column123: Night dual cross country for a student pilot and CFI from ZZZ-RST. Cleared to land RWY 13 at RST; planned full stop; taxi back to RWY 13 for pattern work. Upon landing; clearance from tower was: 'Turn left on A8; taxi to RWY 13 via A; remain this frequency.' Due to abnormal clearance; I as the CFI quickly briefed the response to the student and began to make the call while student departed the runway on A8. Upon exiting the runway; the left main sunk into mud to the left of A8; and soon after; nose gear and right main as well. The plane was unable to be moved without external help; so I called tower to notify them of the event.All lights (landing light; position lights; and red/white anti-collision lights were on during the event. The taxiway diagram was displayed on the MFD. No taxiway centerline was available to follow due to the taxiway exit being a high speed taxiway exit. I believed the mud was the taxiway as they seemed to be a similar color; and difficult to distinguish under the conditions.During post-flight; I saw no damage with the exception of mud on the tires; struts; wing; and propeller/spinner from what looks to be caused by the propwash; and a few small indents on the propeller which looked to be caused by small rocks or pebbles in the mud. No taxiway lights seem to have been struck.In the future; I plan to take extra precautions when exiting runways at night; especially when exiting high speed taxiway exits from the opposite end as primarily intended. I also plan to confirm that I am equidistant from the left and right taxiway edge lights to ensure that I am not falling victim to any illusions or misinterpretations.

column121: On Day 0; I operated a Small UAS for approximately 15-20 minutes along the coastline of the trail. My flight path was primarily over the coastline and occasionally over the water. While my maximum altitude reached approximately 80m (262 ft) AGL; I spent the majority of the flight at a much lower altitude; well below the 400 ft recreational limit. I was accompanied by three friends who acted as informal Visual Observers. During the flight; they spotted a manned aircraft flying at a much higher altitude. Although the aircraft was well clear of my position and way above me; I proactively lowered the UAS even further as a safety precaution until the aircraft passed.After landing; I realized I had inadvertently entered the NAS Whidbey Class C / Alert Area 680 without prior authorization. While I typically verify airspace restrictions on a planning app before every flight; this instance was a complete oversight due to being distracted by the scenic beauty of the landscape. No safety hazards; property damage; or injuries occurred.Corrective Action and Prevention: To prevent recurrence; I have updated my physical pre-flight checklist to include a mandatory 'Airspace Go/No-Go' step. I will now use a dual-verification method by checking two independent airspace awareness applications (e.g.; LAANC and Drone Buddy). Furthermore; I have adjusted my drone's flight software settings to permanently limit the maximum altitude to 60m (197 ft) to provide an automatic safety buffer below the legal limit. I have also briefed my frequent flying companions on how to assist with identifying potential 'No Drone Zones' using these apps before we launch.

column121: During a VFR flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ at 10;500 feet MSL. As described above; the avionics began failing. First the Garmin 430 then the Aperro transponder. I transmitted to ZZZ Approach; as I had been using VFR flight following and informed them of an electrical problem. I received a broken acknowledgement after which all of the avionics failed except for the Garmin G5 AI (Attitude Indicator) and DG which continued to operate on internal battery. The aircraft ammeter indicated in the center position; no charge or discharge and the aircraft had no way to monitor bus voltage. I descended to 8500 to stay out of the ADSB required airspace and proceeded to my destination; avoiding all airspace requiring a transponder. Upon arrival in the destination area I manually extended the landing gear and made an otherwise uneventful landing. The problem was found to be the left generator output wire being secured directly to the intake manifold by a plastic zip tie. The wire chaffed through and shorted to ground. This was in front of the ammeter so gave no discharge indication. The right hand 35 amp generator accepted the load but it was later found that a 50 amp regulator had been installed causing the generator to exceed its output rating; overheat and fail. After this; the battery drained and the system failed altogether. This is a maintenance failure. Improper securing of electrical cabling and installation of the incorrect regulator for the installed generator. The Cessna service manual even makes it clear not to mismatch these components in a precautionary note.

column121: During a routine climb in IMC; the aircraft's ADC1 altitude indication froze at FL230. Prior to the freeze; the altitude had intermittently lagged and the VSI had shown abnormal spikes. Shortly thereafter; the indicated airspeed on (Primary Flight Display) PFD1 froze; began declining; displayed a yellow caution; and was eventually flagged invalid with red X's on both PFD1 and the standby GI275.We were assigned FL270. PFD2; operating on its independent ADC; continued to indicate a normal climb consistent with reaching FL270. Based on the instrument behavior; I suspected a static system blockage or freeze affecting ADC1. I transitioned to hand flying using PFD2 indications and advised ATC that our instruments appeared unreliable. I informed them that PFD1 was frozen at FL230 while we were continuing the climb to FL270 based on the alternate ADC. ATC confirmed they were observing FL230 via Mode C.During this time; the autothrottle was responding to the erroneous low indicated airspeed by attempting to add power. ESP protections in the G1000 NXi attempted to re-engage; increasing workload during a high-task phase of flight. I eventually disconnected the autothrottle and used my free hand to disable ESP in order to reduce automation interference and maintain stable manual control. There was an Airbus aircraft behind us requiring vertical separation. I stated that we were climbing to FL270. Some confusion developed regarding whether we were maintaining FL230 or climbing to FL270 due to the discrepancy between what ATC was observing on their display (derived primarily from Mode C) and what we were indicating on PFD2.I had previously understood that ATC altitude depiction was derived from both radar returns and Mode C; and that discrepancies between the two would be readily apparent. In this case; ATC was primarily referencing Mode C altitude; which remained fixed at FL230. Although separation was ultimately maintained and no loss of separation occurred; the mismatch between actual altitude and transmitted Mode C altitude created the potential for reduced situational awareness and separation risk from both pilot and controller. The issue resolved later in the flight. Post-flight; maintenance evaluation of the static system was requested.

column121: Climbing through 16;000 feet the First Officer's (FO's) airspeed indicator failed with a red flag. After checking all my instruments I determined my airspeed indications and engine indications were completely normal. I then told the FO that I had the flight controls and the radios and to get out the QRH and go to the back of any tabbed page and look for 'AIRSPEED'. The only checklist for our situation is the known as the 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. Having done many sim sessions I am very aware of this 8 page checklist that covers a myriad of possible airspeed malfunctions and things can get extremely confusing when trying to navigate this checklist; and how our relatively stable situation could be easily rectified by doing a simple test. I have seen the exact malfunction on the ground perhaps over a hundred times during my career.It is a very common maintenance issue. Maintenance will be called out to the plane and will simply recycle the airspeed circuit breaker. My intention was to return to ZZZ regardless of whether the First Officer's airspeed was working or not and then write it up upon arrival. But if we could get the First Officer's airspeed indicator working again I would most likely not need to request priority handling. So; I instructed the First Officer to find the First Officers airspeed circuit breaker but not to pull it yet. When the circuit beaker was found and we both agreed that that circuit breaker was; absolutely in fact for his airspeed indicator; I instructed him to pull it and reset it. The result was exactly what happens on the ground. The airspeed indicator reset and went to the appropriate airspeed. In our case it went to 296 kts.; the same as my airspeed indicator. I then tested if his airspeed indicator would follow mine by simply accelerating to 320 kts. As we accelerated my airspeed indicator increased normally and his stayed frozen on 296. I knew immediately that we would need to request priority handling. Moments later; due to the discrepancy between our airspeeds; his airspeed indicator again flagged out.We requested to return to ZZZ and requested priority handling. We landed on Runway XXR with no incidents; returned to gate and wrote up the maintenance issue in the logbook. I recognize; as a Captain I am to simply followed the QRH checklist; however; given the circumstances; I was very concerned about making a relatively simple problem far worse by trying to navigate a very complex checklist in our QRH and end up possibly making our situation more dangerous.

This is contradicted by Jepps Chart DFW 60-7A-4T which shows construction closures.Change AMM chart to show closure of spots 22 and 24 in alignment with Jepps Chart DFW 60-7A-4T. Spots 22 and 24 closure signage in the field is inadequate. Add clear; large signage on field indicating spots 22 and 24 are closed.Ground Control did not advise us of the taxi intentions of the two aircraft. Ground Control should advise fellow aircraft of the intentions of those around them."
column123: Flight DFW - ZZZZ. Position - Relief Pilot. Departed out of Gate XX at XA:15. Upon taxi out Ramp cleared us to spot 23. Approaching spot 23 FO switched from Ramp to Ground frequency. FO noted 2 aircraft approaching on the right on Taxiway K.On Ground frequency we were cleared to 17R via Lima - Echo Hotel. Ground did not tell us where approaching traffic was going; they did not tell us to hold for traffic. We were holding at spot 23 watching traffic approaching not sure what they were going to do so the Captain stopped our aircraft and set the parking brake.First aircraft turned into the ramp over the previously named spot 24. This spot was closed due to construction. We were parked in the center of the taxiway. We believe there was not enough space for aircraft to taxi in with safe clearance distance. There was no time to alert the aircraft because we were on Ground frequency and they should have been communicating with Ramp.Other Relief Pilot called Ramp to notify them of our concerns. They were aware and told the other Relief Pilot that they were trying to get in touch with Ground to have them enter spot 25. We did not hear any communication between the aircraft with Ground Control or Ramp Control.Cause: Jepps Chart DFW 60-7A-4T. Chart depicts that spots 22 and 24 are closed due to construction. This is information only found if opening all taxi pages. These closures are not depicted on that 10-9 Airport Moving Map (AMM) Chart.With so much construction going on in DFW it is difficult to be aware of all the changes and those closures are not depicted. There should be clearer signs and taxiway markings denoting closed taxiways and closed area of the ramp.Ground Control did not clearly communicate with us about the aircraft's intentions. We did not know if the aircraft were taxiing to the runway or holding short to wait for us to taxi out. We have no idea what their taxi instructions were. Ramp did not warn us about any inbound traffic.

column121: We were climbing out on the ZZZZZ departure. There was a radar return at our 1-2 o'clock in the vicinity of our turn to the south. As we climbed out; we could see clearly underneath the clouds and there was no precipitation from the return. Aircraft Y had departed just before us and went through the area with no complaints. As we entered the cloud; the Total Air Temperature (TAT) jumped up to +14c. As we secured the Engine Anti-Ice we got a small flash of St. Elmo's Fire followed by an explosion and brilliant flash of blue light. The Head-up Display briefly turned a blue color from the normal green. It sounded like a stick of dynamite going off rather than a crack of nearby lightning. My hands and teeth felt like I had briefly grabbed a bare wire and my ears felt like they did when I was too close to a grenade simulator explosion. The explosion came from somewhere around the TAT/Pitot Probes. I coupled the autopilot so I could gather my composure and it seemed to have a hard time holding airspeed. Given all of this information the FO and I decided that the most prudent course of action was to return to ZZZZ to have the aircraft inspected. The prospect of continuing to ZZZ at FL400 (our Flight Plan Alt) did not seem worth the risk if we had sustained damage to the nose of the airplane. Cause: ATC vectoring us near the radar return caused this to occur. I thought about asking for an early turn; but given all the other information; it seemed like the turn was acceptable. Suggestions: Insisting on turning early would have prevented the incident. Next time I find myself in a scenario like this; I will be more insistent on an early turn. Just because it is cold outside doesn't mean there's not sufficient energy inside a radar return to cause something like this to occur.

column121: Flight diversion recovery flight to ZZZ. On the recovery flight to ZZZ after landing poor taxi conditions lead to very slow taxi to the gate. Approaching gate XX the Captain lined up with what we thought was the lead in line for the gate as the ground crew scrambled to get vehicles out of the gate area. The line was completely obscured by snow and ice. Once we were lined up we started to taxi into position almost immediately the left wing walker threw up an X with his wands because they had missed a baggage cart that was in the safety area. The Captain stopped and we waited as two of the walkers tried to push it out of the way by hand. They moved it and signaled that we were clear to start pulling in again. We were moving super slowly; cautious of the ice and trying to find the line the whole taxi but especially when entering the gate area. As we were pulling in the Captain noticed the wing walker on his side throw up the X again as we had gotten close to the baggage cart they attempted moving. The Captain stepped on the brakes in an attempt to stop the aircraft but we started sliding on the ice and slid to the left bumping the baggage cart.The aircraft only came to rest after the Captain cracked the thrust reversers. After investigation and coordination with the ground crew and airport ops with clearance we decided it was best to have the tug back us out and tow us in rather than doing it under our own power. Which was a good decision because even the ground ops tow vehicle was not able to get traction with us. The ramp was sprayed and sanded twice before they got the grip to get us to the gate. After we arrived to the gate we ran all procedures as necessary. On post-flight walk around it was found to have a cracked nav light cover with no other damage to aircraftI believe the cause for this event was primarily the poor ramp conditions first and foremost. Had the ramp not been icy; or snow covered the aircraft would likely have been much closer to centerline to start and would not have slid further towards the cart during braking. I think that had either the ground or flight crew stopped and said that the ramp needed to be cleared first that would have saved this event from happening. This is very easy in hindsight but is something I will pay more attention to in the future and not be afraid to refuse a parking spot. I think a secondary cause was the ground crew giving little to no directions as we were entering the ramp area while having better reference to where we should and should not have been; the marshaller had sticks up and was waving straight in until the walker signed the X.In the future I will be more forward about refusing a parking spot if ramp conditions are poor or at minimum request extra caution from the ground crew.  Better training for ground and flight crews about what are and are not acceptable ramp conditions would also likely result in better safety and fewer events like this happening in the future

column121: During a landing rollout in a Piper PA-32R (Saratoga); the aircraft experienced a violent; high-frequency vibration and a sharp pull to the left; resulting in a low-speed runway excursion into the grass. No damage was sustained to the aircraft or airport property.Initial Assessment. Initial symptoms; including a 'humming' noise during taxi and an apparent lack of symmetric braking; suggested a mechanical hydraulic failure or master cylinder bypass.Post-Event Analysis and Corrective Actions. I have taken the following proactive steps to ensure this does not happen again:Technical Consultation.  I consulted with a certified A&P mechanic to inspect the braking system. While the hardware was found to be within limits; the inspection highlighted the extreme sensitivity of this specific aircraft's braking system compared to other models in the fleet.Diagnosis of Human Factors. Through diagnostic taxi testing with the mechanic; I identified that a subconscious 'left-leaning' posture during the flare; combined with an off-center seating position; led to unintended 'brake pressure' on the left toe brake.Instructional Intervention: I have scheduled additional proficiency training with a flight instructor recognized as a subject matter expert in this specific airframe. SOP Implementation: I am incorporating a standardized 'Cockpit Stance Checklist' into my landing flow; which includes seat positioning. Ensuring specific seat-track notches for optimal leg angle.Neutral Position Check: A 'heels-on-the-ground' verification callout during the flare to ensure zero brake engagement. Conclusion. This event was a combination of aircraft-specific sensitivity and a subtle ergonomic error in pilot posture. By standardizing my 'stance' and enhancing my tactile connection to the machine; I have mitigated the risk of future directional control issues. And currently doing instruction with the CFI that is also most proficient with this particular type of aircraft for proficiency and familiarization before I use this particular aircraft for personal uses. My goal is proficiency and safety. I took the time to fully investigate the matter cooperatively with the club; A&P and other CFI; to address the issues and make sure that we resolved the problem.

column121: During a CFII training flight in my aircraft; I was teaching my student how to give vectors to final for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ with WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) disabled. We; Aircraft X; a Piper PA-28 gave ourselves VTF (Vectors to Final) at 2000ft MSL approximately 8nm NE from the airport. We turned into and captured the FAC (Flight Augmentation Computer) of RNAV XX with no other traffic on an approach into ZZZ for runway XX. We descended 500fpm until reaching 1500ft MSL; the FAF altitude listed on the approach plate. We were driving to the final approach fix; level at 1500msl approx 6nm from the airport when Aircraft Y made a 10nm final call over the ZZZ CTAF frequency. The Citation did not appear on our traffic map on the G1000 nxi MFD (Multi-funcion Flight Display)  until he was nearly 1000ft above us and I saw the traffic on the MFD display a downward arrow; indicating the Citation's descent. In a matter of less than 30 seconds; the Citation was approximately less than 1 mile behind Aircraft X; and 500ft above me. This is when I got the TCAS alert and immediately grabbed flight controls and took evasive action; banking the aircraft nearly 60 degrees and turning 90 degrees to avoid a collision from the Citation.My airspeed at the time of the evasion was 78kts and the citation; Aircraft Y was 201kts according to ADS-B exchange data. I started the evasion at XA:36:30. If I had not taken the aggressive and immediately maneuver; I confidently believe the Citation would have crashed into me; Aircraft X and killing myself and my student. No radio contact was established with the pilot of Aircraft Y  outside of his initial 10nm final call over CTAF and a short final radio call that I could pick up. After rolling wings level I made a radio call telling the pilot of Aircraft Y that I had to break off the approach to avoid being hit by him. He never replied to the radio call. I gave VTF again for the approach into ZZZ and landed safely. Prevailing conditions of the flight were VFR; cloud ceilings were approximately 3000-4000AGL. My aircraft; Aircraft X maintained VFR cloud clearance requirements of 500ft below cloud layers at all times during this flight. I do not believe the pilot of Aircraft Y ever saw us on the approach. IF the pilot of Aircraft Y was on an IFR flight plan shooting an approach into an airport with a known flight school; with pilots making radio calls at every phase of flight; I question why he would shoot an IAP going that fast; or why ATC would clear him for the approach while my aircraft is on the final approach segment.
column123: Aircraft: Cessna Citation CJ3+ (Aircraft X)Operation: Part 91 IFRDeparture: ZZZ1Destination: ZZZI departed ZZZ1 as PIC of a Cessna Citation CJ3+; Aircraft X; operating under an IFR flight plan to ZZZ. The clearance was direct ZZZZZ; then direct ZZZ; maintaining 3;000 feet. We picked up our IFR clearance at approximately 1;500 feet after departure.Weather conditions were IMC above approximately 2;500-3;000 feet MSL. While level at 3;000 feet in IMC enroute to ZZZZZ; we were handed off from ZZZ Center to ZZZ Approach Control. ZZZ Approach instructed us to climb to 3;400 feet and cleared us direct ZZZZZ for the RNAV (GPS) Runway XX approach into ZZZ; with a crossing restriction of at or above 3;300 feet at ZZZZZ. We complied with all instructions.Multiple aircraft were observed operating in the traffic pattern at ZZZ via ADS-B; and we had been monitoring this traffic since departure. One aircraft in particular appeared aligned with Runway XX and possibly flying the same RNAV approach. Upon reaching ZZZZZ and beginning descent; we broke out of IMC at approximately 2;800-3;000 feet MSL.At approximately 10 miles from the airport; we reported a 10-mile final for the RNAV Runway XX approach. ZZZ Approach issued a traffic advisory for an aircraft approximately four to five miles ahead of us and below; descending. We had already observed this aircraft on ADS-B and acquired it visually after breaking out of the clouds.Based on closure rate; we determined we were overtaking the traffic ahead and that continuing straight-in would likely reduce spacing. ZZZ Approach was not in communication with that aircraft; and it appeared to be operating VFR.To improve spacing and integrate safely with pattern traffic; we elected to cancel IFR and continue visually. Approximately 5-6 miles from the airport; we initiated a left turn to maneuver toward the published ZZZZZ1 visual reporting point; which is identified in the enhanced operating procedures as the preferred VFR entry for a 45-degree downwind to Runway XX.As we began the left turn; the aircraft ahead also initiated a left turn. At that time; we were approximately three miles behind and slightly above that aircraft. No prior radio transmission was heard from that aircraft indicating its intentions. The turn resulted in a temporary converging flight path.Upon assessing the geometry and maintaining visual contact; I determined the safest course of action was to discontinue the left turn and re-establish on the extended final approach course. We remained in visual contact at all times.During the convergence; a momentary TCAS Resolution Advisory was generated. The advisory was brief and consistent with the converging geometry. Visual separation was maintained; and the RA cleared as lateral spacing increased. No maneuver beyond normal course correction was required.The other aircraft continued turning away from our course and was no longer a factor. Shortly thereafter; the aircraft transmitted that it was breaking off the approach. Another aircraft on downwind stated that he would extend his downwind to provide spacing. We reported a 4-mile final and landed uneventfully at ZZZ. Visual separation was maintained at all times; and the flight concluded without further incident.Contributing Factors:IMC-to-VMC transition during approach phaseHigh volume of VFR training traffic at a non-towered airportMixed IFR arrivals and VFR practice approach operationsClosure rate differences between turbine IFR traffic and training aircraftLimited radio coordination from some aircraft in the patternHuman Factors: Situational awareness was maintained through continuous ADS-B monitoring and visual acquisition upon breakout. The combination of IMC-to-VMC transition; closure rate on slower traffic; and multiple aircraft in the pattern created compressed decision-making during a high-workload phase of flight. The brief TCAS RA reinforced the importance of conservative spacing when integratingmixed IFR and VFR traffic.Safety Consideration: This event highlights the operational challenges of mixing IFR arrivals with high volumes of VFR training traffic in marginal VFR conditions at non-towered airports. While conditions were legally VFR; arriving aircraft descending from higher altitudes and higher speeds may require instrument procedures for descent; which can compress spacing when pattern traffic is established ahead.Increased emphasis on communication clarity and conservative spacing during such mixed-traffic scenarios may help reduce similar occurrences.Corrective Actions / Lessons Learned: Consider earlier speed reduction or spacing adjustments when overtaking slower traffic on instrument approaches into busy training environments.Continue proactive ADS-B monitoring and early visual acquisition during IMC-to-VMC transitions.Maintain conservative lateral and longitudinal spacing when traffic intentions are unclear.Exercise heightened vigilance when integrating IFR arrival profiles into active VFR pattern operations.

column121: ZZZ Tower called me and asked for a heading for Aircraft X.  I was preoccupied with my other arrivals and I didn't understand why they couldn't keep Aircraft X  in the pattern when they had 1 aircraft; so I verified that they 'could not keep the aircraft in the pattern;' to which they replied that they could not.  This is often confusing because of the rules of what a Visual Approach Go-Around is supposed to do - enter the traffic pattern. I opted to get the aircraft back to the airport now.   So I issued a downwind turn (210 heading) ensured the field was in sight still and issued a visual approach clearance.  Meanwhile; I had 2 other IFR aircraft on converging courses with VFR targets that I was doing my best to separate.  While focusing on the other IFR aircraft and making sure they were avoiding the random VFR targets out there; I noticed a VFR target seemingly appearing to depart ZZZ's class D.  However; this target was several hundred feet below Aircraft X and I had no indication that the VFR target would continue their climb; and at this moment; Aircraft X appeared to be in the safest position compared to my other IFR targets.  I shipped Aircraft X to the tower so they could work them in.  Recommendation: We need controlled / protected airspace north of ZZZ.  This area is a mid-air waiting to happen.  We've been told that we can't lower the Bravo airspace out there.  Nor can we create a SATR or otherwise.  We just seem to be in this unsafe situation in perpetuity.  We all see the solution; but the FAA is silent and does not seem to care about fixing the problem.  Every controller can tell you the solution; but only the FAA can act on it; and unfortunately; they sit idle until two airplanes collide.  I'm not talking local FAA.  I'm talking big FAA... the only ones who can make the airspace safer.Get some protected airspace out there in that area ASAP - two airplanes will collide at some point without it.

column121: The First Officer (FO) and I had completed the Before Push Checklist and were waiting to hear from the tug driver that they were ready for brake release. The group crew seemed to be having problems with their headset. I then saw a ramper come into view from the Captain's side window. He pointed to his ears; shook his head no; and gave a broken or no good type of hand signal. He then held up both arms with his hands clenched into fists. I said to the FO; it seems like they're having headset issues... it looks like they're ready for brake release; why don't you call for push. I then held my hands up for the ramper to see my clenched fists and I opened both fists to show all 10 fingers and I released the aircraft brakes.  saw the ramper repeat my hand signal to the tug driver. Almost immediately; the aircraft began to slowly move rearward. I said out loud to the FO; we may have an uncommanded aircraft movement here. I then noticed the ramper who was giving me hand signals move hurriedly toward the tug driver. I immediately moved my feet up on the toe brakes and gently applied pressure to slow the aircraft movement and bring it to a stop. If I had to guess; the aircraft moved somewhere between 5 and 8 feet before I brought it to a stop.I set the parking brake and we waited until the ground crew found an operable headset. Upon completion of our ensuing pushback; I asked the ramper to submit a safety report to document this event and told him that I would do the same.

column121: - This was a two Captain flight crew operating flight #XXXX; with service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. This was the second flight of the day in the airplane and no major mechanical abnormalities were experienced during the first flight. The only notable event was a TLO light (Left Side) that illuminated during cruise. Person A  served as the First Officer and Pilot Monitoring during both the first and second flights. I had not flown in 18 days as a result of a previous reported incident and Person A  was helping me regain proficiency in the airplane.- In ZZZ; the aircraft started up normally and we taxied to the runup area on the 1 taxiway. Upon completing the Before Takeoff Checklist; and with both engines within all parameters; we were given taxi instructions to RWY XX and then cleared for departure. - Both engines eventually developed full power at 103 percent and we rotated around 72 knots. I noted that the engines were surging at times but appeared to smooth out with more airspeed and prior to rotation. When we were around 200 feet above the runway; the left engine began to make a loud popping noise and the power reduced to around 70%.- There was a substantial amount of runway left in front of us as RWY XX is 10;400 feet long. Since we had a headwind and variable crosswind gusting to 22 knots; I initially pulled back power in order to land back on the runway. This is what I had briefed in the Takeoff Briefing.- At this point; Person A stated that we should keep flying and to continue our climb straight ahead. I considered it and then moved both throttles back to full power. We started climbing again. The engine popped one more time but did not lose power. - We were able to climb without incident to 1;000 ft and Person A  notified ATC that we needed to return to the airport for landing. ATC was able to accommodate us immediately back for a left pattern for a return landing on RWY XX. The landing and rollout were uneventful and we notified ZZZ Ops that we had returned. We also informed them that Aircraft X needed maintenance attention and was not airworthy. We also told them that we would need another aircraft to fly our passengers to ZZZ1.- Person A contacted Maintenance Control while I wrote up the incident in the Aircraft Maintenance Log. Person A  then contacted Operations  to inform them of the situation. He was then instructed to contact Person B; the On-Call Duty Manager. He did so and we both chatted with Person B on speaker phone. He supported our decision to return and guided us through the process.- We obtained another aircraft and were able to fly our passengers to ZZZ1 without incident. We remained in our same crew positions for the second attempt of this flight; with myself as Pilot Flying and Person A  as Pilot Monitoring.

column121: While at the gate in ZZZ the aircraft displayed a L OIL LVL LOW status message; with the left engine at shut off prior to blocking out. We (the first officer and I) checked the oil level on the menu page. It indicated that the left engine oil level was at 51%. After referencing the CRJ 900 QRH 0-XX Table 0-1: Oil Level Indication and Duration Table; we determined to be in the 10 hour flight range and above the Do not dispatch" minimum. We continued with the flight as normal. The APU was deferred on this flight so we executed a right engine start at the gate using ground supply air and electrical power. After the right engine start was complete; we pushed back from the gate and taxied to the XXR deice pad on a single engine using all standard procedures. Completed Type 1 deicing process and then began our taxi to runway XXL for departure via Taxiway 1. While on Taxiway 1; the First Officer and I completed a cross bleed start to the left engine using bleed air from the right engine as directed by the QRH. Once the left engine start was complete; all normal delayed start and before takeoff checklist and procedures were completed. In addition to that; the oil level of both engines were check via the menu page and found to be at an acceptable level for departure. Departed runway XXL at ZZZ with no adverse indications. Completed a normal climb to our cruise altitude of FL310 with no adverse indications. Following standard procedures and checklist at every phase of flight. Sometime after reaching our cruise altitude; about 10 minutes after level at FL310; I (the captain and pilot flying) checked the oil levels once again via the menu page. Upon checking the oil levels I found that the left engine was at 15%. We began monitoring the left engine indications as directed by the CRJ900 QRH 0-XX Table 0-1. At that time I began turning to the L ENG OIL PRESS checklist in the QRH just in case it would be needed. About 2-3 minutes after the First Officer and I began monitoring the left engine indications; we received a L ENG OIL PRESS warning message; chime and aural alert. At that time I handed the QRH to the First Officer; I remained the pilot and took over radio communication control; and we began running the CRJ 900 QRH 1-XY L ENG OIL PRESS and subsequent CRJ 900 QRH 1-XZ ENGINE FAILURE/INFLIGHT ENGINE SHUTDOWN checklist. Because both pilots confirmed that the L ENG OIL PRESS warning message was present and the oil pressure was below limits we continued with the intentional shutdown as directed by the checklist. All the while we remained in constant contact with ATC. Primarily ZZZCenter. After the left engine was brought to ideal the aircraft was unable to maintain FL310. So; with clearance from ATC; we descended to FL250. By the time we reached FL250 the left engine was fully shutdown. The aircraft was able to maintain FL250 with right thrust set to tracking. But I elected to descend lower to FL210 in an effort to "take it easy" on the operative engine. Once at FL210 all checklist were completed and that is when I requested priority handling with ZZZ center; informed dispatch and maintenance control via ACARS; and notified the flight attendants of the situation. We did try to contact dispatch through ARINC (Radio) frequency XXX.XX; but had no reply from City X radio. When informing the flight attendants; I told them "the left engine was intentionally shutdown by us to prevent damage. The aircraft is still flying perfectly normal. We are counting to ZZZ1 as planned. We are going to land at ZZZ1 and taxi to the gate just like a normal flight. At this time; the is no need to inform the passengers. If there is need I will inform them. You don't not need to prepare for an evacuation. If anything changes to the situation I will update you". After the flight attendants were informed; the First Officer and I reconfirmed the decision to continue to ZZZ1. We completed all briefings and checklists as we made our descent into ZZZ1. While talking toZZZ approach control; we requested to land on runway XY due to favorable headwinds. Upon switching to tower control; they informed us that fire and rescue would be standing by on the ground. The aircraft was landed safely on runway XZ and made a right turnoff at 2. After landing fire and rescue asked if we needed assistance. I informed them that no assistance was required and they replied by saying they would follow us to the ramp and then head back to the station. We taxied to gate XX; parked; shutdown the right engine and passed the aircraft over to station maintenance personnel.Cause:  The conditions that led to a loss of oil pressure inflight are unknown to me at this time. The post flight inspection revealed a large oil stain under the cowling of the left engine. Indicating a possible oil leak that possibly led to the loss of oil pressure."

column121: During engine start; we received ENG1 GEN FAULT. We followed ECAM procedures and it came back online. I entered it in the ELB (Electronic Logbook); called Dispatch; and finished the procedure with Maintenance Control. We called for taxi; was cleared to Runway XX; taxied out; and departed. At approximately 1500' both the FO (First Officer) and I noticed a sort of shimmy; as though the gear was still down; flaps were down; or maybe the speed brakes were out; but all was normal. It did not seem to me like an engine vibration and we didn't notice any parameters showing high vibes; so we continued. On climb out; beginning at ~3000'; received multiple transient ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE ECAMs. All engine parameters were normal on both engines and the thrust levers were perfectly aligned; so I felt that continuing was the best plan. On the 4th or 5th ECAM; it stayed up almost long enough to run the full procedure; but then it went away again. It came back again as we were passing ~23;000'. It was no longer transient and I decided we needed to start back to the field. I asked the FO to pass the info to Dispatch. They messaged back that they would get the ball rolling. ATC turned us back and began our descent. The ECAM cleared; but we had already started turning back so we continued. We requested priority handling in the turn back to ZZZ. To this point; both engines had been performing normally and it seemed like it may have been an indication issue. On level off; ENG 1 did not spool up; staying at flight idle. The plane commanded LEVER MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust); and performance went into EO (Engine-Out). At this point; I asked the FO to request ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support upon arrival. They said the trucks would be ready. We revisited procedures and both agreed that everything had been completed; to include a report to the (LFA) Lead Flight Attendant. We were vectored to the ILS XX; but the tailwind during the return pushed us too much and we were vectored around for further descent. Upon the next vectors; I thought ATC had requested a ten degree turn to the left; which I did and then our course was promptly blown too close to the localizer - apparently they had given me a RIGHT course correction. They vectored us out once again and gave us much more room to catch the localizer. We commenced the approach; and landed without any further issues. At some point; when were exiting the runway I smelled something odd; so I requested ARFF scan ENG 1 just in case there was something internal to the nacelle. ARFF completed the entire aircraft scan and reported no further issues with the FLIR. I requested to continue into the terminal; to which we were given clearance. At this point; a passenger got up and used the bathroom before the FAs could stop them. Once they sat back down; we continued to taxi to the gate; shut down normally; and deplaned the pax. I'm fairly certain; with everything going on and the previously transient ECAM; something was missed in the approach. We revisited the procedures; although we briefed the passengers later than I would have liked; making sure all the information was covered. I feel like everything was covered; maybe poorly and out of sequence; but so many things were happening that I was doing a lot just staying in front of the problem and making sure that I was prioritizing flying the aircraft. We were constantly checking in with each other to make sure each of us were up to speed and also SA.
column123: After ENG 1 started and stabilized; we received an ECAM: ENG 1 GEN FAULT. We completed the ECAM procedures; and the generator came back online. We contacted Dispatch; completed the ELB (Electronic Logbook) entry; and cross-verified the information with each other. We were cleared to taxi to Runway XX and subsequently departed.During climb; at approximately 1;000-1;500 feet AGL; we noticed a brief irregular vibration; similar to what it would feel like if a gear door were open or the speed brakes were partially extended. All system parameters appeared normal; and the vibration lasted less than 10 seconds. We elected to continue the climb.Beginning at approximately 3;000 feet; we received an ECAM: ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE. The message cleared few seconds later. We verified engine parameters; thrust lever positions; and associated indications; all were normal. We assessed it as a transient condition and continued the climb. The same ECAM message reappeared multiple times (approximately 4-5 times). Then the ECAM remained long enough to begin and finish the ECAM procedure; but it cleared again.At approximately FL230; the ECAM returned. We requested ATC to level off to properly accomplish the checklist and assess the situation. While leveling at approximately FL280; we decided to return to ZZZ. We immediately notified Dispatch via ACARS of the ECAM message and our decision to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of our intention to return; including souls on board and fuel remaining. ATC cleared us direct to ZZZ.Until and during descent; both engines initially displayed matched parameters within normal limits. However; while descending; ENG 1 remained at idle and did not respond as expected. The system prompted us to set the thrust lever to MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust). Considering the ENG 1 condition and the overweight landing; we requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support from ATC.We completed all required coordination with ATC; Dispatch; the flight attendants; and passengers. After setting up for the approach and completing the approach briefing; we requested vectors to allow time to accomplish the overweight landing checklist. Upon completion; we cross-verified all checklist items to ensure nothing was missed.We were vectored for the ILS Runway XX but were unable to intercept the localizer. Requested another vector; cleared for the approach.We landed on Runway XX and vacated the runway. We stopped on Taxiway 1 to allow fire trucks to inspect the aircraft. ARFF reported no abnormalities. We contacted Operations frequency to advise them of our situation and assigned gate. We then taxied to the gate; shut down the engines; and the passengers deplaned without further incident. Being only approximately 50-60 miles from the departure airport; the repeated ECAM messages and evolving situation created a high workload environment. It was not a comfortable experience operationally. In hindsight; I could have taken additional time to review the Manual more thoroughly and attempt to gain a deeper; more systematic understanding of the malfunction. We also could have delegated tasks more efficiently to better manage workload and reduce task saturation.This report serves as a reflection on the event and improvement. While we strive for precision and professionalism; we recognize that we are not immune to human limitations.

column123: Starting with receiving taxi clearance for runway XXR under the lower ceilings and cloudy skies. The CA and I had done proper checklist leading up to taxing and getting ready to take off. As I the pilot flying waiting on the callouts we had set thurst as normal but beginning to accelerate I had noticed a silhouette from a plane in the distance around the middle of the runway had started to cross. I didn't appear to see any lights on the aircraft crossing which could have aided in understanding the situation and making actions sooner. Approximately 2000 ft from the Air Carrier X aircraft crossing I had noticed and took action to reduce power and start braking while calling out plane in the distance. Shortly after reducing power and deacceleration the CA looked up and acknowledged the airplane crossing the runway and took controls while verbalizing reject reject; my controls.  As now reverse roles and pilot monitoring we had veered off to avoid wingtip strike to the 737 crossing. I was observing carefully and making sure we were clear of the airplane crossing. Shortly after; I made call to ATC as instructed by the CA to call rejected takeoff. I was in contact and instructed to taxi off runway XXR onto taxiway 1 left 2 hold short runway XY. We had stopped on taxiway 1 initially clear of runway XXR while CA made PA to passengers to remain seated and aware of situation. The controller shortly asked after if we would like to return to gate or taxi back for take off and we contacted back that we needed to run checklist and cool off brakes. We then proceeded to hold short runway XY. We ran rejected takeoff checklist in the QRH and came up with a plan with letting tower aware of what was going on. column121: I am submitting this report to document an event that occurred during a ferry flight from ZZZ.I was assigned to Reserve Availability Period 1 and was called in for Standby Position 1. I received a call from Customer Service indicating that there was a ferry flight from Gate XX that needed to proceed. Upon arriving at the gate; I met Captain A; who informed me that he was still awaiting a flight release and that there was no gate agent available. I sought assistance from the neighboring gate to gain access to the aircraft; and we both began our duties to prepare for the flight. After completing my walk-around; I performed the cabin equipment check. With our duties completed; we both proceeded to close the main cabin door using the checklist; and we confirmed the door status as green on the EICAS status page.We did not realize that the vent flaps on the remaining three cabin doors were not closed and secured. Being new to ferry operations; I initially interpreted the EICAS messages for the remaining doors as indicating that the slides were not armed; which I mistook for the vent flap issue. We continued to set up for our flight; and on departure we received clearance to climb and maintain FL210.During the climb through 10;500 feet; we encountered a Cabin HIGH ALT warning. Captain A immediately advised ATC that we would level off at 10;000 feet to address the issue. I; as the FO and pilot flying; disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to halt the climb and descend to 10;000 feet. I did not reset the altitude selector to 10;000 feet; and the aircraft briefly accelerated to 325 knots while descending from 11;500 feet to 10;000 feet. Captain A then held the throttles at idle to assist with deceleration and directed me to set 10;000 feet in the altitude selector. The aircraft returned to a normal speed; and the over-speed condition lasted approximately 3-5 seconds.ATC asked about our intentions three times; we confirmed that we would remain at 10;000 feet while we assessed and addressed the issue. After the third inquiry; ATC vectored us to our assigned heading. Following stabilization; I conducted a positive exchange of controls so that I could proceed to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors. Cabin altitude subsequently returned to normal; and we continued the flight without further incident.Cause: I am providing a cause narrative for the ferry flight from ZZZ to document the factors that contributed to the cabin pressurization event and to outline corrective actions. The sequence of events revealed a chain of contributing factors centered on ferry-flight procedures; crew experience; and situational awareness during the abnormal situation.The root cause began with an incomplete preflight and door-status verification for ferry operations. Vent flaps on the three non-primary cabin doors were not closed and secured; a condition that went unidentified prior to departure. This oversight stemmed from a lack of ferry-specific checks and limited experience; which led to the misinterpretation of EICAS messages as indicating slide arming rather than the actual vent flap status. I initially assumed that EICAS messages related to the other cabin doors pertained to slide arming; causing the vent flap issue to be overlooked until the event unfolded.During the climb; I disconnected the autopilot and did not reset the altitude selector to 10;000 feet; allowing a brief overspeed condition as we descended from 11;500 feet toward 10;000 feet. This indicated a delay in crew coordination and procedures during a high-workload; time-critical event. The situation was further stressed by limited ferry-flight experience and delayed identification of the vent flap closure issue and misreading of cues from the EICAS system. In addition; the preflight process did not include a definitive check of vent flap status on all cabin doors; increasing the likelihood of an undetected vent-flap exposure. Communication with ATC under stress also highlighted the need for clear; decisive actions; as initial exchanges were hampered by moments of uncertainty before we could present a unified plan.Immediate corrective actions were taken once the situation was stabilized. A positive exchange of controls allowed me to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors; after which cabin pressure returned to normal and the flight proceeded without further incident. The aircraft was stabilized at 10;000 feet; and ATC vectored us to a safe heading; ensuring continued safe operations.Suggestions: During the recent operation; we faced pressure to expedite departure; but we determined that slowing the pace was necessary to maintain safety and accuracy. We also recognize that we could have leveraged available resources more effectively; including maintenance; dispatch; and company operations; to aid decision-making and risk assessment.Going forward; I have learned that when any aspect of a procedure or condition is in question; it is essential to slow down and seek clarification before proceeding. This approach will help ensure we address potential issues thoroughly and maintain safe; compliant operations.

column121: We started our day two of the trip with two legs on Day 0 in ZZZ. This day we were scheduled to operate ZZZ-ZZZ1 then from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. Initially the inbound aircraft to ZZZ was delayed. Shortly after We claimed the aircraft and started the trip We found the APU to be INOP and MEL-ed (49-XX-XXX). This was observed both in the Engineering change request form as well as informed by the incoming crew. Aside from that MEL the aircraft didn't have any issues or malfunctions. On the ground at ZZZ we observed ' L OIL LEVEL LO' status message. After confirming the indication we checked with QRH and confirmed that the aircraft was still good to go and within the limitations specified in the table in QRH . The flight from ZZZ into ZZZ1 was operated as normal and without any issues. After getting to ZZZ1 and preparing for the second and last flight of the day; a preflight inspection was conducted by me (FO) and nothing out of the ordinary was found. No leakages of either engines or any other fluids were observed. After boarding and getting ready for pushback; We once again checked the Left Oil Level and it showed 51% (engine off); once again we checked the table  and found that the duration of available oil until next service is 10 hours for that quantity. We made a mental note and discussed to let Maintenance know once we got to ZZZ2. Shortly before pushback; We observed snow flurries starting to fall and decided to get de-iced prior to departure. We taxied single engine onto the de-ice pad (XXR); after getting done with de-icing we started our taxi for runway XYL in ZZZ1 and did a cross-bleed start on the left engine. Before; during and after the engine start all indications were showing within the normal parameters. After going through our procedures and checklists We then continued onto the runway and prepared for Take off. During the take off and climb Phases all indications were showing operations within normal parameters. shortly after reaching our cruising altitude of FL310 ( approximately 10-12 minutes ) We once again checked the oil level; at this time we observed 15% on the L side quantity. After checking with the QRH  table; We followed as written and continued the flight while monitoring the oil temperature and pressure. During this time the oil temperature was stable and good while the pressure was flickering and slowly dropping (at this time it was still green and within limits). Shortly after this observation we got a 'L ENG OIL PRESS' warning (approximately 3 minutes after initial observation of pressure flickering). We then confirmed the warning and followed QRH. While running through the QRH; We had two of the three specified indications ( L ENG OIL PRESS warning and affected engine oil pressure below limits). We double and triple checked that oil pressure was indeed below limits and referenced the table in the manual. While running the QRH and having pulled back the affected thrust lever to IDLE (QRH); the Left oil pressure was showing 20 PSI (while 25 PSI being the minimum per the manual). We then again quickly saw the pressure dropping again to 19 PSI. We confirmed displayed indications and followed the QRH for an 'Engine Failure/In-Flight Engine Shutdown'. While running the QRH and just before engine shutdown; Left oil pressure was at 19 PSI. while going through the QRH we communicated with ATC and let them know that we were working with an engine issue we than advised ATC once it was clear that an inflight engine shutdown was imminant. We also continued to communicated with dispatch; and Maintenance via ACARS; and informed them of our situation and that we were still planning to continue to ZZZ2 unless thay would suggest otherwise. We continued the flight to ZZZ2 and completed QRH for a SINGLE ENGINE Approach and Landing without any other issues. During the approach bit; we had already set up and briefed for runway XZ into ZZZ2 ( Per ATIS at the time) as we got closer they informed us to expect XA; after receiving this information we communicated amongst ourself and both agreed that runway XZ would be preferred due to its longer length; favoring winds; and reduced workload on us with it already being programmed and briefed I then asked the approach for the current winds in ZZZ2 ( winds were 280 at 7 knots); We then requested XZ and got vectored for the ILS RWY XZ into ZZZ2. Approach and landing were conducted successfully without any further complications. Cause: After reaching the cruising altitude we check the engine oil level and found it to be 15% for the left engine. Shortly after we got a 'L ENG OIL PRESS' warning due to the pressure dropping below limits. During the post flight walk around; I observed leakage on the L ENG exhaust cone (pictures attached).

column121: On Day 0 at XA:45; a mid-air collision nearly occurred between aircraft I was piloting and Aircraft Y. The event occurred on the final approach corridor to Runway 35 at TRM at an estimated distance of 1 mile; and an estimated altitude of 750 feet. The weather was VMC; light winds; clear skies; and unrestricted visibility.Participating Traffic were a small aircraft in left closed traffic for Runway 17 executing a RH 360 on the LH downwind for spacing; another aircraft 6 miles east inbound to Runway 35; a jet holding short of Runway 35 for IFR takeoff. Another jet taxiing from the ramp to Runway 35; Myself in overhead left traffic for Runway 35 having clearly called number 1 for landing during coordination with the small aircraft on the other downwind and the jet holding short for takeoff; and last----Aircraft Y coming straight-in to Runway 35 making distance calls inbound to 'Cochran.' I didn't clearly hear the jet make a radio call. But I don't doubt the word of the other crew at debriefing given the factors described below. In any case; the crew did not recognize that the pattern was full at the airport they were approaching; and they did not coordinate their plan to come straight-in with any of the other aircraft using the airport.As I was descending from base to final; I was a bit high on approach. I received a TCAS TA while turning final. After rolling out on final the displayed threat aircraft was 100 feet directly beneath me (solid-yellow circle -100).No TCAS RA was issued since both aircraft were configured for landing below 1000 feet. This situation was something like a perfect storm that somewhat defanged the TCAS. Since the initial TA showed yellow and stayed yellow (20-48 seconds); the urgency of the situation was confused; and my initial reflex was to think that there was another aircraft in the vicinity of the airport; but not one on approach. It took me a moment after establishing myself on final to note that the threat symbol; and myself were collocated on the TCAS screen with only 100 feet of separation.Since I did not have full SA or visual contact with the threat aircraft; I was sufficiently confused by the situation to abandon the approach. I executed a go-around and re-entered the left downwind as Aircraft Y landed and rolled out on the runway.A second approach was safely completed without incident.All local traffic were coordinating using the phrase 'Thermal area traffic' to identify the airport and operations. This is normal at this airport even though the airport is called 'Jaqueline Cochrane Regional' airport. The word Thermal contains 2 syllables. The official name of the airport contains 7. This CTAF frequency is often very congested due to the uncontrolled traffic volume at this airport. It was congested at the time of this event.The crew was unfamiliar(first-time to the airport); and did not associate 'Thermal' with the airport they were landing at. As a consequence; they didn't participate in coordination efforts with the other aircraft using the airport. They rightly pointed out on debriefing that 'Thermal' is not printed on any of the airport plates. Thus; local habituated knowledge and telephony understandably contributed to all affected crews' loss of SA.Also a contributing factor was the inhibition of a TCAS RA at low altitude. The yellow-circle symbol did not reflexively indicate the proximate danger present during this event. Even so; without the TA advisory; I am confident that a catastrophic collision would have occurred. This can go up as a TCAS save----if a somewhat confusing one.The traffic situation surrounding this event; and every day at this airport during the snow-bird season can produce a situational-picture that is way too much for any single-pilot in a jet to safely keep track of. I'm a pilot not an air-traffic controller.At 100 feet of vertical separation; and no visual contact made; this was a very close call. This is my second traffic related go-around at this airport in X years due to jet-aircraft coming straight-in to a full-pattern without participating in effective self-coordination.This airport needs an Air Traffic Control Tower----like yesterday!

column121: I had a flight scheduled with a student pilot. The plane was Aircraft X. We both completed a preflight and had a full tank of fuel. Everything seemed normal. We taxied to the runway at ZZZ1 and did our run up. The magnetos showed around 50rpm drop each; as expected. Fuel pressure was normal; oil pressure was in the green arc. Everything was looking normal. We were cleared for takeoff on runway XX and my student applied full throttle rapidly. Immediately we both felt a sputter in the engine and I called for an aborted takeoff. We exited the runway on taxiway 1 and returned to the run up area. I wanted to try to diagnose the issue. I triple checked everything and went through the run up checklist another time. I completed a fouled spark plug checklist just in case that was the issue but I did not believe it was. I concluded that the sputter was due to the aggressive application of the throttle. We agreed to attempt the takeoff again with a smoother application of the throttle but if there was any sign of an issue; we would cancel and taxi back. The second attempt was normal and the engine had no issue so we took off. We took off. The rest of the flight was uneventful. We stayed on flight following while we did a cross country to ZZZ with the plan to return to ZZZ1 after. Based on traffic and our direction of flight; we elected to do a straight in for runway XY. We started our descent checklist and began descending to pattern altitude. We transferred over the ZZZ [CTAF] and began announcing our position. When we had just passed a 1 mile final; we were a little low for the approach and I instructed my student to add more power. I looked at her hand and noticed she had already added power but we weren't getting much power out of the engine. I didn't look at the tachometer but could tell based on the sound that we did not have a high RPM. Additionally; we were not gaining altitude and were still descending. I realized we had an issue and immediately say 'my controls' while trying to do quick troubleshooting. I checked the mixture and the fuel pump were both full rich and turned on. I attempted different throttle settings but had no change in RPM and heard more sputtering in the engine. I hadn't heard this before on this flight but sounded similar to when we aborted takeoff. The engine was still making noise and the propeller was still spinning but we had a partial power loss and would not be able to make it to the runway. At this point we were descending toward trees. I made a right turn for a field and did a soft field landing in this field. There was not more than 30 seconds from telling my student to add throttle and then landing in the field. There was no damage to person; property; or aircraft.

I touched down first on the main landing gear and when the nose gear touched down; the nose veered left. I attempted to correct this with right rudder. The airplane began to fishtail and I continued to try to correct with rudder. After a couple of attempts to correct; the fishtails became worse and I attempted to initiate a go-around. At that time my right main landing gear caught the edge of the snow on the right side of the runway which caused the airplane to turn to the right and exit the runway into the snow. The snow caused the nose gear to collapse which caused a prop strike. I was not injured in any way.

column121: Yesterday shortly after takeoff from ZZZ we had what I was told by the purser was a near miss. Meaning the pilots had to abruptly pull upwards in order to avoid being hit by another aircraft. We were still seated due to turbulence but we had already passed 10;000 ft because the purser was in the middle of his announcements when this happened. I remember myself and the other flight attendant in the back looked at each other in shock and held onto our jump seats. It felt like a roller coaster almost so we automatically knew it wasn't turbulence. It felt like when you are driving and have to swerve quickly in order to avoid hitting something/being hit. The pilots pulled upwards bringing the aircraft higher in such a quick manner that we were instantly concerned. After finishing the inflight service announcements the purser called us and asked if we all felt that and if we were okay. We told him yes we felt it and luckily we were all still seated so we were physically okay. Later on towards the end of the flight the purser came back and told us that during a lavatory break the Captain had told him that we had a near miss with another aircraft and that's why they had pulled up like that so abruptly. The Captain also told him not to mention anything in front of the passengers. The purser then told us not to say anything to anyone and to keep it between ourselves/the crew. We were both stunned and couldn't believe what we were hearing. After landing I was expecting the pilots to at least debrief us since all passengers had deplaned and we were keeping the aircraft for our return flight to ZZZ but they did not. I even waited in first class for them to open the flight deck and come out to and talk to us but they never did. I was still in shock and shaken up so I just went to the lavatory in the back and just cried. I was so scared and feeling so many emotions and didn't want anyone else to see me cry. I am grateful that the pilots were able to get us there safely but it was off putting when nothing was said about the incident after the flight. It does not make me feel safe or comfortable knowing what happened and not being able to discuss it with the pilots after the fact.

column121: Aircraft X was dispatched with MEL 28XXX for the #2 spar valve light; which stayed bright (indicating 'in transit') when the cutoff lever was moved to cutoff. I've had several deferred valve lights recently; this one caught my attention. The MEL allows dispatch but requires a mechanic to verify operation of the actual valve 1x/day. I called the dispatcher; who patched in maintenance control then the Chief Pilot and a Lead Mechanic. None was able to give greater technical insight than my ground-school understanding of the fuel feed system. All of them reasoned that Boeing; the FAA; Air Carrier X; and the union have all signed off on this deferral; and the chances of the valve failing to begin with are pretty small; not zero; but small. With all due respect; no one disagreed with my concern; that just because the valve worked when a mechanic checked it doesn't mean it will work now - and while that is always the case; the lack of an indicator light could lead; in the event of an engine fire; to the possibility of the loss of redundant shutoff valves between the fuel tanks and the burning engine. Not having that information during an emergency could cost the pilots critically. I accepted the aircraft; but in retrospect; not being able to verify the position of the valve seems like unnecessary risk. The analogy I offered is that I would not accept an aircraft with no gear-down indicator light even if the mechanics verified operation of the gear down-locks before every flight. Sure; the valve probably won't fail; and the gear will probably come down; not being able to verify it is the problem. Our first mandate is safety. Everything else comes after.

column121: Inbound aircraft arrived at gate XX later than scheduled.  Flight crew prepared aircraft for departure in a timely fashion.  Upon making contact with ramp agent via interphone; the ramp agent sounded agitated and spoke in a rushed manner.  Ramp agent requested the flight crew to 'release brake we need to reset something'.  CA said 'parking brake released' and released the brake.  The aircraft was not chocked and started to move.  CA immediately reapplied the parking brake.  The movement prompted the CA to query the ramp agent regarding whether or not the aircraft was captured.  The Ramp agent responded by saying 'Sorry it was not captured it is slippery outside' .  The ground crew then removed an apparently disabled tug from the safety area and pushed the aircraft normally with a new tug.Cause: During this event; I was heads down as I had accidentally entered the operations frequency twice in the standby and needed to relocate the correct ramp frequency.  Due to the fact that I split my attention between this task and listening to the ramp conversation; I did not catch all the details which reduced my situational awareness and ability to back up the captain.  The ramp agent was somewhat difficult to understand; was rushing to replace the disabled tug; and did not give any reason for the brake release instruction that would have caused the flight crew to question if the aircraft was secured.  The ramp agent requested that the captain release the parking brake when the aircraft was not otherwise secured; likely due to pressure for an on-time departure.Suggestions: In the future;  I will question thoroughly any instructions from ground crew to release the parking brake for any non-standard reason.  I will make sure the captain verifies with the ground crew that the aircraft is secured prior to any non-standard brake release instructions.
column123: Departing gate XX in ORD; aircraft was ready for block out. Flight crew called ground personnel ready for brake release. Ground informed flight crew they were ready but our tug died so we'll have you release the brake then reset it; and we'll hook up the other tug." Captain released the brake getting an out time 1 minute early; then reset brake. During this release the aircraft rolled back approximately 2-3 feet as the aircraft was on a downslope and the tug was never connected; this is the only aircraft movement of the entire event. Flight crew queried the ground personnel as to why the aircraft rolled and were informed ground personnel did not connect tug because "it's slippery with de-ice fluid on the ground." The second tug was then connected and push commenced as normal. Cause: Multiple causes of this event contributed to the roll. First cause is captain being complacent and trusting ground personnel instead of verifying the ground crew connected the tug. Second cause is the operational pressures put on employees to always get flights out on time; if this pressure was less the second tug would have been connected a minute or so after scheduled departure but this roll would not have occurred. Third cause is the operational norm of the ground personnel that ask for brake release quite often when they are not fully ready so the flight will not take a delay. Suggestions: As captain I always should be verifying all actions are done in the correct way and not allow the aircraft to move unless it is in the safest way possible. Ground crew should also verify the aircraft is in a safe state before asking for any brake releases and have a tug hooked."

Within a few seconds; the aircraft began rolling left and right up to approximately 30 degrees of bank. The Captain (PF) disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to arrest the roll oscillations. Despite opposite control inputs and autopilot disconnection; the aircraft continued rolling for approximately 2-3 oscillations before returning to wings level. The THRUST ASYM COMPENSATION message would not reset again.Approaching the ZZZ [VOR] hold at approximately FL110; the autopilot was re-engaged. The aircraft appeared to respond normally; with the exception of the auto-throttles. FLCH mode and 220 knots were selected and indicated normally.Shortly after leveling at FL100; the aircraft again began oscillating in roll. No yaw oscillation was observed. The autopilot was disconnected; however; the aircraft continued to oscillate and did not immediately respond to pilot control inputs for several oscillations. The flight control diagnostic page was selected. Control surface indications corresponded with the roll oscillations; and no rudder movement was observed. After approximately 2-3 additional oscillations; full manual control was regained and the aircraft returned to level flight.Approximately 5 NM prior to entering the ZZZ [VOR] hold; the Captain (PF) directed the First Officer (PM) to notify ATC and request priority handling for an approach to RWY XXL at ZZZZ.While descending through FL90; all Mode Control Panel (MCP) modes appeared to become inoperative. No modes could be activated. No mode indicator lights were on. At approximately 5;000 feet; on an 14-mile base leg for RWY XXL; MCP functionality appeared to return. LOC capture and APPROACH mode functioned normally. Auto-throttles became available and functioned normally through landing.A normal landing was accomplished. Ground control directed the aircraft to stop on taxiway 1 and contact Emergency Services. While stopped on the taxiway. The FO transmitted that no additional assistance was required. The aircraft taxied normally to the assigned gate and was shut down without further incident.Causal Factors are unknown at this time; without additional information from maintenance post-flight data from the aircraft.

column121: On descent into ZZZ while being vectored to the downwind for runway XX; we received a WING ANTI/ICE fail". We were in IMC with an OAT of between 0 to 3 degrees Celsius. I continued to fly the aircraft and I instructed the FO to run the QRH; as he had stated he flew this aircraft last week and had the same issue. After selecting the ice detector override knob to "all" and I advanced the thrust; the caution went away for approximately 60 seconds. Upon the caution's return we continued the next steps of the QRH and the I advocated to request priority handling. We quickly agreed as a crew and requested priority handling with ZZZ [TRACON] approach control to allow us to receive priority in exiting icing conditions and so I could have the ability to request whatever I thought we needed to safely arrive in ZZZ; as well as having a failure of an aircraft system. The next QRH step required us to push out then push in the wing anti ice button. The caution disappeared for approximately 60 seconds before returning. At this point; I decided we couldn't rely on the indication and to run the QRH as though the message persists. We requested minimum vectoring altitude and a wider base to final from ATC to avoid icing conditions and remain within QRH limitations of 30 degrees of bank and 190 minimum airspeed for flaps 0 and 9 degrees. After transmitting this request the caution went away. We were on our final vector for final when it returned. We agreed that there was no ice accumulation to warrant the "ice accretion" steps and we continued with the approach. Around this time; I had my FO notify dispatch. Due to the possibility of icing; I did not delay the approach and talk to the flight attendant; as we were already below 10;000' and we were more focused on getting the aircraft on the ground.The airport did set up priority handling vehicles as a precaution; and the FO gave them all pertinent information while I contacted maintenance.We landed without incident. My FO did a walk around and noticed no visible signs of damage to the leading wing edges on his post flight inspection.Honestly; maintenance should have had the Captain write it up on the date when my FO had this issue the last time and we wouldn't have had an issue on this day.It sounded like; from the FO's recollection; this aircraft had this issue before with the same aircraft in moderate icing. When his Captain called maintenance after the flight; maintenance convinced him one way or another to not write the airplane up. When I called maintenance; they said I didn't have enough pressure and even though the temperature shows in the green on the Environmental Control System; page; it doesn't mean there's enough pressure. I understand this concept; but I was flaps 9 doing 240kts. I've never had an anti ice fail in this situation; and I even tried having the spoilers open to see if that would give it enough pressure with the advanced thrust setting which did not seem to help."

column121: Incident was with GEU from XA:35 till XB:15….PHX Departure about XB:15 to XB:50.Flight was from Glendale to ZZZ GEU to ZZZ When I called for clearance there were at least seven aircraft already lined up for takeoff.
