Aircraft continued to land and aircraft departed slowly. As I neared the end of the runway; I was given my clearance. It was Cleared to ZZZ; MRBIL; YOTES ZZZ [VOR]; maintain 3000 expect 10;000 3 minutes after; I was given a squawk code and Departure frequency. I do not remember if a heading for takeoff was given at that time or not. I think not. When cleared for takeoff I was given and I heard turn to a heading of 035; I read back 035. On takeoff the controller commented about starting the turn and referenced a direction that I do not remember. I stated I would turn at the end of the runway. I did drift slightly to the right of runway on takeoff. He then changed me over to PHX Departure. I called in and stated the altitude I was leaving; the altitude I was climbing to and that I was on a heading of 035. The controller then stated that he had a low altitude warning to turn to a northwesterly heading and to climb immediately to 3000 feet. I complied and looked out the window and tried to determine where the terrain was. I also later looked at the chart to see if there was some tall structure that could cause the warning there was none. I continued to step climb on headings with the controller.I talked with PHX Approach. He never stated that any separation was lost with any other aircraft and while I was flying; I did not ever see on ADSB or visually any other traffic. I did state that I wanted the tapes at GEU Tower. He stated he could not do that. I said you can't get the tapes at GEU; he said he couldn't. I said I should call GEU and he said I would have to file some special govt paperwork request to get them. I of course wanted the tapes to verify what heading the Tower had told me to fly. He then asked why I turned to the heading that I did. I said because that is the heading the Tower gave me. Basically; he was not going to do anything to get the tapes at GEU Tower. I also stated that this had been my first time IFR out of GEU; that I had never gotten clearance to the north on an IFR departure and that I had never departed even VFR to the north. I stated if I had; I may had recognized if this was not a typical heading. I had nothing to compare it with any other departure; if it may have been an incorrect heading. I also stated that when the GEU Controller had been worried about which direction I was going at the end of the runway; it would have been more helpful to hear from the controller something like 'Verify turning to heading such and such. This would have given a better check to the assigned heading.I stated that I had been startled when the controller gave the low altitude alert; he stated so was the controller. I asked where the terrain was? He stated that it most likely broke a MVA. He started to explain how a controller had to open an area for a heading if it is to be used. While PHX area is hilly; in the immediate area the terrain was flat. As I said before I looked at the charts closely later and did not see any high structures.Other circumstances: Glendale is a very busy airport with traffic. It is tightly confined with Luke airport to the west; PHX Class Bravo to the east and Goodyear to the south. It is a very irregular shaped class Delta. There was ONLY ONE controller working Clearance; Ground; Tower. He was saturated. I heard the controller give another IFR clearance shortly after I got mine and before my takeoff. During this time; hecleared an aircraft to my same destination; ZZZ. I am like is someone else going there. I listened a bit more and the aircraft was doing training and not going to ZZZ and the clearance was corrected. I recognized the controller's voice. He creates a bit of a hostile environment on the radio. He likes to correct pilot errors; but when he makes an error he just moves on and doesn't say anything or apologizes for it. I have spoken to other pilots on the field. They all agree he is difficult to work with. You never know what kind of mood he is in.Finally; If I turned to the wrong heading; I will take responsibility for that. However; if the Tower gave me the wrong heading; I would like to get the answer. I got the feeling that PHX Departure and the supervisor on the phone call wanted me on a 350 heading. Did the controller or I mix up the numbers. Did the relay from PHX Departure give Tower the wrong heading or is there a standard heading that is always given for that area of departure. I don't know; but it seems nobody wants me to hear the GEU Tower tapes

column121: Flight was normal and vectors to ILS XXL was programmed into the FMS as usual. The flight was vectored to final and intercepted the final approach course.  The crew was advised to maintain 3000 until ZZZZZ which is 9 miles from the XXL threshold. Normally the Proline 21 avionics automatically switches from long range nav (pink needles) to short range (green needles); but for some reason this did not occur when expected.  Because vectors to final was selected; only ZZZZZ1(point prior to the FAF) and subsequent fixes were displayed on the moving map.  The FMS generated glidepath came down and the Captain asked why the autopilot did not intercept the glidepath.  He then initiated a descent to capture the glidepath.  Shortly after; the tower called with a low altitude warning and a go around was initiated.  We were vectored around for another approach and landing which was uneventful. I as the non-flying pilot knew something was wrong but could not determine what was causing my confusion.  Both pilots lost situational awareness regarding our exact position ultimately as a result of selecting vectors to final.Neither pilot referred to the moving map display on their ipads and neither pilot looked  at the standby Horizontal Situation Indicator which was presenting ILS information.  Even more importantly; DME position was not compared to the approach chart.There were several lessons learned from this experience. Always program the full approach so that all points on the approach will be displayed on the map. Don't depend on cockpit automation.  Manually select short range nav if this information is needed  before automatic switching occurs.Always use any available information to ascertain position.  Bottom line; get back to the basics and listen to that uneasy feeling.  Don't continue a bad approach.

column121: On Day 0 at approximately XA:30; IP Person A and student Person B were inbound to land at Mankato (MKT) from a flight lesson in ZZZ; flying in Aircraft X. Runway 33 was the active; and we had entered the pattern via a midfield cross. Flying the pattern was uneventful until the final leg.As we turned on final; my student made a radio call stating our position. We had traffic in sight (Aircraft Y) that was holding short of Runway 33. It was a calm and clear day so our groundspeed was probably around 70-80 kts. We heard Aircraft Y make a call stating that they were departing on Runway 33. In my mind I thought 'Wow that's cutting it close but they could probably make it'; but then; I didn't see the aircraft roll across the hold short line after making their departure call. I then thought 'Maybe they just now saw us on final and are waiting for us to land'; but I still maintained vigilance that they might depart anyways. Right after I had that thought; they rolled past the threshold line onto the runway for takeoff. By that time we were less than a mile on final. I had Person B stay on the controls and fly the plane while I watched the traffic outside. We saw them start their roll; but determined we would not be able to land safely without creating an incursion; so we executed a go around. We side-stepped to ther right to avoid catching up to or overflying the departure traffic; but could only side-step so much as there was other traffic on the upwind leg of the pattern (Mankato has an upwind leg for traffic sequencing reasons). At one point we were only separated by 100 feet; and I could no longer maintain visual contact with Aircraft Y due to our nose-up attitude for the go around and our spacing being so close. I'm not sure what our altitude was when we executed the go-around; as I was keeping my eyes outside watching for traffic.As soon as it was safe to do so; my student and I opted to break out of the pattern rather than turning crossdwind in order to recollect and re-assess the situation. When we landed; we each submitted a safety report. We also discussed the situation and determined that we had the right of way. We agreed that something we could have done better was make the go around decision sooner; which would have provided better spacing.

The rundown was then acknowledged by the radar controller and I switched Aircraft X to their frequency when Aircraft X was about a half a mile off of the departure end of runway XX. I observed on the radar scope that Aircraft X appeared to be drifting a couple of degrees slightly east of the runway heading that he was assigned; possibly due to wind. As a result; I called down to the radar controller on the recorded shout line with an approval request for a 150 heading for Aircraft Y to ensure more separation between Aircraft Y and Aircraft X. The radar controller then said that he was going to 'crank Aircraft X on a 090' heading. This did not make sense to me as a 090 would create even more of a conflict with Aircraft Y who was already on a 170. Thus; I reiterated my approval request of a 150 heading for Aircraft Y and the radar controller replied 'approved.' I then switched Aircraft Y to the radar controller about a half mile off of the departure end of runway XX on a 150 heading. After both aircraft were switched to the radar controller's frequency I observed Aircraft X; who was at this point about 2 miles south of the runway; turn directly towards Aircraft Y with targets appearing likely to merge at co-altitude. Ultimately; a 170 heading was coordinated in the rundown for Aircraft Y and another more eastbound heading of 150 was coordinated and approved by the radar controller. The radar controller decided to turn Aircraft X directly towards Aircraft Y creating a near mid air collision. Lastly; I think that it is worth noting that the radar controller is a supervisor who is certified only in one position in the facility and received that certification with zero recommendations from a CPC in the building. I would like to recommend that all those in training whether they are developmentals or supervisors be required to receive a recommendation from a CPC before they are considered for certification.

column121: This aircraft had a L engine exceedance and engine swap prior to report time. This was the first flight after engine change with a MEL deferral It required an ETOPs verification flight (1 hour cruise; all systems normal per FOM 5.60.2) before legal to enter the ETOPs area of operation.  Showing at aircraft about an hour before departure; three Maintenance personnel were working in the cockpit.  The crew gained cockpit access around the departure time. After a few maintenance issues were resolved on the ground (L thrust REV status message; Auto Spoiler EICAS; and previous exceedance that wasn't cleared); we pushed about an hour late.  All was normal until takeoff roll.  Around 80-100 knts; the left engine N1 vibration indicator was higher than normal and the box inverted to white with black digits in the 4.0 range.  Takeoff was continued (no EICAS indications) and vibrations weren't felt on the throttle and airframe until past the low-speed abort phase and into initial climb. One of the Relief Pilots also thought he smelled something not normal.  The FO noted an additional vibration surge above 5.0 occurred during power reduction at 1500 AGL. The non-normal engine indications made ETOPs entry illegal; so the decision was to hold over water and dump 200;000 lbs. of fuel or land overweight   Dumping fuel would delay landing an additional 45 minutes.  AAs the engine was not working normally on its first flight; I decided landing overweight to be the safer option to get on the ground sooner with long runways available back in ZZZ.  This had been coordinated previously with dispatch regarding the ETOPs verification options.  After initial climb out; we completed the After Takeoff checklist as I wanted to clean up and get some altitude to discuss the issue.  The crew concurred to return to ZZZ per our plan with Dispatch on the ETOPs verification.We requested a level off with ATC and were assigned 14;000MSL on the ZZZZZ SID; then a request to return to ZZZ.  ATC cleared us direct ZZZ and descent to 11;000 MSL and to expect the ILS XXR.  While I (PF) and the FO (PM) prepared for the approach; the Relief Pilots assisted by getting a SATCOM with Dispatch.  I had them inform the FAs and Passengers of our plan to return to ZZZ.  We run the electronic Overweight Landing checklist and determined we had to use Flaps 25 for landing as the target speed was over 161KTS.  I believe the final target speed was 167KTS.  The FO pulled up ACARs landing data for RWY XXR that we knew was slightly longer than the takeoff RWY XXL.   Brakes 4 selected.  Approach was brief and Descent checklist completed.  ATC vectored us similar to a ZZZZZ1 STAR down the bay as we slowed and descended.   The approach was uneventful on the ILS to XXR.  Landing checklist and callouts per SOP.  Touchdown was smooth rolling to the end and exiting RWY XXR.  After crossing XXL on Taxiway 1; the brake temps began to increase; so we coordinated with ground to hold on taxiway 1 and have the ear inspected for hot brakes.  APU was started and engines shutdown to allow the parking brake to be released with no aircraft movement.  Brakes began to cool and we verified no fire or fuse plug issues from fire rescue vehicles. We requested to be towed back to gate to avoid using brakes or need to restart engines. After the brakes had cooled around 30 min and began going from amber back to normal; Maintenance and tug crews connected and towed aircraft back to gate XX.  Normal checklists completed at gate and passengers deplaned.  Maintenance write-ups for the engine vibration experienced on the left engine and the BRAKE TEMP EICAS.

column121: While on the STAR inbound to ILS29R at FAT the weather dropped below CAT1 minimums. I was pilot flying; but the Captain would have to fly the CAT3 approach now required.  We requested and entered holding at the point outside the FAF (SANGO). I continued to be pilot flying until the Captain had completed the CAT3 ILS and associated briefing guide. With the Captain as pilot flying he selected flight change for a pitch mode and set the altitude for SANGO (2800) in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window. He and I have a discrepancy in what we remember being set in the altitude window.  I remember confirming 2800 and he remembers setting the altitude for the FAF (1800).  The best way to fly this segment of the approach would have been to stay in VNAV to ensure the altitude restriction at SANGO was protected. I didn't realize the wrong altitude was in the MCP until approach gave us a low altitude warning.  At this time we climbed and corrected the altitude deviation.  I reset the appropriate altitude in the MCP and the rest of the approach was uneventful. Lessens learned are taking more time in holding to prepare for approach; verifying what you see; and use of VNAV.

column121: While at cruise; FL360; a ECAM chime and message appeared and disappeared quickly. I happened to be looking at the ECAM when it happened and registered the words main cargo loop. It happened again; too quickly to read fully. The third time it happened; it stayed on the ECAM and we were able to confirm the main cargo mid 2 loop fault. I ran the checklist for it out of the QRH; page 22-15; without incident. Less than 10 minutes later; the master caution light and bell came on; with the ECAM displaying the SMOKE WARNING and associated items. It went away without any input from us; but then came right back. The captain and I immediately donned our O2 masks and established comms; then accomplished the ECAM items. The warning began to intermittently come back and go away within seconds of each other; so we made the decision to divert. I had just looked at the nearest airfield page; so I knew ZZZ was the closest major airport with Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) capabilities. As a crew we agreed that ZZZ made the most sense; so I  requested priority handling with ZZZ center and got a descent and direct turn to ZZZ coordinated with them. The CA flew a high speed descent while I messaged dispatch our divert intent and got all required information for landing at ZZZ. We flew a visual approach in a 15/20 flap configuration to XXL without incident; stopping straight ahead abeam taxiway 1. CFR used their thermal imaging instrument to ensure no hot spots were detected; which none were. After they gave us the all clear we taxied to the gateway and shut down.We never smelled any smoke; nor had any other indications of it in the flight deck. The ECAM smoke warning went away after we initiated the descent. Dispatch did a good job of letting ZZZ tower know of our situation before we got there; and all ATC agencies were quick and professional at getting us on the ground quickly.

column121: A series of systems failures led to an engine fire shortly after takeoff.Just after raising the landing gear after lift off we; the crew; heard and felt a vibration that was very much like a nose wheel rubbing on the scrubbers; and we smelled what we thought was burnt rubber.  We all thought that a nose tire had perhaps failed and was disintegrating against the scrubbers.   Each of us had experienced this before.  However; this vibration went on too long.  At this point we were at around 1000 AFE and the #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity.The #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity to the standpipe level; but we still had hydraulic pressure.  I decided to wait until we were in a lower threat phase of flight to deal with this issue.  We were perhaps now at 1500 AFE and I noticed that the #2 engine vibration was very high.  I called this out to the crew.  I don't remember the exact number.  All other engine indications were normal; and the N1 and EGT matched the other engines (as far as I can recall). Then; the #2 engine failed. The Relief Pilot called out #2 engine failure.  I decided to run the engine failure checklist.  The FO advised me to wait until flaps were up.  This is the correct procedure following a V1 cut; but I felt that in this case we were high enough to begin the checklist.  However; I agreed to the FO's suggestion.  At this point we were probably 2000 AFE.  I notified ATC and the engine caught fire. The #2 engine caught fire and I ran the fire checklist while the FO flew.  At this point the vibration was gone and we knew what the problem actually was.  The fire went out after the first fire bottle.I now took over pilot flying duties.  We returned to ZZZZ for a landing and the fire department checked the aircraft while we were on the runway.  The fire was out and we had the necessary hydraulics to taxi back to the ramp so we taxied back and shut down.Maintenance later showed me that we had multiple bird strikes all over the aircraft and much damage as a result; including a hole in the right wing root.Perhaps I could have ran the severe engine damage checklist before the engine failed.  However; all engine indications except the vibration were normal.  I would have expected a high EGT; surging N1 and banging noises if we had severe engine damage; and we had none of these.
column123: Upon gear retraction; we heard what we thought was nose gear scrubbing. The sound persisted; and grew louder; and we even commented how none of us had ever had a nose gear make that sound for that long. We then smelled what we thought was burning rubber. Passing through 1500; we got engine vibrations indications on the EICAS engine display. Shortly after; HYD QTY 2 LO caution alert. As Relief Pilot; I kept an eye on number 2 engine indicator; and shortly after called out that #2 was rolling back. We then got ENGINE 2 FAIL alert. Captain notified ATC; called for checklist; but FO (PF) recommended we wait until cleanup. Capt agreed. Shortly after; we received OVHT ENGINE 2 NAC; then subsequent FIRE ENGINE 2. At this time; we were around 3500; climbing to 4000; and decided to run Engine fire 2 checklist. We reported engine failure with ATC; and began immediate vectors back to ZZZZ for an approach to RWY XXL. Being below max landing weight; we had no concerns with the relatively quick vectors; Captain and FO ran checklists and set up the FMS; I ran landing performance; and we reported to ATC our information and Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) requirements. Still suspecting nose gear and hydraulic issues causing the fire; we discussed stopping on the runway for inspection. Capt flew the approach; and we landed uneventfully. We stopped on the runway; ARFF trucks inspected and saw no further damage or fire; and we opted to taxi to parking under power. Upon parking; maintenance teams discovered significant bird evidence and damage. We had discussed birds during the CRM/threat briefing. However; suggestions the future include caution against confirmation bias. The timing of the vibrations and noise were perfectly coincident with what we thought was a nose gear spinning in the wheel well; and further confirmation bias from what we thought was burning rubber. Aside from that; we all acknowledged external factors; such as the recent similar accident; caused a little extra stress that might not otherwise exist. However; this incident certainly cemented the importance of having a full crew; as we all worked together and each was able to contribute to bringing the event to a safe conclusion.

column121: After Right Engine Start and during Left Engine Start the Mechanic verbalized BRAKE BRAKE BRAKE on the interphone I pushed both brake pedals to the floor and verified that the aircraft was not moving and reset the parking brake. I apologized Profusely to the Mechanic for the movement of the A/C (Aircraft) he indicated that there was no injuries or damage.  I estimate that the A/C rolled forward a few feet before the Aircraft was stopped from rolling. The F/O and I discussed the preflight check he noted that he visually saw the parking brake handle up in the set position and I recalled seeing the PARK BRAKE light on the discreet light as being illuminated. I do not recall looking specifically for the PARK BRAKE EICAS message prior to the clearing of the various annunciations after the flight control check and before the first engine was started. Looking back at what may have caused the brakes to be inadvertently released I can only surmise that due to the extreme cold temperatures outside from the preflight that I may have lost some of the feel of my foot position on the pedals as I was completing the flight control check and inadvertently caused the brakes to be released prior to the right engine starting. Going forward I will do a secondary verification of the condition of the parking brake after the flight control check as well as incorporate looking specifically at the light and handle position prior to moving the fuel control switch from OFF to ON.

column121: During transition into DFW from FL310 we executed the appropriate 'Descent Checklist' and set the altimeters to 30.57. Throughout the arrival there was no indication of error from ATC. Upon reaching DELMO at what we believed to be 12;000 MSL we were given a frequency change to 118.42 and instructed to continue our descent to 6000 MSL. During the descent we were instructed to expedite and given additional clearances to 5000msl while turning base; 4000 MSL on base; and 3000 MSL on base to final. While rolling out on a 160 heading to intercept the 18R LOC for the visual approach. ATC asked us to verify our altitude. At this point we were still descending to 3000 MSL indicated. ATC then verified the altimeter setting of 29.57 and instructed us to level at 2300 MSL. Nearly simultaneously ATC issued a 'low altitude alert'. I immediately disengaged the Auto Pilot and pitched slightly nose high to level and reduce speed from 210 kts. While maneuvering the aircraft the  PM was able to get the appropriate altimeter setting and we were able to use his PFD (Primary Flight Display) to verify altitude. Once acceptable altitude and heading for the approach was achieved I was able to set my altimeter to the appropriate setting and proceed with a stable approach to landing. Cause: Multiple factors contributed to causing this incident. Pilot complacency with higher altimeter settings associated with cooler climate therefore not being alerted to the significant change when arriving in a warmer environment. Misinterpretation of the ATIS altimeter setting; failure to verify the altimeter setting; and lastly a lack of warning from ATC that previous altitude restrictions at altitude had been missed by nearly 1;000 MSL. Suggestions: Apply common sense when returning to warmer climates after conducting consecutive operations in cooler weather.
column123: When descending on the boove7 into DFW passing 18k we set the wrong altimeter setting. 30.57 instead of 29.57. We descended down to 12k indicated with approach and when handed off told to descend to 6k and expedite. We continued to descend and were told to continue down to 5k and turn 15 degrees right eventually. We continuously descended from 12k towards our final cleared altitude of 3k as we turned final. Approach asked if we were going down to 2300 because we were cleared to 3000 and I replied were at approx 3300 going to 3k. ATC responded we were already below that and gave us the correct altimeter setting. Fo flying disengaged autopilot to stop descent and begin climbing. We reset the altimeter to the correct setting and were cleared for the approach and handed to tower. FO continued to hand fly the visual to landing. Cause: Usually an altimeter that high would cause a second glance but with this weeks cold front that had been a typical setting. Checking the ATIS against the setting an additional time would have also caught the error. Our printer was having clarity issues and we read our takeoff v speeds off our EFB to verify they were correct due to a misprint. ATC never noticed or alerted us that we had been low on the arrival even when leveling off at the bottom altitude then we were given a continuous descent down until the lower than assigned altitude was noticed. When approach gave us the altimeter on initial contact it wasn't noticed that it was different than what we had set. Suggestions: Double check the ATIS printout more regularly and if ATC notices an aircraft below the level off final altitude it is indicative of an incorrect altimeter setting.

column121: While operating as PIC from FAR to ZZZ; we prepared for push. We had good communications with ramp crew. During pushback; we were cleared to start engines. My FO started the right engine. The push crew pushed us; stopped; and continued the push several times. I had been told my previous trip to Fargo that they were still creating the proper procedures to push aircraft off of the new gates; so we attributed the several stops to the push crew being unfamiliar with the new area and push procedures.At one point; we stopped for a longer period of time. I asked the push operator if we were complete with the push; but got no response. I then noticed we seemed to be moving forward. I asked why we were moving forward and got no response. I looked further down below the nose while trying to determine why we were getting no response and saw what looked like people working near the nosewheel while my FO announced that we were definitely moving forwards.I chose to slam on the brakes to avoid possibly running over the ground grew who appeared to be near the nosewheel. I then told the tug operator to stop everything and tell me what was going on before we continued. He informed me that they had disconnected my aircraft from the tug without telling us or asking for the brakes to be set. After reminding them that communicating this with the crew was a vital safety measure; the tug operator apologized for forgetting and admitted it was his first time pushing an aircraft. There was no training supervisor present.Fortunately; my FO and I were paying attention during the push and I was able to stop the aircraft and prevent anybody from being hurt or any equipment from being damaged.This incident reinforced to our crew the importance of keeping high situational awareness and not relying on the ground crew; even when using reliable headsets. In the future; we will be even more alert during pushback having seen how quickly a bad situation can develop.

column121: Event: Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot B (member tasked to look after the plane 'MX OFFICER') took the C172S for a maintenance checkout flight after the 100hr inspection with Maintenance at ZZZ. The fuel tanks had no visible debris. The left tank had 15 gal and the right tank had 16 gal of 100LL. The right tank had tiny water droplets (about 1 mm); which were poured away. No water observed in the left tank. Three laps in the pattern (.6 of hobbs time) were completed without issue. The plane was placed back in service. No fuel was added given that there was a line at the fuel pumps and the fuel truck was not available. The next flight was scheduled right after the end of this flight. The next flight was an aircraft transition training flight with Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot C (PPL only with about 240hrs). Three laps in the pattern were completed. The first lap was Go Around due to a gust during flare making the aircraft climb. Pilot C initiated a Go Around. The second lap was a normal landing and takeoff (touch and go). During the third lap; Pilot C completed a GUMPSS flow: fuel selector BOTH; mixture FULL RICH; light switches ON and seat and seat belts SECURED. Once abeam the numbers; Pilot C reduced the power and aimed for 1500 RPMs. The RPMs showed 1200 RPMs. Pilot C realized the difference and slightly added power. The MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) displayed 1700 RPMs. Pilot C was distracted by the RPM settings and started to extend the downwind leg while descending. Pilot A noticed a change in propeller sound different from the usual increase in RPMs and similar to an rudder only turn during cruise. Pilot A checked the position of the 'ball' in the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and confirmed it was centered. Pilot A then noticed the altitude of about 600' MSL and prompted a turn to base. Pilot C noticed higher than usual RPM changes and asked Pilot A to take over to rule out Pilot C's improper throttle changes. Pilot A took controls during the base turn and confirmed the propeller sound was still present and decided to do a full stop landing to troubleshoot on the ground. Pilot C agreed. Pilot A turned final and confirmed the fuel selector was BOTH; fuel shut off was IN; mixture was FULL RICH; and magnetos were on BOTH. Oil pressure was in the green arc; oil temperature was in the green arc and fuel flow was still in the green arc. When Pilot A confirmed the aircraft could glide to the runway; he reduced the throttle to IDLE. The propeller slowed down more than usual. Over the numbers; Pilot A set the flaps to 20 degrees (10 degrees already added on downwind). After touchdown the propeller stopped windmilling and came to a complete stop. Pilot A used the energy remaining to let the aircraft roll to the first exit; ([Taxiway] 1) and called [clear of the runway attempting to roll all the way clear]. After crossing the taxi intersection; Pilot A applied brakes and brought the aircraft to a complete stop. Pilot A called Pilot B and reported the issue. Pilot A restarted the plane without prime and the aircraft started without a problem. The aircraft was taxied to its parking spot and shutdown. A magneto ground check did not show any issues. Pilot B met the aircraft with a representative of Maintenance. The aircraft was secured and was not refueled. What I believed caused the problem:I believe the throttle control settings may caused the problem. After repeated use of the throttle controls the settings inside the cowling may have come loose and caused the engine to stop. I believe something was not properly secured during the 100hr inspection. No debris or water was found after inspection of the fuel sumps (left; right and engine). There were no changes in the mixture during flight. The aircraft restarted and taxied without problems on the ground. Not sure what can be done to prevent the recurrence

column121: We were enroute to MWC.  We were eventually cleared direct to MWC.  We were in between layers at 6000 ft with an overcast deck about 2000 ft below.  Handed off to MKE approach.  We rejected a descent to lower stating that we wanted to stay above the deck as long as possible to avoid any potential icing.  ATC cleared us direct IVALY; cross at or above 2600 ft; cleared the RNAV 4L approach to MWC; circle to runway 33R.  We descended to 4500 ft just above the deck; crossed IVALY and began an expedited descent to the next step down of 2300 ft at OWYAL.  We broke out at about 3000 ft  and advised approach with a report of light rime ice at about 3500 and our break out altitude just above 3000. Approach instructed us to contact tower.  At this point we were still about 3 miles from OWYAL.  We contacted tower with position reported as outside OWYAL.  Tower asked if we wanted to land runway 4L or circle to 33R; winds 300 at 10kts.  We elected to circle and tower said 'circle southwest of the airport and enter left base for 33R.'  We had the airport in sight and began to maneuver to enter an extended left base for 33R descending to  pattern altitude of 1745 ft.  Tower calls out an altitude alert saying 'we don't have a standard approach altitude.'  We believe we were cleared on a visual segment of the approach via circling instructions.  We replied that we were entering an extended left base for 33R and asked tower to confirm that we were cleared to land.  Cleared to land 33R ahead of traffic from the NE.  Landed and cleared at taxiway C; B; B1 with no further comment or issue.  Why the altitude alert?  Tower may have been tracking the profile for a straight in approach to 4L which would have alerted the altitude below the stepdown floor of 2300 prior to reaching OWYAL.  Raises another question:  when should you break off your approach and begin circling?  Wait until the MAP?  Or proceed visual when cleared to circle while maintaining visual contact with the airport?    Wait until within the circling radius for your category?  At the MDA the protected area at the circling altitude for category A aircraft is 1.1 nm radius from the approach end of the runway.  But at pattern altitude the whole class D area should be OK.

column121: While flying day; VMC to DEN RWY34R; we were cleared for the visual approach on a dogleg heading and 9000' with instructions to maintain 170 kts to CORDE (FAF). FO had a 2 mile ring around CORDE for SA; and as a spot where he briefed he would drop the gear and call for flaps 15. FO armed the approach but we did not set a lower altitude. CORDE altitude is 7000' or above. Just outside of the 2 mile ring from the FAF I mentioned that we were high and needed a lower altitude set with the autopilot on; did he want 7000?  We then set 7000' and the plane began a shallow descent; but we were still high. Just inside the 2 mile ring (1.5 miles from CORDE) we were 600-700' high and going higher on the path. We lowered the gear; he called for flaps 15; and began to slow to his target speed of 160. We were now over 800' high; and I mentioned that it would be helpful to keep his speed up to lose the required altitude. He responded by increasing the MCP speed back toward 170 with the autopilot on. When I saw that we were over 1000' high on the path deviation scale I told him we that wasn't going to do it; we needed to get the nose down and increase our rate of descent; whereupon he disengaged the autopilot and pitched down a bit. We also went flaps 25 at this point. I assessed that we were too high to use V/S to capture glideslope from above in time to make the stabilization windows; but we were nearing glideslope as he hand flew the plane; at between 165-170 kts. I told him that the 1000' window was coming up; we should reduce the descent rate from what I recall was reading over 1800 fpm.Big failure on my part was that; as I was distracted with helping correct the descent rate and glideslope; I failed to mention that we still did not have final flaps at the 1000' window.FO was able to arrest the rate of descent; but; as we were nearing 600'; I recall that the PAPI was displaying 4 red (low); and we got a couple of 'glideslope' calls. As we were still slowing to our target speed I felt that by leveling off he would recapture glideslope from below about the same time we would hit our target speed; so I figured we'd be able to achieve the 500' stability window. However; as we neared the 500' window we received a 'too low; terrain' call and went around. The 'too low; terrain' call surprised me; as we were completely VMC and nowhere near dangerous terrain on final; but I then realized that we were not at flaps 30. I know that will sometimes cause a 'too low; terrain' call instead of a 'too low; flaps' call; which would've been more obvious as to what was wrong.In hindsight a 'too low; terrain' callout should be followed by a terrain escape maneuver instead of the go-around that we did.The go-around was uneventful; as was the subsequent landing on RWY35R.

After completing this checklist; it called to go to the Alternate Landing Gear Extension Checklist which we completed and the gear came down. The landing was successful and soft but the plane did not have nose wheel steering; so differential braking was used to keep directional control. The Captain was able to slow the aircraft enough to make the high speed exit and clear the runway and make a slight right turn onto taxiway 1. Once on taxiway 1; the aircraft was stopped and we notified tower that we would need to stay there until we could get tugged in.Once tower was notified; the Captain notified the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue. We left the plane in the landing configuration; started the APU and left both engines running until the tug arrived. After waiting 25-30 minutes; tug came and we secured both engines and got towed. column121: On Day 0; I; Captain A; was operating flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ as Pilot Monitoring. While on the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; at around 10;000 to 11;000 MSL; HYD 2 LO PRESS appeared on the EICAS. I looked at the Hydraulics page on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and noticed that there was no hydraulic pressure within system 2. I requested priority handling with ZZZ Approach; notified the controller of the fuel on board; which I believe was roughly 4900 pounds of fuel at the time; and that there were XX souls on board the aircraft. Because I was not the only operational aircraft arriving at ZZZ at the time; I requested with the approach controller to be vectored off the arrival procedure to stay out of the way while I began working on the QRH checklist items. I located the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist within the QRH and began going through the listed items. While completing this checklist; SPOILER FAULT also appeared on the EICAS. I continued with the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist items and completed the checklist. Once completed; HYD 2 LO PRESS remained annunciated. I began working on the SPOILER FAULT checklist. After completing the checklist items; SPOILER FAULT extinguished from being displayed on the EICAS. Following this; I used the non-normal section of the ERJ landing app to set the appropriate Vspeeds for landing. At that point I took control of the aircraft as Pilot Flying from First Officer Person B and had him run the Loss of Hydraulic System 2 QRH checklist.Once the landing gear was extended and all checklist items were complete; ZZZ ATC was notified that we were ready to come in for a landing. The landing runway that we were using was XXL as it is an upsloping runway. It was decided that this would be the best course of action to aid in stopping the aircraft. Additionally; I had also requested that emergency services follow the aircraft up the runway after we land. The landing was successful and soft. Because I had no rudder control or nosewheel steering upon touchdown; differential braking was used to keep directional control of the aircraft. I was able to slow the aircraft enough to make a slight right turn onto Taxiway 1; clear the runway; and make another slight right turn onto Taxiway 2. At that point; I stopped the aircraft; communicated with the tower controller that I would need to remain in the current position; as I was unable to make larger right or left turns and would have to be towed into the gate.After communicating with the tower controller; I informed the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue; and that the airplane would have to be towed to the gate. I left the aircraft in the landing configuration; started the APU; and left both engines running until the tug arrived roughly 25 to 30 minutes later. Once the tug arrived; I secured both engines; the tug was attached to the aircraft; and the aircraft was successfully towed to gate XX. Once at the gate; all passengers were deplaned; dispatch transferred me to a supervisor to notify them of the event; and I conversed with Maintenance Control in the logbook entry for the event.Cause: Aircraft loss of hydraulic system 2.Suggestions: According to the HYD 2 LO PRESS QRH checklist; if the HYD 2 LO PRESS remains annunciated on the EICAS; after turning the associated HYDRAULIC ELEC PUMP to the OFF position; the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist is complete; and I am supposed to complete the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist. Instead of doing this; I went ahead and completed the SPOILER FAULT checklist instead. Had I continued with the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist; as I should have; I would have known that it is stated not to accomplish the SPOILER FAULT checklist.Additionally; because of the feeling stress; I failed to inform the dispatcher; the flight attendants; and the passengers of the situation at hand. Looking back at the situation; I had plenty of time and fuel remaining that I could have accomplished communicating with dispatch; the flight attendants; and the passengers.

column121: In cruise; we noticed lightning on the horizon across a very wide area and activated the on-board radar. The tops were stratiform in all directions. The radar began painting a few isolated cells in the vicinity of ZZZZZ when we were 160nm away. The cells appeared well-defined and reasonably dispersed. We discussed a preliminary plan for diverting around the weather and agreed to proceed unchanged until we were approximately 80nm from the cells where we would have a more clearly-defined understanding of the weather as depicted on the radar. We also coordinated with center to verify the information we were seeing. At approx 80nm from ZZZZZ; we began a left deviation with the intention to later turn right direct the ZZZ VOR and then direct ZZZ. According to on board radar and center control; this was a safe path well clear of cells. As a matter of caution; I turned on the seatbelt sign and ordered the flight attendants to take their jump seats. We were still in smooth air; but conditions began to deteriorate to occasional and then to continuous moderate. The FO said to take over the airplane if I felt it necessary. Suddenly; airspeed dropped precipitously by approx 30kias. I said;Power! Power!" to the FO. He rapidly responded by applying TOGA power and asked if APR was necessary. I said no as airspeed was rapidly recovering. It is important to note the weather radar had previously showed no weather at or beneath the location where this happened at any point leading up to or at this location. Moments later; the autopilot disconnected as the airplane lurched suddenly into approximately 20 degrees of left bank and 7 degrees of pitch up accompanied by a rapid loss of airspeed. I took control of the airplane and called;"My aircraft." I leveled the nose immediately and leveled the wings while simultaneously reapplying TOGA thrust. Focused on maintaining attitude; I allowed deviations in altitude but remained very conscious of airspeed as it fell. I ordered the FO to call a descent to FL340 to ATC as a means of maintaining airspeed as the airspeed was initially completely unresponsive to the increased thrust and I felt a descent necessary to stay on the correct side of the power curve. In approximately negative 2 degrees of pitch; the airplane initially began descending to approx FL355 and then rapidly climbed to approx FL365 while still pitched down as the airspeed rapidly recovered before the FO could inform ATC. The airplane came back under positive control and I modified my instructions to the FO; 'Inform ATC of a severe turbulence encounter with deviations +/-500 feet.' The airplane remained under positive control thereafter; although for 5 or 10 minutes a very high thrust setting (CLB) was frequently necessary to maintain .75M; which we had been flying at before; during; and after the encounter. I returned control to the FO and the rest of the flight proceeded as normal except for a later STALL FAIL caution message in the descent to ZZZ. No one was injured and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft."
column123: In cruise at FL340 we notice build up from weather ahead; our radars indicated widespread perception in direction of our flight. Looking at the on board radar and talking to center about what they're seeing up ahead; we determined it was best to deviate left of course where there weren't any radar echos on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) or what ATC was seeing on their side. We request a deviation left of course and receive the approval. A few minutes into the new cruise altitude; we start getting moderate chop to moderate turbulence with airspeed fluctuations requiring me to put in TOGA thrust to get back up .75 Mach. When then hit severe turbulence getting major altitude and airspeed fluctuations disabling the autopilot. Captain took over pilot flying duties and I took over pilot monitoring duties during the upset recovery from the severe turbulence. We alerted/requested ATC that we were descending from FL360 to FL340; for a greater buffet boundary as we were having a hard time maintaining airspeed and altitude due to the turbulence. After leveling at FL340 the fluctuations continued with moderate chop to moderate turbulence. The turbulence stopped approximately 3 minutes after leveling at FL340; we determined with the radar and ATC that it was clear ahead. I called in the back to talk to the flight attendants to make sure everyone was okay and no one was hurt. The captain gave me control of the aircraft back and rest of the flight proceeded as normal; except for receiving a STALL FAIL caution message in the descent into ZZZ.

column121: After closing the doors and pulling the jet bridge back; we made contact with the ramper crew who was just off the right side of our nose. I (Captain) asked for the phraseology to allow us to release brake. The ramper told us all secure below; FOD walk complete; steering disengaged; ready for brake release." I then released the parking brake and responded with "parking brake released; clear to capture; we are calling for the push now." The aircraft then began rolling backwards at an unusual rate. An operations manager in a truck off the right side of the nose then yelled and told us to set the brakes. Both the First Officer and I applied pressure to the toe brakes however they didn't actuate so I instead pulled the parking brake and we came to a stop.The cause is most likely due to lack of communication between flight crew and rampers; ramper's fatigue; and complacency. After making initial contact via headset; I believe the ramper just instinctively gave his whole prior to pushback brief without fully confirming everything he stated.Suggestions: I recommend rampers to be more thorough with their instructions; making sure that each topic they speak about is true by visually confirming it. As a pilot; we could also start using a double confirmation before changing configurations; such as releasing the brake of disconnecting inter-phones."
column123: Once jet bridge was pulled Captain called for rampers via operations since no one had answered our calls down below. Operations manager pulled up in a truck and spoke with the crew chief who then looked at us. I pointed to my headset and that established comms between the flight deck and ramp. Captain asked if they were ready for brake release for which the crew chief responded with all secure below FOD walk complete ready for brake release." At this point Captain disengaged the parking brake. The aircraft started to roll a little as it normally does but soon it rolled a lot more than usual. Operations manager yelled and we were already trying to stop the aircraft from moving. I used the toe brakes but due to no hydraulic pressure they were ineffective. Captain then engaged the parking brake to stop the aircraft. After that the crew chief walked back over to the aircraft and secured the airplane to the tug. Everything from there proceeded as normal however it took calling ramp twice to get them to push the airplane once cleared.Cause: Lack of proper communication and complacency by ramp crew. We released the parking brake when the ramp agent gave his brief and stated ready for brake release.Suggestions: I should've made sure that the ramp agent was actually focused on the act of pushing the aircraft. By waiting until he was done talking to the operations manager we could've prevented a situation in which the aircraft was in fact not secured to the tug."

column121: On Day 0 while operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We experienced a pressurization issue shortly after departure. During the climb; the cabin was not pressurizing as expected and cabin altitude indications were not responding normally.we had a rapid rate of cabin altitude ascent. We proceed to stop the climb out and stop at 7;000 feet to stop the cabin from climbing.Prior to departure we did write up that the N1 gauges were showing a big split between each other on the ground at the gate. Maintaience came and looked at the issue which was written up a similar way for this aircraft earlier. Maintaience put the right pack back on Mel even though it had been cleared in ZZZ2 just prior to this flight. I questioned that choice and spoke with the dispatcher; duty pilot and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control went through the previous write up and looked to see what was done. I was informed that the problem the aircraft had for the pressurization issue prior was not related with the pack and that they performed tests of pressurization in accordance with Boeing standard procedures. After speaking with Maintenance Control my FO and I were comfortable taking the aircraft as they said what test and checks were done by maintenance and the plane was safe to continue for service.Once we leveled off and communicated with ATC. I immediately directed my attention to the abnormal indication and the FO and I accomplished the applicable QRH procedure for pressurization malfunction. The aircraft was leveled off as required and we began coordinating a return to ZZZ.Given the proximity to the departure airport; ATC coordination; aircraft configuration considerations; and time compression associated with the abnormal condition; my focus was primarily on safely flying the aircraft; completing the QRH; and setting up for the return and landing. The decision was made to return to ZZZ.During this period of high workload and compressed timeline; I overlooked referring the FOM for additional considerations related to overweight landing and did not formally declare an emergency with ATC. ATC was informed about what the situation was and that we were doing a checklist and our plans to return to ZZZ. The QRH checklist was followed for the overweight landing and what to expect and to do a landing assessment. In that QRH under additional items which was after checklist completion it had a few lengthy paragraphs about overweight landing characteristics and a line about going to the FOM for more guidance which I overlooked about the FOM. In retrospect; referencing the FOM would have prompted a formal emergency declaration due to the overweight landing condition.The approach and landing were uneventful. The aircraft landed safely without injury to passengers or crew and without aircraft damage. After clearing the runway; we coordinated with maintenance and completed the appropriate write-ups in the aircraft logbook regarding the pressurization malfunction and overweight landing.Upon reflection; this event reinforced the importance of deliberate consideration of administrative and procedural follow-through such as emergency declaration requirements even when the operational outcome appears controlled and manageable. In the future; I will ensure that; workload permitting; I take a moment to cross-check FOM guidance when abnormal situations involve potential overweight landings or other criteria requiring formal declaration.Safety was maintained throughout the event; and all required documentation was completed.Cause: Aircraft had recent pressurization-related write-up. The Right pack was re-MEL'd after being cleared.Although maintenance stated issue was unrelated; prior history may have increased system vulnerability. There is also a potential normalization of repeat discrepancy.I think to mitigate this would be to not dispatch an aircraft with a repeat item in the same day with similar write up issues and investigate the problem closer.
column123: While completing fms preflight tasks; I noticed that the takeoff N1 settings were mismatched and fluctuating. This mirrored a similar maintenance issue the previous crew had with this aircraft; that resulted in a loss of pressurization. Maintenance was already at the aircraft due to other write ups; and they were notified right away. Eventually; an MEL was applied to the right pack; but as the captain and I were noticing that this event felt very similar to the events leading up to the previous loss of pressurization; the captain called both the duty pilot and Maintenance Control to express our concern. Ultimately we felt convinced that the aircraft would be safe after a thorough explanation from Maintenance Control; explaining that a leak test was conducted; and that the right pack MEL and N1 differential was most likely not associated with the cause of the pressurization issue earlier in the day. After an hour from when maintenance was first called we pushed back. On departure we noted that the actual takeoff N1 settings were not within .5 percent of the performance data setting; but we interpreted that to be in accordance with the pack inoperative MEL. The taxi and take off went normally; but on the initial climb out we noticed cabin altitude climbing at around 2000 feet per minute; and our ears were popping. We leveled off at 7000; and the captain transferred radios to me(I was already pilot flying); and then notified dispatch. The bleeds were set in accordance with the MEL; with the right pack off; the left pack on; and the isolation valve closed. It was then determined that we should return to ZZZ; which was coordinated with dispatch and then ATC. The captain ran the overweight landing checklist; and the non routine landing considerations checklist; while I flew the aircraft and set up the aircraft for a landing in ZZZ. The cabin altitude warning checklist was not completed; as we never received a cabin altitude warning. Unfortunately both the captain and I missed that an emergency needed to be declared when landing overweight. We landed safely; and returned to gate XX; and all passengers were deplaned right away.Cause: I believe that a more thorough investigation by maintenance could have prevented this incident. Both myself and the captain continuously expressed concern about the similarities of our situation and the event described to us by the previous crew. With hindsight I wish we would've held more firm in not accepting the aircraft.

column121: This report is documenting a flight did not operate event for an airplane without an APU that we were scheduled to fly for two legs (ZZZ-ZZZZ-ZZZ1). The day before this; I operated Flight ABCD from ZZZZ1 to ZZZ without an APU. Although the APU was listed as inop in the MEL. ZZZ ops was not aware of the APU inop on arrival. Although we called ops on the ground in ZZZ to ensure power and air would be available at the gate (XX); they failed to have a jetway driver at the gate (so no ground power) and ground personnel were unaware that we would be leaving an engine running for en extended period of time; leading to an unsafe situation with the wing walker moving towards an operating engine and no control of vehicle traffic behind the aircraft.Report narrative of flight did not operate.Just prior to closing the aircraft door for departure out of ZZZ; the APU automatically shutdown. Maintenance accomplished a restart and the APU automatically shutdown a second time for high APU oil temperature. Maintenance informed me of their intentions to MEL the APU as inoperative for our next 2 legs through ZZZZ to ZZZ1. The temperature in ZZZZ was forecast to be 84 degrees; and I felt that would have caused uncomfortable cabin temperatures at the gate and on departure. In addition; my experience with issues of not having a gate agent/jetway driver upon arrival (for ground power from the jetway) as well as potential of having inexperienced ground personnel around a running engine; and language issues complicating communication; had me concerned about safety issues on arrival at these locations. For those reasons; I placed a flight did not operate entry in the logbook. Report narrative of Flight ABCD Day 0.Prior to boarding in ZZZZ1 with no ground power or conditioned air available at gate XY; the APU automatically shutdown. We accomplished the APU fault checklist and coordinated for maintenance; ground power; conditioned air for the cabin and for the potential need for pneumatic air cart. With coordination from maintenance and Maintenance Control we conducted an APU restart and the APU again automatically shutdown. The APU was MEL'd and we proceeded with appropriate supplemental procedures and coordination for departure. The weather in ZZZZ1 was 84 degrees and cloudy. We had conditioned air prior to boarding and all necessary ground equipment standing by. At the time; I felt ZZZ should be a competent station to safely receive an aircraft without an APU. The cabin temperature got uncomfortably warm during the crossbleed start but cooled relatively quickly in flight. The APU was in the MEL and we felt ZZZ should have been aware of the aircraft status for arrival. After an uneventful flight and landing on Runway XX in ZZZ; we called ZZZ ops on the short taxi to gate XX. The FO asked ops if power and electrics would be available immediately on arrival at [gate] XX. Ops said something like 'understand you are asking for power and air; does that mean you have an issue with your APU?' The FO responded that the APU was inop and we would need electrics and air conditioning at arrival. Ops told us power and air would be available but I don't recall their exact words.We taxied to the gate and set brakes. I looked towards the operating engine and saw the wing walker walking from the wing tip towards the operating engine. She took about four steps then stopped briefly before taking another step or two towards the running engine. I opened my window and motioned for her or someone on the ground to get her away from the left engine. I was prepared to shut the engine down if she continued moving towards it. A supervisor yelled in her direction and she moved outboard of and aft of the wing to stop traffic on the road behind us.I then looked at the jetway and realized we didn't have a jetway driver; and therefore had no ground power available. The FO called ops and asked for a jetway driver. The response was that an agent was on the way. The agent arrived at the gate a few minutes later and we waited for the jetway to be positioned before ground power could be provided to the plane.I felt the entire process of receiving an aircraft without an APU was handled without urgency or an understanding from ops or ground personnel of the potential dangers involved. I felt like we were communicating the situation but we weren't understood. To make matters worse; we had an FAA representative on the jump seat witnessing the entire event.

column121: We took off XXC in ZZZ. It was a flaps 5 bleeds on NADP (Noise Abatement Departure Procedure) 1 DEP. After calling flaps up after takeoff checklist; my FO noticed during the checklist that we had a R DUCT pressure of 80 psi and that the L DUCT pressure was only at 40psi. We then told ATC that we wanted to level off. They gave us 15000ft to do so. At that time I transferred the controls over to my FO as well as the radios and I started to focus on the issue. I remembered from previous flights that there is no real guidance on this issue other than a brief paragraph in the limitations section from the FM. Which states '  A duct pressure difference of more than 8 PSI may indicate a mechanicalmalfunction. If a duct pressure split is observed after bleeds are configured forflight; and the lowest indication is approximately 18 PSI or less; contactMaintenance. ' we had exceeded those numbers. when we leveled off at 15000 the duct pressure equaled out and seemed stabilized; but not having more info I had dispatch call us to get Maintenance Control on the radio. Maintenance Control did not have more guidance for us after verifying where gauges were saying at this time. They said that it would be ok to continue.  FO and I talked and agreed to try. Due to the high tail wind and decreasing weather conditions we were concerned with being able to land XX in ZZZ. Weather in ZZZ1 had been similar however wind had been reporting higher. There was a lot of discussion about the pros and cons of shooting the ILS to XX and landing with a tail wind vs LOC XX circle XY. We did run our EFB for both directions and they both worked with current conditions. However with the wind just below the limit at ZZZ1 made Captain nervous with conditions worsening. He called tower directly over the radio and got a weather report. I don't remember what that report was I believe higher winds from the north. He also mentioned tower hadn't had any traffic in a while so no runway condition report. Visibility was reporting plenty good so we opted for the LOC XX circle XY. On the approach we broke out higher than I was expecting however visibility was not what was reported. In particular on the south end of the field. We circled at the published MDA however we forgot about the NOTAM with a MDA 60ft higher. At the time we were both completely unaware we had made the mistake. Around the downwind to base leg tower gave us a low level alert which we confirmed our altitude. Shortly after we lost sight of the airport and went missed. Which leads to the second error. The turn away from the airport. Captain said I lost sight of the airport tell them we are going missed. I call tower and let them know; they acknowledged and told us to fly the published missed. Captian hits the go around button brings power up then makes no call outs. I query him about setting flaps to setting two. He replied flaps two. Then immediately calls gear up. I raised flaps to two and put the gear up. In the time period he started making a right turn away from the airport. I could tell he was behind the plane. I didn't want to cause more confusion or debate with correcting him at this point. So checked the chart for obstacles. When my eyes get back to the PFD (Primary Flight Display) I notice we are well beyond 30 degrees of bank so I called out bank angle. He corrects however is a little aggressive with the controls when he does. At this point we continue on with the missed and divert to ZZZ1.

column121: During pre-departure preparations for Flight ABCD (ZZZ-ZZZ1); maintenance personnel entered the flight deck approximately ten minutes before door closure to check oil levels and advised us they would service the No. 2 engine. We acknowledged and continued normal duties. After receiving matching passenger counts from the flight attendant and release; I authorized door closure. Both packs were operating at that time; and no abnormal odors were present.Seconds after the door closed; while awaiting the flight attendant's cabin secure" report; I detected an acrid; "old socks/burning" odor on the flight deck with no visible smoke. I immediately turned both packs off and opened the DV (direct vision) windows to ventilate. The flight attendant confirmed the odor was also present in the cabin. With windows open and recirculation fans on; the smell began to dissipate. I contacted Maintenance Control and described the situation. They requested that we turn each pack on individually to isolate the source. I expressed concern about reintroducing fumes; but they advised the effect should be minimal with ventilation.We briefed the flight attendant and instructed her to open the service door if the odor returned. Pack 1 produced no abnormal smell. Upon selecting Pack 2 on; the same strong acrid odor immediately returned; prompting us to turn Pack 2 off. The flight attendant opened the service door due to the intensity of the smell. At this point; I determined the aircraft was no longer safe for passengers or crew. I instructed the First Officer to contact Operations and request the jet bridge be reconnected for deplaning. I informed Maintenance Control that I was refusing the aircraft and contacted Dispatch to advise that a new aircraft would be required.After all passengers deplaned; the crew elected to seek medical evaluation out of caution. Vitals and blood samples were taken; no abnormalities were found. I experienced a scratchy throat; and medical staff advised it should resolve within 24 hours.Cause: I believe somehow the oil vapors or oil drippings got into the APU bleed system when they were servicing the engine number 2.Suggestions: Use O2 mask whenever it is needed. I didn't use it because I thought the ventilation with the windows open was enough. I ended up with a scratchy throat."

Now the ZZZ3 should be the destination and ZZZ will be the starting point; but the airplane was already fueled for ZZZ3. I was told that the passengers are waiting for me at ZZZ; at the FBO. And I need to hurry up. I landed ZZZ walked inside the FBO and there were no passengers. I called the dispatch to report it and I told them to update the program. Since the destination was still showing as ZZZ1 instead of ZZZ3; dispatcher told me that I should try ZZZ1 first and then divert to ZZZ3.I immediately reacted and told her that ZZZ1 was well below minimums and most importantly the runway at ZZZ1 was closed since the morning of Day 0. Dispatch finally changed the destination as ZZZ3. 6 passengers showed up after 20 mins with 8 bags; 5 sets of ski and pole; one big black ski sleeve with skies in them; one pair of ski boot; 2 cool case with different liquor bottles in them and 1 full size dog. Passenger weights as follows 265+170+205+165+140+155LBS Cargo Estimated 200LBS. Fuel 2300LBS. Airplane was within weight and balance limits.I took off from ZZZ. I was told to turn to 030 by ZZZ Tower; Gears up/Lights off/YD On/Climbing right turn to 030 degree. Autopilot engaged/Airplane flew through 040 degree/AP Disconnect and YD Disconnect/Hand flying trying to turn the airplane back to 030 degree. Airplane won't turn left; it kept turning uncommanded to the right. Check trim panel. Rudder trim was all the way to the right. Reduced power. Lowered Nose. Fighting the rudder trim/super heavy controls. Cancelled IFR with departure; contacted ZZZ Tower selected runway XX right downwind. All turns to the right. Landed safely with all 6 passengers.Contacted chief pilot described the situation with directional control. I was advised to burn more gas on the ground and finish the flight. No de fueling available at ZZZ. I agreed. I asked the dispatch for a permission to fly the airplane for an hour by myself to burn gas. Permission denied by dispatch. Dispatch wanted me to burn the gas on the ground with passengers inside the airplane. I was burning the gas down at the runup area RWY XY. Dispatched called me again;asking about the fuel quantity. It was 2150LBS Indicated I reporterted over phone they estimated the cargo at 250LBS. With 5 set of skis I clearly saw there were more than 5 set of skis in the cargo plus other items. With all the passenger weights; fuel and cargo they told that I am within limits and I should fly the airplane right awayI rejected to fly the airplane until the fuel weight drops below 2000lbs. They were not happy about it. Dispatch told me to park the airplane at the ramp at ZZZ and put the passengers out and sent another airplane to do the trip. I was told that company had to face losses for my decision making and had to use another bigger airplane.

column121: This is a follow up from my previous report regarding dual FMC failure. We lost both FMC while circumnavigating thunderstorms. ATC had just cleared us direct to ZZZZZ while we were climbing when both FMC locked up. It eventually returned back while we switched to HSEL and V/S and the PM reloaded the FMC. It appeared to be operating properly once everything was back inserted in the FMC. However; it turned out that the ILS was in PARK when we tried to shoot the ILS into ZZZZ. It would not allow us to delete it or put in another frequency. After we were on the ground; we researched this online as no checklist came up and when we did a search in our FM; nothing useful came up. Eventually I found the FMC checklist that should have popped up when all three FMC had failed but it did not come up. As a matter of fact; no EICAS message or STATUS message came up except for the 'Landing Altitude.' It turned out that in order to get it out of PARK; you have to go to ALT NAV; Page 2; Turn it ON; type the frequency in manually and the course and that should fix it. However; as we were close in; and that knowledge was not available with a quick search; we ended up flying more or less a visual approach on the PAPI. As a note; when we did the Descend checklist; the frequency for the ILS had not popped in yet; but that is not necessarily unusual if we are too far out. We just never got back to it again. I think we used to check it at 2500 but that has been out of the books SOP for awhile now.

When it appears a vehicle is stopping and you proceed to begin moving then find the vehicle is not stopping causing the need to quickly stop the aircraft this causes significant risk to our flight attendants that are up walking in cabin as well as potential aircraft damage if a vehicle is contacted. column121: This morning I was having issues with my electrical system in the Arrow I was flying. My radio comms failed and I had talked with the tower over the phone about me receiving my takeoff clearance over the cell phone and using that as two way comms until I was out of the airspace. I was proceeding to an uncontrolled field as my final destination. During my first takeoff attempt I was nervous and accidentally turned left onto Runway XX instead of right onto XY. As I began to throttle up to take off; tower told me cancel takeoff clearance so I immediately idled the power and applied brakes. That was my evasive action when told to cancel my takeoff. Tower told me to make a 180 so I did and taxied off the runway. There was traffic using Runway XZ.After taxiing back to the ramp and recomposing myself; I attempted again but using the correct runway and proceeded to my final destination safely. All while using the telephone to get my takeoff clearance.The series of events that led up to this event was as followed: I had to spend the night due to an electrical issue the night prior where seemingly my battery died. Mind you I had no issues with the electrical system prior to the evening startup attempt. After having it looked at by an airframe and power plant mechanic the next day (today); we addressed the issue and all seemed as normal. I went to take off and when I went to bring my wheels up; lost all electrics in the plane. So I landed and had the system examined again. It was returned to service and I had talked to tower on the telephone about taking off; maintaining VFR; and proceeding to my destination without talking to anyone. I held short of the runway and was handed off to tower and that's when the bit where I am filing this report happened. I was noting my departure instructions; trying to maintain contact via telephone; and get myself going back home so the plane could be examined by the mechanic at my home field. Task saturation and nerves occurred here. I should have remained more calm and just taken one step at a time and thought through the situation more thoroughly instead of trying to be in a hurry to get home as soon as possible trying to avoid weather that would envelope my home field for the next week judging by the forecast.After another attempt; I was able to safely take off and proceed enroute as planned.

column121: While operating a 2020 Cessna 182T (G1000 NXi); under VFR with Flight Following; I experienced an in-flight electrical smoke event.En route with one practice landing at ZZZ1. After departing ZZZ1; I was established in cruise at 6;500 feet MSL in clear VMC conditions. I had completed the cruise checklist shortly before the event; and all indications were normal at that time.While in cruise; I observed a light puff of white smoke emanating from the left side of the instrument panel accompanied by a strong electrical odor. No visible flame was observed. At approximately the same time; the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) went blank; the Primary Flight Display (PFD) and radio panel flickered intermittently; and the secondary radio became inoperative. No circuit breakers were found popped.I immediately requested priority handling with ZZZ [TRACON] and diverted to the nearest suitable airport; ZZZ. I pulled the MFD circuit breaker. The master and alternator were left on in order to retain primary radio communications during the diversion. No windows were opened; and no oxygen was used. The aircraft landed approximately 5-10 minutes after onset without further incident. There were no injuries.After landing; the avionics switches were observed to be heat-deformed/melted. No additional smoke was observed after the initial puff.Post-flight maintenance inspection reported no evidence of active fire. A malfunctioning avionics switch on BUS 2 was identified and replaced. Wiring behind the panel was inspected by maintenance personnel; and an independent avionics shop conducted an additional inspection prior to return to service.This report is submitted in the interest of safety documentation and analysis of an electrical smoke event involving heat deformation of panel components and partial avionics failure in flight.The problem arose in cruise flight at 6;500 feet MSL; shortly after completing the cruise checklist with normal indications; a light puff of white smoke was observed from the left side of the instrument panel accompanied by a strong electrical odor. Avionics degradation followed immediately.The event was first identified visually (smoke) and by smell (electrical odor); followed by loss of the MFD and intermittent operation of other avionics.The precise initiating failure is undetermined from the pilot's perspective. Post-flight maintenance identified a malfunctioning avionics switch on BUS 2. The relationship between that component and the in-flight smoke event was not independently determined by the reporting pilot.The presence of smoke in the cockpit was assessed as a potentially time-critical situation. Immediate priorities were aircraft control; communication; and expeditious landing. Priority handling was requested promptly. A decision was made to pull the MFD circuit breaker while leaving the master and alternator on in order to retain primary radio communication capability during the diversion.The event occurred unexpectedly during routine cruise flight. The presence of smoke created a heightened workload environment requiring rapid prioritization of tasks. Maintaining situational awareness and communication while managing a partial avionics degradation required focused attention.The aircraft was diverted to the nearest suitable airport (ZZZ) and landed within approximately 5-10 minutes of onset. The MFD circuit breaker was pulled. Other electrical components were not de-energized in order to preserve communication capability during the emergency descent and landing.The aircraft was removed from service pending maintenance evaluation. Maintenance reported no evidence of active fire. A faulty avionics switch on BUS 2 was replaced; wiring was inspected; and an independent avionics inspection was conducted prior to return to service.
