column121: We departed ZZZ on runway XXL with a clearance to 5000 with a heading of 110 degrees after takeoff.   I was the pilot flying and shortly after VNAV was selected at 1000 AGL the airspeed tape appeared abnormal as it showed yellow caution tape on the airspeed indicator while well above flaps maneuvering speed. All three airspeed indicators were indicating the same airspeed and it was reasonable but my airspeed tape was indicating yellow and an EICAS Message of Airspeed Too Low displayed. The First Officers airspeed tape was indicating correctly. We got a momentary stick shaker even though we were well above the flap maneuvering speed. Also during this time the Captains and First Officers flight director pitch bar disappeared. Cycling the Flight Deck switches brought them back but only momentary. Once the flaps were retracted and accelerated to 250 kts I selected the alternate air data computer which eliminated the airspeed too low message. We continued to climb and continue to a safe altitude to attempt to resolve the issue. At this point I suspected that the captain air data computer had failed but as we continued it was apparent there was more to the situation. The aircraft would level off about 150 low on every altitude captured. In addition to that the Autothrottle Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) would indicate ALPHA at level off and then change to SPD.I transferred control to the First Officer with the Relief Pilot backing him up while I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control via satcom. After a discussion we jointly determined that a return to ZZZ was the best option. We then requested priority handling with ATC and were cleared direct to the airport. We planned for an overweight landing but it was only projected to be approximately 5500lbs overweight. During the descent we noted that using FLCH caused a aggressive nose down pitch and added power. The FMA for the auto throttles displayed ALPHA.  After some experimenting it was noted that with the auto throttles OFF and use of V/S the autopilot worked normally. We were vectored for the ILS Z XXR and landed with no further issues. Upon block in we were met by maintenance personnel and they informed us that the captain side AOA probe was broken. There was a previous write up from the inbound leg that the crew stairs hit the aircraft and the AOA probe was likely damaged but not detected. No one was aware that the probe had been compromised by the crew stairs.  It was likely cracked and not detected and once airborne it failed. The AOA vane was replaced by maintenance and we departed ZZZ with no further issues.The success of the safe return and landing rests on the tremendous job of the First Officer and Relief Pilot who were indispensable in making this happen.

column121: ATC cleared us for 170 KIAS to the final approach fix. CA called flaps 2-to-3 at the fix; then flaps 3-to-full as we slowed toward approach speed. While flaps were transitioning from 3 to full at ~155 KIAS; the aircraft pitched down significantly- FO called out an instantaneous VSI of ~2;200 fpm. This happened as we descended through 1;200 ft AGL; with intermittent ground contact.By ~1;100 ft AGL; we gained intermittent visual contact with the runway and started correcting toward the glideslope (about 3/4 dot low). At ~800 ft AGL; tower issued a low-altitude alert; we acknowledged and continued. No GPWS warnings sounded--likely because the deviation stemmed from the earlier pitch excursion rather than terrain proximity.  Go around was not called at 1000 ft AGL because the aircraft was correcting and we gain visual reference.  The aircraft was stable with runway insight at 500 ft AGL.Cause:  It is believed the rapid flap extension from 2-to-full; combined with high deceleration; created a strong nose-down moment that overwhelmed auto pilot pitch control momentarily. In future;  especially in intermittent IMC conditions; earlier and slower flap transitions will help create better conditions for a smoother approach.
column123: ILS XXR at ZZZ: Told to fly 210 on final and subsequently told to slow to 170. Aircraft intercepted GS as we were still slowing to 170 and we selected flaps 2 (2000 ft) and gear down (1700 ft) as we intercepted the GS. After I called for flaps 3 and very soon after flaps full we got 1 dot above GS. The Autopilot rapidly lowered the pitch in response to being slightly above GS (coupled with the large flap configuration change). The excessive pitch down change resulted in slightly more than 2000 FPM descent rate and the aircraft going 1 dot below GS. I was milliseconds from performing a Go Around; I doubted the Autopilot would have remained engaged during the rapid pitch change and was preparing to disconnect the Autopilot and perform a manual Go Around. We had just broken out of the weather and the Autopilot was correcting back to GS with a normal pitch attitude and I decided to let it recapture the GS while monitoring it very closely. The Autopilot got back on GS and speed and we were stable before reaching 500 ft.  The Autopilot remained engaged and slowly corrected the pitch to recapture the GS and continue to slow to approach speed. The tower did alert us to a low altitude alert during the event - I'm not sure if that was a result of the Vertical Velocity Indicator (VVI) or the altitude.Cause: I should have put the gear down and selected Flaps 2 earlier (as soon as tower slowed us to 170). This would have given the Autopilot a better chance to stabilize on GS at a slower speed. The rapid flap change from 3 to full caused the Autopilot to get above the GS and overcorrect. I believe this rapid flap change (3 to full) was the catalyst to this entire event. This rapid flap change should have been avoided by being more stable with the gear and flaps 2 on GS earlier. Initially I was frustrated with the Autopilot performance and focused the blame on the aircraft. But I realize I was asking too much of the Autopilot all at once. *The decision not to Go Around during the high VVI/below GS event was based on my prediction of how disorienting the Go Around would have been and my doubt that the autopilot would've remained engaged during the subsequent rapid pitch up. We would have also went back into the weather; further adding to the disorientating effects. Regardless of those factors; I was still moments away from performing the Go Around (after debriefing with the FO he told me he was about to call Go Around as well - right around the same time as the Autopilot started recapturing the GS and stabilizing the pitch). The FO did a good job throughout the event calling out the excessive VVI. **I realize that once the Autopilot was correcting we were still technically unstable on the approach...and should have performed a Go Around. I elected not to because we were below the weather and the Autopilot was leveling off and predictably correcting back to GS. We were very rapidly getting back to the stable criteria.

column121: I had purchased a Cessna 340A on Day 0. The same mechanic who performed the annual inspection also performed the pre-buy inspection as well. Everything appeared to be in order and we took ownership and ferried the aircraft from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. Over the next few months I had accumulated approximately 27 hours in the aircraft from training and familiarization flights to and from various airports. All were uneventful. However; as I continued to log more and more time in the aircraft; I endeavored to continue to familiarize myself with the specific maintenance requirements of the Cessna 340A as well as keeping track of relevant Airworthiness Directives; that I would need to accomplish to maintain airworthiness of the aircraft. However; in my studies; I discovered a discrepancy a few days ago with the propellers - I found that both propellers are listed in an AD - which indicates that the lag screws; which are a vital component in securing the propeller blades to the propeller hub; are defective in certain MT composite propellers manufactured/installed between certain years. As it turns out; both of the propellers on Aircraft X are flagged under this Airworthiness Directive as having the defective lag screws. Under certain high-load conditions such as heavy turbulence or maneuvers; these defective screws can fail; leading to potential inflight blade separation and severe damage to the engine and airframe. Continuing to go through the propeller logbooks; there is no evidence that this AD was ever complied with whatsoever. The aircraft mechanic who performed most of the maintenance on Aircraft X in the 4 years prior to our purchase of the plane; made no mention of it either.Because of this; the aircraft is not airworthy and has not been for several years at the earliest; and the previous owner flew it during this time as well. Immediate corrective actions had begun the moment I discovered the propellers had an outstanding AD. The aircraft was immediately grounded. First; the aircraft will have its propellers removed and shipped to an authorized repair facility; and the aircraft will have another annual inspection performed to rectify these issues. I exercised poor judgment in assuming that everything was in order with the aircraft and did not do enough due-diligence on the aircraft logs or AD records; as I perceived the aircraft to be in excellent shape with everything else in order on the pre-buy inspection. Ultimately; it falls to the pilot in command to ensure the aircraft is airworthy; and I incorrectly placed the entirety of my faith in the mechanic that did the annual and pre-buy; as well as the previous owner. Said corrective actions will continue as swiftly as possible to correct this oversight and return the aircraft to a fully airworthy condition. In addition; going forward; I will heavily scrutinize and cross-check any and all maintenance performed on this airframe; ensuring everything is in order for each flight and not allowing any assumptions to fall into place.

column121: I was flying from ZZZ to BUR I got a little distracted had passenger wanted to sit in copilot seat and was asking questions for landing but weather was clear then reported few at 600 I was on ils Y runway 8 into Burbank with the sun in my face i had auto pilot coupled on ils and was planning on landing visual so didn't notice the min on that approach was 800 I was surprised when I heard min because I was still high I was in visual conditions but with sun in my face didn't see a thin fog layer was forming so I couldn't see the end of the runway. But after I landed I looked at the plate then realized 800 ago was min I wanted to see if I entered the wrong min the first time. Lesson learned trust your first instincts I should have went missed because I didn't see the runway at 800 feet with the sun in my face and haze and assumed my min were 200 without confirming. Moral always brief approach at new airports really good even though it was clear skies when I started approach. I was always in the clear never went into the fog but touched down 500 feet longer than I planned when I saw the runway. column121: I was working Local control west position and owned runway XXL and runway XY. We were landing runway XXL and departing runway XY. It was IFR and snowing; visibility was 3/4SM.  I had Aircraft X cross runway XY at 1 taxing to runway XXL. Aircraft Y was lined up on runway XY. My next transmission was for Aircraft X to cross runway XXL and 2. Once Aircraft X finished the crossing I issued a clear for takeoff clearance to Aircraft Y. Since no one was on final for runway XXL I was able to line up Aircraft Z on runway XXL. I scanned the asde-x and noticed Aircraft X didn't make the turn on 2 and was heading to runway XY. I tried to reach out and have Aircraft X stop and then my next transmission was Aircraft Y cancel takeoff clearance. When Aircraft Y read back the cancel takeoff clearance the asde-x alarmed through out the tower warning and highlighted the 2 aircraft on the asde-x. Once I was able to see Aircraft Y came to a stop I asked them if they were able to go back to the runway or needed other assistance. They said they the were able to taxi back to the runway but would need a few minutes. I knew I had to continue working the position. Since Aircraft X  was in the intersection of runway XY at 1 so the best thing to do was keep him going on 1 and send him to runway XXL. Next I had to clear up runway XXL and issue takeoff clearance to Aircraft Z. Once Aircraft Z was airborne I taxied Aircraft Y back to runway XY with a right turn on runway XXL and a right turn on taxiway 2. Both Aircraft Y and Aircraft X departed at XA:57Z and XB:58Z. I asked for a break moments after it happened and due to short staffing it wasn't available at that time. About 10 minutes later a controller came up the stairs from break and was able to get me out of position. I was asked to take a short break because the controller on clearance delivery was almost at 2 hours on position. I took a 20 minute break and came back to work clearance. Within about 10 minutes on clearance I asked the supervisor if I could go home when they would get me out. At XC:27Z I was able to get off position and then went home. .

column121: On approach to ZZZ for the ILS XX I called for flaps 1. We immediately got an EICAS for TE FLAP ASYM (Trailing Edge Flap Asymmetric). We notified ATC and discontinued the approach. We requested to hold our current altitude of 4000 feet and were able to enter a holding pattern while we worked the QRH. We selected the appropriate checklist and started working through it. Given the steps we had to action we eventually got the aircraft configured to slats down and flaps less than 1. When we got to the deferred approach and landing sections we discussed what we should do next. We briefly discussed the possibility of diverting over to ZZZ1 but ruled that out as we were now in a configuration with drag and would be speed limited and couldn't be sure what the fuel burn would be to get there. ZZZ had ample runway and VMC weather so we were comfortable continuing the approach there. We also felt saving the gas was prudent to give us multiple attempts at the landing should we need to go around. I gave control of the aircraft and ATC comms to the FO. He requested priority handling with ATC while I sent dispatch an ACARS informing them of what was going on and our decision to land in ZZZ. Dispatch asked if we needed anything else or other assistance and we said we were all set. I briefed the flight attendants and made a PA to the cabin. I reassumed flying and we briefed the threats of tail strike; hot brakes; and being close to tire limit speed as well on landing. We recommenced the approach and completed the deferred approach and landing checklists. We touched down on speed in the zone and I selected max reverse. I had adjusted the autobrakes to 3 and let them cycle normally. We vacated at 1 taxiway and proceeded to the gate. No other abnormals were noted. The brakes peaked at 4. The appropriate debriefs with maintenance and emergency responders was completed and an ELB (Electronic Log Book) entry made. The Chief Pilot was also debriefed via phone.
column123: On approach for ILS XX in ZZZ; the captain as PF called for flaps 1. Flaps 1 was selected and we received a TE FLAP ASYM (Trailing Edge Flap Asymmetric) EICAS message. The captain decided to level off at 4;000 and ask for a hold. After the hold was established; we ran the appropriate QRH. This had us extend the leading edge slats using the alternate flap system; and TE Flaps remained at less than 1. We requested priority handling with ATC. The captain then coordinated with dispatch; advised the flight attendants; and made a PA. We then proceeded inbound on the approach; and the captain made an excellent landing. We cleared the runway at 1 and taxied to the gate. Crash fire rescue followed us to the gate; and a maintenance report was submitted.

column121: This incident occurred during takeoff at ZZZ at approximately XA:24 on Day 0. I was taking off runway XX with calm winds; >10sm visibility; and skies clear. Once airborne; I encountered mist; but it did not impact actions on the ground during takeoff. I initiated a rolling takeoff and accelerated to my published Vr speed of 86. I rotated and leveled the aircraft to accelerate in ground effect per my company's pilot training. Once established in my level acceleration; I retracted the gear. Either as the gear retracted or shortly after retracting; the cockpit door on the right side of the aircraft popped open. Prior to takeoff; I had verified the door was secure twice: once before taxi (personal technique); and again short of the runway in accordance with the before takeoff checklist.Due to the increased airflow and noise within the cockpit from the door popping open; I lost situational awareness of the aircraft and failed to continue my climb out. The nose of the aircraft dropped; and the airplane lost altitude over the runway. When my attention returned to flying the aircraft; I recognized the nose-low attitude and pulled back on the yoke to resume climbing; but had lost enough altitude that resulted in the right propeller struck the runway; causing damage. Indications of the ground contact were a spark-like flash and a scraping sound loud enough to be heard over the engine and airflow noise.Following the ground contact; I recognized that my gear was retracted and there was insufficient runway; so I continued my takeoff and executed a left traffic pattern to land back on runway XX. I did not receive any cockpit warnings; cautions; or advisories. While in-flight and during my deceleration to land; I noticed a mild vibration that further indicated damage to the propeller; but I felt no significant loss in controllability or performance. Upon landing; I immediately taxied to the FBO ramp and shut down the plane.After parking; I completed a thorough inspection of the aircraft. I found that all three blades of the right engine propeller were damaged; curled up about 3-4 inches each; with some pieces of the propeller broken off. I found the passenger's footstep aft of the right wing was bent upwards with a crack in the tubing and abrasion damage on the bottom. Additionally; I found punctures to the fuselage skin on the right nose; inboard of the right nacelle; and below the nose baggage compartment; moving towards the leading edge of the right wing. I did not find evidence of the right wing; or any part of the fuselage; including the nose; belly; and tail; making contact with the ground. The left propeller also appeared free of damage.I immediately notified my flight controller; who notified the Director of Operations; and then notified my Director of Maintenance; who initiated recovery. After debriefing my company's safety officer on the events; it was determined that the takeoff profile I used did not align with published procedures; but was corroborated by other BE58 pilots as what was taught in our training. Contributing factors: This was my first time flying in and out of this airport. Runway illusions induced by an unfamiliar runway at night may have given me the perception that I was higher off the runway surface than I actually was when I retracted the gear during my level acceleration.Human Performance Considerations: I had received approximately 16 hours of rest following my previous duty; and about 7-8 hours of broken sleep in the preceding 24 hours; but had been awake for approximately 11-12 hours by the time the event occurred. An additional factor affecting performance was that the cargo pickup was delayed by an additional hour; resulting in almost 2 hours of waiting on the ground at ZZZ in the dark and cooler weather. Actions/Inactions: I failed to maintain aircraft awareness and was distracted by the door pop event; despite knowing from training that it could not be resolved while airborne. I also believethat the pitch trim; set during ground checklists; had been set slightly nose-low within the takeoff range indicated on the trim indicator wheel; which required more effort to keep the nose up; rather than nose down during the takeoff; so when my focus was pulled from flying; the nose was able to dip. After the takeoff; while returning to the airport; I assessed the condition of the aircraft; mostly certain of the propeller strike; but unconfirmed; and determined the aircraft was still flyable and therefore did not shut down the engine to avoid complicating the scenario and requiring a single-engine landing.

column121: Aircraft X departed ZZZ VFR to ZZZ1; climbed to about 020 on about a 120 heading. Right after that; Aircraft Y departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan but flying the VFR departure procedure. I called ZZZ tower to ask why Aircraft Y was stopped at 010 and they replied that he should be climbing. I tried to climb Aircraft Y and then he turned south below the MVA; at almost the same time Aircraft X turned south too.  As this was happening the two data blocks were overlapping and it was difficult for me to determine which aircraft was doing what.  As I noticed the turn; I asked Aircraft Y if he was in fact turning and he said yes he was maneuvering due to the traffic above.  I stated that he was IFR.  I issued a low altitude alert and turned to get out of the lower MVA and issued another climb. I would not launch a fast guy right behind a slower aircraft when they are both flying the same route

column121: This incident report is for flight ABCD which was later flown and completed on a different aircraft with a different aircrew following our refusal for the reasons as detailed below.Our duty day began at XA:13 in ZZZ1 beginning with a deadhead to ZZZ followed by three flying legs scheduled afterward: ZZZ-ZZZ2; ZZZ2-ZZZ; ZZZ-ZZZ3On the second flying leg (ZZZ2-ZZZ) we encountered a possible (what I believe to be likely) lightning strike during the descent into ZZZ. Initial reaction was surprise but thankfully all aircraft systems appeared to continue functioning without fault or issue. We did note a brief but apparent smell of burning electrical cable or wire; which dissipated within several minutes. There was no associated smoke or fumes beyond that. After querying the cabin crew if they saw anything irregular they also noted the brief smell but otherwise cabin and occupants were not experiencing anything out of the ordinary during our descent. Given no aircraft faults; we were able to continue the arrival and landing uneventfully and arrived at ZZZ for a normal shutdown and deplaning. During the flight we notified maintenance of the observed lightning strike by submitting a maintenance request requiring a post-flight inspection. The maintenance team was able to meet us at the aircraft shortly after the cabin door was opened and we described the incident and they conducted their exterior inspection. The conditions at the time were light periodic rain; at night with marginal ramp lighting. I also conducted a thorough inspection during my routine exterior walk-around to see if I could find evidence of a lightning strike. With our limited visibility from the ground using only handheld flashlights; both the maintenance personnel and myself were unable to find specific evidence of a strike with only a visual inspection. So we continued our preflight; maintenance cleared the forms and we planned to continue the next leg ZZZ-ZZZ3.However; during the flight deck preparation; shortly before our preflight checklist and briefing; an ECAM fault appeared that was either TCAS or RA related. We noted that was unusual but maybe just a system fault that may automatically reset or require a procedural reset. Before we could evaluate further; a second ECAM appeared within 60 seconds or so; followed by a complete array of faults that would normally only be visible in flight. Some of these were cautions and several were warnings including 'All Engines Failed' with a continuous bell ringing in the cockpit (during boarding); in addition to 'Stall; Stall; Stall' and other significant warnings and aural alerts. This was all while we were still completing boarding; with passengers walking right behind us. We were only able to silence these alerts and alarms by continuously holding the 'EMER CANCEL' button on the ECAM system selection panel. This continued for at least 3-4 minutes; at which time maintenance was able to observe some of these indications.Eventually; after about 5 more minutes; the faults cleared and the ECAM screen went back to normal; but there was clearly something abnormal to trigger those warnings during ground operations. While our exterior inspection was inconclusive; maintenance had done their check and recommended a full system power down and reset; with passengers aboard. This took about 5-10 minutes. Upon power up; the aircraft did not seem to have any faults noted; so maintenance again cleared the forms and gave us a clean release. Shortly thereafter; we got one additional ECAM fault (at XA:36; picture attached); reducing our confidence that the issue was fully corrected or otherwise absent. At this time we suspected there might be something deeper within the avionics that got damaged but without a further inspection we could not be certain. For this reason the captain and I agreed that it constituted an unreasonable flight safety concern; which we did not feel comfortable accepting. We decided to refuse the aircraft and return it to maintenance.
column123: Aircraft refusal of flight ABC is due to events occurred on flight ABCD ZZZ2-ZZZ on Day 0.While on the arrival phase of the flight; passing 13000 ft at 280 kts on the ZZZZZX RNA's arrival; we went through an area of thunderstorms when a sudden bright light and an immediate thundering sound were perceived; followed by a pressure wave felt by both pilots. The FO was flying pilot; we immediately acknowledged the lightning strike and we kept monitoring the aircraft systems during the descent. No indication of system damage or alerts were present. Shortly after a faint electrical burnt smell started appearing; we called the flight attendants to make sure the situation in the cabin was under control and they reported the lightning strike and the burnt smell; but reported no irregularities in the cabin. The smell dissipated quickly; approximately 2 minutes after the strike. We sent an ELB report requesting a lightning strike inspection. Given the proximity to the destination airport and the regularity of all systems we continued to ZZZ; where we landed and taxied to the gate without issues. Maintence met us at the gate; performed an inspection and the FO conducted a detailed preflight inspection. No strike marks were noted on both inspections. After preparing the plane for the next leg; flight ABC to ZZZ2; with boarding almost complete; we had a NAV RA 2 fault message appear; and approximately a minute later; all systems were faulting. We had GPWS warnings; Stall warnings; Engine failure warnings; wind shear alerts; many more and we had to press the emergency cancel to silence the warnings. Photos of the warnings are available if needed. Maintenance was called; and while they were on the way; the warnings cleared themself. Shortly after; NAV RA 1 fault presented itself. Maintenance run a system diagnostic and all systems presented no fault. A supervisor was called and advised to run a full aircraft reset. A PA was made to the passengers to advise them that the aircraft would go dark for approximately 3 minutes. After the system reset; no faults were noted. Approximately 20 minutes later; NAV RA 1 fault message appeared again. Maintenance run their diagnostic and no faults were found. In the meanwhile; I called the chief pilot to explain the situation and obtain new informations that could aid the resolution. Maintenance cleared the aircraft and issued a new release. At this point; after consulting with the first officer and chief pilot; I communicated my decision to be unable to operate the aircraft. Given the shared experience in the flight deck; corroborated by the flight attendants in the cabin; we knew a lighting strike had occurred. The sudden appearance of all systems warnings and aural alerts told us there was something wrong with the aircraft. The fact that maintenance couldn't find any faults at the moment didn't give us the peace of mind it wouldn't happen again in flight; at night; through the thunderstorms surrounding the ZZZ airport. Both flight crew concurred that the aircraft was unsafe to fly in the current condition without a in depth inspection.

column121: On takeoff Rwy XXL ZZZ; Capt flying pilot; I was the F/O; at approximately 1000 instrument pitch bars disappeared followed by yellow caution airspeed tape displayed on the Capt side.   We were above flap maneuvering speed.  Airspeed indicators (all 3) were indicating the same speed and seemed normal.  Airspeed Too Low EICAS msg followed.  Momentary stick shaker occurred.  We continued the departure climb to a safe altitude and when flaps were retracted the Capt selected Alternate Air Data.   After level off it was noticed the acft was approx. 150 low and the A/T (Auto throttle) FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) would change to ALPHA then back to SPD.I became the pilot flying as the Capt coordinated with Operations to troubleshoot and determine our course of action.   We then advised ATC; returned to ZZZ for a 5500# overweight landing by the Capt.During descent we found that V/S was the better choice since FLC caused unusual pitch down movement followed by ALPHA displaying again.We received vectors for the ILS Z XXL ZZZ and Capt made an uneventful landing.  After block in maintenance told us the Capt side AOA probe was damaged possibly by ground crew positioning the stairs during the previous flights block in.   Earlier in the day; during our pre flight walk-around when we initially arrived at the acft there was no indication that this AOA probe was damaged.   The AOA probe was replaced; ops checked and we departed for our leg to ZZZZ.I'd like to say the Capt set the tone during this unusual occurrence to bring it to a positive outcome.   And the Relief Pilot was outstanding in backing us up multiple times having the big picture from his observers seat.

column121: Almost immediately after takeo' from Istanbul; we experienced GPS jamming. By top of climb; we suspected GPS spoofing. The checklist was run and GPS updating was turned o'. I had the first rest so I went back to the bunk. When I returned later and signed in as PIC I reviewed the status of the aircraft and noticed that the FMC time was four minutes and 36 seconds faster than the aircraft clock time. At about four hours into the flight we started to receive a GPS signal; but it was unreliable showing the GPS position between 38 to 45 nautical miles ahead of our IRU (Inertial Reference Unit) position with DME/DME updating (this position was also checked against land based VOR signals). By the time we crossed into the Astana FIR we were receiving a reliable GPS signal to the captain's iPad the FO's iPad started to receive a reliable signal about an hour later. We kept GPS updating turned o' and let ATC know about our situation. With our 3 IRUs updating our ANP was between 0.38 to 0.45nm. Crossing position SARIN entering Chinese airspace (Urumqi FIR) we began a turn to TCH on airway A368. We then received the EICAS caution message UNABLE RNP. Our ANP was noted at 15.4nm and fluctuating. I was about to call Urumqi control when they called with a heading of 130. Again we let ATC know of our spoofing encounter. Within two minutes our ANP showed 0.39nm. After a few minutes on the heading; Urumqi control asked if we were able our own navigation and gave us direct position SALMO. About 25 minutes later we were alerted to the EICAS caution message AUTOPILOT; with LNAV and VNAV faults shown. We also noted an ANP of 12.3 that almost immediately decreased to 0.43nm. We selected HDG (Heading) SEL and FLCH and the re-engaged LNAV and VNAV; with no disruption to the flight path. The flight continued to destination with no other anomalies.
column123: As per note on release and activity in the area we experienced GPS interference on our route.  Earlier we had run through the GPS data unreliable QRH and had GPS update off.Approaching SARIN and in the turn to our next position TCH we received an UNABLE RNP EICAS message. SARIN was our entry point into Chinese airspace and ATC issued us a HDG (Heading) 130 after the turn. Not too long after issuing the heading ATC cleared us own navigation to our next point. We notified them that we had been having GPS issues. They said to notify them if we had any further issues and couldn't maintain our own navigation. The PF mentioned he had noticed the RNP jump way out in the turn. ANP was now back in limits. In the GPS unreliable QRH is mentioned we may get this. We then ran the UNRELIABLE RNP QRH and continued as normal. We presumed that we may have had some lateral deviation during the turn hence the heading from ATC. 25-30 mins later we got AUTOPILOT EICAS message. FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) showed LNAV and VS with a line through. I had noticed that the ANP had gone out to 13.2nm then went back to .38-.40 where it was sitting most of the time. We ran QRH which just mentions degraded autopilot and roll mode or pitch mode failure. PF cycled through different mode and then reactivated LNAV and VNAV and we continued as normal. We continued to monitor RNP/ANP without further incident during our flight. Cause: GPS jamming in the Middle East. Ground based navigation not too accurate in certain areas. Suggestions: Just have to pay closer attention to navigation accuracy during turns and overhead waypoints. Keep ATC updated if necessary.

column121: Center asked us if we could climb from FL350 to FL360 for a direction of flight change ahead and coordination with ZZZZ.  Center also reported smooth rides at FL360. We checked the VNAV cruise page and determined that FL360 would work at 0.78M with a 400 foot buffer. We had a discussion about lower level weather topping around FL280-300 and decided together that with the weather and ATC ride reports to accept FL360.The radar was on to depict weather; we were running our EFB and WSI (Weather Stress Index) as well. We made the decision while going over the weather by greater than 5000 feet to seat the passengers and flight attendants prior to approaching it. I made the required announcements. We also noted some taller thunderstorm activity about 30-40 SSW of our position and blow off might cause a few bumps.At approximately XA30 we encountered an immediate and sudden area of severe turbulence. There were no radar returns; nothing at our altitude on WSI; and our EFB showed no adverse rides. The duration lasted approximately 10 seconds. Initially we encountered a strong updraft showing a rapid airspeed increase from 0.78M to an overspeed of approximately 10 knots and a vertical speed showing +2000FPM. The aircraft climbed to approximately FL362. Suddenly the trend reversed; autopilot disconnected; and we experienced decreasing performance; airspeed decreasing; vertical speed -2000 FPM and we descended to FL358. I immediately took manual control of the aircraft; instructed the FO to report the severe turbulence to ATC; and request FL340. They instructed us to standby and at nearly the same time we were through the isolated severe turbulence and maintained FL360 until given a descent few minutes later. Automation was re-engaged me no further issues happened.We checked in on the flight attendants and they reported no injuries; and that the cabin was good.
column123: While at Cruise at FL360 in IMC; an area of severe turbulence was encountered which lasted approximately 10 seconds. While there was convective activity in the area; our onboard weather radar depicted it 40nm west of our course. There were no radar returns along our course and ATC had reported the altitude as smooth. We did however experience rain on the windscreen during the event.IAS increased from 260 KIAS to 280 KIAS and then down to 240 KIAS. Vertical speed fluctuated from +/- 2000 FPM. Autopilot disconnected during an overspeed. Altitude fluctuated +/- 200' while we requested an immediate descent to FL340. The event lasted about 10 seconds and we entered VMC conditions. We were assigned and subsequently initiated a descent to FL340.The seatbelt sign had been placed On and the Flight Attendants had been instructed to take their jump seats prior to the event. No injuries were sustained.The flight continued to destination without further incident. column121: We received aircraft services on the remote ramp used by the FBO. After fueling was finished; I entered the updated fuel load and adjusted the passenger seating from zone 1 to zone 2 as they had moved from when they got on the plane.  I do not recall if I actually heard the lead FA say 'cabin secure'. We were marshaled from our parking spot and began our taxi. The lighting from the surrounding area and the wetness of the ramp made it difficult to see obstructions on the ramp so all of the forward lights were turned on. As we came out of the back of the remote ramp I noticed a vehicle on the right side of the aircraft driving parallel to the aircraft. We were taxiing a little slower than you would on an unobstructed taxiway. As we approached the hold bar at Taxiway 1; I called ground to get taxi clearance; at this time the vehicle was still driving parallel to the aircraft. ZZZ ground gave us the clearance to join Taxiway 2 and hold short of 3. We noticed the vehicle in the vehicle road make a left turn and not stop at the intersection; and the now continue towards our aircraft. The PIC started to apply the brakes to slow the aircraft in case the vehicle did not stop. The vehicle; now clearly a van; continued at speed not slowing and crossed in front of the aircraft. The PIC applied full braking in order to avoid a collision; and the van passed approximately 20 feet in front of the aircraft. The flight attendant fell during the braking and hit the floor near the jumpseat and the aft of the center pedestal. The PIC stopped the taxi and checked with the flight attendants to confirm that everyone was ok. We received confirmation from the flight attendants that they felt ok to continue; and that the owners were safe. I notified ZZZ ground that we had a near collision with the vehicle and received a secondary taxi clearance. After entering taxiway 2; the aircraft lighting was reduced. ZZZ ground was also notified that the flight attendant fell due to the near collision; but was not injured.  As the flight continued the flight attendant that fell indicated that his ankle and side were sore. The PIC went to check on the flight attendant and to talk to the owners. It was determined everyone was okay to continue to the destination of ZZZ1. Out of an abundance of caution the flight attendant went to get checked out after landing.Suggestions: We could have had a better confirmation of Cabin Secure. Due to waiting for fuel I was mindful that the passengers may have changed seats. My mind may have associated the FA telling me the new seating positions with the cabin being secure as these are usually stated together.

column121: Time: Day 0; Approx time of event XA:45Weather: Night IMC; navigating rain storms with minor convection imbedded.Location(s): Approximately at waypoint ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZ1 departureAirspeed about 300 KIAS; Altitude FL260Aircraft: Aircraft XCA: Person A (PF)FO: Person B (PM)FO's Narrative:Departing out of ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 at FL260 crew experienced a dual generator failure.  CA retained control of the aircraft by using the standby instruments; he remained on altitude and maintain a safe airspeed; manually adjusting the thrust and 'hand flying'. He also turned on the DOME light immediately.  FO; referenced the QRC and stated this is not a 'Quick Action Item or an ECAM exception'.  The crew had to wait as the RAT (Ram Air Turbine) deployed and this took approximately 2 to 5 minutes to provide emergency power.  When the upper ECAM became available; the crew was reassured the engines were operating normally; which was evident in the ability of the CA to maintain altitude and airspeed; and the crew had situational awareness that the aircraft control was being maintained in ALTN LAW (Alternate Law) with no auto thrust.  After the audio panel initiated a boot up sequence; the FO requested priority handling with ATC and began coordinating with ATC to proceed back to ZZZ1. Weather at ZZZ1 was received from ATC and reported OVC 200' 1/2 mile visibility.  CA instructed FO to get weather at ZZZ; which was better with OVC 600'; with light easterly winds.  CA instructed FO to begin coordination to divert to ZZZ.  After the aircraft was safely moving in the direction of the divert field; the FO began ECAM actions which regained generator 1 after one attempted reset and did not regain number 2 generator after one attempted reset.  ECAM did not direct the crew to disconnect the bus tie to attempt a second generator reset on the number 2 generator.  Other ECAM actions were to reset the FACs (Flight Augmentation Computer) and ENG (Engine) N1 MODE OFF (1/2).  The autopilot was functioning now in direct law after the FAC reset but the auto thrust wasn't functioning after ENG N1 MODE was selected OFF; as expected by the crew.  At this time the crew elected to not address any ECAM follow ups due to conditions and crew workload.  During system initialization; after restoration of aircraft power; the FO didn't have a map on his side and primary instruments were unreliable.  The CA regained full functionality of the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and Map; and the FO regained PFD; but the Map did not function on his side.  This condition persisted for the reminder of the flight.  CA/FO elected to not run the APU because the crew was satisfied with the electrical power being supplied from the RAT and gen 1; and the cause of the ELEC malfunction was unable to be immediately identified by the crew with the information presented.  The crew didn't want to introduce another electrical component to the system if they didn't know the exact cause of the malfunction.  Additionally; no immediate procedure drove the crew to turn on the APU; it is in the ECAM follow ups.  During the decent into ZZZ; the crew addressed all remaining non-normal and normal checklist; ran the land app using the 'normal' tab for the overweight landing.  In the land app the non-normal tab; under the failure tab; did not have an 'additional system failure...' selection that fit the current condition.  Additionally; the crew accomplished the overweight landing checklist in its entirety.  The only communication with Dispatch was through the ACARS diversion message; which the FO accomplished.  The CA maintained PF duties for the whole duration of the event and the rest of the flight. The FO maintained PM duties for the event; and briefed the FAs about the nature of the event and the crew's plan to divert into ZZZ.  Of note; the #1 FA has enhanced systems knowledge of the Airbus fleet and understood the RAT was deployed because she heard the 'humming' of the Turbine.  She knew the flight crewwas dealing with an electrical problem and/or a hydraulic problem and was able to relay to the FO during this conversation of her situational awareness.  This is above and beyond for her position and her actions need to be commended.  She enhanced the other FAs awareness of the gravity of the situation and maintained passenger confidence that the pilots had the situation under control.  The CA directed the FO to address the passengers that we experienced a 'power interruption' and brief them of our plan to divert into ZZZ where there will be company assistance to continue their travel to ZZZ2.  The crew was vectored by ATC to 4;000' MSL on final for RWY XX at ZZZ.  The crew set up and briefed the ILS to RWY XX after a few turns in holding on final.  This gave the crew time to reassure themselves the aircraft was in a safe configuration to accomplish a safe recovery to the runway and taxi to the gate.  Additionally; this low holding help reduce the aircraft weight.  The crew flew a non-eventful ILS to a min rate of descent to touch down; and taxi to gate with no additional malfunctions.  After safely at the gate; the CA turned on the APU and shut down the engines.  The APU started and functioned normally.  No additional ECAM displays were noted after shutdown.
column123: Day 0Flight: ZZZ1-ZZZ2 Dep XA:30Aircraft Airbus A321 Event Location: Approx 75 Miles West of ZZZ1 @ FL260CA Person A (PF)FO Person B (PM)CA's Perspective:Normal Preflite ;Brief; Taxi; Departure Off RWY XXL - ZZZ1. Climbout Normal; FA's Briefed To Stay In Seats (Turbulence Expected). Wx Radar In Use. We Leveled At FL260. Suddenly Both Generators Tripped OffLine - Cockpit Immediately Dark except For Standby Instrument Panel. Master Warning Lights On w/Chimes. I Immediately Pressed The Emergency Cancel Button Several Times on ECAM Ctrl Panel To Silence ALL That Noise. We Both Stated 'My Aircraft/Your Aircraft' and I Began To Hand Fly And Use Thrust Levers and Stby ISS (Integrated Standby Instrument System) to Maintain Aircraft Control - Every Other Display is Dark. FO Was Able To Request Priority Handling With ATC And Request Return To ZZZ. I Referenced Only The ISs To Maintain  Altitude And Turn Back East. It Took A Few Minutes After 'Auto RAT (Ram Air Turbine) Deployment' For My Emergency Power Displays To Become Operative. We Then Commenced 'QRC/ECAM Actions' We Were Very Methodical With ECAM Directions For Which P/B To Use Gen's; FACS (Flight Augmentation Computer); Eng (Engine) N1 Mode; Etc Gen 1 Came Online ; Gen 2 Would Not Reset..left Gen 2 PB (Push Button) 'Off'. We Verified Via 'Elect' Page What Buses Were Powered - We Then Discussed APU Usage. We Agreed To Level Off - Since We Did Not Know What Caused PWR Failure - And Did Not Want To Risk A Power Surge. (In Retrospect- We Should Have Started APU; deselecting APU GEN PB...to Have Ready As A Backup). Once I Had Normal PFD (Primary Flight Display) /ND (Navigation Display) Usage...we Began Our Descent. I Had FO Communicate With The FA's And Pax (Passengers). The #1 FA Had Exceptional Knowledge About Airbus RAT...she Relayed That To Her Crew and Pax; Keeping Everyone Calm. When FO Back In The Loop ; I Had Him Ask ATC for ZZZ1 Wx. It was Now 200/1 ish. I Was Concerned That ZZZ1 Was Gonna Get Worse so I Asked For ZZZ Wx (We Passed By There Earlier in The Day And Saw Area Wx Was Improving From The SouthWest) ATC Said ZZZ 1000/7 I Believe - So We Decided That Would Be Better For Our Situation. I Then Realized AP (Autopilot) might Be Avail And Turned It On. From Then On While Descending We Used ACARS Diversion Prompt; I Also Used 'Free Text' To inform Dispatch of Diversion. FO Did All Of FMS Programming; Change Destination; Load RWY XY ILS. We Then Completed Descent Checklist; Overweight Landing Checklist; Approach Briefing; Landing Distance Assessment; Etc. ATC Provided Us A Box Hold w/Vectors @ 4;000' To Give Us Time To Complete Our Procedures and Burn Down Our Fuel. ATC Was FANTASTIC with All The Help They Provided Us. I Wish I Could Thank The Controllers In Person For Their Part In The Successful Outcome For Us. FO and I Then Discussed If We Both Comfortable With AC (Aircraft) Status and All Our Threats Covered. We Began Approach; I Disconnected AP Approx 600' And Touchdown Around the 1;500' Mark with Minimal VS at a Weight of 188;000 lbs. Taxied To Gate XX; I Called Dispatch and Maintenance after AC Shutdown. We Started APU on Taxi In - Deselected APU GEN PB. Switched To APU PWR Before Engines Shutdown with No Bad Result.

column121: While working the flight there was a situation that arose from ground crew-to-flight deck communications. Upon reaching the gate; the ground workers gave us the 'stop' message with the batons in the shape of an 'X.' The manor in which we received this signal was abrupt and nonchalantly given. Our original thoughts in the flight deck were about the idea that we had rolled too far on the parking job and that it could potentially be possible that a tug would have to push us back. We deducted that this was a possibility due to the nature in which we were told to stop. The abrupt order to stop from the ground crew helped us draw this as a potential conclusion. The head ground personnel had given us the 'x' and stood stationary for almost 2 minutes while the captain and myself later assumed he had forgotten to give us a 'chocks-in' signal. We proceeded to run shutdown flows and checklists because of the ground workers approaching the airplane for post flight duties despite the forgotten chocks in gesture. It was at this moment that we received hand signals from the lead ground Marshaller; to disconnect our parking break. This was later found out to be the ground controller signaling us about the beacon light still being on. The hand signals he gave us were incorrect and were interpreted as a 'release brakes' message.In some scenarios; it had been known that being pushed back from the stopping point is a possibility at some airports because of the lack of motion in some gate docking devices. We assumed this was the case; and that a tug had been hooked up as well to the nose; to also prepare for the next quick turn on this aircraft.With the assumptions made; that we were asked to release brakes; and that the tug could be connected; like it possibly; and many times is after shut down; we elected to turn the parking brake off after the shutdown checklists. Our thoughts were that we had received word from ground that we were too far forward and needed a small push from ground crew to correct this. So we complied with what we thought was happening; which was a small pushback correction. We had wing walkers come to the wings as if we were actually pushing back from a gate to fuel the idea that this was a serious possibility. So as the brakes were disarmed; the captain and I were attentive to the controls. We were ready to act at any moment in this sterile environment.We were both under the impression that we were in an active push back discussed via the common sign language used between flight decks and ramp crew. It was at this moment that we also realized the wing walkers followed us back as if we were getting pushed. At about 10 feet back from where we had originally stopped; we became alarmed to see that the tug was still at the stopping line at the gate; and began to immediately question why we were moving and why there was crew doing nothing to stop us or explain what was occurring. I had opened my window on the first officer's side to inquire about why were still moving with ground crew if there actually was no tug attached. The same moment; we came to an abrupt stop; which was a required action as we had realized that the plane was rolling backwards with no indication from ground crew that; that was our reality. The parking break was pulled in an effort to immediately stop the potentially dangerous roll; and thankfully; no damage; injury; or potential to put someone else in serious danger had occurred. The seatbelt sign was unfortunately off due to the shutdown flow being completed. The events that had unfolded happened in a very short time frame; that the primary consideration was with what was happening to the state of the aircraft.The nature of this entanglement with the parking situation was grounded in miscommunication from the start. The nonchalant nature of the ground crew made it near impossible to realize that we were in an entirely dangerous scenario where we thought they signaled to push in a non-controlled ramp. We were able to quickly act by stopping the aircraft; and having a direct verbal conversation with ground personnel to get towed back in to the gate.Cause: Miscommunication; no action taken by ramp workers.Suggestions: To avoid this event again; my suggestion would be to emphasize the need to not move the aircraft until absolutely certain the message received was correct and based on fact. It would be beneficial to also emphasize the idea that ground ramp personnel can't always be trusted and that a pilot's judgement needs to be separate from what ramp may indicate.
column123: The issue began in the parking phase of the flight at the gate. The marshaller ushered us forward until he showed the 'X' signal with the wands indicating us to stop and set the parking brake. He did so very abruptly which made us believe there was potential the aircraft had been parked too far forward. With the parking brake set; I began my Captain Shutdown Flow. I was waiting for the chocks in signal from the marshaller for what seemed like almost 2 minutes. The marshaller then signaled to us with an open hand then closed fist which at the time was interpreted to us as a 'Brake Release Signal' and confirming our original thought that the aircraft was parked too far forward. Later; we realized the signal he was trying to communicate to us was that the beacon was still on; and that he could not attach the chocks until the beacon was turned off. Me leaving the beacon on was my mistake; and the one and only item that I missed on my shutdown flow. Complying with the marshaller; I made the decision to release the parking brake; and after a few seconds the aircraft slowly began rolling backwards. We had assumed a tug was already attached as it often is right after parking the aircraft. We were a bit confused as to why we were being pushed without further coordination from the ground crew. The wing walkers also walked back with us indicating at the moment that everything seemed ok and the aircraft was indeed being pushed by a tug. This all happened very quickly and both me and the FO were very unsure about what was going on and instantly began questioning what was taking place. About 10 feet back I realized the tug was still at the gate and the marshaller; and other ramp personnel near the aircraft essentially stood there with zero urgency not letting us know that the aircraft was abnormally moving backwards. The ramp personnel didn't wave to stop; they weren't yelling at us and one ramper even looked at the aircraft moving backwards and then nonchalantly walked back in to the office as if nothing was wrong. All seemed completely unalarmed which led to further confusion about what was transpiring. When the aircraft was very clearly past the E-175 mark and we were not conducting a small correction push back on the parking line I sensed that something was very wrong and made the decision to pull the parking brake. The parking brake was pulled in an effort to immediately stop the potentially dangerous roll and to maintain aircraft control. Unfortunately due to the Shutdown flow being completed the seatbelt sign was off at the time. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop. I immediately contacted the flight attendants to verify everyone was ok. They mentioned one passenger had fallen down; but that they reported they were ok and did not require any further assistance. The ramp personnel came up to the front of the aircraft; connected the headset and began communicating with us via interphone. A tug was then brought over to pull the aircraft back into the parking spot. With no damage to the aircraft and all passengers disembarked safely we handed the aircraft off to the next crew.Cause: The failure to turn off the beacon during the shutdown flow which led to what was interpreted as a brake release signal from the ramper; which then began rolling the aircraft backwards. Furthermore; an inadequate display of urgency and alarm from the ramp personnel lead to further confusion about the nature of what was occurring; or if a tug was connected to the aircraft..Suggestions: To avoid this happening in the future; first off the beacon needs to be turned off as required by the captain shutdown flow. Secondly; some other means of communication to let us know that the beacon was still on would have helped in this situation. The flashing fist' signal from the ramper's hand looked almost identical to a brake release signal. Prior to the parking brake being released there should have been explicit; preferably verbal; instruction from the ramper. Furthermore; an inadequate display of alarm or that anything was wrong from numerous ramp personnel as the aircraft slowly rolled back is cause for concern and I would have immediately stopped the aircraft had I known we were not undertow or that something else was wrong.

column121: Weather over and around ZZZ. We waited until the cells have passed east to start making our way to the runway for departure. column121: During walk around; found NLG strut completely compressed (bottomed-out). Contract Maintenance serviced it to in-range extension with N2. Taxi and takeoff were uneventful until gear retracted. NLG green down and locked extinguished; red unlocked light illuminated and remained illuminated. Pilots ran Gear Disagree Checklist. Noise level and vibration seemed nearly normal on climb out and fuel flow was nominal for phase of flight. After weighing options; Captain decided to continue to ZZZ1 and continue troubleshooting on way to ZZZ1. Manual Landing Gear Extension Checklist was reviewed just in case it would be needed. Contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control to determine any other possible action. Maintenance Control informed us that the maintenance tech in ZZZ left his flashlight in the NLG compartment.  This was the most likely cause of the problem. Pilots agreed to extend the landing gear early for landing since fuel state was not a concern. During approach; when the gear handle was moved to the down position; the NLG red unlocked light remained illuminated. The green down and locked light remained extinguished. Overhead panel NLG green light also was extinguished. Both MLG lights indicated down and locked. PM (at this point it was the Captain) referred to the manual landing gear checklist and attempted a manual extension. This was unsuccessful. NLG indications did not change. PF abandoned the approach and called for the go-around. ZZZ [TRACON] vectored us northwest of the airport at 12;000. Crew referred to the landing with Partial Landing Gear Checklist. Dispatch and Maintenance Control were consulted. Briefing with brace instructions was provided to the flight attendants. After running all applicable checklists the Captain performed a normal approach and light landing while reducing loads on the nose gear for as long as possible.  The nose settled on to the extended NLG. Ops and Airport Rescue and Firefighting inspected the aircraft; pinned all landing gear before exiting runway.  The flashlight was located in the NLG compartment. A normal taxi to the arrival gate occurred without further incident.

column121: We pushed off the gate on time for a departure from ZZZ. There was a front to the west of the airfield approaching quickly.  We were up with ground and got a full reroute which added quite a bit of fuel required. We taxied to a spot to get in touch with dispatch and come up with a plan. We decided to drop the alternate so we could takeoff legally as there were many good options along the route clear of the weather.We taxied to the runway and were number 6 for departure. ZZZ was doing 20 in tail spacing for departures. As we waiting for turn the weather hit the field; with wind shear of over 25 kts at 500 being reported. Tower stopped all departures and was estimating a minimum of an hour till the weather was going to clear.Around this time the flight attendant called me and said it was pretty hot in the back. I asked the FO to use the max cooling procedure from the Flight Manual.  We talked again to dispatch and decided a return to the gate was necessary due to fuel and the weather.As we were taxing back the FAs called again and said it was very hot. We switched the pack temperature controllers to manual and full cold (737-700).  We parked the plane after a long delay to get the self park system to operate. The jetway driver would not bring the jetway to the aircraft due to the ramp being closed. I called ops; ramp; dispatch and the Chief Pilot to get my passengers off the plane. I requested priority handling at the gate due to heat; It was approximately 95 degrees in the back.  After around 30 minutes the jetway was driven to the aircraft and passengers were deplaned.

column121: Previous flight that we flew in for assigned (737 NG) aircraft Y had a pneumatic maintenance issue. I was unhappy with maintenance effort to rectify problem. They cleared the warning electronically and did a leak check of right ACM (Air Cycle Machine) bay. Basically; they turned on APU and told us to call them back if light came on again; but would not check the wing strut or leading edge despite our requests and explanation of system. After a discussion with Dispatch; she agreed it was a problem; and offered a solution of another aircraft; Aircraft X; that was scheduled to ferry to ZZZ with two pilots we had deadheaded in. This plan was put in motion. I was told the ferry paperwork needed to be changed to a revenue flight and aircraft brought from hangar. Deadheading crew was to fly back with us.While we waited; we reviewed the aircraft history. Apparently on Day 0 Aircraft X (737NG) experienced a #2 engine failure that tore up the turbine blades and sent debris into the horizontal stabilizer. The logbook documented that the engine was replaced at ZZZZ; ground run only; and horizontal tail holes speed taped. FO and I discussed concern on putting revenue pax on aircraft with new engine that had never been flown; and concluded this was indeed FAA approved company policy and all paperwork appeared in order.When we arrived at aircraft; it was clear it had never flown; and cockpit was in configuration of last single engine landing (flap inhibit up; trim adjusted). Duty day was beginning to become concern due to delays and it was brought to my attention that customs closing was an issue. At some time dispatch notified me that customs would stay open; but we needed to hurry up. The usual delays of switching aircraft (bags and catering) occurred; and I was notified some bags had to come off for pax that had not re-boarded. Start up and push was normal; but upon After Start check we discovered that EECs (electronic engine controls) were in ALTN. Called dispatch and conferenced in Maintenance Control to discuss (item is flight crew placardable). Discovered EEC were not on; FO said he must have missed on pre-flight flow (very easy to do). Maintenance Control could find no reason they were off; but I asked about ground run test card that was in logbook and on a hunch she got the actual mechanic that did the ground run (he was still in ZZZZ) who admitted it was part of the test and that he left them off. Maintenance Control then cleared us to turn them on and proceed and with concurrence with dispatch; FO did so. Dispatch then had to check to see if customs would still stay open at ZZZ for our late arrival; which they did and she gave clearance to proceed.Taxi; takeoff; and initial climbout was normal for night VMC at ZZZZ. We had just negotiated a isolated line of thunderstorms that were putting out a little light turbulence and FO as PF had slowed the aircraft for turbulence when he decided to speed up to ECON speed at about 31000 ft. I felt a rumbling vibration and a slight yaw as PM and asked 'did you feel that?' Before he could answer I felt more vibrations and looked over to the engine instruments to see #2 engine rolling back and 'ENG FAIL' displayed. He said 'MY Aircraft' at same time I said 'your aircraft' and clicked off autopilot as aircraft was slowing and yawing. I realized that we would immediately be drifting down; and requested priority handling with ZZZZ Control asking for lower and a return to ZZZZ (we were 20-30 min out and this was closest suitable airport). Immediately started getting calls from back of aircraft saying they had seen a flash and 'sparks'. Executed QRC Eng Severe Damage or Separation checklist due to prior vibrations; and subsequent One Eng Inop Landing and Nonroutine Landing checklist while FO navigated back through weather towards ZZZZ and I followed along with charts monitoring minimum safe altitudes (low chart and 20-1 page) as identified threat was also terrain. Communication was difficult dueto constant communication with cabin and language barriers with ATC. ATC told us to expect ILS Y XX which is a teardrop turn from ZZZ VOR to the ILS XX. Neither the FO nor I could get it to load without placing a discontinuity in the middle of the approach. We tried numerous techniques but it kept leaving a discontinuity in middle of approach. Normal checklists also completed sometime in here. I am familiar with ZZZZ and knew they vector on one side of the airport; so asked for vectors for the ILS Z which they approved. This removed a major distraction. FO flew the aircraft on FD1 (Flight Director) and AP1 (Autopilot) (CMD 1) to downwind as I briefed the approach; and set up for Flaps 15; brakes 3. I decided to fly the approach as I had just done a flaps 15 in there that morning and was more experienced in the aircraft. Took aircraft on base leg and intercepted LOC on vectors at 2;500 ft. For some unknown reason; I saw flight director disappear in HUD and looked down at PFD (Primary Flight Display) to see lateral disappear and shortly after vertical to disappear. Immediately transitioned to HUD raw data and continued hand flying while asking FO to troubleshoot by resetting FDs. Field was in sight and PAPIS operational.Flew overweight landing to a smooth touchdown about 1;500-1;700 ft down and stopped short of a taxiway (1 maybe) about 8;000 ft down 10;500 ft runway. FO moved flaps 40 and spoilers down while I spoke to people in back. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) rolled up to inspect aircraft. We quickly discovered we had no contact with ARFF and tower wanted to relay all communications to them which became really awkward as we relayed our condition; what we wanted checked; and tried to warn them to stay clear of operating #1 engine. Additionally; we checked brake energy and discovered for our weight and speed were in 'caution zone'. Through a series of awkward communications (language barrier and 'pass the message' barrier) we asked tower to have fire chief aware and eventually we got back info that one tire/brake was indeed smoking. I asked tower to have ARFF chock nose so I could release brakes with a plan of allowing brakes to cool some and eventually taxi to gate. This seemed to not be understood or confusing to those on ground. FO at this time was also trying to get hold of OPS for gate assignment and to notify maintenance. We attempted visual signals but mostly just got quizzical looks. At some point a random individual showed up on FO side and he believed this individual (which was not a uniformed fireman) was asking us to shutdown. Since we had not gotten hold of anyone at company yet and fire chief had not cleared us off; I was reluctant to do so. I told him to signal the fellow to come over to my side and tried to communicate to this very animated individual who was not responding to my chocks signal either. Had to shut down in order to hear him. Turns out he was company maintenance of some sorts and basically just took over from Fire Chief telling me he would get tug to tow us in. I told him we had hot brakes (assuming he might not want us immediately in a gate area) but he did not seem to care. Tug showed up and we towed to gate area. Once at gate and checklist complete; I sent FO down to ensure wheels were chocked twice and released brakes to cool. FO told me that maintenance got a bit aggressive downstairs stating he was in charge and how we should have listened to him immediately (even though we had no idea who he was or why he was there). My FO says he corrected him in the conversation as to who was in charge-us and ARFF at that point in the situation. Later I found out that they had run from hangar straight out to us; but had no headsets; radio; or chocks with them. I am not sure they were communicating at all with Fire Chief on ground. Ops never answered on radio. I called dispatcher; who had gone home; asked replacement for chief pilot; who could not be found; so called safety. Filled out logbookfor engine failure and overweight landing. After that; things seemed to move along. Through ops coordination and the app eventually secured 8 rooms for crew. Assigned to fly Aircraft Y (original aircraft) home next morning. My original refusal write-up as signed off with requested inspections when we showed up.Cause: What started out as a simple 'turn' ended up being very long day. The length of day and darkness exuberant the 'startle affect' for all involved; but front and back end of crew worked well together. Terrain; weather; and communication barriers were a constant distraction. FO and I reviewed/debriefed with safety software. I discovered a few errors and pointed that out for us both to learn. I found out that when I asked for flight directors to be reset; he did not turn his off (just mine) as he was afraid he would lose his flight director. I suspect had we recycled; that problem would have gone away. We are not sure why approach would not load. I suspect it was some combination of direct to IAF and constraints somewhere. The next day I was able to put in the FMS for Aircraft Y no problem.Maintenance in ZZZZ seems to have a bit of attitude working with aircrews and ARFF. If they are going to insert themselves with ARFF they really need comm gear (radio/headsets) and if planning on towing; chocks. ARFF at ZZZZ really needs comm capability with priority aircraft. Finally; I really don't think the first flight after an engine change needs to be with revenue pax on board.
column123: On climbout from ZZZZ approaching 31;000 ft MSL I felt and heard two distinct high frequency vibrations. I immediately looked at the engine gauges and saw the #2 engine N1 RPM rapidly winding down. The EGT maintained at this point. I verbalized this to the CA and called My Aircraft. We analyzed what was happening and I clicked off the Autopilot to fly the aircraft. My focus was to keep the aircraft in coordinated flight; maintain speed with minimal altitude loss. This was at night and I knew there was mountainous terrain underneath us. ZZZZ1 was to our left around 30 miles or so and my thoughts were that returning to ZZZZ was the best option since it was low altitude and was clear of terrain to the west and south. The #2 engine N1 wound down below idle and ENG FAIL showed on the EGT. Since we had engine failure with associated vibrations the CA pulled out the QRC for Engine Failure or Shutdown and followed the path for Airframe vibrations with abnormal engine indications. We followed the QRC and QRH and shut down the #2 engine. The CA requested priority handling and asked for a return to the ZZZZ airport. I maintained the flying role while the captain then ran thru the checklists and took care of the people and flight attendants. I turned the aircraft back to the airport; turned the autopilot back on and flew back to vectors to downwind for an ILS to runway XX. The CA had flown a flaps 15 into this airport that morning so he took that aircraft and flew the approach and landing. This return to the airport; approach and landing was mostly uneventful except for two minor avionics oddities which didn't affect our ability to safely return and landing the aircraft. The first was that we could not get the ILS Y Rwy XX to fully connect without discontinuities. We tried a couple different methods to fix this but to no avail. We simply executed vectors to the south of the airport and picked up the final portion of the ILS. We were able to get this approach to load the next day without issue on a different aircraft. The other issue was that when the localizer was captured the CA's flight directors (FD) disappeared. Everything else appeared normal - generators on the APU; radar altimeter reading correctly and the FO had normal FD and indications. This also didn't affect the approach and landing since we were VMC and had PAPIs; HUD; raw ILS data; etc but it is noteworthy. Landing was over max landing weight and after coming to a stop I set the flaps to 40 and we used the brake cooling tables to assess that we were in the caution zone. 'Wheel fuse plugs may melt.' 'Delay takeoff and inspect after 1 hour.'The fire trucks and emergency personnel were in position to check us over but the only way to communicate with them was with replay comm thru Tower. I was able to tell Tower what we needed from the emergency crews etc and they would relay that to the emergency crew. The crew would then relay what they see back to Tower and Tower would then tell us. Realize that there is a bit of a language barrier due to accents and terminology. I was able to clear the emergency crew; thru Tower; that they are cleared to inspect the plane. I informed Tower at least twice that the right engine was shutdown; the left engine was running and asked to tell the crews to look for damage; debris on the runway; damage to the engine; wing and tail and to stay clear of the running engine. This took a significant amount of time to relay to the emergency crew to get in there and inspect because there was no way to talk to the ground crews via direct radio contact.The CA and I were also concerned about the hot brakes. I asked Tower to get them to look assess the brakes as well. From what I remember there was indication from Tower that the brakes were hot or abnormal; and nothing else abnormal with the engine; FOD damage - so in the CA and my mind our priority now is to get the nose wheel chocked so we can release the brakes. I communicated this to the Tower numeroustimes and there was basically no action from what I could see from the crews to chock the plane. They were walking around but no chocks. At this point a new person to the scene was waving at me and trying to get my attention. He was not part of the emergency crews and he eventually yelled to the CA that he was a part of company maintenance. I opened my window to be able to yell or get my 'chocks in' signal more clear. He gave me the shut down the engine signal. I went back and forth with him a few different times trying to get him to confirm that the chocks were in. He held up his finger to indicate 'not yet - wait for it' I was trying to get Tower to give me confirmation that the chocks were indeed in but there was no winning comm at this point. Since it was dark and the crews were looking confused we couldn't tell what they accomplished or didn't accomplish. From what the Tower indicated was that the emergency crews were trying to find chocks somewhere. The maintenance person was telling us to shut down the #1 engine but was not part of the fire crew so I was confused on what exactly was happening. Again no radio comm available to anyone on the ground. The CA and my priority since we were told everything was fine by Tower was to get the plane chocked so we can release the brakes. Our overall plan was to let the brakes cool; have the fire crew inspect and then - as we are trained to do - decide to taxi or not single engine back to the gate. The maintenance person went to the CA's window and they were able to yell back and forth. He said we were to be towed in to the gate. I was also talking with Tower and they told me that our company was going to tow us back to the gate. During all this I had tried to call ops on their freq but no answer - late at night or out here at the jet - unknown. The CA and I were happy to be towed back to the gate but the big issue was that maintenance was aggressively trying to get us to shut down the other engine without understanding our situation. This was highly frustrating but we worked as a team to eventually get the plane chocked; shut down the engine and get towed back.The main issue we have is the lack of ability to communicate with the emergency crew. The second is that as far as we were concerned the emergency crew is the ones to be handling this aircraft especially considering the hot brakes situation. The maintenance person just popped in to the situation and tried to take command of what we were doing and it added negative value to this situation.I spoke with him on the ground at the gate and I explained that we had hot brakes and were not going to shut down the engine without being chocked. Additionally we were told by the emergency crew - thru Tower - that there was no danger so why was he trying to get us to shut down the #1 engine. He said that in order to inspect the aircraft we had to shut the engine down. I said we were never trained to do that and additionally if there wasn't a fire or some more severe issue that we weren't going to just shut down the engine without chocks or a signal from the emergency crew. I told him our plan was to chock the nose; assess the brakes and then taxi back; get towed back or evacuate if something bad occurred. He put himself in the middle of our standard game plan and caused confusion at the least. He said 'This is ZZZZ and we do things differently. We have to have both engines shut down to inspect.'Regardless I thanked him for having this debrief with me and he can discuss this with the captain once all the passengers are deboarded.Cause: Mechanical. We found out a couple days later that the engine experienced multiple compressor stalls and fuel starvation. The HMU (Hydro-Mechanical Unit) was the cause of these issues. The previous flight experienced the same #2 engine failure but with material failure and shredding of turbine blades which caused damage to the engine; wing and horizontal tail. The removed and replaced the engine; testedit on the ground; but never test flown. We were the first flight to fly this jet with passengers with a new engine.
