column121: Approximately half an hour into the cruise; while resting in the cabin; I heard the master caution chime; and autopilot disconnect alert. Upon entering the cockpit and seating in the observers seat I saw the captain reading a QRH checklist and observed the EICAS Caution message 'HYD PRESS SYS 1' along with the lower EICAS displaying the HYD SD page; and the number 1 hydraulic tank indication empty. I then opened the HYD PREES SYS 1 checklist on my IPAD and monitored the actions of the PM and PF.  Following the selection of the alternate gear extension; the right hand wing gear indicated hashed/in transit; and an EICAS gear disagree message was displayed. The crew actioned the gear disagree checklist and that did not remedy the situation. I contacted Maintenance Control; Deputy chief Pilot and the Supervisor on the sat phone. I asked the question to the Supervisor if; (as we had used the alternate gear selection ) would there be any negative repercussions with selecting the landing gear handle down; as this was not a step that the gear disagree checklist advocated. Upon receiving the 'no objection' from the Supervisor the gear handle was selected down and the right wing gear indicated green. We then landed in accordance with the loss of hyd 1 system; and were towed to the ramp following shut down on the runway.I wish to commend the Captain on his excellent crew management and command handling of this malfunction.Suggestions: I suggest that the B744 QRH GEAR DISAGREE checklist be amended to direct the crew to step XX (Landing gear lever (if possible)…DN. Currently the checklist directs crew to step XY bypassing the gear lever down selection.

column121: On Day 0; I departed ZZZ to ZZZ1 for the purpose of practicing tower operations at an unfamiliar airport. After two landings at ZZZ1 with a couple hours of leisure flight in between the landings; I departed ZZZ1 for my return to ZZZ. My eta at ZZZ was approximately XA:00; and; based on the weather data available through my EFB; my expectation was an arrival on RWY XX at ZZZ. The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was unremarkable in all regards. Approximately 10 miles east of ZZZ; I obtained the weather via the ZZZ AWOS system; which indicated winds from 020 at 9 kts. As expected; the winds favored an arrival on RWY XX; so I set up for a slightly wider than normal righthand base entry for RWY XX. There was no local traffic in the pattern; and the only radio traffic was from a single inbound plane approximately 10 miles out for RWY XX.I descended to pattern altitude at approximately 5 miles from ZZZ; added 10 degrees of flaps; and entered the right base for RWY XX pitched to approximately 90 kts. Upon turning north for final; approximately 2-3 miles south of ZZZ; I noted the winds aloft at pattern altitude seemed brisker than the AWOS report and I felt slight gusting; which was consistent with my prior experience at altitude and generally unremarkable. Because of the ground level crosswind and the gusting at pattern altitude; I decided to make my landing with 20 degrees flaps; rather than my normal 30 degrees; and adjust my final approach speed up from my normal 65-70 kts to something in the low to mid 70 kts range.During final approach; I added the second 10 degrees of flaps approximately one mile from the threshold and I maintained a crab angle into the wind; which meant my heading was east of the runway heading; as expected. I adjusted my pitch after adding the second notch of flaps and was holding a pretty steady 72 kts airspeed with 20 degrees of flaps. Upon reaching short final; I added left rudder to transition from a crab heading to runway heading using a 'right wing low slip technique' and continued to hold approximately 72 kts. The slight gusting I had experienced at pattern altitude was no longer evident at short final altitude. Overall; the final approach felt stable and my airspeed and heading varied very little from the initial turn final until the threshold; except for the intentional airspeed adjustment associated with adding the second notch of flaps.As I crossed the threshold; I pulled power to idle; compensated for the slight nose down action associated with the 182 when power is brought to idle; and entered the ground effect. Flight in the ground effect was stable; and my runway placement was slightly left of center but certainly within the middle third of the runway.When my airspeed dissipated sufficiently; I began my flare for touchdown. At this point; I experienced a gust (presumably) that caused the plane to yaw noticeably and abruptly to the left; which resulted in me being in a 'right wing low' bank with the right main leading the left main. I was expecting to touchdown any moment; so my reaction was to correct the left yaw by adding right aileron to bring the nose to the right and toward the center of the runway. In doing so; I believe I overcorrected for the left yaw and ended up pointing too far to the right when I touched down; which occurred immediately after making my correction.The touchdown led with the right main; which would have been oriented farthest to the south at this point due to the overcorrection. After the right main touched down; the left main and nose gear followed; either at the same time or perhaps with the left main slightly ahead of the nose. The touchdown itself was not particularly hard; although I wouldn't hold it out as my smoothest landing by any means.At this point; elapsed time became a little difficult to judge; but it seems like within a second or two after touchdown; I felt a force acting on the plane that I hadn't experienced before; and that caused me to pause for another second or two in order to evaluate what I was experiencing. I determined the force was sideloading toward my left; and I also noticed the left wing of the plane was dipping and the right main had come off the runway; resulting in the plane rolling only on the left main and the nose gear. I responded to the side loading by adding what little remaining right aileron I had left and pressing the left rudder pedal aggressively. Unfortunately; neither control input seemed to help; and I believe the sideloading actually caused the nose wheel to turn to the right because the plane began rolling across the runway in a right arc. The tilt to the left gradually increased to the point where I actually leaned to the passenger side of the plane in an attempt to offset it. At some point; I heard a rubbing noise I didn't recognize; and my first reaction was to look out the left window to see if the left wingtip was dragging the ground. It did not seem to be close to dragging; so I assumed the rubbing noise was coming from the nose gear being in a bind or something along those lines (I later learned the noise was the prop contacting the runway surface).After arcing to the right across the runway for a couple seconds (which felt like an hour) with all the right aileron and left rudder I had to provide; the plane leaned back to the right and settled on all three gears. At this point; I engaged the brakes pretty aggressively and came to a stop about three feet from the right edge of RWY XX with the engine running smoothly at idle. I'm guessing at this point; but it seems the nose of the plane was pointing about 040 or 050 at the time. Suffice it to say; the rightward arc I traveled across the runway was significant in any event.I looked out the windows of the plane and noted a runway light less than a wing width away toward my left; and; based on my proximity to the runway edge; I didn't think I had enough room to attempt a left turn on the runway without risking an impact with the runway light. As a result; I elected to exit the runway to the east; make a lefthand arc through the RSA; and reenter the runway between the next set of runway lights; so that's how I proceeded. The exit and reentry of the runway was smooth and uneventful; so I proceeded north down RWY XX to the next taxiway intersection and exited the runway. While taxiing down the runway; I heard the plane behind me call a five-mile final; so I announced myself upon exiting the runway and noted the traffic was on short final at that point.I taxied uneventfully back to the hangar and shut down the engine; and when the propeller came to a stop; I realized the tips were all curled; hence the unexplained noise I heard while arcing across the runway. This was the first time I realized a prop strike had occurred.At the time of the occurrence; I held a private pilot license with an instrument rating; as well as high performance and complex endorsements. I had 314.9 hours of total time; with 287.2 as PIC. Specific to C182 time; I had a total of 81.0 hours and 100 landings; 40 of which were night landings. Thats when I took controls and immediately started turning towards ZZZ. I figured I had power still enough right now so I elected to climb as much as I could to gain some altitude an use the tailwind to at least get us away from trees and give better gliding distance to a field. Told my student to run the loss of oil pressure checklist and sqauwk XXXX while i handled comms and advise on ZZZ ctaf. At about 2400ft is when I pulled the power back to prevent overheating of the engine and kept just enough to try and hold altitude but temps kept climbing so I reduced more which eseentially gave us a drift down with some power. We were about 14 miles southeast ish away from ZZZ when I noticed the oil pressure dropping. By about 6 miles away the engine began losing more rpms but by then I had a good feeling we'll make the runway but it'll have to be a tailwind landing. There wasn't enough power to get into the pattern so I just elected for a straight in runway XX at ZZZ. After we landed we still had some power to roll off the runway and started rolling towards the ramp by then temps were really hot so I shutoff the engine and continued rolling on to the ramp. As we get out there's oil all over the bottom and noticed no oil in the dipstick. Shutdown terminated and then made some calls.

column121: On the walk-around prior to the flight the captain noticed that the nose landing gear strut was fully compressed. I (FO) was the pilot-flying and the captain noticed upon retracting the gear that the red Nose Landing Gear light illuminated. Although there was a very slight vibration difference we agreed the gear was up and potentially not locked. We decided to continue on to ZZZ1 and we maintained the slowest practical airspeed during the flight as to not exceed gear limitations. We briefed the arrival and approach into ZZZ1 and elected to configure early in case the gear did not operate properly. When the gear handle was extended the unsafe indication remained and I called for the go-around. We climbed and were vectored north or the airport where we ran necessary checklists in an attempt to get the gear down and locked. Our efforts to get a safe gear indication failed so we prepared for landing and decided it would be best to swap flight controls so the captain could control the tiller in the event the nose landing gear operated abnormally. The landing was uneventful and the gear pin was inserted before we taxied to the gate.

column123: On the arrival for runway 30 visual approach into HTS; the winds were stronger than previously reported. column121: Day 0; Learjet 60; departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ. The forecast for ZZZ indicated ¼ mile in FZFG which caused the crew to delay takeoff for 1 hour to allow our arrival at ZZZ for the estimated forecast at XA:00z to be 200 and ½ mile visibility. The crew departed ZZZ1 at XB:51z and arrived in the area at approximately XC:06z just after the control tower opened. The crew acknowledged the new ATIS '1' indicating winds Calm; ¼ FG; Ceiling 100; Temp -1C/Dewpoint -1C; and Altimeter 30.17. There was no mention of Freezing Fog. RNAV (GPS) Rwy XX was in use. The ILS Rwy XX Glidepath is NOTAM'd out of service. As a crew; we decided to 'take a look' and performed the approach. At minimums; the approach lights came into sight and then the runway was in sight. However; due to a loss of visual to the runway missed approach was conducted. During the missed approach the crew noticed the weather seemed to be improving. We talked about it and thought that we would be able to complete an approach and land. After being vectored to the final approach course by ZZZ Approach Control; we performed a second RNAV (GPS Rwy XX approach. On this approach; we again had the approach light system in sight at minimums and then the runway in sight. The Flying Pilot maintained a stabilized approach speed of approximately 140 Knots based on a calculated VREF speed of 137 Knots. During the landing flare the plane floated for about 2 to 3 seconds before touching down. The flying pilot immediately deployed the thrust reverser system and began braking. The Pilot Monitoring noticed the 1000 foot marker quickly approaching and made the callout. The Pilot Flying went to maximum braking and the aircraft overran the end of the runway approximately 20 feet in soft mud.The calculations from the aircrafts Aircraft Performance Program  indicated that based on the criteria of a wet runway and flaps 40° and using 115% performance numbers; our landing distance based on a 18;361 pounds was 3794 feet. Unfortunately; because of the 3 second of floating time; much of the runway was used up during the landing.After shutting down the engines and notifying the tower of the incident; we exited the runway to assess any damage and coordinate with our company to recover the aircraft. I noticed that the runway was very slick in spite of being grooved which I believed contributed to the overrun. No obvious damage was noticed and recovery efforts were accomplished with no further problems.

column121: At ZZZ; I was attempting to Taxi to Runway XX at ZZZ for a cross country flight when winds caused the plane to drift off the runway to the left when perpendicular to the runway prior to lining up with the centerlines. Of note; the flight had been delayed one hour due to gusting winds. Winds had reduced prior to taxi and were predicting to continue to decrease according to regulated weather sources. The rate of drift was slow; but rudder control was reduced; leading the tires of the plane to be slightly to the left off of the runway when control was re-established. Due to the position; the tire was stuck and the plane was unable to move forward to be re-established on the runway. The pilot communicated the issue to ATC; who directed upcoming landing traffic to go around. Due to the plane's inability to move backways (due to the manufacturing limits of the plane); I communicated with ATC that I would need to physically push the plane backways. I then turned off the plane; pushed the plane backward and then in line with the runway. After starting up the plane; I regained contact with ATC and let them know that the plane was now in line for takeoff. I was able to takeoff without any issues with winds or gusts. The plane was landed without incident at ZZZ1. There was no damage to person or aircraft during the incident. Incident occurred due to wind gusts and the pilot underestimating the extent of the effects of the gusts when perpendicular to the runway prior to lining up on centerline. Corrective action includes further training on effects of wind; especially in Cessna 152. In addition; although the flight was delayed due to the wind; further delay or cancellation would have avoided the incident completely.

On inspection of the wheel it was noticed that the cotter pin for the wheel retaining collar was missing. column121: Date: Day 0Location: Practice area east/northeast of ZZZ near the ZZZZZ fixAircraft: Aircraft X; Aircraft YOther Aircraft Involved: RV-4 On Day 0; during a training flight operating in the practice area northeast of ZZZ; a near midair collision occurred between our aircraft and an RV-4  near the ZZZZZ fix. The conflict developed as both aircraft converged while climbing and maneuvering in the same airspace. Evasive action was required to avoid the other aircraft.During a training flight on Day 0; I was instructing my student pilot departing from ZZZ. They are working on their Private Pilot Airplane Single Engine Land training in the Cessna 172 Skyhawk. They have nearly 100 hours and was doing one last flight to prepare for their end-of-course progress check. After departure; we transitioned northbound from ZZZ and proceeded into the local practice areas commonly referred to as City X and City Y at 7;500 MSL. These practice boxes are below ZZZ1 class Bravo.We remained in the practice area for a short while; conducting normal training maneuvers for a private pilot. After completing those maneuvers; we transitioned eastbound; positioning ourselves slightly south of ZZZ2.While in this area; we conducted two ground reference maneuvers: turns around a point and S-turns across a road. These maneuvers were performed at approximately 1;000 feet above ground level. Which; for this given area; was roughly 5;900 MSL. We were making routine traffic calls on the North Practice area frequency of XXX.XXX throughout the entire flight. We made sure to comply with 91.119 and maintain an altitude allowing for an emergency landing without power; without undue hazards to person or property on the surface. This is a sparsely populated area consisting mostly farmlands underneath the ZZZ1 class bravo.Upon completion of the ground reference maneuvers; we began a climb to 6;500 feet MSL while turning westbound to return to ZZZ. This put us roughly 1;500 ft AGL.While en route westbound at approximately 6;500 feet MSL; shortly after; I observed a traffic advisory on the aircraft's MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) indicating traffic off our right side. The traffic was identified on ADS-B; an RV-4; and was initially displayed approximately 500 feet below our altitude.Because I did not yet have visual contact with the aircraft; I instructed my student to initiate a climb to 7;000 feet MSL in order to increase vertical separation. The student began the climb; and the aircraft reached approximately 6;770 feet MSL when I observed the aircraft passing below. I pointed out the traffic to my student and notified them that it should soon be passing under the nose and appearing on their side (left) of the aircraft. We continued climbing to increase separation. I monitored the traffic information on the MFD and observed the altitude separation decreasing rapidly. The traffic indication changed from 500 feet below to 400 feet below; then 200 feet below; and eventually indicated the same altitude and the same position.At that point; it became clear the other aircraft was climbing directly toward our altitude. I immediately took control of the aircraft and initiated a right-hand evasive turn to the north.As I initiated the right turn; the RV-4 also began a right-hand turn toward the north; indicating the same altitude the whole time; further reducing the lateral separation between the aircraft.Based on the maneuvering and flight profile; it appeared the RV-4 was performing aerobatic maneuvering in the area and was likely unaware that we were operating nearby.I personally did not obtain visual contact with the RV-4 during the conflict. However; my student; who was seated in the left seat; did acquire visual contact and estimated the aircraft passed approximately '3-5 feet off our wing'. They told me; 'They are right next to us and turning into us'. I then steepened the bank to roughly 50 degrees and pushed the nose forward to accelerate us to 129 KIAS.We lost roughly 1;000 ft attempting to break away from this aircraft and were still indicating the same altitude throughout the evasive action. This lasted almost a minute.Following the evasive maneuver; we successfully separated from the traffic. We then continued east briefly before turning northbound to reestablish our route back toward ZZZ while maintaining separation from the other aircraft. We then went north of the class Bravo and climbed up to 8;000 MSL. The aircraft continued to the south. We attempted to contact the aircraft on both practice area frequencies of XXX.XXX and XXX.Y. We received no communication back from the traffic. No further traffic conflicts occurred during the remainder of the flight.This event is concerning because the practice areas northeast of ZZZ are routinely used by student pilots from multiple training organizations. Many students conduct solo operations in these areas and routinely transition through the same airspace.The behavior and maneuvering of the RV-4 suggested the pilot was likely conducting aerobatic maneuvers and may not have been aware of other aircraft operating nearby. The lack of apparent situational awareness by the RV-4 created a hazardous situation in an area that regularly contains high volumes of training traffic.Given the frequency of student pilot operations in this region; this type of maneuvering presents a significant risk for future conflicts. Given the maneuverability of the RV-4 and the spontaneous maneuvering; it was extremely difficult to decipher which direction/altitude would clear us of traffic. No contact was made with the aircraft.

column121: I arrived and began preflight planning for a maintenance flight to test a diode on the right engine. I conducted a weight and balance form; a dispatch sheet and spoke with maintenance about what had been done to the aircraft in order to plan accordingly. I planned to travel to the midway practice area and perform basic maneuvers to include steep turns; slow flight; and stalls at 3;000 feet over water southeast of ZZZ. I conducted a preflight and noted no defects with the airplane; all fluids were filled to an acceptable level and no notable damage was found. I got into the airplane and started the engines; taxied to the runup; completed the before takeoff check checklist and taxied to the runway without any issues. I did a normal takeoff from runway XX full length at ZZZ and noted no issues on the takeoff roll. Approach let me know that there were two other airplanes in the practice area so I talked to them and determined I would work the east side north south at 3;000 ft. I got into the practice area; got set up for maneuvers and started with steep turns. No issues with steep turns so I moved on to slow flight. Once I began slow flight I pulled the power to 25% load on each engine and lowered the landing gear handle. Upon landing gear extension I noticed a strange yaw to the left and looked down and noticed my right main landing gear position indicator light was not illuminated and my gear unsafe light was illuminated.I continued to fly south and I began to trouble shoot starting with the gear fire test button which illuminated all landing gear position indicator lights and proved that all lights were working. I then called Aircraft Y and asked if they could fly below me and check if my gear was down. They did and confirmed the right main was in the wheel well. I then asked if they noted any change as I ran the manual extension of landing gear checklist and pulled the manual extension handle. The pilot of Aircraft Y confirmed that the landing gear was still stuck in the up position. This confirmed that there was a real problem and I began to maneuver with the gear handle down in an effort to try to pull the landing gear out of the wheel well. Once I had tried this a few times I determined that it was not working and wanted an official answer from the tower confirming that the right main landing gear was stuck up. I swapped frequencies to approach control and requested priority handling requesting to return to ZZZ for a low pass. I did and the tower confirmed that the right main appeared to be in the wheel well.I responded to the tower that I would return to the midway practice area to troubleshoot and burn off fuel. I returned to the midway practice area; continued to maneuver the aircraft and asked over our company frequency if anyone could get maintenance on the radio. Maintenance had me try a few different methods to lower the gear including going 180 kts and lowering the landing gear; pushing the manual gear extension handle back in and cycling the gear a few different times and adding constant G forces in a 60 degree banked steep turn. None of these methods worked. Eventually Aircraft Z; containing a representative of the FSDO and my Chief Pilot; departed ZZZ and flew close to me while I troubleshot the problem. Once I had tried everything and burned 10 or more gallons of fuel; I determined that the gear was not going to come down. I then returned to ZZZ. I entered left traffic XX. On short final for XX ~100' I pulled the power to idle and turned off the left then right engine masters and landed. I opened the canopy as I was coming to a stop. Once stopped I turned off the electric master and departed the aircraft.

column121: 10 to 15 miles NE of Danville (DAN); ATC was hesitant to lower us below 12;000 feet because another aircraft (Aircraft Y) did not close out the flight plan and ATC needed to figure that out first. Eventually; they descended us to 6000 feet but kept us there because of traffic below at 4000 feet. The captain was very concerned about making the runway so he prioritized making the descent and canceled IFR with ATC to enable us to go lower - the field was in sight (CAVU day). The Captain instructed me as the first officer; and as the pilot flying; to descend at a high rate and he recommended 4000 ft./min. I asked about the traffic and he said 'it's ok; start the descent'. Thinking he was clear on where the traffic was I complied; especially as the captain was reaching for the VS knob to scroll it down (though I was the one to command the v/s knob). I started the decent while looking to gain perspective on where the traffic was. I looked down at the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and as I did that; we received an RA which required us to pull up. We complied with the RA and added power. The next RA was to level. We complied at 4000 ft; and the traffic was clear after that. At our closest point; (to my recollection); we were 400 ft from the traffic.  From there; we descended in plenty of time to make a normal approach into Danville with a safe landing.

I continued my takeoff roll; believing we would be clear of the runway in time for the landing aircraft. The landing aircraft announced they were going around and side-stepping to the left. We briefed this incident on the ground and agreed the better course of action would be to announce your intention to take off and give enough time for someone you may not see to respond before crossing the hold short lines. The next best course of action would have been to stop or clear the runway as soon as possible without taking off.

column121: Was assigned TipToe 28L; with initial clearance for course only at 6;000ft. Was cleared to 3;000ft where Level Change was selected by PF. After visual contact with field; was cleared for the visual tiptoe 28L approach. Was past IAF EDDYY; where PF instructed PM to set touch down elevation (100ft). Plane was configured for landing appropriately and continued to descend; where around 1;000ft; PM recognized below Vertical path and lack of engagement of VNAV when we cleared the visual approach. Due to error; level change was still engaged below 1;000ft. PF disconnected AP (Autopilot); and corrected/regained flight path. Approach was continued to uneventful landing. Debriefed. Determined both PM/PF could have used better Monitor/Crosscheck and Automation Management when cleared for the approach to prevent error.
column123: Occurred during day; VMC conditions on a return leg to SFO airport. Crew flew the SERFR arrival into the TIPP TOE visual approach. We were initially cleared for course only guidance on the approach and given a descent to 3000 feet MSL. As a pilot flying; I selected Level Change approximately 6000 feet for the descent down to 4000 feet. During that descent; approach control cleared us for the full approach. The PILOT monitoring set TDZE in the altitude window and pointed it out; which I acknowledged as pilot flying. At the 1000 foot check point; the pilot monitoring observed that the visual side picture was lower than expected. I disengaged the auto pilot leveled off. We recognized that we were in Level Change and not in VNAV. We continued in level flight until we intercepted the correct altitude checkpoint and continued the approach uneventually.My personal assessment as pilot flying was that I was monitoring the Flight Director needles and outside visual reference and did not utilize a proper cross check to notice the incorrect flight mode selection.We used the debrief tools to assess what happened during the event on landing and discussed for the failures occurred in CRM that resulted in the condition. We also discussed how to use VVM (verbalize; verify; monitor) techniques in the future to avoid the same condition.

column121: On decent into El Paso International Airport; we were cleared to descend VIA the BEAHR3 for the RNAV 26L Y approach. The Captain (pilot flying) set LNAV/VNAV and the bottom STAR altitude 8000 ft; shortly after Approach control asked us to cross the (IF) BUSEY at 7000 ft and cleared us for the approach. Captain set the bottom Altitude on the altitude selector for the RNAV 26LY approach 5700 ft and set 7000 ft in the FMS for BUSEY and activated the hard altitude for BUSEY crossing restriction. We were descending in PATH mode at around 3200 FTM; nearing 10000 ft I called for speed check as the aircraft was descending at high rate in Manual speed mode; trying to make the crossing restriction. The Captain told me to let Approach control know we will not make crossing restriction; and the Captain change the decent mode to Vertical speed. I informed Approach control of the unable to make restriction; Approach control asked us to cross BUSEY at or above 8000ft. I asked if we ate still cleared for the approach; ATC confirmed cleared; I called for speed check again and mentioned our FMA vertical mode change and reminded Captain we are cleared for the approach. I asked the Captain do you want me to set the new hard altitude crossing 8000 ft at BUSEY. Captain mentioned not necessary but go head; I bugged 8000 ft at BUSEY and activated; our (altitude selector was still selected for our bottom RNAV 27 approach altitude 5700 ft ) after inserting new information into FMS below 10000 ft; I looked up called check speed and altitude and mentioned cleared for approach as the vertical mode was still in Vertical Speed and decent rate was excessive. At that time ATC mentioned low altitude alert and to climb to 6500 ft we started the climb; ATC then asked us to climb to 6700 ft; I asked if we were cleared for the approach; they confirmed cleared and transferred us to tower.Suggestions: As a crew we could have asked for a decent sooner as it's known for El Paso approach to bring aircraft in high then descend fast to meet a restriction. Better awareness during heavy workload; with last minute changes below 10000 ft with head down; While bugging new information not noticing new FMA changes made by Pilot flying. Being more assertive with altitude and speed restriction callouts.Less talking on the radio with ATC during critical phases; Captain mentioned couldn't hear or understand ATC instructions so I pilot monitoring had to keep confirming instructions; which increased workload during critical phases.
column123: ATC instructed at FL200; cleared to descend via the BEAHR3. At FL200 I set 8000 for BEARH and armed vnav. As we were descending ATC then said cleared direct FABAN cross FABAN at 8000; we vertical direct to FABAN but we were high; so I pulled the boards to get down; so we could make the new fix with the altitude restriction. ATC then said cross FABAN at 7000; cleared for the RNAV Y 26L; I set the final approach fix altitude; as we were cleared for the approach; I asked the FO to let ATC know we were not going to make that altitude restriction at 7000; I put it in VS to try to get down and slow down; somehow I missed ATCs response to now cross FABAN at or above 7000; I never put it back in path; or set the alt back to 7000; the alt was set for 5200 for the final approach fix; as I caught it we were already descending below the appropriate altitude; leading to an altitude deviation. We corrected the altitude deviation and completed a stabilized approach and landing. Suggestions: There was a lot going on in this phase of the flight; several things could have made this better; setting the altitude back to 7000; so we didn't blow through it; until me met that restriction then resetting the final approach fix; and/or putting the aircraft back in VNAV. Both would have prevented the deviation. The big one is I thought it was cross it at; not at or above; my misinterpretation of the clearance. Because we were given direct FABAN while we were high; I was distracted by trying to get down and slow down. Our CRM could have been a lot better also.

column121: On Day 2 at approximately XA:00 prior to aircraft door closure I was informed by the ground crew that they had observed an uncontrolled fuel leak coming from the right main wing tank on the outer edge of the tank towards the winglet.Immediately I grabbed my safety vest and air protection; exited the flight deck; and went out to the ramp to confirm that yes indeed there is a pencil width sized leak coming from the vent hole on the fuel tank. This leak was uncontrolled; could not be stopped; and required immediate attention. I returned to the flight deck and made a PA and told the passengers the situation and mentioned that because it was a fuel spill that had not been contained yet it was advantageous for everyone to grab their belongings and exit the aircraft as soon as possible. I then called my dispatcher and told them exactly what I had done and the event that had occurred outside. He was in agreement; deplaning the aircraft was a good idea. In the meantime; the ZZZ Ground crew flawlessly contain the spill so that there is minimal impact to ramp safety.I got off the phone with the dispatcher so that I can make the appropriate entries into the aircraft electronic logbook. My first entry into the logbook; stated that there was a new leak coming from the main wing tank. This issue had previously been written up and addressed on Day 0.After making the logbook entry; I called back dispatch and asked to be connected with the maintenance desk. The tone of the maintenance technician on the phone sounded frustrated; but eager to help. They simply said without any investigation or asking me any questions that I had just been over fueled and the situation was normal. The situation was not normal. We were already at our recommended fuel release load. Between us inspecting the leak and approximately 10 minutes later we had lost almost 200 pounds of gas due to a leak. When I advised the technician of this they did not change their judgment. They simply said yes that happened because you were over fueled; even though we are at the correct fuel load given our flight conditions as a matter of fact; we took off out of ZZZ1 with a higher fuel load on the previous flight and never encountered a leak.Once I was finally able to make my point across the technician on the other end of the phone; they decided it would be worth calling contract maintenance to come out and look at the aircraft.Roughly about an hour later maintenance arrived to the aircraft and began inspecting the wing for leaks . Maintenance personnel asked me to fully extend the flaps and slats so that they can fully inspect the wing to find other leaks. The contract maintenance technician then asked me to move fuel from the fuel control panel inside the aircraft to different tanks. I told him I was not comfortable doing that because it violated our SOP's. And I was not fully taught how to do this. Less than one month prior to this incident I remember an email being sent to all pilots asking us not to perform maintenance functions on the aircraft.The contract maintenance person was frustrated with me after I politely told him that I would not be able to comply with that request. I offered him my seat so that he could do it himself. The contract maintenance personnel moved roughly 1000 pounds from the right main wing tank to the left main wing tank and told me that the leak has stopped and that we were good to go. He became very frustrated with me when I told him that that doesn't comply with Company SOPs. And that we are not allowed to take off with a 1000 pound and balance between the wings. I also informed him that both main tanks had to be full of fuel before the center tank could be filled. The leak simply stopped because we moved gas away from the hole not that we did not actually solve the problem or find the source of the leak.After this diagnosis and attempt to fix the problem; I refused the aircraft and made a corresponding info item notation in theelectronic logic book. I had lost faith that this problem was gonna be solved to a satisfactory and safe nature and I elected that it would be best to remove myself from the situation. And not fly an unsafe aircraft.I then received a call from the chief pilot. The chief pilot did not give me their name and immediately became a line of questioning that seem to escalate and tone and speed; spinning a tighter and tighter web trying to find a fault in my story and trying to find a weakness in the narrative that I had told them. The told me not worry; the aircraft was actually fine and I was being overly cautious. I was told we had just been over fueled and it happens sometimes. For the record; I have almost 6;000 hours in this aircraft and that has never happened. I also informed them that we were at the correct few release number. This fuel release number is also not very large and it's very normal for this route and altitude.Their line of questioning seemed to invalidate my concerns for safety. Had I not been so confident in my judgment and prior experience; I could've easily been manipulated into making an unsafe decision that merely would've only benefited the company by moving an aircraft. This line and reasoning for questioning is very concerning to me. It seems unsafe; unprofessional; and against the norms that I had become to expect from Company.Thankfully; the first officer had taken a video of us finding the leak. I sent the video to a number that texted me saying that they were with the management team and they needed to talk to me immediately. I wanted to also let it be known that every contact attempt by the company did not include the dispatcher. I found that very concerning because any communication with the dispatcher is on a recorded line.I talked to a new maintenance control supervisor named Person A. He told me that the contract maintenance personnel also found a fuel leak coming from the fuel service panel on the right wing. Person A then asked me to perform more function checks on the aircraft. I told him I did not feel comfortable doing that. Although Person A seem frustrated; he did not seem frustrated with me. Merely just at the situation. I fully understand the inconvenience and impact this maintenance issue caused; but unfortunately the facts are undeniable. Taking an aircraft off the ground full of people that is leaking fuel is unsafe.A new contract maintenance personnel member came out to the aircraft approximately 2 1/2 hours after our initial report of the fuel leak at this point the leak had stopped; but we had lost approximately 400 pounds of fuel. The maintenance technician went to the flight deck; asked to sit in my seat and begin working with the fuel panel. The technician moved fuel from both wing tanks into the center tank and claimed that he had fixed the leak and that everything was good to go. I asked him how he fixed the leak and he said he had moved fuel from the wing tank to the center tank and you should be fine while both tanks were balanced. The center tank was grossly overloaded. This goes against Company standard operating procedure of fueling the wing tanks first then fueling the center. I asked if the hole and leak had been located and fixed he said no.Despite and obviously known outcome; I remained on duty to ensure that the maintenance situation was dealt with accordingly; I was fearful that another pilot would be given this aircraft with it fully not fixed and have an issue. At approximately XE:45 the dispatcher working my flight had called me and said 'hey; I am at shift change. I just wanted to call and see why things were and how things were going.'I informed him that nothing really changed. There is still a leak. There is fuel moved away from it; which is simply why it stopped leaking. I still don't fully understand how this is deemed a reliable and practical fix. I then told him for a third time I am still refusing the aircraft. I will not go into crew rest only to come back out to the airport and fly the same aircraft home if nothing had been fixed. I noted that I had said this for three times; and put it according info item in the electronic logbook hours ago. It was at that point we were finally released from duty given a min rest overnight and a new aircraft to fly home the following morning. Cause: Safety can at times be inconvenient; however should not cut corners to find a substandard resolution.

column121: During the pushback sequence from gate XX; engines 4 and 3 were started in accordance with approved company procedures. Ground handling personnel failed to adhere to standard operating procedures in several critical respects:-They did not issue any verbal instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake prior to initiating disconnection of the tow bar and tug.-Without prior authorization from the Pilot in Command (PIC); and while engines 1 and 2 had not yet been started; they proceeded with disconnection of the towing equipment.With the parking brake unset and the nose wheel steering bypass pin installed (disabling hydraulic steering); as engines 4 and 3 stabilized at idle thrust; the aircraft began to move forward and yaw uncontrollably to the left.Ground personnel immediately shouted instructions to 'release the parking brake;' to which the PIC promptly responded; 'parking brake is released.' Shortly thereafter; ground personnel urgently directed the crew to 'set parking brake.' The PIC applied the brakes without hesitation upon observing the aircraft's forward and leftward movement.Despite the immediate brake application; the aircraft's residual momentum caused the nose landing gear to strike the tow bar; resulting in damage to the scissor link (torque link).Immediately following the incident; the flight crew overheard; via the interphone; the headset operator (ground personnel) state: 'I [expletive] up.'Upon return to the gate and subsequent opening of the aircraft door; the flight crew promptly disembarked to inspect the damage and assess the situation. The headset operator involved in the pushback was no longer present in the vicinity.The root cause of the incident was procedural non-compliance by ground handling personnel; specifically:Failure to follow the standard pushback sequence; including the omission of any instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake.Initiation of towing equipment disconnection without clearance from the PIC.Premature disconnection attempt while two engines (1 and 2) remained unstarted.No injuries were reported.Suggestions: Reinforce ground personnel procedures and communications.
column123: After completing all ground checks on either; crew side and ground crew side; we started the push back procedure from gate XX in ZZZ; first by the broadcast where aircraft Y behind us was pushing back first. We meanwhile once cleared by the ground staff; pressurised the hydraulic and ran our before start checklist. After aircraft Y started taxiing; we then proceeded to make another call on the broadcast frequency and receiving no reply; determined it was safe for us to initiate the pushback. The ground crew initiated the pushback at XA:00. During the pushback; the PIC; using standard phraseology at all times; requested from the ground crew the authorisation to start engines; after an initial 'stanby by;' the clearance to start came while the aircraft was still in towing motion. While starting engine 3 and 4 on autostart; the plane came to a stop in what appeared to be an intermediate position; far from aligned with the taxiway 'aircraft offset on the left of the taxi lane with nose in by 20 to 30 degrees.' While monitoring the engine start; we heard nothing from the ground personnel nor any commands from them prompting us to think that the tow was still in progress to the final start stop 'E2 in that case.' The crew then felt a motion forward that would be similar to a tow then came again to a stop. Still awaiting any commands from the ground staff; we then finished to monitor engine 3 and 4 starts. The aircraft then sustained a mid to strong shake; again happening sometimes during a tow; came to a stop; to then a violent shock and a stop followed by a motion forward and yaw to the left.The ground personnel then eventually start talking ;shouting on the headset 'realease the brakes; release the brakes;' command that both startled us as not being able to have any idea of what was happening downstairs. Looking at the EICAS showing no 'parking brake set and the PIC feet that were not commanding any brakes; we asked the ground staff to confirm if he wanted the brakes to be set; where he simply yelled back "Brakes; brakes.'The PIC then set the parking brake and seeing the motion stopping; we realized that the ground personnel disconnected the equipment and the motion forward was induced by the engines and not commanded by the tug. During all that time; the mic of the ground staff remained open and we could eventually hear the staff on the headset verbally confirming 'I [expletive] up man; i [expletive] up' to his co-worker driving the tug. Following this; the ground supervisor came to take charge of the tow; assess the situation and tow us back to the gate. It is important to note that at this moment while we are still waiting in the cockpit to clearly understand what happened; that the towing personal in charge of the headset left the scene; and the tug and tow bar involved in the incident also were removed and swapped from the scene. After confirming damages to the NLDG; the new staff then proceeded to tow us safely back to the gate to asses damages. Notes : - After confirming that a report on their end will be completed; the ground supervisor 'who promised to come back with the involved staff;' never came back to the aircraft. - The crew nor the onboard mechanics; never had a chance to see the involved tow bar. - Nor the crew or the onboard mechanics had a chance to see or talk to the involved personal.Potential causing factors. - Lack of standardization from the ground personal using wrong phraseology in normal and under pressure situation. - Heavy breach of SOPs on the ground crew side that did not respect the standard actions and calls on the following :     - Never asked for the parking brake to be set nor confirmed or established communication about this subject with the flight crew.    - Initiated a disconnection of the tug and tow bar; during engine start while SOPs assert that a disconnection cannot be initiated without consent and positive contact from a flight crew member after the parking brakeis set and all engines are started and stabilized; with parking brake confirmed by the PIC 'verbally and on the EICAS' and visually confirmed by a light on the NLDG.    - Used under panic; incorrect terminology; making the situation worse.    - ultimately damaged the equipment by incorrect actions.It is important and fortunate to note in this situation that nobody on the ground got injured by what could have been; really fast; a life threatening situation and/or causing further damages to neighboring aircraft's or equipment. Reinforce the strict adherence to SOPs and sequences at all times and circumstances to mitigate potential risks. While it is impossible to judge at that precise time in the process; if a motion of the aircraft is provoked or unwanted; the only solution would have been a clear communication from the ground staff.Suggestions: Review and reinforcement of SOPs and safety procedures for all ground personnel during towing operations; with an emphasis given to the fact that flight crew on specific aircraft cannot see the ground crew operate."

However; it is possible that I missed it after takeoff. We did a TO-1 (max power) takeoff due to approaching storms which often kicks the packs offline. column121: Immediately after executing a base leg turn from downwind for RWY XX; inside long downwind base traffic; at approximately 400-500ft AGL; I observed Helicopter final traffic to my immediate right; west of the field at approximately 300ft AGL.  Last I saw this traffic I was ahead of them and from my sight view there would be no traffic conflict caused by my early base turn to final.  I did not hear the helicopter traffic's base and final radio calls for the midfield grass area for landing; due to my passenger stepping on the radio call over Intercommunications Systems (ICS).My early turn to base/final; coupled with the missed radio calls created the potential for a midair collision between my aircraft and the helicopter final traffic. Early turns to final with potential conflicting traffic should be avoided at all times if traffic is not seen.  Additionally; no turn to base should be initiated until final traffic is clear.  It is better to avoid the early turn to final and extend the downwind than risk a potential for midair collision.Enhance lookout doctrine for traffic closer into to the field; especially helicopter traffic routinely operating at the field; not just the traffic you are attempting to turn inside of.  Additionally; avoid turns inside of other traffic; even if sufficient space is available.Brief the importance of a sterile cockpit for ICS communications with passengers to avoid blocked radio calls from other traffic; Emergency calls only.Even though in the landing phase minimize overflight of airport hangars and buildings.  To minimize risk for other personnel and equipment in the event of unexpected aircraft emergencies.

I verified we were not over any houses or people before performing the turn. While in the turn we lost more altitude then expected and exited on final around 500 feet. In the debrief I discussed that this maneuver was a nonstandard maneuver and shouldn't have been done unless we had actually had an engine failure. This maneuver could have been dangerous given how low we were. In the future I will advise students that the 360 could be an option but I won't demonstrate it at those altitudes. I got too low because I started the 360 from too low of an altitude initially. This discussion was caused by my fixation on demonstrating the importance of flying the aircraft; setting up for a good approach; and hitting your desired touchdown area under positive control during an emergency scenario. I also felt that the student had resignation over being high and I wanted to prove that there were still things we could do to get a positive outcome.

column121: The flight diverted to ZZZ1 due to increasing crosswind gusts at the destination and a developing fuel margin concern.During preflight planning; a threat-forward approach was used. The First Officer; dispatcher; and I evaluated the original flight plan; which had us landing near maximum gross weight with no alternate listed. Additionally; forecast gusts at the destination were near the aircraft's Flight Manual maximum crosswind limits. Given these conditions; we coordinated with dispatch to revise the plan to include a suitable alternate with improved margins. A thorough fuel and performance discussion was conducted during the approach briefing; including crosswind limits; landing performance with gust factors; and contingency planning should a go-around become necessary.The approach was conducted in high velocity; gusty crosswind conditions. The approach was primarily in IMC. Appropriate precautions were taken to balance gust additives with stopping distance considerations. The approach was turbulent; careful automation management was utilized to maximize pilot Situational Awareness. Below approximately 500 feet AGL; high crosswind gusts appeared to increase significantly and momentarily; requiring large control inputs; to maintain the desired flight path while remaining within stabilized approach criteria. During the flare; at approximately 20-10 feet AGL; with thrust just brought to idle; the aircraft encountered a strong sustained lateral gust that required substantial control inputs to maintain runway centerline. Simultaneously; the gust produced a noticeable performance increase; resulting in altitude gain of 20-30 feet. Based on recent performance training and anticipating the potential for an equally rapid loss of performance as the gust potentially subsided; along with the risk of airspeed decreasing below Lowest Selectable Speed; I immediately initiated a go-around. The gust began to subside and the aircraft did appear to momentarily descend.During the maneuver; careful attention was paid to pitch attitude to mitigate tail strike risk. Flap retraction and pitch changes were managed deliberately; ensuring a positive rate of climb prior to significant changes.Given that a possible go-around scenario had been thoroughly briefed in the context of our general fuel state; the wind conditions; and considering the largely IMC conditions associated with lower ceilings on the approach end of the field; the crew recognized that a second attempt (if unsuccessful) would introduce downstream fuel concerns. After coordinating and assessing the situation; we elected to divert to ZZZ1.The diversion was conducted in a smooth and controlled manner. The FOM diversion guide was utilized. Dispatch was notified. The crew was very efficient; having thoroughly discussed and prepared for this possibility during the threat forward departure and approach briefing. Threat forward briefings; and recent performance training were pillars in insuring a safe outcome. The diversion recovery guide was utilized upon landing. We departed ZZZ1 with additional fuel; and landed in ZZZ uneventfully.

The CA was flying and the FO was monitoring.  Conditions were VMC and the flight was under IFR control by Denver Center.  The crew had been working well together over the previous days and continued to after this event.On extended vectors after the previous aircraft had not canceled their clearance upon landing; Aircraft X was level at 14;000 feet to the north west of GEJYU flying direct to GEJYU when cleared the approach ILS 17.  Not expecting to be vectored as far north as they were; the crew had loaded the approach starting at MEYRS which included a crossing restriction at GEJYU of +12;300.  About 6NM prior to reaching GEJYU the crew initiated a descent to cross GEJYU at 12;300 in approach mode with 8100 selected in the altitude window.  About 3NM prior to GEJYU Center asked if the crew was established on the approach.  The CA matched the aircraft's course to the course on the approach plate and believed the aircraft to be within the RNP 1 bounds of the DIRDY to GEYJU leg and its lower +11;000 restriction.  The CA replied in the affirmative and confirmed that terrain was in sight; which the FO relayed to Center.  Center then directed the crew to maintain 14;000 until reaching GEJYU.  The crew immediately commanded a level-off passing 12;800 and was level at 12;500.  The CA momentarily selected a positive VSI to initiate a climb before canceling it as the plane neared GEJYU where a further descent would be required to fly the approach.  The approach and landing was conducted without event after GEJYU.After parking the aircraft the crew discussed the event and concluded that; even if the aircraft was on the DIRDY-GEJYU leg; the approach clearance began at GEJYU and so they should not have descended until crossing GEJYU (as required by FAR 121.659(a) and FOM.  Moreover; even if they had been cleared the approach from DIRDY; the flight computer was not loaded with DIRDY as the feeder fix so determining when established on the RNAV portion of the approach would be; at best; difficult and counter to the FOM which directs that RNAV procedures be selectable in the FMC and flown using autopilot or flight director guidance.  In heat of the moment; while monitoring area traffic at a non-towered airport; with the field and terrain well in sight the crew inadvertently got head of themselves did not comply the IFR established approach requirements.

column121: After climbing through FL200 we were checking our systems pages and noticed there were xx in place of the volts reading for both generators. Shortly after; the First Officer noticed his flight director had failed as well as some data on the PFD and ND. We came to the conclusion that it could be an ADC fault even though it was unannounced. He selected the FD and ADC switches on the switching panel to recover data. Having lost the ADC; we found we were unable RVSM and began a descent to FL270. During descent we heard a boom and looked at each other thinking it could be a load shift; however; the lower forward cargo door light came on as well as the Lower Forward Cargo Door ECAM message. We felt an irregular cabin pressure. We also received a pack 1 fault and Bleed air fault with the cargo door ECAM message. We donned our oxygen masks and requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ where we landed uneventfully. We performed all required checklists and my decision was the cargo door was not safe. Per the checklist one of two choices; abnormal cabin rate; with accompanying door light confirmed diverting was the safest option.
column123: I was pilot monitoring during this flight.  As we climbed through FL200 we scanned the systems pages and noticed XX in place where the generator volts should read.  Shortly after we required anti-ice and got the #1 Air Bleed fault ECAM message and followed the checklist reseting the switch.  The fault reset and we continued to climb to FL300.  After level off we were no longer using anti-ice and got the #1 Air Bleed fault a second time and again it reset.  The FO then noticed multiple data missing on the Navigation Display and the Primary Flight Display.  The Captain took the radios while flying as the FO connected the dots of the data lost in the AOM to a possible Air Data Computer #2 fault that was not annunciated on ECAM.  Following the recommendations in the QRH the FO was able to get the Flight Director and ADC instruments back switching to the Captains side.  After discussion on RVSM compliance we notified ATC we were no longer compliant and were given a descent to FL270.  Around this time while descending and still working clean up on checklists we both heard a loud bang and immediately thought a possible load shift of cargo possible.  We noticed a shift in pressure in the cockpit and received a new message on ECAM for Lower Fwd Cabin Cargo Door open with an accompanying #1 Air Bleed fault and Pack #1 fault message.  The Captain maintained flying and the radios while the FO continued running checklists.  With the change in pressure we felt and confirmation from the sound we heard we donned oxygen masks; requested priority handling; and followed the checklist to descend to 10;000ft.  We were over ZZZ at the time and elected the safest course of action to divert into ZZZ.  The approach and landing into the airport was uneventful and we were met with the EMTs to confirm we didnt have any effects of decompression.

When we switched from tower to departure; ATC mentioned we were low; due to terrain. The non flying pilot mentioned we were VFR and had the terrain in sight. At the same time our attention was diverted on the climb due to GA traffic. We were asking for vectors to avoid traffic. We had the traffic in sight and were clear of the traffic. It was a little late; but we finally got a climb and a turn from ATC. Noticed immediately upon switching from tower to SoCal.Cause: Late communication in a traffic saturated air space; on a short flight from VNY to ZZZIdentified traffic visually; and remained clear; and complied with ATC vector and climbSuggestions: Upon debriefing with other pilot; we recognized lack of communication between pilots and ATC. ATC was busy with GA traffic; and we were distracted by identifying traffic to remain clear of.

column121: Arriving in darkness after tower closed into ZZZ we were cleared for the RNAV Visual XXR as we requested direct ZZZZZ. This to avoid the no transgression upwind runway XX/R area. 2 things happened that could have been done better. We approached a bit fast for being under the Class B shelf of 5000 and this contributed to a steeper than normal descent rate to get down to at or above 4500 at ZZZZZ to establish on the glide path for the approach. Not exactly sure what transpired with the mode control as I was more concerned with being outside the aircraft for terrain and traffic avoidance and my co-pilot was flying. Additionally I was canceling with Approach; getting a phone number to contact them for clearance/cancellation on the ground and preparing to switch to  CTAF. My co-pilot was being proactive to get us down and capture the glide path and get us slowed down. At one point the descent angle and rate increased to a steeper than stabilized value which; to no surprise to both of us; activated the EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) SINK RATE; TOO LOW; PULL UP; to correct; which my co-pilot disconnected the Autopilot. We were still on the Downwind so we elected to continue the approach; which we completed without incident. However; with the APPR armed VNAV armed FMS showing captured we could not get a capture of the glidepath until 700 or so AGL. And we think this was also a contributing factor to why the plane did not arrest the rapid descent rate that set off the EGPWS previously. Again FMS was capture on the mode selector scoreboard; but perhaps we were not close enough to the course to capture the vertical guidance. Either way; VMC prevailed and there was never the perception that there was a CFIT risk. However we could have done better not to set off the EGPWS and that our speed may have been slightly above 200 under the class B at one point or another during the descent. And we were a bit confused as to why the plane did not capture the vertical guidance and why it steepened its descent rate right before the EGPWS warning.Suggestions: We will endeavor to approach ZZZ from the south at a slower speed for the Class B shelfs and to allow for more time to descend and capture. Additionally; we tried to adhere to the attention all users guidance to avoid the XXR/L Upwind. But I couldn't help thinking that it might have been better to track the course completely from ZZZZZ1 off the arrival and cut through this non transgression zone; especially since it was after tower was closed with little to no traffic. That way we could have been flying a prescribed course and altitude from the get go ; giving us more time to concentrate on configuring etc. As it was my primary focus was CFIT awareness given the fact that we were maneuvering visually to the direct ZZZZZ to avoid the no transgression zone. We were on frequency and the EGPWS occurred around XA:29. Incidentally we offered to to preposition earlier than scheduled during daylight and prior to the 3 hour sit in ZZZ; but we were backing up trips on the coast and it was determined best to wait to ferry from ZZZ to avoid possible double ferry legs.
column123: On Day 0 around XA:32 local time in Aircraft X we experienced a GPWS event where the PULL UP" command was annunciated. We were transitioning from the ZZZZZX arrival to the RNAV VISUAL XXR into ZZZ. We were instructed to depart the arrival structure and proceed direct to ZZZZZ waypoint on the RNAV VISUAL approach.  NAV with FMS; VNAV; APPROACH; along with AUTO THROTTLES and AUTOPILOT were armed.  When we were issued the direct to ZZZZZ; VERTICAL SPEED was added so that we could increase our rate of decent to be a little closer to the 4500' at ZZZZZ.  I recall the captain was on com2 when the instruction to fly direct ZZZZZ and cleared the visual approach was issued.  Lateral navigation and vertical navigation were stable; but as we approached ZZZZZ the aircraft increased its descent rate significantly.  I was monitoring the instruments trying understand what the avionics were trying to do.  The captain then indicated that I need to arrest the descent as to prevent a GWPS event; as I reached up to disconnect the autopilot and correct the pitch we got the PULL UP annunciation; and responded in kind; and the annunciation quickly went away.  We were in VMC and continued the downwind and approach via raw data and reference to the approach plate.  As we turned base I noticed the command bars on the Flight director were indicating an extreme pitch down and turn to the left.  Prior to departure from ZZZ1; we did a full departure and arrival brief with a focus on the "all users page" for the RNAV visual to XXR  and discussed FQOA concerns.  One of the biggest factors that lead to this event was my low experience in this aircraft.  Normally; when an aircraft responds in an unexpected expected manner I immediately disconnect the autopilot and hand fly; but in this case I wanted to gain insight to what the jet was doing in this situation.  The initial sensation of the event mimicked a configuration change from flaps 2 to full flaps and then progressed to a steeper descent.  There was no configuration change taking place.  Another contributing factor was speed.  We were in excess of 200 knots approaching ZZZZZ waypoint requiring a steeper descent; but not the rate which triggered the GPWS response.Also; when cleared to descend from our last assigned altitude to commence the approach; I just spun the Altitude select down to an arbitrary altitude; just to start the descent.  I will never do that again.  The Captain was on Com 2 when this happened.My main concern is; although I am aware that this can happen; I still do not know why this situation developed.Suggestions include improvements on my performance; which include slowing the aircraft down sooner; being proactively particular on setting the AAD in all situations; and quicker response to unexpected flight path situations."

column121: Taxiing on inner line to spot XX at CLT west ramp our clearance was spot XX to join the line to 5W. Approaching the spot I looked left and didn't see anything. We were slowing to make a right turn and the FO said clear right. I looked left to say clear left and saw Aircraft Y approaching which appeared close and I applied brakes. Firm at first then eased off. We sat at the spot for a minute and the Aircraft Y pilot asked ramp controller what going on. Who was giving way and why weren't they notified. Ramp controller said that she didn't think Aircraft Y was going to turn the corner that fast and it wasn't going to be an issue. Well it was. The ramp controller told Aircraft Y to give way to us and we proceeded to take off. I didn't call the cabin to see if everyone was ok. I thought they would call us if something was wrong. We flew to ZZZ without incident and had normal communications with the cabin. After shut down and leaving the flight deck a couple of F/A's asked what happened taxiing in CLT. When we got to the top of the bridge by the gate we told them what happened. The number 1 said she bumped her arm in the galley and the number 3 bumped her head. The number 2 said her back hit the galley wall. I asked why they didn't call us in CLT. They were preparing for takeoff was the answer I got. I asked if anyone needed medical attention and was told not yet. I called dispatch per the FOM for a follow up since everyone was able to preform their duties.Cause: Ramp control to give specific instructions as to who is following who. Communication from the cabin telling us they were injured before we depart. Not after completing the flight.
column123: When departing the west ramp from the gate in Charlotte we received instructions to taxi to spot XX; then join the line to 5W and contact ground. As we approached spot XX I looked out the right windows to make sure we were clear for the turn on to the line. After I said clear right" the captain applied the brakes as there was Aircraft Y coming from our left. The braking was firm but did not seem like it was an aggressive or instantaneous stop; especially as it appeared we were at an appropriate speed to begin the turn on to the line. There was confusion as to which aircraft was to proceed. Aircraft Y was first to ask; and ramp told the jet to let us go first; and ramp admitted that they didn't expect Aircraft Y to have caught up to us so quickly. We continued our taxi and the flight resumed as normal. Only after landing did the flight attendants ask about the firm braking in CLT; and then explained that the 1; 2; and 3 FAs had potential injuries. The captain asked if anyone needed medical attention; and none of the FAs said they did at that time. The FAs did not mention any issues or injuries during the flight; even during cruise communications to discuss en-route turbulence. Cause: If ramp had given instruction to either us or Aircraft Y to clarify which aircraft would be first then we could have avoided any confusion. The braking did not feel hard enough that I would have thought any injuries would have occurred; otherwise we would have called back to check if everyone was ok. It would have also been helpful to have had a call from the flight attendants if there were any concerns until waiting after landing."

column121: Flight was dispatched with MEL 24-XXX (inoperative IDG (Integrated Drive Generator)) configuration requiring use of APU during flight as a secondary electrical power source. Approx 120 West of ZZZ APU failed in flight. QRH requires land ASAP with one power source; several attempts to restart APU were unsuccessful. While discussing our diversion a ACARS was sent to our dispatcher to coordinate/discuss our intentions. After receiving an additional ECAM (ECAM IDG 1 OIL OVERHEAT) and noted IDG#1 temperature increasing; IDG#1 was disconnected per the second ECAM and we requested priority handling with the decision that we would be diverting to ZZZ. During the descent dispatch acknowledged our status and suggested a diversion to ZZZ but in the interest of safety (after the overheat msg) we decided to not fly further than required. A normal precautionary landing was made with a taxi to the gate. FO was the flying pilot and did an excellent job having the diversion airport/approach and a few ATC calls handled during time period I briefed the Flight Attendants and advised the passengers about our diversion; his efficiency was very much appreciated and he completely reduced my workload during a very short time frame from cruise at altitude to landing.
column123: We were dispatched that day with MEL 24-XXX which was an imperative #1 IDG (Integrated Drive Generator). Per the MEL we were able to depart with the APU continuously running to provide backup electrical power and generator. While in cruise flight at FL330 (max altitude per the MEL) and approx 120 miles west of ZZZ the APU  performed an auto shutdown. The FO announced my aircraft and took over radio communication with ATC while the CA ran the ECAM and subsequent QRH. The QRH led him to attempt a restart of the APU which was momentarily successful (less than a minute). The FO then began to look for nearest suitable airport to divert to per the QRH. At that time ZZZ was directly in front of the flight path and less than 200nm away. The FO asked for a decent to FL270 and was granted this by ATC whom was then notified by the FO that the flight was requesting priority handling and likely diverting to ZZZ. The CA agreed that was the nearest suitable airport and related this information to dispatch via ACARS message. At FL270 the CA attempted another APU restart which was unsuccessful. While descending out of FL240 a third and final APU restart attempt was made but unsuccessful. The FO continued to fly to ZZZ via new ATC clearance of direct and set up the MCDU (Multi-purpose Control Display Unit) for an ILS to runway XXR and entered the performance information for arriving at ZZZ. The CA made a call the inform the FAs of the diversion and made an announcement to the pax regarding the diversion. At this time the FO noticed IDG temperature of the #1 IDG began rising continuously until an ECAM message alerted the crew of IDG #1 OILOVRHEAT. The FO checked the reference sheet to ensure this was not a quick action item and not an ECAM exception. After verifying the ECAM was nether; he ran the ECAM procedures while conferring with the CA on each item. This led to a disconnection of IDG #1. After ECAM actions were complete a decent checklist was initiated by the CA and a normal precautionary landing was made at ZZZ runway XXR. We were able to taxi on our own power to the gate where we parked; shutdown; and all pax got off the aircraft for rebooking.Cause: APU failure caused our aircraft to be reduced to sickle stage electrical system. Increasing IDG temp on the #1 IDG resulted in ECAM that directed us to disconnect the #1 IDG. Mitigation suggestion would have been to shut down the APU whole on the ground in ZZZ1 to reduce its workload.

column121: We were on a heading of 065 between two lines of weather to intercept the XXL localizer between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 at 7-8;000 feet with an assigned speed of 200 knots configured to flap 1. We were assigned 4;000 feet with at least a 45 knot tailwind trending high. I advised the FO to keep coming down due to the tailwind. He extended the speed brakes fully. ATC then assigned us 180 knots. I acknowledged the clearance then got distracted by something. The FO slowed to 180 knots which was about 5 knots below flaps 1 maneuvering speed. We hit a gust and had a momentary stick shaker which I called out. I realized the situation and moved the flaps to 5. The rest of the flight was relatively uneventful. (LLWS advisories).
column123: We were flying the ZZZZZ2 arrival from ZZZ. Prior to commencing the STAR; multiple ATIS updates indicated rain conditions at the airport.At approximately 12;000 FT; ATC began providing radar vectors and advised that two preceding aircraft had executed go-arounds due to wind shear. We were assigned a heading of 065°; which positioned us between two lines of weather. We subsequently received vectors to intercept the ILS for runway XXL.While descending through 8;000 FT; ATC instructed us to reduce speed to 200 knots. I had already requested Flaps 1 in anticipation of slowing below 220 knots. At that point; I observed significant airspeed fluctuations caused by a tailwind component in excess of 45 knots that continued to increase. I was required to make multiple vertical speed (V/S) interventions because the speed brakes alone were insufficient to achieve and maintain the assigned speed.ATC was delayed several times in issuing further descent clearances due to multiple aircraft ahead executing go-arounds; resulting in us being slightly high on the approach. When ATC subsequently directed a reduction to 180 knots; the airspeed oscillations remained pronounced; and the stick shaker activated for approximately one second. Flaps 5 were promptly selected; and the remainder of the approach was flown in accordance with standard operating procedures.The aircraft was landed safely on runway XXL despite the challenging weather conditions. No further anomalies were noted.I am submitting this report to document the event and support any safety review or analysis.

column121: Maintenance had signed off the aircraft for an intermittent pax (Passenger) door indication which was written up by the previous crew. During the climb out we noticed our ears continuously popping and that the pressure didn't seem normal. CA asked me to reduce my rate of climb as we had been cleared to climb to 18;000 ft. At 10;000 we got the CABIN ALT caution message; this is when CA advise ATC we would need to level off. CA assumed PF duties and we advised ATC we would need to run our checklist which is when we entered the hold. After running the QRH for CABIN ALT we determined we would return to ZZZ. We staid in the hold while we re configured the aircraft for an approach into ZZZ. After getting our data and briefing the approach and FAs we made our way back to the field. Since we caught the pressurization issue early and did not continue climbing; we did not declare an emergency. Our return to ZZZ was uneventful and maintenance met us at the gate. After correcting the issue and running a few verification test we were able to depart a few hours later.Cause: The aircraft did not pressurize during the climb out.Suggestion: Maintenance could have verified the pressurization prior to signing off.
column123: On Day 0 at approximately XA00 we were operating flight ABCD ZZZ to ZZZ1. Maintenance had signed off the aircraft for an intermittent pax (Passenger) door indication written up by the previous crew. On the climb out we started to feel pressure that didn't seem normal and I asked my FO who was the pilot flying to reduce her climb. We were cleared to I believe 18;000 but at 10;000 we got the cabin alt" caution message. I advised ATC we needed to level off and we did at 10;000 feet. I took control of the aircraft and we ran the QRH for the "cabin alt". We advised ATC that we would be returning to ZZZ but we needed a few minutes to get ready. We entered a hold and ran all of our checks and briefings. Since we caught the issue early and didn't continue climbing; which would have created a bigger problem; we did not declare an emergency. Then we advised ATC we were ready to return to ZZZ where we landed without further incident. ATC did a great job handling us and my FO and FAs did terrific dealing with the situation. After maintenance corrected the issue several hours later we were able to board back up and complete the flight.Cause: The aircraft did not pressurize as it should have during climb out.Suggestion: After we returned to the gate the maintenance crew did a pressurization check. They saw the aircraft was not pressurizing. They corrected the issue after several hours."
