column121: On the date of the event; the flight departed ZZZ1 en route to ZZZ. During the initial climb; at approximately 1;300 feet AGL; the aircraft received a windshear warning. The windshear escape maneuver was executed in accordance with company procedures; including the application of maximum thrust. I assumed control of the aircraft from the First Officer during the maneuver. Once the aircraft was clear of the windshear condition and stabilized; ATC was notified of the event; and a PIREP was issued for traffic in the area. Control was then returned to the First Officer.During the enroute phase; weather conditions along the route and at the destination were continuously monitored. Given the reported gusty winds;  I elected to assume pilot flying duties for the landing.Transfer of control occurred during cruise flight. At that time; the autopilot was transferred to the Captain's flight director; and the transponder was switched from position 2 to position 1; allowing ADC 1 to provide the associated data.The approach to RWY XX at ZZZ was stabilized by 1;000 feet AGL. Surface winds were reported as approximately 160 degrees at 13 knots; gusting to 23 knots. The runway was wet; with braking action reported as good (5/5/5). The calculated gust crosswind component for RWY XX remained within the CRJ-200 published crosswind limitations of 27 knots throughout the approach and landing attempt.During the flare at approximately 10 feet AGL; with thrust at idle per normal procedure; the aircraft encountered a sudden and severe wind disturbance consistent with windshear or a strong localized microburst. This resulted in a rapid uncommand roll displacement; with the left wing rising and the right wing dropping. Control inputs were applied as trained to counteract the roll and maintain alignment with the runway. Within approximately less than 2 seconds; a second abrupt wind disturbance occurred during the same low-altitude flare regime.As a direct result of these sequential; uncommand wind disturbances in the flare; the left wingtip contacted the runway surface momentarily. The landing was completed without further incident; the aircraft was decelerated normally; and it taxied to the FBO at ZZZ under its own power.A post-flight walkaround inspection revealed damage to the left wingtip.This report is submitted solely to document the sequence of events; the prevailing environmental conditions (including low-level wind disturbances/gusts); and to support identification and mitigation of potential hazards associated with similar windshear/gust encounters during the critical flare phase on the CRJ-200 in gusty; wet runway conditions.
column123: We departed from runway XZ; out of ZZZ1. We did a flaps 20 takeoff. We climbed out on a heading of 079 and climbed greater than 600fpm. The ceiling was 800 overcast and visibility was 3 sm. As we reached 1300 ft above the ground; we got a 'wind shear warning' message. We performed the wind shear escape maneuver; and resumed our climb. We then advised ATC to report the wind shear out of ZZZ1; and they did. As we got closer; the weather was deteriorating. We briefed this on the ground so we were expecting it. There were storms along the route. As we got closer; we re-ran the landing distance numbers. We saw that with a wet runway; we were going to be too heavy to land on runway XY into ZZZ. We decided to go with runway XX. The crosswind component was 23 kts; which is in legal limits for a wet runway. We got the updated weather which was '1'. We decided to perform a risk assessment and I decided to transfer the controls to the captain. We transferred the autopilot and the transponder to the captain side. Controls were transferred in cruise. The approach was briefed already; so we continued on to the descent and approach as normal; for the RNAV XX. Winds were 160@13G23.  We were stable at 1000ft. I made the appropriate callouts during descent. I then called runway in sight and we continued in for landing. At 10 ft above the ground we were idle and in our flare. We had two wind shear encounters within a few seconds. The left wing ended up touching the ground. We parked at the FBO and did a walk around and discovered the wingtip strike. We reported the winds shear to the tower.

column121: While cruising at 5500 ft on a heading of 110 I noticed an aircraft; Aircraft Y; on ADS-B that was traveling on an approximately 150-180 heading and would appear to be on an intercept to my course. ADS-B data showed the plane had come from the direction of N82; I noticed that the aircraft was continuing to climb on that course; as I was 'on the right' I would have had the right of way in this scenario. When I gained a visual they were approx. 500 ft below with no change in course or climb rate; with this I began an emergency climb to avoid this aircraft when the GTN650 collision avoidance began to alert. I also took evasive action and turned to position myself out of their path. This aircraft ended up flying directly under me; about 300ft below and horizontally by approx. 2-300 ft. then continued at an altitude of 5500. I am sure that we could have been extremely close to or could have collided if no action was taken and I did not have ADSB-in. I believe that the other aircraft's lack of situational; or visual awareness was a direct factor; and if not; a blatant disregard for; or perhaps a lack of knowledge of; aviation collision avoidance rules. I confidently say that ADS-B; and particularly ADSB-IN was responsible for the safe and uneventful outcome of the situation. Maintaining visual and situational awareness at all times is extremely important for all aviators as well as knowledge of how to handle close encounters such as these.

column121: When cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival to ZZZ; I read back the clearance and the altimeter setting and subsequently entered the altimeter setting in the standby attitude indicator. When we completed the descent checklist we used the altimeter setting set in the standby attitude indicator for each PFD (Primary Flight Display). Just outside of the FAF the FO disconnected the autopilot and the auto throttle as was previously briefed. Inside the final approach fix and somewhere between approximately 500 and 1000 feet the FO asked me if I thought it looked like the automation was bringing us in on a very shallow approach. I agreed and instructed the FO to maintain our altitude and transition to the PAPI. The FO re-intercepted the glideslope and landed without incident.Cause: When we were on the ground we realized that I had input a much higher altimeter setting in the standby attitude indicator which we later used for both PFD altimeter settings thus causing us to fly lower than the automation believed we were at.Suggestions:--In the future I'll write down the altimeter setting from the ATIS or weather request and cross check it with the altimeter setting given on the arrival. If the setting is close then I'll use it for reference in the standby attitude indicator. If it's significantly off then I'll use the predetermined altimeter setting and query the controller.

Which caused issues later on approach. After reaching 4000 feet with stable cabin pressure we entered a hold to burn gas to get below max landing weight. During which time checklists; communications and procedures were completed. The CA who was initially PF for the flight had me as PM take over due to his recent time off. The autopilot was on the CA side after exchange of controls. During the approach I had the autopilot captured the localizer in white needles due to the crosswind; and at approx 12 mile final switched to green needles and the LOC captured. At the minimum glide slope intersect the GS captured but the autopilot did not descend despite the GS mode being captured which causes the aircraft to be high on approach. As PF I disconnected the autopilot and flew the approach visually which allowed for the aircraft to be back on the glide path and stabilized by 1000 feet for stabilized approach criteria.Cause: High workload and task saturation due to high stress from pressurization loss and diversion. The transfer of controls should have included the autopilot and transponder as required by Standard operating Procedure.Suggestions: In the future despite workload I will make sure to check the autopilot side in my scan.
column123: During cruise at FL290 heard loud sound from behind fight deck. Checked door and pressurization synoptics and all systems were showing normal. The ramp is uncontrolled and the ground crew did not push us back far enough that we were able to make the turn without crossing the zipper road.Once we completed the after start checklist; we advised ground and confirmed taxi instructions to the de-ice are. I looked and cleared right; looked left; then checked to make sure the Radio Tuning Unit (RTU) was on the correct frequency. As I looked back to the right; a de-ice truck was approximately 30-45 degrees off the right side of the airplane. I called 'Deice Truck right side' and started to put my feet on the pedals when the Captain hit the brakes. The deice truck went off the zipper road into the gate area to avoid us; and was traveling approximately 25-30 mph.As the airplane came to an abrupt stop; I heard a grunting noise from the cabin. We immediately advised ground control of the incident and the Captain called the flight attendants to see if they were injured. I could overhear the Captain ask about how the flight attendants hit the ground; and we started the process of deciding to gate return.After confirming with several people from ops; duty pilot; and the flight attendants; the flight went on without further incident. It should be noted that both Flight Attendants were the ones who had and made the final decision to continue the flight. Upon arrival at our destination we asked that paramedics meet us at the gate to ensure there was not any unseen injuries; or any other medical issues that could arise.One Flight Attendant was taken to the hospital and the other was released and continued on with the rest of their flying schedule. Suggestions: Push the airplane back further; retrain the driver of the truck.
column123: We were in front of and nose to the zipper road in ZZZ gate XX. We had just completed after start checklist and cleared both left and right sides and I had just began to make the hard left turn to join the ramp lane  behind us to go de ice. We were single engine. After fo cleared right side visually and verbalized and I looked left and verbally cleared my side I glanced back straight ahead and slightly right to ensure we would clear the ramp equipment in the turn when we were at about a 40 degree angle to the zipper road at this point and we would.it was then out of my right periphery that I saw the de ice truck zoom at about what I estimated 25-30 mph off our Immediate right hand side  at a sharp angle and from slightly behind us to the other size of the zipper road which we were on the immediate other side of. At the same instant the fo saw it as well and verbalized its presence. I had no option and was already applying the brakes. We were moving maybe 2-3 knots as we had only just began to make the turn. The plane decelerated very quickly and I heard a thump noise in back. I immediately set the brake advised ground we would be stopped for a bit and what had happened and then called the FAs in the back to see if there were injuries. Person A advised me they had hit the wall but was ok but that Person B had fallen into the wall and hit her head. She was able to come on the interphone and advised she had fallen into the wall by the emergency exit and hit her head I asked if she needed medical attention and she advised she did but wanted to continue and that she was now seated. I advised them to sit for a few minutes while I figured out a plan on what to do. I called dispatch / duty pilot to build my team and advised them what happened; dispatch  listened to my call with the duty pilot. Duty pilot advised that if they said no to medical in ZZZ and that they wanted to continue we needed to continue. I acknowledged. I talked about it with my FO.I called back to them to get more info on their injuries. I believe I asked if they had worsened or if the were bleeding they said they had/were not and that Person B had an ice pack on her ear. I again reiterated that if they wanted medical attention any way In ZZZ that we could just pull back into the gate and have paramedics check them out. Person B refused said she wanted to go. Person A said that they had also wanted to see medical as well when we arrived at our destination because they had hit their back and shoulder but that they did not want to go back to the gate to ZZZ. I again triple checked with them that they were refusing medical in ZZZ and wanted to continue as we could gate return as I was somewhat uneasy departing ZZZ under the circumstances but i talked about it with the team that i had built and the FAs and went with the consensus and departed. Rest of flight was uneventful and we requested paramedics / customer service meet us at the gate at our destination; which they did. Person A worked their next flight and I believe Person B went to the hospital with the paramedics. I believe the de ice truck cut the corner of the zipper road through the ramp from around the corner of the terminal at a high rate of speed and that why we did not see it. I could not see it at first because it came from an angle behind it off our right. I judged I had no option but to hit the brakes in that split second.Cause: Flight attendants were injured due to rapid declaration when I applied the brakes to avoid a de icing truck that went by us in close proximity and at a higher rate of speed while turning to taxi out of the ramp area. Our failure to see the vehicle approach us.Suggestions: Maybe ensure we as a crew double/ triple check left and right before taxiing.

column121: I was PIC in Aircraft X enroute to SBP cruising at 10;500ft approximately 40NM East of SBP. Flight conditions were clear VFR in stable air. I received an ADSB traffic warning 6 o'clock high. Observing the garmin display; and recorecting the zoom it appeared an aircraft was overtaking my position while descending from above me; with less than 700ft of vertical separation; and a 80knot closing rate. I identified the aircraft from it's ADSB transponder and made a radio call on 121.5 to that tail number; which received no response. I made a 45degree descending left turn down to 10;000ft until making visual contact with the aircraft. Due to the aircraft proximity during the evasive maneuver I did not have high fidelity situational awareness of the other aircraft's location until making visual contact. Aircraft Y had been enroute VFR from ZZZ to SBP on what appears to be a direct course at 12;500ft. Aircraft Y began its decent into SBP; at 174kt. At this time Aircraft X was 1.6NM ahead; 1000ft below and at 130kt. Aircraft Y accelerated to 210kt in the decent; making the closing speed at the incident 80kt.Aircraft X made an evasive descending right turn. There was a less than 200ft of vertical separation; less than 200ft of horizontal separation and Aircraft X was unable to make contact with Aircraft Y on 121.5. The evasive action allowed visual contact to be made; and both aircraft arrived without incident to SBP. In summary: Aircraft Y began an enroute decent; and accelerated during the denent. Uncertain of obstruction or telemetry inside the Aircraft Y aircraft; the pilot was likely unaware of the high speed overtake on the same course and position. Aircraft X was only able to identify the situation through ADSP and Garmin 275 display; and made evasive action avoiding a mid-air collision. It is recommended contact be made to the operator of Aircraft Y to discuss if the onboard ADSB equipment was able to identify the imminent collision; and if so were warning systems functional; to ensure the operator scans the airspace in front of the aircraft when making course/altitude changes; and to remind the operator maintaining auxiliary radios on 121.5 could have allowed air-to-air deconfliction over radio communications.

column121: The aircraft operated was under MEL for a failed B fire detection loop. A loop only selected per the MEL and tested ok on preflight. Shortly before reaching cruise altitude we noticed the fire loop A FAULT light flashing intermittently. A message was sent to dispatch and we were patched through to Maintenance Control. After some confusion in relaying the system failure due to poor radio connectivity we sent an ACARS to Maintenance Control explaining that we had a failed B fire loop and now a fault in the remaining A fire loop.  Maintenance Control advised it was Captain's discretion whether to continue the flight or not. After conferring with the FO we decided it would be better to divert back to ZZZ because we had no working engine fire detection system on either loop. Our thinking is that we had another 4 hours of flying ahead and it would be bad to continue since it would be possible to have an engine fire with no flight deck indication. We coordinated with ATC for a return to ZZZ and ran the appropriate checklists. Flight attendants and passengers were notified. We ran the checklist for overweight landing and opted to land on the longest runway; XXL; with auto brakes 2 to avoid hot brakes. We advised ATC that we wanted fire and rescue to examine the aircraft after landing to verify no smoke or fire on the brakes and no signs of an engine problem. ATC advised that if we wanted the trucks they would have to request priority handling for us. We agreed out of an abundance of caution to have fire and rescue look us over after landing. Subsequent approach and landing were uneventful. Upon exiting the runway post flight inspection showed no signs of engine problems or hot brakes. We taxied uneventfully to the gate. Maintenance entries were made for an overweight landing at 174;000 pounds and the failed fire detection loops.

column121: ZZZ was meant to be a fuel stop on our trip. When we fueled up and departed ZZZ; called for gear up; the gear handle raised but the gear did not retract.  We continued to climb to a safe altitude of 6000 feet and get vectors from the controller while we ran the checklist. The gear handle would not go back down to the 'gear down 'position for some time. Upon reaching the point of the 'gear will not retract' checklist; it called for gear handle down and with some force; the handle finally moved to the down position. The gear indicators throughout the entire time remained 'three green' down and locked. There was never a 'gear unsafe' red light illuminated. There was never a hyd pressure light illuminated to indicate pressure to gear . Never received any other abnormal indications.  Once sufficient fuel had been burnt off to make landing weight; we returned to ZZZ with Airport Rescue and Firefighting positioned   just in case. The landing was uneventful. Two days later we ferried plane for maintenance on a ferry permit. Crew was fine and passengers were sent another aircraft for remainder of their trip.Suggestions: The checklist for 'gear will not retract' addressed some of what we were seeing but not everything. Our concern was that the gear handle being left in the up position might cause a gear collapse on landing if left in that position. Luckily; we were able to move it back to the down and locked position.  With the gear handle down and the gear never having retracted; the checklist was complete.  I believe that ultimately the entire gear handle mechanism got replaced but would like to know for sure what failed in the system to cause this problem.

column121: Around 6;000 feet the auto throttle failed and I called for the Captain to cancel and identify. I asked the Captain to delay running the checklist until we got to 10;000 feet as it was busy. I was in controlling the throttle while monitoring the airspeed and the other instruments. After reaching 10;000 feet; the Captain completed the after take-off checklist and I took the radios and flight controls so he could focus on running the QRH. The Captain ran the QRH for AUTO THROTTLE FAIL" and we waited 10 seconds and attempted to reengage the auto throttles which remained failed. We decided to continue the flight to our destination without the use of the auto throttles. I gave the radios back to the Captain. The Captain notified ATC that we would need to amend our final cruising altitude as we were no longer able to enter RVSM. ATC then asked if we needed any assistance and the Captain replied "No". As we continued to climb and at approximately 14;000 to 15;000 feet the aircraft switched into Flight Path Angle (FPA) mode from FLCH mode. I tried re-engaging FLCH mode; with no success. I changed the FPA to 3 degrees up and started monitoring the VSI and ASI. Next the aircraft went into roll mode. I attempted to engage HDG (Heading) mode; with no success. Then the auto pilot disengaged. As we continued climbing through 16;000 feet; we received a Total Air Temperature (TAT) 2 failure message on the EICAS and we lost the FMS Speeds. We entered IMC and we received an icing conditions EICAS message. We were having multiple cascading failures that were increasing our workload while heading to our destination. We decided to return to the field. I leveled us off at 17;000 feet and the Captain requested a descent to exit icing conditions with vectors back to ZZZ. We were given a descent to 13;000 feet and a heading to return to the field.  The Captain briefed the flight attendants and built; bugged and briefed the RNAV approach to runway XXL into ZZZ. We regained FMS AIRSPEED; while descending through 10;000 feet.I hand flew the aircraft for the remainder of the flight and completed a successful landing without further incidence. The emergency equipment had not been requested; but they rolled the trucks as a precaution."

column121: During climbout from ZZZ; #1 engine vibrations fluctuated wildly; oscillating between 2.0 and 3.5.  High vibrations continued until power was reduced to maintain cruise altitude.  I contacted dispatch through VHF radio and we did a 3 way call between myself; dispatch; and Maintenance Control.  Maintenance informed us during the conference that the #1 engine had a recent history of several writeups for high vibrations and that there was a technical item assigned to that engine to track its performance.  I expressed my concern that this aircraft was assigned to a destination like ZZZ1 (our original destination) given its history.  The three of us agreed that it would be prudent to return to ZZZ given the limited contract maintenance available in ZZZ1 and the high terrain in the area that places a high demand on the engines  in the event of a go-around or takeoff from runway XX.  At the time we were about 6;000 lbs over max landing weight; so we coordinated with ATC to hold until we were under max landing and we returned to ZZZ.  Known history of bad performance on an engine that was also assigned to a destination which has limited contract maintenance.Aircraft with engines that have a recent history of questionable performance should not be assigned.  The lower display in the 737 should be turned on during the after takeoff checklist so that all secondary engine indications are displayed to catch this and other engine situations that slowly creep up on the crew.  The time to be prepared and do something is early before the situation arises; not when the display automatically pops up. This should be standardized across all Boeing fleets.
column123: I was performing PF duties flying Aircraft X from ZZZ Airport to ZZZ1. During climb out it was noticed that the left engine vibration was fluctuating. The CA; performing PM duties; and I each looked and noticed the engine vibration fluctuating in an erratic pattern. I noticed that the initial fluctuation grew from approximately 2.0-2.5 to 1.5-3.5 rapidly and unpredictably; while the right engine remained steady at approximately 0.2. As the PF; I scanned other instruments and all other indications seemed normal; we continued the climb while watching the engine vibrations. The CA opened and referenced the engine vibration checklist in the event we might need it; so that we would be prepared - however we did not perform the checklist as the fluctuations did not go out of limits.We had a brief discussion; which resulted in us not being able to say why the engine was vibrating like that; and that the captain could actually feel the vibration on his side of the cockpit. Shortly after the CA asked if I was comfortable handling the aircraft and radios so that he could try to call dispatch; to which I concurred.Around this time passing through FL280 and leveling at FL290; over Location X I assumed those duties. I noticed that the engine vibration fluctuations lessened but did not resolve at cruise power settings. As the Captain was working through his call to dispatch; I was focused on aviating; navigating; and communicating - having to work route deviations and climbs to avoid weather over Location X. I did note that when we climbed from FL290 to FL330 for weather; the engine vibration fluctuations increased at climb power as they had before - and settled a little lower but did not resolve at cruise power at FL330.I was able to hear a small portion of the conversation the Captain was having; most notably the discussion from the maintenance representative that this aircraft had some form of history of this engine vibration; and that there was a concurrence with dispatch that a return to ZZZ was prudent. The CA informed me after their call that we would return to ZZZ.It was my understanding having discussed with the CA after his call to dispatch that this return to ZZZ was based on there being a known history of fluctuating indications on the left engine for an unknown reason. Our discussions revolved around ZZZ1; the single engine profiles; performance; and potential for the engine to have some form of failure at the wrong moment on those complex departure procedures. After the decision to return to ZZZ the discussion was had weather to land overweight; or to burn down fuel to land under max landing weight. Based on: strong and gusty crosswinds; the potential to damage the aircraft landing heavy; the engine remaining within limits and settling lower at cruise power; I recommended to descend and burn down fuel in holding to below max landing weight; to which the CA agreed. We then returned to ZZZ uneventfully. An engine with a history of engine vibration presentation; which was fluctuating rapidly close to the upper limit. Engines with known issues such as this should not be dispatched. The lower display is turned off per SOP; however passing 10k this screen should be turned on to be monitored during the remainder of the flight.

column121: Just prior to beginning our descent we noticed the green hydraulic quantity was very low just above the amber. Once we started the descent just prior to the fix ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZX arrival; we got an amber HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR ECAM. I continued as PF while my Captain ran through the Ecam procedure. He had me fly the aircraft and run radios while he dealt with this procedure. We elected to level off and enter a hold over ZZZZZ to develop and analyze a plan. The ECAM had us shut down the green ENG 1 PUMP which displayed numerous inop systems; including the possibility of manual gear extension; gear retraction ; nosewheel steering; etc. After advising maintenance; Dispatch; and FA's we determined the best course of action was to request priority handling and divert to ZZZ. I continued flying while my Captain contacted ZZZ ops; reviewed procedure manual pages and briefed FA's of a precautionary landing in ZZZ. We notified ZZZ tower we would be stopping on the runway and would need possible tow off runway as well as Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) to give a quick inspection. Joining final for RWY XXL; we turned on GREEN ENG 1 PUMP as directed by the STATUS page APPR PROCEDURE. We regained back all our inop systems and the aircraft was operating as normal. We landed as normal; came to a stop; and the captain made a PA to the passenger notifying that ARFF would be inspecting the aircraft out of caution. We were able to taxi back to the gate under our own power with no further issues. Event was caused by hydraulic abnormalities. Only mitigation is to continue to be proficient in emergency procedures.
column123: Enroute we received a HYD G SYS LO PR ecam and other subsequent ecams. We performed the ecam methodology as trained. We entered a holding pattern between ZZZ1 and ZZZ. FO remained PF while I spoke with dispatch; ATC; FAs; and passengers. The decision was jointly made to divert to ZZZ; only 45 miles away at that point due to the long runway; acceptable Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) and maintenance personnel. The FO remained PF during the duration of the flight and did a great job. Per the ecam we were able to turn the G pump back on and get the gear and flaps down normally using whatever fluid was left. We stopped on the runway; ARFF performed their inspection; and we we able to taxi to the gate on our own power. We took our time and were deliberate in our actions and decisions. Air Carrier X was a great resource and very helpful during the entire event as was ATC. We are trained very well such that two pilots who have never met or flown together until the day before can be professional and standard and work together in a setting like that.Nothing really from a flight crew perspective. Per the logbook closing actions looks like a faulty hydraulic drain valve and busted o ring. Not sure what we as flight crew could do different for a maintenance item like that

column121: Just after reaching cruise altitude at 36;000FT with the First Officer as PF;  a FA called from the aft galley saying there was a loud wind noise coming from door 2L in the back of the aircraft. I checked the overhead panel and verified no door lights were on; the cabin Altitude was steady at 8000ft with a differential 7.8PSI. I had the FA verify the door 2L handle was secure in the latched position and she verified the door was secure mechanically. The FA said the ambient noise was so loud that they would need ear plugs to continue the flight. I could also hear the loud ambient noise through the intercom as we talked.I told the FAs that the door seal most likely failed or did not engage properly; and that the door was mechanically secure so there was no safety risk of it opening inflight. I told the FAs that I would have a conference call with Maintenance Control and Dispatch to come up with a plan; but most likely we would be returning to ZZZ.I informed the FO/PF who had been listening in what the situation was and had the FO continue to manage the aircraft and ATC coms while I talked to Dispatch and Maintenance Control. After establishing a phone patch with Dispatch and Maintenance Control I relayed the information from the FA and Maintenance Control had me verify the cabin altitude and DIF pressure readings. Ultimately a decision was made to return to ZZZ and that the airplane would be landing about 7500-8000LBS over the max structure landing weight. I had the FO coordinate with ATC new clearance to return to ZZZ and to request lowest altitude possible to burn off as much fuel as possible on the return as well as attempted to lower the Cabin ALT and reduce the ambient noise if possible. An emergency was not declared at the time.I did a Brief with the Purser; then made a cabin PA for the passengers explaining the situation. After referencing the 737 Flight Manual for overweight landing I ultimately decided that due to our landing weight being close to 8;000LBS over the max structure  the need for runway XXR in ZZZ (longest available) as well as the possibility of hot brakes after landing that requesting priority handling and having fire trucks on standby for the brakes was the most conservative plan of action. I informed ATC of the change of status to priority handling and why; then requested runway XXR and to have the fire trucks on standby for a brake check once clear of the runway. ATC passed along all the information and verified our FOB and SOB. I did another briefing revision with the purser due to the change to priority handling status. I then made a PA to the cabin about the reason for the fire tucks meeting the aircraft after landing.After the FMC was set up; Briefings and checklists were complete I took over PF duties of the aircraft. I did this due to the need for a soft landing and the FO was coming back form a leave as we were conducting the FO's requalification training on this trip.A soft landing was made with a VSI of about -210FPM (3.5FPS) at 153;800lbs landing weight. After clearing the runway the fire crew did a circle around the aircraft and reported the brakes looked normal with no glowing or any signs of overheating. A normal taxi to gate XX was made and aircraft parked and passengers deplaned. Maintenance techs met the aircraft and took the details from me after I sent in the Log Book reports for the door and overweight landing. Flight XXXX continued out of gate XX with a different aircraft 90 min later.

column121: Approximately 15 minutes after departing ZZZ and climbing through 28;000 for FL330 over Location X the cabin interphone call chimed.  As pilot monitoring I took the call and was alerted by a very panicked flight attendant that there was a fire in the forward galley.  Details were not very clear but I understood they were getting fire extinguishers and starting to fight the fire.  Without delay I hung up the phone and took control of the aircraft.  The FO immediately informed ATC and we began a turn and descent back towards ZZZ.  Once the aircraft was on the desired path towards ZZZ we were able to speak with the purser and found that the fire was contained to the forward galley oven and had been extinguished using one halon extinguisher.  Control was transferred back to the FO.We communicated with ATC the fire was out but since there was no way to be sure it wouldn't reignite we continued to ZZZ and informed them that it would be an overweight landing.  Dispatch was notified via satcom.A PA was made advising the passengers that we were heading back to ZZZ.The FAs were briefed.A normal approach and landing was made on XXL.We were met by airport vehicles to ensure no issues with brakes or tires.After inspection we taxied to the gate without incident; Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) boarded the aircraft and ensured the fire had been fully extinguished.Passengers were deplaned and a new aircraft took them to ZZZZ.
column123: Fifteen minutes into our climb; at 28;000 feet; the forward galley flight attendants called the flight deck to inform us of a fire. The Captain slid the phone halfway off his cheek; looked at me; and said fire". I asked; "Is it contained?" Given the panic in the galley; we initially believed the fire was not under control. Aircraft controls were transferred to the CA; who initiated a descent and a turn towards ZZZ. I informed ATC of our actions. Shortly after our turn towards ZZZ; the flight attendants called back with additional information. They reported that the fire was located in the forward galley oven and that one fire extinguisher had been used. I repeated this information to the flight attendants to ensure clear communication. The fire had been extinguished. I then relayed this information to the CA. Ultimately; since we could not determine the source of the fire and could not guarantee that it would not reignite; we decided to continue our diversion to ZZZ. We discussed the potential threats associated with an overweight landing and the increased pace of flight deck duties associated with a quick return. We prioritized the important threats appropriately; and trapped them with mitigation strategies. We performed an overweight landing and stopped on the runway until we could assess brake temperatures. The most incredible moment of this flight unfolded when we arrived at the gate. To our astonishment; all of our wheelchair passengers walked off the airplane."

Winds were calm so we took the closest and longest runway which was XXL. On final for runway XXL we heard a rattling/tapping sound coming from the engine. We asked tower if they could visibly see anything wrong with the aircraft which they said no. Once the runway was ensured my instructor performed a forward slip and we landed. column121: In the interest of safety; I am writing this report to help pilots be more aware of the risks of improper fuel planning. On Day 0; a passenger and I made our way to ZZZ for a joyride. When we arrived at the airport; I immediately began my preflight with Aircraft X. My standard walk-around includes checking all control surfaces; propeller; tires; brakes; oil; and fuel. Fuel is always my last task. On this particular day; I visually verified that both tanks were full. I also strained the fuel to ensure no contaminants were present. Since this was a day VFR joyride; I calculated the distance and time we would be flying; and it was agreed we would just go where we wanted to.The flight was uneventful for the first portion as we made our way from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 4;500 feet; where we conducted a landing and then flew up to Location X for pictures. We then flew from Location X to ZZZ2; where I flew the RNAV XX approach. At that point; I decided not to stop and check the fuel and performed a low approach; believing I had plenty of fuel to make it back to ZZZ.I knew the aircraft held 38 gallons of usable fuel and estimated a burn rate of 8 GPH. At the time we executed the low approach at ZZZ2; we had only been flying for approximately 3 hours; which I believed was sufficient to return to ZZZ.I then began setting up for a practice RNAV XY approach into ZZZ. After crossing ZZZZZ on approximately an 8-mile final and descending through about 2;500 feet; the engine began to sputter. I checked the total flight time; which was approximately 4 hours and 5 minutes. I immediately looked for the nearest airport on the GPS and initiated a 180-degree turn to attempt to return to ZZZ3; which was approximately 4 miles behind us.The engine continued to sputter and then completely lost power shortly after leveling the turn. At that point; it was clear we did not have the altitude or power to reach an airport. I immediately began running the emergency checklist and pitched for best glide and began looking for a suitable field.Around 100 feet AGL; I noticed the airspeed decreasing and added full flaps. The selected field was clear of crops; and I executed a soft-field landing. There were no injuries and no damage to the aircraft.Upon review of the aircraft; it was determined that both fuel tanks were empty due to higher-than-expected fuel consumption during the flight. Even though we departed with full fuel; I did not adequately calculate the fuel required for the flight we ultimately conducted.Additionally; the mixture was not properly adjusted during portions of the flight; which likely contributed to increased fuel consumption. The decision to continue from ZZZ2 without verifying fuel quantity was also a contributing factor and; in hindsight; could have prevented the situation.As PIC; I take responsibility for the outcome of this flight and the planning decisions that led to this situation. This experience highlighted a lapse in judgment that resulted in a scenario I had not intended.I am proud of how the situation was handled. I remained calm; followed established procedures; and relied on my training to safely land the aircraft without injury or damage.I learned more from this experience than any single flight lesson. It reinforced the importance of thorough planning and disciplined decision-making.In the future I will ensure fuel requirements are properly calculated; including legal reserves; even on shorter or 'joyride' flights. Properly adjust the mixture throughout all phases of flight. Stop and verify fuel status rather than relying on assumptions.This is an experience I will not forget; and it has reinforced the importance of completing all calculations thoroughly and maintaining situational awareness throughout the entire flight.

column121: Not long after leveling off at cruise altitude from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 we experienced both a green hydraulic system low level and low pressure ECAM. I continued to fly the aircraft and took over comms while the Captain ran the ECAM. The ECAM directed us to turn off the PTU (Power Transfer Unit) and the hydraulic engine 1 pump. After completing the ECAM and consulting the flight manual and calculating landing distance; reviewing gravity gear extension procedures; and tow in procedures we coordinated with dispatch a diversion to ZZZ. We knew we would be landing overweight so we requested FL240 with ATC and requested priority handling after reviewing overweight landing procedures. We set up for a long final to runway XXL. The Captain took control of the aircraft after we turned direct to ZZZ. On about a 15 mile final I gravity extended the gear and the captain landed the aircraft. Emergency personnel were standing by as we vacated the runway using only rudder steering. Company X operations came out and towed us into gate XX after the assessment was made that we did not need any emergency services. We ended up landing around149;000lbs; roughly 8000lbs overweight.

column121: On departure; flaps up was called for; followed by the after-takeoff checklist. The flaps were positioned to up; and it was noticed that the LE FLAPS TRANSIT light was still on (the flap indicator was showing flaps up). The OVHD LE Devices indicator showed that the #8 leading edge flap was extended. The aircraft and radios were handed to me while the LE FLAPS TRANSIT light QRH was accomplished by the Captain.      It instructed us to extend and then retract the flaps; which we did. The light extinguished briefly and then came back on. We stayed at 8;000 feet; received radar vectors near ZZZ1; and decided to call maintenance. Maintenance had us execute the same checklist once again; and we received the same result. At this point; we collaborated with dispatch and had them run the numbers with the restrictions to continue in our current configuration (FL200 and speed restricted to 300 KIAS). Dispatch advised that we had the fuel to continue; so we advised ATC of our restrictions; climbed to FL200; and continued to ZZZ while being extremely vigilant in monitoring enroute alternate airports in case conditions deteriorated further.      Upon checking in with ZZZ ATC; we requested priority handling due to a flight control issue with excessive target speed and a non-normal flap configuration. We asked for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to be standing by just in case; but advised that we fully expected to be able to land and taxi with no issues. We landed uneventfully with Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate after ARFF confirmed no visible issues; and the tires appeared normal with no overheating noted. During the flight; we gave the lead FA a briefing; advised the passengers; and kept dispatch in the loop. After arriving at the gate; we spoke with maintenance and wrote up the malfunction

column121: During cruise about 5 hours into a flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1; we had set up for a bathroom break. As FO came back from break he noticed EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) was quite a bit higher on the right engine vs the left engine also the fuel flow on right engine was about 2000 lbs/hr than left engine. Fuel appeared balanced at that time. Except for EPR other indications N1; N2; N3 and EGT all appeared lower on right engine. A call was made to dispatch and Maintenance Control. After short discussion Maintenance Control suspected a bad EPR probe or something similar. Now fuel inbalance began to occur. I discussed with dispatch  about divert to ZZZ2 which was about 135 miles away. Dispatch also threw out ZZZ3 which was about 200 miles away. Maintenance  added the engine maintenance  was available in ZZZ2. The decision was made to divert to ZZZ2 in concurrence with dispatch and my FO. An emergency was NOT declared. An uneventful approach and landing occurred and maintenance  was debriefed at plane. I provided them with picture I took and also performed 2 event records at altitude. Chief Pilot  was also debriefed. We deadheaded home on a flight about 2 1/2 hours later to ZZZ1.

column121: Flight xxxx ZZZ1-ZZZ2; level cruise at 340.  ECAM message G HYD RSVR LO LVL with gauge indication of the green system fluid empty. Dispatch advised the would make all notifications.   We then contacted ATC; requested priority handling and requested divert to ZZZ runway XXL. We then reviewed the landing gear gravity extension procedure; the overweigh landing procedure; obtained landing performance data and discussed the runway exit plans as the nose wheel steering was inop.  The ILS for runway XXL was intercepted on a 17 mile final at 3000 MSL.  The gravity gear extension was accomplished; the aircraft slowed and configured and an uneventful approach to the runway was accomplished.  The aircraft was slowed to taxi speed and I determined I had sufficient control to exit onto the high speed taxi exit and parallel taxiway.  The aircraft was stopped and communications established with Crash Rescue.  Nothing was reported or observed.  The company tug then made contact and aircraft was connected and tugged to the gate.

column121: After what should have been the completion of the pushback the ramp crew had difficulty removing the towbar. As always; he had the aircraft until he tells me to park brakes so I waited for the call to set brakes not knowing if he would move us forward or back more. Then I noticed the aircraft moving slightly forward and I thought he was towing us forward now. While the aircraft was moving forward very slowly he says "set brakes" and; even though I could tell we were moving slightly I applied brakes and set them and said "brakes set". At this point as far as I know they are removing towbar then they pulled back for salute and nothing else was said. I knew of no issue until arriving in ZZZ and was notified by ZZZ1 chief pilot that there was some kind of issue about possibly moving forward after the brakes were supposed to be set. I immediately realized that was not what happened from my perspective as I parked the brakes when the driver said. Perhaps the driver forgot to call for brakes set at the proper time and the towbar was removed without the brakes being set and we began to move forward and he then called for brakes set. column121: I was PF.  We were holding short of runway 07 waiting for takeoff while a Aircraft Y landed in front of us.  After they landed we were told to line up and wait.  The Aircraft Y appeared to clear the runway at the other end and we were cleared for takeoff.  Just after the FO made the '80kt' callout; tower told us 'Aircraft X cancel takeoff clearance.'  After a 1-2 second hesitation I initiated a rejected takeoff.  Asking tower for details on the problem we were told that the Aircraft Y never cleared the hold-short line at the other end.  We exited the runway and reviewed the rejected takeoff considerations.  Because it was >80kts an maintenance logbook entry was required.  I contacted dispatch and maintenance control who directed us to return to the gate for inspection.  After the inspection was complete and brake cooldown times were observed we departed again.Cause: Lack of taxiway and gate space in LIR leads to planes stacking up on the only 2 exits for runway 07.  The aircraft that landed did not have room to clear the runway.  Every takeoff also requires a back-taxi which is very often 'expedited' for traffic.  It seems like the airport does not have the ramp or taxiway space to support the number of operations.
column123: On Day 0; I was pilot monitoring of Aircraft X as first officer with scheduled service from LIR to ZZZ. The captain and I arrived to the airport well-rested after a 23-hour overnight and the arrival to the airport and airplane was standard. There were no issues with any of the aircraft origination or checklists; and no anomalies with respect to preflight duties or clearance delivery/routing. We were given clearance for push back and start from gate XX; which was accomplished normally and we joined the line for taxi to the departure end of the runway. The airport had been on runway 07 operations for the entire time we were there; so a full-length back taxi was required. Upon reaching the runway; we waited in the turnaround for arriving traffic behind an aircraft. There was an arriving Aircraft X that landed a few minutes after the aircraft departed that; once past us; we were issued a line up and wait clearance; which we accepted. After waiting in position for approximately two minutes; we were given a takeoff clearance by the tower. Initial power up and acceleration was normal. I called 80" and almost immediately after; tower calls "Aircraft X; cancel takeoff clearance." The captain and I were a bit confused as there was nothing hazardous immediately apparent in front of us; but we initiated a rejected takeoff. The deceleration was smooth; and callouts were standard. Once stopped; I started a timer and dropped the flaps to 40° and the captain retracted the spoilers and made an announcement to the cabin to remain seated. Once slowed; we were asked if we could make a 180 on the runway to return to the departure end; which we were able to accommodate. I was instructed to perform an after landing flow; and the captain and I began to discuss the requirements for a rejected takeoff and brake cooling requirements from the table in the AOM. The auto brakes did not fire; so we knew we were below 90kt when the reject was initiated; however with the adjustments for the length of taxi and the headwind; we determined that the most conservative cooling time was 45.9 minutes. We were not in the caution or melt zone; so we set the parking brake when coming to a complete stop.When queried the reason for the rejected takeoff clearance; the tower responded that an airplane had not fully cleared the runway. They tried to issue us a second takeoff clearance while we were calculating cooling times and contacting dispatch and maintenance control; and ultimately we were instructed to return to the gate for a visual inspection. We were caught in a lot of traffic; but made our way back to the gate and maintenance was waiting on us. We elected to not give the opportunity to deplane given the efficiency with which we were parked and accommodated by maintenance. The airplane was determined to be safe to continue on; so we closed the main cabin door; and pushed back for a normal flight arriving to ZZZ about an hour and a half late. No injuries were reported and no further problems with the airplane were experienced. Cause: We were issued a late cancellation of takeoff clearance for a runway incursion that was impossible to see from the departure end of the runway. Flight and cabin crew followed SOPs to mitigate injury or escalation of the event."

column121: During the arrival into ASE; the aircraft was fully configured as we passed abeam Red Table. At that point; we reported Runway 15 in sight and were subsequently cleared by ATC for a visual approach to Runway 15.Autopilot pilot was disconnected; flight directors were selected off; and the runway QDM was set. The landing checklist was completed; and then landing clearance was received from ATC.Aircraft was maneuvered between the surrounding mountain ranges and finally aligned with the runway centerline. While turning final; four red PAPI lights were observed so a slight level-off was initiated to correct the approach profile.While established on final and aligned with the runway; a TAWS Mode 2B caution (Caution Terrain") was triggered. Approximately 10 seconds later; a "Terrain; Terrain; Pull Up" warning was annunciated.This warning was assessed as being caused by lateral terrain proximity due to rising terrain abeam the aircraft; despite the runway being at the 12 o'clock position. Given the visual meteorological conditions (VMC) and full situational awareness; the alert was treated as precautionary.The approach and landing were continued without further incident.Cause: Being low on the approach and with the close proximity of rising terrain to the right of the aircraft this infringed the lateral envelope of the EGPWSSuggestions: For visual approaches into ASE the company needs to approve and provide crew with some vertical guidance profiles for visual approaches that the PM calls in support of superior outcomes."

column121: Flight proceeded normally during our pre-flight duties. We were slightly delayed pushing waiting for wing walkers. Once pushed; we were cleared to start engine 1. Upon starting engine one I had noticed the EICAS message 'PACK 2 VLV CLSD'. I ran the QRH; which did not resolve the issue. Captain and I decided that we needed to go to a hard stand and call maintenance for further troubleshooting/possible deferral of the pack. During our taxi; (starting from gate XX; to the west hard stand) as a means of troubleshooting and isolating variables; we decided to start engine 2; and see if the message would persist with engine bleed air instead of APU bleed air. After starting engine 2; the message persisted. We informed ramp of our issue; pulled into the handstand and the Captain proceeded to call maintenance.Pack 2 inop is flight crew deferrable item; so we followed maintenance's procedures for the deferral and then worked on the next task. As part of the deferral; we were restricted to FL250 (originally FL360) and since this was an MEL affecting our performance and fuel consumption calculations we needed to call dispatch and see if we have enough fuel; and if so; get a new release. Upon calling dispatch we were able to continue with our current fuel on-board; and obtain a new release. After getting our new release we rejoined the departures and the taxi-take off was completely uneventful. The take off was normal until the climb portion where I had noticed the EICAS message 'ENG 2 BLV VLV CLSD' during my after take off flow. I consulted the Captain on the appropriate QRH procedure and conducted the QRH procedure. Upon completion of the procedure the message had cleared and we continued. As we leveled off at FL240 (our final filed altitude); I smelled a burning smell; simultaneously the Captain had noticed the same thing. As we looked at each other; I noticed smoke coming above the Captain's head. We then dawned our O2 masks; and we informed ATC that we needed to immediately return to ZZZ due to 'smoke in the cockpit'. The flight attendant also contacted us about a burning smell. The Captain flew and coordinated our return while I ran the QRH; during this time I transferred radios to the Captain while I continued the QRH. We then descended and received vectors back to ZZZ; we joined the localizer for XXC. Since I was not fully caught up on setting up approach/speeds; I informed the Captain that I 'needed more time' we informed ATC. We continued on that heading for a brief minute; then the Captain determined that the safest course of action was to continue for XXL instead of delay vectors; as we did not know the source; nor the severity of the possible smoke and fumes. I was able to load in the approach speeds and we joined the localizer XXL. He landed very smoothly; we pulled off the runway and asked crash; fire; rescue to confirm that there was not any visible smoke or fire on the exterior of the aircraft. They confirmed that it was clear on the exterior. We then determined that it was not necessary to evacuate the aircraft as there were no signs of persisting smoke or fumes and the flight attendant also did not have any signs of smoke in the cabin. We elected to taxi to the gate. From our brief ACARS message; I said that we were told to go to gate XY. As we taxied into the ramp; ramp control informed us that it was occupied. We then stressed that we need a gate ASAP ! They then directed us to another gate on the concourse. I cannot remember the exact gate; possibly XZ or XA. We then taxied over to the 'vacant' gate; but there was a fuel truck in the way and no rampers. We immediately called operations and informed them that we needed it moved immediately; we proceeded to wait for another few minutes; despite another call. However; we confirmed that there were still no signs of smoke or fumes from the aircraft during the taxi and waiting period; and had a fire truck follow us. We pulled into the gate; deplaned the passengers in an organize manner; and shut down the aircraft.Maintenance determined Pack 1 exhaust duct had blown; and it was ingesting pack exhaust into the cabin (preliminary)

column121: Holding for runway XX in ZZZ for weather to improve to have a better chance of getting in for landing at waypoint ZZZZZ at 4;000ft. After 20 minutes of holding (estimate) weather improves and approach descends us to 3;000ft to proceed inbound. It was my leg (first officer) and began to configure for the approach that would be near minimums. Once inbound; I recognize that the plane ahead of us (corporate) is relatively close but approach permitted us to continue. I would estimate we were in trail by 4-5 miles. Fully configured prior to GS intercept; as we cross ZZZZZ1; the autopilot disconnects; and I lose guidance from the Flight Directors (FD) but continue raw data. Captain and I recognize he still has guidance; and so we transfer the controls at around 1;400ft with the autopilot off. We are stable at this event. Approach then directs us to break off the approach and turn left 90 degrees (cannot remember the specific heading) and climb to 3;000ft. As PM; I turn off the FD's; spin the heading bug and altitude bug while clicking LVL Change and Heading (HDG) select. I believe I did this with the flight directors off; but due to the subsequent events; I am not so sure. As I am doing this; the Captain is calling for flaps 15 and gear up. It is during this that I realize; the Captain is still descending because of the flight directors giving him an improper guidance. The Captain was following the GS down but had began the turn to the requested heading. After setting the flaps to 15; I tell the Captain to climb" repeatedly. He recognizes what he is doing; and corrects to our assigned heading and altitude. The lowest we got was approximately 1;050ft. We also got an audible callout of which I assume was "sink rate" and approach asking us to check our altitude and notified us of the MVA. I cannot recall those 10 seconds exactly; but I assume those were the events that occurred to my best knowledge. From there we cleaned up the plane; and set up for the approach again. To get proper automation; I flipped the NAV frequencies from the LOC to the VOR; and then clicked HDG and LVL change. Captain asked if I wanted to take the plane back; and I did. After I had controls; we both decided leaving the autopilot on the Captains side would allow for better situational awareness and we proceeded as such; and landed the plane with that configuration. We saw the approach lights at around 400ft. There weren't many things that I felt went right if I were to do the situation again. I believe that handing the plane to the Captain at 1500ft; albeit low; was the right decision at the time. I tried to be preventative and cycle the FD's to get to the proper automation; but that did not work as planned. Only once the NAV frequencies were flipped; a preventative action was taken. I also believe the Captain handing the plane back to me for the second approach was a containment action from him; I do not know if he was shaken up or had gotten disoriented by what had just occurred; but I felt very comfortable with flying the plane from the position we were in and do believe it was safe to do so given what had just happened. Not once do I think that CRM had fallen apart; in fact; I think we both excelled at communicating what was happening once the event had happened. I want to bring up that after we had completed our duties as flight crew-members; the Captain did not waste time asking about what happened; what went wrong; etc. Again; I want to emphasize that I never felt that CRM was an issue and the Captain was very approachable about the event afterwards."

column121: 6 minutes after the sterile light went off the forward galley oven closest to the flight deck caught on fire. I was getting ready to take the food out of the oven to put in meals from the mid galley when I noticed the oven fully illuminated orange. At this point I didn't realize it was fire. When I went to pull the tray out a piece of the ember flew back on me. As I jumped back; that's when I realized there was fire. The purser was coming back to the galley. I couldn't make out the words to tell him fire; but he realized what I was pointing at. I called pilots right away and said fire. The Captain told us he was turning around. We closed the oven until we got the halon. At this point I waving for the fa in the mid galley to come up. I told the purser to let the others know what was happening as we were trying to put the fire out. The fa from the mid galley closed the curtains before we opened the oven so that passengers couldn't see what we were doing. The purser opened the oven while I extinguished the oven. After some time I stopped because I wasn't sure if I should keep going. The purser told me to keep going until it was empty. At that point the Captain called back and asked the purser all of the questions about the fire. He then gave the purser brief information for a land emergency since we were landing overweight. I forgot to mention the aft fa brought up a halon just in case after the purser let the others know what had happened. We all met in the mid galley for the information and had about 10 minutes or less until landing. We were told we didn't need to do an evacuation at that point and if anything changed they'd let us know. After we landed the Captain told us our brakes were okay to continue to the gate so no evacuation needed. Once we got to the gate it was determined that everyone would deplane and the aircraft would be taken out of service. The Captain also acknowledged a part outside of the oven where I believe got burned. One of the maintenance workers also said the fan probably caused the spark on the aircraft.

column121: I decided; for the safety of Flight; and perhaps a good discussion; to post a little educational rant about a very close midair my student and I watched happen on Day 0 at XA:20 at ZZZ. We were holding short of RWY XX and watched a prior plane on a somewhat long final make a touch and go. A Cherokee then turned their base behind them appropriately and I pointed out to the traffic to my student. Interestingly; we then noticed a subsequent Cessna turn a very low tight left base. The Cherokee by this time was already on final; and had made their call. They then asked if the Cessna had them in sight. They replied in the affirmative and that they would 'extend their base.' For the record; they were already on their base leg. I watched as both planes continued on a collision course right above the Street X intersection with the Cherokee finally climbing and side stepping and the Cessna staying low and flying due south probably about 50 feet of separation between them; then making a radio call 'that was close!' I spoke to the Cherokee pilot afterwards and fortunately they did have the Cessna traffic in sight throughout the incident; so I suspect while it looked close that it would have had a safe outcome regardless of how it looked from my vantage point. A few thoughts for all of us to ponder. I am convinced that the Cessna never had the Cherokee in sight. I presume; perhaps falsely; that they were looking at an ADSB return rather than out the window. We all need a reminder that ADSB is NOT visual separation. When ATC asks you if you have traffic in sight; they mean with your eye balls. Not on your 'fish finder'. Please; for the love of God; do not call it that. Even more importantly; when another pilot asks if you have them in sight; do not reply in the affirmative if you do not. Instead; take action immediately to increase the separation between you. In formation flying when you lose sight of your wingman; you immediately call blind and increase the separation between the aircraft. This isn't checkers; it's flying. And a simple screw up will kill you; or much worse; someone else. ADSB isn't perfect. It has a lag. Sometimes a fraction of a second and sometimes 20 seconds. Are you using a third party device that then wirelessly connects to your foreflight app to show you? Are you holding a phone in your lap? Or is your system installed in the plane and displayed on a Multi-function Flight Display (MFD)? Even primary radar has a lag. Nothing is perfect. More importantly  not everyone has ADSB. It's not required. I don't have it in my plane. It is for situational awareness. It is not meant to replace your eyeballs. When someone on the frequency calls a position you should look outside the plane first; not at your panel or your phone. I presume we all know 91.113 about right of way. Read it again if you haven't this year. Landing traffic has the right of way. If someone is already on final; turn your left base once they are at your 9'o'clock; not while they are still at 11 o'clock. The C210 on Day 0  turned their base low at least a half mile before the Cherokee. In the left seat; low; with a high wing; they had no chance of seeing that Cherokee. Why then did they say traffic was in sight? And what does extending your base leg even mean when you are already on your base?The question I pose to myself; sitting at the threshold; is should I have been empowered to play ATC and demand a go around? My thought was to not clog the frequency while these two worked it out. However in hindsight; there was no negotiation between them. I would have felt very guilty if I had not said something. Kudos to both pilots afterwards for being kind and professional. Neither of them got nasty on the radio (something that I hear too frequently these days) and neither of them chastised each other. The Cessna exited the area and the Cherokee got back in the pattern. I presume both had honest debriefs when they got home. However; the rest of us can stand to learnsomething from this close call before the flying season gets busy. Every year in our country someone dies due to this situation because of two reasons: 1.) they misinterpret 91.113 or 2.) they are too hard headed to realize that even though they are in the right; they neglect to knock off their approach and create separation because - dang-it - they have the right away!!! I argue that this Cherokee; due to the fact that they could see the Cessna making a mistake; could have aborted their touch and go 30 seconds earlier. They could have sidestepped on an upwind to keep the Cessna in sight and learned a valuable lesson that being courteous; even when you were the one that was wronged; is the right thing; and the safe thing; to do. Don't think this thing happens a lot? How many classic 91.113 see and avoid mishaps come to mind right off the bat?  DCA accident?  Centennial accident between the metro liner and Cirrus. Or maybe all of us need to have a little common sense and remind ourselves to be courteous. This means if you are working with a student on instrument work and the pattern is really full; it's not the time to do your circling maneuver. This means if it's clear and a million and you're on an instrument plan in a single engine piston; you shouldn't fly a 10 mile straight in and you should join the pattern in a VFR manner - even if your bladder is about to explode! It means if a turbine is arriving; that the rest of us make way and let them land. We only have one sand box to play in. We should keep it pleasant for every user…we all have a right to be there.

column121: I was providing flight instruction near ZZZ Airport  when we experienced a total engine failure at approximately 2;500 feet MSL and about 4 NM from the airport. The engine failure occurred without prior warning. The engine abruptly made an abnormal sound and then lost all power completely. A review of the engine indications confirmed a full loss of power; with the engine instruments showing a significant drop.At the onset of the emergency; the student transferred flight controls to me. I confirmed there was no useful engine power and no meaningful response from the engine. I immediately began evaluating available landing options and determined that ZZZ Airport was the best available landing site.Once the airport was selected; the student and I coordinated duties. The student assisted with navigation and frequency management for ZZZ; while I maintained aircraft control; maneuvered toward the airport; and executed the in-flight engine restart checklist. During the restart attempt; the engine tried to relight but did not successfully restart. Instead; it produced backfire-type sounds without developing usable power.I then transmitted on the ZZZ UNICOM frequency that we were experiencing an engine failure and intended to land on Runway XX. At approximately 500 feet AGL; the engine attempted to produce power again and momentarily developed approximately 1;200 to 1;400 RPM for about 10 seconds; but then lost power completely once more.I continued the forced landing and landed the aircraft safely on Runway XX at ZZZ Airport. There was no injury to either occupant and no damage to the aircraft or other property. After touchdown; using the remaining landing energy; I was able to clear the runway and stop on the taxiway.While on the taxiway; I evaluated whether the engine would produce any usable power. With full throttle applied; the engine produced only approximately 400 to 650 RPM; which was unstable and accompanied by significant vibration. Using that limited power; I was able to taxi the aircraft to the FBO area.Maintenance personnel responded and conducted a full inspection of the aircraft. The discrepancies were addressed; documented in the aircraft maintenance records; and the aircraft was subsequently returned to service later that same day.This event involved a sudden and unexpected total engine failure without meaningful prior warning indications. Positive crew coordination between instructor and student; prompt identification of a suitable landing site; emergency checklist execution; and timely radio communication contributed to a safe outcome.

column121: I was flying with 3 passengers on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ to 1V6. When passing approximately 8 miles west of APA (location and time is approximate; I did not mark it on the chart) at 9000ft MSL; we encountered two objects that appeared to be drones flying very near our position.I spotted the first object a few hundred feet ahead of us. It reminded me of encountering a bird in flight. It was clear it was slightly lower and to the right of us; so I left the autopilot engaged and didn't take any evasive action. I pointed it out to a passenger (my wife; who is not a pilot; but is familiar with GA due to several hundred hours as a passenger with me). Our initial reaction was 'what was that?' The object was grey/silver; reflected a fair bit of light; but was much more boxy and angular than a mylar balloon would be. It did not look like a typical quadcopter; but was also far enough away that we couldn't really identify any means of flight (wings; propellers; etc). The object was a 1-2ft across; similar in size to a medium bird; but much more metallic/machine looking.Several seconds later; I spotted a second object ahead of us. It was at approximately the same altitude as the first object; but this time to the left of our flight path. I pointed it out as it went by. The passenger in the back seat behind me saw it go by as well. It appeared similar to the first object.Given our groundspeed of around 150kt; we passed by both objects very quickly. It was as if they were standing still. Given the large difference in our speeds; I could not tell whether the objects were moving; or their direction of flight; except that it was much slower than us.I can't think of anything different that I or ATC should have done. Assuming that the objects were drones; whoever was operating them should not have been flying them there without significant coordination with ATC. Given how busy the airspace around Denver is; the danger this kind of operation poses is obvious.

column121: After a regular departure and climb out from ZZZ to ZZZ1 over approximately ZZZZZ the aircraft leveled off at FL310. Right after level several loud bangs were heard from the left side of the aircraft as well as indications of a surging engine or compressor stall. Flight attendants then made contact as they had heard and felt the bangs and saw sparks from engine 1. Control was established and the duties of flying were then given to the First Officer and the Captain then ran the QRC and QRH checklists. After the autothrottles were disconnected in accordance with the checklist the engine then ran normally. Decision was made to return to ZZZ in the interest of safety and a turn and declaration was made. Checklists were then completed as we returned to ZZZ for a normal landing on runway XXC. Crash and Fire inspected the engine and aircraft found no damage and as it was deemed safe we taxied to the gate and parked. Casual factors include long day; multiple legs and maintenance write ups as well as delays. Mitigation was good CRM and use of any and all information available to us to make the safest decision possible.
column123: The flight was normal until leveling off at cruise.  As we were leveling at FL310 the number one engine N1 begin to roll back.  There was a pronounced yaw and roll.  There was also a loud bang.  I did disconnect the Auto Pilot as I was uncomfortable with the autopilot performance.  Just as quickly as it started the engine recovered and began to operate normally. The First Officer said that acts just like a compressor stall.  During this time of what I believe was a compressor stall we also got a calls from the front and aft Flight Attendant position.  They heard the banging they reported they saw sparks coming from the engine number one and vibration in the cabin floor.  I gave control of the aircraft to the First Officer talked with ATC and got a turn back to ZZZ.  We did request priority handling with ATC and were cleared direct to ZZZ.  We ran the QRC for Engine Limit or Surge or Stall; which lead us to the QRH.  Which we completed.  Since the engine was performing normally now; per the QRH we left it running.  We did complete the non routine landing check list.  We told ZZZ approach we would like XXC and to have ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) standing by.  We would be stopping on the runway and I would like them to check for any visible damage or leaks.  That was approved but latter they came back and asked since we would be stopping on the runway if we could accept XYC.  As a crew we felt we had time to make the change so we approved ATC request and switched to XYC.  Landing was normal.  We stopped on the runway.  I did an after landing announcement that the safety vehicles  would look us over.  Then contacted the ARFF command.  We did start the APU after landing and shut down engine number 1.  ARFF approached looked over engine number 1 they reported everything looked normal.  We called ops got a gate and I asked to be followed to the gate by ARFF (another human factor incident was fore most in my thoughts).  We arrived at the gate with out further incident.  ARFF left us and MTX arrived.  We made our calls and Logbook write up and talked to MTX; FA's and Dispatch.Cause: Casual factors.  MTX did mention this was an older engine that was scheduled for replacement.  I have no idea of how close it was for replacement.   Upon arrival MTX did check the engine oil and said the smelled jet fuel in the oil.  Is there a better way to monitor the engines condition as they get closer to overhaul?  Mitigation of Risk.  I think our training department had us well prepared for this situation.  I am flying with a newer First Officer who is on probation and 271 hours on the airplane at the start of our trip.  We did like we are encouraged to in training (assigning the first officer to be PF.  He has really good stick and rudder skills.  He assistance was invaluable.  Very calm and professional.  He help make busy and stressful situation flow smoothly.Recommendations:  One thing I should of done sooner was start the APU instead of waiting till we go on the ground.  Neither of the check list directed us to start it but should have thought of that sooner.  There are a couple other recommendations that came to mind.  Single frequency with ATC and ARFF.  I asked for that while airborne talking to tower they said we will give that to you after you land.  Did not think much of it till we came to a stop on the runway.  I talked to the people while the First Officer was getting the frequency to talk to ARFF. Looking back this was kind of disjointed.  I feel it would been easier to talk to them and coordinate what we wanted before we landed.  That may not work for every situation but I felt it would worked better for us.  The last suggestion is to reconsider getting rid of the paper QRH.  On a good day with out a lot of use of WSI (Weather App); sky path; company page; and FMS Plus I am good for 2 legs.  This was leg number 3.   We had some time before this departure so I was able to charge my IPad some.  My concern is a situation where the FO's outlet is deferred (I'm not sure it can be) if we have two older IPads and no way to recharge them and no paper QRH that would not be a good situation.
