column121: On Day 0; my private pilot level student and I took off from ZZZ1 Airport at approximately XA:40. Our intended lesson was to fly to the practice area where I would introduce stalls; slow flight; and steep turns in the Piper Archer before returning to the airport for landing. Before the flight we did a thorough preflight where we determined that the fuel was full in both tanks with no contaminants found in the fuel; the oil level was at 6.5 quarts; tires; brakes and rotors appeared in good condition; and the flight controls were all functioning in their correct manner.We started the engine and noted that the oil temperature and pressure were all in the green and were at acceptable levels. There were no illuminated lights when we checked the annunciator lights and the amperage was at a normal range. During the run up we leaned the mixture out for best power. Both magnetos had a normal drop of less than 175 RPMs and the difference between the two drops did not exceed 50 RPMs. On takeoff; we received normal RPM output and our temperature and pressures all remained in the green; normal range. On climb out we maintained a normal climb out rate with normal airspeed; we maintained 80 knots and climbed out at 500 FPM. We turned crosswind for our departure at 2;700' and continued our climb over the cement plant to exit the airport environment to the north. We continued to climb on a northern heading until we reached 5;500'. At 5;500' we leveled the plane out and brought our RPMs back to 2300. Shortly after bringing the RPMs back to 2300 we heard a loud noise from the engine. The noise sounded like a boom. We immediately lost all RPMs and both the vacuum and oil light illuminated. I increased the throttle to see if we could maintain altitude or climb but we could not. I then turned us to the south to circle to keep us close to the small airpark west of us. while I attempted to restart the engine by ensuring that the fuel pump was on; putting the mixture full; and switching the fuel tanks. I then cranked the starter but there was no indication that the engine would turn over and restart. At this point I knew that we would not make it back to the airport; we were 7 miles north and we did not have adequate altitude to return back to our original point of departure. I knew that we were going to have to land at ZZZ Airpark so we turned northwest to head directly to the airpark. I did not have adequate time to advise ATC. We started a slow descent at our gliding speed of 76 kts. I added in the first notch of flaps (10°) when we were a mile away from the airport. I added another notch of flaps (25°) when we were short final. We didn't have excess altitude so we had to come in low. On our approach; our right wing grazed through shrubs but it did not cause us to falter off of our path. We touched down on the runway and the plane veered to the right slightly because of the gravel but we maintained control and brought the plane to a stop in the center of the runway. We then shut down the engine and performed the engine securing checklist.

column123: On Day 0; I was receiving dual instruction in a PA 28R-180 with my instructor while completing the required flight time needed in a complex aircraft for my commercial requirements.We were returning to ZZZ Airport following a cross-country flight from ZZZ1. Approximately 4-5 nautical miles from the airport; we began our before-landing checklist and initiated the GUMPS flow. At that time; our airspeed was at or slightly above the maximum allowable speed for landing gear extension; so we made the decision to delay extending the landing gear until the aircraft slowed and continued with the rest of our checklist.As we continued toward the airport; our workload increased due to pattern entry; radio communications; and configuring for landing. During this time; although the checklist had been initiated earlier; we did not complete a final verification that the landing gear had been extended.On final approach; both my instructor and I were focused on maintaining a stable approach and landing. We did not visually or physically confirm gear extension prior to touchdown. Another pilot attempted to alert us via radio; however; we misunderstood the transmission and did not recognize it as a warning regarding the landing gear.The aircraft touched down with the landing gear retracted. After landing; we secured the aircraft and exited safely. There were no injuries.Upon reflection; I recognize several contributing factors; including initiating the before-landing checklist too early; delaying gear extension without establishing a clear follow-up trigger; increased workload in the pattern; and a breakdown in final verification procedures. This resulted in a loss of situational awareness regarding the landing gear status.This experience has reinforced the importance of strict adherence to checklist discipline and redundant verification of critical configuration items. Moving forward; I will ensure that landing gear extension is verified multiple times during the approach; including on downwind; base; and final; with a positive confirmation of 'gear down; three green' prior to landing. I will also incorporate physical verification of the gear position and avoid performing critical checklist items prematurely.I take this event seriously and am committed to applying the lessons learned to ensure it does not happen again.

column121: On Day 0; we were conducting a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 in Aircraft X. I was serving as Pilot Monitoring (PM) for the departure from Runway XXL.Due to ambient temperature and aircraft weight; Continuous Alcohol Water Injection (CAWI) was required for takeoff performance. Prior to takeoff; the Before Takeoff checklist was completed.During the initial takeoff roll; upon reaching approximately 35% torque; the Pilot Flying (PF) called for water injection. I confirmed activation of the CAWI system; including pump indications and an initial increase in torque on both engines. Shortly thereafter; the right (No. 2) engine torque indication began fluctuating; with uncommanded decreases and increases observed. I announced the abnormal indication; and the crew elected to reject the takeoff. The rejected takeoff was completed without further incident; and the aircraft exited the runway.After clearing the runway and completing applicable checklists; the crew assessed the situation. A potential contributing factor considered was improper positioning of the right engine speed lever. Based on this assessment and normal indications at that time; a second takeoff attempt was initiated.During the second takeoff roll; the right (No. 2) engine again did not produce expected torque with CAWI activated. The crew rejected the takeoff a second time. The aircraft was brought to a safe stop; exited the runway; and returned to the ramp for further evaluation. No injuries occurred.This event highlights the challenges associated with diagnosing abnormal engine indications during high-workload phases of flight such as takeoff. The fluctuating torque indication on the first attempt created ambiguity regarding whether the issue was mechanical or related to configuration.The decision to attempt a second takeoff was influenced by a perceived; correctable configuration issue and the absence of persistent abnormal indications while stopped. However; recurrence of insufficient torque on the second attempt suggests the possibility of an underlying mechanical or system-related issue.This event also underscores the importance of conservative decision-making when abnormal engine indications are observed during takeoff; even if a potential explanation is identified.

column121: I (FO) was pilot flying with AP (Autopilot) and AT (Autothrottles) engaged during the climb to cruise altitude of FL370. Climbing through FL355; through clear and smooth air; we experienced sudden windshear causing airspeed to increase 20-30 kts and VSI increasing to around 4500fpm. As I saw the airspeed approaching redline I reduced thrust and as the clacker sounded the CA took the controls; disengaged AP and AT; continued to reduce speed below red line and began to level off. CA returned flight controls to me just before we got to the back side of the windshear and quickly lost 20-30kt and approached minimum maneuver speed. I told the CA I will be descending to FL 360 in order to reduce pitch and regain airspeed at that altitude and he made the request to ATC. ATC continued our descent to FL350 where we leveled off on airspeed and reengaged AP and AT. CA made an Airplane Maintenance Logbook entry for the over speed. Flight continued to ZZZ with no issues. Cause: The event's main causal factor was meteorological. Unknown windshear at altitude. I would say another causal factor could be my monitoring of speed as I could have noticed the speed increase slightly sooner; however the dramatic performance increase and decrease would have occurred regardless of reaction time. Proper training and execution of that training were essential in regaining airspeed control. Performance demonstrations at high altitude in the simulator were helpful during this event. Because of those demonstrations and knowledge it was clear that after the loss of performance on the back side of the windshear; a decrease in altitude was necessary for proper and timely airspeed recovery. More of these demonstrations and relating this meteorological/performance possibility to other factors that we talk about; such as microbursts; will help in mitigating risk by helping pilots with timely recognition and recovery.
column123: FO was PF.  At XA:30 climbing through FL360 in the vicinity of ZZZZZ intersection we experienced an immediate vertical wind sheer of +22 to +30 knots.  CA took controls; disengaged AP (Autopilot) and pitched up and reduced thrust. We experienced what we believe was high speed buffet; which felt like cobblestone" or "washboard" turbulence; but felt more like shaking which we felt in the simulator. Airspeed then immediately dropped to min maneuvering speed +5 knots.  Pitch limit indicators were in view. We transferred controls back to the FO and exercised emergency authority and descended immediately to FL360. The flight attendants were up in the cabin at the time. No injuries were reported. We notified dispatch. We completed an Airplane Maintenance Logbook entry.Cause: When the airspeed dropped dramatically on the other side of the windshear; we knew to pitch down and descend to quickly regain flying speed. Just like the simulator. Both pilots were on the same page about what was needed. I recommend that during recurrent training; a high speed buffet is demonstrated in the simulator. As a former check pilot; I've experienced this; but it is not in the curriculum as far as I am aware. In the simulator; we'd have to fly to red line +40 or +50 to see this effect.  This flight showed high speed buffet around redline +20 knots.In hindsight I would not have reduced thrust as much as I did knowing that this was a transient condition; with an imminent reversal in trend.  Much like an increasing headwind / decreasing tailwind condition like we see in microbursts."

column121: Flight experienced GPS interference consistent with jamming/spoofing while operating in the Turkey region. During this phase; one or both GPS receivers were intermittently lost or unreliable. Standard degradation of navigation capability was observed and managed.Continuing for the remainder of the flight; or nearly the remainder of the flight; after exiting the interference region; anomalous system behavior continued while one GPS remained offline. The aircraft clock began oscillating between correct time and an offset of approximately five minutes. This was not a steady offset but a repeating switching between time sources.This time instability resulted in multiple downstream effects:• CPDLC instability; including repeated logoff/logon requests from ATC (LPPO); likely due to message timing/sequence issues.• ADS-C / ADS-B discrepancies. (On a prior flight) ATC reported position inconsistency on approach to DEL; with the aircraft depicted approximately 0.5-1.0 NM north of actual position while established on the ILS. Approach and Tower control seemed to think we were not on the localizer; and maybe believed we were lining up for the wrong runway. They seemed very concerned. Other crew members on the flight related being directed to go around on a prior flight to DEL for the same reason.• NAT ADS Position reporting becoming unusable due to reporting over a fix at a time in the future. We reverted to HF Voice position reports for the entire crossing.• Nuisance EGPWS alert (WHOOP WHOOP PULL UP") at cruise altitude (FL360). (Prior flight)The aircraft flagged the GPWS TERR POS; however; nuisance alerts continued to be generated. In the absence of company guidance addressing this condition; I selected TERR Override to suppress repeated false warnings and reduce distraction during flight. Various conditions persisted well beyond the geographic area of known interference; and one GPS position never recovered. Mitigation actions included increased cross-checking of navigation sources; use of procedural separation techniques (including HF position reporting when appropriate); and cautious use of datalink functions. However; no flight deck intervention was available to isolate or reset the affected time source.Cause: This condition presents more than a nuisance. Incorrect time and position outputs can lead to:• Misleading ATC surveillance displays• CPDLC communication failures or delays• False terrain warnings; including at cruise altitude• Increased crew workload and distraction during critical and non-critical phases of flight.Consider system-level mitigation to prevent corrupted GPS-derived time and position from being intermittently accepted after initial rejection. A more robust isolation of unreliable inputs; or a crew-selectable means to inhibit GPS-derived time and/or terrain alerting when flagged unreliable; may improve resilience.A means for resetting an individual GPS receiver inflight. With the incidence of jamming/spoofing likely to increase; there needs to be an emphasis on making our aircraft more resilient. Another aircraft type flew through the jamming/spoofing areas with considerably less bother."

column121: My student who is training to become a private pilot was planning to solo today. They had completed the initial solo; but this flight was supposed to be a pattern solo. It had been some time since they had flown solo; we had flown a pattern lesson the previous week with ten landings to smooth out their landing flare technique (tended to not flare enough leading to hard landings); and towards the end of the lesson the landings were pretty good. So today just to make sure everything was good I decided to run a few laps in the pattern with them before they went solo today. We did three laps in the pattern and had no concerns with their takeoffs and landings. After the third lap in the pattern; I had my student drop me off at the FBO and I was going to observe the rest of the lesson from the ground. The student then proceeded to complete seven laps in the traffic pattern using runway XX at ZZZ with no issues. The weather was 10SM Visibility; sky CLR; with winds 220 at 7KTS. After the seventh landing the student then proceeded to take off. I was told by the student that after they increased the power; they were rolling down the runway and glanced over to the right side of the cockpit to make sure the oil temperature and oil pressure was in the green. At that time the right wing started to roll moving the plane to the left on the runway. The student then proceeded to pull power and tried to maintain control and drove the plane into the grass on the left side of the runway. I then ran over to make sure the student was okay and that the plane was okay. After assessing the situation and seeing my student was okay and the plane seemed to be fine; I taxied the plane out of the grass and back to the main ramp. Plane had no damage and the taxiway; lights; and signs on the side of the runway by [taxiway] 1 had not been damaged. Upon review from what I saw on the ground and from what I was told by my student the contributing factor to this accident was an incorrect input of the flight controls and not correcting for the crosswind on takeoff. As the flight instructor I need to be more vigilant on teaching cross wind corrections and make sure my students know the importance of them. Also to keep their eyes down the runway during the takeoff roll to see the trends and movement of the aircraft so the correct crosswind corrections can be made.
column123: While accelerating for take off on runway XX at ZZZ a cross-wind gust of wind lifted the right wing of my plane just prior to rotation speed causing it to veer off the runway and into the grass. I came to a stop in the grass along the runway and determined there was no damage to the plane or airport property. I was uninjured. Contributing factors include the plane has a STOL kit installed so lift can occur prior to recorded rotation speeds. Also; lack of enough aileron turned into the wind allowed the right wing to be lifted prior to the left one.

column121: I am a video editor by trade. I was recently hired as a Social Media and Content Coordinator. My role is to manage social media channels for them and gather content and edit it to post to social media. I was informed that the company owned a drone; so I waited until there was an opportunity to use it. I have never flown a drone before and I have never been trained to. Today; I operated the drone at a residential site from about XA:25 - XA:55. The goal was to capture photos or videos of a completed backyard that has been designed and built by the landscaping firm. I did not have any issues with operating the drone and I did not fly above 300 feet; and that was only for a brief moment to begin descent of the property. Most of the flying was close to the ground. While I was operating the drone within 10-20 feet in the air; I did hear and notice a helicopter overhead. By reflex; I soon landed the drone. When the helicopter returned (or it may have been another); I had already ceased operating the drone. I did not believe that I was doing anything improper at the time. Still; it prompted me to conduct an online search about laws regarding drone usage. I then learned that I am required to be licensed to operate the drone; and also that I cannot fly within 5 miles of an airport. I performed a Google search and realized that this address was within 5 miles of ZZZ Airport. This news brought me anxiety; for I did not intend to violate any FAA laws and I had no idea that the airport was so close to the job site. I do not know if my inadvertent action was discovered or reported to or by the FAA; as it could have just been routine helicopter operation; but I did later learn that my drone has a digital ID that can appear and be noticed. I informed my employers right away about this; in case they are contacted. The drone belongs to the business owners and I was using their drone on site; operating alone with no training or awareness of the laws. I regret operating the drone today and I wish I had been aware of the requirements. I do not plan on operating the drone again until I am licensed and have obtained approval to fly in any airspace requiring it.

column121: Unintentional UAS Operation in Class D Airspace (First Flight Experience)During my first-ever recreational drone flight; which occurred at approximately XA:00; I unintentionally operated within Class D airspace without prior authorization.The flight took place in an area that I later learned corresponds to a 100-foot LAANC grid within Class D airspace. column121: Runway 16R was the active. I (training on Local Control) had control of Runway 16R. Ground Control (GC) had control of runways 16L; 10; and 4. GC had a vehicle that needed to mow the area immediately surrounding the intersection of runways 16R and 10. Ground would request permission from me to have the vehicle enter the intersection. When I needed Runway 16R clear; I would inform ground; and they would have the vehicle exit Runway 16R and remain on Runway 10 for quick re-entry. Each time I give GC permission to enter the runway; I put my memory aid up on the Runway Incursion Device (RID); as required by our SOP. I had a VFR helicopter maneuvering about 300 feet above ground level (AGL) several miles south of the field inspecting a power line. I had Aircraft X ready for takeoff at Runway 16R at Taxiway Papa. Another aircraft was taxiing northbound on Papa and would be ready to depart shortly. Because the helicopter was in the way of the departing aircraft; I coordinated with the departure controller and received a left turn heading 100 or heading 110; which would get the departure well east of the helicopter. I wrote the coordinated heading on the flight strip as a not-required memory aid to give the aircraft the turn when clearing it for takeoff. At that time; the vehicle was in the intersection of runways 16R and 10; and my memory aid was where it should have been. After seeing the helicopter out the window to the south and turning to look at Aircraft X to the north ready to depart; I cleared Aircraft X for takeoff. I issued the left turn and gave the aircraft the wind and the position of the helicopter. Aircraft X then entered the runway and began powering their engines up; all the while the pickup truck is parked on the runway. The ground controller noticed Aircraft X moving and mentioned it to me; then exclaimed that the vehicle was still where I had coordinated that it could be: halfway down the runway directly ahead of the departing Aircraft X. I told Aircraft X to cancel takeoff clearance and turn right at Taxiway Mike. The pilot promptly read back my instructions; slowed the aircraft; and exited the runway at Mike. The pilot then asked me why their takeoff clearance was cancelled. I informed them that there was a vehicle on the runway. The ground controller had the vehicle exit Runway 16R. The other departing aircraft was ahead of Aircraft X at this point and departed first. Aircraft X next; but this time runway heading because the helicopter was not a factor. Aircraft X never got closer than 3;250 feet to the vehicle.If I had had direct communication with the vehicle; rather than the vehicle being on GC's frequency; I would likely have been more aware and would have talked to the vehicle before talking to the aircraft. I need to ensure my normal scan (including the RID and runways) does not get compromised when I have additional things to include in my scan (in this case; the helicopter in a specific place out the window and the heading in a small box on the flight strip). If I had looked at the RID and seen the memory aid or looked at the runway and seen the truck; I would not have cleared the Aircraft X for takeoff.
column123: I was training a developmental on the Local Control (LC) position. Traffic had been average; and the session up to that point was uninteresting. The Controller in Charge (CIC) position was de-combined; and the CIC and Ground Control (GC) controller were having a conversation. A vehicle had been proceeding onto the intersection of the active Runway 16R and Runway 10 periodically. The developmental cleared Aircraft X for takeoff from Runway 16R; which is approximately 5000 feet from the intersection. It appeared to me that the vehicle was near the edge of the safety area; so I was unclear if he had exited. I was about to ask the developmental; when the GC controller jumped up and said that the vehicle was still in the intersection. The developmental cancelled Aircraft X's takeoff clearance and taxied them back around to the departure end. When exiting the runway; Aircraft X asked the reason for the cancellation.The memory aid for the runway being occupied was used.The primary failure here was in the scan; the developmental failed to scan the runway for the vehicle; and failed to acknowledge the memory aid they had displayed. As the trainer; I failed to acknowledge with certainty that the vehicle had not yet exited the runway. I gave the developmental; who is close to certification; too much leeway and benefit of the doubt that my memory was lacking and not his actions.I also feel that this developmental sees extra scrutiny and harassment from other controllers due to his personality. This may cause me to give him extra space to work traffic to prove them wrong; which may have contributed to this scenario.

The flight attendant contacted the flight deck and reported that passengers had heard the noise and that some appeared concerned. We advised the flight attendant to stand by while we focused on aircraft control and the immediate abnormal procedures.I remained PF and continued flying the aircraft. The Captain requested priority handling with ATC and requested descent to FL230. The Captain set began the applicable engine-out QRH; and turned the APU on. During the procedure; I monitored aircraft control; guarded and confirmed the required actions as appropriate; and continued the descent.After the No. 1 engine was safely secured; the Captain coordinated with Dispatch and we elected to divert to ZZZ. ATC then cleared us direct ZZZ and issued descend and maintain 11;000 feet. During the descent; the Captain made a PA advising the passengers that we had experienced an engine failure and were diverting to ZZZ for a safe landing; while I set up the FMS and prepared for the approach.During the descent; we also observed a PACK 1 OVHT (Overheat) message. The Captain selected PACK 1 OFF. Later; we observed a Rudder Hardover Protection Fail message. After ensuring the aircraft remained stable in the engine-out condition; I transferred control of the aircraft to the Captain; and the related QRH was completed while continuing the diversion.The flight attendant continued her procedures and kept the cabin under control. The approach and single-engine landing at ZZZ were completed without further difficulty by the Captain. After clearing the runway; Engine 2 was shut down and fire/rescue personnel performed an external inspection of Engine 1. We were advised that there was no visible external fire or smoke. Afterward; Engine 2 was restarted and the aircraft taxied to Gate XX.At no point did I perceive a loss of aircraft controllability. Workload was elevated but manageable; and CRM among the Captain; myself; the flight attendant; ATC; and Dispatch was effective throughout the event.Suggestions: The company's engine-out training was very helpful during this event. I advised her to stand by while we focused on aircraft control and immediate actions.I then requested priority handling with ATC:I requested a descent; stating We need lower;" and ATC cleared us to descend to FL230.While First Officer continued flying the aircraft; I initiated the applicable QRH procedure. We positively verified the correct engine prior to taking action and secured Engine 1 in accordance with QRH guidance. Passing through approximately 28;000 feet; the APU was started.Once the engine was secured and the aircraft stabilized in descent; I contacted the Flight Attendant and provided the following briefing:"Everything is under control; so remain calm. We lost Engine 1. We have approximately 15 minutes to prepare the cabin for a normal landing. I will call you if anything changes. Please read that back and report to me once the cabin is ready."She acknowledged and began cabin preparation.After securing the engine; I coordinated with Dispatch regarding a suitable alternate for single engine operations. Dispatch recommended ZZZ. We advised ATC of our intent to divert and were cleared direct ZZZ; with a subsequent descent clearance to 11;000 feet.During the descent; I made a PA to the passengers:"Folks; this is your captain speaking. We've experienced a loss of our number one engine and will be diverting to ZZZ. There is no need for concern; we will have you safely on the ground in approximately 15 minutes."The announcement was delivered in a calm and controlled manner.First Officer configured the FMS and prepared for the approach while I continued coordinating with ATC; Dispatch; and the cabin. The flight attendant later confirmed that the cabin was prepared.During the descent; we observed a PACK 1 OVHT (Overheat) message; which was addressed by selecting PACK 1 OFF in accordance with QRH procedures. We also received a Rudder Hard Over Protection Fail message. After confirming the aircraft remained stable; the associated QRH was completed and no additional action was required.We verified that the aircraft was below maximum landing weight and completed performance calculations using QRH; along with obtaining current weather for ZZZ from ATC.Once all QRH and abnormal procedures were completed; with the exception of the landing checklist; I briefed First Officer that I would assume control of the aircraft for the approach and landing. A positive transfer of controls was completed at that time.I then hand-flew the aircraft from base to final to better assess handling characteristics; trim; and aircraft response in the single-engine configuration. First Officer continued in a monitoring role and handled the landing checklist at the appropriate time.We maintained a methodical and disciplined approach throughout the event; verbally confirming actions and ensuring all procedures were completed.The approach and single engine landing at ZZZ were completed without further issue. We landed using Flaps 22 on Runway XXL and exited the runway at taxiway 1.After clearing the runway; we stopped at Taxiway 1 and shut down Engine 2 to allow emergency personnel to approach the aircraft. Fire andrescue crews performed an external inspection of Engine 1 using thermal imaging equipment and reported no signs of fire or abnormal heat.Following the inspection; Engine 2 was restarted; and we taxied to Gate XX; where the terminating checklist was completed.Post-flight; we coordinated with Company; Maintenance; and Union representatives to complete all required reports and write ups.At the gate; I addressed the passengers; informing them of the next steps; including that a replacement aircraft would be provided for transportation to ZZZ3. I also thanked them for their patience and cooperation. The message was well received.Suggestions: CRM was a key factor in the successful management of this event. I could not have asked for a stronger First Officer or Flight Attendant. We worked cohesively as a team; maintaining clear communication while continuously supporting and cross-checking one another. Although the situation involved a high workload; it remained manageable due to this coordination; discipline; and adherence to SOPs."

column121: After departing ZZZ for ZZZ1 we received a call from the number one flight attendant climbing through approximately 10;000ft. The number one stated that there was an extreme amount of noise coming from the forward entry door. As he was speaking to me on the inter phone I could audibly hear the loud rushing air noise and the flight attendant was having to yell to communicate with me. The pressurization was on schedule and there was nothing on the gauges to alert us of any kind of issue with the system. We discussed with the number one that we were going to climb a little higher to see if the door will get a seal on it. Some aircraft need a little more pressure to create a good seal. As we climbed we contacted the number one and he stated that there was no change it was still loud. I then called dispatch and Maintenance Control and went over the issue with them. They all agreed this was not normal. As I was talking to them the cabin crew was calling to let us know the passengers were uncomfortable. It was at this point we decided to take the plane back to ZZZ instead of continuing over the ocean to ZZZ1. We discussed that the plane would be slightly overweight for landing and given the unknown situation with the door we advised ATC and started coordinating with ATC for a return to ZZZ. On our way in to ZZZ we ran the overweight landing QRH procedure and the non routine landing checklist. The rest of the flight was unremarkable and we made our way to the gate for a normal deplaning via jet bridge. At the gate I made the entries in the logbook for the pressurization issue and the over weight landing. Cause: Casual factors in this event are mechanical failures as well as communication and crew coordination. This is the type of event that could really only be discovered during flight as the AC is not pressurized enough on the ground to know. I did follow up with the actions of the mechanics and it seems there was a tear in the door pressurization seal. Mitigation may have to occur on overnight maintenance checks of door pressurization seals.
column123: I was the flying pilot of Aircraft X. During the takeoff phase of flight while climbing through 10;000 ft. Upon communicating with the flight attendants; The pilot not flying indicated that the Flight attendants had to scream next to each other in order to communicate. he also explained he heard loud consistent wind noise while speaking with the flight attendants. He called Maintenance Control and tried to trouble shoot the abnormality however after communicating with Maintenance Control they came to the same conclusion we did that there was something defective going on that we couldn't see and that the pressurization gauges weren't indicating. So we discussed and decided that landing back in ZZZ was the safest course of action. We proceeded to make the necessary reports when requesting priority handling with air traffic control. After going through all the appropriate checklist for the non routine landing and the over weight landing. We executed a safe landing on runway XXC in ZZZ. Cause: Our crew took the necessary steps of migrating risk by returning to the destination airfield. We did not feel it was safe to continue on to ZZZ1.

column121: The flight crew arrived at ZZZZ to operate Aircraft X to ZZZ1 on-time on Day 0.  While completing our receiving checklist; the CA noticed that the CA's oxygen mask (interphone) would not test properly; and that there was not a proper 'switch over;' to the mask-microphone function.  After confirming that the First Officer's mask was working properly; and attempting to resolve the issue multiple times; dispatch was informed and maintenance was called to the aicraft.  Maintenance confirmed that the CA's mask was not working properly; and upon further investgiation; damage was found to the cables connecting the mask to the aicraft in the flight deck.  Maintenance informed us that they would 'swap;' the mask assembly box with the second observer's mask to resolve the issue.  This process took several hours as it proved to be a difficult task to accomplish due to the ergonomics of the assemblies. After the procedure was complete; the maintenance technicians proceeded to begin the 'sign off;' process; and took the logbook to 'close out;' the open write-up.  While this was happening; the aircraft unexpectedly rolled forward completely uncommanded into the chocks.  The Captain first noticed this; and it was confirmed by the remaining maintenance crew still onboard the aicraft.  We verified that the parking brake was still engaged by first looking at the E/WD; and then looked at the 'triple indicator;' to see that both the accumulator and both brake pressure indicators were showing zero pressure.  After coordinating with maintenance; the yellow pump was turned on which immediately pressurized the yellow system.  Hydraulic cavitations were felt and heard; and the 'triple indicator;' immediatley showed tha the system was pressurized. At this point; we realized that there may be an issue with the accumulator.  At no point did we suspect that the indicator was incorrectly reporting the pressure; as it was confirmed on two separate 'known states;' that the pressure was first 'lost;' and then 'recharged.'  During the next 35-40 minutes of troubleshooting and invesgitation; we noticed that the presure in the accumulator was dropping rapidly; and the brake pressure indicators were also showing a loss of pressure. The manual states that 'EFFECTIVE ON A/C ALL - Accumulators maintain the parking pressure for at least 12 hours.  Yellow accumulators can be pressurized by pressuring the yellow electric pump switch. Brake and accumulator pressure are indiciated on the triple indicator.'  The total time elapsed from first parking brake application (aircraft block-in from ZZZ1) to the aircraft moving into the chocks was approxmately 3 hours -- clearly outside of the normal expectation for the system. At this point; we were notified that the airport authority had instructed us to move the aicraft off of the gate because it was needed for another aircraft.  We proceeded to 'deplane;' the customers; and maintenance moved the aicraft to another suitable gate.  This process took several hours; and during this time; on-site maintenance worked to test the aicraft and seek a resolution.  Ultimately; the flight was cancelled due to the extended delay as the inflight crew had worked the incoming flight from ZZZ1; and we were rapidly approaching our MOT (Minimum Off Time). We were notified that we would be operating an extra section for the route; Aircraft Y on Day 1.The next morning; after waking up in ZZZZ; I noticed that the schedule stated that the flight would be operated with the same tail number; Aircraft X and there was an MEL applied -- MEL 32-XX-XXX.  In my opinion; after reviewing the MEL details; this was an incorrect MEL for the situation; instead referencing the indicator not being correct.  At this time; I felt that maintenance control was attempting to apply the MEL that would allow us to depart while the aicraft was still in an unsafe condition to fly.  Ultimately; the issue was resolved via a 'tail swap;' to another aicraft; and AircraftX was grounded.

column121: I was assigned from reserve to operate Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1.During preflight; the First Officer and I reviewed the aircraft logbook and MELs. Multiple MELs were noted; including two related to the air conditioning system. Neither MEL contained Operations Procedures or notes indicating degraded cabin temperature performance. During cockpit preparation; I observed the PACK FLOW selector in the HIGH position. As this was not required by any MEL or procedure; it was returned to NORM.Pushback was slightly delayed due to ramp congestion. Taxi and takeoff were uneventful. During climb; passing approximately 10;000 feet; the flight attendants reported increasing cabin temperatures in the aft cabin. In response; I selected all temperature zones to full cold and set PACK FLOW to HIGH. A subsequent report from the cabin indicated that conditions were worsening; with very hot air from the vents.The COND page was reviewed and indicated increasing cabin temperatures and elevated trim air temperature (approximately 150°C). I made a PA to inform passengers that we were working to address the situation. At that point; I transferred aircraft control to the First Officer and requested a level-off from ATC to allow time for system evaluation and troubleshooting.No ECAM messages were present; and no applicable non-annunciated procedures were identified in the QRH. Based on system indications; we selected the HOT AIR pushbutton OFF; no improvement was observed.I established communication with Maintenance Control via SATCOM and provided a summary of system indications and cabin reports. In coordination with Maintenance Control; we selected the HOT AIR push button OFF and performed a pack reset. These actions did not result in any sustained improvement. Cabin temperatures continued to increase; reaching approximately 105°F forward and 100°F aft. Concurrently; the cabin crew continued to report worsening conditions and increasing passenger discomfort.Given the lack of response to corrective actions; continued adverse temperature indications; and ongoing cabin reports; the First Officer and I assessed the situation as a safety concern and elected to discontinue the flight and return to ZZZ.The First Officer coordinated the return with ATC while I remained in communication with Maintenance Control. During the return; trim air temperature briefly decreased; however; cabin temperatures remained elevated and subsequently increased again. Based on this trend; the decision to return was reaffirmed.I advised the cabin crew and passengers of the return. Due to workload during the approach phase; I contacted ZZZ operations via VHF to advise of the return and request notification to dispatch.The approach and landing were uneventful. After arrival at the gate; a logbook entry was made and the aircraft was subsequently removed from service.

column121: Shortly after departure from ZZZ Airport; while climbing through approximately 1;500 feet AGL; the crew received an amber ECAM message: DOOR R AFT EMERGENCY EXIT.The message appeared after the Takeoff Inhibit phase; at which point we leveled at 5;000 feet and requested vectors to troubleshoot. ECAM and QRH procedures were initiated.Per QRH guidance; continuation of flight may be considered if pressurization is confirmed normal. However; during coordination with the cabin crew; a physical inspection of the door revealed that the handle had become detached and the door appeared unsecured (unlocked"/not properly seated).This created a discrepancy between: System indications and QRH conditional guidance; and Direct physical observation from the cabin crew indicating a potential door integrity issue.Additionally; due to the early phase of flight in which the ECAM message occurred (approximately 1;500 feet AGL); there was limited opportunity to reliably assess cabin pressurization performance prior to reaching higher altitudes where any degradation could become operationally significant.Given: The uncertainty regarding the mechanical status of the emergency exit; The abnormal condition of a detached handle; The limited ability to confirm stable pressurization early in the climb; The planned routing over the ZZZZZ/oceanic segment; where diversion options are more limited; I assessed that continuing the flight would introduce unnecessary risk; particularly in the event of a pressurization or structural issue. Given these factors; delaying the decision until further climb would have reduced available margins and increased exposure to risk in a less favorable operational environment. After completing the QRH; I coordinated with Dispatch via SATCOM; briefed the passengers; and elected to return to ZZZ for a precautionary landing. The aircraft landed without further incident."

column121: Shortly after liftoff; we raised the landing gear; noticed the Nose Pitch Trim was not corresponding correctly to the flying pilots (Captain) input. As the aircraft accelerated through 800' feet; both pilots recognized the excessive pressure it took for me to keep the nose at the proper pitch angle for climb. Although I could command the Blue" electronic pitch trim speed bug forward; there was no airspeed trim vector "Green" indicated. As the airspeed increased and the aircraft continued; it was harder to keep the nose down at the proper climb angle. Upon level off at 5;000; I was forcefully pushing forward pressure constantly to keep the aircraft nose from pitching back up. I was able to control and eventually level the aircraft and reduce the speed; as the speed trim bug was 30-40 kts above the FMS preselected climb speed in the climb. I was able to eventually ease the forward pressure on the stick and level the aircraft off. The First Officers side seemed unaffected by the problem. We both made the decision that he would fly the aircraft and I would handle ATC and programming the FMS for the approach back into ZZZ. I elected to return the aircraft back to ZZZ; RW XXR. I did not declare an emergency; simply because I did not feel assistance on the ground was warranted at the time. I did not brief my Inflight; as time was a virtue. However; all items of a briefing were accomplished. Getting the aircraft back on the ground SAFELY was my main priority. We were cleared back to join the ILS approach for RWY XXR and to descend to 3;000. My inflight was instructed to prep the cabin for landing. I made an announcement over the PA to the passengers. The aircraft did not auto-call 1;000 RA while on final approach. The aircraft handled as expected through flare & touchdown; while the First Officer flew the approach. Once on the ground; I contacted dispatch; Maintenance control and the duty chief pilot."

column121: I was arriving at ZZZ in gusty southerly wind conditions. The reported winds were approximately 170° at 11 knots; gusting to 18 knots. Visual observation of the windsock indicated variable and gusty conditions.On the first approach; I experienced instability on short final related to gusty conditions and airspeed management. Recognizing the unstable condition; I executed a go-around.On the second approach; I increased my approach speed and initially maintained runway alignment. However; during the landing phase near touchdown; I encountered a gust while applying significant control input to maintain directional control in the crosswind. The aircraft deviated left of centerline and exited the runway into the grass; where it came to a stop in soft ground.There were no injuries; and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft. The aircraft is being inspected prior to return to service.This event highlighted the importance of maintaining adequate control margin in gusty crosswind conditions. While the reported winds were within expected limits; the variability and gusts resulted in higher control input requirements than anticipated on short final.In reviewing the event; I recognize that increasing control demand earlier on final approach was an indicator of reduced margin. Continuing the approach into the flare under those conditions reduced my ability to respond effectively to a gust at touchdown.Going forward; I will use earlier decision points based on control input and stability; and will discontinue the approach if increasing control demand indicates diminishing margin. I will also ensure appropriate energy margin is maintained in gusty conditions.

column121: Our flight was from ZZZ.  We boarded Aircraft X and found the flight deck and forward galley in a bit of disarray; with gear pins; papers; and rags on the cockpit floor and a mechanic's headset and pitot tube covers in the galley.  The aircraft had been sitting in ZZZ for what I recall was a few days from the logbook.  We requested that a mechanic come to retrieve any items that didn't belong on the airplane and ensure that everything that was required to be onboard was accounted for; which they did.  My FO verified that no gear-pins; collars; reverser locking pins; etc. were in place on the exterior of the aircraft.We departed on time and taxied to runway XXL for takeoff.  The takeoff was normal and we received a vector of 230 and clearance to 10;000 feet from ZZZ departure.  Passing through approximately 6;000 feet; an ECAM message appeared; ENG 2 EGT OVER-TEMP" with engine parameters in agreement.  I was the pilot monitoring and began the non-normal plan strategy; which led us to reducing thrust to see if the EGT would come below the high-limit.  It did; but after a brief discussion of our situation and about how such a reduction in thrust didn't make flying all the way to  our destination seem very practical or wise; we decided that returning to ZZZ would be prudent.  This discussion was cut short by a second ECAM; "ENG2 EPR MODE FAIL"; so the plan strategy began once again.  The ECAM action led us to a reversion to N1 mode of thrust control and subsequent loss of auto-thrust; and that went smoothly.  My FO; whose capacity to fly the aircraft extraordinarily well and handle high task-loading with apparent ease (while I was quite busy with QRH followups; STATUS page updates; the ECAM Supplemental manual; diversion notification; etc.); was able to observe that increasing the thrust on the affected engine close to climb would cause another over temperature condition while decreasing the thrust to idle also caused a sharp increase in temperature up to the limit.  Unusual.  I notified the flight attendants and passengers of the need to return to ZZZ for a mechanical discrepancy.  We notified ATC for a more immediate return to the airport; although the situation was quite under control; the strange behavior of the EGT on the affected engine gave us enough reason to think being on the ground sooner than later would be a good idea.  We performed an overweight landing checklist for what would be a landing at approximately 4;000 pounds over maximum landing weight.  During landing the #2 engine thrust reverser didn't deploy; and displayed amber when selected to reverse.  After clearing the runway we noticed that the #2 engine; when at idle; was approximately 150 degrees hotter than the #1 engine at idle; but within limits.  After shutdown; we also noted an "ENG2 FADEC" Class 2 status message.  Before I had the chance to pick up my iPad to begin making all of the necessary logbook entries; we were greeted on the flight deck by two mechanics who noted that they weren't very surprised by our return because the airplane had "quite a history".  They mentioned that the work done on the airplane over the last day or two involved replacing pieces of a wiring harness; but the reality was that the airplane simply needed an engine change.  I can't speak to the veracity of that statement; but it was said to me.  I spoke with our dispatcher; Chief Pilot.  We swapped to another A-320 at the neighboring gate and departed about 2 hours late for a successful flight.Cause: The specific causal factors; at least in so far as what caused the EGT to over-temp in such a way with the follow-on failures (Engine Pressure Ratio mode failure; thrust reverser failure; Full Authority Digital Engine Control fault) aren't available to me at this point; so I could only speculate.  My decades of experience flying turbine engines would lead me to believe that the engine's turbine tolerances had become excessive and the engine was simply out of time.  That would agree with the statement the mechanics made to me; but I can't verify that.  As I sit writing this; it's not immediately apparent to me why an EGT exceedance (at least one that's not severe) would cause the other issues; too.  Concerning this; I don't have any recommendations for this situation to be prevented; but I can speak to the effectiveness of the planned strategy and of course recommend the reinforcement of its teaching.  An EGT over-temp on a high-time engine for a brief period during takeoff isn't exactly unheard of; and in fact is even allowed in some cases with a maintenance discrepancy item; but this event unfolded in a rather unexpected way after the over-temp occurred; and the planned strategy is indispensable in such a situation."

FO saw the n1 roll back some then heard a second loud bang saw the n1 roll back some then got an amber ecam 1 engine compressor stall. The ecam message then extinguished not to come back on. While i was coordinating with dispatch the FO asked at his time if we should request priority handling. He was flying and working with atc to get us to ZZZ2; We agreed to get priority handling to the airport; (with engine issues that could be unknown we wanted to get on the ground as quick as possible ) and proceeded to ZZZ2. I used the iPad and contacted our dispatcher informed of the issue and our intention to go to ZZZ2. I then went to the qrh and non routine landing page went through that. I talked to the FA's and made a pa to the pax. At this point the FO had us descending toward ZZZ2 and had the plane ready for approach. We reviewed the approach; briefs and decent checklist; and they were completed at this time. We did a normal approach and landing with no issues. We pulled off the runway and had ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to look over to make sure there were no issues with the engine. We got the all clear and proceeded to the gate with no further issues . This was not an overweight landing as well.

column121: On departure out of ZZZ we received an engine exceedance Crew Alerting System (CAS) message briefly. PM observed the message and called for the low speed abort. We cleared the runway and taxied back to ramp to contact maintenance and company.Cause: Tail wind component was within limits and winds were variable in direction. We determined we were within safe and legal tailwind component limit of ten knots. We believe the tailwind component may have shifted which generated the momentary CAS.Suggestions: Crew will be even more conservative below the published tail wind component maximum to help ensure the possibility a shifting tail wind component does not necessitate another low speed abort.
column123: We were attempting to fly from ZZZ after landing on runway XX. We deplaned our passenger; fueled; and prepared to takeoff on XY. We had collectively decided that runway XY was the more favorable runway due to the local ceilings as well as the fact this was the only runway where a Departure Procedure existed. We had shifting and gusty winds for our landing and departure; but had made a determination that we had not exceeded the 10kts tailwind limit for the CE-700. We also determined that the performance assessment and associated limitations were met for this strategy. We lined up on the runway; ran up the engines for static takeoff; checked the engine instruments; and began our takeoff roll. My role was PM at the time; and as we proceeded in the low speed section of the takeoff roll. we received an amber Crew Alerting System (CAS) message stating that one of the engine limits was being exceeded. I believe the CAS message was 'ENG EXCEEDANCE'; which engine I cannot recall. I immediately called for an aborted takeoff; and the PF complied. We exited the runway; called clearance to cancel our release; ran our checklist and called maintenance to proceed with whatever they needed. We waited for maintenance to get back to us; and they determined that we were released to attempt another takeoff. We never did; as there was no legal way to depart the other runway; so we taxied back to the ramp.Cause: I believe that this was likely caused by the winds at the time of the event. While we had determined that the aircraft's tailwind component limitation was respected; the wind was highly variable as it gusted through the mountains near ZZZ. I believe that what happened was that during our takeoff roll; there was a change in wind that either caused a momentarily exceedance of the tailwind component or a change in crosswind loading on the engines. Either way; the change in engine intake airflow likely caused the engine to momentarily near an exceedance. The checklist for this CAS message explains that it appears when the engine N2 is in the transient region and close to exceeding an operating limit.Suggestions: While I believe that we were within the limitations of the aircraft; I also think that this instance is a great example that the limitations we fly with are legally defined sharp lines; with a good side and a bad side. In reality; the equipment's ability to perform is not as sharp as the limitations that try to define the ability to perform. While we were legal to attempt takeoff; it is clear that between the gusty and shifting winds and the existing tailwind component; we had managed to find an area where the machine was unable to perform despite what the book says. Perhaps the wind momentarily gusted past 10 kts of tailwind; but we will never know. What we both seem to be taking away from this instance is that we need to consider the totality of the situation a bit more in-depth before simply relying on exactly which side of a limitation we are on. We should have taken into account all of the wind shifting and gust factor as well as the tailwind component and simply declined the takeoff. I will be more cautious of these types of situations in the future; and will be ready to discuss with flight support why we were unable to take off even if we seem to be in limitations on paper.

column121: Requested priority handling on a the approach segment to runway XX into ZZZ. The aircraft was on its second flight after maintenance. Leg one was a no passenger test flight / reposition all systems checked and functioned well. Second flight everything worked great until 1.5 miles from the FAF a dot above; I put the gear down. Gear symbols went to transition but took longer than normal. Finally the nose wheel turned green; however; the mains turned a red box. I got the following Crew Alerting System (CAS) messages: landing gear disagree; hyd low pressure; break fail. I was already talking to ZZZ [Tower]; I was already visual. I advised them of the issue that I'd like to level over fly the airport and climb to 12;000 for safe maneuvering to run checklists and return to the field. I advised that we would be requesting priority handling because the hydraulic failure meant we would have to shut down on the runway and be towed in. As we flew over the field the main landing gear due to the airflow over it locked in place and received three green indicators and the landing gear disagree message disappeared. I requested the trucks as a precautionary; hydraulic fluid is highly flammable. ZZZ [Tower] transferred me back to ZZZ [ARTCC] who gave me a heading and an altitude. We coordinated further details for the priority handling. I ran both my break fail check list and the hydraulic low pressure checklist. Upon completion I got the final vector to the IAF ZZZZZ and started the approach there. Though we were in visual conditions I requested the ILS due to the nature of the situation. Once established ZZZ [ARTCC] passed me back to ZZZ [Tower] and provided them with further details and information of the nature of the situation. I landed runway XX; stopped the airplane with the parking brake. Set the brake I advised ZZZ [Tower] we would be unable to exit the runway due to loss of hydraulics and limited pressure in the accumulator. He advised it be okay to shut down. We shut down the engines; priority handling vehicles; Maintenance and tow crew came out and made sure all were okay. We inserted the gear pins to prevent a potential gear collapse during towing; disconnected the nose torque link and were towed off the runway. NO aircraft damage; no passenger or crew injuries; and no airport damage.

column121: I departed in Mooney with a destination of ZZZ. The weather was exceptionally favorable--clear and sunny; with some ground fog in the region. I climbed to an altitude of 13;000 feet; enjoying a smooth IFR flight.As I began my descent towards ZZZ; everything seemed normal. I arrived and made my approach for landing. During the landing phase; I touched down at the typical speed of 55 to 60 knots. Upon landing; the steering did not feel normal; and the aircraft began to veer left of centerline. My first thought was that I might have a flat nose wheel tire. I provided control input to correct the course; and while the aircraft initially responded; it soon began to veer to the right. It wasn't long before the nose gear collapsed; causing the nose to drop and the propeller to strike the pavement at an approximate ground speed of 30 to 35 knots; resulting in the engine shutting down.After communicating with the tower about the collapse of the nose gear and informing them that I was evacuating the aircraft on the runway; I pulled the mixture knob; switched the fuel selector to the off position; turned the master switch off; switched the ignition to the off position; removed the keys; and placed them on the dashboard. I then grabbed my handheld radio to remain in contact with the control tower before evacuating the airplane.Once outside; I conducted a visual inspection of the aircraft and noticed no damage other than the collapsed nose gear and bent propeller. Additionally; there were no fuel leaks or indications of leaking oil. The nose landing gear doors remained unscathed; as they did not contact the pavement due to the collapsed nose gear's ability to keep the aircraft elevated. I also noted that the nose tire was fully inflated.Soon after; personnel arrived to assist me. A forklift was utilized to lift the nose of the aircraft using cargo straps attached to the propeller and to pull it to the ramp.

column121: Got to the airplane about an hour before a scheduled departure and Maintenance was on board fixing a problem with our Elevator Aileron Computer (ELAC) system. This caused a delay of about an hour. Flight was not very full but we were boarded up and had to stay at the gate until Maintenance finished their job and paperwork was signed. We eventually pushed back and everything was normal. 2 engine taxi out to runway XXR for departure. There were 2 other planes waiting at the end to takeoff but we were given a takeoff clearance by tower since they were waiting for en-trail spacing. I remember thinking that our takeoff clearance was given a little early; as we were still probably 500'-800' or so from the end of the runway. CA was PF and I was PM on this leg; our first flight together. CA pushed the throttles up and we began the takeoff roll. Everything was normal up until about the 50-65kt range when the Takeoff Hold Lights suddenly changed from green to red. At this point I was looking at the engine pages but I remember seeing the change from green to red happen out of my peripheral vision. I also remember looking down the runway and even though it was dark; I saw an airplane crossing downfield. The captain immediately used MAX braking to slowed the plane to a stop. We skidded a little bit due to the wet runway. He set the parking brake and made a PA in the back. At the same time; I advised ZZZ Tower that we were aborting the takeoff on the runway. They seemed a little confused but one thing that stuck with me is that they NEVER asked us why we discontinued the takeoff. I asked Tower to roll the fire trucks in case our brakes were hot or locked up or there was any other outside damage they were able to see. We were able to taxi so we decided to turn off the runway on an upcoming taxiway and that's where Airport Rescue and Firefighting met us. They could see no such damage and our brakes were not on fire or anything like that. We sat on the taxiway for a while to gather ourselves and to run appropriate checklists. We decided that it was best to go back to the gate because we were getting close to our min fuel for takeoff and we also wanted Maintenance to do a quick inspection of the plane in case one of the wheels locked up since we skidded during the abort. We taxied back to the gate without issue and myself and the captain walked up to the terminal to debrief what had happened.In my opinion; there needs to be better communication between controllers and pilots. I'm still not sure if this was a case where ZZZ ground cleared a plane to cross XXR while ZZZ Tower cleared us for takeoff; or if the crossing plane did so without a clearance; or what exactly happened. It was very strange (in my opinion) for tower not to ask us a reason for the abort. They NEVER recognized the reason why we had to abort the takeoff or maybe they did and said nothing about it. Either way; there was a massive communication breakdown between ground; tower; us; and another aircraft.

column121: I was the pilot flying on flight to LBB.The flight and approach to landing on runway 26 in LBB were all standard and normal. ATIS was reporting gusty winds about 25-35 kts. right down the runway and low level wind shear advisories.We briefed the go-around procedure in case we did get a wind shear advisory.The weather for LBB was reporting VFR.I turned the autopilot off around 200 ft above the minimums. At approximately 200-300 AGL we received a wind shear warning. I called for a go around and pushed the thrust levers forward and pitched up for the recovery.I initially pushed the auto throttle button when I pushed the thrust levers forward on the go around. While the plane was climbing I realized I hadn't pushed the TOGA button so I did; and at the same time while I was doing that my FO said push the TOGA button.Tower instructed us to climb runway heading to 5000 ft.During the climb out around 1200 ft the airspeed got slow and the shaker went off. I lowered the nose and my FO assisted in pushing the thrust levers forward.After we recovered; the FO re-engaged the auto throttle and engaged the autopilot. We climbed to 5000ft and cleaned up the aircraft. We got vectored back around for runway 26.We landed uneventfully with no further encounters of wind shear.Suggestions: I should of had my finger on the TOGA button.

column121: During cruise at FL370 on flight to ZZZ; approximately 100 NM prior to the ZZZZZ fix; both FMS units failed nearly simultaneously; resulting in FMS1 and FMS2 failure advisories and an associated Autothrottle FAIL caution. The aircraft reverted to basic modes; maintaining altitude and roll. The Captain; acting as Pilot Flying; maintained control of the aircraft and communications; while the First Officer; as Pilot Monitoring; executed the appropriate QRH procedures.Attempts to recover or select an alternate FMS were unsuccessful; as both units were inoperative. In accordance with QRH guidance; the crew transitioned to alternate navigation methods and promptly notified ATC of the dual FMS failure; requesting assistance and exit from RVSM airspace. ATC issued step-down descents from FL370 to FL350 and then FL270 and provided radar vectors for navigation.The crew attempted to navigate using raw data via the ZZZ [VOR] by selecting V/L (green needles) and tuning NAV radios; however; no reliable lateral guidance was received. ATC continued to provide vectors. Dispatch and flight attendants were informed; and the crew used additional resources such as Jeppesen charts and flight tracking website to maintain situational awareness. Fuel status was manually calculated and monitored; confirming sufficient fuel to continue to destination. An emergency was not declared.Approximately 200 NM from ZZZ; the crew manually computed top of descent and landing performance data. Weather at ZZZ was VFR. As the aircraft approached the terminal area; VOR navigation became available; and the crew conducted an ILS approach to Runway XXR using raw data. The landing and taxi to the gate were uneventful.After arrival; the Captain coordinated with Dispatch and Maintenance; and the aircraft was turned over for evaluation and corrective action.

column121: Aircraft X was placed on a maintenance hold prior to boarding when maintenance discovered a hydraulic leak on the left wing. Maintenance cleared the issue; and we proceeded with an approximately 45-minute delay. The crew briefed the issue as a potential threat that would be mitigated by monitoring the hydraulic system prior to entering ETOPS airspace.Shortly before level off; the First Officer initiated a log to monitor the hydraulic system quantity and pressure. Very quickly; the HYD synoptic showed a steady decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side at a loss of .01 every 8-9 minutes.If that rate were to remain steady; we calculated that the left hydraulic quantity would read 55% by the time we reach ZZZZ1. Complicating the matter was that the Flight Plan Release included a ZZZZ1 Field Report that indicated a wet runway; with a 500/500/500. As a restricted Captain; I am not authorized for a CAT III approach. If those conditions had persisted; we would have been eligible for a CAT II approach using the exemption. However; during our previous threat briefing; it was discussed that fog at ZZZZ1 tends to be the most intense at dawn rather than around midnight; which was the time of the Field Report.As we typically do not monitor the HYD synoptic page in flight; we initially reviewed the Aircraft Systems Manual (ASM); Quick Reference Handbook (QRH); and Aircraft Operating Manual (AOM) to determine if a continued decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side is normal in flight. We could not find any information in the manuals that indicated it was normal. At this time; we were near ZZZ airspace and initiated a SATCOM call to dispatch to confer with the Maintenance Control. At the conclusion of the initial call with Maintenance Control; we determined the best course of action to be to continue monitoring the hydraulic quantity to see if the trend persisted and to call back on SATCOM prior to the ETOPS Entry Point if the trend continued.Upon entering ZZZZ [ARTCC] airspace; the trend of decreasing HYD quantity on the left system continued at the same rate. We subsequently contacted dispatch and requested a second conference call with Maintenance Control. During the second call with Maintenance Control; we inquired about the normalcy of the decreasing loss of indicated HYD quantity on the left side. Maintenance Control informed us that this situation was not normal. At this juncture; as a crew; we determined the most suitable course of action to be to divert prior to the ETOPS entry point. ZZZ1 was the closest option; but considering redundancy in the HYD system; maintenance facility; and the ease of rebooking passengers; we concluded that ZZZ was a more appropriate diversion field. Upon arrival at ZZZ; we executed an overweight landing (23;000 lbs. above the maximum landing weight) without incident.Cause: Causal factor for the divert was a steadily decreasing Hydraulic Quantity on the A System.

column121: Received takeoff clearance on runway XXR @ ZZZ. Aircraft lined up and FO was given control. Normal engine spool up and normal thrust setting technique applied. As engines were placed into FLEX detent and just as FO called out FLEX; loud bang from #1 engine with aircraft immediately veering left. I commanded control of the aircraft; brought aircraft to a complete stop while FO issued radio call to ATC to inform. I applied brakes and made pa to passengers to remain seated. Initial ECAM messages was ENG 1 STALL; followed just after bringing aircraft to stop to ENG 1 FIRE. Simultaneously with both crew members calling out engine fire; a Air Carrier X aircraft that was given line up and wait behind us on runway XXR made a radio call that our left engine (#1) was on fire and that they could see flames from their position under and behind the engine. FO began the QRC proceeding with Quick Action Item for ENG FIRE (on the ground). I moved to start APU and establish contact with cabin. It was at this time; that I realized that due differences in button location between Basic and Enhanced aircraft and multiple versions of both; that I may not have actually broadcast initial remain seated" pa using the proper function on Audio Control Panel. After placing #1 FA into loop and asking for them to look from windows to see if we were missing anything; I used handset to make addition pa to passengers to explain our situation; that they were to remain seated and that equipment was approaching aircraft. Dispatch was notified of our situation. FO finished checklist; initiated contact with Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF); maintained contact with ATC and then did the most important thing; added a pause to our procedure to make sure we were still working towards the completion together. ARFF contacted; stated no further fire or flames noticed and that the temperature; that had been upwards of 1000C; was in fact reducing. They also inspected left landing gear. I kept the #2 engine running during event while we completed checklist and determined if an evac would be required. I felt evac was not required so we agreed and coordinated with ARFF; ATC and cabin to taxi back to gate under our own power with ARFF following.  No further issues and passengers deplaned normally.Cause: I felt we as a crew performed well; but the multiple configurations of radios and switches to include multiple locations that we face on the A319/320/321 can cause confusion especially when task saturated."

Weather was IMC. I was prompted to switch to departure; then we were given direct to ZZZ [VOR]. I was about to call '3000 feet' and prompt for the after takeoff when this occurred. After I had got confirmation and executed the direct; my FO said something about the autopilot being degraded. I then looked at the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) and saw 'ALT HOLD' with an amber line through it indicating a degraded vertical mode; then noticed our airspeed was quickly rolling below 200 kts and nearing 180 kts. We were in the amber airspeed band with the Performance Limiting Indicator (PLI) visible. There was a startle effect and a moment of disbelief or confusion in what I was seeing; but I called out the speed; and prompted the FO to accelerate as the PLI was floating near the limit. I remember saying something like 'lower the nose'. When the PLI contacted; I called 'STALL' took control; and rolled wings level to initiate the recovery. It took a few seconds for me to realize we were not accelerating at which point I realized I was unconsciously working against the auto throttle at which point I pushed the throttles all the way forward and clicked the autothrottles off. The aircraft began accelerating; the descent arrested and began climbing. During this I also had to tell ATC we were responding to a situation and we'd get back to them. They gave us a vector to 270 and to advise them when everything was okay. Airspeed reached approximately 270 kts as we were climbing again where I started to easy the climb and the airspeed to re-automate. I called for Autopilot Center Command; and once it engaged it resumed the turn to the heading we had been assigned (270). However we immediately got a 'bank angle' aural alert; which confused us because although the Autopilot was banking slightly beyond the Flight Director; the angle was not any higher than 25 degrees while at about 240 knots. Nevertheless; I disconnected the automation again; eased the bank and hand flew with the Autothrottles engaged at 240 kts. Once rolled onto our heading of 270 and steadily climbing to our altitude (we had gotten 7000 and then 11000 assigned during this); I called for the Autopilot again; and then never had another issue. I asked the FO if they were ready to retake the controls; and they took over just before 10;000. We then accomplished the after takeoff checklist. I did not notice at what point we went into altitude capture; when the vertical mode degraded; or when airspeed began rolling back as I was in the middle of ATC responses etc as is typical for this phase of flight. The events all happened very quickly. I only remember seeing the degraded mode; and then the pitch and airspeed which I was immediately fixated on along with the VSI and the altitude; the usual instrument scan. Automation modes were secondary to me at the time as they were being disconnected. I did not think to reset flight directors or try other autopilots since I was focused on the recovery and keeping the plane flying. We descended about 700' during recovery starting from about 3700' regaining altitude at about 3000' and climbing. We talk about; and practice upset recovery in every sim session. We talk about startle effect in CRM every year and in sims. We are trained to expect the unexpected; but it's not until it happens to you in the real environment where you fully realize the effect it has on you.

column121: Our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was uneventful until we started our approach.  The First Officer and I planned and briefed our approach to Runway XXR.  When we got handed over to ZZZ Approach; we were advised to expect Runway XYR.  After a runway change and new briefing; we completed the Before Landing Checklist to the line.  Shortly after we were instructed to descend to 4000 feet and fly direct to ZZZZZ to intercept the XYR localizer.  We were instructed to cross ZZZZZ at 4;000 feet and cleared for the ILS.  At 4;000 feet; I selected LNAV/VNAV and closed the speed window to engage VNAV PTH but remained in VNAV SPD.  Approach instructed us to reduce speed to 170 knots. I opened the speed window to reduce speed.  While slowing down; I requested Flaps 1; VNAV PTH engaged and I selected 2;300 feet for the FAF altitude.  At this point; the Master Caution light illuminated; extinguished and then illuminated again; we saw the HYD light illuminate of the Right Annunciator panel.  The aircraft had already started a descent on the approach path but no more that 100 to 200 feet; we requested to abandon the approach and maintain 4;000 feet as well as a vector to the right.  Autopilot was disengaged momentarily and then re-engaged when established on an altitude and heading.  We selected the systems page on the Lower DU (Display Unit); at this time we noticed that the hydraulic quantity was zero and we had lost pressure in Hydraulic System B.  At this time the LOW-PRESSURE lights on the overhead panel also illuminated.  I declared my aircraft and communications and requested the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH procedure.  While completing the QRH procedure; we noticed the Flap Indicator needle was between the Flaps Up and Flaps 1 position.  We requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of the aircraft status and intentions; we requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) shortly after.We completed the QRH procedure; I then transferred control and communications to the First Officer; I proceeded to complete the NON-NORMAL LANDING CONSIDERATIONS procedure contacting Dispatch and Maintenance Control and informing our cabin crew and our passengers of the current situation.  ATC advised us to expect the ILS to Runway XXL; we selected and briefed the new approach.  ATC vectored us for the approach; we lowered the gear and landing flaps while on base leg and completed the Before Landing Checklist.Our landing on Runway XXL was normal; we vacated the runway and were able to vacate to the left and stopped on Taxiway 1.  We asked Fire Command to inspect the aircraft exterior and were informed of smoke coming from the right landing gear but did not detect excessive temperatures with their thermal imaging.  ARFF requested we shut down the right engine which we did after the 3-minute cool down period; at which time they advised smoke was no longer detected. We decided to continue our taxi to our assigned gate as we were confident in our ability to stop the aircraft normally.  Even though we had no issues stopping the aircraft; we requested to stop on the ramp short of the gate area and have the aircraft towed to our parking position.  After parking; we completed the shutdown checklist; completed the logbook and our maintenance team took over the aircraft.Cause: Mechanical failure of the onboard hydraulic system.  I believe the airlines training for non-normal procedures was evident in this situation.  A recommendation for myself as a new captain was to have let the First Officer fly the aircraft and communicate and I complete the QRH procedures.
