column121: On Day 0 starting at approximately XA:50 local; two near-collision events occurred within a short amount of time at Sequim Valley Airport (W28); involving myself (Aircraft X); an Aircraft Y; and Aircraft Z.Incident 1 -- Runway Incursion by Aircraft Y Causing Me to Abort Takeoff.(The conflict data entered above on this form refers to this specific incident. The 2nd incident described below; concerns a 3rd plane; has even smaller margins for their near-miss.)I was operating Aircraft X and had completed all pre-departure checks. I made radio calls on CTAF 122.7 announcing my intention to taxi onto and depart Runway 09. After lining up at the Runway 09 threshold; I observed Aircraft Y move from the parking area to the runway edge at midfield (2100' ahead from me); then taxi onto the runway and proceed toward Runway 27 -- the opposite end from where I was positioned. No radio calls were made by the aircraft at any point during this time. I made multiple calls to the aircraft and multiple radio checks; no response was received. I elected to abort my intended takeoff and vacate the runway rather than risk departure with an aircraft of unknown intent on the runway.After I vacated; the Aircraft Y pilot then disclosed he had been on the wrong frequency the entire time. Despite this; his first action upon returning to the correct frequency was to announce his departure without first assessing the traffic situation or acknowledging the conflict he had caused.Incident 2 -- Near Midair Collision between Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z:At approximately XB:04 local; while Aircraft Y was positioned at the Runway 27 threshold preparing to depart; Aircraft Z executed what appeared to be a go-around or touch-and-go on Runway 09 and climbed out directly over Aircraft Y at an estimated vertical separation of no more than 100 feet. Aircraft Y appeared unaware that Aircraft Z had passed overhead. Aircraft Z subsequently called on CTAF to apologize; disclosing they had also been on the wrong frequency throughout their approach and pattern.Contributing Factors:Two of three aircraft at the airport were simultaneously tuned to the wrong CTAF frequency; rendering the standard self-announce separation system ineffective.W28's runway configuration requires prolonged runway occupancy to reach thresholds; increasing exposure time and collision risk.The Aircraft Y pilot; after discovering his frequency error; did not pause to assess the traffic situation before proceeding with departure.The narrow runway (40 ft) with no parallel taxiway significantly reduces margins for error.What Prevented a Worse Outcome:I visually detected Aircraft Y before initiating my takeoff roll and held position.I elected to vacate the runway rather than assume the other pilot's intentions.Aircraft Z's go-around (likely triggered by sighting Aircraft Y on the runway) provided vertical separation.Recommended Preventive Measures:Encourage pilots who discover a frequency error to pause; listen; and build situational awareness of the existing traffic situation before taking any further action.At narrow runways like W28 where no parallel taxiway exists; hold-short lines should be positioned to provide greater lateral clearance from the runway edge; and pilots should be explicitly encouraged -- through signage or Chart Supplement notes -- to perform a thorough visual check for aircraft already on the runway before entering.

column121: On Day 0; at approximately XA:20; I was pilot in command of Aircraft X; a Cessna 172S NAV III; departing Runway XXR at ZZZ on a personal flight with one passenger. I hold a Private Pilot certificate; ASEL; with approximately 163.5 total flight hours; all in Cessna 172 aircraft; and 16.6 hours in the preceding 90 days. I was well-rested; of sound mind; and had completed the IMSAFE checklist prior to flight with no concerns. No hazardous attitudes were recognized.The aircraft was rented from the FBO at ZZZ. Prior to flight; I taxied to the fuel tank where the FBO personnel topped off the fuel. A preflight inspection and walkaround were completed with no abnormalities. Fuel was sumped with normal results. Engine oil was observed at approximately 6.5 quarts; one quart was requested and added. A weight and balance computation was completed and confirmed the aircraft was within limits. The fuel selector was verified on BOTH. Aircraft loading was as follows: PIC at 180 lbs; one passenger at 255 lbs; and approximately 20 lbs of baggage in the rear seat area; with full fuel.ATIS Information 1 was current at XD:53; reporting winds 120 at 10 gusting 18; variable between 070 and 140; visibility 10 statute miles; ceiling broken at 4;000 ft; broken at 7;500 ft; temperature 27°C; dew point 17°C; altimeter 30.18. Increased bird activity was noted in the vicinity of the airport. The wind presented a right crosswind component on Runway XXR. Density altitude was elevated due to the 27°C temperature; however; the conditions were within the normal operating envelope for the aircraft type and loading.During the engine run-up at 2;000 RPM; a magneto check was performed. The left magneto dropped to 1;930 RPM and ran smoothly. The right magneto dropped to 1;910 RPM and ran rough. The idle check was satisfactory at 840 RPM. A second magneto check was performed; during which the right magneto ran smoothly. Both drops and the differential were within limits.I contacted ZZZ Tower and reported holding short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1; ready for departure. Tower instructed line up and wait due to traffic on the downwind. Subsequently; Tower cleared me for takeoff on Runway XXR with an assigned heading of 080.I began the takeoff roll from the full length of Runway XXR. Full throttle was applied with mixture full rich; flaps up; and trim set for takeoff. Engine instruments were checked and indicated in the green. Airspeed was confirmed alive. The takeoff roll felt normal in terms of acceleration. I noticed the crosswind component during the roll consistent with the reported winds.Rotation was initiated at 55 KIAS with approximately 10 degrees of pitch. Immediately after liftoff; climb performance was sub-optimal and the aircraft was barely gaining altitude. At a few feet AGL; the stall warning horn activated. I reduced the angle of attack; but airspeed was not increasing. I observed the engine RPM between 2;400 and 2;500. The engine sounded smooth and was not surging or running rough. The aircraft drifted left of the runway centerline.Within a few seconds; recognizing the aircraft was not climbing and was drifting off centerline; I made the decision to abort the takeoff rather than risk running out of usable runway or being forced to land off-surface. I pulled the throttle and mixture fully out; shutting down the engine. The aircraft touched down on the remaining runway approximately abeam Taxiway 2; roughly 1;600 feet from the Runway XXR threshold. I continued on Runway XXR; slowing down and turning right onto Runway XY; where I came to a full stop.I transmitted to Tower that I was aborting the takeoff. Tower initially instructed a right turn at Taxiway 3 to contact ground; then corrected to exit on Runway XY and contact ground. I acknowledged and advised that the engine was off. I contacted ZZZ Ground and reported engine-off on Runway XY after the aborted takeoff. Ground asked if I needed assistance; I requested a moment to assess. After confirmingeverything was in order; I successfully restarted the engine and requested taxi back to the Southeast ramp. Ground cleared me to taxi via Runway XY and Taxiway 3.Upon return to the ramp; I completed a squawk write-up documenting the event. Maintenance was contacted. The aircraft is pending inspection and the cause of the degraded takeoff performance has not yet been determined. No injuries were sustained by either occupant. No aircraft damage was observed.Chain of Events and Contributing Factors:The problem first arose during the run-up when the right magneto ran rough on the initial check. Although the second check was smooth and within limits; this may have been an early indication of a fouled spark plug or developing magneto issue. The problem became apparent immediately after rotation when the aircraft failed to achieve a normal climb rate despite full throttle application; and the stall warning activated at a few feet AGL. Engine RPM was observed at 2;400-2;500; which; combined with the initial rough magneto; suggests a possible partial power issue such as a fouled spark plug or intermittent magneto malfunction.Human Performance Considerations:I was well-rested and had passed the IMSAFE checklist with no concerns. My perception of the initial rough right magneto was that it had cleared on the second check; and I judged the engine fit for flight based on the smooth recheck and all indications being within limits. In hindsight; the initial rough magneto warranted additional scrutiny. My decision to abort was made quickly once I recognized the convergence of poor climb performance; stall warning activation; and lateral drift from centerline. I prioritized remaining on the runway surface and bringing the aircraft to a safe stop over attempting to continue a climb that the aircraft was not performing.Corrective Actions and Prevention:The aircraft has been squawked and is pending maintenance inspection; which should identify the mechanical cause. In future operations; if a magneto runs rough during the initial check -- even if a recheck is smooth -- I will perform an additional magneto verification while holding short prior to takeoff to confirm the issue has truly resolved rather than accepting a single smooth recheck. This additional step adds minimal time and could catch an intermittent ignition issue before committing to a takeoff. I will also establish a more deliberate go/no-go gate at the hold-short line for any anomaly observed during run-up; treating an initial rough magneto with greater caution.

column121: Chain of events and discovery: During an introduction flight I followed checklist usage; however after the run-up I demonstrated to the student that it is important to lean out the mixture while waiting to take off to prevent the spark plugs from fouling. I aggressively leaned the mixture as prescribed; but forgot to re-apply the appropriate mixture for takeoff (full in this case with a density altitude in the negatives). As the aircraft began to accelerate with the student's full application of power; the engine stuttered and stopped on the takeoff roll. I scanned the cockpit and noted the problem. I immediately felt a sinking feeling in my stomach; but was simultaneously struck with fear for how dangerous that situation could have been if we were off the ground. I notified other airplanes on the CTAF that we were stopped on the runway; re-started the engine and taxied off the runway. This event shook me up. As a new instructor; it was a wake up call that it is harder to diagnose issues without my hands on the controls. It was also a shock for how fast everything occurred. I have replayed the event many times in my mind and considered what I should have done differently. I am so thankful that we both walked away safely; and for the instructors that demonstrated aggressive lean procedures to me. This technique caused the engine to stop on the ground rather than in flight.Contributing factors: As a new instructor I was undoubtedly focused on the new students performance during the takeoff. The previous mental space that I would have devoted to re-applying mixture was now distracted with my student. This inadvertently and unnecessarily lowered my situation awareness. Another causing factor was lack of a final flow or adequate takeoff checklist before applying full power.Correcting actions: A learning lesson for me from this was to always use the demonstrate / performance method. An external factor at play was me trying to make the introduction flight as fun as possible by letting the student takeoff. In retrospect; I should have simply let the student put his hands on the controls to feel the correct application. If I would have focused on the demonstrating the correct configuration; the next time the student would also have knowledge of the correct mixture configuration. Additionally; my attention would be less on the students control inputs and more on an overall scan for improved safety. Another learning lesson is two fold: 1) Updating the takeoff checklist in the airplane to include mixture configuration (3rd party checklist and manufacturer's didn't include this). 2) performing a final takeoff flow in all airplanes to cover the most important items; especially ones like mixture that might have changed. For example; once on centerline; I will callout as I confirm: mixture set; props forward (if applicable); throttle forward. Closing notes: This was a very humbling event for me. I feel thankful that nothing serious happened; and I hope to do the most learning I can do from this to prevent another occurrence like this from happening. I also hope that others can learn from my mistake. I apologized for/debriefed my mistake hope that it does not negatively influence his training.

column121: While conducting Flight Instruction in a helicopter (CFI positioned left seat; Pilot-Student Right Seat) at the local high traffic-use un-towered airport; we had conducted our approach to the predominant wind use runway XX; making the CTAF radio report of the approach; and runway XX mid-field intersection termination point.    The mid-point area of the runways intersect; with Runways XX and XY crossing; with the winds indicated by windsock on the airfield of 350-010°; 10 knots with occasional gusts during our traffic pattern training.  The runway alignment angle of Runways XX and XY does not allow a direct view on final for Runway XY if positioned near the intersection or north on Runway XX for reference.  This positioning makes it necessary to verify conflicting approach path is clear of course; if directly holding short (responsibly announced) or prior to an initial departure intention from runway XX; neither of which was the case in this situation.  Upon completing our approach to the mid-field intersection on Runway XX; I was allowing the student pilot to stabilize their hover in the wind prior to our take-off checks and prepare for next departure / right traffic pattern.  I heard an aircraft in-bound over the CTAF; making a call with the intent to use Runway XY; despite the winds and traffic pattern in use already; so as to avoid back-taxing to parking; as only Runway XY has a parallel taxiway directly accessible easily to & from the apron / ramp area.  I made another CTAF call stating we were a momentary delay; midfield intersection RWY XX.   I did not hear another CTAF call; however just a few moments later the American A-5 Tiger landed in front on us on Runway XY; (from my right; angled and blocked by the Pilot-Student / Door) rolling directly by within 50' or less from our hovering position on Runway XX; just south of the intersection.   The pilot while; rolling out after landing; proceeded to chastise us over CTAF; stating we 'were too close to the runway and shouldn't be there'.  I restated we literally had called our position on our approach and again just prior to his approach; stating we were still occupying the predominant wind runway at the intersection; using the crossing runway XX as established by us and other aircraft in the recent traffic pattern operations. There was no inquiry about if we were holding short on Runway XY; or if we could reposition away from the crossing runway (which we can & will do routinely); nor any attempt to abort his landing approach; despite knowing we were still there. column121: Arrived at ZZZ for preflight. Preflight was normal with no abnormalities. Oil level was at 4 quarts; which led me to add 2 more quarts to bring it above the normal 6 quart range. No contaminants found in fuel during sump. No oil leaks in or around the engine. Aircraft had full fuel tanks and I was the only occupant in the aircraft for this flight.Started the engine; contacted clearance and ground frequencies for taxi to run-up area. The taxi was normal with no abnormalities.The run-up went smoothly with no abnormalities. Magneto checks were very smooth and well within range. The engine sounded normal and I continued my taxi to the runway.Departed ZZZ with no abnormalities. The engine sounded completely normal during climb out. I exited the airspace and started to head North-West towards ZZZ1; which was my destination for this flight. 4 minutes after my departure; I reached my cruising altitude of 2;000 feet due to a cloud layer above me and my relatively short flight plan to ZZZ1. My RPM setting for the flight was 2300 rpm's; and the mixture was leaned slightly due to the high density altitude for the day. 12 minutes after my departure; I noticed a steady decrease in rpm's. The drop started at 2300 rpm's and decreased on its own to about 1500 rpm's. I checked to make sure that the throttle did not back itself out. Everything looked normal. The engine started to shake violently. I immediately added full mixture and pulled the carburetor heat. Neither of those inputs made the problem any better. I backed off the throttle enough that the shaking wasn't as violent; but kept it high enough that I could mostly maintain altitude. I first thought that the propeller could have been knocked out of balance; however I decided that that was more than likely not the issue. There was too much shaking for it to be a normal bad magneto; so I also ruled that out. However; in case there was a bad magneto; I did not attempt a magneto check. I checked my engine gauges and the fuel pressure was green; the oil pressure was green; but the oil temperature was gradually decreasing. I monitored the gauges throughout the remainder of the flight. I was monitoring guard on 121.5 as soon as I had gotten the frequency change call from ZZZ tower. ZZZ approach responded to me on 121.5 and asked what kind of aircraft; how many souls were on board; and how much fuel I had. I responded that I was a Cessna 172; 1 soul on board; and full fuel as I had just departed ZZZ. I did my best to report my location before I was contacted by approach; however they made radar contact with me fairly quickly. They eventually asked me to switch to their frequency.I started to look for somewhere to land near me in case my engine decided to quit. I eventually made my way to the Highway that leads into the Bay and the city. I observed traffic patterns of the vehicles on the highway to see if it would be a safe option to land on. Traffic was relatively light; so I stayed over top of the highway until I could find a possible landing location at an airport. Approach gave me a few options to the North. Those airports were private strips. After hearing my options; I decided that ZZZ2 was the best option. Approach informed me of runway length; width; and winds available to the best of their knowledge. About 6 miles away from ZZZ2; I started to turn towards the airfield. I utilized the 3D imaging on ForeFlight to see what the strip would look like since it was private. I made visual contact with the field and continued my flight towards it. Approach informed me that an aircraft was above me and following me in case I had to ditch elsewhere.I had enough power to maintain my altitude for a normal left downwind entry for the field. I added 10 degrees of flaps to help me maintain my altitude while the aircraft slowed down. Once I was confident that I could make the short runway; I added full flaps. There was nearly a 90 degree crosswind for the runway (runway XX). The landing was smooth and did not require any substantial abnormal procedures. I taxied the aircraft off of the runway and shut down immediately. Postflight inspection resulted in seeing that there was a substantial amount of oil pooling on the ground on the right side of the nose wheel coming from the cowling and around the exhaust. I was not able to take the cowling off of the aircraft due to the amount of screws and lack of tools. Nothing looked abnormal in the engine other than the obvious oil leak. I believe that most of the oil leak came after the engine stopped; or at least when I was on the ground. The oil pressure never fell out of the green range and the engine stayed on throughout the flight until I was on the ground and shut it down myself. To my knowledge; I do not believe that any FAR's were broken or deviated from.

I opted to continue the approach; but I was still confused on how I got the caution. I then decided to do a go-around for a reset and do the approach again just for good measure. I then broadcast my intentions to taxi to runway 33 for departure on the RYW Unicom frequency and monitored that frequency until I was ready to depart. I completed my preflight checklist at the departure end holding area of 33 and then called Austin approach for my release. After a few moments on the phone I was given my departure instructions and release. I then broadcast my departure from runway 33 on the unicom frequency; again hearing and seeing no other traffic. Part way down the runway I saw another single engine aircraft on short final for the opposite runway (15). At nearly the same time I also noticed the traffic warning on my TIS-B unit. column121: An Aircraft X departed SDL requesting VFR flight following. Aircraft X established communications with me approximately 10 miles northwest of SDL in a slow climb and moving quickly. Firstly; Aircraft X called me in the blind for flight following. UHF radio stepping on the VHF frequency. It took several transmissions for me to determine his callsign and type aircraft. Contributing to this difficulty was poor radio and reception quality making it difficult on first listen to determine the callsign if you aren't expecting it. Secondly; Aircraft X was not transmitting an ADS-B callsign. If the aircraft was transmitting the ADS-B callsign; I would have determined his callsign much quicker. ADS-B is required to operate in the airspace Aircraft X was flying in. Because of the delay in inputting the necessary information into STARS; I was unable to issue the aircraft control instructions to more effectively avoid traffic. Recommendation: SDL Tower should solicit high performing aircraft for flight following and input; or have Biltmore input flight plan information into STARS/NAS. This would eliminate the back and forth the radar controller has to do to determine the pilots callsign and intentions. In turn; we could provide a much better service. IWA tower does this already and it is very helpful. SDL tower should too. Alternatively; SDL tower can give the Biltmore controller a heads up of what's about to happen.

column121: When departing ZZZZ; we experienced an Airspeed Unreliable due to speed limitation followed by MACH TRIM FAIL and AUTO SLAT FAIL.  During the diversion planning phase; I was the PM.  While trying to contact dispatch to coordinate diversion; I inadvertently caused a communications gap with ATC and had incomplete communication my dispatcher. My first method was to use SATCOM.  The SATCOM system on the aircraft worked fine; but the operations phone would only ring for several calls without an answer.  Finally; on one call the dispatcher answered; but I only got a few words in before the call dropped.  After the failed SATCOM attempts; I went to the CALL ME" button on ACARS.  The dispatcher messaged me to come up on the Company X VHF frequency.  When I dialed in the Company X frequency on VHF2 (I thought it was VHF2); I was able to hear them but they couldn't hear me.  This compounded the mess; as not only were we unable to communicate on VHF2; but a new distraction was introduced as Company X continued to re-SELCAL us every few minutes until we were on the ground.  I then resorted to just using ACARS messages; and the dispatcher and I successfully coordinated over ACARS from that point onwards.  At some point during our descent to ZZZZ1; I saw (On my Radio Tuning Panel) that our VHF1 was incorrectly tuned to Company X; switched it back to ZZZZ [ARTCC]; confirmed we hadn't missed any ATC instructions; and we left it that way for the remainder of the flight.  When trying to contact dispatch via Company X on VHF2; I used the FO's radio tuning panel to change the VHF2 frequency.  However; I didn't notice the Offside Tuning Light was on nor that the FO's Radio Tuning Switch was selected to VHF1.  As a result; I made the Company X VHF frequency ACTIVE in VHF 1; but was listening to both VHF1 and VHF2; and transmitting on VHF 2.  I was therefore unable to communicate with dispatch via Company X and abandoned that idea after a few minutes.  Then I noticed on my own Radio Tuning Panel that VHF1 was on Company X; and switched it back to ZZZZ [ARTCC]  We completed the diversion to ZZZZ1; using VHF1 normally.  After arriving at the gate; I called the dispatcher by cellphone and learned that he couldn't hear any of my transmissions on the Company X frequency (but I could hear him).  At that point; I finally realized that I had been tuning the wrong radio the whole flight due to the selection of VHF1 on the FO's Radio Tuning Panel."

column121: I was completing a round trip flight from LGB in Aircraft X. My right-seat passenger was an instrument-rated private pilot. We were descending to land at Long Beach 26L with VFR flight following; on SoCal Approach. Route of flight was direct from the southeast; descending through 3000 on a 303 degree heading; descent to 2500 authorized. ATC issued a traffic alert for a converging aircraft at 2500 feet indicated. I added power and held 3000 feet until further advised. I never saw the other traffic; so turning away was not an option. As the other aircraft (Aircraft Y) passed directly beneath us; my copilot snapped a ForeFlight screenshot showing the tracks crossing; the other aircraft was shown at 2600' on ADSB-in.The other aircraft was not in communication with SoCal so far as I could tell. It is possible the other pilot was on the practice area CTAF; though I was not. The near-miss happened very fast. Collision was avoided due to my evasive action of aborting descent in response to the ATC alert. My analysis is that my choice to use ATC flight following; and a quick response to the ATC traffic alert; likely saved our lives. My attention was divided between managing the descent; visually scanning outside; descent checklist; navigation; and communications. My iPad was not showing traffic consistently; as it would not maintain a steady WiFi connection to my Sentry Plus. Yet I should have been able to note the conflicting traffic on my own ADSB-in on the G1000 Multi-function Flight Display (MFD). Had the other aircraft been on frequency; likely there would have been ATC intervention to deconflict. Had I been monitoring the CTAF; I might have heard the other aircraft make a position announcement; but the extra radio work would have increased my workload and delayed my imminent handover to LGB Tower.See-and-avoid is a fantasy in situations like this one. Again; though I was actively looking; I never saw the other traffic. I will redouble my own efforts to maintain situational awareness of traffic using all resources available. I would support a requirement for all aircraft to transmit ADSB-out in all US airspace. I would also support a change in the FARs to allow general aviation copilots to log Second in Command (SIC) time; in order to encourage pilot-passengers to serve as Pilot Monitoring. Thank you.

The second mistake was turning the wrong knob for heading change (two identical knobs - one does altimeter the other heading).  The third mistake was trouble shooting the autopilot.  I should have disconnected it and hand flown.  If I had done that I would not have veered far off course. What I did well was call ATC quickly and they helped me get my head back on straight.I discussed with two respected ATP/CFI's and gained additional insight.  I've shared my story with other pilots.

column121: We were being vectored to the final approach course for ILS 32 at TBR; and I cancelled IFR when the field was in sight as there was no other traffic in sight or indicated on my traffic display (ADS-B and Garmin 800). I switched to VFR on the transponder and switched to the CTAF to report my position and intention to land on Runway 32. A few seconds after I reported my position and intentions on CTAF the runway lights came on bright. I had not activated that so I concluded that someone at the non-towered airport had heard me and out of courtesy turned the lights up bright.As I turned onto the final approach course at the final approach fix I noticed a single white strobe light at the departure end of the runway. I wondered if it was an aircraft on the runway or a single Runway End Identifier Light. Since I had not heard any other transmissions or position reports on the CTAF and observed no traffic on my traffic display I concluded it must be a single REIL; even though I had never seen such a thing.I made a short-final position report but still was unsure what the strobe like was. Just before crossing the runway threshold I looked down and saw what I thought was an aircraft at the end of the runway--the source of the single strobe light.I immediately added power and initiated a go-around. I climbed out and turned to a left downwind. At that point I questioned if I had tuned the correct CTAF; so I checked Airport Info on Foreflight and discovered I had tuned 122.75 instead of the correct frequency; 122.72. I reported my position and intention to land on 32. A helicopter pilot responded and said they had been on the runway. I explained my frequency mistake and apologized. The pilot said something to the effect of 'No problem.' I saw the strobe light move off the runway onto a closed diagonal runway so I continued my downwind.Just before touching down another voice transmitted; saying he was the instructor in the helicopter and claimed we were just 10 feet above them when I initiated the go-around. Given that I was busy with the landing I did not respond. And that was it. No other transmissions from the helicopter.The next day I attempted to find out who was flying the helicopter so I could discuss the situation with the instructor; but the airport said they do not know of anyone who is training there in a helicopter.My mistake in tuning the incorrect CTAF frequency was obvious. But the sudden change in runway lighting made me think someone heard me and turned up the lights; so I had no reason to think I had the incorrect CTAF. Plus; I wasn't surprised that no other aircraft responded to my initial calls because it was nighttime and there was no traffic shown on my traffic display. I've learned from that to double check every frequency input. But I wonder why the helicopter would remain at the very end of the departure runway for several minutes without any movement; and why they did not appear on my traffic display. That's what I wanted to talk to the helicopter instructor about.That experience was a dramatic and sobering example of how an unrelated series of events and circumstances can lead to a disaster. Pay attention to details!

column121: During departure from ZZZ; the aircraft was operating with a deferred item: ENG 2 FIRE LOOP (no indication as to which loop) along with other unrelated deferrals.Shortly after departure; we received multiple intermittent ECAM alerts for ENG 2 FIRE LOOP B. The alert appeared and cleared several times; prompting further review of the aircrafts maintenance history and current status.Upon re-examining the aircraft logbook; I noted that a similar discrepancy involving ENG 2 fire loop B had been recorded two pages prior out of ZZZ1. The associated maintenance comment indicated the issue had been entered into the maintenance software; however; there was no clear documentation specifying the corrective action taken and if that was the current deferral we had. This lack of clarity made it difficult to determine whether the previously recorded issue corresponded to the currently deferred LOOP A; or if there had been an error in deferral.I cross-checked the Deferred Item (DI) list and logbook entries and discussed the situation with my First Officer. To clarify information; I contacted Dispatch; who confirmed that LOOP A was the deferred system. However; due to the ambiguity in the maintenance records and absence of a clear timeline or action history; uncertainty remained as to whether the correct loop had been deferred or if both loops were potentially inoperative.Given the possibility that both fire detection loops on ENG 2 could be non-functional; effectively leaving the engine without fire detection capability; we assessed this as a potential safety-of-flight concern. We communicated our concerns to Dispatch; including the possibility of an incorrect deferral and the operational implication of having no fire detection on ENG 2.Dispatch concurred with our assessment and requested a return to ZZZ; with an amended release issued. The return was conducted uneventfully.Upon arrival; we coordinated with Maintenance to clarify the discrepancy. After additional review; Maintenance confirmed that the deferral was correct and that both fire detection loops on ENG 2 were inoperative; LOOP A having been placed on deferral a while ago; and LOOP B being inoperative now without deferral. To me this event highlighted a significant gap in flight crew access to detailed and time-stamped maintenance actions and deferral history. The absence of clear documentation regarding when a system was deferred; what exact corrective actions were taken; or whether previous discrepancies were related to current deferrals. It created uncertainty during an in-flight abnormal situation.In my opinion this lack of transparency led to an unnecessary increased cockpit workload during a critical phase of flight by the difficulty of verifying a system status and MEL applicability.I would like to see an improvement of flight crew access to detailed maintenance records; to enhance our situational awareness and support more informed and timely decision-making.

Approximately 100mi from the coast; all messages cleared and GPS 2 began getting information again. We continued with no further issues or erroneous information. column121: I was holding short of rwy XX at ZZZ getting my ifr clearance/release for a flight. The field was 1000 overcast.  I was on the phone (through my headset) with ZZZ clearance delivery and radio background noise and poor telephone connection were very distracting and makde for difficult communication. I turned the volume on comm 1 way down to hear ZZZ. Once I got my release; I heard no traffic on ctaf (I didn't realize that comm 1 volume was at zero); and I announced my taxi onto the runway for departure. With a quick glance; I saw no traffic on final and taxied onto the runway. Sight of the traffic on final was blocked by the airframe and I gave a cursory; at best; visual check of final. I didn't expect to see any traffic and therefore I didn't.  As I turned on the runway; I saw a flash of an airplane overhead and stopped immediately. After a few seconds to analyze what I'd done; I realized that comm 1's volume was at zero. Therefore; I hadn't heard the traffice making their calls. Unbelievably; I had taxied onto the runway with an aircraft on short final. I realized my mistake; corrected my comm 1 volume; and taked with the aricraft that was on the go and going back into the pattern. I told them of my error and thanked them for being aware and taking corrective action for my mistake. They were quite gracious. I then took  quick second to analyze things and decided to proceed with my departure. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Background distractions with comm 1 and the telephone both in my headset caused communication difficulties and I turned comm 1 volume to zero. There was a failure to check comm 1 volume before taxiing onto the runway. I felt rushed (self imposed) because of a 5 minute void time; and my connecting flight pilot (leg 3) was up against a tfr at the final destination. I was trying to gain as much time for him as possible. I allowed myself to feel rushed in the moment and made a critical error that could have had terrible consequences. Only a cursory glance of final was a factor since i didn't expect to see any traffic because I hadn't heard any radio calls in several minutes. I will not turn the volume on comm 1 or 2 to zero ever again. Turn it down a bit perhaps; but never to zero. I have an acute awareness now of the issues with being rushed in the cockpit. I will be very careful to not allow myself to rush. I am incorporating a slow and methodical final cockpit check before taking the runway.A slower and more intentional check of final before proceeding onto the runway will also be a corrective action. I never imagined (wiht my varied experience) that I'd make such stupid and compounding mistakes leading to such an incident. I believe that I am a more diligent; aware and intentional pilot moving forward.

column121: When departing ZZZ Airport in Cherokee; an engine incident occurred during the initial climb out. During taxi from the ramp to the runup area just off of runway XXR at Taxiway 1; there were no bad engine indications on either the standard engine gauges or the installed engine monitor. The engine runup was conducted; and all indications were normal and in the green; including Fuel Pressure; Oil Pressure; Oil Temperature; and Cylinder Head Temperature. Magnetos were also checked and were within specifications. After the runup; we were told to cross XXR at Taxiway 1 and hold short of XXL at Taxiway 1. Before we entered XXL for departure; I verified that the aircraft was properly set up; including the electric fuel pump on; the fuel selector on the fullest tank; and the mixture full rich. We were then cleared for takeoff on XXL at Taxiway 1. We rolled onto the runway centerline and smoothly increased power to take off. My student is fairly new; so I pointed to each engine indication and called out each of the following for him. Fuel pressure in the green; Oil temperature in the green; Oil pressure in the green. I then verified with the digital engine monitor. We climbed on the departure leg to 1;100 feet indicated; then started our left climbing turn out to the southeast. Up to this point; there were no indications on the engine gauges other than positive indications. While in the left-hand turn; there was a loud bang and a thump that I felt through my seat. This was followed by shaking throughout the aircraft and the flight controls. Oil began spraying onto the windshield. This was followed by smoke filling the cockpit. My first action was to turn downwind and reduce power. I contacted ZZZ Tower and requested a short approach to land on Runway XXL. The tower responded; saying they were unable due to landing traffic. I then responded to the tower; informing them that I would need a short approach to Runway XXL. The tower then told the landing traffic to go around. I made a left turn toward the runway and landed safely. At the time of the landing; I did not know if there was a fire due to the smoke in the cockpit; so I used full braking power using the parking brake handle and exited Runway XXL at Taxiway 2. As I was rolling off the runway; I brought the mixture lever back to idle cut; turned the magnetos off; and removed the key. At this point; I saw that there was no fire; and smoke was coming from the hot oil and exhaust gas. I notified Tower that we would not be needing emergency services. I then turned off the master switch; opened the door; and my student and I exited the airplane. I; as Pilot in Command; did everything in my power to properly pre-flight the aircraft; including verifying that the required inspections were complete; required documents were in the aircraft; and the aircraft was airworthy; verifying the engine was running properly before takeoff; and swiftly and safely returning to the airport when the incident occurred. After landing; I inspected the engine and found that the #1 cylinder had cracked and the pushrods had been forced from their seat. There was nothing further I could have done to prevent this issue from occurring.

column121: Immediately after starting descent from FL340 multiple ECAMS illuminated: ENG 2 EPR MODE FAULT N1 DEGRADED MODE along with AUTO FLT A/THR OFF. We had a third ECAM but I can't remember what it was. We lost #2 EGT and Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR). We executed the QRC and then proceeded with the ECAM action. I immediately formulated a plan to not go to ZZZ1 due to the #2 thrust reverser being inop coupled with a short runway; the current EPR issue and fuel possibly becoming an issue; I communicated this with the FO for his input and he concurred; so I coordinated with ATC and asked for holding at FL300 to give more time to work the issue. I was the pilot flying and the FO was monitoring so we maintained those  positions for the remainder of the flight. After finishing ECAM actions I had the FO go to the follow up items as I continued to fly and communicate to ATC. After a brief discussion with the FO I favored the notifying ATC option and communicated that with ATC followed with Souls on Board and 1.5 hours of fuel. We did three turns in holding which allowed for us to finish everything we needed to do inside and outside the aircraft to include the comms to dispatch; FAs; the passengers and ZZZ ops to make sure they were ready for us. We setup the arrival and approach and slowly worked towards ZZZ. We completed all checklists and landed without incident. Tower wasn't sure as to our plan for leaving the runway after landing so we told them we would clear immediately after landing. Fire trucks still responded even though they weren't requested; followed us to the gate and we shutdown the engines.The FO and I did a post flight inspection walk around of the aircraft specifically the right engine and saw no anomalies. I communicated with chief pilot who passed on the info to the IOC Duty pilot; dispatch informing them the plane was grounded awaiting contract maintenance; and Maintenance Control due to the out of base write up.The FO did a great job of remaining calm and helping me work the issue. His input and dedication to the task at hand was perfect and the interaction between us was seamless. SIDE NOTE: Major issue with the wording on the ECAM vs what's on the switch- wording is mismatched which caused an unnecessary distraction and wasted time in proceeding to the 2nd ECAM which was turning off AUTOTHRUST; which almost led to an MMO overspeed. The ECAM says: ENG 2 N1 MODE ONENG 1 N1 MODE ONWhile we presumed this was actually the Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC)s it doesn't say that and I was concerned about the result of turning them on during flight (it's labeled GROUND POWER and a guarded switch for a reason?!) and possibly exacerbating this issue or creating another issue. So I had the FO scrub the manual to confirm that N1 MODE= FADEC during holding in an attempt to complete the first ECAM action. Meanwhile the airspeed was slowly creeping up as we delayed doing the third item of the 1st ECAM - move the thrust levers; since we hadn't resolved the 1st two items of the first ECAM . This distraction brought us real close to an MMO overspeed but I caught it prior to it occurring. I retarded the thrust levers appropriate to the speed needed. We then circled back to the 1st two items of the first ECAM and the search for N1 MODE.Cause: there seems to be a mismatch of ECAM procedures and the name of the switch which should be looked into further.

column121: I was training on sector 40/41. During the session; Aircraft X was handed off to us from NCT with destination to APC. The pilot stated he had the ATIS for APC. I cleared the pilot direct RRIBT; a transition fix on the RNAV 19R.The pilot said he could not find RRIBT on the approach plate; I spelled it for him and he was able to find it and go direct. I then cleared him to cross RRIBT AOA 060 and cleared him for the approach. During this time we were sequencing for STS and went into holding for SFO. We were also discussing sector operations and procedures given that SFO/Norcal was in an unusual/uncommon configuration (landing SE). At some point my trainer observed Aircraft X descending below 059; which was low for the segment of the approach he was on; but still above the MVA. My trainer brought it to my attention; at which point the pilot descends below the MVA; and we issued a safety alert. The pilot climbs to 045 as instructed; but does not follow the lateral guidance of the approach; at which point I canceled the approach clearance. I vectored him back around for the approach; he flew it with no problems this time and landed at APC.Recommendation: Confirm pilot is familiar with approach being given. Notify pilot of deviation from approach segment altitude prior to it requiring a safety alert.Better low altitude alert phraseology. Wouldn't have prevented it; but could've been better regardless.
column123: We were flying inbound on the REBAS1 arrival and were told to join the approach after REBAS. We had briefed and loaded the approach loaded via vectors; so we didn't have anything loaded in the FMS prior to OIINK we asked the controller how he wanted us to join the approach and he told us to go direct RRIBT. Due to how we had the approach loaded we didn't have RRIBT. At this point we were behind the airplane and ended up loading RRIBT manually to get headed in the right direction. We looked in the FMS to try and load it via RRIBT but we were not able to since it wasn't a IAF. We ended up manually putting in BARKZ and POPES. Because we had manually put in the points they had no altitude protection. We were VNAVing down to 1900 at NAAYY. Because we had fell behind we didn't catch the altitudes at BARKZ and POPES. We got as low as 3700 feet before OIINK and had the TAWS page pulled up and got no terrain warnings so we didn't think anything of it until we received a low altitude alert from ATC and were told to climb and maintain 4500 feet. We ended up being told to climb to 6000 and got vectored back to POPES to do the RNAV 19R again. The second time we understood where we went wrong and complied with the remaining altitude restrictions and eventually landed with no issue. After landing we were then told to copy down a phone number. This could've been prevented had we loaded the approach Via the IAF Rebas. We also could have asked for delay vectors and taken the time to figure out how to set up the approach correctly.

column121: On visual approach to approach to Runway XX at ZZZ; I was PM(Pilot Monitoring)  and Line Check Pilot (LCP) conducting Operating Evaluation (OE) training for my FO(First Officer) who was PF.(Pilot Flying).  During the approach we were slowing and configuring to land.  Upon calling for Flaps 30; we encountered a wind gust that increased our airspeed and caused a 'FLAP RELIEF'  EICAS CAUTION message.  I return returned the Flap handle to Flaps 25 until we got out of the gust and slowed back to return the Flaps to 30.  At this time we received a 'LE SLAT DISAGREE' and 'TE FLAP ASYM'  EICAS  Caution Messages.   We executed a Go Around and per SOP retracted the Flap handle to Flaps 20.  The Flaps retracted to about 21 degrees and stayed stuck there as we tried to retract them on the Go-around.  I returned the Flap Handle to correspond with the Flaps at the '20' detent.   We retracted the gear and flew the missed approach per ATC instructions and remained at 180 KIAS.  We advised ATC of our condition and requested priority handling.  After completing After Takeoff Checks we ran the QRH procedures for the above listed malfunctions.  They directed us to accomplish an approach and landing using FLAPS 20 Ref + Target speeds.   We completed all checklists.  I spoke to the Flight Attendants and advised them of our situation and used our brief model.   I then spoke to the passengers and advised them of the situation.  I sent an ACARS message to dispatch to advise them of the situation and we were in the pattern for landing and would speak on ground if needed.   We finished our briefs and checklists and I took over the aircraft as PF due to my FO being a student on OE .  We then advised ATC we were ready to return for landing.  They vectored us to a visual approach to Runway XYC as we had requested that as a longer runway per our configuration.  We landed uneventfully and cleared the runway where we spoke to and were followed to the gate by the airport responding vehicles.  We taxied safely to the gate without further incident.
column123: On a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ Airport; I was the First Officer acting as PF while undergoing Operational Evaluation (OE); with the Captain serving as PM and Line Check Pilot (LCP).During descent and landing configuration; I called for Flaps 30. Afterward a large wind gust increased our airspeed; triggering a FLAP RELIEF EICAS caution. The Captain selected Flaps 25; and once we were clear of the gust and slowed appropriately. Soon after; There was a LE SLAT DISAGREE and TE FLAP ASYM cautions.We initiated a go-around and; in accordance with procedures; selected Flaps 20. The flaps moved to approximately 21 degrees and stopped. The flap handle was then matched to the indicated position. We retracted the gear; followed ATC instructions for the missed approach; and maintained 180 KIAS. ATC was advised; and we requested priority handling.After completing after takeoff checks; we ran the appropriate QRH procedures; which directed a Flaps 20 landing using adjusted reference speeds.Once checklists and briefings were complete; the Captain assumed PF duties due to my OE status. We requested and received vectors to Runway XYC for a longer landing distance. The approach and landing were uneventful. Priority handling vehicles met us after rollout; and we taxied to the gate without further issue.

column121: While completing cruise duties at initial level-off and preparing for ETOPS entry; the PM checked the status page on the lower EICAS as part of normal system checks. It was then that both pilots noticed the status message 'AIR/GND DISAGREE'. After checking circuit breakers; we discussed the meaning of the message and the fact that status messages are not controlling in-flight and do not require crew action. However; we discussed the possibility of the issue developing into an 'AIR/GND SYS' EICAS Advisory which drives a non-normal checklist. We considered about 10 minutes into discovering the discrepancy that we may need to air return. We considered the weather forecast at ZZZ1; ZZZ2; and ZZZ. ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 were forecasting rainy and gusty conditions with thunderstorms in the vicinity; ZZZ was dry with light winds. We also considered that if we received the EICAS Advisory that our auto brakes; auto speed brakes; and thrust reversers would be inop all while navigating near thunderstorms approaching ZZZ1. We completed an HF phone patch to Maintenance Control to discuss the issue; attempt to gain more awareness about this message; and rope in dispatch to get their latest information about local weather. We researched more and discussed the risks which worked in our favor to burn more fuel to get our gross weight below max landing weight. At about 1+30 into the flight; we decided that the workload to take this potential issue into the islands with unfavorable weather would not be the safest course of action. Additionally; the MEL mentioned that the issue does not have MEL solutions once on the ground. We coordinated with dispatch; ATC; and flight attendants to start heading back to ZZZ. On the approach; we configured early including gear to see if the ground/flight mode anomaly would appear and force the AIR/GND SYS advisory. It was a normal approach; however; I noticed that the aircraft sank faster than usual while pulling power during the flare. This may have been because the jet allowed the engines to go to ground idle before touchdown; but I added power to re-establish a normal flare and descent rate then gradually reduced power to idle as the jet touched down. While deploying thrust reversers; the EICAS Advisory 'AIR/GND SYS' appeared and remained on until we cleared the runway. We passed all this info to maintenance who was able to capture it in the write up.
column123: Leveled off at FL330 waiting to accomplish a cruise check and begin departure using the ZZZZZ guide.  I noticed  a status message alerting us AIR/GND SYS.  FO continued flying while I looked up the status message approaching ZZZZZ1.  We had been radar service terminated from ZZZ CTR.  FM was not much guidance so we decided to contact ZZZ radio for a SELCAL check and position report as we elected to continue on the track.  After establishing contact with ZZZ radio; I requested an HF Phone Patch and was given a separate HF frequency at which time a phone patch to Dispatch and Maintenance Control was established.  The phone patch was limited and we could barely hear Dispatch and Maintenance Control.  Maintenance Control was not sure nor could verify if the aircraft was in air mode or ground mode.  We tried several times to check circuit breakers and EICAS to see if we could determine which mode the aircraft was in and what to expect when we put the gear down.  We were not sure if we would get Air/Gnd System which would affect braking and thrust reversers.  The Wx in ZZZ1 was gusty winds with rainy showers and wet runway.  The Wx in ZZZ2 (Mx base) was worse and forecasted to get worst.  We continued flying given we were tankering fuel with 14;000lbs extra which put us landing over weight with an air return and also landing heavier than normal with rainy weather and gusty winds with terrain.  Given these threats; we elected to continue towards the fix to burn fuel down.  The extra flying time would allow us to brief an air return; close out the HF phone patch by also notifying the company and dispatch; speak with FAs; and develop a plan.  We accomplished all; referenced the diversion guide in the FOM; and communicated our plan with ZZZ radio.  We executed a diversion from our track turning right flying directly North and returning back to ZZZ.  We requested an early descent while also encountering holding for traffic delays in ZZZ which was to our advantage to burn fuel down to help with our overweight landing.  We held for ten minutes at 10;000 ft and took delayed vectors landing runway XXR about 300 lbs overweight.  We put the gear down early to make sure no further issues or status/EICAS messages were present.  We received AIR/GND SYS on the EICAS upon putting the landing gear down.  In anticipation; we previously referenced the AIR/GND SYS checklist and had already prepared for non-normal landing distance and any configuration differences.  We accomplished the landing checklist while configuring early and landed with no issues.Of note; approximately 50-40ft above touchdown; we did notice the aircraft loose airspeed and drop unexpectedly to which the FO added slight power to arrest the descent due overweight landing considerations.  I briefed a shallow touchdown due to overweight landing as a threat and to use the entire runway for braking.  We landed and stopped turning off at taxiway 1 with no issues using minimal braking.  No emergency was declared.My decision to air return was based on several considerations; mostly unknown conditions from the air/gnd computer with bad weather in the islands.  The FO was excellent in executing the air return as the PF allowing me to coordinate the divert with no issues.

column121: We were about 30 miles from destination ZZZ we were descending through 6000ft spoilers were fully deployed and engines were at idle speed was around 230kts. When I looked at the speed I wanted 250 until 10nm from destination so I slowly brought in power. This was first sign of a problem. We got a weird fluttering noise. Brought power back.. I looked at the other pilot said that's not right. I proceeded to stow the spoilers to see if they had anything to do with the noise but they did not. The I slowly added engine power same noise. Back to idle. Then I added power on the number 2 engine no noise power smooth. Next I added power to number 1 engine and it made a lot of noise like a helicopter. At that moment I smelled oil in the cabin. I looked all the engine parameters and both engines in the green and matched up. I then made a decision having the runway in sight and a good number 2 engine to shut number 1 down as to avoid fire or damage . I told Person A to use the fuel cut off. He let approach know that we had and engine issue and we shut it down and that we would like straight in to runaway XX. . I joined the ils and on autopilot made the approach even though we were cleared for the visual. We made a safe and secure landing..Cause: The aircraft is at maintenance at ZZZ they have not told me yet what exactly went wrong with the engine.Suggestions: Stay calm focus on flying the aircraft which i did.

column121: This was the last leg of a 4-day trip. Boarding was normal. We were completely full plus a Company X Pilot in the cockpit jumpseat. We were cleared for takeoff full length on runway XXL at approximately XA:06 UTC. We were cleared on the ZZZZZX RNAV departure out of ZZZ. Takeoff was normal. We were instructed to contact ZZZ departure at approximately 1000 ft AGL. I checked in with ZZZ departure; the controller instructed us to climb to 5;000 ft. As I was replying to that instruction I received a call from the cabin. I answered the call and the purser alerted me that they may have a fire in the cabin. The forward galley was filing with smoke and it appeared that it was coming out of one of the ovens in the forward galley. I told the captain what was going on in the cabin. At that time we began smelling a strong acrid odor as well as seeing a haze of smoke in the cockpit. The captain; myself and the jumpseater all donned our oxygen masks and established crew communications. The captain told me that they wanted to return to ZZZ immediately. I alerted ATC that we would like to stop our climb at 5000 and we would probably be heading back to ZZZ. ATC gave us a 280 heading to put us on a downwind for runway XXL and began giving us a descent to 4000 feet. As we leveled at 4000 feet we received an Off Schedule Descent light.I pulled the QRC down from the glare shield and looked at the immediate action items for Smoke/Fire/Fumes. I saw that we had already accomplished the steps of donning our oxygen masks and establishing crew communications. I pulled out the QRH from my side of the pedestal and was about to go to the fire protection section as it was the next step from the QRC but was distracted by the purser calling up from the back. She confirmed that the smoke was coming from the oven. She told me that she didn't want to open the door of the oven. She was afraid that it would make it worse. She told me that she shut the ovens off but there was still a lot of smoke coming out.  I instructed her to pull the circuit breakers for both ovens in the forward galley. We continued to receive transmissions from ATC. They wanted to know what the issue was; souls and fuel onboard. it was at this time that we received priority handling with ATC.At the captains direction; I began setting up the FMC for the ILS XXL at ZZZ. I loaded the approach; set the ILS frequencies and minimums. I also loaded VREF and target speeds for landing. The purser called up front again. I answered and was told that the smoke was starting to dissipate. I told them we were heading back to ZZZ and we would be on the ground shortly. I told the captain that the smoke was dissipating in the back. We noticed that we did not have the acrid odor or smoke in the cockpit anymore either. We decided it was safe to remove our oxygen masks. We had some issues communicating with each other. I remembered to close the oxygen mask door and test it on my side to return the audio to normal. I failed to remind the captain of this and they continued to have some issues with communication that I wasn't aware of at the time. I pulled up the divert page on the ACARS portion of the FMC and told the captain that I was going to send a divert notice to dispatch. I glanced over the page briefly and thought that I pressed the send button. I later found out that dispatch didn't know about the divert. So I either didn't press the button hard enough or it didn't go through. I began going into the ACARS section to get landing data as I knew we were overweight landing back at ZZZ. I typed in 161.0 for our landing weight and XXL for the runway and pressed send. I didn't see until we were on short final that I received an error for our landing data. I believe that I didn't enter ZZZ as our landing airport. The landing data page defaulted to ZZZ1 for the landing airport and the error was because there isn't a XXL runway at ZZZ1. At this point we were on downwind for XXL. The captain transferred the controls to me and they briefed the approach. I believe at this time the captain also made an announcement to the passengers. I transferred the controls back to the captain. ATC began turning us on a base leg and descending us further. The captain began to call for flaps and the gear down. We were given one more turn and then cleared for the ILS XXL. I pulled out the checklist and accomplished the descent checklist and after we were fully configured for landing I accomplished the landing checklist. When we were on short final I received the error for the landing data. I showed it to the captain. I can't remember if the captain acknowledged it or not. The captain later told me that they felt we had plenty of runway for landing considering the headwind and dry runway conditions.The landing was normal and uneventful. We cleared the runway to the right at taxiway 1. There was ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting ) equipment that was waiting for us as we cleared the runway. They followed us to the gate. I spoke to them on the frequency at one point and they told me that they would be on the jet bridge as we pulled in to make sure the fire in the oven was contained. There was about a 5 minute delay holding short of the gate as we waited for a ramp crew to guide us in. Parking and shutdown was normal. The captain called the fight attendants and instructed them to disarm the L1 door and allow the firefighter on the aircraft to look at the oven. We deplaned the passengers and our maintenance crew came out to look at the write-up for the smoke coming out of the oven as well as the overweight landing. Maintenance determined that there was a lot of grease all over the top of the foil on many of the meals. They think that the grease dripping off of the foil on our takeoff roll and climb out caused the smoke event.
column123: Climbing through 3000 the purser called reporting smoke in the cabin. She said it was either coming from the oven or behind the oven. Looking at the flight deck door camera we could only see solid white since the smoke was rising to cover the camera. At this point smoke began entering the flight deck so I commanded oxygen masks on and had the FO requested priority handling with ATC. I requested an immediate return to the airport. We were given a left downwind vector and subsequent turn to base. The flaps were already at 1 and I began configuring. Brakes were selected to 3 and an abbreviated descent check was completed to include speeds and gust factor. The purser at some point in this called to say the smoke was slowing down after they had turned the oven off and pulled the circuit breaker. I made the decision to continue our quick return rather than diving deeper into the smoke checklist. I made a quick announcement to the pax (Passengers) as to the plan of action and what to expect when we landed. My concern was that there was a fire that couldn't be seen and could reignite. Rescue vehicles were dispatched and followed us to the gate where fire personnel boarded the aircraft and used thermal imaging to make sure all was okay. The oven was taken out of service and an overweight landing inspection was completed. We departed again about 2 hours late with an uneventful flight to ZZZ1. As for TEM (Threat and Error Management) during the air return; VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor) was done to the best we could with the challenge of oxygen mask use. Someone was always flying the plane. If I had the event to do over once I heard the smoke was decreasing I would have asked for a delay on the approach to readdress the smoke checklist. Everything was conducted safely but was more rushed than it ultimately needed to be with the smoke decreasing. I think total flight time was 12 minutes. It was a definite learning experience and has put additional tools in my 'toolkit'.

column121: Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1. Normal boarding and pre-departure checks. Pushback and started engine 2 at XA:08. Due to flow metering into ZZZ1; waited to start engine 1 at XA:27. No abnormal engine indications on startup or during taxi. Both engines had 8 minutes of warmup time and oil pressure/temperature/vibrations within limits before taking the runway. Flight OFF at XA:35. No abnormal indications during climb phase or cruise phase until approx XB:12 at FL340. At XB:12; an audible bang could be heard from the flight deck and cabin; followed by vibrations and a left yawing moment. EICAS indicated N1 decreasing to approx 22% with ENG1 OUT caution message. After confirming with the PM/CA verbally that I would be the Pilot Flying and that I had controls; the PM/CA immediately began consulting ENGINE 1(2) out QRH. To start the APU in accordance with this procedure; PM/CA requested priority handling and requested a descent to FL280. Once below FL300; the APU was started. An engine restart was considered. An additional descent to FL240 was requested and the APU-assisted engine restart procedure according to the QRH  was attempted once below FL250. The engine restart was unsuccessful. After coordination with dispatch via ACARS and air traffic control; a decision was made to turn right direct to ZZZ2 for diversion and continue descent. The flight attendant was briefed on special procedures according to company SOP and PM/CA turned the fasten seatbelt sign on and provided an announcement to the passengers regarding the requirement to divert to ZZZ2. Inflight Engine Shutdown QRH was completed for Engine 1. One Engine Inoperative Approach and Landing Procedure QRH was completed. Landing speeds and landing distances were calculated for ZZZ2 XXL according to QRH. We confirmed that the aircraft would be under max landing weight. A single engine approach briefing was given by the PM/CA. ATC provided delay vectors for an extended right downwind for a visual to ZZZ2 XXL to coordinate airport services to follow the aircraft after landing and for us to complete the approach checklist and one engine inoperative go around procedure. We then requested a right turn to join the ILS XXL (in lieu of a visual approach). ATC cleared us for ILS XXL approximately 9nm beyond the FAF for the approach. At 3nm from the FAF; the QRH landing checklist was completed to fully configure the aircraft. The autopilot was disconnected approximately 1nm from the FAF and the ILS XXL was hand flown to a normal landing. The after landing checklist was completed. We taxied to the gate; shut down the aircraft; and completed the parking checklist. We consulted airport services and airport operations and began appropriate company reports regarding the incident. A post flight walk around was conducted and found no obvious damage to the aircraft exterior; nor the cowlings; intake fan blades; or exhaust section of Engine 1.
column123: The flight began as normal. Pushed back in ZZZ; started engine number 2 and then engine number 1 about 10-15 minutes later. No abnormal indications during either engine start. We took off normally and climbed up to our cruising altitude of FL340 as normally. During cruise at FL340; about 45 minutes after starting the number 1 engine (based on a timer started at engine start); we heard a loud thud and felt a large jolt and then immediate pull to left. We looked at the EICAS and saw that engine number 1's N1; N2; and Fuel flow were all decreasing rapidly. The N1 stabilized at approx. 25%. N2 and fuel flow dropped to 0% and 0PPH. Followed shortly after was the EICAS caution msg 'E1 OUT' add some associated msgs like shed busses off bus. It was verbalized by both of us that the number 1 engine had failed and rolled back. I then pulled out the QRH and started turning to E1 OUT QRH. The FO was the pilot flying and I restated verbally that he had the controls and he acknowledged. I then began running the ENGINE OUT QRH. ''The QRH directed us to start the APU. At this point; we needed to descend so I called ATC on the radio and requested priority handling and requested a descent to FL280 in order to be low enough for an APU start. After passing below FL300; I continued with the QRH by starting the APU. When reaching the section that asks us to consider a restart; we both looked closely at the MFD systems pages and the EICAS engine instruments to determine if there was any obvious reason for the failure. We could find no indication that was abnormal or expected. The oil quantity was showing 10 qts and all other indications were normal. (the E1 fuel flow and oil pressure were 0 due to the failed engine and I considered them expected). We decide that we would attempt a restart and then followed the QRH reference to the Inflight Restart Procedure. Before attempting the restart; we descended to FL 240. We followed Engine Airstart for an APU assisted start. Engine failed to start with no N2 rotation. We then finished the QRH and then decided to divert to ZZZ2 (as we were nearby). This decision was confirmed with Dispatch via to ACARS and they agreed. ATC was informed and we were given vectors towards the airport. We then continued with the Engine Failure/Shutdown normally. I then informed the flight attendant and gave her a special procedures briefing informing her of the issue and plan to divert. We then set up and briefed the ILS XXL at ZZZ2 and I ran performance numbers for the landing. We made sure the aircraft was under max landing weight. After Setting up and briefing the approach; we then ran the One Engine inoperative approach and landing procedure. At this point the flight was mostly uneventful. I asked ATC to have the emergency equipment ready for us just in case. The FO performed the landing and we then taxied to the gate.  A post flight walk around was accomplished and we found no obvious signs of damage to the aircraft or engine.

column121: On Day 0 Aircraft X had a Main and a Back up trim failure during the initial climb out. Flight crew got to the aircraft at the scheduled time of XA:30 in the morning. A GPU was not available for the initial start up of the APU. Started the APU soon arriving at the aircraft. Had PAXs and cockpit ready to go at XB:10. Was given a EDT time of XB:45 local. I chose to stay at the gate and only run the APU. At XB:35 I gave the order for a push back. Now running 20 minutes late. Started both engines and was at the RWY XXL at XB:40. At XB:46ish was given clearance to take off. Gave the control to the first officer for his takeoff. Takeoff was normal and uneventful. Climb check was complete and was handed off to departure. Climb through 4;000ft we got an EICAS message of PTRIM Main INOP fallowed by PTRIM Backup INOP. ATC had just cleared us to FL230. I said the FO let stop the climb and go down to 4;000ft. FO said we have to go back to the field. I agreed and said maintain 4;000Ft and will get radar vectors (RV) and set up for the ZZZ ILS XXR approach. I called approach and said we have an issue and will need to stay at 4;000ft and RV for the ILS XXR approach. Dispatch ACARS us asking us if we were OK. I ignored the message. I had to keep it simple and Aviate; Navigate and Communicate.ZZZ1 Approach was very helpful and wanted to give us RV directly right to the ILS XXR. I requested delay RVs to burn gas; run through a check list (QRH) and set up for the approach.  Approach gave us 3-4 more RV as I figured the weight of the AC; got Vspeed numbers; set up the approach in the FMS and on the flight panel. I quickly briefed the approach. All during this time Dispatch was trying to get a hold of me via ACARS. I gave back to two quick replies about my intentions. The 2 replies to dispatch came in between a call to the FA and announcement to the passengers. Due to time and  the quickness of situation I did not use the full special procedures. Basically; I said we were returning to ZZZ due to mechanical issues. The landing will be normal.For the final RV to final I took the controls and had the FO give me back pressure on the yoke. I brief the FO he would be my trim by providing back pressure on the yoke as needed by my verbal commands. This worked out well and I have to commend my FO. He did a great job. The approach was good and straight down the pipe. Landing was smooth as butter. Touchdown at 1200-1400FT down the RWY. I got the AC stopped and turned off the RWY by taxi way 1". Received a taxi clearance from tower to cross RWY XXR and taxi via taxiway "2" and Taxiway 3 to the gate.  Passed by the fire truck that had been rolled for us and gave them a thumbs up and a friendly wave.Upon reaching the gate the rampers guided us in to a stop. Did the nominal parking flow. The rampers said there was no gate agents at the gate. So I made announcement to the passengers "to please remain seated until we can get a gate agents. " 10 minutes later the gate agents showed up. Then were able to deplane all of the PAXs normally. I stood by the cockpit door said to each passenger thank you for your patience and sorry for the inconvenience.After once the passengers were off of the airplane and were working with the gate agent on rebooking. I started making phone calls. I called dispatch and then maintenance for the write up of the Main and Backup pitch trim.  Also called the Chief Pilot to cover all my bases."

column121: On initial climbout from ZZZ RWYXXC at approximately 3;000 FT MSL the purser called the flight deck to alert the Captain that there was a 'large amount' of black smoke coming from the oven at a flight station. For the duration of the entire event I was not in communication with the back of the aircraft. At this time the Captain was hand flying the aircraft to 5;000 feet and I was PM. ATC gave us an initial vector and a climb to 15;000 feet; I read back the clearance but delayed input into the control panel for concurrence with the Captain. We decided to call back and request priority handling and request vectors to land back at ZZZ. At this time we split duties with the FO flying the aircraft and handling ATC; Captain ran the Fire Protection checklist. Received short vectors back to land RWYXXL. The Captain loaded the ILS XXL into the FMC for a back up to the visual and then continued to run the non normal checklist. I called the airfield in sight at approximately 9 miles. A faster than normal airspeed was flown while turning onto final due to the unknown status of the galley fire. No ILS frequencies were tuned and the FMC was not re-cruised to our current altitude. Flight directors were ignored and the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) was referenced for runway alignment verification. Gear and flaps were dropped to 30 on speed to be configured at approximately 700 feet AGL. Normal flare and touchdown was made for an overweight landing; on landing rollout is when I noticed that we had not selected an autobrake setting. Manual braking was used to slow down and vacate the runway at the last high speed taxiway. Crash Fire Rescue met the aircraft right after vacating the active runway and we taxied on Taxiway 1 to hold short of runway XYR.  At this time we slowed down and verified all appropriate checklist were completed and passengers were seated. We communicated with operations for a gate and taxied back to gate XX with no further issues.
column123: I was PF and my FO was PM. Shortly after takeoff and climbing through approximately 3000MSL; we received a call from the cabin. I took the call while my FO answered a call from departure to continue the climb. The lead FA said black smoke was emanating from one of the forward galley ovens. We noticed a burning smell in the flight deck and executed immediate action items. We did not observe smoke in the flight deck and did not don O2 masks. Instead of continuing the climb; we leveled off at 5000 while my FO referenced the QRC. Departure queried us about the climb and instead we requested priority handling. My FO supplied departure with Souls on Board and fuel. I failed to remind him to include information about the hazmat we had on board. After referencing the QRC; I gave flying pilot and normal ATC duties to my FO while I referenced the QRH for Smoke; Fire or Fumes. I began running that checklist and in the process called the lead FA back to brief her; as well as send a message to dispatch. The lead FA said she would make a PA to the passengers. ZZZ approach asked us if we had a runway preference; and considering that we did not have any aircraft performance issues; I suggested any runway; not thinking about the fact that we were over maximum structural landing weight. As we were vectored onto final for rwy XXL; I was only about half way done with the Smoke Fire Fumes QRH and decided I didn't have the time to finish prior to landing. To this point; my FO had masterfully piloted the aircraft and communicated with approach back to the airport. I abandoned the QRH and began setting up the FMC for the approach. I entered the ILS for runway XXL and sequenced the box; but failed to re-cruise it. I selected V ref and target for flaps 30; but failed to select an autobrakes setting. By this point my FO was hand flying on final and calling for appropriate flaps. Unable to select approach mode or vnav; my FO verified the correct runway from the magenta line and continued the approach entirely visually without vertical guidance. In the compressed time; we got on short final before final configuration. I suggested to my FO to level off to bleed off speed in order to fully configure prior to continuing the descent. I don't know if we were configured prior to 1000 AGL; but we were stable prior to 500 AGL. The flair; touchdown and rollout were textbook excellent; as my FO applied manual brakes to exit the runway. We taxied off the runway with Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) following; and stopped to assess; coordinate with the FA and call ops. The lead FA notified us that the smoke had stopped and the fumes were dissipating. We received a gate assignment and taxied with ARFF following us to the gate uneventfully.
