column121: During climb; the #1 [FA] called and said that they smelled an electrical odor in the forward galley; near the R1 door. I sent the FO back to check. He returned and said that he wasn't certain; but the floor near the door felt hot. I was about to call back to ask the FAs if that was normal when they called up again to say that the floor material was melting. We were just about to level at FL350 approaching ZZZ [VOR]. I asked the FO to request priority and ask for a return to ZZZ. While he had been in the cabin; I looked for nearest airports and determined that the closest large airport was ZZZ. If the FAs had said that there was smoke; I would have dropped into ZZZ1 as I know they do have airline service and a long enough runway to stop. Gave the plane to the FO and he got the plane going to ZZZ at a high speed. About halfway back I called back to see how things were going; the #1 said that the area was growing but still no smoke. I discussed that we were going to stop on the runway to be checked out and that I hoped we wouldn't need to evacuate but to listen if I called for that. She agreed that we didn't want to evacuate but would be ready and would let me know if she saw any reason to do so. ATC gave us as direct of a routing as they could with the mountains and we proceeded to XXR. Informed ATC that we would be stopping on the runway. After we stopped; ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) came to check us out; they saw a heat signature in the R1 door area- not blistering paint or any sign of an active fire so they asked us to proceed to the gate so they could check from inside. Coming inside; the burn area was still showing about 107 degrees. They looked inside the cargo compartment and the E&E (Electronics and Equipment bay) area and saw no damage. The circles over the right side of the floor heating pad had disappeared by the time we landed. We deplaned using the L1 door after we determined that it was safe to do so.Cause: Don't know why the pad decided to overheat. There is NO circuit breaker information. I was fairly certain that it was the heating pad overheating but I could not find someway to turn off the power to the unit. With an electric jet I don't want to be pulling breakers without any information as to what they control. However; after the turn to ZZZ; if a fire had broken out I think I would have started to pull anything that sounded like galley power. A little more info about things that can catch on fire in the plane would be nice.

column121: The entire length of the flight was 10 minutes in duration. Shortly after engaging the autopilot after takeoff from ZZZ; the yoke rapidly began violently pitching the plane forward and back suddenly. We previously had been experiencing unexplained issues with the autopilot including but not limited to: failure to capture localizer course; flight directors disappearing; red elevator trim annunciations necessitating the disconnecting of autopilot and trimming manually. I disconnected the autopilot; and the uncommanded pitch ceased. Minutes later; ZZZ [TRACON] control instructed me to fly direct ZZZZZ descend and maintain 2000 for the RNAV XX into ZZZ1. The autopilot at this time was engaged in Nav/Vnav mode and 2000 was preselected in the altitude selector. What had occurred was the autopilot did not capture the altitude; instead descending below it. Rather than disconnecting immediately and maintaining my assigned altitude manually like I should have; I was late to react appropriately to the error and attempted to rectify the issue using the abnormally behaving automation; all the while the aircraft continued its rapid descent. We were several hundred feet below our assigned altitude before I disconnected and began climbing back to 2000. I then hand-flew the rest of the approach; landing on runway XX. There were no terrain or traffic alerts. I understand had the circumstances been different this could have been a fatal mistake; and I regret the actions I took. I should have taken control immediately upon discovering the deviation instead of trying to diagnose the problem. I am thankful that no other aircraft were affected.

I then entered Runway XXR from Taxiway 1. An aircraft was still on the runway but in the process of exiting; and after it cleared the runway; I started my takeoff roll.Sometime during the takeoff roll; I heard 'monitor tower;' which led me to recognize that I may not have been on the correct frequency or had not received a valid takeoff clearance. Around liftoff; I attempted to contact tower on the assigned frequency (XXX.X) but did not receive a response and then switched to the other tower frequency (XXX.XX) to establish communication. During this time; I heard another aircraft execute a go-around. I adjusted my climb profile by shallowing the climb to reduce the risk of conflict but still maintain a safe distance above the ground.The problem arose from a misinterpretation of flight following information as a takeoff clearance. I believe some of the contributing factors included high workload due to traffic volume; frequency congestion; extended ground delay leading to expectation bias; and the similarity in cadence between the transmission and a takeoff clearance. Receiving the flight following information while holding short of the runway; in a position normally associated with an imminent departure clearance; likely increased expectation bias and contributed to the misinterpretation. Additionally; in busy environments it is common for flight following to be delayed or unavailable; and because no earlier indication was given that flight following would be issued later; I did not anticipate receiving it at that point; which likely contributed to the confusion. My perception that I was on the appropriate frequency and ready for departure influenced my judgment and decision-making. The issue was discovered when I heard 'monitor tower' during the takeoff roll; which prompted immediate recognition of a discrepancy.Corrective actions included attempting to establish communication with tower; switching frequencies when necessary; and modifying my climb profile to maintain safe separation from other aircraft. No further conflict developed.To prevent recurrence; I will ensure I'm on the correct frequency prior to departure and will positively verify that an explicit takeoff clearance has been received from tower before entering the runway. I will also deliberately pause at the hold short line; particularly in high workload environments; to confirm clearance and reduce the effects of expectation bias.

However; I question if there is not a better and safer way to handle interaction between GA aircraft and UAS operations. If there were indeed extensive UAS operations in the area that posed a hazard to GA aircraft; why was there not a TFR?

column121: I was busy following a runway flow change and sector split when I released Aircraft Y from ZZZ. After establishing radar contact; Aircraft Y reported a scary close call with another aircraft approximately 400 feet from his position. I didn't see a primary anywhere in close proximity to Aircraft Y. I issued traffic advisories for the only aircraft observed in the area but both were well above Aircraft Y and on my frequency. Aircraft Y indicated the conflicting aircraft was talking with ZZZ [Tower]. I advised that we would coordinate with ZZZ [Tower] to see what was out there.Shortly thereafter; Aircraft X contacted me just outside ZZZs Class D airspace. I issued a discrete code. The pilot reported a position southwest of ZZZ and stated he did not have a transponder. I instructed the aircraft to remain clear of the ZZZ1 Class B airspace.Based on the pilots position; timing; and degraded radio quality; I suspected Aircraft X may have been the aircraft referenced by Aircraft Y. I did not ever call him radar contact due to the lack of a transponder and only an intermittent primary target. I told Aircraft X to exit the ZZZ1 Class B Mode C veil due to operating without a transponder. The pilot objected; stating he had a right to be there because he doesn't have a generator. I asked for his altitude and relayed that information to the next sector for traffic awareness. He flew NW bound through the veil until NW of ZZZ2 field when I briefed the next controller.After being relieved from position; I reviewed the AIM regarding operations within the Mode C veil with the supervisor. The AIM notes that certain older aircraft not originally equipped with certain equipment may be permitted to operate without one but it also indicates that aircraft intending to operate within the Mode C veil without a transponder are expected to coordinate with ATC in advance to ensure situational awareness and safety. Further review of 14 CFR  91.215 says that operations within the Mode C veil generally require an operable transponder; with limited exceptions outlined in  91.215(b)(3) for certain aircraft not originally equipped with the required systems. Additionally;  91.215(d) requires prior ATC authorization for deviations from transponder requirements when applicable.Regardless if the exception applies to him; the lack of coordination reduced our ability to provide traffic advisories and maintain situational awareness. I believe that operations within the Mode C veil without a transponder and without prior coordination increases the risk of potential unsafe situations.  Aircraft intending to operate in the Mode C veil without a transponder should coordinate with ATC in advance to prevent unsafe situations EVEN IF they are allowed to be there due to equipment limitations.  ZZZ [Tower] could have coordinated with us about the aircraft with equipment issues or no transponder.  Somehow; we need to reinforce pilot understanding about how potentially unsafe this would be operating in the veil without coordination.

Prior to descent; the pilot monitoring and I briefed the arrival; approach; stabilized approach criteria/considerations; landing; and taxi items. We briefed the threats of high density altitude; increasing temperatures; and a heavy aircraft. The plan was to fly the ILS XXL; even if cleared for the visual; in order to protect against Class B airspeed infractions and to fly a stable/predictable approach.Flying the arrival and ILS approach were uneventful; meeting stabilized approach criteria we had earlier briefed. Winds were variable according to the ATIS. At approximately 700 ft I disengaged the autopilot once I believe the managed thrust had properly adjusted for the winds. At approximately 650 ft I observed a tailwind on the display. I adjusted to a more nose down attitude in order to keep the aircraft from landing long with the tailwind. At 500 ft the aircraft and PM announced '500 Feet' and I responded 'stable' referencing my airspeed on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). When I referenced the PFD at 500 ft for speed; I noticed the wind had shifted from a tailwind to a crosswind. In order to correct my previous tailwind inputs; I shallowed my pitch inputs inside of 500 ft to maintain my aim point.At the 50 ft automated callout I remembered I had previously briefed I would keep the thrust in longer than normal due to the high; hot; heavy conditions. However; I do not remember exactly when I began my thrust reduction. At 30 feet I started my flare but noticed the controls were not as responsive as I was accustomed to on other landings because the airspeed had slowly decayed prior to my flare input. The following events happened in very quick succession. The aircraft bounced; I heard an automated 'pitch' annunciation; the PM said 'continue' ( or something similar); and I flew the nose wheel to the ground and simultaneously engaged the thrust reversers. It was definitely a startle event because of the firm bounce and by the time the thought of 'go-around' entered my mind I was already flying the nose wheel to the ground.We exited the runway and pulled into a de-ice pad while we waited for parking. After providing the flights attendants and passengers an update on our gate; the PM told me what he saw and experienced. We taxied to the gate and conducted a more thorough debrief using the crew debrief card. The Captain conducted a walk around of the aircraft after we pulled into the gate and I began preparing for the following flight. After the box was prepared for the following flight; I conducted a walk around to visually inspect the aircraft before the following flight.

column121: During our climb up to FL320; we began to feel a moderate airframe vibration passing through FL230. We immediately looked at engine indications and captain ask me to reduce power to see if it was engine related. Engine indications looked normal and vibration did not change. Captain called FA to ask if she could hear and feel the vibration from the cabin. She could. We continued a slow climb while we diagnosed the issue. We then felt our ears pop and we immediately checked cabin pressure. Cabin pressure was slowly rising at 400fpm. Captain asked ATC for a level off and we leveled at FL250. In level flight we noticed the cabin climb rate increase to 700fpm and cabin alt increase to approximately 5000. Captain requested a descent and ATC gave us PD (Pilot's Discretion) down to 10000. At this point there were no caution or warning messages. We began a descent at about 2500fpm. In the descent; the cabin rate was still climbing 800-1000fpm. We then increased our descent rate to 4000fpm with flight spoilers deployed. Captain called for oxygen masks on and we donned masks out of caution. Captain requested priority handling. Passing through FL180 the cabin alt caution came on. Cabin alt was 8000' and climbing. Since we were already in a preventative descent; I continued to fly as Captain coordinated with ATC. The cabin alt warning came passing through 14000 and initiated the QRC for emergency descent and changed controls. We almost immediately leveled off at 10000' and warning message went out and cabin alt showed 6500'. Captain asked me to tell ATC we'd like to divert to the nearby airport. Since we were stable at a safe altitude; captain decided to switch controls back to me. He then requested 8000' and we began descending again. The FA called and mentioned it was very hot. He asked if the oxygen masks had deployed and if everyone was ok. Masks did not deploy and everyone was ok. Captain then continued with the QRC even though warning/caution lights went away. During completion of the QRC; captain decided to not deploy passenger oxygen because warning messages were out and the cabin alt was 5000-6000'. We also noticed the cabin temp was at 32C. We both thought deploying the masks unnecessarily would cause undue panic in the very hot cabin. We then descended to 6000' and asked for delay vectors to run QRH and setup for the approach. The captain completed the QRH procedures; messaged dispatch; notified PAX (Passengers); and coordinated with FAs. He then setup and briefed the approach. We completed normal checklists. When we got the landing data; it showed we would be landing about 200lbs heavy. We decided an immediate landing was necessary with cabin temp now at 33C. Captain took controls and I advised ATC we were ready for the approach. Approach and landing were normal. During taxi; I called ops for a gate. They said they had a gate ready to go. I then made a PAX announcement stating we were aware of the heat and we already had a gate and we'd have a short taxi. We arrived at the gate; CA made an announcement and PAX deplaned normally. I completed a post-flight inspection and CA contacted company. Cause: The initial cause of this event was an uncommanded depressurization of the aircraft.Suggestions: Nothing could have been done with the maintenance issue causing depressurization. We might have been able to hold or add drag to increase fuel consumption but ultimately made the decision that cabin temp was more of a safety issue than landing 200lbs overweight.
column123: On a scheduled flight; during a climb up to FL320 we started to feel a moderate airframe vibration passing through Approx. FL230. We did not see any engine indication or messages on our EICAS. I directed the FO to slightly reduce power to see if it was engine related; but the vibrations did not go away. I then called the FA to see if they could hear/feel any similar indications and they could. We continued climbing as the FO and I diagnosed the issue. Shortly after I noticed my ears beginning to pop and it immediately brought my attention to the cabin pressure gauges. I noticed the cabin pressure was climbing at a rate at 400 FPM and our cabin ALT was at approx. 4000 ft. I then asked ATC to level off and we leveled the aircraft off at FL250. In the level flight we noticed the cabin climb rate increased to 700 FPM and the cabin ALT increased to approx. 5000 ft. I then requested a descent from ATC and they gave as PD (Pilot's Discretion) to 10;000. At this point there were no caution/warning messages.I instructed the FO to start a descent at 2500 FPM down to 10;000 feet. In that descent we noticed the cabin rate was still climbing at about 800-1000 FPM. We then increased a descent rate to about 4000 FPM and used the flight spoilers to aid us in in the descent. I put my oxygen mask on and instructed the FO to do so as well out of precaution. Passing through about FL180 the CABIN ALT Caution appeared and the cabin alt was at 8000 feet and climbing. During this time we also requested priority handling with ATC. Since it was only a CABIN ALT caution the FO continued to fly as I coordinated with ATC. We got the CABIN ALT Warning message through about 14000 ft. Then we switched controls and Initiated the QRC for emergency descent. Almost immediately after; we leveled off at 10;000 feet and the warning message went away and the cabin alt showed 6500 feet. I instructed the FO to ask for a diversion to ZZZ since we were almost directly above them when this situation occurred. The FO was still working on starting the QRC; but since we were at a safe altitude I decided to switch the controls back to him again. I then requested a descent to 8000 feet and the FO executed the descent. We received a call from the FA; I answered; and she mentioned it was hot. I then informed her of the situation; asked her if the masks had deployed and if everybody was okay. She said everybody was ok; the mask did NOT deploy; and they did not even notice we were descending. Even though all caution/warning lights went away; I still cross referenced the QRC. During completion of the QRC I elected to not select PASX OXY (Passenger Oxygen) on. That decision was made because all warning/caution lights were gone; the cabin alt was between 5 and 6 thousand feet; the pax (Passenger) mask had not dropped yet; and the cabin temp was at 32 degrees C. The FO and I both agreed the deploying the mask unnecessarily would create undue stress or panic in the cabin.  We then continued to 6000 feet asked for delayed vectors to the airport so that we could run through checklists. I completed all the required QRH procedures. I messaged dispatch and spoke to the passengers. I briefed the FA that it would be a normal landing; no evacuation required; on the ground in 20 min. After that we set up and briefed the approach; got landing date/weather; and completed normal checklist. This all took about 10 minutes. When we got the landing data back; it showed we would be landing 200 pounds heavy. I elected to continue due to cabin temp reaching 33 degrees C. After everything was complete; I took the controls for the landing and the FO advised ATC we were ready for the approach. The approach to landing was normal and the touchdown was at about 200-300 fpm. During the taxi back the FO reached out to ops to make sure the gate and ground crew were ready for us. He also made a pax announcement stating that we were a short taxi to the gate and we are aware it is very warm back there. We arrived at the gate and completed normal checklist. I made an announcement to the Pax and we deplaned the aircraft.After this; I called dispatch; the manager; and maintenance. The FO noticed a portion of the door seal was loose. We closed out of the flight and wrote up all maintenance actions. Cause: The cause of this event was an uncommanded depressurization of the aircraft. Suggestions: There is nothing that we could have done to prevent the depressurization of the aircraft. It was a maintenance failure and we had no indication of any door or hatch being open. When it comes to the over weight landing; it is possible that we could have done a hold or create drag to increase our fuel consumption resulting in a lower landing weight. However; I was more focused on the passengers safety then only being a couple of hundred pounds over weight.  When it comes to not selecting the PASX OXY button; I could have followed the QRC so that I was not causing any confusion. However; that decision was made because all warning/caution lights were gone; the cabin alt was between 5 and 6 thousand feet; the pax mask had not dropped yet; and the cabin temp was at 32 degrees C.

column121: Early morning flight departing ZZZ at XA:00am. Deferred APU. Ground crew understaffed and in training. So we had to sit there for 25 min waiting for Ground Crew to show up with no PACK (Pneumatic Air Cycle Kit). Passengers complained about stale air and rising temperature. Ground crew showed up and proceeded with engine start with external air. After engine 1 start;  we lost ac power for split second due to a small error when transferring ac from ground ac to Gen 1. Captain quickly fixed it.  As a result all the V speeds were cleared out. It was a very short taxi and we were behind schedule. Neither CA or myself noticed the speeds cuz we both verified it previously. Captain is PF. On take off roll; I called V1; Rotate. Captain started rotating; stall horn went off that's when I realized the speeds are off; the speeds were bunched up together and were were below rotation speed. Stall horn went off; stick shaker; Captain lowered nose and increased thrust. We eventually gained enough airspeed and continued without further incident. Did not impact runway or lose control; or get into a real stall. Cause: Early morning departure; behind schedule and complaining passengers. Weather conditions was nice weather and very light wind. It looked like nothing could go wrong on that take off.  Complacency and external pressure definitely contributed to our errors. AC power was only out for 1 second; nothing else was affected except the speeds so neither CA or myself noticed. On take off roll; I called 'V1 Rotate' without double checking the actual speed until I noticed V2 was there too and we were below the planned speeds. I should've double checked if these numbers made sense before calling them out. And it took me too long to realize what was going on. I should've realized the number were off sooner and made call outs off my take off data print out. Suggestions: Need to not let external pressure get to us; like complaining passengers and unusual engine start proc. and delays. Need to not let compalcency get to us either; especially on a calm vmc day with very light wind where 'nothing could pososibly go wrong'.Need to be aware of things that can potentially be impacted by temporary power loss.Take my time; verify things; and not rush through things.

column123: FIt ABCD ZZZ1-ZZZ; requested priority handling due to complete loss of Hyd 2 fluid after putting the gear down and flaps 5 on Visual XXC into ZZZ. The message did not clear; so we kept the LG down as per the QRH. We asked the approach to give us a vector for 5-10 minutes as we run the QRH.Then we ran the Hyd 2 Lo Press QRH as it was the root message. Message did not clear; and at that point I decided to request priority handling with the approach as I was unsure if the HYD 2 was still actively leaking out of the aircraft and possibility of the hydraulic fluid catching on fire. I also considered the possibility of fuel issue as we had our gear down and our fuel flow rate was relatively high at 200 kias - although we had a precautionary alternate; I remained on the safer side in case of unexpected go-around.Once we landed with flaps full; we had the CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) meet us on the runway to visually inspect the right aft fuselage for any hydraulic leaks. Once we were told that there were no active leaks; we proceeded to the gate with differential braking and thrust. We requested to be towed into the gate; but we were able to park with no problems.Once we parked however; CFR and ramp reported that once we parked; they saw a 'poof' steam of some sort coming near the landing gear. There were residual hydraulics that started dripping near directly below right inner slat; so they sanded the leak on the ground. column121: While on my rest break; one of the relief First Officers came back to brief me that the aircraft had lost GPS Navigation capability. Symptoms included Transponder Faults; ADSB Fault ICAS; and IRS Nav only messages on the FMC and the loss of the GPS nav indication on the NDs (Navigation Displays). He briefed that they had actioned all Checklists and also ran the GPS Nav Data Unreliable Unannunciated Checklist which directed them to select GPS NAV DATA OFF. The decision was made to continue to our destination PEK and monitor the system while informing each ATC FIR of the failure. Upon my return to the flight deck; I was briefed that nothing had changed with the GPS system and ANP was good everywhere we had DME DME reception. We briefed the Threats of the downgraded nav capability would have on the approach emphasizing a detailed brief of terrain around the airport. As expected the Terrain Display was not available. We decided to leave the EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) active; but be aware that we may get false warnings and if they became a distraction we'd override that system. We received no warnings during the approach and landing in PEK.While we suspect this was a GPS Jamming/Spoofing event; we can't verify that and this may have also been some sort of system fault.

column123: My trainee and I received an ACARS from the crew on the event flight saying: HI; ENG 1 SOURCE OFF LIGHT. RAN THE QRH TO APU. APU DID NOT START. My trainee and I worked on getting the flight manual open to the applicable non-normal checklist and open the flight in FPM (Fleet Program Manager); and I had my trainee look to see what ARINC frequency area the aircraft was in. The FM (Flight Manual) directed the crew to land at nearest suitable due to the loss of 1 source of AC electrical power and the fact that the APU was not starting; leaving the aircraft in a state of single system redundancy. I saw the flight had ZZZ1 off to their right approximately 104 NM away. ZZZ was over 260 NM behind them at the time. I called ZZZ2 ARINC to try to connect me to the flight since I had no luck raising them and I sent the crew the following message:SHOWING ZZZ1 CLOSER. NOT HEARING YOU ON FREQI had the dispatcher at the next desk advise the Maintenance Dispatcher of the situation and that the flight would likely be diverting to ZZZ1. The ARINC operator connected me with the flight and the captain recapped what was going on. I advised that I had reviewed the FM checklist and saw that it didn't require using a non-normal landing distance table and asked if they concur; which they agreed with. I reiterated my recommendation to divert to ZZZ1. The captain voiced concern about the fact that they'd be well over max landing weight; which I acknowledged; and told them I was working on getting them ZZZ1 landing data to address their concern and updated  burn info but was having technical issues; so I would get Maintenance Control on the line while I continue to troubleshoot. FPM kept on giving me an error saying there was no PET (Point of Equal Time) between ZZZ3 and another airport; or something similar. Despite reactivating the current release; re-doing the CHG (Change) DEST (Destination) on the FPM Details tab; and deleting ZZZ3 in the quick EROPS box on the EROPS tab; it still wouldn't calculate the diversion to ZZZ1. The conversation between the flight and Maintenance Control was relatively short in respect to any systems recommendations. The event flight had already turned around to the west; and the captain stated to Maintenance Control their intention to go to ZZZ; with Maintenance Control responding they would notify local maintenance. I advised the crew that I was unable to get a calculation to go to ZZZ1; but that ZZZ4 was suitable; and closer than ZZZ. ZZZ4 was WNW (West North West) of their position; then off to their right; approximately 140 NM away; with ZZZ still at least another 100 NM further. I was able to calculate a diversion to ZZZ4 and recommended that they divert there; and stated despite their high landing weight concerns; they would still have enough runway distance available  even if the runway condition code were to deteriorate to 3/3/3 (which would be unexpected.) I didn't send the current ZZZ4 weather or NOTAMs to the crew at this point since we were still discussing on the call; but I saw that neither of these factors would prevent a safe landing there.The captain responded that they still wanted to return to ZZZ. I said to the captain So you are intending to continue to ZZZ under emergency authority? The captain remarked they weren't sure if they considered their flight an emergency yet; and that they were concerned with the idea of stranding their passengers at a random airport. Since I had made several attempts to get the captain to land at what I considered to be the nearest suitable airport(s) at the time and the captain was not budging off their intention to return to ZZZ  despite me implicating that they would be continuing under captain's emergency authority to go there  I decided I could not continue to argue with them and would rather have them focus on getting on the ground safely. I told them I would work on calculating their diversion back to ZZZ; send them landing data; and asked them if they needed anything else from dispatch. The captain didn't have any other requests; so we ended the call. I continued to follow the Dispatch Emergency / Irregular Ops Checklist for MECHANICAL  SINGLE SYS (System) REDUNDANCY and LANDING AIRPORT SELECTION. I sent the landing data to the crew; entered the DV (Divert) FLIFO (Flight Information) Divert command; re-released the flight; and sent the information to the crew. I had my neighbor call the Maintenance Dispatcher again; advising of the air return to ZZZ and their emergency status. I had my trainee call the ATC desk; the OM; and the Chief Pilot to advise the same. I entered the MECHANICAL shift into the log. I advised the crew I sent the landing data to their printer and asked if they needed anything else. They responded that they just needed to know which gate they would be going to since ATC was asking. I responded with their gate information and the flight proceeded to land at ZZZ without any further issues.

column121: Shortly before beginning the descent for arrival into PVR; we lost the GPS-R and then the GPS-L signal (GPS-R/L INVALID FMC messages). Over the last many (6+?) months; I have seen loss of usually one; occasionally both; GPS signals in this same vicinity; en route to PVR.  The CA and I discussed that we'd both seen it before and that it was a known issue for local ATC; and that the signal(s) usually returned shortly.  That I am aware of; this is general knowledge only and cannot be found in any Jeppesen company pages; Pilot Bulletin; manual entry; etc.  Yesterday; the event lasted longer than usual; and in addition to the Unable Reqd Nav Perf - RNP message in the scratchpad; it also displayed this message on the navigation display; and the UTC time on the clocks was blanked out.  We ran the Unable Reqd Nav Perf - RNP non-normal checklist and the GPS Data Unreliable Checklist; notified ATC of our equipment loss; and requested a VOR approach. While flying direct to the VOR to be vectored to VOR final and at approximately 19;000 feet MSL the GPS-R returned.  We notified ATC and were directed to the IAF for the RNAV approach.  Somewhere on the approach the GPS-L returned as well and the approach and landing were uneventful.  We spoke with a maintenance representative; who was also aware of this issue happening; but he said a good GPS reset would just get the GPSs back to where they were - there was no indication of an issue on the ground.  Dispatch was notified.  The CA and I definitely had expectation bias that the GPSs would come back before we started our descent; which delayed our running of checklists and briefing the VOR approach.  This gave us a high task load during an already busy time and we needed to pay special attention to briefing the VOR approach; which is not an approach we normally do; and has specific safety considerations mentioned on the MMPR company page.
column123: These past few months I've been flying often to PVR and have noticed a consistent loss of both GPS signals about 150 miles north of the OBRUG fix on the OBRUG1A arrival.  Normally this lasts no more than a few minutes. Fellow pilots who fly PVR often have indicated that this is very common.  PVR predominantly uses the RNP runway 22 and today our loss of both GPS signals lasted until descending through transition altitude.  Although manageable; this was a marked increase in workload as we switched from an RNP approach to VOR approach and ultimately back to the RNP approach when the GPS signals returned at about transition level. ATC was of course advised and they are very much aware of the GPS signal loss in that location. Dispatch was advised. GPS signal checked and stable on approach and landing. Conditions were VFR. Local PVR station maintenance personnel have had numerous reports from pilots about GPS loss and speculate military jamming.

column121: During climbout; all indications were normal until right at 8;000 feet; at which point the cabin began to rapidly over pressurize. Initially; the condition was physically noticeable through ear discomfort and a message on the EICAS: PRESSN AUTO FAIL. We then referenced the Cabin Pressure Acquisition Module (CPAM) indications on the bottom of the EICAS and became fully aware of the situation.At one point; I observed approximately -3000 fpm on the cabin VSI. Eventually the Cabin altitude and Cabin VSI indications are dashing out yellow on the EICAS and the Delta Pressure rapidly went to 8.0 PSI. Due to the increasingly uncomfortable and mildly disorienting conditions; I elected to engage ALT HOLD before we even reached 8100 feet and stop the climb. At this point the First Officer took over the radios as well and began to inform ATC of our intention to hold 8000 feet and for the moment continue on course. Manual control of the digital controller was unresponsive and inoperative which led to a cabin dump. After completion of the QRH I knew we would have to return.We were in contact with ATC and advised them of the situation; stating our intent to return to ZZZ. We requested delay vectors in order to reduce weight and arrive within landing limits. The flight attendant had contacted the flight deck when we were still running the QRH and still in sterile; clearly recognizing that something was abnormal with the obvious ear pain and expressed concern from himself and the passengers. I advised him I would provide a special procedure shortly; as we were still managing a high workload at the moment. Once workload permitted; with the First Officer handling flying duties and radios; I provided the flight attendant with a proper report; explaining that we were experiencing a pressurization issue and would require approximately 30 minutes to land; because we needed to burn fuel; I instructed him to prepare the cabin for a normal landing and deplaning; with no special instructions or brace commands anticipated.I made a PA to the passengers advising that the situation was under control; that the aircraft was safe; and that we would be unable to continue to ZZZ1 and would instead be returning to ZZZ.No cabin aural warnings were triggered; as the event occurred at 8;000 feet. Passenger oxygen masks did not deploy. At no point did I or the First Officer declare an emergency; rather; we communicated to ATC that we were returning to the field and requested delay vectors to reduce weight. As this was not assessed to be a time-critical emergency; I exercised judgment to avoid an unnecessary overweight landing. We elected to drop flaps 9 and gear significantly early to increase drag and fuel burn to get on the ground sooner and there were no exceedances of any limitations.On final approach; I observed the fire trucks had rolled out. I queried ground regarding this; as no emergency had been declared from the flight deck. It is possible that ATC provided priority handling on our behalf; however; this was not communicated to us. After landing; we contacted the fire chief on their assigned frequency and advised that no assistance was required. We then taxied to the gate; parked; and deplaned normally.Suggestions: It would be nice to get confirmation from ATC on if priority handling was provided on their behalf.

column121: I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying to ZZZ; operating Aircraft X. During the approach to Runway XXL; winds were reported from 160-170 degrees at 10-12 knots; gusting to approximately 18-20 knots.Prior to initiating the approach; I briefed the Captain that I had limited experience landing in gusty crosswind conditions in this aircraft; as I am new to it. The Captain acknowledged this and suggested that completing the approach would provide a valuable learning opportunity; which I agreed to.At approximately 1000 feet AGL; I disconnected the autopilot. I noted that the crosswind effects felt stronger than anticipated; requiring continuous aileron inputs to maintain alignment with the extended runway centerline. At 500 feet AGL; the aircraft was stabilized in accordance with company criteria.At approximately 200 feet AGL; a gust resulted in a brief loss of energy and a slight deviation below the glide path; which was promptly corrected. The correction caused the aircraft to pick up energy. As the aircraft approached approximately 50 feet AGL; I assessed that the approach could result in an undesirably firm touchdown. I initiated a go-around; however; during the initiation; the main landing gear made brief contact with the runway; followed by a bounce. I called going around; flaps 9; check thrust while advancing the thrust levers. The captain who was the pilot monitoring said ok but the flaps were still at 45. I reached for the flaps to avoid over speeding them and was intending to retract them to 9 but accidentally got them to 0. Landing gear horn started going off. Captain took flight controls. A positive rate of climb was established; and the landing gear was retracted. Tower was advised of the go-around; and we were instructed to maintain runway heading and 1700 feet; followed by a climb to 3000 feet. Climb check was done at acceleration altitude. We were subsequently vectored for another approach and cleared to land on Runway XXR. The Captain conducted the second approach and landed it. After parking; both pilots visually inspected the landing gear with no visible abnormalities noted. Maintenance was contacted regarding a brief; less than 2 minutes; ETO reserve thrust; which was reported to have been within allowable limits by maintenance who said it didn't require inspection.Suggestions: Providing additional guidance on how gust factors should be applied in conjunction with published crosswind limitations for pilots with less than 100 hours in type. Clearer interpretation may help crews better assess overall crosswind risk in variable wind conditions.Reinforcing collaborative decision-making between Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring when evaluating approach conditions may further enhance safety margins.

Checklist was completed; and within QRH 5.5 the blowdown handle was pulled out. Once checklist was completed; captain briefed the FO to let them know that they would exchange controls again so the captain could make the landing. Captain and FO briefed and decided that there was no need to declare an emergency as the gear was down and locked. FO commenced a positive exchange of controls with the captain; and an uneventful landing was made. Upon landing; captain briefed passengers on the issue being non-emergent. Passengers deplaned. column121: Initial descent into ZZZ; I was PF (FO) and the CA Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) went black. As we were descending through below 18k ish; my MFD also went black. So now we had no MFDs in the airplane. Ahead was a few buildups; we did our best visually to avoid these. That being said the CA were both pretty task saturated due to us both losing our usual info. Things just felt off when you are missing all MFD info. As we got closer we got our runway assignment; as briefed. We were getting vectors for the visual. All looked okay; as we got our final intercept turn; i noticed the CA never sequenced the FMS. So this Autopilot (AP) was going to blow through the course. As I was visual at around 3k; I disconnected the AP because it was going to be a lot of button pushing rather than just turn and line up. CA cleaned up box; and we were back on track. ATC then told us 180kts until 5 mile final. This was a challenge with no MFD and my localizer(I was green needles) not giving me any DME. The CA did something in FMS to get us distance from runway threshold. In the meantime I am 'heads down' trying to get info from my ipad about what altitude is the FAF at and such. Obviously this was all briefed in cruise but it isn't something that I had memorized . So we get 6 miles from runway and call gear down. I start slowing and get the flaps 30 just after 5 miles. As I can visually see us close to runway; as soon as possible. I called for final flaps. At this point things are happening really quickly as I am hand flying and very busy. But I recall hearing '1000' prior to having the before landing check completed. I am not sure what our true MSL altitude was at the time in relation to Height Above Touchdown (HAT).  I flew an ugly hand flown approach. As I was mainly following the PAPI; most of my scan was outside. The CA called 'vertical speed' and I said correcting. When I looked I was at 1.3VS. Shortly there after we heard 'OBSTACLE' Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGWPS) callout. I corrected VS and had an unobstructed clear path to the runway so we continued. The last few hundred feet of the approach stabled out and had an uneventful landing. Cause: Task saturation; due to dual MFD failure. Poor vertical path control by me; PF.  In an already busy airport environment; I should have reconnected the AP while on the approach to alleviate task saturation. The FAF ZZZZZ is relatively low (I guess from what I'm used to). So I thought we had more time than we did. Suggestions: Use AP for approaches when necessary. Make stronger mental notes of charted altitudes/GS intercepts (maybe write them down). Incorporate the VSI into my scan below 1k more often. Most importantly; go around!

column121: Runway XX.  Last reported wind:  250 at 10; gusting 20.  Demonstrated crosswind component and company standard for captains is 25 kts.We were hit by significant crosswind on landing.  Initially added slight power while in flare to stabilize before touchdown.  Touched down on centerline and corrected a slight swerve.  Was then hit by a significant crosswind component from the left.  Despite left aileron deflection; right rudder; differential power (right engine in deep reverse); and right brake applied; the aircraft tilted forward and to the right; traveling on the nose-wheel and right main tire.  The aircraft slowly moved to the left and exited the runway.  The left main then came down.  Shortly afterwards; I applied full reverse on both engines and locked both brakes in the soft ground; bringing the aircraft to a stop between the runway and parallel taxiway.  We crew-members checked that each other were OK.  We then confirmed that the passengers were OK.  Both engines appeared to be running normally.  After confirming that both main tires were intact; I added power and aft elevator; entered taxiway 1 near the midpoint; and taxied to the ramp.  Checklists and shutdown were completed normally; and the passengers disembarked.  A walk around inspection revealed that the right wingtip sustained damage; including the outboard flap bracket.  Subsequent observation of the tire marks on the runway asphalt and in the dirt confirmed that the aircraft was sliding at an angle pointed towards the left; towards the wind; for a significant distance.Other considerations:1.  Crosswinds from the west can be partially blocked by a large hangar west of the touchdown point.  From there; continuing the landing touchdown and rollout northward can be followed by a very abrupt return of a 'slotted' crosswind.2.  Runway XY-XZ was permanently closed last year.3.  The general opinion of those who fly this make and model for my employer is that it has particularly challenging ground handling characteristics.

column121: I was operating Aircraft X on an IFR flight departing SNA on a leg of a personal IFR proficiency flight. During the initial climb; I experienced a loss of situational awareness resulting in a heading deviation.Prior to takeoff; during the run-up; all instruments appeared operational. However; approximately 3-5 minutes later; while holding short of the runway; I observed that the vacuum-driven heading indicator had drifted. I reset the heading indicator to the runway heading prior to takeoff and set the heading bug to the assigned departure heading of 220°.Aircraft instrument lighting was suboptimal. The magnetic compass was difficult to read due to inadequate illumination.After takeoff; I conducted a normal climb. At approximately 800 feet AGL; I requested and received approval from the tower to begin a right turn and was subsequently handed off to SoCal TRACON. During the turn; I misinterpreted the heading indicator. Instead of recognizing that the heading indicator was indicating that 220° was to the left; I initiated a right turn as previously instructed by the clearance delivery controller; resulting in a 100° deviation towards a heading of approximately 020°; effectively creating a 360-degree turn in the wrong direction.The controller identified the problem and issued corrective headings. During this time; I recognized that the heading indicator was no longer providing reliable information. I informed ATC that I was experiencing issues with the directional gyro. At this point the controller engaged in a series of disparaging remarks over the radio adding to the stress of the situation. The controller responded to my notification of the loss of directional gyro with 'I do not care'. This took me aback because this should have let the controller know that for the moment I had no idea of what heading I was truly on. The controller also asked if 'Do you know how to fly the airplane?' followed by 'I have to hold departures for you.' Conditions were VMC therefore; I switched from instrument flight momentarily to looking outside to gain some sort of bearing on course.Due to the poor cockpit lighting; the magnetic compass was not readily usable without additional illumination; requiring the use of a handheld light. This increased workload during a critical phase of flight. After some back and forth with the operation of the aircraft and the controller; ATC continued issuing vectors; and I complied using GPS-derived heading information. The controller also issued multiple instructions in rapid succession while managing other traffic and attempting to correct my course. I experienced elevated workload and stress while troubleshooting the instrument issue; maintaining aircraft control; and complying with ATC instructions. I managed task saturation by focusing on aircraft control and navigation until situational awareness was regained. I transitioned to using the Garmin 650 GPS display as my primary source of heading information; as it was the most immediately legible and reliable instrument available.The flight continued to the destination without further incident.Contributing factors included heading indicator drift and unreliability of the vacuum-driven system. Inadequate instrument lighting; particularly affecting compass readability. Night IFR conditions during initial climb; increasing workload. Misinterpretation of heading indication leading to incorrect turn direction and increased workload and task saturation during instrument failure and ATC vectoring.

column121: Date: Day 0Time: approximately XA:10pm  Location near / before fix ZZZZZFlight stage: beginning decent Description: we had just begun decent from ZZZ. Also; weather in area meant we needed to correct course more towards the north. We elected to continue. We were only 15-20 minutes out and had plenty of altitude. I began transfer of fuel at 200lb imbalance; and also utilized anti ice and cross flow as we had to decent through precip. As we descended; I continued to asses the situation. I briefed passengers that we'd had an engine rollback; but all remaining systems are normal and explained our intentions to continue. I initially opted to not attempt a restart for fear of taxing unknown systems faults with the starter sequence; but once we were given our discretion for altitude; I realized I could remain higher; conserve speed; and utilize the steeper decent to get to required restart parameters. I discussed with my copilot; and we agreed to the attempt in decent. We built excess speed of 230kts; and followed air restart procedures. They were successful. I asked her to notify Atc we successfully restarted motor; but remained cautious and continued to monitor for any faults. (Pic) After restart we got another warning that said 'N1 REF CIC' on the fms. We were unable to get a photo before it went away.We made a normal landing; briefing for if the issue returned at any stage of the approach. I then taxied to and parked at vip parking; where we were asked to present documentation for the flight to local officials. I inspected what I could of the motor; and did not note any leaking fluids or score marks on nacel. Oil was checked; and was over the minimum line (pic). I contacted our maintenance in ZZZ1 to make sure he was in loop; and we'll start prepping plans for either a flight to the service center or on site maintenance.

column121: Aircraft X was in my traffic pattern and was told to continue for traffic holding in position.  Aircraft Y had called up ready at R21R; I told Aircraft Y to LUAW and but before I could give the associated final traffic I realized Aircraft X was too close to the runway for a departure to work; so I then said disregard; disregard hold short of R21R.  I then went and cleared Aircraft X to land; he read back his landing clearance.  Unbeknownst to me Aircraft Y had taken and read back the LUAW clearance; I did not hear that.  A few moments later Aircraft X said they were going around for an aircraft on the runway.  From the tower to the approach end of R21R it is almost impossible to see a small aircraft on the runway's approach end; so I got my binoculars and at that time I could see what appeared to be a C172 on the runway; and then I had to check the ground radar to see who exactly was on the runway and that is when I realized that Aircraft Y had LUAWed. Aircraft X reentered the pattern and landed safely and Aircraft Y took off without incident. column121: On an otherwise uneventful flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; severe turbulence was encountered south or in the ZZZZZ FIR. There were no forecast indications in cockpit weather radar or WSI (Weather App) of this event. ZZZ assigned FL 330 for our final altitude. There was a forecast FPG (Flight Plan Guidance) along our route of flight and low level radar returns on both WSI and the onboard weather radar. All indications were that we were topping any radar returns by approximately 20;000 feet. Both Captain and FO determined that actual ride conditions allowed for the seat belt sign to be off and flight attendant up and about the cabin. Approximately 80% of the way through this forecast FPG; the aircraft encountered severe turbulence. What started as appearance of mountain wave (i.e. small fluctuations in speed and altitude) quickly progressed into rapid airspeed and altitude changes. Unexpectedly the aircraft accelerated into the MMO (Maximum Operating Mach Number) tape while simultaneously gaining approximately 1500 feet of altitude. The captain as pilot flying quickly disengaged the auto pilot to more precisely control the aircraft. During the event; I as pilot monitoring instructed the flight attendants to be seated immediately and turned on the passenger seat belt sign. In addition to air speed and altitude fluctuations it was noted that the aircraft entered IMC conditions with intense static discharge and Fire observed on the windscreens. The captain was able to level the aircraft at approximately FL350. Once radio traffic permitted I advised ATC of our deviations and requested a block altitude. Turbulent conditions continued so we requested and were approved for a turn to the south; as this seemed like the most expeditious manner of exiting turbulent conditions. Once the aircraft was again under control; the captain re-engaged the auto pilot system. After a short amount of time of smoother air flight attendants were advised to take their jump seats. After a few minutes of smoother ride conditions; the captain request requested a check-in from the flight attendants who noted that they were all without injury and in their jump seats. A PA was made by the captain asking any passengers who needed medical attention to ring their flight attendant call button; there was no initial response. Sometime later closer to our top of descent point a flight attendant called forward advising of a potential injury as a result of the turbulence. Medical advisory services procedures were initiated but unable to establish voice contact due to poor connectivity. During descent flight attendant advised of another possible injury. Both injured passengers requested no immediate medical assistance but asked for EMS personnel at the gate. Dispatch was advised of both potential injuries. An ELB (Electronic Flight Book) report was submitted via the ACARS system to advise of the over speed.Flight proceeded without incident and landed safely in ZZZ1. EMS personnel met passengers at the gate. Captain established phone contact with Maintenance Control.

I heard the aircraft accelerating and noticed on the ISI (In Service Information) that our speed was increasing. I immediately called out unreliable airspeed and the first officer started the memory items while I grabbed the card. We ran through the card and then proceeded to QRH 13-XX. We started the checklist. I requested priority handling with ATC as we continued our descent. Both our airspeed tapes decreased and then disappeared. As we continued through the checklist we got some the associated messages with unreliable airspeed in the QRH. The First Officer appeared to lose his AHARS system with all the associated red flags. At approximately FL240 my airspeed tape reappeared and matched the ISI. A few minutes later the First Officer's airspeed tape appeared at approximately 10;000 feet and also matched mine and the ISI. We completed the checklist and decided I would land the aircraft and the First Officer would take the radios after I talked to dispatch; the flight attendants; and passengers. I sent Dispatch an ACARS but didn't receive a response. I talked to the flight attendants and gave a brief. I then advised the passengers. After everyone was briefed we swapped roles. We then told ATC we would like a long final and would like to start the approach. They gave us a long final and I configured the airplane level at 3;000 feet. Everything appeared normal and the first officer verified pitch and power levels with the QRH. We landed without incident and taxied to the gate. I gave a brief statement to ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire and Fighting) and airport ops. Then proceeded to call company and write up in logbook.Cause: TBD by maintenance. Unknown at this time.

Brake temps were fluctuating on our right outboard brake and often resting at 20. We decided since we just took off and figured a return back to field would the airport most suitable. We requested priority handling with ATC and had them send a fire truck out to meet us when we landed to make sure that there was no fire threat. We told dispatch and maintenance our situation. column123: After takeoff at approximately 1000 ft MSL; we received a BRAKE OVHT warning message. BTMS (Brake Temperature Monitoring System) temperatures for the right outboard brake were initially indicating a red '07'; spiked to a red '20'; displayed amber fault lines consistent with a sensor anomaly; and returned to '20'. The indication was non-decreasing throughout the event. The captain and I executed the Company Procedures. As BTMS indicators were non-decreasing; the QRH directed a return to the nearest suitable airport. We leveled off at 8;000 ft MSL and maintained 200 KIAS in accordance with QRH limitations while evaluating the indication. We requested priority handling; accomplished all remaining checklists; and determined the nearest suitable airport was ZZZ. We requested and were met with crash and rescue services upon landing. When we taxied off the runway we requested crash and rescue to inspect the right main landing gear for possible overheating -- they did not observe any abnormal heating of the brakes. We taxied back to the gate; documented the warning message in the Logbook; and deplaned the passengers to coordinate with maintenance; customer service; and company dispatch.Cause: There was a mechanical failure of a sensor part of the brakes that led to this indication - this was physically determined by maintenance after we had landed.Suggestions: The lack of QRH guidance for diagnosing this as a genuine overheating scenario resulted in the turn back to ZZZ. The BTMS indication behavior -- including an initial red '07'; spike to '20'; amber fault lines suggesting sensor anomaly; and return to '20' -- was not addressed by any available checklist or decision tree. If written guidance existed to diagnose indications as anomalous based on specific observable criteria; a continuation to destination could have been more easily justified with appropriate documentation. Development of a BTMS anomaly assessment decision tree within the QRH or Standard Operating Procedure manual  would provide crews with a defensible; procedure-backed pathway for these scenarios.

column121: Before Event:I was on my second solo flight ever. I did a normal walk-round and pre-flight; and had some trouble starting the engine. After two attempts to do so; I requested help from my instructor; who told me to prime and attempt again. The engine successfully started on the third attempt. I then did my pre-taxi as normal; then called for taxi clearance.Event:I called ground control for clearance to taxi VFR West. Ground control relayed a clearance back; and told me to wait for traffic exiting runway XX. I relayed the clearance back; but did not acknowledge the traffic. Ground called again asking me to acknowledge traffic. I located the traffic; acknowledged it; and waited for it to turn onto taxiway 1.It turned onto taxiway 1 moving away from my position. After waiting a moment to give it room; I then pulled onto taxiway 1 and began proceeding in the same direction as the other plane. The other plane; a long way down the taxiway; then turned around while still on the taxiway. At this time I concluded that I had misinterpreted ground's instructions; and stopped for a moment to think. After a moment; I called ground and said 'Aircraft X trying to turn around.' I received no response; and exited the taxiway left back towards the hangars. My intention at that moment was to circle the hangar and get back to where I had started.There was a gate where I needed to go in order to do that; and I did not realize it was too narrow for the plane to get through. I continued taxiing until impacting the gate.I then attempted to shut down the plane by pulling zeroing the throttle and turning off the magnetos. The engine did not stop. I communicated with ground to let them know the situation; and that my engine would not stop. I then ran my shutdown checklist; and when I pulled the mixture back to full lean; the engine stopped.After Event:I was helped to exit the plane by another pilot/instructor who was in the area. I found the airplane completely covered in oil; which appeared to be coming out of all openings on the engine cowl. With help from the rancher; I got the aircraft secured. column121: I was planning to go to ZZZ1 for a couple landings from ZZZ. During my preflight; fuel was full and of good quality. Oil level was at 5 qts; the oil was pretty dark in color. I got VFR Flight following to ZZZ1. I was going a runup; everything was completely normal; mag drop was checked within limits; carb heat was checked; fuel tanks were swapped; all performed by flow; backed up with checklist; nothing was missed in runup. On departure I was cleared into ZZZ2 Class B airspace at or below 2;000; however I stayed at 1;500 to stay away from cloud layers near my intended route of flight. I was cruising at a low power setting; around 100mph indicated and 2;200 RPM. At approximately XA:00 local; I felt a small amount of engine roughness; which was typical for that specific aircraft. Normally; that issue can be fixed by adjusting the power setting; so I did. As a precaution; I also applied carb heat; as well as turning the fuel pump on. The problem went away for a little while. Shortly after that; approximately at XA:06 local; the engine started running extremely rough; as well as the RPM fluctuation between 1800 and 2400. The throttle lever immediately became unresponsive; so I immediately started a turn back to the departure airport and advised ATC of the amended destination. ATC requested fuel and souls on board; as well as asking if I needed any assistance; so I provided the information and declined assistance. I turned back to ZZZ and started troubleshooting the issue. I made sure my memory items were compete and they were. I referenced the checklist; and everything was complete. I turned the carb heat off; and the roughness went away. I advised ATC that the issue had ceased; however; I was still going back to the original airport to troubleshoot more on the ground. I got cleared to ZZZ right downwind RW XXL for a full stop landing. I exited the runway and parked the aircraft; and completed my shutdown checklist items. I got the airplane put to bed and went home. If I could be in the situation again; I should've requested priority handling due to the immediate threat to safety of flight. I believe a root cause could have been spark plug fouling; because after inspection of the maintenance logbook; it had been approximately 60 hours since the last spark plug service. In the future I feel like there isn't much that can be done to prevent this from happening just due to the fact that there are so many issues that just end up happening with very little control being had from a pilot's point of view.

column121: The aircraft is used for flight training; but I am the owner and not a student pilot. We had a report of a C0 alert in the aircraft and so the PIC made a precautionary landing at ZZZ on the Day 0. When our mechanic was available; we went out to the aircraft on the Day 2 and I assisted in his repair of the issue; which was an exhaust manifold separating from the header due to the bolts coming off. We inspected the remainder of our fleet and discovered that the other aircraft also had loose or missing bolts also on the rear exhaust headers; these were accordingly tightened and will be routinely checked.After the repair; I performed a run-up and; satisfied that the engine was operating normally; obtained clearances to taxi out and depart Runway XX. Just after takeoff; I heard a noise from the engine; and almost immediately started seeing the C0 numbers climb and an alert warning (as the aircraft is equipped with a monitoring system). As the numbers were quickly approaching 100ppm (and did pass them before landing); I opted to return to the field immediately. I had been assigned a straight-out heading; and was unable to reach Tower due to communication congestion; but given the situation started my turn anyways; at which point Tower contacted me and asked the situation. I explained that we were having engine problems; as we did not yet know what they were; and he cleared me to land. I landed and taxied in without further incident.Upon examining the engine; we determined that the exhaust springs had stretched; allowing the muffler to separate from the right side exhaust headers when full power was applied quickly for takeoff (we believe the more gradual application of power in the run-up had not done this). The following day; our mechanic replaced all exhaust springs and re-sealed the system; we performed extensive run-up testing; and I flew the aircraft home without incident and returned it to service.Due to the occurrence of loose exhaust header bolts across all the RV12 aircraft; which we believe is being exacerbated by an existing gearbox issue impacting the Rotax 912is motor; we are implementing a regular inspection interval of 50 hours on all exhaust header nuts. I believe this should be expanded via an SB (Service Bulletin) or AD; as applicable; to all 912is-equipped RV12 aircraft; until the situation is better understood. The RV12 has an exhaust system manufactured by/for Van's Aircraft; and not the stock Rotax exhaust; so we have no reason to believe that this issue necessarily affects other models using the same engine.

column121: Coming into El Paso landing east; runway 08R. Tower breaks us off the arrival and assigns a 260 heading for the visual. From the arrival and assigned vector; we were arriving on the north side of the airport. During the flight; I warned my FO of the threats involved with El Paso and being known for unstable approaches. This was his first time in El Paso; and my first time landing east. On downwind; we tried to slow but the winds at altitude kept us fast leading to the gear being dropped to slow down. Both pilots had the terrain feature pulled up for visual reference due to the blinding sun and low level haze layer obscuring the mountain directly ahead. Once the sun dropped below the mountain the fog immediate disappeared and the mountain was only several miles away. I recognize it and immediately start a mountain escape with vectors and altitude from ATC after I successfully escaped. We came around from the south side and had zero issues and landed 8R.Cause: GPWS message for terrain west of EL Paso airport.Suggestions: Being cleared the visual from the north side for runway 8R is NOT safe. I have lost sleep realizing how close I actually was. There is ZERO warning of terrain regarding El Paso; no published app procedures for 8R; (due to mountains); but no company pages for suggestions; the AOM suggests creating a PBD of 5nm (FAF) and 1500 AFE to keep a standard 3.0 glideslope. (This is the procedure of a visual approach per the book). That was what I followed; and due to the lack of general company pages on Jepp; I had no idea terrain was inside of 5nm. Due to the terrain feature being pulled up on my own; it saved us from the mountain. There was no warning; no prior training in visual app; no company pages; new pilots with no experience landing east; and sunlight blinding us as it set were definitely factors. I hope this almost crazy accident is investigated further to realize that landing from the north for Runway 8R is WAY too close for comfort.
column123: On approach into El Paso; ATC assigned us the visual for runway 08R. We accepted that clearance and they brought us in from the north instead of the south. This approach is affected by the mountain range immediately west of the airport running north east and southwest. While on approach on the left downwind for runway 08R we got a GPWS terrain warning because of the upcoming mountains. The captain executed a go around and we came in from the south on the second time around without issue.Cause: GPWS AlertSuggestions: My suggestion would be to create a suggested visual approach procedure for runway eight right coming in from the north. A detailed explanation of speeds to fly and markers to hit when we fly that approach would have helped us immensely on this specific instance. For any pilot flying into El Paso I would say be 160kts gear down flaps 3 at the maximum abeam touchdown point and start your turn 10 seconds after that point. That being said; the procedure from the north is very tight and if I had to do it again; I wouldn't do it at all.During the event; the captain and I both noted that it was hard to make out the distance to the mountains when the sun is setting over them; causing the backside of them to shade. It was only when the sun set behind the mountains that the captain and I noticed how close we were.

column121: On Day 0; while operating Aircraft X from ZZZ to BOI; we were initially planning the RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 28L. My prior examination of the BOI notams were confusing for this approach as it stated procedure NA" and later provided adjusted specific altitudes for specific legs of the approach. During descent toward the end of the Kourt 4 arrival toward LITTL; ATC informed us that the RNP Z was out of service due to crane operations. The approach controller offered us a visual to 28L or the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L. The first officer quickly pointed out on our company arrival pages that the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L was not listed as an authorized procedure. Finding out it was completely out of service; given our location and workload in mountainous terrain; lack of destination framiliarity/procedures and the offered approach not being authorized; I elected for the radar vectors to a visual approach 28L given the favorable VMC conditions. We accepted radar vectors for a visual approach to RWY 28L. To ensure a stabilized approach and maintain terrain awareness in the mountainous environment; I elected to retain the HOBSI fix in the MCDU (Multipurpose Control Display Unit). I programmed a hard altitude constraint of 3;900 ft at HOBSI (the published FAF altitude for the RNP Z) to serve as a safety barrier and provide vertical guidance for a 3-degree glidepath. Again; we were being radar vectored on to the visual approach in VMC conditions with a final vectors of 260 descend to 3900ft. These vectors pointed us directly to HOBSI fix.We conducted the arrival using a managed descent profile toward HOBSI with 3;900 ft set in the FCU (Flight Control Unit). The aircraft was fully configured and on speed just prior to reaching HOBSI to meet FOM stabilized approach standards and to account for a lack of local airport familiarity. As we were in the managed descent approaching 4;000 ft; just prior to HOBSI; the EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) issued an 'Obstacle' alert. I immediately verified our position visually and confirmed we were clear of all terrain while the aircraft leveled at the 3;900 ft FCU altitude. Shortly after; at or around HOBSI; the system issued a 'Terrain; Terrain; Pull Up' warning. Although we were in visual conditions and clear of obstacles; we immediately executed the full EGPWS escape maneuver in accordance with SOPs. At the start and during the maneuver; I noted that no prominent guidance was displayed on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) VSI.During the climb we made ATC aware of the go-around actions; received a heading/altitude assignment and cleaned the aircraft up. We then conducted a briefing to discuss the event and plan the next arrival. We subsequently flew the RNAV (RNP) X RWY 28L to an uneventful approach and landing. It is my assessment that the crane operations near the approach path likely triggered the EGPWS logic.Cause: A significant factor in this event was the late-stage transition to a visual approach in an unfamiliar; high-terrain environment; which was made more challenging by confusing NOTAM information. The decision to keep the HOBSI fix and a 3;900-foot altitude constraint in the system was a proactive effort to ensure a stabilized descent and maintain safety margins. The election for a visual 28L inadvertently brought the air carrier into EGPWS threshold for the temporary crane operations even though we were well clear with of any conflict. The limited selection of authorized backup procedures also added to our workload; as we had to quickly adapt our plan while navigating mountainous terrain. Based on the timing; unclear notams; mountainous terrain if we had more time at altitude with the issues at hand we could have researched the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L;  found it to be legal and optimum to fly. This was discussed post flight with the first officer on how and why we could have flown the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L. Again; he did a stellar job looking at the company arrival pages and I was focused on descent inmountainous terrain. It was my decision for the radar vectors to 28L approach based on workload; timing; terrain.To help manage these types of situations in the future; it may be beneficial to clarify ambiguous NOTAMs with Dispatch or ATC as early as possible. When a primary approach is out of service due to temporary obstacles; using a slightly higher vertical buffer than the published FAF altitude can provide extra peace of mind during a visual approach. Additionally; identifying and briefing a secondary authorized procedure; like the RNAV (RNP) X; can help keep the workload manageable if the primary plan changes and in this case if flown would have mitigated this event.  A thorough debrief was conducted and the lessons learned in this write up as well as additional items were noted between the two of us."
column123: During the approach phase when we checked on with BOI Approach; they told us to expect the RNAV Y to 28L. We told approach we were unable the RNAV Y as we did not think we could fly that approach and requested the RNAV Z. Approach told us the RNAV Z was unavailable but we could be vectored for a visual approach. We elected to fly the visual approach with a RADAR vector to final for 28L. The PF entered the FAF from the RNAV Z in the DIRECT to with the altitude constraint on the chart and managed the autopilot. As we descended through 4200 or so I noted the prominent boxes on the ND (Navigation Display) displayed with an aural OBSTACLE sounding. I looked left and spotted cranes up south of the aircraft course near some construction. At around 4000 feet we received the GPWS warning and the PF executed the GPWS Escape maneuver into a go-around. We followed tower's instructions and reloaded the box for the full RNAV X approach from the north; briefed it and flew it to a successful landing on runway 28L.Cause: It had been a few years since I had flown into BOI and I was unfamiliar with the airport and failed to call that out during the arrival briefing threats discussion. That may have lead to the election to use an instrument approach instead of a visual. I incorrectly reviewed the approach authorization table as meaning that we could not fly the RNAV Y approach but after reviewing the charts post flight realized the RNAV Y was a GPS approach not an RNP approach and we could have flown that approach from the east successfully; that also could have lead to a better outcome. During review of the NOTAMS for the flight we failed to identify that the RNAV Z was unavailable because of the cranes being 3500ft MSL which is probably the biggest risk factor we had for this approach and would have led us to overfly the field and choose the RNAV Y approach which was the eventual solution to getting to the runway anyway.Overall I will be more mindful of my threats during approach briefings and of being more careful when reading NOTAMs for airports we are heading to. As a secondary measure; if the ATIS had the RNAV Z was unavailable on it due to cranes it may have also caused us to elect to overfly and use the RNAV Y.
