column121: During this flight I was the Captain and Pilot Monitoring. On final approach to runway XX at ZZZ the departing aircraft on the runway began their takeoff roll; momentarily stopped; then began rolling again.  Tower cancelled their takeoff clearance and directed us to go around. The First Officer (PF) had disconnected the autopilot in the descent at 1000ft AGL and was hand flying the aircraft during the approach and go around.  The FO immediately initiated a go around at 400ft AGL as directed. All initial go around procedures were executed and call outs made. The aircraft was established in a climb; gear up; flaps 3.The aircraft had established a very high rate of climb and we were on the way to the published missed approach altitude of 3000ft. At 1000ft MSL the PF moved the thrust levers to the Climb detent. Also; at 1000ft MSL tower switched us to departure frequency. Immediately upon establishing radio contact with departure they told us to maintain 2000ft. Given our very high rate of climb; both of us immediately focused on altitude awareness and the need to level at 2000ft. Both of us reached for the altitude set knob to put 2000ft in the window. Eventually; it was set; and 200kts was set in the speed window. The PF began to lower the nose and rate of climb in an attempt to catch 2000ft. At that time; we heard the flap overspeed warning. I immediately set the flaps to 2 and the PF manually reduced thrust and raised the nose to control the speed. The aircraft slowed below flap overspeed and the PF placed the thrust levers back in the Climb detent. Shortly after that we reached 2000ft; still in a climb. The PF pushed the nose over at 2200ft and began a descent to 2000ft. The aircraft began accelerating again towards a flap overspeed.  I raised the flaps to 1 and the PF once again manually reduced thrust.  Once level at 2000ft and safely below flap overspeed the thrust levers were again placed in the Climb detent; and the autopilot was engaged.The flap overspeed was approximately 5 knots; which was confirmed by maintenance during their inspection.Cause: The causal factors for this event were a combination of Human Error; Automation Management; and Task Saturation.  The initial go around procedures were executed in accordance with SOP; but the maneuver got away from both of us at 1000ft with the radio switch to departure.  The unexpected level-off clearance at 2000ft was the first distraction that took my attention away from aircraft configuration and speed monitoring. It had the same effect on the PF whose full attention went to altitude control.  The high rate of climb and proximity to the new level-off altitude became the primary concern of both of us. So much so that the PF reached for the altitude knob to make sure 2000ft was set in the window as quickly as possible.  There was a moment where we both were reaching for the altitude knob and had to establish whose responsibility it was to set it. This momentarily took us both away from the primary flight instruments at a critical time. The result was that we did not configure the aircraft to flaps to2 on cleanup schedule.This failure to continue to maintain the normal configuration schedule was a direct result of task saturation and monitoring error on my part.  I allowed my attention to be drawn to the altitude issue and away from monitoring the aircraft configuration and aircraft performance.  So; task saturation led to an error in monitoring.Additionally; the PF's decision to hand fly the entire go-around with no autopilot added significantly to the workload for both of us. Not engaging the auto pilot earlier in the maneuver required significant attention to be paid to basic flight control and added to the task saturation.The first recommendation I have is to utilize the autopilot as much as possible during a busy maneuver like a go around. That allows both crew members to focus on aircraft trajectory; performance; and configuration; rather than monitoring basic aircraft control.The other recommendation is for me as PM to establish crew duties immediately as soon as it gets busy like that.  As Captain and PM I should have told the PF; since he was hand flying; to concentrate solely on the primary flight instruments and let me listen to departure; set altitude/speed window parameters; and keep him informed of any necessary changes.  Had I focused his attention back to flying the aircraft immediately; he probably would have caught the overspeed before it happened. I also should have recommended that the autopilot be engaged early in the process.The lesson learned for me is that I need to ensure a very thorough brief on pilot duties and automation management during a go-around.  I also need to take a more involved approach during the maneuver to make sure that the PF is solely concentrating on flying the aircraft and controlling its trajectory; velocity; and configuration.

column121: During pushback I notified the push crew first to standby;" then when cleared by ramp I said "cleared to push tail north". I did not release the brake and I failed to say "brakes released."  An unusual sound was heard and I immediately realized that the brake was still set.  The push crew stopped the push and investigated for any damage - I informed him that the brake had not been released. They advised that tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. I released the brake and the push continued. About 50 yards into the push the crew stopped and had me set brakes. Something was not right with the tow bar and they had to swap it out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push.  Nearing the desired drop point; the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as I waited for the driver to advise me to "set brakes." Just then the tug and the aircraft began to roll forward and the driver said "Captain brakes brakes."  I immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes and stated "brakes set; cleared to disconnect inter phone."  I had assumed the aircraft was still being positioned by the tug driver; but perhaps we had been disconnected without brakes being set.  On taxiout we entered the hardstand. The FO researched tow bar pin shear (FOM requires inspection) as we both began to wonder if that may have occurred. Since we were off gate we contacted Dispatch and were patched through to Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control did great work to coordinate with ZZZ Maintenance and OPs to find out if there was a shear.  While we waited in the hardstand the FO and I decided it best to taxi back to gate and get the nose gear inspected just in case there was a pin shear. We taxied back to Gate XX; shutdown and entered an logbook entry.  There was notably good collaboration at the gate from our Maintenance team including the original ground crew providing their inputs so that the inspection could be done properly. With the inspection complete we departed without further issue.Cause: Causal was my failure to release the parking brake prior to authorizing the push.  My normal habit is to say "standby" after receiving the guide person's "all secure below" advisory; which I did.  But when I reviewed the ECAM just prior to clearing the pushback I only noted the NW STRG DISC memo and failed to note the Park Brake memo. And I didn't state "Brakes released" nor did I release the brakes. I am going to add a technique of pointing to the parking brake handle and then to the ECAM prior to stating "brakes released; cleared to push."  This was suggested by the FO who has seen other CAs using this technique.  And while I didn't feel rushed; I think making this process a slower and more deliberate execution will do me well in the future. I'm certain that the drop point rolling issue was part of this cascade from the non standard pushback. The guide person was very quick to catch the issue and call for brakes."
column123: We were given the brief from the pushback crew but had not completed our Before Start Checklist and had not received our pushback clearance from ramp.  The Captain told the push crew to standby."  Then once we were cleared by ramp to push he informed the ramp crew  "cleared to push tail north".  At that point the parking brake was still set. (Normal call "brakes released; cleared to push (tail north)").  When the ramp crew went to push we heard an unusual noise.  Then we realized that the parking brake had not been released. The Captain then notified the ramp crew to stop the push and investigate for any damage.  Additionally; he informed him that the parking brake had not been released. After the ramp crew investigated; they advised us that the tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. The captain released the brake and the push continued. After about 50 yards; the push the crew stopped and had us set brakes. They informed us that there was an issue with the tow bar and it needed to be swapped out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push. Nearing the desired drop point; the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as the captain waited for the driver to advise "set brakes." We then noticed the tug driving away and the aircraft appeared to be rolling forward.   Shortly after this the driver said "Captain brakes brakes."  The Captain immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes.  Then he notified them that the brakes were set and they were cleared to disconnect the interphone.  To us what had appeared to have happened was the aircraft was still being pulled by the tug driver; but other indications made us question what was happening.  I believe the tug driver was a little shaken from the previous events that had occurred but the error had been trapped and damage/injury was prevented..On taxiout; I researched the publications for tow bar issues and discovered we may have sheared a tow pin and needed an inspection.  We coordinated with ramp to hold in the hard stand and worked with Dispatch; Maintenance Control; ZZZ Ops; ZZZ maintenance; and ramp to setup an inspection.  We proceeded to a new gate for the inspection.  The Captain made an logbook entry and maintenance performed the inspection.  We then proceed with the flight with no further issues and as a crew talked about what had happened and ways to prevent such a miscommunication in the future.Cause: The cause of the event was a miscommunication between the Captain and the push crew.  He did inform them that we were cleared to push but never said that the brakes were released.   I can see why this was confusing for the push crew.  Depending on the situation; Captains sometimes release the parking brake immediately after the brief is received from the push crew but tells the push crew to standby for the push clearance.   Also I'm curious how often the push crews ensure the light is out prior to initiating the push.  If the push crew would have referenced the light this would have been trapped and no error would have occurred."

column121: Around ZZZZZ intersection on the ZZZZZ1 arrival we received an ECAM message HYD Y RSVR LO LVL. We did an assessment; followed by QRC; ECAM actions; QRH follow-ups; and the procedure. We advised ATC and requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) standing by on runway XXL. I notified dispatch of the situation and briefed the flight attendants for a precautionary landing. Lastly; I made a PA notifying the passengers of the precautionary landing that would be followed by an exterior inspection from safety vehicles. The subsequent approach and landing went uneventful. After landing ARFF inspected the aircraft and told us there was hydraulic fluid on the right landing gear. I decided to have ARFF follow us to the gate for safety and to avoid a possible similar situation as a recent incident. Before starting the taxi; I made another passenger announcement to reassure the passengers. After arriving at the gate; the fire marshal came in the flightdeck and updated us on the break temperatures. During deplaning I stood and greeted all the passengers as I do during most flights and I did not observe any distraught persons.Cause: I don't have any further recommendations. Our training worked great in this instance.
column123: On descent into ZZZ we had an ECAM indicating the yellow hydraulic system reservoir was low. I continued flying and the CA ran the ECAM. The fluid level was mostly empty and the ECAM had us turn off the yellow pump and PTU (Power Transfer Unit). Since we were down a hydraulic system we decided to advise ATC. Due to where we were; we also decided that ZZZ was still the best option to land. The CA informed the FAs and passengers. Out of caution we also requested XXL as it was a longer runway. Also; for safety we requested to stop on the runway and get inspected. On final approach; we turned on the yellow engine pump according to the ECAM procedure. The remaining fluid leaked out in less than a minute. The CA had me continue to fly and land the plane. Upon landing; we stopped on the runway. I talked with Fire and Rescue and they reported that our right main landing gear had some fluid on it and was smoking. I assumed it was caused by the hydraulic fluid on the brakes. Fire and Rescue reported the right brakes were showing hot. Our wheels page didn't show any high temperatures on the brakes. We took the airplane off the runway and began taxiing to the gate. During our taxi; Fire and Rescue reported our right brake temperatures were decreasing pretty steadily and there was no more evidence of any smoke coming from the main landing gear. We pulled into the gate with no more events.Cause: Training really kicked in and everything happened in a way both of us expected; as far as who did what and when. It really helped to keep the stress levels low. We did use a procedure to help with the precautionary landing and they also helped to make sure we didn't miss anything.

column121: After aircraft shut down and parking checklist accomplished; the FO and I had begun disembarking the aircraft.While the FO was exiting the aircraft during deplaning; and I stood with my bags at the flightdeck door; I heard 4 (or more) chimes which could be either the FAs calling the front or the ground crew.  I did not see any indication of a call from the FA's; and noticed the ground crew trying to get my attention on the right side of the aircraft.  The FO must have heard these chimes as well as he managed to make his way back to the flightdeck.I opened FO's side window to talk to ground crew from the flight deck.  After about 20 seconds I realized they were indicating a fire in the right engine.  Looking back toward the #2 engine there was no indication of any fire.  No smoke was noted and no flames were visible.  Routinely; the ground crew will see something and think it is a problem when in fact it is not.  The FO left to investigate from the ground.I saw the FO return to the right side of the aircraft where I was still located and he indicated there was a fire back there.  I still could see no visible smoke or fire from my viewpoint.  I queried if he thought fire trucks should be called.  The FO indicated that he believed it would be a good idea to call them out and assess the situation.I immediately grabbed the hand Mic (as all our belongings had been stowed and some were on the jetbridge) to call ground and ask them to send the trucks out due to a fire that the ground crew had told us about.  I also advised it was the #2 engine that was in question.  Ground asked a passing by jet if they saw any fire from our #2 engine.  The jet confirmed they did see some fire located at the 6 O'clock position of the back of the motor.With still zero visual evidence from the flightdeck of smoke or fire; I proceeded to call the Air Carrier X maintenance Control office to let them know of a possible fire and give them a heads up" of an upcoming Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) entry.  By this time; while on the phone with maintenance; my FO returned to show me a picture he had taken of the fire.  It was; in my opinion; not anything major; but had been now burning for approximately 10 minutes.  I described the fire to the mechanic through the phone as being between the exhaust nozzle and the rear blades.  The mechanic indicated he thought it was a "candle flame".  Right about the same time; I herd the FO say; "They're foaming the engine".  A quick glance out the window; and I could see foam flying by the FO's side window.  When I indicated this to the Mechanic he said that the action of foaming was a big problem and that I needed to find out what type was used for my AML entry. At this point we were nearly deplaned.  I did not make any special PA's to the passengers since most the people were already off and all remaining passengers were in the aisle with their bags in hand.  The two forward FA's were made aware of the situation by the FO.  The cleaning crew that had tried to come onto the aircraft were told; by me; to leave the aircraft.  I had contemplated making a PA but feared at our current point in the deplaning process; the PA could create some unnecessary panic and do more harm than good.  I allowed the deplaning to continue normally which took another couple of minutes.After the passengers were off; I got word from the FO; that the fire chief wanted the APU shut down.  All the passengers were off the aircraft at this time and the FA's were gathering their belongings for their layover.  We did not have any ground power attached; the APU was shut down as if it was the last flight of the day.The FO and I went down to the aircraft to talk with the firefighters.  We ended up talking to the firefighter that sprayed the aircraft.  He mentioned that he had never seen that type of fire and did attempt to spray it with water first; this did not yield the desired result.  I assume this to mean that the fire would not extinguishby water alone.  He then resorted to the foam and mentioned he also foamed the wing as an extra precaution.  When asked the type of foam used for my AML entry; he said it was the "latest and greatest F-3 foam".  Later he indicated the new foam being used was non-corrosive.Having the information we needed and the AML entry complete; the FO and I grabbed our already packed bags and proceeded to the hotel for our scheduled layover.  While walking up the jetbridge I contacted our assigned dispatch at Air Carrier X to make them aware of the aircraft state and that maintenance had been contacted.Cause: During the event a tailpipe fire never entered the conversation.  On our return flight we discussed about the potential being there and that neither of us had really witnessed a persistent tailpipe fire; if one exists.  Myself; I've flown for decades and a majority of that has been in jets.  Pictures of tailpipe fires and possible expansion of QRC to include all steps if this occurs well after engine shutdown."

column121: While near the end of the ZZZZZX arrival; RWY XX transition; we experienced two uncommanded roll events to the left while autopilot B was engaged. The aircraft was below 10;000' on the segment of the ZZZZZX before the slight left turn at ZZZZZ; on the straight-ahead sequence of fixes between ZZZZZ1 and ZZZZZ when both of these uncommanded roll events occurred. Neither event could be attributed to any change in aircraft configuration; input; or other factor that I can identify; both happened without any identifiable cause. Before the first uncommanded roll event; we were descending via the arrival in LNAV and VNAV with autopilot B engaged. Without warning or identifiable reason; the aircraft suddenly began rolling to the left. The autopilot initially stayed connected; and the autopilot system turned the yoke significantly to the right in an attempt to counter the roll. However; the autopilot was unable to stop the roll; the aircraft continued rolling; an amber 'ROLL AUTHORITY' displayed on the attitude indicator; and an aural alert sounded (this all happened very quickly--I cannot clearly remember what the aural alert was; since at that point I was already reaching for the disconnect to take recovery actions. My captain later said that he recalled it being a 'BANK ANGLE' aural alert). I called out 'my aircraft;' disconnected the autopilot; and applied right aileron and some right rudder to stop the roll and return the aircraft to level flight. Since the aircraft was notifying us that the autopilot's aileron authority alone was insufficient to keep control of the aircraft's bank angle ('ROLL AUTHORITY' annunciation); I determined that some amount of rudder was necessary to ensure we could overcome whatever unusual force was causing this uncommanded roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron alone. My inputs successfully stopped the roll; and I returned the aircraft to level flight and re-established the aircraft on the flight path. Feeling that the aircraft was now under control; my captain and I searched for any reason why that might have happened and couldn't identify anything. For that reason; we initially suspected wake turbulence. The captain asked ATC if we were following a heavy aircraft on the arrival; but ATC responded that we were following another 737 MAX. We did not think that a fellow MAX miles ahead would cause such an aggressive effect on our aircraft. Since the aircraft was stable and showing no further signs of control issues; we elected to re-engage autopilot B to monitor its response. Shortly thereafter; the same thing happened: an uncommanded continuous roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron input. I was already prepared to disconnect the autopilot quickly at the first sign of a recurrence; so I did so; applying the necessary inputs to stop the roll and re-stabilize the aircraft. In both instances of this uncommanded roll; it felt as if the autopilot had been commanding some sort of continuous control input that then released when I disengaged the autopilot; because the aircraft was responsive to my control inputs and recovered without difficulty after the autopilot was disengaged each time. Since the aircraft annunciated 'ROLL AUTHORITY' on the attitude indicator; indicating that 100% of the autopilot's roll authority was insufficient to control the aircraft's roll; I wondered if perhaps the aircraft had experienced an uncommanded rudder deflection that the autopilot was unable to overcome with ailerons; which then released when the autopilot was disconnected. However; that is just a possibility that crossed my mind; we could not identify any cause; nor did I feel any sort of yawing or rudder pedal movement prior to each event. After two uncommanded roll events in a row on autopilot B; we were convinced that we had a genuine problem with something in the autopilot system; as two events in a row like that did not seem like a wake turbulence encounter with anaircraft of the same type that was miles ahead. column121: Took off of XXL at ZZZ assigned a 080 heading. Right after takeoff; around 2500 feet; we recieved a L PITOT HEAT caution message on Engine Display 1. The captain flew the airplane while I ran the QRC and QRH. The QRH lead us to the source selector panel and changing the air data source to 2; which created a plethora of red Xs on the captain side Primary Flight Display (PFD). The plane briefly climbed through our assigned altitude of 10;000 feet at this point (reaching 10;400) so the captain disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the plane back down to 10;000 and stayed at 250 knots. I asked air traffic control for present heading and present altitude while we troubleshoot an issue. The captain handed me the airplane; transferred flight directors; and ran the QRH themself; leading to the same issue. The end of that checklist led us to the air data failure QRH which led us to the unreliable air speed QRH. It was at this point that we decided it would be best to return to the field. The captain notified dispatch; and then flew the airplane while I briefed the flight attendant on the brief items. We asked ATC for vectors back to ZZZ airport. In my recollection; ATC didn't tell us what runway to expect; so the CA directed me to load the RNAV for XXL in. I started working on setting up the approach and getting landing performance. As we received further vectors; ATC informed us that we can expect runway XXR; so I reloaded the correct approach. At this point; the captain handed me the aircraft while they double checked my work; double checked the unreliable airspeed QRH to make sure there were no signs of discrepancies; and I was given instructions to intercept the approach and a clearance for the visual approach to XXR. Instead of clicking approach mode; I accidentally clicked the speed mode button. This prompted the captain to take controls; disconnect the auto pilot; and hand fly the intercept. It initially looked like the captain was lining up for runway XXL; so I clarified with them; and we corrected to the correct runway; XXR. The captain kept a buffer above Vref as a precaution for unreliable air speed. Once we landed safely and got off the runway; I called operations to get us a gate. Once we were stopped with the parking brake set; the captain delivered a PA to the passengers. A taxi to the gate without issue and had maintenance meet us there.Cause: I believe the lightning strike that the aircraft suffered the day prior may have affected certain systems that led to this failure. However; I'm not certain.'Suggestion: I should've discussed with the captain about declaring an emergency; and taking a little bit more time up in the air to set up the aircraft properly and calmly before commencing the approach. I should've also flown the airplane the entire time while the captain managed the aircraft and the situation. Tunnel vision and adrenaline were running high in this situation and I failed to speak up and instead deferred to the captain for decision-making.
column123: Got a Left Caution Pitot message at 3;000 I had the First Officer run the QRC and the QRH while I continued the climb. We blew through 10;000; I corrected manually and notified ATC we needed present heading and 10;000 ft we needed to trouble shoot and that I was correcting back to 10;000. We ran the Left PITOT caution QRH again and it did the same thing;  I had coupled everything to the First Officer's side so it would knock the Auto Pilot off. We ran the next QRH for ADC failure which then lead us to the unreliable airspeed QRH. At this time I told the First Officer to notify the Flight attendants that we would be returning to the field for a small flight control issue and to remain seated no emergency. I told ATC I wanted Vectors back to ZZZ airport. We were not an emergency at this time but we were returning to field. We got vectors for the approach; we had XXL loaded got switched to XXR reloaded that as we were being vectored. We double checked the unreliable airspeed QRH and we didn't see any signs of unreliable airspeed with the pitch but I flew cross panel off the first officers side and the standby for reference and kept us 10 kts faster from VREF just to make sure I had a buffer. On intercept of course the First Officer accidentally hit my speed mode. This caused my side to black out and clear everything and I clicked off Autopilot and deselected both Flight Directors then hand flew the approach. The First Officer made sure we were lined up with the correct runway XXR since we never really intercepted the course so we corrected to XXR and landed safely. I delivered a PA once we exited the runway and were stopped to inform passengers we had a small flight control issue and needed to have Maintenance check it out and I would be getting a new aircraft to continue to our destination and to remain seated everything was fine.Cause: Electrical damage to systems from the lightening strike the night before.Suggestion: This plane was struck by lightening the night before; it needs to have all of its wiring replaced. I believe quite a few items got fried which lead to our situation.

This flight took place around XA:00 and was the second flight of the evening; the first went well with no issues. On the return trip around 20 minutes from ZZZ we decided to proceed to ZZZ2 and do a practice approach before continuing on to ZZZ. We decided on this course of action after verifying with the fuel gauge that we still had roughly 9 gallons of fuel (estimate of around 2.5 hours of flight). After completing an approach at ZZZ2 we then planned and flew directly towards ZZZ. However; on the flight at about 10 nm from ZZZ at 8000 Msl we experienced engine failure. Over the course of less then a minute our engine became very rough and had a large drop in RPM; we increased throttle and had no change; and then the engine fully died. We verified that the gauge still read 4 gallons of fuel; the battery still had 13.1v but the oil pressure read 0. The PIC for this flight contacted ATC and landed in a field close to ZZZ when it became clear we would not make it to the runway. After landing we verified that we were both unharmed and then contacted emergency services. The main factors that contributed to these events were unfamiliarity with the plane and over reliance on fuel gauges rather than our planning. Both the PIC and I had flown this plane before but neither of us were 'experienced' in it and while we had both read the POH neither of us were knowledgeable in it. Additionally; we should have trusted the flight plan and calculated fuel burn and trusted it rather then our instruments mid flight. What can be done in the future is ensure that pre flight planning is the number one source of planning information and that it is stuck to unless forced to change.

column121: I was piloting a hot air balloon on a passenger flight. We launched from a field just west of ZZZ; and our flight path took us approximately 8 miles to the northwest.I was flying a Cameron Z105 with passengers.Weather was clear with visibility greater than 10 miles. Surface winds were 7 mph at launch and approximately 6 mph at landing; both from the southeast.The takeoff and flight were uneventful. I approached a large open grass field (approximately 7 acres) to land near the driveway leading from the road to the house. I was approximately 5 to 10 feet above ground level; moving about 6 mph toward the driveway. The passengers and I scanned the area for power lines and poles but did not see any in the field. We did see and discuss the power lines along the road; and we agreed the area between us and the driveway was clear.As we approached the driveway; a passenger and I noticed two single-strand power lines running from the road on our left to another pole north of the house. The lines were about 80 feet in front of us.  This occurred at about XA:40 PM; sunset was XB:43 PM.  Factors affecting the visibility of the power lines would have been background clutter with the background field and trees.   The balloon chase crew was also turning onto the driveway at the same time and called out the power lines over the radio.  This occurred just seconds after the pilot and passenger noticed the power lines.  I immediately opened the parachute valve to put the basket on the ground short of the power lines and allow the balloon envelope to lay over the lines. This is considered a 'rip out' situation as described in the flight manual and the FAA Balloon Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-11B). This is the safest maneuver to perform when contact with power lines is inevitable. If not performed; the basket could have contacted the power lines and injuries; or further damage could have occurred.There were three electrical arcs with two power lines. On the third arc; the fuse on the street power pole opened. The basket came to rest on its side; and all occupants were uninjured. We were able to exit the basket on our own. The balloon remained draped over the power line. There were no injuries to the pilot or passengers.A power company removed the balloon envelope.  The power was restored to one residential property.   The balloon and equipment were packed and transported to our storage facility. The next morning; I inspected the aircraft.  Four panels within the first 10 feet of nylon fabric had burns and holes. No load tapes or structural members of the aircraft were damaged. Per the Continued Airworthiness Manual; the holes were not required to be repaired because they were below the first 10 feet of nylon fabric.I plan to develop a near-miss presentation to share with fellow pilots and balloon crew members.The envelope has been repaired by an authorized repairman and returned to service.   The event arose from late identification of two single-strand power lines along the intended landing path. The balloon was already very low and moving toward the driveway when the lines were recognized; leaving limited time and distance to fully avoid contact.Contributing factors-	Low-visibility hazard: The wires were single-strand and therefore harder to see.-	Background clutter: Trees and the field behind the wires reduced contrast/visibility.-	Operating environment: Landing near a road/driveway/house increases the likelihood of utility spans and service runs that are not as obvious as roadside distribution lines.-	Expectation/attention: Attention was drawn to and discussion occurred about the roadside power lines; reinforcing the assessment that the area between the balloon and driveway was clear.-	Time/distance constraints: Wires were detected at close range (~80 ft) during a low-altitude; high-workload phase of flight.The wires were discovered visually on short final when the pilot and a passenger noticed two single-strand lines spanning from the road to a pole north of the house; approximately 80 feet ahead. The chase crew also called out the lines over the road seconds later as they turned onto the driveway.Corrective actions-	Immediate operational action: Pilot opened the parachute valve to execute a stop-short landing ('rip out' procedure) intended to keep the basket short of the lines and reduce occupant risk.-	Utility coordination: Local power company responded; removed the envelope from the lines; and restored power to one residential property.-	Recovery and inspection: With permission; balloon and equipment were packed and transported to storage.-	Maintenance disposition: Damage assessed; envelope repaired by an authorized repairman and returned.-	Lessons learned dissemination: Plan to develop a near-miss presentation for pilots and crew members.Human performance considerations-	High-workload phase: Approach and landing require continuous control decisions while scanning for obstacles; time available to detect/confirm thin hazards can be limited.-	Attention management: Visual attention may narrow toward the touchdown zone; making small; low-contrast hazards (single-strand wires) easier to miss until close.-	Team scanning and shared assumptions: Having passengers assist with scanning can increase coverage; but agreement that the area was clear can also reduce continued challenge/verification.-	Lighting/angle considerations: Late-day conditions and low sun angle can reduce contrast and increase glare risk (sun angle noted in the report).

column121: The push began normally after receiving clearance from the ramp controller. Once we appeared to be in the correct position for disconnection with both engines started; we sat for what seemed like an unusual time without communication from the ground crew. The captain eventually inquired if they were ready for him to set the brake; and they said 'please set brake.' Before the captain set the brake; we felt the plane shudder as if it was being dropped from the tow tractor and it started rolling forward. At this point the ground crew said 'set brake; set brake; set brake!'. The captain brought the aircraft to a stop and set the parking brake. At no point did the captain verbalize to the crew 'parking brake set; pressure normal' which would have indicated that it was safe to disconnect. We also did not receive the 'breakaway' command that would have indicated a problem with the tug. Following the event; the ground crewmember did advise us that they were having trouble with the tow tractor; though it's unclear whether they disconnected the tug without clearance; or the tug had a mechanical failure such that it was still attached to the aircraft and the aircraft was able to push it under idle thrust.Following the disconnect; we taxied to the assigned spot. I called operations on the radio to ask for the final weights; as the taxi would be short and the response to the message was that the ramp had not completed their document. The operations person advised us to the return to the gate so that the dangerous goods on board could be re-secured. We did as requested. During the second pushback; we received clearance from ramp and the captain gave push clearance to the ground personnel. We sat for several minutes without moving; at which point the captain queried the push crew. They stated that they were having issues with the tow tractor; and that a supervisor was coming to assist with a reset. We cancelled the push clearance; and the captain advised them of this. The problem was eventually fixed; and we pushed. I did notice that the crew used nonstandard phraseology when communicating with the captain.

column121: The incident involving Aircraft X arriving from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was extremely concerning from a safety standpoint and presented the potential for a severe accident involving both personnel and aircraft movement.As the Ramp Lead; I observed that the jetbridge had been positioned improperly by the jetbridge operator. The jetbridge was raised to an excessively high level; which caused the cage holding the ground air hose at the gate to become lifted off the ground and stuck. This created an unsafe condition because when the cage becomes jammed; movement of the jetbridge can force sudden or uncontrolled motion; increasing the risk of damage to equipment; the aircraft; and nearby personnel.Due to this hazard; I immediately gave the pilot the X signal to stop; and one of my agents positioned on the number 1 engine side also reinforced the stop command. The pilot did initially stop. I then turned my attention to assisting the jetbridge operator in correcting the hazardous condition so the area could be made safe.While I was actively addressing the issue; the pilot began taxiing the aircraft into the gate on his own without receiving clearance to continue from me as the Ramp Lead. This was done after a clear stop command had already been given. I was still on the taxi line and was not aware the aircraft had started moving again. At the same time; the jetbridge was still involved in correcting the original hazard. This created an extremely dangerous situation in which I was placed directly at risk by an advancing aircraft.Once I realized the aircraft was moving; I immediately began giving repeated stop commands to the pilot multiple times. My agent also gave stop commands. Despite these repeated signals; the pilot continued to taxi forward until the aircraft came dangerously close to me; forcing me to move out of the way to avoid possible serious injury. The pilot then pointed at me in an aggressive manner; appearing to indicate the self-park system as justification for continuing into the gate.This is deeply concerning because a direct stop command from the Ramp Lead was ignored multiple times during an active safety hazard. The pilot's decision to continue taxiing without clearance; while personnel were still exposed in the movement area and while gate equipment was not yet in a safe condition; created an unacceptable risk of severe injury or fatality. This incident reflects a serious breakdown in communication; situational awareness; and compliance with ramp safety procedures; and it should be treated as a major safety event.

column121: The flight began as normal and uneventful. Both engine starts along with taxi for takeoff were all normal with no abnormal indications. During the takeoff roll we didn't notice or feel any abnormalities beside the runway being very rough and bumpy (which is normal for ZZZ). After rotation and during climb out I noticed that I could feel a slight vibration from the airplane engine and looked at the VIB indicator and notice it was sitting around 3.9. We initially followed immediate action items (non involved); then I called for the QRC; then captain assigned me to continue PF duties while he conducted the QRH. While we ran the checklist I asked ATC to level off at 12;000 feet and stay there while we were troubleshooting. Once I brought the thrust levers back to a normal 250kt cruise speed the engine vibs returned to a normal green range; we continued with the checklist and it directed us to continue with the flight while monitoring the engine vibes. We both agreed that declaring an emergency didn't seem appropriate since the engine was operating normally at lower thrust settings. We communicated with dispatch and came to the agreement to return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight we asked ATC for 'speed our discretion'. We flew back to ZZZ without any other abnormalities. During the landing we didn't feel anything abnormal and even during the taxi to the gate. When we arrived at the gate XX we heard a ramp truck report to ramp control that the aircraft he was looking at had a blown tire. We asked ramp to confirm if it was our aircraft he was talking about; and he confirmed it. During the walk around I saw that the inboard left main tire had blown; I also noticed dents and tire marks on the underside of the wing and flap. The engine showed indications that tire debris had entered the engine. We then notified ground control of potential FOD on runway XXL and XXR.Would have been helpful if someone had noticed our tire blow out during departure. We had no indications that a tire had blown.
column123: Tail swapped into Aircraft X for unknown reason. Push back; engine starts; taxi all normal. During takeoff we assumed runway was poorly textured. After we decided to return to field; dispatch also got in contact with Mx (Maintenance) who agreed that we should return. We determined that we could safely contain the vibration in CRZ setting and deemed that declaring an emergency was not necessary; however had priority to the field. I communicated with FAs; dispatch; then made a PA to the passengers telling them that due to the 'loud vibrational noises from Aircraft left; we would be returning to ZZZ out of precaution'. Completed the rest of the flight as routine standard; landed safely; coordinated gates and specials with operations. We fully taxied to the gate before a ground person told ramp that our left main inboard tire was completely blown and it was communicated to us. We deplaned; contacted maintenance; dispatch coordinators; scheduling; and the chiefs. This resulted in 3 write ups from us directly. We did notify ATC about the tire issue for possible FOD on the runway (either on takeoff or landing); ground called us back to say yes; FOD was found on XXR.Would have been nice to know we had tire damage before parking; but it seems like nobody was around to see it and we didn't believe to have had any indications stating otherwise.

column121: Flight purpose was to regain proficiency after not flying for several months. Checked fuel quantity using sight gauges and found 2 gallons in the right tank and 5 gallons in the left tank. I expected to use about 4 gallons during the flight. Other aircraft were parked at the fuel pump; so I decided to fill up after the flight.After some airwork and practice landings at another airfield; I headed home. As I was initiating the descent from 3000 MSL (about 2000 AGL); I got a fuel pressure warning from the Dynon system. The fuel pressure indication was fluctuating widely. I decided to stay at my present altitude until within easy gliding distance of my home airport. Roughly a minute later; the Dynon system gave me an engine speed warning and the engine stopped.I glanced at the glide ring on the Dynon system and my home airport was right on the edge. Knowing that the glide ring was based on conservative glide data; I was tempted to continue to my home airport. Then I thought about the reason that I had used conservative glide data (because I might encounter sinking air) and decided that a farm field nearby was a better option. After an uneventful landing in the field; I contacted a neighbor and had him bring fuel to the field. We added five gallons to each tank and I made an uneventful flight home.After getting home; I reviewed the POH. It states that the pilot should alternate between the left and right tank. I had been in the habit of setting both fuel valves to open assuming that; if one tank became empty; fuel would flow from the other one. The POH stated that is not guaranteed with both valves open. In the future; I will follow the POH recommended practice for setting the fuel valves.

column121: This incident happened on Day 0; XA:15. It was a cloudy day with a very low 300ft ceiling. I arrived at my friend's house at around XA:10; and I decided to take my drone out while I was waiting. I have altered the maximum distance to around 500m(1640ft) horizontally; and did not change the maximum altitude at 120m(400ft) before handing it to him. I saw he started the motor without any problem; and started climbing; clearing nearby objects. I turned around and went inside my friend's house to use his restroom.After 5 or 6 minutes; when I went out; I saw the drone was descending below the cloud. After he returned the drone to me; I found it was slightly wet on the hull. I checked the drone; and I found the altitude limit was lifted to the max at 800m(2625ft); and the flight log indicated a 798m(2618ft) maximum flight altitude and probably busted B airspace at my location; which was where I realized it is a clear violation for both losing VLOS and busting altitude.I do understand the risks of flying UAS above 400ft; especially into B airspace; and now I also know the risk of putting drones into the hands of someone you do not know. I truly regret letting an unfamiliar person operate my drone; and the lack of continuous supervision. In the future; I will not allow others to operate the aircraft without direct supervision and will never let incidents like this happen again.

column121: I took the radar handoff on Aircraft X from ZZZ1 [ARTCC] at 090. I was working other traffic waiting for that aircraft to check in when I noticed him descending. With no answer or correction I then asked am aircraft to relay the low altitude alert. I turned off my Low Sector XX transmitter to allow for that while working my Low/Hi Sector XY  traffic. I removed the strip and continued my session.ZZZ arrivals are a weak point in the sector. The ZZZ1 RCAG could potentially be moved to ZZZ to allow for better communications with these aircraft with I believe minimal impact on the sector. column121: I was working a combined feeder and satellite sector for ZZZ.  VA (Visual Approach) RWY XXL/ ILS RWY XXR was in use.  With almost no notice we lost the use of RWY XXR because of a tall vessel in the RWY XXR approach area at approx XA:00z.  This forced all AC to use RWY XXL.  I was vectoring all of the ZZZZZ arrivals to blend flows with the other feeder sectors; working arrivals into a satellite and working overflight AC.  This is not uncommon; but it does create a heavier workload.  Once RWY XXR reopened there was a bit of a scramble to reassign AC to the appropriate runways.  I had a lot of things to do and I had released an IFR from ZZZ1 Aircraft X.  I am not trying to assign any blame; but things were busy and the situation was just bad in general and a lot was happening. At approx XA:35Z Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z had a Conflict Alert (CA) in the final box.  Same altitude and closing; and I was honestly kind of in shock.  They were same altitude and the targets were nearly merged.  It was extremely distracting to say the least.  Aircraft X had departed ZZZ1 and was nearing the edge of the class D. He never checked in; so I had to call ZZZ1 to have them switch him.  I got him; radar ID'd him and put him on a heading away from the final box.  I couldn't climb him yet; so I assigned a 270 and went on to the next task.  Aircraft A was seeking flight following to ZZZ2 and was nearby so I gave him info about pattern traffic and changed his frequency.  He never read this back; then called me after to change his destination.  I was having an issue with his data tag and he them went to a vfr tag on his own.  He was leaving my airspace so I quickly assigned him a tag to try and get a handoff to ZZZ3.  At the same time Aircraft B was looking for flight following and for some reason his tag had been terminated.  I had basically 4 things going on in different corners of my airspace.  I couldn't get Aircraft B  to tag up because of a STARS flaw.  Aircraft A was pulling my attention away and messing with his transponder; and I was trying to sequence AC in a complicated RWY config.  Aircraft X called my to ask for higher about 10 miles into ZZZ4 airspace.  He was at 2000 in a 3000 foot MVA for approximately 5 miles.  I immediately coordinated with ZZZ4 and turned him back into my airspace.  I then climbed him and transferred him to the appropriate sector.Recommendation: This was honestly such a tense moment; and a high workload that you can pick your poison.  The supervisors were helping coordinate; but stupid things were drastically making my life harder.  Sequencing in these instances is typically the priority; but having to call a tower to talk to the IFR they just departed; 2 separate automation issues; and an honestly terrifying proximity of 2 AC made for the right blend of distractions.  The action was not on the left side of the scope; and I let an IFR get away from me to fix radar tags on 2 VFR AC and sequence jets to ZZZ.  I guess it was the straw that broke the camels back.  I think the biggest problem is that we get these tall ships in the harbor and they throw the operation into disarray.  There was no notice except; hey this is the last AC to XXR; make it work.

column121: We departed the gate and had a quick taxi to XXL @ Taxiway 1.  The takeoff was a normal with a strong crosswind from the south.  After takeoff (Approx. 1000ft) an ECAM appeared.  HYD Y RSVR LO LVL followed by I believe a PTU (Power Transfer Unit) Fault and a low pressure.  We told departure that we needed to stop the climb and take care of an issue.  At this time we had not declared an emergency.  We leveled at 5000ft; maintained 220 kts; on a heading of 270; and the autopilot was ON. The ECAM was announce and we decided that I would continue flying and the PM would run the ECAM.    The PM went through the items instructed by the ECAM.  I was flying and working the radios; but I believe the PTU was turned off and possibly the yellow engine pump.  After the ECAM was completed and the screens were normal; the PM contacted dispatch via ACARS and was given a frequency so that we could have verbal communication.  According to the PM communication was difficult due to poor reception.  After we discussed the situation; we decided that returning to ZZZ was the best option.  We discussed requesting priority handling and decide to do so because of the spoilers 2 and 4 being inop.  After our plans were settled I requested priority handling and notified ATC of our intentions; souls; and fuel on board.  ATC began vectoring us for an ILS to XYC.  The PM informed the FA of the situation and gave them a briefing.  Dispatch sent us landing distance numbers approx; 8900 feet which was well within the 10800 feet for XYC.  The PM ran through the Overweight Landing Checklist.  I configured early and dropped the gear early to burn more fuel to reduce the overweight landing issue; and the flaps would be moving slower than normal.  The autopilot came off at about 1000 feet.  The flight controls felt spongier than normal but not so much that aircraft was difficult to control.  The strong crosswind remained present.  I would consider the touchdown to be smooth. The Capt took the controls at 80 knots and taxied off the runway at Taxiway 2 and held on taxiway 3 short of 4.  Emergency vehicles were behind us.  We went to frequency XXX.XX where ground and emergency services were accessible.  Emergency service circled the aircraft and found no evidence of damage or fire.  The brakes topped out at 505C on the number 1 caliper.  The other were 380 to 425.  We discussed our ability to taxi in but were hesitant due to the brake temp and we had been made aware that a fluid was now leaking from the belly of the aircraft.  A tug arrived and we decided out of an abundance of caution that we would be towed in.  This took a while.  Mx (Maintenance) arrived and asked for the gear pins.  We had trouble locating the gear pins. They asked if the aircraft taxied fine. We stated yes and since the brakes had cooled significantly; we decided to taxi it back to the gate.  The aircraft was choked at the gate and the maintenance requests were sent in.
column123: Departing ZZZ on our third flight to ZZZ1; climbing out of 1000 feet we had yellow hydraulic reservoir low ECAM. Additional messages came up with that failure. I was the pilot monitoring; and I informed ATC that we needed too level off at 5000 feet to work a problem. I asked the FO if he was comfortable flying and working  the radios so I could run the checklist; and he was. He turned on the autopilot and continue to fly and work the radios. We ran through the procedure together; verifying everything was done correctly. At that point I tried a call me message for a frequency with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since we were at 5000 feet; we had a hard time hearing dispatch and I've ended up telling them our plan was to return to ZZZ; the dispatcher was phenomenal and getting us landing data and information we needed for landing.  We advised ATC. We set up for a return to ZZZ and briefed the plan. I then called the flight attendants and advised them of the situation as well as notified the passengers. We were aware of the possibility of an overweight landing and had a discussion on burning the fuel or just going into land. We elected to land as we were down one hydraulic system. The landing was incredibly smooth and uneventful. Being that we were overweight and heavy; we had the fire trucks meet the airplane as a precautionary measure. Once off the runway; the fire trucks notified us that we did have hydraulic fluid leaking out of the belly; it was described as a slow drip. I communicated with dispatch and Maintenance Control on the ground for the safest course of action with hot brakes. I'm not sure who; but somebody sent us a tug so we thought we would use the tug to get back to the gate. Unfortunately; in the midst of the chaos; I could not find the gear pins in the flight deck as that back closet was dark and the gear pin holder was a dark color. This is no way in excuse that I could not find them; just telling you the real time situation as I was trying to communicate with everybody and find gear pins for the tug in. At this point; the brakes had cooled down enough that we discussed with maintenance and they thought it would be better if we could just taxi in so that's what we elected to do. (once maintenance arrived at the airplane. We did shut the engines down in preparation for being towed in). We started the engines back up and order a taxi back to the gate uneventfully. We coordinated with operations to chock us ASAP as the checklist says that the brake accumulator may not hold the aircraft in position. Maintenance personnel met us at the gate where we continued the discussion of what happened.

column121: Abnormal Aileron Control Feel. During preflight; the First Officer and I reviewed the logbook and noted a previously closed write-up stating: 'Noticed excessive yoke movement up to 2 units without aileron response.' The write-up was discussed during the departure brief. Control checks after start were normal. During departure from ZZZ; during departure while hand flying in moderate turbulence; the First Officer noticed an abnormal aileron control feel. During right aileron input; resistance was sometimes normal; sometimes significantly lighter than normal; and at times initially normal before abruptly becoming very light. Left aileron inputs were initially normal. The First Officer advised me of the condition and elected to continue hand flying while we discussed what he was experiencing. I subsequently hand flew the aircraft and immediately experienced the same abnormal and inconsistent aileron control feel the First Officer had described.Throughout this period; the aircraft responded appropriately to all control wheel inputs. However; the feel or resistance of the ailerons was highly variable; at times heavier than normal; at times lighter; and occasionally transitioning from heavy to very light during a single control input. We elected not to use the autopilot and to continue the climb to FL300 (planned FL370) to evaluate the condition; and coordinate with Dispatch and Maintenance before making further decisions and determining the safest course of action. There is no published QRH procedure that directly addressed the abnormal aileron control feel. The Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls QRH was reviewed as the closest reference; although it did not precisely match the condition observed. In accordance with our plan strategy; I transferred aircraft control and radios to the First Officer; who is very experienced and had a good feel for the aircraft. I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control via Crew Phone. Maintenance Control stated they were not aware of known issues with the aileron system that would produce the symptoms described and advised that the aileron system does not share characteristics with elevator systems that typically experience bearing-related feel issues. No additional guidance was provided. The abnormal aileron feel persisted; remaining variable.After further discussion; and considering the current condition in combination with the recent prior closed aileron write-up; we determined that although the aircraft remained controllable; we could not ensure an adequate margin of safety to continue to destination; nor could we be confident the condition would not worsen. We notified ATC and elected to divert to ZZZ1 which was previously coordinated with Dispatch. ZZZ1 was chosen to allow sufficient fuel burn to reach landing weight with minimal maneuvering; favorable weather; long runways; and crew familiarity. We started the APU; and initially remained at FL300/275 KIAS and did not change airspeed. To continue assessing controllability while burning fuel; we later descended to FL260 and further slowed to 250 KIAS to stay in smooth air and then later descended slowly to 16;000. Airspeed changes were then made in 5 knot increments; closely monitoring control feel with each change. The abnormal aileron feel remained variable throughout all speeds. We extended the landing gear and began configuring early to assist with fuel burn and continue evaluating controlabillity. As a precaution; we elected to limit bank angle to 15 degrees and elected to land Flaps 15 to maintain higher approach speed and roll margin. The aircraft was hand flown for the remainder of the flight; as we were unsure how the autopilot might respond given the abnormal aileron control feel.Below 10;000 feet; continuous light turbulence required frequent control inputs. The aileron feel remained abnormal and variable; however; aircraft control remained effective. The Non Routine Landing Considerations QRH was completed. We requested theILS Runway XXC at ZZZ1 and requested ARFF to observe the aircraft after landing. Descent and before landing checklists were completed; with continuous updates provided to the flight attendants and passengers. The landing was normal. We remained on the runway for a post landing Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) inspection; no abnormalities were observed. ARFF accompanied us during a normal taxi to the gate. The shutdown was normal. Passengers were reaccommodated onto another aircraft. After completion of the flight; both pilots discussed that we did not feel fit to continue flying. The ZZZ1 Chief Pilot assisted in removing us from further duty.  Threat and Error Management (TEM) was used throughout the event; including the decisions to notify ATC; divert to ZZZ1; restrict bank angle; slow and configure gradually; and land Flaps 15 to preserve controllability and safety margin.Cause: The following day I noticed a maintenance write up for this aircraft that air was suspected in the hydraulic lines. That would be a condition I believe would be consistent with what was felt on the controls.  However; that was not something considered during the flight as our attention was more about safe recovery of the aircraft.

column121: The First Officer was flying a normal approach to Runway XXR. As the aircraft settled on to the runway; FO said that the braking felt a little weird and that the aircraft was not decelerating correctly. FO disconnected the AUTOBRAKES via brake pressure; and I said let's go to the next high speed [exit taxiway] 1 because I did not want to try and stress the brake system more. I took control of the aircraft and finished the rollout to 1; made a left turn and the aircraft brakes appeared to be grabbing; and letting go. I then made another left on to taxiway 2 and began taxing EAST on 2. I slowed for a second to gain a better understanding of what was going on. FO asked if I wanted him to tell ATC that we were having brake problems; I asked him to hold off until we got EAST of the next turn off taxiway 3 going eastbound because that was a NORMAL turn off and I wanted to get EAST of it before the next aircraft landed. After I past [taxiway] 3; we called ATC and told them we may need to taxi slowly because of brake problems. As the ground speed dropped below ANTISKID engagement speed; 27 MPH; the aircraft began to roll normally. NO more wobble; no more grabbing; so we continued.The tower asked if wanted different taxi routing because of the brake problem. I told them NO; I then explained to FO that I did want to heat the brakes up any longer on the longer route. I then said; FO; I'm not sure what is going on so we will leave both engines running for idle speed; control and avoid braking.ATC immediately cleared us across RWY XXL so we didn't have to stop; then taxied to 4; 5 and ramp on the bridge. I asked FO to input an ELB (Electronic Log Book) for the anomaly and he did. As I turned on 5; FO then got a clearance for parking via 5; 6 to the alley for gate X. I asked FO to contact maintenance because we need to have a discussion with them and because it was an international flight; I needed them to catch us before we went on to customs. On initial contact with Maintenance; they informed us we had a wheel FIRE; we notified RAMP to dispatch ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to our location. FO asked if I wanted to evacuate and I said no we simply did not have enough information to that. I stopped the aircraft and made an announcement to the passengers and crew and told them we were not on the gate yet; and Fire rescue will be inspecting the rear tires. After a few minutes; I engaged with MX (Maintenance) Control and Ramp to find out where the ARFF was on the field and an ETA. Numerous employees gathered and took pictures from afar; but no one could tell me if it was getting worse. I made another announcement to the pax reassuring them that we were safe and the ARFF would be pulling up shortly.  Each announcement had to be translated for our passengers by the flight attendants. I made announcements every 5-7 minutes.ARFF arrived and got on the RAMP frequency; asked us to shut down the RIGHT engine; so they could inspect the right wheels; we complied. The Left  Engine was still running; the APU was running. FO asked about shutting down the LEFT engine; we did; and now the packs were running off the APU bleed air. We spoke with ARFF on ramp frequency for a minute and no one said an ACTIVE FIRE was present. As we sat there for about 5 minutes; no communication with ARFF; they elected to spray fire retardant on the brakes; 1st the RIGHT SIDE; then the LEFT side brakes. This forced Smoke and fumes into the cabin because the retardant struck the hot brakes; formed a smoke and the South wind blew it right into the PACK INTAKE system. As soon as it happened I reached up and turned off the packs; and made an announcement to the passengers and crew to remain seated. I later found out the Flight Attendants were getting ready to evacuate until they heard my announcement. This whole sequence of events took less than 20 seconds.I called MX on radio one and notified them I was no longer communicating with ARFF and that they just created a problem with smoke in the cabin. Poor communications between ARFF and the crew.Then ARFF told me to taxi into the gate; I told FO to tell them MX would be towing us; both engines were shut off. After a few minutes; I elected to turn the PACKS back on; made an announcement and asked the passengers to be patient.Numerous vehicles airport ops; MX; baggage handlers; police; etc.; were around the aircraft; but NO ONE was telling me about an active fire. Then MX showed up and requested that I through down the gear pins. RIght then I knew we were NOT on fire; and MX was going to set the gear pins for pull in to the gate. Again; no verbal confirmation from anyone.Ground personnel finally showed up; some frequency communication problems with them; then they pulled us into the gate about :40 total time from the fire notification by MX (Camera - not sure how they knew) and in at the gate. The passenger deplaned; I contacted MX again and requested a face-to-face with someone so I could give them a quick debrief. Someone came up; took my statement. I was informed right then… for the 1st time by the MX guy that we DID NOT HAVE a fire; only the hub cap melted. Good thing we didn't evacuate on just a report of a fire and not confirmation. I wanted to go down to the ramp but Customs had not released the aircraft yet. FO and I proceeded to customs; cleared customs got on the bus and called the Chief Pilot from the employee parking lot.

This led to some confusion on the flight deck. I verified with the controller what he meant; and he clarified that he wanted us at SAMPA at 6;000 feet. We rectified the situation; though the phrasing was non-standard.Before reaching LOMEN; ATC cleared us for the ILS 10L approach. At this point; we were slightly higher than the glideslope; and I noticed that the FO had not armed approach mode on the Mode Control Panel (MCP). I informed him that we were cleared for the approach and prompted him to arm the Approach button.By the time this was completed; he became preoccupied with the high altitude; he selected FLCH and dialed 3;000 feet in the MCP altitude window. Before I could warn him; he disconnected the autopilot and decided to follow the flight director (FD); which was providing incorrect guidance at that moment.Consequently; we received a GPWS 'GLIDESLOPE' alert. I told him; 'You need to go up; you need to capture that glideslope;' as I noticed he was below the slope and continuing to pitch the nose down.We were stabilized by 800 feet RA and completed the landing checklist. The weather was VMC; the field was in sight; and the glideslope was captured. Despite the instability prior to the 1;000-foot AGL stable approach gate; I decided not to call for a go-around; as I felt it would have caused further confusion in the cockpit. We landed without further issues and discussed the event during the van ride.Cause: One of the contributing factors to this event was the fatigue. Even though we all felt fine at the beginning of the flight; with rolling delays for a couple days; ever changing departure times and multiple long delay made things a bit harder on us.Suggestions: We were delayed due to aircraft maintenance; which caused rolling delays. I woke up on my own for the early departure; but there was no wake-up call.When I called dispatch; they told me they were having customs issues. Nobody updated the departure time until we were on the plane. Once we boarded; there was no ground crew available to load the aircraft; which caused further delays. Eventually; we were delayed by almost four hours; which contributed to our fatigue.

column121: Enroute to ABQ I had the Colter4 arrival loaded and the RNAV (RNP) 26 approach loaded into the FMS. ABQ ATIS was calling winds 260/08 and RNAV 26 in use.  We checked in with ZABQ and were not given any other information other than got you check in".  Several other aircraft checked in with ZABQ and then center stared letting people know "Whites Sand is testing GPS and ADS-B jamming." As we started setting up for the arrival and RNAV I noted we had high accuracy on the prog page; however we had zero satellites and no GPS signal.   We asked ZABQ how people are doing the RNAV app road into ABQ with no GPS and he said to do the RNAV visual.  We said we're not doing a night visual around mountains.  We asked for an early switch to ABQ approach to see what other people are doing.  Switching to ABQ approach two aircraft were in the same predicament we were in.  One aircraft elected to do the ILS runway 8.  They noted a 30kt tailwind until 300 feet AGL then a 5 kt tailwind at touch down.  At this point we only had about 7;000 of fuel and no listed divert.  The second aircraft did the same ILS 8 approach and reported them same.  I elected to do the same. We briefed the approach and I briefed the FO.  We flew the approach as advertised at 300 get the tail wind died off.  This caused our indicated airspeed to jump about 10kts at 300 for a brief moment the. Quickly captured back to on speed.  Landed and taxi in was uneventful.Cause: WSMR (White Sands Missile Range) regularly conducts jamming.  If this is known ahead of time we should add fuel and an alternate for a situation where the only approach to the runway in GPS.  Center and approach control need to communicate better to each other and aircraft inbound.  Center seemed to not think this was a big deal; approach was overworked with four inbound aircraft all unable to shoot the approach do to jamming; weather and all other runways beside 08/26 being closed."
column123: Immediately prior to top of descent into ABQ as we were setting up the cockpit for the RNAV (RNP) Z Rwy 26 approach we discovered that that our GPS was being jammed and operating in a greatly reduced capacity only receiving between 3-5 satellites at any given time with an operating mode of AIDED instead of NAV. This completely precluded us from preforming the approach to runway 26 which was the only runway open at the time with winds being reported as 270/8 kts and winds aloft being out of the west at approximately 30 knots until 300 feet above the ground. This put added pressure into preforming a tailwind approach in challenging conditions at night using the only available approach. As we crossed the mountains just east of the airfield I observed GPS 1 receiving only a single satellite and GPS 2 receiving no satellites. Multiple aircraft were adversely affected by this GPS jamming at and around our arrival time. This is a major safety of flight issue in ABQ when the winds are out of the west as this completely inhibits us from using any approach to runways 26 or 21. If the winds would have been above our max tailwind component we would not have been able to legally land anywhere as we were not filed with an alternate and did not have the fuel to make any airport without dipping significantly into our fuel reserves. We assessed after the fact that the closest company airport to us would have been ZZZ and at 200 miles away would have used up a significant portion of our remaining fuel. In my estimation if we would have had to divert there we would have arrived with around 30 minutes of fuel remaining onboard the aircraft given we arrived with around 70 mins of fuel in ABQ and assuming the approx 40 minutes of flight time to cover the 200 miles down to ZZZ. In the end we conducted a tailwind approach within limits to runway 8 however there is in my opinion a significant risk of aircraft flying to ABQ with jamming in progress not carrying the fuel for an alternate and not being able to land in ABQ because of tailwinds on the only useable approach as we were only between 2 and 7 knots of wind; depending on the exact aircraft; away from being unable to legally land in ABQ without using emergency authority.Cause: White sands missile range GPS jamming creating a significant threat to aircraft approaching ABQ with no filled alternate under clear weather in particular at night. It is my belief that as long as GPS jamming is underway at white sands every aircraft arriving at ABQ should have a filed alternate and carry sufficient fuel to reach it. In particular aircraft operating at night when winds are forecast to be out of the west.

column121: We were cleared for the RNAV XX approach to ZZZ by ZZZ center. The tower was closed. After passing fix ZZZZZ began descent from 3200 to 2000 as published. I was slowing and configuring per non-precision profile. I was fully configured by 3mi from FAF(ZZZZZ1). I chose to set the missed approach altitude but did not notice we had not Altitude Select (ALTS) capped 2000. We continued descending approximately 800fpm. The captain saw the deviation about 1700ft and called ALTITUDE; I said CORRECTING. We climbed back to the 2000ft published altitude prior to the FAF and then began normal descent to the runway. No further problems. The cause was my setting the missed approach altitude prior to ALTS capping the published altitude and not recognizing. Due to terrain the altitude change between segments on the approach is larger than no terrain areas and my feel for elapsed time was off for the altitude change compared to other non-precisions I have done. I did not verify the ALTS cap. From the start of the approach thing had progressed nicely and I got lulled into a complacency after we got fully configured.Suggestions: This is a sobering lesson knowing we were so close to the ground and I put us into a premature descent unknowingly. And only the captain recognized it. This will stay with me for a long time. I know to make sure we have captured an altitude before spinning the knob. Take a moment to be sure it's the correct timing for the input.
column123: On the RNAV Rwy XX approach in VMC; after crossing ZZZZZ at 3200' my first officer began descending to 2000' at ZZZZZ1. Shortly thereafter he called for the Flaps 45 & before landing check; so I went head down to run the checklist. As I was running the checklist; he set the go around altitude of 5600'; and as soon as I finished he stated go around altitude set since we were in visual conditions. I confirmed the altitude selection. However; I did not immediately notice that he did not let the plane reach Altitude Selection (ALTS) CAP; so we unintentionally descended below the altitude on prescribed on the chart roughly 4 miles before the final approach fix. As I began to scan I realized the mistake and called Altitude"; to which he immediately began a climb back up to 2000'. We continued the flight and landed uneventfully. We debriefed the event at the gate.Cause: Mismanagement of automation systems is the primary factor; but in talking to my first officer we also agreed that fatigue played a large role on his part- He had been awake for a long time. On my part; I needed to verify the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) right after returning from the checklist. Additionally; complacency could have had a part to play in it too; as it was visual conditions and an overall simple approach.Suggestions: In debrief I mentioned the dangers of creating unintentional; unlimited descents and how important it is to allow the plane to level off at assigned altitude on approaches; especially when low to the ground as the ALTS CAP mode is a safety feature installed for this exact reason."

During this time; we maintained communication with ground personnel; the flight attendants; and passengers.Both engines were shut down at the request of Fire and Rescue personnel. As a result; fumes entered the cabin. column121: During a landing rollout on Runway XX at ZZZ; the aircraft encountered a localized; quartering tailwind gust that was not reflected in the previous AWOS report. Despite following established traffic; the aircraft experienced significant directional instability shortly after touchdown.The combination of the high groundspeed from the tailwind and the LSA's free-castering nosewheel led to a diverging yaw that could not be corrected with full rudder deflection or differential braking. Recognizing that a high-energy ground loop on the asphalt was imminent; I utilized my PIC authority to make a deliberate; proactive transition off the pavement and onto the wide; level grass adjacent to the runway. This choice utilized the grass's lower lateral friction and higher rolling resistance to stabilize the aircraft. The aircraft was brought to a safe; controlled stop on the grass with no damage or injuries.Human Factors & Contributing Factors:Environmental: Rapidly deteriorating surface conditions were confirmed by METARs showing a 70-degree wind shift in just 20 minutes (from 130° at 08KT to 200° at 11KT); transitioning the runway from a headwind to a quartering tailwind while I was in the pattern.Herd Mentality: I initially deferred to the 'de facto' runway in use by other aircraft (two landed just before me) rather than independently verifying the current windsock indication during the final approach.Aircraft Design: The light wing loading and free-castering nosewheel make it sensitive to 'tripping' or pivoting on high-friction pavement during a tailwind-induced swerve.Corrective Actions & Lessons Learned:Personal Minimums: I have established a new personal minimum of a zero-tailwind component for this aircraft due to the narrow safety margins it provides during rollout in such conditions.Checklist Revision: I have modified my short-final flow to include a mandatory visual verification of the windsock to ensure surface conditions match my expectations; regardless of radio traffic; 'runway in use'; or AWOS.Safety Training: My previous tailwheel transition training was critical in recognizing the point of 'no return' on the pavement and choosing the more forgiving grass surface to dissipate energy safely.Systemic Recommendation:It is recommended that LSA manufacturers and flight/transition training providers include specific warnings in the Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) and Flight Training Supplements regarding the hazards of tailwind landings in these aircraft. Documentation should explicitly address how light wing loading and castering nosewheels can lead to rapid loss of directional control on pavement; which may not be intuitive to pilots transitioning from heavier GA aircraft.
