column121: Uncommanded Nose Wheel Steering Turn Event.We had a normal pushback from ZZZ Gate XX into the west alley and were cleared to start both engines. During the engine start the Ground Crew reported some difficulty removing the Tow Bar (not uncommon event) and during the process; a 'Nose Wheel Steering' message displayed briefly on the upper EICAS. The message disappeared shortly after both engines completed the start process which happened just as the Ground Crew were able to disconnect the Tow Bar. The entire pushback seemed smoother than most without any sharp movements; turns or noises.We were cleared by ZZZ Ramp to right on Taxiway 1 to Spot XX; at Spot XX we were cleared by ZZZ ATC Ground for an immediate left onto Taxiway 2; right on Taxiway 3 for a full length departure off Runway XXL.This was a very short taxi and required two immediate 90 degree turns after initial taxi. My estimated speed was approximately 5 knots or less due to the planned short taxi and other traffic. Nose wheel steering and feel was normal for the first right 90 degree turn. Approaching the second left turn for 2 after passing Spot XX the aircraft performed an uncommanded hard right turn to a 45 degree angle along with an immediate total loss of Nose Wheel Tiller authority. I immediately applied full braking to a stop and notified Ground Control followed by ZZZ Operations and Maintenance.I would describe the right turn like as quick as one could turn right 45 degree with the Tiller. It wasn't a gradual failure. Even with an immediate braking response; it appeared our nose position ended up 10 -15 feet right of the Taxiway centerline. Nose wheel steering remained non responsive and Tiller movement felt stiff; maybe 2x-3x normal force required to move the Tiller. The Tug lined up at the approximate Nose Wheel Steering angle for tow back.We were eventually towed back to Gate XX where the aircraft was taken out of service.Cause: None.

column121: In cruise at FL400 light chop. Heavy thunderstorm activity 56 nm to west of our position; with tops estimated at 45;000.Position was south of nav point OHLAA off coast of Florida. Heading 210 due to 56 kts wind from 287/52kts.Experiences what felt like a mountain wave which I assumed was due to the the upper level winds caused by the ++THR [severe thunderstorm] activity 56nm to the west of us.In anticipation of an increase in speed I informed the PM I was selecting manual speed; and reduced our Mach # from M.85 to M.83. There was a 39 kt spread between our IAS and the BARBER POLE. Airspeed continued to increase and auto throttles slowly started to reduce. As it was evident that the speed was increasing faster than the auto throttles were responding I again informed PM I WAS disengaging the auto throttles and manually reduced the power back further and then to idle!. Within a second the airspeed increased into red line activating the aural OVERSPEED warning.I extended the AIR BRAKES AB1; and the speed stopped increasing but was still within overspeed regime by 10 kts. I decided not to disengage the autopilot but rather press the Touch Control Steering (TCS) button to raise the nose as the only option to reduce the speed out of the overspeed envelope. This did reduced the speed to below the BARBER POLE causing the aural OVERSPEED to cease.I released the TCS button allowing the Autopilot to immediately engage selected VS MODE on the guidance panel  to descend back to our assigned Flight Level; and manually took command of the throttles manually. I instructed the PM (Second in Command) to inform MIAMI CENTER what had happened and explained why.Miami asked if it was due to severe turbulence; to which we replied NO; it was type of mountain wave or rather severe thunderstorm wind turbulence wave that caused uncontrolled speed deviation most likely caused from the severe thunderstorm 56 nm west of our position.Other aircraft were also experiencing the same type of effects after our encounter.Once things had settled down and I felt we were away from any possible reoccurrence; I engaged the auto throttles keeping the M.83 (our turbulence penetration speed) set to manual.  We then verily reviewed the automation confirming we would keep the autothrottles (AT) / manual M.83 set until we both felt we were away for the area of concern. Miami ATC  seemed fine with our immediate explanation and we were not asked to call anyone; nor have we been asked to explain further to anyone.Suggestions: I have experienced mountain waves around the world many times as well as thunderstorm rotor turbulence. However after many hours I have never encountered such a rapid uncontrolled  speed increase (within seconds) as I experienced with this one. On reviewing our actions to control the rapid speed increase; I don't think we could have done anything different. Hindsight is always 20/20 and one could say had we waited with power at idle and AB1 (Air Brakes) extended; the speed would eventually certainly started to reduce.Although on reflection this might very well have been so; yet I could not be sure that the speed might not have continued to increased into a very critical regime where structural damage might have been encountered. Therefore utilizing the TCS and using pitch as a last resort to control the speed was;  I think the best cause of action.56 miles away from a ++THR is generally considered ample distance.

column121: CA PM FO PFWe were cleared for the visual approach XX backed up with the ILS. The FO had briefed me that he was just off low-time hours in type. We had done one leg together which I flew. On the approach we identified the traffic to follow and proceeded inbound. The FO was delayed in calling for configuration as we became established on the LOC. I am not the type of CA to micromanage speed reductions and flap configurations as long as it does not affect stabilized approach criteria. However; I prompted that we need to begin configuring as we are getting close to the aircraft ahead and do not know their ground speed. I believe we were at flaps 3 gear down when ATC notified us of a 60kt overtake and that S-turns to the right were approved. We slowed to final landing configuration and were stabilized at 1000'. I told the FO to perform S-turns and he proceeded; reaching 1000 fpm momentarily and getting low - hitting 3 red lights on the PAPI before he rejoined the course and corrected - but otherwise we continued to remain stable through 500'. ATC told us at about 200-300' to go around and the FO hit the TOGA button but I did not hear him make the call-out as he was a very soft-spoken individual. I looked down to make sure the throttles were in TOGA detent and made the call-out myself then retracted the flaps to position 2. We performed the gear retraction properly and at that time ATC told us to climb 2000' and turn heading (I believe) 270. I bugged the panel and selected Heading and was monitoring the FO hand flying when I prompted him to take the Autopilot (AP) to reduce our workload; which we engaged. It is hard to remember the exact sequence of events that followed because of the momentary stress but after I engaged the AP; we received another instruction to climb 3000' and turn heading (I believe) 330. It was at this time I noticed our speed reducing and realized we missed the FLCH 210 call out and were still bugged at our Vap of 131. I noticed the speed around 140kts approaching 131 quickly and because we were in a turn; the low speed tape was higher; buffering Vap speed. I called out Speed 210 Speed 210" as the speed turned amber and instead of spinning the speed bug the FO disconnected the AP and pushed the nose down; which threw me off since I was not expecting the action and now I was back to manipulating the control panel. We did not receive a stick shaker. I spun the speed to 210 and at the same time I saw we were in a nearly 40-45 degree bank and approaching 3000' with a high rate of climb. I told the FO "altitude" "bank". I pressed forward on the controls and we managed to level and the FO reduced the bank angle. I engaged the AP once more and we continued to speed up and clean up the aircraft. We came back for a second approach without incident and landed uneventfully. We parked and debriefed the event. It was the FO's first go-around. We discussed fixation which led to the omission of speed on both our ends and the importance of aviate-navigate-communicate. We discussed the speed tape and how at higher bank angles it can lead to accelerated stalls and that there was no need to turn to the heading so aggressively. I also encouraged him to call for AP early in order to reduce workload."

column121: Preflighted the aircraft normally and performed initial start up and run up checklists as usual. No unusual readouts or abnormalities. On takeoff and climb out all indications were normal. Outside of the airport environment I had my student put on the goggles and directed us to a gps fix for some simulated IMC practice. Upon leveling out at cruise I took controls and had my student remove the foggles; handed control back and had him run through his initial checklist for maneuvers. We loaded in the nearest fields frequency and made a call that we would be maneuvering 15nm NW of the field at 5;700. I demonstrated a set of steep turns and then we went over the importance of running our cruise checklist and scanning all instruments every time in between. Student attempted a set of steep turns and requested to practice another set. We ran through the cruise and instrument scan and noted no abnormalities. We went over the importance of finding good visual reference points; and he attempted a steep turn to the left. After completing and leveling back off; I re-scanned the instruments and noted the Ammeter read out was low (around 2 or 3). I looked to the annunciator panel and noticed there was no illumination and the engine instruments digital screen was flickering and dim. Upon noticing this I took controls and had my student get his checklist to check the alternator low / inop checklist. At this time the Primary Flight Display (PFD) gave an AHRS failure notification and inop readouts for our attitude indicator and heading. Simultaneously both of our G430s went black and our PFD /Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) flashed off and back on. We ran the troubleshoot checklist and verified circuit breakers had not popped; they hadn't; attempted to reduce the load by shutting off the fan; shutting off lights; tried turning battery master and alternator off and back on; turned on the power for the standby attitude indicator and it worked alright for a couple minutes before flagging that it was inop. Nothing worked; and at this time we were a little over what looked like 10nm from the closest airport ZZZ. I made the decision to head to ZZZ and as it was an untoward field and G430s were black screened; I squawked 7600 for loss of comms and attempted to transmit in the blind. Called that we were approximately 10nm NW of the field and inbound for a landing with no electrical power. ZZZ center responded asking if we could hear them; if we needed assistance; and informing us we were transmitting on guard. I responded with our location and intentions and that was when we lost our standby attitude and our PFD / MFD went black. ZZZ center asked if we were able to swap and transmit on the local CTAF. I responded unable as we still did not have the 430s. A nearby aircraft also on guard called center and offered to transmit on our behalf on the local CTAF. Center agreed and we continued inbound to ZZZ prior to landing we lost all electrical. We landed; taxied to the ramp; secured and post flight inspected the aircraft. The only abnormality we found was a significant drop in oil level. In pre-flight it was 6.5 and in post flight it was 5.5 at most

column121: I was on short final at ZZZ for runway XX. It was sunset. The entire runway was in shadow. The sun was in my eyes from the sunset at my right. I had repeatedly tried to activate the PAPI using 5 clicks on the radio; but it was not activating and was discussing with my pilot/passenger in the right seat why it was not activating. I did not realize that I was on the wrong frequency and not on ZZZ CTAF. I made a call that I was on final runway XX at ZZZ about 3 miles out. I did not see any other aircraft on ADSB north of the field; and I'm not sure I looked south of the field on the map to see if there was anyone on ADSB. The wind was calm; so either runway was a candidate for takeoffs and landings. At about 500 feet AGL/MSL my right-seater and I both noticed at the same time an aircraft's landing lights on the runway. I was doing a short field landing; so was slow; and so I carefully broke off to the left without adding G loading; adding full power; and gently entered a climb with full flaps; gradually working the flaps out. The aircraft must have just landed on runway XY without me hearing them on the radio because I was on the wrong frequency; and without realizing I was on final for XX because they didn't hear my transmission; and they probably didn't notice me on ADSB; if they even have it. Once I was in a stable climb; I realized I wasn't on frequency and changed to CTAF and heard the other pilot calling me. I replied explaining it was entirely my fault because I had been on the wrong frequency; and the other pilot was gracious about the situation. I'm assuming the other plane must have taxied off the runway and to the ramp because I didn't see them after that. We set up for another landing; which was uneventful.The problem was that I don't have a correct-frequency check as a checklist item; and skipped verifying that I was on the correct CTAF. This was compounded by the runway being entirely in shadow and the sun in my eyes. The PAPI not turning on should have alerted me to the fact that I was on the wrong frequency. The short field landing I was doing also had me in a nose-high attitude behind the power curve; which made it slightly harder to see down the runway. I was also focused on maintaining the plane at a low airspeed; lined up for landing; during the slow approach; which is a bit more demanding and may have been an additional distraction from the issue unfolding. The plane that had just landed on XX may have turned on their landing lights on the runway to alert me of their presence; because neither my right seat pilot/passenger or I noticed them until the plane appeared halfway down the runway. To avoid this in future I plan to add a frequency check to my checklists; make sure I run my checklists every time; make sure my landing lights are on for takeoffs and landings; and consider what else may be wrong when I notice something 'weird' like a PAPI not activating.

column121: I was acting as a safety pilot for another private pilot. We were coming in to land at ZZZ airport and we were making left traffic for runway XX. The pilot flying made a base turn that was closer to the airport than usual and this put us up for a high and fast final. We landed after using up most of the runway. This was a touch and go so we immediately took off again. After takeoff; the pilot flying pitched up for our best rate of climb speed and we continued climbing. However; I can see obstacles at a distance. We were going to clear them. However; after reaching those obstacles and climbing over them I realized we were uncomfortably close to them. If I were in this position again I would have asked the pilot flying to initiate a go around after recognizing we were going to be high and fast. This would have prevented us from landing long. If we did land I would have told the pilot flying to make this a full stop and do a standard takeoff. Upon climbout after our landing; instead of climbing at the best rate of climb; I should have told the pilot flying to climb at the best angle of climb. These actions would have prevented the issue. While I did recognize the issues; I did not speak up since we were both private pilots and I felt I wasn't in a position of authority to tell another pilot how to fly. I should have spoken up when I recognized the issue and will do so next time.

column121: The Captain and I were doing a leg of a multiple day trip. It was a flight to ZZZ. Captain was the PF and I was the PM. We were setting up for the ILS XXR into ZZZ. Weather was about 4sm and overcast around 1500'. We were vectored for the approach around ZZZZZ at 2500' and cleared for the approach. Captain armed the approach. The MAX9 captured the LOC and GS roughly at the same time causing the airplane to aggressively pitch down attempting to catch the glideslope. Airspeed was increasing rapidly toward the barber pole; decent rate was increasing rapidly and Captain attempted to override the autopilot by pulling back on the yoke. He did not disconnect the autopilot. As he saw the airspeed increasing he extended the speed brakes. Airspeed is at the barber pole; aircraft pitching down aggressively and we hear Sink Rate; Sink Rate." Captain disconnects the autopilot (AP); pitches up very slightly and banks right. I said "roll wings level" he rolled wings level momentarily; still high on the GS and turned to the right again; ignoring the flight directors. I said again; "wings level" and put a little pressure on the yoke to get the airplane level. Captain said "UPSET!" We were not in an upset condition and I was afraid Captain was going to pitch the aircraft down; I said "my controls". I took control of the aircraft and executed a go around procedure at 1200 Agl in IMC. We got runway heading up to 4000'; cleaned up the airplane and I asked the Captain if he wanted the controls back; he said "yes". I gave him the controls and requested vectors for the approach again with an extended final. Once on the ground we debriefed the situation. The Captain admitted he was disoriented and was very confused about what had happened. We talked in depth about what happened and I made it clear how scary the situation was. The Captain just came off the 777 and just completed 737 IOE."
column123: Uneventful leg from ZZZ1 to arrival on the ZZZZZX arrival.  We briefed by the card and identified a possible short vector as well as the weather as potential threats.  I was vectored off of the arrival to a 300 heading to intercept XXR ILS's final; turned to 280 and maintain 4000 feet.  I was then turned to an ILS intercept heading; don't remember it; and cleared to descend to 2500 feet.  The airplane was at flaps 5 and slowing to 180 knots.  We were then cleared to maintain 2500 feet and 170 knots till a 5 mile final.  I started slowing to 165 at about a 6.5 mile final. The vector brought us just inside of ZZZZZ at 2500 feet.   I called for gear down and flaps 15 then 25 a few seconds later.   The airplane intercepted the LOC and GS at the same time and I called to set TDZE.  The airplane was a a half dot high and still in a 20-30 degree turn intercepting Final Approach Course.  The airplane dumped the nose to get on the path and the speed rapidly increased to almost 190-195.  I recognized the speed increase and pulled the speed break out to control it.   It was not slowing and we got a sink rate; pull up call.  (lowest alt was 1000 feet) I clicked the autopilot (AP) off; pulled up and turned to the right; which was the wrong way.  My FO recognized that I was disoriented challenged me twice to roll wings level; which I though I was doing.  He took the controls and executed the go around (GA).  The GA was challenging due to the confusion; but he executed it.  I took the comms; we cleaned up the aircraft and completed the after takeoff checklist.  Tower directed  to fly runway heading and climb to 4000 feet and later boxed back around to the right to try again.  We resequenced the box for the ILSXXR.  I felt fine; so I retook the controls on the downwind while the FO did the descent checklist.  The FO asked for a longer vector and I flew the approach and landing uneventfully.  Once at the gate; we thoroughly debriefed the event and determined that between the short vector; intercepting the LOC/GS simultaneously; the steep decent (high airspeed) and disorentation led to the event.  We determined as well that the CRM skills of Situational Awareness; and monitor/cross-check by the FO fixed the situation.

column121: While operating flight from ZZZ1; we received a cabin altitude warning indication and associated master warning and horn. We were passing FL260 to our assigned cruising altitude of FL320. We performed the immediate action items (O2 masks; established communications; seatbelt sign on) and FO advised ATC that we had a pressurization issue and requested an immediate descent lower and then clarified 10;000 ft. The autopilot and auto throttles were disconnected and I requested LVL Change and 300 KIAS. The speed brake was utilized as well. While descending I observed that the cabin pressure was slightly above 10;000 ft and it didn't get much higher than that. It got very busy due to initial difficulty communicating (mask and volume issues); ATC requesting details and the FAs immediately trying to contact us multiple times as well. We didn't initially request priority handling since the focus was flying the airplane first and dealing with our issue; but we eventually did due to the fact that we were going to land overweight. When FO was performing the Cabin Altitude Warning or Rapid Depressurization/ Descent QRC he discovered that the pressurization switch was already in manual when he got to step 6. While he was performing the checklist; i was still hand flying in the descent to 10;000 ft. The FAs were concerned that we were concerned about our well being and tried to enter the Flight Deck (FD) utilizing the FD door EMERGENCY ENTRY button. This occurred after they attempted to call the flight deck a few times and knocking on the door as well. What they didn't know was that we were very busy dealing with the checklist and ATC concurrently. When we heard the DOOR DOOR DOOR audio; FO performed the immediate action item for the flight deck door and pressed the HARD LOCK switch. We were able to eventually advise them that we were very busy and that we'd contact them when we get a chance. After completing up to step 17 of the CABIN ALTITUDE Warning non-normal; we discussed diverting to ZZZ. We informed dispatch of our issue and our intentions to go to ZZZ. They eventually replied and asked if we requested priority handling and we informed them that we did. I slowed the aircraft to 250 KIAS at 10;000 ft as to not feel rushed dealing with our issue. The FAs were contacted and the brief was performed. The passengers were also briefed of our issue and our intentions to divert to ZZZ. Everyone was also informed about the emergency equipment on standby and they were going to be there as a precaution. The divert* function had been completed; aircraft re-cruised and set up for the arrival into ZZZ. Since we were landing overweight; we calculated our landing distance utilizing the LANDING DISTANCE NORMAL CONFIGURATION - FLAPS 30 (800) table. We were given vectors for ILS XXL and conducted a FLAPS 30/AUTO BRAKES 3 landing. After landing; we exited runway XXL and came to a complete stop so Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) could inspect the aircraft exterior for any damage. After none was noted; they departed the scene and returned to their base of operation. We eventually taxied to the gate. After we completed the parking checklist; we spoke to one of the maintenance technicians. They were debriefed. Afterwords; I contacted the Chief Pilot and advised him that we were ok to continue. Electronic Log Book entries were made for the cabin altitude (occurrence altitude and cabin altitude indication noted) and overweight landing (smooth landing and weight noted (…approximately 8200 lbs overweight). Outside the flight deck; we had to opportunity to conduct a thorough debrief. We discussed aspects of how we handled the situation (workload management and situational awareness) and the fact that we were able to cover all the steps dealing with our issue and safely divert to ZZZ. Communication is what could've gone better. We discussed how the warning horn was a distraction before cutout was selected; establishing communication with masks on; ATC callingus while we were doing checklists and the FAs immediately trying to contact us numerous times as well. The primary issue though was how we both missed the pressurization switch in the manual position. We discussed about the possibility of confirmation bias regarding the switch position; but we also discussed ways to prevent a repeat of undesired outcome of events.
column123: On climbout to FL320 at approximately FL270 the CABIN ALTITUDE warning light illuminated and warning horn started sounding.  We accomplished our immediate action items(O2 masks on; establish communications; and seatbelt sign on); and I asked ATC for a descent to 10000' stating we had a pressurization issue.  The CA; PF; initiated an immediate descent.  The CA called for the 'CABIN ALTITUDE Warning or Rapid Depressurization/Descent' QRC.  As I was accomplishing the QRC and got to item 6 I noticed the pressurization controller switch was already in manual and the MANUAL green light was illuminated.  I looked at the cabin altitude and saw approximately 11000'.  Also at this time the FAs began trying to call the cockpit. I attempted to establish communication with them but was unable initially; and was prioritizing the checklist and communication with ATC.  This quickly escalated to banging on the flight deck door and sounding of the 'door; door; door' alarm.  I pushed the hard lock button and attempted again to get in contact with the FAs.  I was able to very faintly hear them over the speaker and advised them we had a pressurization issue; we were descending to 10000' and to stand by. With the O2 masks on and with how busy we were I was unable to discern if they had heard me very well at this point.  I continued with the QRC and eventually the QRH.  We leveled at 10000'; took the O2 masks off and I established better communications with the FAs; restating the situation and asking if they passenger O2 masks had dropped; they had not. 	Level at 10000' at 250 kts and with the masks off and the QRH completed to the deferred items;  the CA spoke with the passengers about the situation and we discussed options between ourselves and with dispatch; eventually concluding to divert to ZZZ. ATC had already asked for souls and fuel onboard but we confirmed with them that we were a priority aircraft.  I then checked the LANDING DISTANCE NORMAL CONFIGURATION - FLAPS 30 (800) table in the Flight Manual (FM) for an overweight landing at 155.6lbs.  After confirming the runway length required we completed the deferred items checklists and the CA made an uneventful landing at ZZZ.  Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) was standing by and checked the aircraft out after we exited the runway with no findings.  We then taxied to gate XX. We debriefed the event as a crew thoroughly; the CA called the Chief Pilot and we put in Electronic Lob Book report for the CABIN ALTITUDE warning; and the overweight landing.   	On the descent while accomplishing the QRC was the first time that either of us noticed the pressurization switch to be in manual.  Both the CA and I remember verifying the pressurization panel was in the correct configuration during the initial flow; the preflight checklist; and the before takeoff checklist. Whether it was confirmation bias and the switch was in fact in the wrong position prior to takeoff or the switch was bumped during flight we are not entirely sure.

column121: Contacted MIA ground for taxi. Controller advised expect Rwy 8L for takeoff and to taxi via Txy K to holding point for Rwy 8L.  We had loaded Rwy 8R during preflight; so during the taxi; I loaded Rwy 8L; entered the takeoff data; and confirmed waypoints.  The CA called for the Runway Change checklist and it was completed halfway to the holding point.  Ground then directed us to monitor Tower frequency approaching the holding point.  When tower contacted us; they directed us to cross runway 8L and hold short Rwy 8R and expedite for traffic on 5-mile final. As we crossed the hold short line for Rwy 8L; tower advised us to proceed onto hold for Rwy 8R.  I advised that we would need a few minutes to run checklists.  Tower replied with hold short Rwy 8L and the CA applied brakes; but we were past the hold short line by about 50 feet.  I advised tower and he said to then expedite and hold short Rwy 8R; traffic on 2 mile final. CA advanced throttles; but we did not clear Rwy 8L in time and traffic on final was directed to Go Around.  Holding Short of Rwy 8R we completed all the runway change items one last time and rest of departure was uneventful.Cause: Change of Runway assignment followed by expedited instructions to cross and then on to the new runway and hold before crew could run required checklists.  I also should have been more vocal about our requirements before attempting to cross Rwy 8L; but with the hold short instructions initially provided for the other side; I thought we would have time while holding short of Rwy 8R.Suggestions: When workload is high and expedited instructions are received to cross an active runway; request hold short of that runway to ensure all requirements are completed to prevent conflicts.
column123: Our preflight was normal.  We had the aircraft set up for a departure off of runway 08R and also had the numbers for 08L.  We blocked out early.  Upon receiving initial Taxi clearance we were told to taxi via K to runway 08L and expect 08L for departure.  We immediately reconfigured the aircraft for 08L and had the runway change checklist completed before crossing taxiway K7.  Around approximately taxiway Z the ground controller had us switch to tower and monitor.  We were approximately abeam the beginning of taxiway K1 when the tower controller said 'Aircraft X; cross runway 08L hold short runway 08R traffic five miles out I need you to expedite.' We proceeded to cross 08L and were waiting to reconfigure for 08R until we were stopped and holding short of 08R.  All numbers and  power settings were exactly the same.  We had discussed and noted this before initial taxi. We just had to select runway 08R; reenter V speeds;  and repeat the runway change checklist. As we were crossing the runway 08L hold short line the tower controller said 'Aircraft X Line up and wait runway 08R.'  We responded we'd need a minute to change the numbers and run the checklist.  The controller then said 'Aircraft X hold short  runway 08L.' We responded 'Unable we have already crossed the hold short line.'  The tower controller then said 'Then I need you to expedite crossing 08L and hold short 08R traffic two mile final.' We had stopped when he initially told us to hold short and were now trying to expedite again. At that moment I immediately observed the aircraft on final begin their go around.Cause: When receiving our initial taxi clearance the controller initially gave us 08R then said 'hold on ….'  there was about a three to five second pause then he came back and said 'Taxi via K to runway 08L.'  I believe during that pause the ground controller likely checked with the tower controller or someone else and asked if it was ok to give us 08L. We did not ask for this however I think they were just trying to be accommodating. I think there was some sort of miscommunication between ground and tower and that translated into the tower controller giving us 08R when the ground controller had given us 08L.  In the moment the tower controller got audibly agitated with us as I felt he thought we weren't prepared.  In reality we were fully prepared for either runway and were set up for the runway given.  I just should have refused to cross runway 08L at the initial instruction until we were fully set up again.  In past experience I have also had them do almost the same thing previously to me. The previous time I stopped prior to 08L; reconfigured for 08R; then they eventually came back and reassigned us back to 08L prior to takeoff.Suggestions: In hindsight when the controller initially issued a runway different than we were expecting I should have just held short of runway 08L and told him we were going to have to change numbers and run the runway change checklist there.  I was trying to make it work in the wrong place.  Going forward I that's what I will do.

column121: On Day 0 around XA:37 in ZZZ; Aircraft X blocked OUT for its flight to ZZZ1. Weight of aircraft on pushback: 75;100 lbsI communicated with tug driver to confirm that she and the rest of her ramp crew were ready for pushback off gate XX. She confirmed that they were ready. I called for the pushback checklist; which my FO and I then completed. My FO then called ramp for push clearance. We received push clearance straight back off [gate] XX. Once we received push clearance; I turned the beacon ON; released the parking brake; and verified once more the nose wheel steering was OFF. At this point I stated to the tug driver; Beacon ON; Brakes RELEASED; Nose Wheel steering OFF. You are cleared to push straight back." If I had to venture a guess; it was maybe 10 yards off the gate when the tug driver brought the push to a very abrupt stop. There was a very sharp jolt to the airplane associated with this abrupt stop. I queried the tug driver as to what happened and she relayed to me that a wing walker had given her the signal to stop the push due to traffic on the roadway behind the aircraft. Once the traffic was clear; she attempted to restart the push and gave us clearance to start the right engine. However; shortly after the push started it was evident that something did not feel or sound right. We stopped the engine start attempt and the tug driver brought the aircraft to a stop. She got off the tug to inspect the nose gear and tow bar and told us that something was not right and the tow bar was possibly broke. At this point I told her I would set the parking brake; which I then did. I immediately called Maintenance Control through my dispatcher. My FO then told ramp control our situation and then called local maintenance in ZZZ. Maintenance came to the aircraft and conducted their inspection. Fortunately; it was a shear pin on the tow bar itself that broke and the inspection of the nose gear was satisfactory per maintenance personnel. Once the paperwork was completed and the logbook returned; we proceeded on our way to ZZZ1.Cause: The tug driver stopped the push too abruptly resulting in a shear pin event on the tow bar."

column121: After completing the training flight with the student; we were was taxiing the aircraft back to the hangar to be parked. The student was on the control taxing. There is a light pole by the fuel pumps at the flight school that we have to clear on the right side for a turn. There is usually cars parked along on the left side that we also have to clear; but due to the timing of the lesson; there were less cars. This is a tight spot the aircraft has to clear. During this time; there were conversations in the flight deck which caused a distraction to both the student and instructor resulting the right side of the wing running into the light pole.There is structural damage towards the end of the wing. Maintenance observed the damage and reported that the dented parts will need replacement. No spars were damaged but would need to inspect to see if there are internal damages along with the root of the wing as there were small wrinkles observed.The student is a current commercial applicant that is also training for their commercial multi-engine training at the same time. To prevent this; instructor should never get complacent with any student and what rating they hold. Also need to make sure to follow the taxi lines to ensure the clearance and not have expectation bias as aircraft wing spans all differ. During taxi; should always still practice sterile flight deck while engine is still on.
column123: After completing the training flight; the instructor and I taxied the aircraft back toward the hangar on the school parking lot; with me at the controls. The area requires careful maneuvering due to limited clearance. During taxi; both the instructor and I became distracted by another aircraft on final performing a power-off 180 approach at what appeared to be a steep angle. Weather conditions was clear; with visibility greater than 6 statute miles and wind gusts exceeding as high as13 knots from the north. Concerned that the aircraft might undershoot and was descending rapidly; our attention shifted away from taxi operations; resulting in the right wing striking a light pole near the fuel pumps on the right side; which must be cleared during the turn. The aircraft was taxiing at a minimal speed with both engines at idle power.The wing skin near the tip of the right wing was damaged. The maintenance team assessed the issue and determined that the dented sections will require replacement. While no spars appear to be affected; a more detailed inspection is necessary to check for any internal damage; particularly around the wing root; where minor wrinkling has been noticed.I am a commercial pilot candidate currently undergoing multi-engine training. As I operate multiple aircraft with varying wingspans; it is essential to strictly adhere to taxiway centerlines to maintain proper clearance and avoid assumptions driven by expectation bias. To mitigate similar situations; I should actively scan for obstacles while maintaining precise centerline tracking during the taxi. A sterile cockpit environment must also be maintained during all taxi operations while the engines are running. This experience provided a critical learning point that I will carry forward for the rest of my career.

column121: I was scheduled to operate flight from ZZZ on Aircraft X. As part of my preflight duties; I reviewed the aircraft logbook history for the preceding days and noted that the 'IAS DISAGREE' EICAS message had occurred multiple times within the past couple days. During the threat-forward preflight briefing with First Officers A and B; I highlighted this recurring discrepancy and reviewed the applicable memory items.Pushback; taxi; and takeoff were uneventful. This was First Officer A's leg. After gear and flap retraction and completion of the takeoff checklist; between approximately 5;000 and 6;000 feet during the climb; we received an IAS DISAGREE EICAS message. We immediately accomplished the applicable memory items. As we transitioned from the Quick Reference Checklist (QRC) to the Non-Normal Checklist; the EICAS message cleared; however; the Captain's ADI speed tape continued to display a 'SPD LIM' flag.We discussed the situation and agreed to initiate a three-way conference with Dispatch and Maintenance Control. Following coordination with both parties; we elected to return to ZZZ. This decision was based on the recurring nature of the discrepancy and the potential for re-occurrence; which could lead to an undesired aircraft state; including unreliable airspeed indications; nuisance or erroneous warnings (e.g.; stick shaker; overspeed); and abnormal handling characteristics; as outlined in QRH 2.100.21.I requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of our intention to return to ZZZ. Crew duties were clearly assigned: First Officer A remained the pilot flying; International Relief Officer B handled ATC communications; and I coordinated the return with Dispatch while also updating the flight attendants and passengers.At the time of the decision; the aircraft was approximately 16;000 pounds above maximum landing weight. With no fuel in the center tank available for jettison; burning down to landing weight would have required approximately one hour. Given the operational risk associated with the recurring IAS DISAGREE condition; I exercised my authority and elected to proceed with an overweight landing.ATC provided priority handling for our return. First Officer A executed a safe and stabilized landing on Runway XXR; with a touchdown rate of approximately 200-300 feet per minute.Once at the gate; we conducted a debrief among ourselves and afterwards provided a detailed briefing to maintenance personnel regarding the event.
column123: I was the pilot flying on Flight from ZZZ operating Aircraft X. During preflight review of the aircraft logbook; I noted multiple occurrences of an 'IAS DISAGREE' EICAS message within the past couple days. I briefed this trend during the threat-forward discussion with the Captain and International Relief Officer; including a review of applicable memory items.Departure was uneventful. During climb; passing approximately 5;000-6;000 feet after completion of the takeoff checklist; an IAS DISAGREE EICAS message was annunciated. Memory items were accomplished immediately. During transition from the QRC to the Non-Normal Checklist; the EICAS message cleared; however; the Captain's ADI continued to display a 'SPD LIM' flag.The crew assessed the situation and coordinated a conference with Dispatch and Maintenance Control. Given the recent history of repeated IAS DISAGREE events and the potential for unreliable airspeed indications; nuisance/erroneous warnings (e.g.; stick shaker; overspeed); and abnormal handling characteristics (QRH 2.100.21); the decision was made to return to ZZZ.Priority handling was requested with ATC. I remained pilot flying; the International Relief Officer handled communications; and the Captain coordinated with Dispatch and cabin crew.At the time of the return decision; the aircraft was approximately 16;000 pounds above maximum landing weight. Fuel jettison was not available; and burning down to landing weight would have required approximately one hour. Due to the operational risk associated with a potential recurrence of the airspeed discrepancy; the Captain exercised authority to conduct an overweight landing.ATC provided priority handling. A stable approach was flown and a safe landing was accomplished on Runway XXR with an approximate touchdown rate of 200-300 FPM.Post-flight; the crew debriefed and provided a detailed report to maintenance.

column121: On descent into IXD we were given the option by ATC  to fly the ILS 36 approach or fly a visual approach. We had briefed the ILS prior; but having the field insight I elected for the visual. We were cleared for the visual and told to contact tower. We switched frequency and cleared to land. I glanced at the approach plate and saw the glide slope intercept at 1580. Being visual I asked for 1500 in the ALT select. I began my a gradual descent and adjusted my heading to intercept final. As we leveled at 1500 I noticed that we appeared much lower than anticipated and further away than I initially believed. I elected to stay at 1500 and intercept the glide slope as we got closer in.As we were looking outside at the field as we got closer; the terrain actually was beginning rise; triggering the aircraft to alert Landing gear; Landing gear. I asked for the gear. The gear was selected and I began requesting flaps. Flaps 1 and 2 were selected as we began to configure to land. As we were configuring I looked down at the PFD (Primary Flight Display) just in time to see the terrain turn yellow and get a terrain proximity alert then a pull up command.Cause: After shutdown; we debriefed the incident. After reviewing the approach plate I saw I had mistakenly seen and requested the altitude at ZIXAT not the altitude at the FAF SKINI. Complacency stemming from a nice early morning flying into a scenic area. Not reacting to multiple clues of rising terrain. No additional advisories from approach or tower to check altitude. Not excusing my mistakes or complacency; but may have triggered us to take action sooner.I pitched up adding power to climb. I leveled off still at roughly 2000 were I waited to intercept the glideslope before continuing descent on the approach. Once on the glideslope I continued the approach to land.Suggestions: Moving forward if an approach has been programmed and briefed; given the option to fly the approach or take a visual I will elect to continue on the approach as the difference would have been a few additional vectors to final. With regard to visual approaches I will continue to back them up with vertical guidance when available and be more cognizant of both information available to me on approach plates; airport information; and visual cues.

column121: At XA:30pm while conducting the visual approach into XXR at ZZZ I called for the landing gear down.  At that time we received a GEAR DISAGREE R CAS (Crew Alerting System) message and the right amber X on the gear indication for the right main.  I decided to go around when I saw the indications.  After the after takeoff checklist we asked for delay vectors to run the appropriate QRH checklist for the CAS message.  After running the checklist we still had an amber X for the right main gear indication and the CAS message. We then climbed to 10;000 ft where I was able to get a hold of the Chief Pilot who was Person A at the time. He confirmed with me that all of the items were done on the checklist.  He then stated we should request priority handling since we still had the amber X for the right main gear indication.  We did request priority handling.  We then discussed the landing and the threats associated with a potential unsafe gear and also an emergency evacuation if needed.  After the approach checklist I requested a low approach to see if the right main was out. It was dark but I thought I would try.  When the flaps were selected full; the amber X turned to a red X and we received the audible 'landing gear' warning that was very loud and continued which made it hard to communicate between us and tower.  The first attempt the emergency vehicles could not tell because of the runway light reflection.  They asked if we could do it again and they would aim spotlights at the landing gear.  On the second low approach they were able to see that the right main was down.   We then came back around and ran the approach checklist again and landed. The plane landed without incident but I elected to stop on the runway until emergency vehicles could inspect the airplane for any anomalies with the landing gear. They saw none so made a left turn on 1 and exited the runway and shut the plane down on 1 and was towed in from there.  Person A the Chief Pilot was helpful along with ZZZ tower and emergency vehicles.

column121: During takeoff from ZZZ in VMC conditions and LNAV deselected due to vectors from ATC; the CA nav display and Flight Director (FD) lost heading guidance. I (CA) was flying. Following completion of the After Takeoff checklist and once at a safe altitude; it was determined that the FO had full FD and NAV guidance; so controls were transferred and COMMAND B selected while I referred to the QRH. There were no FAULT indications on the overhead; and no procedures in the QRH to address the loss of heading guidance. No Circuit breakers were tripped. I assumed control of the aircraft to allow the FO to search the QRH for an applicable procedure with the same negative result.I transferred control back to the FO; did a thorough scan of the overhead and discovered that that the Inertial Reference System (IRS) 1 selector switch was in ATT vice NAV. With concurrence from FO; decided to switch the IRS to NAV mode; which led to a complete loss of navigation data on both sides and autopilot disconnect. We had attitude guidance and altitude guidance from the FD; but were down to magnetic compass for heading. Notified ATC; and let them know we were trouble shooting the issue. There were no procedures in the QRH or AOM to restore the NAV. We coordinated through Dispatch with Maintenance Control (Crew Phone was down due to loss of WiFi); but Maintenance Control only asked if there were and circuit breakers tripped and had no alternative solutions. We decided that proceeding to our destination without navigation was a poor choice so requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ1; which was reporting VMC. With vectors from ATC; we hand flew the aircraft to an ILS/visual intercept where we regained FD guidance for the approach using raw data and landed without incident.Cause: The major factors that we identified as a crew that led to this were the inadvertent selection of ATT during preflight by the FO; not catching the lack of Flight Mode Annunciator 'HDG SEL' annunciation; lack of FD guidance at TOGA during the takeoff roll and selection of NAV inflight after the original issue was identified. There is a procedure in the AOM for inadvertent selection of ATT during pre-flight on the ground; but nothing for discovering the condition once airborne. In retrospect; without guidance we should have left the switch in the ATT position with the good data on the FO side; but it would be helpful if there were procedural guidance for this condition inflight.
column123: During takeoff from ZZZ; in VMC. LANV deselected; radar vectors on departure.CA PF; his Nav display lost heading guidance and Flight Director (FD). I FO PM; completed after takeoff checklist. Once at safe altitude. We determined FO side had all information; so aircraft control was switched to FO .CA was now PM and referred to QRH. There were no fault indications; no procedure addressing loss of heading guidance. No circuit breakers tripped. CA took aircraft back to be PF; and I also verified QRH for appropriate procedure. I agreed with CA not seeing an applicable procedure.CA transferred aircraft back to Fo to be PF again. CA did a review of overhead panel Inertial Reference System (IRS) 1 was on ATT not NAV. We agreed that was issue switched to NAV. Lost everything only had attitude and altitude; magnetic compass. CA advise ATC; dispatch and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control asked to verify circuit breakers. No reference in QRH to restore the NAV.  At that point requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ1. CA took control again PF; I resumed PM duties. Landing in ZZZ1 without incident.Cause: Factors we identified; inadvertent switch position. Not trapping the error with before start checklist. Not recognizing missing information on Flight Mode Annunciator; lack of FD at TOGA. Without guidance we should have left the switch in the ATT position with good data on FO side.

column123: Landing on runway XXR at ZZZ we were slowing and directed to exit on 1 and contact ground.  As I turned the aircraft onto taxiway 1. column121: Enroute to ZZZ1; requested cruise climb from F340 to F360 per flight plan. At approximately F352 the number 2 engine EGT surged into caution range. Checklists were accomplished (autothrottle was disengaged and thrust lever retarded until back within normal EGT range). Red line was not exceeded. QRC and QRH were accomplished. Continued climb and leveled off at F360 and autothrottles were re-engaged. EGT was in normal range but was 100c greater than number 1 engine EGT. Radio was contacted and phone patch requested to dispatch and Maintenance Control. As we discussed options; number 2 engine EGT climbed up to 115c greater than number 1 engine. Due to warmer trending EGT; captain and I decided to request priority handling and divert to ZZZ. Preparations were made for an overweight landing (approximately 10;000 lbs over Maximum Landing Weight.) Emergency vehicles were asked to standby. Descent; approach and landing were normal and uneventful. Taxied to the gate under own power.
column123: While climbing to FL360 noticed Engine #2 surge into the caution range without any other abnormal indications.  Disconnected the autothrottles and reduced the thrust on the #2 Engine to get it out of the caution range. Accomplished the Checklists/QRH items.  Aircraft stable with the Number #2 engine running 100C degrees hotter than the left engine.  Consulted with maintenance and dispatch on the situation with the high EGT.  Maintenance was recommending on continuing to destination which was more than 2 hours away.  We agreed initially although after the phone patch was complete myself and the First Office continued to evaluate our situation and were formulating options as ZZZ1 was at least 2 hours away.  Shortly thereafter the EGT was increasing to 115 degrees C hotter in the wrong direction without any surging or vibrations or other abnormal anomalies.  At that point we made the decision to divert. Did not see any reason to continue away from close by airports or continue into high terrain and possibly have to shutdown #2 Engine.  Priority handling was requested and dispatch informed and a diversion to ZZZ the closest and smartest decision.  Decision to land overweight was executed as the status of the #2 engine was in question. Landing accomplished uneventful and aircraft taxied to the gate under its own power.

column121: The flight began with a normal and smooth pushback; taxi and take off. As we were climbing through 18;000 feet; Relief Pilot left for his rest break and as he closed the door behind him FO noticed a significant long spark on R2 window. At the time I was checking in with ZZZ [ARTCC] on a newly assigned frequency. FO brought into my attention about the spark on R2 and as we started to ascertain if that could have been St. Elmo's fire; EICAS suddenly displayed 'Window Heat (R)' message. I advised the FO to continue flying and I would do the Window Heat non-normal checklist procedure. The checklist directed us to check the window in question if it had any visible arcing or cracking. Since it was night time and the cockpit was too pitch dark; I advised the FO turn on the flash light and see if there was any damage to the window. On doing so we both discovered large arcing on left bottom side of the window. Checklist dictated to land at a nearest suitable airport if such damage was visible. I immediately decided to call Relief Pilot back and as he was stepping back into the flight deck he observed a large crack had also developed on right bottom side of the window. We decided to request priority handling and land back ASAP. Roles were delegated as per the SOP; FO was asked to continue flying while I and Relief Pilot completed the necessary checklists including diversion guidelines; obtaining weather and performances data. I advised the ATC of our intention; spoke to dispatch and Maintenance Control. We decided to return to ZZZ1 and ATC offered us Rw XXL for landing considering it was longer than XXR and we were going to make an overweight landing. I asked the purser to pull up his briefing card and briefed him accordingly. Made an announcement over the PA and apprised passengers of the safety concern and that we were returning to ZZZ1. Told them upon reaching the gate customer service would be there to arrange for their alternate travel. Also gave heads up to them they would be noticing emergency vehicles on the ground and they didn't need to worry about it as their presence was totally going to be out of abundance of caution. Due to heavy weight; high VREF approach and potential liability issues I decided to land the plane. An uneventful landing was conducted at the end. Briefed local maintenance and Chief Pilot thereafter.
column123: All was normal through takeoff. Upon climbing through FL180 the Relief Pilot was in the process of leaving the flight deck to go on break and I noticed a line of small electrical sparks coming from the lower left portion of the R2 window. Initially I thought it might be St Elmos fire but I could see it had left a crack where it was sparking. I brought the sparking up with the captain after he checked in with ZZZ [ARTCC]. About one minute after seeing the sparks; EICAS displayed 'R window Heat' message. I was PF so I continued flying while the captain worked the checklist. The checklist directed us to check for visual arcing and/or cracking which would lead us to land at the nearest suitable airport. The captain made the decision to call the Relief Pilot back up and when he got back he noticed a large crack on the lower right portion of the window. At this point we requested priority handling and I took over radio communication along with flying the plane while the other two worked on the proper checklists and worked the situation per SOP. We diverted back to ZZZ1 and ATC offered XXL for a longer runway for an overweight landing. The captain took over the controls during the approach and landing due to the overweight landing and  possible liability. We landed about 20;000 lbs overweight and made it back to the gate with no further issues.

column121: During a night visual approach to runway XXR in ZZZ with the first officer flying while I monitored; we received a low altitude alert from ATC and elected to abandon the approach and try again. We were initially expecting runway XXR; but when the ATIS was advertising that runway XYL was in use; we changed the approach in the FMS and briefed for runway XYL. Upon contacting approach control; the controller advised that the winds were from the south and gave us the option of XZ or XXR. We chose XXR; due to the runway being longer; and a runway assessment indicated we had adequate runway to land with a slight tailwind. As we descended to 2000 feet for the approach; we picked up the runway visually and were cleared for a visual approach. The final approach fix altitude was 1600 feet; and the first officer selected 1600 as the next altitude while arming the ILS XXR approach. However; when the autopilot captured the ILS signal; it turned away from the runway and paralleled the course instead. It was then that I realized that the ILS signal must have still been set to runway XYL. The ILS frequency for both XXR and XYL were the same; and I had not seen the IDENT displayed on the Primary Flight Display (PFD). The other issue was that the PAPI for that runway was out of service; so it was difficult to determine our glide path. The first officer disconnected the autopilot and tried to return the aircraft to the centerline while I disengaged the flight directors. While I was trying to find an RNAV approach to quickly load into the FMS; ATC alerted us to our low altitude; and I saw we were at 1000 feet and still outside the final approach fix. We attempted to regain altitude to salvage the approach; but ATC offered to vector us back for another approach; and we agreed. At this point; we had already been configuring for landing; and we had the gear down and the flaps were at config 3. As we continued to climb; we were slow to reconfigure; and the aircraft was still at approach speed (160-170 knots) when I instructed the first officer to select TOGA; and we were finally able to climb to 2000 feet and reconfigure the aircraft. On the next approach; I noted the correct IDENT on the PDF for runway XXR; and we were able to successfully land. In hindsight; I should have known something was wrong with the ILS signal when I did not see the IDENT displayed. I also should have been monitoring the approach better and corrected the altitude deviation sooner; or at least commanded a full go-around once ATC alerted us.Cause: It has been many years since I've seen a situation where the ILS frequency is the same for both runways. I did not consider that multiple runways changes might cause the wrong runway to be selected by ATC; and I should have confirmed the correct IDENT before allowing the FO to arm the approach.

column121: We were conducting stop and gos; but did not have enough runway to take off; so we got clear of the runway because Aircraft Y was on final (we had been coordinating with them the entire time in the traffic pattern). As we entered the runway to begin our back taxi; Aircraft Y made a call on CTAF that an aircraft (Aircraft Z) was on final. We didn't see them turn base to final and when we heard Aircraft Y make that call and then saw Aircraft Z on final; we swiftly exited the runway. We were off of the runway by the time Aircraft Z would've touched down; but Aircraft Z executed a go-around out of precaution.Cause:  Lack of coordination from Aircraft Z; and I didn't zoom out on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) because I still had it zoomed in to determine if we had 2000ft to take off. It was a fault on both ends. Certain fatigue on my end too since this was a late afternoon flight and the second consecutive day where I had an early morning flight and a late afternoon flight in the same day.Suggestions:  All aircraft in the traffic pattern should be coordinating with each other. Also checking the MFD before entering a runway; because traffic might not be talking. I was scanning final as Aircraft Y was coming in to land but at the time; Aircraft Z was likely on base which I didn't see.

No conclusive data was determined except that it was a Air Carrier X main landing gear re-tread tire. The FO and I had an extensive discussion of multiple outcomes and possibilities. We descended to a lower altitude to reduce landing weight and continued to ZZZ1.  Briefed with the flight attendants was conducted. Requested priority handling with ZZZ1 [ARTCC].  A soft  landing was made followed by a fire and rescue inspection at the end of the runway that revealed damage to the left Main landing gear outboard tire. The outer tread had separated from the tire leaving marks under the wing and flaps.  With an all clear from Airport Rescue and Firefighting and the tire still inflated.; we taxied to the gate without further incident.
column123: Upon reaching cruise altitude; ZZZ [ARTCC] notified us that ZZZ [Tower] had an aircraft departing runway XX out of ZZZ behind us; that saw what appeared to be tire material falling from the aircraft. column121: Our aircraft was parked at the FBO in TEB.  It had been towed into place and backed into a spot alongside other aircraft with our tail facing a hangar.  Aircraft Y; was parked slightly behind us and to our right.  We had a clear path in front of us to taxi out; and we discussed the nose of Aircraft Y being a little close but that we would keep an eye on the distance and taxi slow in case we needed a wing walker.With pax (Passengers) onboard; we cleared the area and started engines; ran the after start checklist; and got our taxi clearance.  Before we started moving; the captain announced 'Clear Left;' and when I looked to clear the right side; I was alarmed to see that Aircraft Y; parked with it's left wing behind our right wing; had begun to taxi forward.  I immediately notified my captain and threw up my arms to the window in an X signal to the other crew as it didn't look like they would clear.  My captain did the same.  The other crew appeared to see us motioning and stopped briefly; but then started moving again and subsequently struck our wing.  To our surprise they continued taxing out toward the runway and we called them on ground to inform them that they had hit us.  They said they didn't realize they had hit us; and we asked if they saw us motioning them to stop.  They said that they saw us motioning but their marshaler signaled them to go.  They aborted their taxi and returned to the ramp.We shut down our aircraft and tended to our passengers.  No one was injured.Suggestions: Suggest that the FBO use wider spacing with no overlap when positioning aircraft.  It is already a tight ramp with a high incidence of collisions.  Crew of Aircraft Y should use wing walkers when necessary and confirm wingtip clearance before moving.  It seems they were in a hurry; and I believe a slower pace could have helped them avoid this as well.
column123: Arriving at FBO X; we were tugged and placed in front of Aircraft Y. Loaded pax (Passengers); briefed and started engines. We gathered our taxi clearance; upon checking left and right; copilot brought Aircraft Y to my attention. From the cockpit it did appear fairly close and at an odd angle; nose pointing slightly towards us; more so than it did on my walk around; where I felt we should clear easily since they were parked behind us. We were discussing how to taxi; either immediately tillering to the left and slowly advancing or calling for extra wing walkers. During this brief discussion; Aircraft Y started moving and attempted to swing hard to their right to try and squeeze out from behind us. Copilot and I were shocked watching them attempt this though recovered and both threw our arms up in an X; universal sign to stop. The crew did stop momentarily; though continued to taxi while we continued to hold our arms in an X in an attempt to stop them. As their wing slid underneath ours; it lifted our wing slightly and dropped it back down as their wing slid clear. The owners saw the event unfold and were as shocked as we were; Person A (one of our passengers) called out the tail number to me as he had a clear view. I hailed Aircraft Y over ground frequency and told them not to take off; that they just struck our wing. They acted surprised. I asked them if they saw my partner and I yelling stop and folding our arms in an X; they replied that they did see us but that the marshaler waved them on so they continued. I believe I responded with 'ok' at that point; I was pretty stunned. I cut the engines; and went back to check on the owners and ensure them a recovery would be in the mix soon. Afterwards; met with authorities; gave a succinct written statement; a verbal statement to the police and met with the FAA shortly. After coordinating with the Chief Pilot and maintenance; applied the AOG and buttoned the jet down.Suggestions: One thing that struck out was the police telling us this happens far too often at TEB. I was unaware of that; at FBO Y south ground ops does a far better job of parking aircraft. FBO X should utilize more marshalers and should use wider spacing when parking aircraft. I can't speak for the crew of Aircraft Y but I would hope they are receiving additional training on spatial awareness and aeronautical decision making; this incident could have been avoided if they slowed their pace.

Once we realized that we were going to have to do a single engine approach and landing; we requested priority handling and told ATC we wanted to return to ZZZ. We followed our checklists. We advised dispatch through ACARS of our situation; we notified the FAs and passengers; and we set up the aircraft for the ILS XXL and ran the QRH checklist for single engine approach and landing. column121: Pre-departure (Doors closed; Jet bridge retracted).After cabin doors were closed and the jet bridge was retracted; ground personnel notified the flight deck of a 'propane-like' odor detected near the aircraft. The source of the odor could not be immediately identified by the ground crew.I immediately briefed the flight attendants on the situation and instructed them to disarm all doors in anticipation of a possible emergency deplaning.Contacted Maintenance Control to report the odor and seek technical guidance. Logged the discrepancy in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook as: 'Ground crew reported propane smell; source undetermined.'Maintenance personnel arrived for an initial assessment and reported that no odor was detectable at that time. However; to comply with fume protocols; Maintenance determined the aircraft needed to be taken out of service for a more thorough investigation.Based on the lack of any detectable odor or smoke in the cabin; I determined that an emergency deplaning/evacuation was not required. I maintained frequent communication with the passengers; explaining that the delay to push was a proactive safety measure to allow Maintenance to investigate an external report. We coordinated with Operations to reconnect the jet bridge; deplaned via normal procedures; and completed a ship change. The flight subsequently departed without further incident.Cause: An unidentified odor reported by ground personnel created a potential safety hazard. The fact that the source was not determined warranted further investigation. The threat of having a fume event in the cabin remained until the source was positively identified.Maintenance requirements necessitated removing the aircraft from service to ensure airworthiness; despite the odor being transient.Early notification to the cabin crew and passengers prevented alarm; primed the crew and passengers to be able to detect any abnormal smell in the cabin; and ensured the crew was prepared for a rapid deplanement if the situation escalated.Staying at the gate and performing a ship change was the most appropriate course of action when the source of a reported combustible smell could not be verified.

column121: While climbing through 10;000ft we noticed a bad smell which became stronger and began to bother us. Given our path ahead we talked about a return to ZZZ as it was only becoming more bothersome. We stopped our climb at 25;000ft and decided to don our oxygen masks and notify ATC of our intentions along with requesting priority handling. We ran all appropriate checklists and set up for the longest runway due to an overweight landing of around 153;000lbs. We planned on meeting ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to inspect our brakes on the runway upon landing. The landing was uneventful and when we came to a complete stop I opened my window and we removed our masks and continued communications via headset / hand mic. This helped to greatly dissipate the odor. With the aid of the fire chief we calculated that we were not in the caution range with our brakes and vacated the runway. We took a few minutes to coordinate some things with the cabin and return to a gate. We requested ARFF to follow us due to a long taxi and check our brakes upon shutdown. They simply said that we were 'ok'. Paramedics met us at the gate as our Flight Attendant was feeling ill. Both Captain and I were not feeling great as well and could taste this strong odor in our throats and elected not to continue with a new aircraft.Cause: The aircraft underwent a check for severe turbulence upon landing and we were told the stick shaker was activated on the previous leg. Possibly this had something to do with the odor.
column123: After departure while climbing through 10;000 we noticed a smell on the flight deck that was becoming stronger and more unpleasant; the FO and myself started to experience discomfort in our throats. I made the decision at that point to return to ZZZ. We donned oxygen masks and established crew communication; I then checked with the flight attendants if there was any odor in the cabin; they told me that there was no odor in the cabin. We requested priority handling leveled off our climb at FL250 and told ZZZ [ARTCC] ATC that we were going to return to ZZZ. We also told him we would need a short delay so that we could accomplish all of the non normal checklists.We received vectors back to ZZZ for runway XX; we asked for and were granted a single frequency approach frequency and called for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to meet us once we stopped on the runway.The heavy weight landing (153;000lbs) was uneventful; when we stopped; we briefed the fire chief to check our brake temperatures. The fire chief reported normal temps.We calculated the brake energy; determined that we were not in the caution range and made arrangements to taxi to the gate. ARFF followed us to the gate. Once at the gate the fire chief rechecked our temperatures and reported normal.We had paramedics standing by to check on our number one flight attendant who felt nauseous and light headed.After landing and once the door was opened she began to feel better and agreed to stay on the airplane until the passengers deplaned.After the passengers disembarked; we discussed the smoke issue with maintenance; and I debriefed the flight attendants.I completed two AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) entries.Cause: None apparent

column121: On Departure from ZZZ and climbing through approximately 14;000 feet; the crew received a Left Engine Oil Pressure High Crew Alerting System (CAS) message (which was intermittent twice more) and there was a positive exchange of controls to the captain as we went through the process to troubleshoot with the QRH2.  Shortly after; this was followed by a Left Bleed Leak.  Crew reduced thrust on the left engine and performed the immediate action item per the QRH2 of addressing the bleeds. We advised ATC of our desire to run a few checklists and need to level off at a lower altitude. Following our checklist (and having known previously that the aircraft had just come out of maintenance for a Left Engine Remove & Replace); crew opted to return to ZZZ and advised Dispatch; ATC; and the passengers of the return. No emergency was declared. ATC recleared crew to ZZZ via vectors and crew continued in for the ILSXXR with no further issues excluding the possibility of an overweight landing. Landing was made smoothly and Thrust Reversers were applied. Once on the ground; crew advised Dispatch; Chief Pilot; as well as Maintenance. The passengers were offloaded as well and kept informed of the situation. Suggestions: We can always use events like these; to improve in many facets; whether it be operationally; procedural; etc..even with events that are caused by a malfunction in the aircraft equipment or system.
column123: Crew elected to return to departure airport due to LEFT ENGINE OIL PRESSURE HIGH EICAS message; this was confirmed with the engine gauges.  The same crew had flown the plane on a maintenance flight check the day prior with no issues. The plane was then subsequently flown to ZZZ on a positioning flight; also without issue.  The OIL PRESSURE light would extinguish then come back three separate times. We also received a LEFT BLEED LEAK. the decision to return was made swiftly; a message sent to Ops. Eventually; both messages would not return; but I did not want to work the engine too hard to possibly re-aggravate the issues. Minimal throttle adjustments were made. The aircraft flew normally during vectors and descending back to ZZZ. We may have landed overweight by (later calculations) 228 pounds.  I did not want to remain in the air with a questionable engine; so elected to land. We did a visual approach to runway XXR; backed up by the ILS. Approach and landing were normal; as was taxi in and shut down. Operations was called then Chief Pilot and maintenance.Cause: Extra fuel had been put on the aircraft before departure due to an ATC reroute.Suggestions: I was confident our weight was not excessive; and did not want to overwork a temperamental engine.  In hindsight; a few S-turns or delay vectors for a short time may have been prudent.

column121: I was operating a flight from to ZZZ. The aircraft was a CRJ-700 without VNAV and with a single FMS. We experienced a low-altitude event during the RNAV XX Y approach into ZZZ. I was pilot monitoring and the captain was pilot flying. Conditions were VME from the initial approach fix until landing. At 4000 ft MSL; we were cleared direct ZZZZZ for the approach. Shortly after; we were told to switch to the tower frequency. At 4000 ft; prior to ZZZZZ; the vertical guidance snowflake had not populated; so the PF initiated a descent to 2700 ft using Constant Speed mode for the crossing restriction at ZZZZZ. The PF then reached up to set 900 ft in the altitude pre-selector for minimums and I confirmed the altitude. Vertical guidance populated shortly after; and the PF adjusted the VS mode descent to track the snowflake. I cross-checked the altitude at the next fix to verify we would meet the crossing restriction. At ZZZZZ1; the approach was stable. The captain then asked what the ref speed was for the approach. I did not remember off the top of my head; so the captain used the FMS to find the ref speed on the LEGS page. I was also heads down; looking at the FMS with him. He found the speed and verbalized it. At that moment; we received a caution obstacle alert. I scanned the Primary Flight Display (PFD); and we were at 1080 MSL crossing ZZZZZ2. The crossing restriction was 1500. At the same time; tower called with a 'Low altitude alert; please check altimeter 29.76'. I responded '29.76; Aircraft X'. The captain disconnected the autopilot and initiated a climb. As soon as I finished responding to tower; I stated that we should be at 1500 ft. After climbing and reestablishing a stable approach; we continued the approach to landing uneventfully.
column123: As pilot flying we were landing GPS XX in ZZZ. When clear for the approach; I armed NAV and set Decision Descent Altitude (DDA) and started down to intercept the snow flake. Once I intercepted the snowflake I shallowed my descent and followed the snowflake and glide path down. We fully configured and completed the before landing checklist. One that was done I glanced outside and we looked low. At this point we were around ZZZZZ on the approach. I looked down and saw we were on the glide path. I decided to pull off the autopilot and level and further analyze what happened and get back on the visual glide path as I already had the runway in sight and was in VMC. As I pulled off the autopilot I ran the altitude we were at vs required altitude for the next fix and we were below it. As this happened all at once we for a too low Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) alert and ATC alerted of a low altitude alert and said check altitude. I also noticed the snowflake shot up and showed the glide path was above us and showed us low. I correct and flew the rest of the approach visually and off the PAPIs. The rest of the approach was uneventful.
