column121: I was flying touch and goes at ZZZ Airport; in Class D airspace. As I was taking off on runway XXR to do the touch and gos on XXL; 2 other planes already in the pattern has just reported significant wind shear on the approach to XXL; in the order of 10-15 knots. The tower when reported 'calm winds' along with the wind shear pilot report. As I came in on final for my first touch and go; I strongly felt the wind shear at about 500 AGL; about 100 yards from the runway. I initiated a Go Around on the first approach and let the tower know the wind shear was still there.On the 2cd and 3rd approaches; I was able to complete the touch and go without a lot of difficulty-the wind shear was still there but I felt it moving farther south away from the approach end of XXL.On the final approach; again I felt the wind shear about 400 yards south of XXL; but is seemed to calm down by the time I was over the runway threshold. The landing was very smooth without any significant crosswind. As was was rolling out preparing to do another touch and go; I reached to raise the flaps; I was going maybe 40-45 knots on the runway at that moment. Very suddenly the aircraft veered hard to the right. I felt if I tried to brake or try too much left rudder the aircraft would tip over; as the plane was moving quite hard and fast. I elected to accept the fact I was going to go into the grass off the right side of the runway. I did not hit any landing lights as I entered the grass. Once in the grass the plane slowed considerably; and I gave it left rudder and a little power and was able to exit the grass and get back on the runway without damaging the plane or any runway lights. The area of the grass I was in was flat and almost level with the runway; so the propeller did not hit the ground during this event.I then contacted the tower; told them I had entered the grass and was back on the runway; and was done doing any more touch and goes. I taxied down the runway to an taxiway and then the tower asked if I needed to stop and check the aircraft for damage. I told them no and was going back to my parking area. They gave my taxi instructions.Once back at the tie down; I inspected the aircraft and it looked undamaged.As to why this happened; I am just not sure. I did not feel I had a significant crosswind on the last landing. I also do not recall my right foot hitting the rudder pedal hard enough to swerve the plane over to the right like it did. I have recorded over 1;000 landings and that has never happened to me before. I also felt like the wind shear was moving away from the airport on the prior landings. The weather was partly cloudy with good visibility and reported light winds; save for the wind shear. The plane taxied with out difficulty and the brakes appeared to be functioning normally before this event. I guess it must have been something I did; but I can not determine what that was. I did have a passenger with me- an old friend who is also an old pilot; he was uninjured.

column121: Prior to the incident; the PIC (Instructor) conducted all appropriate checks on the aircraft; including run-up procedures; to ensure it was in an airworthy condition. After the pre-flight checks were completed; the student (acting PIC) conducted a takeoff briefing with the PIC. This briefing included all required items; including what would be done in the event of an aborted takeoff. After concluding the briefing; takeoff clearance was requested by the student. Takeoff clearance was shortly received; and the aircraft lined up for departure. The student then increased the throttles to verify correct engine performance and that all gauges indicated normal. The student then applied takeoff power and began to accelerate the aircraft down the runway. Both the PIC and the student expected to see the airspeed indicator begin to increase after releasing the brakes. However; the airspeed did not increase. The PIC immediately called 'REJECT' to abort the takeoff; notified the tower; executed a positive exchange of flight controls; and slowed the aircraft back to safe taxi speeds. The aircraft was then taxied clear of the runway and back to parking. Once the aircraft was fully shut down; the PIC exited the aircraft and performed a visual inspection. There was no damage to the aircraft and no hot brake condition. The pilot then continued the visual inspection of the aircraft and was able to identify that the pitot cover had been left on the pitot tube. While the student and PIC did conduct a preflight inspection; both missed the pitot tube cover. While the student is in training and is expected to know how to check for these items; the PIC ultimately is the one responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft and determining airworthiness. The corrective action is for both the student (but more importantly) the PIC to ensure that they are conducting a thorough inspection of the aircraft prior to accepting it for flight using approved checklists. The PIC elected to terminate flight operations for the day to allow the student and PIC the chance to debrief; reflect; and try again on another day.

column121: Climbing through about 34;500 MSL; we felt a sudden jolt and then pretty severe airframe vibration. We initially thought it may have been a flight control issue. Engine instruments were normal until we scanned down to the Vibration (VIB) gauge and noted it was pegged at 5.0. There was definitely a startle factor to the whole thing but upon noting the VIB; we both said we needed to reduce thrust on the left side. I started pulling the power back slowly but the VIB stayed high until I got all the way to idle. Then it settled around 1.8. We noted an odor but it fairly quickly dissipated. I asked the captain to ask for a lower altitude and he found the engine out page in the FMS to get our driftdown speed and altitude. Once we had it I set that in the Mode Control Panel and set max continuous thrust on the right engine. I think at this point I had the autopilot off because it had gone into Control Wheel Steering (CWS) at some point so I just took over until I could get it set back up. We decided to go back to ZZZZ1 so we coordinated that with ATC. We elected to go there because the captain and I both fly in there a lot so we are very familiar; and because we have Air Carrier X ops there. The right engine had all normal indications. We briefly discussed ZZZZ which was almost directly under us; but felt more comfortable going back to ZZZ1. That would also give us more time to run checklists and get set up without rushing through things. Around this time I took over the radios and the captain got into the QRH for engine vibration. I believe he sent a quick message to dispatch that we were turning back to ZZZZ1 and had also answered a call from the FAs. I got us all set up for our approach and landing in ZZZZ1; and after running the VIB checklist we decided to request priority handling so we would have Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) standing by. We discussed brake temps and our planned overweight landing and that we were unsure what was going on with the engine or how much damage it had. At this time we also decided to put on our oxygen masks for the remainder of the flight. I think this was after speaking with the FAs and asking if there was any odor in the back and they said there was a little bit. The initial odor we smelled up front lasted for less than a minute and then we were kind of distracted by the immediate issue of the vibrations and possible damage. Then the smell dissipated. But since the FAs said there was an odor and to play it safe; we donned our masks and established communications; and the captain ran the one engine approach and landing QRH. We never shut down the left motor as the vibration stayed below 2.0 at idle. He asked if I was comfortable landing it and I said I was as long as he would back me up with any info from the Head-up Display (HUD) as far as trends. We discussed the high ref speed due to flaps 15 at just above max landing weight. We completed that checklist and flew the RNP XX. Landed without incident just a few knots above ref; rolled down to the end of the runway and had ARFF check our engine and brake temps before taxiing back to a hard stand. After shutdown; mechanics came up to the flight deck and said there was severe fan blade damage. It appeared that a piece of the spinner hub broke off and was ingested by the engine. It damaged about 5 fan blades and took a quarter sized chunk out of the trailing edge of at least one of them. To prevent in future: Maybe mechanics should be checking for metal fatigue in these older 737-800s. I know we also have engines that run at a high VIB level but below 4.0 and we're requested to let maintenance know about that but just continue operations. Sometimes it's audibly noticeable like your old prop sync is out of whack and I've even had flight attendants call saying it sounds abnormally loud in back. I guess in hindsight we sort of treated this like 'engine severe damage' initially and ran the memory items for that rather than getting the QRH out for high vibration first. Maybe this was the right call and we saved the engine from shredding itself by leaving it at high RPM for too long. I don't think we ever attempted to increase the power on it again after going to idle. The sudden jolt we felt seemed to indicate that something had broken internally and I know we briefly discussed that out loud. We probably should have donned our oxygen masks right away and in the future I would do that as soon as an odor is noted. If it had not almost immediately dissipated I'm sure we would have donned them sooner and I realize that we should have because a fume could've still been lingering in the air. Other things we could have done better - probably should've started the APU in flight and had it ready to use in case the left motor fully seized at some point.

column121: During pushback I started the right engine then asked the mechanic if we were clear to start the left engine. We were told the left engine was clear to start. I get uncomfortable with this period especially when we are starting an engine or the towbar is being disconnected. There are so many things that could happen while the mechanic is unplugged from us. column121: After block out and engines started with after start checklist complete.  We had an ICASS message HEAT P/S CAPT. We briefed prior to takeoff that there may be a discrepancy of airspeed since the system had been worked on.  On takeoff roll the captains airspeed indicator was up to 20kts less than the FO airspeed indicator prior to 100kts.   Above 80 kts and approaching 100kts the airspeed indicators matched within 2 kts.   I elected to continue weather was CAVU and the airspeeds were within reasonable match to continue a normal takeoff.  We had no ICASS messages during takeoff roll.In cruise the Capt and  FO airspeeds stayed within 2-5 kts indicated.   In the descent airspeed indicators also stayed within 2kts   Approach and landing were normal.  During deceleration on landing again below 100kts the airspeed indicators began to separate between the Capt and FO up to 20 Kt difference as we slowed to turn off the runway.  The captains airspeed was again the lower airspeed indicator. Aircraft was written up in ZZZ1 after block in stating the discrepancy in speeds reference above.In ZZZ with the initial write up of HEAT P/S CAPT.   We observed the maintenance crew unbolting; cutting the seal and attempting to remove the Captains Pitot Static Tube.  Is it normal procedure to Defer the CAPT pitot under MEL 30-XX-X-X by just reattaching  the failed Pitot Tube and no further testing or action required?
column123: We pushed back and started normally. After engines were started; checklists complete; and aircraft began to move;  we received a EICAS message HEAT P/S CAPT .  Did the non normal; then called Dispatch and Maintenance Control; the conversation resulted in a Back to Base.Once in the blocks; maintenance ran tests and determined it was the Captains pitot static probe had failed.  They began to work on the airplane and said it would take anywhere from 1.5 to 5 hours.  We returned to the ready room to wait for word from Maintenance.   After an hour; they called and said they were going to defer the item. The deferral was under 30-XX-X-X; in addition to 35-XX-X-X-X.We blocked out again; this time the captain briefed we would watch closely for any anomalies.  On takeoff roll thrust was set. The Relief Pilot mentioned that the captains airspeed was not responding to the movement. As I looked over the captains airspeed jumped up to about 40 kts. At 80 kts the Captains airspeed was trailing the FO and Stby by about 20 knots. The captain said lets see what it looks like at 100 kts. I agreed .  At 100 kts the airspeed on Captain side was within 2-3 kts of FO and STBY.  The Captain elected to continue.In climb and cruise the Captains airspeed was within 1-2 kts.On arrival into ZZZ1 the speed was within 2 kts until touchdown.  After touchdown the airspeed on CAPT side began to deviate as much as 20 kts until we turned off the runway.  The captain decided to write up the deviant airspeed indicator.Unfortunately we could only put pieces together once airborne. Looking back; we all recalled that the Left Pitot tube was being unsealed and removed as we were leaving to go to the break room.  Somewhere in a that hour they decided to just defer the Aircraft.  So what happened to the work that was done?  The same part was put back on the plane; was it pressure tested?  It is my belief that had they not touched the airplane; and just deferred it; that the airspeed would have been fine.

No squealing sound was heard from the tire; so I had no indication that the wheel was locked up until the tire deflated. The blown tire cause drag that pulled the aircraft to the right; but I maintained control and was able to turn the aircraft onto a concrete driveway surface in order to clear the runway. A tug arrived within 10 minutes to pull the aircraft further away from the runway.Cirrus maintenance was contacted with a request for aircraft grounding support and they sent a technician to the location who was able to replace the wheel tire assembly. He stated that the sign-off for the repair would be sent electronically as he had no access to print a label version at that time. I believe that this met the requirement for a sign-off of maintenance performed.We advised the technician that we would be taking off to return to our home base. This technician acted as a runway observer to watch out for deer known to be in the area as I conducted the takeoff.As for the locked wheel; I have long believed that Cirrus Aircraft should install anti-lock brakes on the Vision Jet. This would have prevented this event from occurring.

As part of my routine flight preparation; I failed this day to do a complete check of NOTAMs when reviewing the airport information before takeoff. Upon what seemed a normal arrival and announcement into the airport pattern; I could see some localized work being conducted next to the T hangers at the far end of the runway. The runway was clear; unobstructed; and did not appear to have visible markings. Approach was normal and without event. In preparation to flare as I crossed over the runway end I observed what I first believed to be a cover/possible aircraft cover of sorts wrapped and balled up near the end of the asphalt near the grass edge. With the intent to land and report the debris near the field; I continued. The entire runway was clear and unobstructed. As I was beginning my flare crossing the threshold; I overserved sandbags and quickly realized the airport was likely closed and the debris was likely a fabric X placed originally on the threshold. Given the current wind conditions at the time; (10/12 gusting to 18/20) and the short field I felt the safest course of action was to land and immediately stop as opposed to aborting the landing. Once stopped I shut down and walked down to make contact with personal working to advise them of the condition of the temporary airport marking as well as to arrange to restart and taxi safely to the ramp which were both conducted without incident.

column121: We pushed off the gate and started both engines. We completed the after start checklist and requested our taxi clearance. Upon increasing power on both engines the captain and I heard a loud whirring noise but assumed it was just the engines spooling or coming from the Nose Wheel steering but we both commented that it was louder than normal if it were the engines. Shortly after the noise; the flight attendants called and informed us that white smoke and a burning odor is filling the mid cabin. I informed the captain and we immediately stopped the aircraft. I informed ramp we were stopping and to standby then pulled out the Smoke/Fumes QRC and ran that. During that; the captain elected to turn on the APU and shut down both engines as we didn't have any abnormal flight deck indications and assumed the smoke was engine related because the noise we heard got louder as power increased. After the QRC was completed; I informed ramp and ops we needed a tow back to the gate due to the event. I also informed maintenance of the smoke event and gate return. The captain handled coms with the cabin until his radio panel quit working and he was unreadable over the mic. I then handled all coms inside and outside after that point. A few minutes after engines were shut down we received a PACK 2 OVHT ECAM but we were unsure if that was related to cutting out all airflow into the cabin. We were also receiving a nuisance  RMP 1 FAIL ECAM that would chime every few seconds leading to the failure of the captains coms. After a few minutes; I checked back in with ops to determine the time for a tug to show up because it was getting extremely warm in the cabin with zero airflow. They indicated no more than 5 minutes. Maybe 2 minutes later the tow crew arrived and hooked up to the aircraft. Once they established communication with me; I queried ramp for clearance back to the gate. Once cleared; I gave the clear to tow to the ground crew. I then informed ops that we would like the paramedics to meet us at the gate in case any passengers or crew experienced any symptoms from the smoke inhalation. We returned back to the gate and deplaned the aircraft.

column121: While on the takeoff roll on Runway 28L at SFO at XA:00; a super tug with an aircraft attached taxied from one of the Runway 1s (relatively confident it was 1R) directly up to the edge of our active runway. The speed and timing of their approach left us with essentially zero margin to initiate a safe rejected takeoff had the vehicle/aircraft not stopped in time.The tug was not on Tower frequency; so I did not hear any clearance or acknowledgment. Given the circumstances; I believe a rejected takeoff would have been fully justified. I elected not to call for one only because of trust in the ATC system - a trust that has been called into question recently.There is no hold-short line painted on the Runway 1s. As a result; the tug proceeded all the way to the edge of the white runway designation line for 28L. This created another serious time/distance dilemma for deciding whether to reject. Runway monitoring systems and stop-bar lights on the Runway 1s are presumably inoperative due to ongoing construction and vehicle traffic. Had they been active; the lights on 28L probably could have illuminated given the tug's rate of closure.SFO's runway width is published as 200 feet. Aircraft X exceeds this; as do larger aircraft. While it was impossible to accurately judge lateral separation at night during the takeoff roll; the absence of a hold-short line raises legitimate concerns about wingtip clearance. From my observation; the tug and attached aircraft stopped right at the edge of the 28L runway line.

column121: Boarded in ZZZ. Passengers were the first to notice and report the smell to the flight attendant. As I came on board I also smelled something that was faint but smelled like potential burning oil. I called a mechanic out for a second opinion before writing it up and he came out and said it was definitely not coming from the plane and instead was caused by the belt loader near the aircraft and that once we started engines and pushed back from the gate the smell would go away. We agreed to that plan but once we had pushed back from the gate the smell was still present so we returned to the gate. As far as symptoms go; I had a headache pretty much as soon as I stepped on the aircraft. After taxing out the FO and I both had a strange sensation of a metallic taste which later the #1 FA also commented she had. Upon return to the gate the #1 FA also said she felt slightly nauseous. The crew agreed that we were no longer fit to fly and needed to be seen by medical personnel due to our symptoms. I called the emergency line first who then directed me to call a medical advisory service. The medical advisory service asked about my symptoms during the event and that of the crew members which I explained in detail. Then the medical advisory service asked if any of us were still experiencing symptoms which none of us were. Then the medical advisory service said that in their professional opinion since no one was still having symptoms they would like to medically clear us to fly and continue on the sequence. I explained that we would still be seeking medical care. It took about 20 min with each crew member answering questions before they directed us to go to the Hospital. I was removed from the rest of the sequence and deadheaded home although my schedule does not reflect that at all. It simply shows me ending in ZZZ with no way home. I was told by my chief pilot that it was as if I were removed due to a family emergency. I explained that my schedule was altered due to a company failure to maintain its aircraft; not because I called in sick or with a family emergency. However; due to the lack of contractual language I learned I will not be getting paid for the extra day of the trip. Not only did I lose pay but my schedule for the purpose of FAR 117 work and rest schedules is completely inaccurate.Cause: Oil was found in APU inlet after the fact. This is a known problem with airbus and the mechanic should have recognized it and backed me up in writing it up. Instead he dissuaded me from writing it up and instead convinced me it had nothing to do with fumes coming from the aircraft. In the future I will immediately deboard if I smell anything even slightly abnormal.

column121: We took off from ZZZ normally; and climbing through 13;000' or so we both noticed the secondary engine instruments screen turn on; which only happens when an engine parameter has been exceeded.  We both noticed it right away and looked at what limit was exceeded.  Upon seeing the #1 engine vibrations exceeding 4.0 and varying between .3 and over 4.0 I called for my aircraft and the captain began working on the QRH for the high engine vibrations.  We never felt any vibrations from the flight deck. I reduced thrust in the #1 engine until the vibrations remained within limits; as called for by the QRH.  I had to reduce thrust back to near idle to keep the vibrations low enough.  The captain and I then discussed the situation and decided to return to ZZZ. He had me continue to fly the airplane while he talked to dispatch; ATC; the flight attendants; and the passengers.  While he did this I accepted vectors to a STAR and set up for an RNAV approach to runway XXL.  We discussed an overweight landing; briefed the approach; and landed normally.  We taxied off the runway and then stopped to get checked out by Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF).  They told us they saw no damage so we taxied back to the gate as they followed.  No further abnormalities.Cause: It seemed like just a maintenance issue.  The procedure to blank out the screen with the secondary engine instruments with the idea being that when one is exceeded the screen suddenly turning on would get the pilot's attention.  I have personally flown with captains that both like and dislike this idea. In this instance the screen popping back up worked very well and immediately got both of our attention.

column121: On Day 0; I was the pilot flying on Aircraft X from ZZZ to JAN. On the visual approach for Runway 16L; we started configuring the aircraft with flaps 8 and 20 at about 10 NM on a right base leg. We slowed to the maneuvering speed for flaps 20. We then intercepted final in white needles (RNAV) at about 7 NM from the runway. Then we put the landing gear down; configured flaps 30; and slowed to the straight in speed. We started descending on the approach using vertical speed 0.2 NM prior to the fix HARAG. We then noticed that the PAPIs for 16L were not visible. This caught us off guard because there wasn't a NOTAM saying they were inoperative. The captain tried to turn the lights on using the radios without success. We decided to continue the approach since it was visual conditions and we had an electronic glideslope from the ILS. Reaching 1000 feet; I called out one thousand;" and the captain replied "stabilized; cleared to land." On short final; at about 300 feet above ground level; we got a "terrain" Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) callout; which confused us since we were on the glideslope. A couple seconds later; we got a flaps aural alert; which made us realize we were still at flaps 30. We immediately initiated a go-around. We were then vectored back to a 10 NM final by Approach Control. We continued to a landing without further incident. At the gate; we debriefed the reasons for the go-around.The primary contributing factor for the unstabilized approach was fixation / distraction by the unexpected inoperable PAPIs for 16L. This caused us to forget the final flaps configuration and the before landing checklist. A secondary contributing factor would be complacency with the 1000 feet stabilized call. It can become habitual to say the callout without fully verifying all of the stabilized approach criteria.Going forward; I will focus on preventing distractions and fixation during critical phases of flight; and I will verify all of the stabilized approach criteria at the 1000 foot call. A helpful tool would be to use the "1;2;3;4;5" memory aid to verify proper aircraft configuration. 1 is cleared to land; 2 are the two thrust reversers; 3 is down three green; 4 and 5 are flaps 45."

column121: I am writing this to explain the series of events that led me to run off the left side of the runway on XXL at ZZZ airport on Day 0 at approximately XA:00 and strike a taxiway sign in Aircraft X.Weather at the time of airplane dispatch was 310@13G18. I decided to do a landing lesson with a PPL student pilot to prepare him for his upcoming prog check. Winds throughout our instruction had been variable; gusting up to 24 during our laps in the pattern. During instruction; I was teaching the student how to execute crosswind correction during landing.On the sixth lap in the pattern; while we were in the downwind; the weather conditions at the airport deteriorated rapidly. At this point; ZZZ tower released a weather report stating severe low level windshear; winds 250@20G35; and a dust storm at the departure end of the runway.At this point; ZZZ tower had cleared us for the touch and go; and I instructed my student to turn base for runway XXL. While turning onto the base for XXL; I saw the massive dust storm that ZZZ tower had reported quickly approaching the departure end of runway XXL; blowing left to right. At this point; my student dropped flaps 10.Turning base to final; I instructed my student to come in at 70kts due the excessive wind. He dropped flaps 20. After this; I instructed him to maintain flaps 20 and emphasized coming in at a higher approach speed.Now on short final; I could feel the crab angle required for our ground track to run parallel with the runway increasing as we were descending. The idea for a go around had entered my head; however looking down the end of the runway; I could see the dust storm; at least 800ft tall; moving toward the approach end of runway XXL. Seeing this; I knew going around at our current trajectory would involve penetrating the dust strom at a low airspeed and altitude; and I immediately took the controls with the understanding that I needed to get the airplane on the ground.I was able to use a crosswind landing technique to touch the airplane down on the centerline of runway XXL. I immediately initiated flaps zero and instructed ZZZ tower that this was going to be a full stop. As I was attempting to slow the airplane down on the runway; the nose of the airplane began to drift from the center line to the left at a rapid rate. I immediately acted by exercising full aileron correction left; and full rudder deflection to the right in an attempt to prevent the airplane from weathervaning into the wind. I had reached the control limit of both the aileron and the rudder while still on the runway; but I had lost complete directional control at this point.Now completely at the mercy of the wind; I could see that our direction of movement was veering us off the runway and into a taxiway sign. I initiated full back pressure to reduce as much kinetic energy as possible; causing the airplane's nose to rise. We struck the taxiway sign with the underside of the airplane.Now at a reduced airspeed; I was able to get the nose of the airplane pointed back toward the runway. I allowed the airplane to coast back in the direction of the runway. I did not apply toe break pressure for the sake of preventing the nose landing gear from digging into the grass. We came to a full stop with the right main landing gear on the runway; and the nose wheel and left main landing gear in the grass.The first thing that I did was turn to the student and ask if he was okay. He told me he was. I called up to the tower and told him that everyone on the airplane was okay. I asked tower if we should taxi onto a taxi way. He told me to shut down and stay where I was; and I complied.

column121: A complex go-around created by an ATC landing/take-off conflict led to an undesired aircraft state in which the PM perceived safety was in jeopardy and took control of the aircraft.The flight began eventfully with a passenger and service animal issue that caused a delayed departure. Once resolved; the taxi out through initial approach was unremarkable. The workload and complexity began during the latter stages of the arrival and clearance for the approach.The weather was approximately OVERCAST010 to FEW050 and there was a NOTAM for our landing runway (XXR) that advised 'Special Authorization Cat 1 (ILS) procedure Not Authorized; unless advised by ATC that cranes are down.' As we were cleared for the approach and above the glideslope (~2000' AGL); I directed the PM to inquire on the status of the cranes. We were informed multiple times that the 'cranes are up' and there was an unfamiliarity from ATC about this NOTAM; but eventually a declaration that 'we are authorized for the approach.' Meanwhile; I had disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle; accelerating about five knots; but intercepted the glideslope configured gear/F15; slowing from 165kts to target speed at the FAF/1500' AGL. We briefly discussed that we felt safe continuing the approach; completing the landing checklist prior to 1000' AGL and entering IMC. This phase was the first element of complexity during this approach.Upon breaking out of the weather at approximately 800' AGL; I observed an airplane on the runway and queried the PM if he saw the same thing. He confirmed there was an airplane there; followed by ATC providing instructions to it and the preceding aircraft. Next; we verified stable at 500' AGL and were discussing the probability of a go-around as the aircraft was slow to begin the takeoff roll. ATC instructed us to go around at approximately 300' AGL; but with noticeable closure on the impending lift-off of the other aircraft. I initiated the go around in accordance with the SOP; while offsetting to the right (away from the other runway) and remaining under the weather layer; keeping the departing aircraft in sight. I was unable to verify any of the PM go-around actions as I was primarily concerned about flightpath deconfliction with the other aircraft and verbally said 'what does he want us to do' as I estimated our distance to the other aircraft nearing 3000' nose-tail separation. ATC then gave us a left turn to 060 (nearly across the taking off aircraft's flight path) and climb to 3000' MSL; and after a slight delay; I complied with that instruction; beginning the climb back into IMC. This phase was the second element of complexity during this approach.As we climbed into the weather and I transitioned to instruments; I observed the aircraft passing through approximately 1200' MSL at approximately 12 degrees nose high pitch; but with an airspeed of approximately 190 KIAS and decreasing rapidly with the trend arrow approaching 160 KIAS. I immediately lowered the nose towards 5 degrees nose high as I scanned across the other side of the cockpit to analyze the poor aircraft performance. During this time; I believe I said '(check) Flaps' or possibly 'level change; set Climb Speed (CMS); Flaps 5;' but more attention was narrowly focused on determining the throttle setting/engine performance and aircraft gear/flap configuration. I continued to lower the flight path towards level flight; advanced the throttles slightly; and did observe increasing airspeed; as well as a momentary sink rate of approximately 500' FPM. There was comm from both ATC and the PM during this point that I did not fully interpret while focused on precisely controlling the flight path; while also still attempting to diagnose the performance degradation. At this point; without any Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) aural warnings; the PM perceived 'red terrain' on the Navigation Display and said 'climb' and then 'I have the aircraft.' Obviously; this was also startling; but I released control of the aircraft and tried to make the mental shift to gain Situational Awareness (SA) as the new PM. I did not immediately notice any 'red terrain'; but did perceive a significant increase in pitch attitude. Still without certainty of the flap position; I begin moving the flaps to a lower setting; neither the FO nor I can definitively say who moved the flaps to 5; though we know he did press LVL Change and set CMS at some point in this immediate sequence of transitioning PF/PM roles. While still gaining SA; I observed 'yellow terrain' on our nose starting at approximately five nautical miles and made a request to ATC that 'we need a turn away.' ATC subsequently provided a frequency change; the new PF also said things during this time that I did not fully comprehend. I observed the aircraft continuing to accelerate; nearing 250 knots and I raised the flaps to UP; the 'FLAPS; FLAPS' aural warning also sounded at some point during this sequence of me functioning as the PM. The PF at some point engaged Command B and we cleared the weather back into VMC. This phase was the third element of complexity during this approach.Now on top of the weather with a stable aircraft and on a good vector and altitude; we were able to restore normal CRM; and executed the after take-off checklist. We double checked each other and the aircraft; returned to the original PF/PM roles; completed a descent check; and uneventful landing and taxi-in (though there was still concern/uncertainty regarding the NOTAMs referencing the cranes; but we had not noticed any on the previous approach).  Due to being late; we only very briefly debriefed in the airplane after completing the parking checklist and I said we would discuss prior to the next flight. The FO left the jet as I stayed to wish passengers farewell and apologize again for the inconvenience. Upon exiting; I saw the CA of the next flight on the jetbridge and we discussed the passenger service animal and NOTAM issue for several minutes. I arrived to the next aircraft and began a deliberate debrief with the FO; recognizing that we will probably be late departing. During our discussions; it became apparent to me that we may have oversped the flaps; I then left the middle of our debrief to go back to the other aircraft to inform the Captain of our suspicion; stating that it was less than 10 knots; for less than 10 seconds; at Flaps 5 or less at ~2000' MSL. I returned to satisfactorily continue our debrief; double checking on the fitness of both the FO and my own fitness for duty for the next flight. He stated that he was; I agreed with his assessment; and did not have concerns regarding my fitness. The next flight was conducted uneventfully.To recap and summarize; the slightly varied and out-of-sync SA among the PF; PM; and ATC resulted in multiple missed/delayed comm and lack of shared mental model on the flight deck (degraded CRM); ultimately producing a poorly executed go around.

column121: I was flying at FL350 with FL370 as final. ZZZ Center was the controlling sector during this time. I was given a climb to FL370 at 1;000 FPM or greater. I set the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) to VS +1000 and told the FO that we will monitor the airspeed and bleed off as much as we feel comfortable with or make it to FL370-but not going to get too slow or be dangerous. We started the climb with an indicated mach of .752At approximately 36400 I was 10-12 knots above 1.3VSO and decide thats enough. The FO told ZZZ Center that we can no longer maintain 1;000 feet per minute but can take a turn. We were given 10 degrees left. Then told to turn RIGHT 090. We start the turn and almost immediately told then turn LEFT 300. When turning left the FO goes oh thats because another plane is right below us. I then look at the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and see they are 400 feet below. Immediately we get a TCAS RA to climb. I disengage the automation; go full power and comply with the RA per the procedure in our 737 AOM. When we were clear of conflict I reengaged the automation and continued our climb to FL370. The other aircraft also got a TCAS RA to descend. Then given clear back to ZZZ [VOR].Cause: The climb to 370 was not that imperative-we could have just waited for the other aircraft to pass and climb then. Also there was a SIGMET on the weather app for MOD turbulence up to 350 shortly after Top of Climb. To get above it faster for flight attendant safety and passenger comfort I flew the climb at max rate on the VNAV page which was 256 indicated and that become .752 MACH when we started our climb to 370. Typically we fly 280-300 and then .76-78 so if the conditions allowed a faster climb perhaps I could have had more speed to bleed off to get to FL370. Also with the price of fuel I know we are really paying attention to ECON speeds and everything where our usual 300 and .78 may not be the more desirable speed anymore-but that could have given me more speed to bleed off.

column121: PA30 was approaching the airport and announced a 5 mile final. Cessna proceeded to Runway XX Hold short line and completed final checks for departure. The Cessna pilot made a radio call 'taking Runway XX for departure'.  The PA30 pilot shouted 'Hey we are on short final; what are you doing!'  The Cessna pilot immediately stopped the aircraft approximately 150 feet from the runway edge but beyond the hold short line. The left seat pilot looked again; saw the PA30 and judged the aircraft to be about 1 inch wide on the windscreen. The pilots exchange dialogue for a few moments to verify positions; and eventually the PA30 executed a go-around  which seemed to be several hundred feet above the threshold; Contributing factors: Overcast; grey sky; and Cessna was position perpendicular to the departing runway.  Lessons Learned: Angle the aircraft prior to the hold short line as appropriate to get a clear view of the final approach course. It may have been possible to see the PA30's landing lights.Human Factors: Cessna crew was alert; fatigue was not a factor. Cessna crew used pre-takeoff checklist; and briefed the takeoff prior to departure. The crew heard the distance calls and judged and concurred the separation to be safe and sufficient for departure.

column121: While performing a normal take off for a flight to ZZZ1 oil sprayed onto my windscreen. At the time I was unsure of what the issue was so I began to prepare to land straight ahead. My passenger; another pilot; assisted me by stating that we still had good oil pressure and that perhaps we should go around and land on the same departing runway XX. I agreed; increased power to full; climbed to pattern altitude and told tower that I'd like to land XX. They asked me if I was requesting priority handling and I responded that I was; and that I had oil spray across my windscreen. I was cleared to land on XX; and I landed on XX. Other traffic on final to XX was directed to clear out of the way. I landed; exited via Taxiway 1 to the ramp and taxied back to the hangar. I was met by airport fire / rescue. Upon inspection after shutdown it was found that the oil filler cap wasn't secured or came loose during takeoff / flight. SOP procedures are currently being updated to stop the practice of taking the cap off after flight to allow the crankcase to exhaust. The positives of this practice seem to me to be far outweighed by the negatives. I also have altered my procedures to never fly an airplane that I haven't physically checked that the oil cap and any other removable caps are secure. I've also discussed with CFIs to update my abort briefing to be adjusted that I only land straight ahead or turn back to land in the event of a power plant failure. If I am able to still safely climb; I will do that and return to land on the departing runway.

Upon landing we quickly got to the gate and the EMT came onboard to check on the PAX before the rest of the plane deplaned. I was told the PAX was ok and he was take into the terminal via wheelchair. After this event ended; I called maintenance and MEL'd the portable oxygen bottle as it was used and still indicating 1000 psi.Once we returned to ZZZ1. I had enough time to talk with our flight attendant. She described the situation and told me how the passenger had two portable oxygen (batteries) that are personal. The first tank was depleted on his previous flights and the tank used for our flight became depleted because of the turbulence and his heavy breathing during the flight. our flight attendant described the actions she took and I think she did a fantastic job in addressing the situation. She was filling out her medical form to provide us. However; the turbulence was so strong. It was not feasible to complete that task or for us to reach out to medlink. There were no medical professionals onboard the aircraft.During this flight we had previously requested priority handling. We had the field in sight and cleared for the visual to RW XX. I had selected 2100 which was the faf altituded and was pointing the plane towards the fix to land asap due to situation. ATC gave us traffic to follow and instructed us to turn right an additional 15-30 degrees. We were in a decent at 1000fpm and the 'Terrain Terrain' caution alarmed followed by a warning 'Pull Up'. We were visual with the ground so I disconnected autopilot and climbed to 3000. The alert went away. This occurred about 10 miles east of the final approach course. I then hand flew the rest of the approach and landed without any further issue.Cause: PAX O2 supply became depleted due to heavy breathing with associated turbulence. The actual descent rate exceeded the planes threshold for issuing the warning.Suggestion: Inform pax requiring O2 to come with a greater supply if possible. Priority aircraft should have priority to the field; especially medical in nature. PAX was on O2 with a breathing issue.

column121: We were holding short of runway XX at ZZZ on the east side of the runway. We had just received an IFR release from air traffic control who gave us a three minute void time. There was one aircraft on downwind for runway XX. We made a radio call to the common traffic advisory frequency to advise that we were going to take the runway for departure. As we began to power up past the hold short line; the first officer said stop stop. I stopped the aircraft with the nose just passed the hold short line for runway XX at the approach end. As I looked over the shoulder of my first officer towards the 3 o'clock of our airplane; I saw a C130 approaching low and fast on a severely short approach. The C130 operator had not advised us of his intention to make a short approach. Due to the close proximity and high approach speed of the C130 I chose to stop and remain where we were and advise the C130 our nose was just passed the hold short line. The C130 made a radio call on the common traffic advisory frequency to say they were on left base. In the interest of safety and out of an abundance of caution; I chose to allow the C130 to execute his procedure first before taking the runway. The C130 accomplished a touch and go in front of us and then afterwards we departed without incident.Suggestions: It's incredibly important; especially in an uncontrolled airport environment to be aware of the type of aircraft sharing the airspace. This particular C130 was a firefighting tanker out doing practice maneuvers. The aircraft commander of the C130 never indicated to us the type of aircraft they were or the nature of their fighter pilot type of approach that they were planning on accomplishing. The aircraft descended very quickly from 1600 feet above the runway on a downwind in a hard left bank straight to the runway threshold. This type of approach caught us off guard as we assumed a normal approaching landing which would have given us more than enough time to depart safely without conflict. I'm thankful to the first officer for having his head on a swivel and calling out the closure rate of the surprise maneuver.

column121: The First Officer was the PF. CA was PM and had just finished transition training a few weeks ago. We departed runway XXR in ZZZ; APU Bleed On takeoff. Shortly after takeoff we received an EICAS message for L Bleed Fail. The FAIL light was also illuminated on the L Bleed switch. We continued to climb out on ZZZZZX departure; cleaned up the airplane and ran the after takeoff checklist. We decided to leave the APU on and start running the L Bleed Fail Checklist in case the APU would be needed. The FO continued to fly the departure and took over the radios while the CA ran the checklist. After closing the XBleed per the checklist and working through a few decision trees; the checklist asked if oceanic or high terrain is an issue. There was terrain along our route with the first critical point about 17 mins into the flight. Since we were not there yet; we took that into consideration and continued with the checklist. The next step had us reducing the L Thrust Lever to idle. This step took us both by surprise. The CA tried to scroll thru the checklist to see what the next steps would be and if the engine would remain at idle or be shutdown; but it was too difficult to tell thru the checklist. We determined the best course of action was to contact mx (Maintenance) via dispatch over satcom. We talked with mx to see what they showed and to verify that we needed to bring the engine to idle. They looked thru the QRH and verified the engine needed to be brought to idle; and the need to remain clear of icing conditions. They also showed that the PRSOV (Pressure Regulating Shut Off Valve) was showing failed open. Since dispatch was on; the told us a reroute would be needed to remain clear of icing and they were working with the duty pilot and chief pilot. While the CA was coordinating with mx and dispatch; the FO had pulled up the MEL for the L Bleed Fail. It had a long note about the possibility of a duct burst that could cause a major event." The CA confirmed with mx that a duct burst was a possibility. We were now approaching the first terrain area. There was a broken layer of clouds out ahead of us that would prevent us from remaining out of icing. We were also unsure if we would get engine thrust back. We were dispatched Method 2 and not yet at our cruise altitude. Taking all of this information into account; CA and FO decided the best course of action was to return to ZZZ so we could continue the checklist. The CA informed mx and dispatch of our intentions. Mx agreed and dispatch worked on amending the release. The CA asked dispatch to notify ZZZ ops. The FO notified ATC of our intentions and we were cleared back to ZZZ. Once workload permitted; the CA continued the checklist; reducing the L engine to idle. The checklist permitted use of the left engine upon completion. We were overweight so the overweight checklist was also run. ATC worked us back into the arrival flow and we landed uneventfully in ZZZ. Since ATC provided us with priority handling; CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) was standing by but not needed. We taxied to the gate and wrote up the Bleed Fail and overweight landing."

column121: Departed XXR on the ZZZZZX; FO flying; bleeds off take off.  The usual turbulence in the climb.  Uneventful initial climb out.  After passing ZZZZZ he called for the after take off check about the same time as initiating the right turn in LNAV/VNAV.  Seeing that the aircraft was turning north away from terrain and meeting all vertical path requirements first (flight path forward priority here) thus far I diverted my attention to reconfiguring the bleed panel and ensuring we were pressurizing.  All normal thus far.  Approaching ZZZZZ1 I completed the after take off check list and at the same time the controller called and said we were off course and asked if we needed assistance.  This was both alarming and confusing; but at this time I did notice we were slightly left of the magenta line by maybe one half mile (.5) but he was correcting back.  I checked our altitude to be 6;200 feet - within vertical path limits.  I responded with 'negative he is turning back.'  Controller came back with 'you are below the MVA'.  At this point we were passing ZZZZZ1 and on or above vertical path and returning to the magenta line heading east.  Normal ops at this point handed off to ZZZ center.  I work a fair amount of flights out of ZZZ; I was surprised to hear this from the controller.  We were absolutely never in any position of being in danger of terrain.  It was day VMC and all vertical path criteria were met and as I said maybe 1/2 mile left but pointing where we should be.   I will say this:  in cruise the FO and I de briefed this and he said to me 'maybe it's because I didn't use all the bank' to which when I queried this he mentioned we were heavy it was bumpy he didn't feel comfortable with 25 degrees of bank so he used less.  Intent to fly safely was there; but possibly this contributed to the controller seeing on his radar a slower rate of turn and slight track deviance.  I told the FO that unless we are single engine and below the shark tooth and in VNAV/LNAV we are protected for 25 degrees bank.  The FO is a stand up guy and has time in both seats at two other airlines previously but I do think the lower bank contributed possibly to this.

column121: On a planned IFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; weather conditions at departure were VFR with ceilings approximately 2;800 feet AGL and visibility around 6 statute miles. My planned route was direct from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I received my IFR clearance on the ground from Clearance Delivery with a straight-out departure; radar vectors; maintain 3;000 feet; and expect 6;000 feet ten minutes after departure.After departure; ZZZ Approach subsequently cleared me to 4;000 feet and later to 6;000 feet. The aircraft appeared to be operating normally during the climb. At approximately 2;800 feet MSL; I entered IMC conditions. The operation was single-pilot; hand-flown; and conducted without autopilot assistance.While climbing through approximately 5;000 feet MSL and about 8 NM northwest of ZZZ; I heard an abnormal noise through the intercom/headset system. Shortly afterward; I observed an undervoltage indication on COM 2; and the ammeter showed a discharge condition consistent with a possible alternator or electrical system malfunction. Immediately after observing these indications; I lost two-way radio communications with ATC.I attempted to reestablish communications with ATC and squawked transponder code 7600 for lost communications. Due to concern over a potential alternator failure and possible continued degradation of electrical systems while operating in IMC; I elected to begin a descending left turn toward known VMC conditions; which I knew existed below approximately 2;800 feet. At the same time; I accomplished checklist procedures to reduce electrical load by turning off nonessential electrical equipment in an effort to conserve battery power and restore communications capability.At approximately 3;500 feet MSL; I was able to reestablish communications with ATC. ATC subsequently cleared me back to ZZZ via visual approach and assigned 3;000 feet. Shortly thereafter; I exited IMC conditions. I advised ATC of my intention to cancel IFR in the air; however; full communications were lost again immediately afterward. I again squawked 7600 and proceeded to enter the traffic pattern at ZZZ; landing without further incident.In hindsight; I recognize that the published IFR lost communications procedures could have been followed after the initial communications failure. However; during a high-workload; single-pilot IMC situation involving a suspected alternator failure; I prioritized returning to VMC conditions and landing as soon as practical. Additionally; after communications were briefly restored; I believe it would have been beneficial to request priority handling and request direct routing back to ZZZ. At the time of the initial communications failure; I attempted to request priority handling but was unable to confirm transmissions were being received and therefore selected transponder code 7600 under the assumption ATC would recognize the abnormal situation.

column121: During a recent cross-country flight; I departed with full fuel and conducted fuel tank changes approximately every hour after the initial 30 minutes of flight. En route; I continued monitoring fuel burn and engine operation; and no abnormal indications were observed during the flight. However; as the flight progressed and fuel levels decreased; I did not adjust my fuel management strategy to a more conservative approach. Specifically; I should have switched tanks more frequently at lower fuel levels and should have more seriously considered making an additional precautionary fuel stop.While complying with ATC instructions during the arrival and landing phase into ZZZ; I began noticing engine roughness. Recognizing the potential seriousness of the situation; I immediately contacted the tower and requested an immediate landing. ATC accommodated the request; and the aircraft landed safely without further incident. After landing; it was determined that approximately 10 gallons of fuel remained onboard.The issue arose primarily from inadequate conservatism in my fuel management decision-making. Contributing factors included over-reliance on planned fuel burn calculations; confidence that the remaining fuel quantity was sufficient; and failure to fully appreciate the reduced margin for error as fuel levels became lower. Although the aircraft landed safely with approximately 10 gallons of fuel remaining; I later recognized that my operational decisions unnecessarily reduced available safety margins.The concern was identified during post-flight reflection and review of the flight. After evaluating the circumstances; I realized that while regulatory fuel requirements may still have been met; my decisions did not reflect the level of conservatism and risk management expected for safe aeronautical decision-making. In hindsight; an additional fuel stop would have significantly improved the safety margin and reduced operational risk.From a human performance standpoint; several judgment and decision-making factors contributed to the situation. My perception during the flight was that fuel status remained acceptable based on calculations and expected fuel burn; however; this perception reduced my willingness to make more conservative operational choices. Plan continuation bias and confidence in the original flight plan likely influenced my reluctance to stop for additional fuel. Additionally; I recognize that I did not sufficiently account for the increased importance of proactive fuel management as usable fuel decreased.Corrective actions taken since the event include additional study and review of aircraft performance data; fuel burn calculations; and fuel management procedures. I have reevaluated my personal minimums and fuel reserve standards and will adopt a significantly more conservative approach moving forward. In future operations; I will switch fuel tanks more proactively when fuel quantities become lower and will not hesitate to make additional fuel stops whenever they improve operational safety margins.This event served as an important learning experience regarding aeronautical decision-making; risk management; and fuel planning discipline. I take full responsibility for my decisions and will continue working to improve my judgment; situational awareness; and operational conservatism in order to become a safer and more professional pilot.
column123: During a recent cross-country flight; I was onboard the aircraft as a passenger/backseat occupant while another pilot was acting as PIC. column121: Summary:  I experienced a low speed runway excursion on landing; in a lightweight tailwheel airplane without differential brakes; due to the airplane weathervaning into the crosswind against a full opposite rudder input.I went for a 1.3 hour personal flight in a Sonex Waiex airplane out of ZZZ airport.  Due to preparations for an upcoming airshow; runway XX/XY was closed; and the airport was operating on runway XZL with winds from 200 degrees at 8 kts.  When returning for landing; the ATIS stated the wind had increased to 12 gust 19; creating a significant left crosswind condition.The Waiex is a tailwheel (conventional landing gear) airplane without differential brakes.  It has a single hand brake; and the tailwheel is steered with a pushrod link to the rudder.  It is an experimental amateur-built airplane.As I began the landing flare; I was using nearly full right rudder to align the aircraft heading with the runway; but was able to align it and opted to continue the landing.  The landing roll initially stayed straight; then the airplane began to weathervane left into the crosswind as I slowed; and the airframe began to shudder due to the rightward deflected tailwheel skidding on the pavement (the crosswind on the tail surfaces overpowered the traction of the tailwheel).  The airplane rolled off the edge into the grass at 20-25 kts and came to a stop about 30 feet from the edge of the runway; nearly aligned with runway heading.I notified tower that I had departed the runway into the grass due to crosswind gust exceeding my control authority; had not hit anything and would like to taxi clear; and tower cleared me to taxi back onto runway XZL and then exit at Taxiway 1.  From Taxiway 1 I contacted ground control and taxied back to the hangars.  There was no damage or evidence of the runway excursion on the airplane.

column121: I was on a pleasure flight taking a pilot rated passenger who had never flown in a tailwheel aircraft. I was PF from the rear seat. It was a nice VFR day; with winds reported by tower as 310/9 knots. We entered a right downwind for runway XX and I took control of the aircraft to make the landing. I flew a normal approach; compensating for the right crosswind; and touched down in a three-point attitude. During the rollout; I lost directional control and the aircraft ground looped to the right; exiting the right side of the runway. We stopped in the grass just off the edge of the runway. I estimate the speed at which point directional control was lost was less than thirty mph. Tower asked if there were any injuries or damage; we replied negative and that we could re-enter the runway and taxi to the next intersection and exit. We did so; were handed off to ground control and then continued back to the hangar. After shutdown I did a visual inspection of the aircraft and noted no damage.Contributing factors as I see them were a right quartering tailwind which was different than reported by the tower. As we taxied by the windsock I noticed the direction appeared to be northerly or northeasterly than the tower had reported. Another factor was that I have limited time flying from the rear seat. The majority of my 7AC time has been from the front; this was only my second landing from the rear seat in several years.In retrospect; I should have requested runway XY or XZ to mitigate the crosswind and tailwind components. I do not feel a go around would have been appropriate; as the speed at the initiation of the ground loop was very low.

Although I hold an active FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate and have approximately 150 hours of small UAS flight time; this flight was conducted recreationally as detailed in the LAANC authorizations. The drone was equipped with the required anti-collision and navigation (NAV) strobes: one top-mounted Firehouse Technology ARC PRO (flashing white on top) and four additional ARC PROs (flashing red on the port side and flashing green on the starboard side). These strobes and mounts increased the takeoff weight (TOW) of the drone to 352 grams. I maintained visual line of sight (VLOS) with the sUAS throughout the entire flight. My home is located just outside the controlled airspace of both ZZZ and ZZZ1.I was flying under two active LAANC authorizations (ZZZ) (ZZZ1). Both authorizations were valid from XA:00 to XM:00 and authorized a maximum altitude of 300 feet AGL.Purpose of the flight: I intended to take photographs of Aircraft Y that was on approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. The approach path passes almost directly over my house. I had not set the drone's maximum altitude limit to 300 feet AGL before takeoff because I originally planned only a very short flight to capture the photos; land; and possibly fly again later (the LAANCs remained valid until XM:00. I climbed to approximately 385 feet AGL. Aircraft Y was approximately 0.25 miles west of my location at 2175 feet AGL when I was taking the photos. After taking several photos; I continued southeast to perform a loop. During this maneuver; I crossed into ZZZ1 airspace while still at 385 feet AGL (where the authorized maximum was only 300 feet AGL). I immediately turned north after crossing the highway and entered a grid with a 400-foot AGL maximum; but I remained at 385 feet AGL (still above my LAANC clearance of 300 feet). Continuing north; I then turned west at Road X (crossing into Class G airspace) and proceeded to the intersection of Road X and Road Y. While circling south near Road Y; I realized I had been operating above the altitude authorized by my LAANC. I immediately returned to my residence; landed safely; and began preparing this report. I am submitting this report voluntarily to promote aviation safety. I will provide my complete flight log and any additional information or data requested.

column121: Aircraft X was delivered to the FBO for annual inspection. After initial completion of the annual inspection; a pre-return to service run-up about a month later revealed a fuel leak on the right engine. Both engines' throttle controls and fuel assemblies; because they were the same vintage; were removed and sent to Company X for overhaul. Both throttle controls and fuel assemblies were overhauled and reinstalled; and the aircraft was returned to service on Day 0. I arrived at ZZZ to pick up Aircraft X on Day 8. After an extended pre-flight; I executed a runup to the tarmac. All engine indications were normal; oil pressures; oil temperatures; cylinder-head temperatures (CHT); fuel flows and exhaust gas temperatures (EGT). The runup was as usual with appropriate indications of oil-pressure and RPM drops as the propellers were exercised. I requested a taxi for full-length of the Runway XX; but changed to an intersection take-off at Taxiway 1. Take-off procedures were normal; i.e.; brakes held until released and engines' indications in the green. Take off roll was normal with full RPM's; manifold pressures; and fuel flows. I extended my upwind flight along the runway center to 500' AGL; then entered a turn crosswind. That is a point at which I normally start another check of the engine instruments; starting with the EGT on the far right of the panel and working left across the RPM; throttle; and mixture in the middle of the panel; then to the lower left for the triple gauges and oil pressures; oil temperatures; and cylinder head temperatures; briefly before a normal RPM reduction to 2500 RPM at traffic pattern altitude or about 1000' AGL. That check showed the left engine EGT spiking to maximum temperature. I called ZZZ Tower for a return to the runway stating I had an instrument problem. The crosswind turn required additional right rudder to correct a slight roll; which keyed me to check the other indications for the left engine. They showed low RPM; low MP (Manifold Pressure); and zero fuel flow. I then automatically pushed all engine controls forward; which they mostly were anyway at that stage of flight. Because of the aircraft's known single-engine climb capability at ZZZ's elevation; I was able to obtain 800' AGL to 1000' AGL on downwind. After executing the emergency checklist; I adjusted the downwind-to base and base-to-dual turns to accommodate the critical engine out; extended the landing gear and flaps and landed on Runway XX; rolling out to Taxiway 1 and eventually taxiing to Taxiway 2 to exit the runway. The aircraft is undamaged and no one sustained an injury. Another aircraft on Taxiway 2 reversed and exited the taxiway as ZZZ personnel and the fire truck arrived. After shutting down both engines and securing the aircraft; I was handed paperwork by the ZZZ airport personnel; which I filled out. The maintenance shop was notified and came out to tow the aircraft back to the shop. Post event; the maintenance shop found a loose connection on a left engine fuel system hose which may have admitted air enough to disrupt normal mixture control. Further; after the event and after additional runups; the left engine boost pump was found to exhibit low pressure and is being replaced. Currently the aircraft is still in the shop awaiting the new left engine boost pump. An additional flight test upon return to service is anticipated. On the human performance considerations; a positive factor is my more than 1000 hours in this aircraft and regular participation in type; make and model specific re-currency training programs. These programs over the years made my responses to this event practically automatic.

column121: I was training a trainee on sector XX. The sector wasnt super busy but for him at 25% hours; it may have felt slightly busier. The complexity turned fast when Aircraft X went missed at ZZZ on the ILS Z Rwy XX because of wind shear. Aircraft X was a chinese speaker and definitely didn't understand english perfectly nor did he understand approach procedures correctly. More on that in a minute. After going missed; we vectored Aircraft X and another aircraft toward Rwy XY at ZZZ. Aircraft X was then giving instructions to fly to ZZZZZ direct ZZZZZ1 direct ZZZ for the RNAV X Rwy XY. Procedurally; if you do the approach over ZZZZZ; then there is no procedure turn authorized. Well; Aircraft X did the procedure turn! And as we had another aircraft right behind him; the complexity shot through the roof. I tried to handhold my trainee because I think I have a solid amount of experience and could help him through the situation. I think I did a pretty good job. So I was speaking to my trainee during most of his transmissions. I told my trainee to cancel the back aircrafts approach clearance; maintain 130 thousand; and make him do a left 360 for spacing. As soon as my trainee gives that clearance; Tower calls us to switch the runway again! Which in turn; brings more complexity to the situation. My trainee cancels the approach clearance of Aircraft X. Once that happens; the back aircraft requests something that we dont quite hear; and thats when I step in. I tell the back aircraft that Tower just switched runways on us; and to fly back to Runway XX; and climb him to 140 thousand knowing that my next move would be to climb Aircraft X. Then Aircraft X asks if he should be on a heading. He was currently climbing through like 123 thousand; and flying through a 120 thousand MIA box; but was going to momentarily be in a 129 thousand MIA box. My Trainee told Aircraft X to fly heading 070 which I knew wouldnt be good in a moment. So I keyed up and told Aircraft X reaching 130 thousand to fly heading 270 which would get him away from the other aircraft and be good with terrain. Aircraft X never turned to the heading my trainee gave; and technically did go into the 129 MIA box at 128 thousand briefly before reaching 130 thousand and turning northwest bound. The aircraft never turned below terrain and I felt that we handled the situation very well and the trainee and I both learned some things.RecommendationMy trainee thought he was doing the correct thing by terminating the approach clearance for Aircraft X; when in retrospect; we should have told him to fly the published missed approach and climb to an appropriate altitude to stay separated from our other aircraft and terrain. I think once we did cancel the clearance for Aircraft X we had our hands tied and I think the next course of action we took was the correct one; except we should have issued a low altitude alert as well!My only other recommendation would be for Aircraft X and that would be to correctly learn that procedure turns have to be authorized from a controlled if they are charted non-authorized in the pubs. We never had a chance to talk to Aircraft X again about that as we needed to finish cleaning everything else up from all the missed approaches and runway changes.

column121: Departure and climb were routine. I was the Captain/PM and the First Officer was PF.After leveling off; we received an L HYD RESV EICAS message. We accomplished the applicable QRH non-normal checklist; which did not resolve the issue. A review of the status page indicated left hydraulic quantity decreasing; suggesting a system leak. Based on indications; we anticipated progression to L HYD SYS PRESS.The leak appeared slow; and after reviewing the L HYD SYS PRESS non-normal checklist; we assessed that continuing to destination was acceptable. We contacted dispatch via SATCOM; requested Maintenance be advised; and asked for concurrence on continuing. Dispatch confirmed preference to continue to ZZZ.We advised Dispatch that we would likely request priority handling in the terminal area and anticipated the need for a tow off the runway. Requested they notify ZZZ operations.Approximately 30 minutes later (about 90 minutes from ZZZ); we received L HYD ENG PUMP. We accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the engine-driven pump within approximately 90 seconds of the EICAS message.Approximately 5 minutes later; we received L HYD SYS PRESS. We accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the electric pump within approximately 60 seconds.  Dispatch was updated and confirmed all parties had been notified.We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center upon check-in and were vectored toward ZZZ. We requested direct ZZZZZ (final fix on the ZZZZZ arrival) to support our configuration planning.The First Officer and I developed a configuration plan; including Flaps 1 at ZZZZZ. Subsequently; ATC issued a STAR change to ZZZZZ1 arrival; and we requested direct ZZZZZ1; which supported our plan.We were initially advised to expect the ILS XXL and completed the approach setup and briefing. Approximately 20 NM from the airport; ATC reassigned us to ILS XXR. I initially declined due to workload; but advised ATC we could accept XXR if doing otherwise would disrupt the ZZZ operation. After being cleared for the ILS XXR; we were unable to obtain a valid localizer ident or glideslope. Upon query; ATC advised the ILS was out of service and offered the RNAV approach. Due to proximity to the airport and workload; we declined the RNAV and advised we would need to execute a missed approach with the gear remaining down the rest of the flight. ATC issued a  heading and climb to 3000 ft. ZZZ Approach then offered the ILS XXL; which we accepted. The remainder of the approach was uneventful.The First Officer performed the landing. I assumed control at approximately 100 knots for rollout. Rollout was uneventful. A company tug met the aircraft and towed us clear of the runway to parking.The CRM training we received was extremely helpful to us in navigating the challenges we faced as a crew. We were task loaded with a complicated non-normal checklist. We had multiple changes by ATC  on the arrival.  Specifically; reviewing the checklist before executing it; developing a what if plan such as considering an unanticipated missed approach with the landing gear down and the flaps in the alternate configuration; and using our resources such as ATC and dispatch to obtain support in the terminal area.  The company procedures also prepared us well for this challenge.  A recent intensified focus on fuel planning led to an enhanced awareness of our fuel status; which became critical on the missed approach. We both experienced this situation in the simulator many times so we felt very well prepared for this event and felt we; as a crew; maintained good situational awareness.For an aircraft operating under distress with a complex non-normal checklist; the number of late changes (arrival and runway assignment) significantly increased our workload. Minimizing changes in the terminal area would improve safety and reduce crew task saturation.

column121: At approximately XA:00 in ZZZ. I was occupying the right seat of Aircraft X with my partner that day in the left seat. We have completed dual route verification and we doing our pre-departure briefing. We got up to the before start checklist. At that time ground control called us and told us one of our globals was returning to the ramp and they might need to switch airplanes with us. At that point we got out of the cockpit. The parking brake was inadvertently turned off during this process. Next we were standing in the back waiting for the company airplane to park. Then at or around this time Aircraft X started to roll forward down the sloped ramp. The airplane rolled approximately 30 to 50 feet where my partner reoccupied the left seat and applied the brakes. No damage to the aircraft or any other aircraft was done.Suggestions: This was classic case of task interruption. Our company has very specific procedures on the removal of chocks and the occupying of the pilot seats during the removal of chocks. Proper and immediate adherence to these procedures would've prevented this from happening. I would recommend in training we talk about the procedures we do every day and verify if we're actually doing procedures correctly. I would respectfully suggest covering procedures such as towing; jet blast on the ramp; chock removal; the discharging of coffee or ice and other liquids on the ramp. Also vehicle operations on the ramp around our airplanes; These but a few things that might be covered and reminded during training. I would further suggest some additional day to day operations that need covered include uncontrolled airport ops; standard instrument departures with an engine failure after the divergent point.I am not trying to shift blame from what was most probably my error. What I am suggesting is sometimes we need to reaffirm the day-to-day operation and make sure we're doing things correctly.

column121: On flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; I was the PF and the Captain was the PM. Departure; climb; and cruise were normal. We were cleared to descend from 4;000ft to 3;000ft. While descending into ZZZ at approximately 3;500 feet; we were cleared for the visual approach to Runway XX. During the approach; the left engine fuel flow indication displayed 0 PPH. The left mixture was moved full forward. The PM referenced the QRH and no checklist item was identified specifically for a 0 fuel flow indication. The PM notified Operations of the indication issue and potential write-up; and requested Runway XY. ATC cleared us for landing on Runway XY.At approximately 3;000 feet; left engine roughness was noted. The PM selected the auxiliary fuel pumps to LOW. Following an RPM drop; the PM selected the auxiliary fuel pumps to HIGH. Engine roughness continued. Ran memory items. Reduced thrust from the left engine was observed and additional right rudder was required to maintain coordinated flight. Airspeed was maintained above Vyse. The PM accomplished the engine inoperative in-range and approach checklists in the QRH. The crew briefed continuing the approach in the current configuration due to the left engine continuing to produce partial power. At that point the aircraft was turning base to final. The approach and landing on Runway XY were otherwise normal. A positive exchange of controls took place and the Captain assumed control of the aircraft during the landing rollout.After landing; I briefed the passengers regarding the presence of vehicles approaching the aircraft. The left engine subsequently lost all power after exiting the taxiway. The aircraft was secured without further incident.
