column121: Soon after takeoff from Rwy XX in ZZZ; the secondary eicas came on to show a partial compact engine indication.  Eng #1 oil quantity was down to 1.We were not surprised.  The previous crew had reported their engine oil quantity having dropped after heir takeoff from ZZZZ and maintenance in ZZZ had topped off the #1 oil by 11 QTS.The oil pressure was slowly decreasing; but without any eicas msgs I decided to continue climbing as much as we could because of the mountains ahead and below us.  We were very heavy; about 355 Tons.Some time later; the ENG 1 OIL PRESS advisory msg came on.  With oil P below the red line limit; the qrh directed us to shut the #1 engine down.  We continued to climb but only to 29;000 Ft to comply with the FMC engine out drift down guidance.15 or minutes later; I was in the process of telling the crew that I preferred not to return to ZZZ (RVRs reporting around 2000) and were about to call dispatch; when the HYD PRESS DEM 1 msg came on.  The hyd quantity was good; so I suspected a failed pump perhaps.Some time later and without an operating eng #1; the HYD PRESS SYS 1 msg came on.I was familiar with this qrh procedure; having done it at the training center a few times.   Gravity landing gear extension would be needed and the flaps would be on secondary mode.  My mind was then made up to continue to ZZZ1 where I was very familiar with the airport.  The weather forecasts I had obtained at the hotel before departure were good and were now checked again to be great.  No threat of nearby mountains like ZZZ and the winds would be almost lined up with the long ZZZ1 rwys.We sat-called dispatch/maintenance and after explaining our predicament; they were in agreement that continuing was the better option.  I was concerned that if ZZZ1 refused to handle our emergency arrival; we'd have to go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 (our planned alternate) but ZZZ1 fortunately agreed to handle us.  I insisted with the dispatcher that we'd need a tug to tow us off the rwy.It was at about this time that I took over PF duties from my FO.  I was going to let him fly and land the plane with an engine inop; but not with the #1 hyd system gone also.The former PF FO; now PM then did an amazing job of balancing fuel which became the real focus and hassle for the rest of the flight.We had advised ATC after shutting the engine down much earlier; but the ZZZ Center controller took it upon himself to give us priority handling.  I was glad he had done so; as I suspected that priority handling to still be better understood to everyone; as opposed to our declared advising".ZZZ1 had reserved their longest rwy; XXR for our arrival.  I managed to keep the plane on the rwy CL with the rudder and an occasional tap on the left or right brake as needed; but was happy at how steady the 747 remained without nose wheel steering.The good people of the ZZZ1 FD (Fire Department) had dispatched 4-5 trucks and did a visual inspection of our plane and #1 engine.  They reported seeing nothing unusual.The tug pre-arranged by the dispatcher and ground operations was waiting and promptly towed us to the ramp.After blocking in; the mechanics opened the nacelle on engine #1 and saw a lot of oil (or hydraulic fluid; they said they didn't' know which) pour onto the ground.I called ground operations the next day to ask if someone had determined by now why we had also lost hyd system 1 after losing the  #1 engine.  They said they really couldn't be sure.  They suspected either a failed demand pump or the entire accessory gear box having failed.  They were considering changing the entire engine.Cause: Not sure.  The engine had a massive leak of oil to the outside of the engine; not inside.  The previous crew experienced a loss of engine oil in ZZZZ; but never got an eicas msg; so didn't shut the engine down and continued all the way.I thought operations was closely monitoring the engines and trends remotely from their office.  Maybe everyone was off.Suggestions: I was concerned that in secondary mode the flaps would take longer to deploy than in the simulator.  I voiced my concern to my FOs and briefed that I would slow down early.  I really didn't want to go around because I had not allowed enough time for the gear and flaps.The qrh says to allow extra time for flap extension from 1 to 5 (4 minutes).  I slowed down and asked for flaps much too soon; before downwind.  I timed the flap extension with the stop watch.  It took only 3 minutes and 30 seconds.  The gear came down in alternate mode with all greens indicated in about a minute; or so.  If this ever happens to me again; I won't slow down and configure so early."

column121: First flight since annual and also my first flight in months. Pre-flight checks were perfect so I proceeded onto runway XX. I took the runway and powered up half way well holding brakes to make sure engine data was good before releasing brakes and going full power. Plane had lots of power and took off as expected with all engine data as expected. I turned cross wind at pattern altitude 2400 feet; raised the flaps and started reducing manifold pressure to 25'. I then started to reduce RPMs as I started the downwind turn as I had climbed to 2600 feet. At this point the engine went to idle and fuel pump alarm came on. I turned on vapor suppression pump and switched tanks from left to right. This made no difference so I turned off vapor suppression and pressed the primer button. This brought the power back temporarily; at this point I announced aircraft in distress and intent to land runway XY and asked traffic starting on runway XX if they could clear runway XX. They were able abort takeoff and vacate . During call I had pressed fuel primer again this added power again and put me a little higher than expected and over XY. I did a S type descent deploying speed brakes and landing flaps to runway XY and engine died on rollout. I believe this because I forgot to turn on fuel vapor suppression on rollout.My first move should have been to turn back for runway XY and 2nd move to turn on backup fuel pump instead of vapor suppression and switching tanks. I need to review my emergency flight procedures well sitting in airplane so I can 'dry' practice as part of keeping current. I believe I did well. I had delayed this flight many days due to not feeling up to par; busy traffic pattern and sub optimal weather.

column121: At just past XA:00 on Day 0 I was returning from ZZZ to LOM and requested RNAV 6 from PHL Approach Control (123.8) for practicing my IFR flow (the field was visual). A request that was accepted by PHL Approach. I was directed to the LASBE (IAF-RNAV 6) and cleared for the approach. On turning to the final approach course; I told PHL approach that I had visual of the field. They advised me that there was no traffic observed. At this time; I canceled my IFR. I switched to CTAF and made a 9-mile final call on the CTAF; followed by a 5-mile final call; followed by a short final call. I did a quick scan of the runway on short final; and everything looked good to land.As I touched down; I see a plane on 24 at the opposite end of the runway; and that is the first time I heard him. His call was to warn me of his presence on the runway. He had just rolled on to 24 and was fortunately stationary at that end. There was no danger of any collision since I stopped within 1500 feet or so of touchdown and taxied off the runway. Once the runway was clear; the other plane departed as soon as I was off the runway. When I walked into the FBO (there is a speaker tuned to CTAF); the people there told me that they heard my 3rd call - the short final call; but not the first two (or did not pay attention). They said they never heard the other plane till he piped up to warn me of his presence when I had already touched down and I was on my landing roll. What did I learn? When I am on a short final; I am generally focused on the touch down point; typically the numbers at LOM; and once I pass the threshold and begin my level out and flare is when I raise my eyes to the end of the runway. I think that is what I did on this landing as well and by the time the presence of the plane at the other end registered with me; I was on the ground and slowing down. It was too late to go around. I should not assume that the runway is mine even if I have been making calls; scanning and hearing nothing on the radio. I should always be more watchful and continue scanning the entire runway environment; including at this late stage in my landings.

column123: Previous crew told us they had seen a RA flag on previous flights but did not write up because it quickly disappeared. Our preflight and taxi was normal. We chose to continue as the plane was stable and we had the runway in sight. I tried to trim the plane but electric trim was not working. I told the captain who took control and also could not operate electric trim. He continued flying while I manually trimmed the airplane for him. We requested priority handling out of an abundance of caution and elected to continue the approach since we felt a go around with no trim could put us into an undesired aircraft state. column121: Flying the visual approach backed up by the ILS 3. Prior to commencing the approach; it was briefed with knowledge of terrain and obstacles; and I had my terrain display present on my MFD. I was PIC and PF.ATC provided us with a descent down to 3000' at midfield downwind; and then provided us with an initial base leg vector; prior to receiving clearance for the visual approach. Being approximately 5 miles from the FAF SIPME and already on a tighter base leg; I requested 2600' to beset in the altitude selector; which is the minimum altitude at the FAF SIPME. After being cleared for the visual approach; the plan was to continue the descent down to the minimum altitude at the FAF and capture the glideslope.At about 4600' and recognizing that we were slightly high turning into our base leg; I increased the descent rate briefly in order to trend towards the glide slope intercept altitude. After I recognized that we were trending towards it I began to intermittently shallow our descent out; ultimately setting less than -1000 FPM as the final vertical speed setting. At no point did we descend below the minimum segment altitude prior to the FAF of 2600'.At approximately 3 miles from the FAF SIPME; and approximately 2700 - 2800 feet; we received Terrain Terrain Pull Up." I initiated the escape maneuver; but almost immediately after initiating it and having a pitch up attitude; the terrain caution concluded. Since this message cleared almost instantly with a slight pitch up attitude; and no visual obstacles were in our path; it was determined that we were clear of the terrain threat. Being in complete VFR; and back to a desirable aircraft state at an appropriate speed prior to the FAF; I determined we were in a safe position to continue and execute the approach. We proceeded inbound to complete the approach; having no exceedances or other events occur.Afterwards; we had noted on the Jeppesen Approach plate that the approximate location just prior to receiving the terrain caution has terrain listed at 1785'. I had briefed terrain and the highest obstacles; but what could have been done better is to emphasize this specific point as it pertains to my descent plan for the approach. Being in VFR conditions; we had maintained a visual on the terrain prior to the base leg; and it wasn't until we were above it that it was out of sight.In hindsight as PIC and PF; recognizing that we were high and having been turned onto a shorter base leg; this could have been preemptively resolved by communicating with ATC; and potentially even requesting vectors to provide more time to descend.As a crew we debriefed this event on the ground; and talked in depth about exactly how this could've been prevented. We concluded that more in depth briefings on the terrain we will encounter at specific points; a more clear and shallowed descent plan; and avoidance ofcomplacency in VFR conditions could've worked to prevent this from occurring."

By this time most messages had cleared. Around 25k I engaged the yaw damper. I then asked for lower at which point they gave us shock at 12k. We determined the system was back online and engaged the autopilot. At this point the system was still only using GPS 1 and AHRS 2 was in backup GPS and AHRS 1 was not online. We then told Albuquerque we seemed to be back online and things seemed ok. We got cleared to YOLOW at 7k and I called the airport in sight and got cleared the visual. column121: Was conducting a repositions flight for Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 after dropping off a different diamond in ZZZ that same day. Everything was routine/ normal / in limits until about 300 ft - 400 ft AGL in the upwind. Noticed an abnormal noise/ slight vibration/ engine roughness coming from the left engine. A few seconds later probably around 500agl received a Left hand engine ECU (Engine Control Unit) A and B caution. No change in performance or engine output/ engine indications noted. Immediately after this communicated a decision to come back to land as a precaution. First coordinated with Pilot Monitoring (Person A); then Communicated to ATC that we were turning back to land XXR due to abnormal annunciation. Person A then was helping run/ find checklists while I continued flying. They cleared us to land in the upwind. Everything was normal until reaching midfield/ approach end of the downwind; when ATC advised that they potentially had seen a puff of 'smoke.' We then scanned and noticed in the left engine that we were leaking fluid pretty heavily. Initially was thinking it was coolant due to location of leak (fins on the inboard side of the nacelle). Other than ECU Annunciations engine page looked normal and engine output felt normal. Continued to setup for landing and focused on flying the aircraft while there was still available engine power. During the turn from downwind to final; we both realized that it smelled like fuel was potentially leaking. I continued to fly the aircraft and focus on landing when PM suggested we secure the engine just in case to negate a fire hazard. We then ran secure items and engine was feathered by about 300 AGL on final. Left gear down; but brought flaps back up to APP in order to not lose airspeed; maintained approximately 85-90 knots down to the runway and landed safely. Attempted to make turn off of runway; however was unable to continue due to asymmetric thrust overpowering steering. Stopped on taxiway and requested a tow.Suggestions: Keep two pilots on reposition flights. It was infinitely helpful having a second set of eyes and hands assist with the problem.
column123: On takeoff from ZZZ I was pilot monitoring (PM). Pilot flying (PF) was Person B. In the upwind; approximately 500 AGL; two CAS messages appeared; followed by slight engine roughness of LH engine. CAS messages were: LH ECU A FAIL & LH ENG ECU B FAIL. I verbalized the non normal in the flightdeck and PF called ATC requesting landing back on rwy XXR at ZZZ. No emergency was declared at this time since the engine appeared to be running mostly normal - load and RPMs were unchanged; thrust seemed stable; and PF did not report any unusual control pressures. Tower cleared the aircraft for right traffic and cleared us to land at that time. As PF turned crosswind I performed the landing checklist to the line; verified that the PF was in control of aircraft; and let him know that I was pulling out AFM for simultaneous ECU (Engine Control Unit) A&B failure. As the aircraft began the initial descent to land; tower called and let us know that they might have momentarily seen smoke; but it was no longer observed. At this time I noticed that the LH engine was leaking fluid from the cooling fins. I verbalized this to PF; and initially thought that it was coolant; but as we turned onto final i began to smell fuel and suspected a fuel leakage. ~500 AGL verbalized this to PF and suggested securing the engine to mitigate fire risk. PF agreed; I asked him to pull the LH throttle idle so that his control wouldn't be compromised and then I performed the remainder of the engine securing checklist as published. Landed XXR at ZZZ and taxied off the runway but was unable to continue further taxi with the LH engine secured. Tower coordinated a tow off of the movement area back to the maintenance hanger. Dispatch & maintenance were notified; I wrote out the aircraft squawk; and then this report was submitted.Suggestions: Keep two pilots on Maintenance ferry flight pickups.

column121: Situation 1:While operating from Location X at the intersection of the 50 ft and 100 ft LAANC grid; we moved the Landing Zone (LZ) for safety reasons but failed to properly reassess the new location. I didn't account for the offset of the new LZ being farther east than we originally calculated; and I failed to make the necessary adjustment in the field after relocating. After moving; we were positioned under the 50 ft grid but did not adjust our operational assumptions accordingly.Situation 2:Because the change in LZ was not fully accounted for; we continued the flight using the 50 ft operating plan without adjusting for the offset. This resulted in operating at 100 ft when the correct authorization for that location was 50 ft.Main cause:The primary issue was not fully re-verifying the updated LAANC grid after relocating the LZ. The offset shift was not recalculated in the field; leading to the incorrect assumption that we had exited the 50 ft grid when we were still inside it.Going forward:Anytime the LZ is moved during operations; I will stop and fully reassess the new position before continuing flight. This includes confirming the exact grid location (especially 50 ft vs 100 ft boundaries); verifying any offsets in the field; and verbally calling out the corrected altitude limit before resuming operations.

column121: During a review of my UAS records; I discovered that I had inadvertently conducted commercial small UAS operations while my recurrent training was overdue by approximately two months. At the time of the operations; I believed my Remote Pilot recurrent training status was current and that I had a reminder system in place to alert me before expiration. After reviewing my records; I realized the reminder had either failed or was not properly configured; which caused the lapse to go unnoticed.The flights conducted during this period were completed normally and safely; with no injury; property damage; airspace conflict; loss of control; or known hazard created. Once I discovered the issue; I immediately stopped conducting commercial UAS operations until the recurrent training requirement was corrected. I then completed the required recurrent course and updated my records.The primary contributing factor was overreliance on a single reminder system instead of actively verifying pilot currency before each commercial UAS operation. As a corrective action; a new UAS credential and training verification SOP was introduced. This SOP requires confirmation of Remote Pilot currency before accepting or conducting any commercial UAS mission; periodic review of pilot credentials; redundant calendar reminders for recurrent training deadlines; and documentation of credential status in the mission file.Additionally; as an extra safety and compliance measure; we will complete the FAA ALC-515 recurrent training course annually; even if the regulatory recurrent training interval allows a longer period. This annual review will help ensure continued familiarity with current Part 107 requirements; operating limitations; airspace procedures; and UAS safety responsibilities.This issue was unintentional and was corrected immediately upon discovery. The lesson learned is that currency requirements must be verified through a formal process; rather than relying only on memory or a single automated reminder.

I told Aircraft X that traffic had him in sight and would maintain visual separation when Aircraft X was about 4 mile final and there was about 2 miles between him and Aircraft Y. I had heard the controller working Aircraft Y tell Aircraft Y to maintain visual separation and caution wake turbulence which is how I knew that Aircraft Y reported Aircraft X in sight.I noticed that Aircraft Y was flying a shallower downwind than was usual and was doing about 120 kt. on the downwind which is considerable faster than what similar aircraft do on the downwind. I told the controller who was working Aircraft Y to 'watch for the slop over' because of the way Aircraft Y was flying. I then observed Aircraft Y turn base wide and 'slopped over' or veer into the path of Aircraft X. I could not tell who was in front or behind from my perspective; but I then saw Aircraft X turn sharply to the right as if he was afraid that Aircraft Y was going to impact his left side. I then told the controller that Aircraft Y was too close to Aircraft X. The controller then proceeded to instruct Aircraft Y to start a climb and go around. Aircraft X then said that Aircraft Y was way too close to which I just replied 'Roger.' About 30 seconds later Aircraft X said he was executing missed approach so I issued the standard missed approach instructions which is heading 195 and climb and maintain 3000.I would strongly recommend to suspend all flight training at SNA. The runways at SNA are 500 ft. apart which is extremely close. We are depending on low time or student pilots to turn the base in such a manner as to avoid colliding with airlines and jet traffic inbound on Runway 20R. The AFD instructs pilots to do a 15-degree offset dog leg for base to final turn. That is a lot to ask a pilot who is training or who just got the license. It's a complicated maneuver to begin with but it is a vital necessity due to the proximity of the runways.I see it constantly where the pattern workers on Runway 20L will slop over and veer into the final for Runway 20R. It happens constantly and no matter how many times we tell pilots not to do it or correct the pilots; it happens on a regular basis. Luckily when there has been slop over; either nobody is on final for Runway 20R or the inbound traffic is far enough in front or behind the pattern worker to take enough corrective action. It is my own personal belief that someday a small aircraft will slop over and collide with an airliner or business jet inbound on Runway 20R. In my mind; if flight training is allowed to continue; it's not a question of 'IF' but a question of 'WHEN' a catastrophe will occur. Mixing commercial jet traffic and VFR pattern workers who are either learning or have low time at SNA is a recipe for disaster that will cost a lot of people their lives. There are a number of neighboring airports where the student pilots can go and do their flight training without putting the lives of airline passengers at risk; I believe that right to live of 200 plus passengers on an airliner supersedes the right of a student pilot to learn to fly at SNA.
column123: Aircraft Y; in the traffic pattern and on the downwind leg; reported Aircraft X in sight. Pilot stated that he would maintain visual separation from Aircraft X. Aircraft Y was then cleared for the option" on Runway 20L. Aircraft X was on short final; arriving Runway 20R; which is 500 ft. laterally separated from the parallel Runway 20L.Runway 20R is the air carrier and primary IFR runway here at SNA at 5;700x150 ft. Runway 20L is the primary traffic pattern / light GA runway here at SNA at 2;887x75. Aircraft Y turned final to Runway 20L off the left wing of Aircraft X; but overshot the centerline of Runway 20L; flying too-wide of a turn; and nearly cutting off Aircraft X; who had to take an evasive turning maneuver to avoid an NMAC. Aircraft X executed a go-around. John Wayne Orange County Airport (SNA) is a very busy Class C airspace air carrier airport in Southern California. The airport handles about 11.5 million passengers per year; while handling a high volume of arrivals and departures daily between XA:00 and XQ:00. The airport has two parallel runways (see above); and is situated on a 500-acre plot of land. The airport has a large terminal that has 22 regularly used airline gates. It also has a ramp just south of the terminal used for air cargo operations. The airport has 3 FBOs on the field with a very high volume of corporate and private jet traffic.Through the years; there have been several close calls between pattern working light GA aircraft and airliners. There have been many light GA airplane incidents that have been attributed to wake turbulence. In my years at SNA; I have witnessed several very close calls between airliners and small aircraft conducting flight training. As a controller; and as one who worked this high volume of traffic daily; I am baffled by the pressing need by these local flight schools to conduct flight training here at a busy air carrier facility. It is not uncommon to have 6 or 7 low time student pilots in the traffic pattern; right next to arriving and departing large and heavy aircraft. The airspace and airfield is so limited in space that it is a requirement for departing GA aircraft off Runway 20L to conduct an immediate left 15-degree offset turn to avoid "drifting" into departing jets off Runway 20R. The margin for error here at SNA is virtually none. Airline pilots and passengers should not be put in this dangerous situation day to day. It is a common occurrence here to see student pilots soloing for the first time; in close quarters with airliners.I rarely feel the need to file a report regarding anything that will hinder the flying public in any way; but I've seen enough here at SNA to prompt me to do something to look out for peoples' lives. I highly recommend that SNA suspend flight training indefinitely. VFR itinerate traffic; no problem. Furthermore; to increase safety here; I recommend that Runway 20L be permanently decommissioned and recommissioned as a taxiway. Furthermore; I recommend that an EMAS be installed at the departure ends of Runway 20R and Runway 02L. I would also recommend that a displaced threshold be built at the approach end of Runway 20R in order to increase the length of takeoff rolls for larger aircraft. The current 5;700-foot runway; in my opinion; is not enough of a safety margin when the land space currently exits for a displaced threshold for departures."

column121: Leaving 10k feet as we begin accelerating; we heard multiple loud bangs which felt to be under the right side of the cockpit. The captain was pilot flying; and he immediately turned off the auto pilot and auto throttle to begin leveling and slowing the airplane. We requested to level off at 12000ft and begin trouble shooting the issue. We had no indications on the EICAS; and the engines were within normal parameters.  We requested priority handling and informed that we would be returning to the field. The loud bangs continued ever few minutes in intervals of 2 or 3 bangs. We initially believed that it was a panel or door because it occurring during the acceleration period and seemed to occur when in turns. We decided to do a airport fly by to see if it could possibly be a gear door; but tower said they did not see anything. The flight attendant in the rear also stated that they felt the same sensation from the rear of the plane which led us to believe it had to be something different. We returned to the field with the bangs only occurring normally in turns. We landed below max landing weight and exited the runway. The fire trucks did not see anything of note; so we taxied back to the gate. We also received a remote Circuit Breaker trip; 'TAXI LT RH'. During the walk around everything seemed normal until 3 passengers seated behind the number 2 engine said they saw flames shooting out the rear of the engine every time the loud bangs occurred. This led us to believe that the number 2 engine was having intermittent compressor stalls that were not severe enough to show and create surges in thrust.

column123: I was acting as a safety pilot for my friend who owns a Cessna 182H after getting fuel and doing a thorough preflight we departed on a cross country flight to an uncontrolled field. We landed at our destination airport and on the roll out as the airplane slowed the front tire felt slack and the nose of the aircraft settled slightly lower than normal. I tried to call the Unicom frequency for the FBO but no one answered. We were close to a taxi way and did not see or hear any other traffic in the area so we shut the engine down and pushed the aircraft off the runway and on to the taxi way as to not damage the tire and to get it clear of the runway. We then walked to the FBO where the manager of the airport who was also a A&P offered us some air so we could pump up the tire and see if it was leaking. We pumped up the tire and inspected it and did not see or hear any leaking. We then taxied to the end of the runway and departed to our home airport and landed safely. When we were taxiing in on our arrival we could feel the front nose wheel felt slack again and after we parked on the ramp we could see that it had definitely lost more air. Once we tied down the aircraft we discussed what we should have done differently. We should have had a mechanic take the tire off and inspect it for leaks or just replaced the tire all together. Ive learned from this event that it's never a good call to takeoff with a tire that's in question even though we thought it just needed air.

On rollout of the third landing I was correcting for left crosswind when the gust abruptly shifted to come from the right and I was unable to reverse my correction fast enough. My last glance at the airspeed near the threshold was about 85 mph; but the airspeed needle was bouncing back and forth and not stationary.  On the last final approach; after round-out; I sensed that my airspeed was a little too fast as I seemed to be floating longer than usual.  Perhaps I should have opted to go around at this point.  Another thing that maybe I should have done is just ended the flight after first or second circuit; however how could I know that the last circuit's gusty conditions we going to worsen so quickly.

column121: VFR arrival to ZZZ; flying the profile of GPS XX approach (straight it to XX).  Aircraft type: Lake Amphibian.  Normal pre-landing checks completed; gear down; green light; 3 wheels visually and hydraulic pressure up. Normal landing was executed in the touchdown zone. On rollout; after cresting a hump in the runway (ZZZ runway is not flat; there are multiple large undulations); the left main gear collapsed and the left wing float contacted the runway.  Aircraft veered left and came to rest between the centerline and the left edge of runway; between TWY 1 and 2. I shut down the engine and master switch; shocked and confused.  Gear handle appeared down; but hydraulic pressure was indicating zero.  I turned the switches back on and pressed the gear handle down (it moved slightly further down) and saw hydraulic pressure coming back up.Upon further investigation at the maintenance shop; it was discovered that the landing gear handle detent stop was misaligned and the gear handle was free to move up and was not held down by the mechanical stop as it should be. By design; the landing gear selector valve vents pressure back to the hydraulic reservoir if the handle is between detents. They were able to re-rig the mechanical stop to restore proper function.The benefit of being a Lake with the engine on a pylon is that damage was minimal and limited to the wing float and scrapes on the lower fuselage keel where it also contacted the runway.

We scanned the engine page to look for any abnormalities and noticed the left TIT (Turbine Inlet Temperature) and CHT were lower than right by a good amount. FO turned on autopilot and once we leveled out at 5;000 feet we tried different power settings to try and smooth out the vibrations. We also looked out at the engines; the right engine seemed to be running normal and the left engine was shaking a good amount. Off of this we determined it to be the left engine with the issue. We had about a 45 knot tailwind at so we covered a lot of distance in a short time thus making returning to ZZZ a much longer diversion. After cruising for a few minutes the vibration got worse so I asked ZZZ approach for a 030 heading to stay closer to the coast which they then proceeded to ask if we were an emergency aircraft. I advised them negative emergency however left engine was running rough. After coordinating with Dispatch about the diversion to ZZZ2 I asked approach to divert into ZZZ2. We were given a discretion descent to 2500 and vectored in for a visual approach runway XX. ATC asked for souls plus fuel onboard and rolled the trucks as a precautionary measure. I advised them of the fuel and souls while also saying the situation has not improved nor gotten worse. FO landed runway XX without issue we taxied to the ramp advised the passengers and received positive feedback from the passengers. Myself and the FO made phone calls to Dispatch; Maintenance Control; and the chief pilot. Recovery flight was sent up and took the passengers from ZZZ2-ZZZ1.

column121: We were on final approach to runway XXL with Flaps 2 selected. When we attempted to select Flaps 5 the flaps did not move to the selected position. An attempt was made to get the flaps to move by selecting flaps 10 however; the flaps remained at the 2 position. At this pointed we executed a go-around and the flaps retracted normally. A second attempt was made to deploy the flaps and they got stuck between 5 and 10. A review of the trailing edge flap disagree checklist was completed. A 3rd attempt to deploy the flaps prior to executing the checklist and they worked normally. A landing on XXL was made using normal flap settings (30) and braking. We proceeded to the gate and after we parked the ground crew notified us of a significant leak emanating from the left wheel area. I went down to investigate and saw hydraulic fluid leaking from the union between the caliper and brake line onto the tire and brake assembly. I asked the ground crew to step back and went to the flight deck to contact operations to have them request ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) assistance on my behalf. I then contacted Maintenance Control to advise them of the issue and entered the discrepancy into the logbook. I then noticed the SYS A quantity decreasing fairly rapidly so I called Maintenance Control back to see if there was anything I could do to slow or stop the leak. I was advised the releasing the parking brake may help but I needed to ensure the aircraft was properly chocked prior to doing so. I went back under the aircraft to coordinate this with the crew chief and other ground personnel. After this was completed I went back to the flight deck to release the parking brake and observed that contract maintenance had arrived to the aircraft. I did not observe any ARFF presence during this process.Time compression was a factor as we were on final approach when we noticed the flaps were stuck. In retrospect we should have not attempted to move the flaps; immediately executed a go-around; and executed the TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE checklist.In regards to our hydraulic leak after we arrived to the gate I should have contacted ATC instead of company operations. It is possible this could have generated a faster ARFF response to the aircraft.
column123: On final to XXL; While configuring the flaps; with the flaps at 2; we selected flaps 10. The flaps did not move. We attempted to move flaps by re-selecting flaps 2; then 10. column123: Aircraft X had an MEL 21-XXX for One Auto Cabin Press Control.  Logbook; placard; mechanics; and crew complied with the MEL instructions and verifications. During the climbout; the flight crew felt increased pressure in their ears.  ATC cleared us to FL120; and somewhere between 10;000 and 12;000 feet; we received the EICAS Master Warning red lights and aural alert.  I was the pilot flying; so I took control of the aircraft and radios; disconnected the autopilot; stopped the climb; and informed ATC we needed an immediate descent to 10;000 feet.  The FO announced the type of aircraft condition; and all pilots donned our oxygen masks and established communications. I requested priority handling; requested a 180-degree turn back towards the ZZZZ airport; and a lower altitude.  We held in our present position below 10;000 feet and completed all required checklists; briefings; and reports.  Then we proceeded to ZZZZ [VOR] and held while we briefed the plan for an overweight landing.  We landed on runway XXL; Airport Rescue and Firefighting checked our aircraft on the taxiway; and followed us back to our parking spot.  I made two logbook entries for the pressurization problem and for the overweight landing.  I stayed on the flight deck to confer with the maintenance about the aircraft's issues.  ZZZZ ATC was very professional and helpful throughout and should be commended for their prior preparation and calm demeanor.Cause: Aircraft X had an MEL 21-XXX for 'One Auto Press Control;' a Technical Standby Instrument (TSI) to monitor a component in the pressurization system; and a yellow placard for a mechanic to check before every flight.   I am surprised this aircraft was approved for ETOPS service across an ocean.  Our failure could have occurred in the middle of the Ocean at 36;000 feet at night.  IF that had occurred; we could have had multiple injuries due to extreme pressure changes; an emergency descent to 10;000 feet; and then a diversion.During our in-flight pressurization failure; while we were running our checklist; we received several interruptions on the COMM page from Dispatch.  I am not sure whether these were sent manually; automatically via automatic function; or by rescheduling the aircraft for its next takeoff.  One message was sent to us with our new flight plan; and I believe the other concerned crew duty legalities.  These messages pop up; and my FO must verify them and then cancel them because they concern another flight that we are being scheduled for.  Suggestion: Don't send non-essential messages to aircraft during their procedures that should be conducted in a sterile cockpit.  Don't send any scheduling messages below 10;000 feet during the sterile period.  Let us land the aircraft safely; then we can consider reassignment; rescheduling; or a new flight plan.ZZZ ATC asked us if we needed speed relief during the approach.  Instead of 160 KIAS until a 4-mile final; we needed 175 KIAS due to our heavy landing weight.  The autothrottles worked as normal; but I had to override their normal idle timing.  The Overweight Landing checklist in the QRH addresses this; but it's regarding 'using throttles manually'.  Suggest a note about being ready for the autothrottles to move to idle after 30 feet; because this isn't always the best scenario.  I had not considered this during the brief.  I was fortunate to feel the autothrottles reduce before I wanted them to; so I overrode them very slightly; resulting in a normal touchdown.

column121: There has been a good deal of helicopter training here over the last few years. Generally we never have a problem with the helicopters; as they try to account for the normal traffic here and are rarely a problem. Mind you; I'm not necessarily blaming the helicopter here; just trying to give some background about our particular airport.I made the usual radio calls at 10 and 5 miles; and I was following a Cirrus in about as closely as prudent. There was a helicopter making right traffic above us; and he seemed to be a new guy; but we were all making the appropriate calls. Because of the fact that I was hundreds of feet lower; had clearly announced final at a mile and a half out; and the helicopters are usually good about waiting for us to pass; I thought all was well. But he did descend fairly quickly; and landed on our end of the runway instead of the far end at about the same time I did.I thought it might be unwise to go around; since a helicopter could do almost anything. I always land at the start of the runway in a short distance -- since I always make the first turn-off -- so I did that; but did get a nasty comment from a pilot flying overhead. I don't think he was particularly blaming me. But I didn't like how it played out really; and I said at the time that it was probably my fault to mollify him.If you go by who is in front; well yes; he's a helicopter and he turned in front of me. If you go by who is lower; then I was. I think that I should have gotten a direct answer from him instead of just assuming that he was waiting for us both to land; but I was working with the Cirrus so closely on the radio that I didn't think he would try to get in between us.The safety lesson? Be careful around students? I'm not entirely sure; since I'm still thinking about it. I have always held that the helicopters have just as much of a right to be here as we do; but then again; they've been very considerate too. In this case; I probably figured that I had made radio calls and they would do as usual; and they probably figured that since they had made previous radio calls; it was all good.

column121: This was a scheduled cargo flight between ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 with two operating crew and two company jump-seaters.  This event occurred within ZZZZ FIRWhile operating ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 as First Officer and PF we were established at initial cruise at 31100.  We were continuously in and out of cloud tops during this portion.  After a few minutes the wing and nacelle anti-ice systems automatically turned on.  Almost immediately we had a bleed #2 EICAS alert with associated inop light in #2 bleed air switch.  The PM ran the bleed #2 checklist; after complication we got L; R EICAS msgs.  While working that checklist we received bleed's 1;3;4 EICAS alerts as well.  This was followed shortly by the return of bleed 2 EICAS alert. We noticed cabin altitude climbing and at an altitude of 5700' we elected to put on O2 masks and activated supernumerary o2 switch.  The captain ran those checklists and managed to get two bleeds back on but we eventually lost all 4 bleeds a second time.  Unable to maintain cabin pressure; we advised ATC and coordinated a rapid descent to 3000 meters.  During rapid descent the highest cabin altitude noted was 12000' and highest rate of cabin climb was 2000 fpm.  Once below 10000 we removed masks and continued running the litany of EICAS generated non-normal checklists (Cabin Altitude; Bleed 1; Bleed 2; Bleed 3; Bleed 4; Packs 1+2+3; Cabin alt auto; Outflow valve r/l; Suprnmry oxy on; Pack mode 2; Pack mode 1; Pack mode 3). Once below 10000' we struggled to maintain communications with ZZZZ Control even using XXX.X; we required multiple relays with other aircraft.  Also during this low altitude cruise with center AP (Auto Pilot) engaged and no other crew engagement; power began to increase with a corresponding climb commanded by AP.  PF disconnected auto-pilot and auto-throttles and returned aircraft to level flight at 3000 meters.  We also noticed lights in MCP (Mode Control Panel) flickering continuously bright to dim.  Once stabilized the left AP was selected and auto-throttles were re-engaged.After evaluating options and communicating with dispatch we elected to continue the short flight to ZZZZ1.  Once in terminal area we requested short delay vectors to allow for flaps to extend in secondary mode due to lack of bleed air to actuate leading edge in primary mode and landed safely off ILS-Z to runway XX.  We maintained our ATC handling status until landing due to abnormal aircraft condition.This was a fairly challenging situation.  Time of day; complexity of system failures; communications with foreign controllers; cabin altitude and use of oxygen mask all contributed to high workload.  I was surprised how much the O2 mask decreased our ability to effectively communicate and maintain a high level of situational awareness. I recently completed annual training which involved use of oxygen mask which definitely helped in this situation.

column121: Aircraft X filed ZZZZZ. ZZZ to ZZZ1 and was level at 090. They were a P28A and not a jet or high-altitude aircraft so they should not have been on jet airways; which don't have an MEA through the terrain around ZZZ2. They should have filed a victor airway as they were not technically capable of flying jet airways. I had just taken over the sector from the previous controller. About 5 minutes later the MSAW for Aircraft X started flashing as they were about to hit an increased area of terrain where the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) went up to 095.Neither myself or the previous controller had noticed the aircraft was on a jet airway with no MEA/MOCA and was headed towards higher terrain. I gave a low altitude alert and the aircraft climbed to 100.At the time this event happened I was completely task saturated. I was working 5; YES FIVE; sectors combined over 3 different frequencies ALL BY MYSELF.  I had multiple calls from approach; the missile range; FSS clearances; ZZZ [Center] calls; and other sectors. At one point an aircraft started broadcasting 'in the blind' because I was so busy answering other aircraft several hundred miles away from his position that he thought ATC was gone. I had numerous low altitude aircraft that I was providing approach control services for; 2 IFR drones that were hovering over the western arrival/departure corridor for ZZZ1; and weather deviations; and high altitude overflights. In order to do all this I was essentially on a MID configuration and super zoomed out so I could see all the airspace under my control.  I replayed the Falcon.  I had 23 data blocks on the scope at the moment the MSAW started going off. I should have had a D-side just to help with all the data block separation; not to mention the phone calls.The CIC (Controller in Charge) was planning to split off 2 sectors whenever someone came back from break or the XA:00 am people showed up; but that didn't happen fast enough. The TSD (Traffic Situation Display) was obviously showing that my sectors were ready to get stupid busy. I told the CIC I couldn't wait any longer and that they needed to abandon the CIC desk and split off sectors X and Y. They agreed and did so. It took probably about 5 min afterward for me to fully regain control of the sectors I had left: Z; A; and B. Safety was compromised without question.The combined configuration of C; Z and A was already deemed unsafe for day shift operations and requires manager approval since we have had numerous safety events with that combination. The MAP number for when those sectors are combined is only 14. YET STUPIDLY if you add EVEN more sectors and complexity and combine up C; Z; A; D; and B all together the MAP number jumps up to 20 and is not an illegal day shift combo.  So we are actually incentivized not to split sectors. If we think it is unsafe to have more than 14 aircraft in the combined low sectors in what world does it make sense to allow 20 aircraft if we do all that plus add two additional high altitude sectors into the mix?!!This event 100% happened because myself and the controller before me were trying to do the job of 3 people and couldn't keep up. The manager was super busy dealing with all the other stuff and didn't notice we hadn't split anything off.We had a controller on break when this event happened; they should have been recalled. Trying to provide approach control service to aircraft when you are looking at 300 miles of airspace is not safe on anything other than a slow MID shift.  Working 5 sectors combined on day shifts should not be allowed unless the volume is like 14 or lower like it is when only 3 of the sectors are combined.I should have shut off ZZZ [Center] and ZZZ1 approach until I could get the sectors split off and safely take on more airplanes. I prioritized efficiency over safety.CICs and FLMs (Front Line Manager) need training to understand that the TSD (Traffic Situation Display) is a predictor; and that it is not accurate tothe exact minute. Sectors are not split in a timely manner because they wait because the TSD says the volume doesn't happen until XB:03am and will say I have someone coming back right at XC:00 am.  Ignoring the fact that it takes several minutes for a briefing to occur; but also not understanding that the TSD time is an estimate; a prediction; and can be of by 5-10 minutes; is a common problem is my specialty.Due to staffing; we rarely have a supervisor in the morning.  CICs tend to take more risks and prioritize breaks and don't like to page someone back early because it is one of their peers and people complain.  A supervisor in the area would have reduced the chance of this event happening..

column121: During cruise; near Albuquerque; we began to lose GPS due to jamming in the area. Several other aircraft in the area were complaining of the same issue to ATC. The nav data page showed GPS 2 completely lost; and GPS 1 degraded to an AIDED" status and momentarily back to "NAV" status before completely being lost. With the autopilot engaged; the aircraft began a standard bank turn to the left; upon which I quickly selected "HDG" mode to regain the plotted ND (Navigation Display) course to our next fix within .2 NM laterally. After reporting the incident to ATC; we completed the approved QRH procedure for GPS Interference. After being unable to regain GPS accuracy; we deselected navaid function to continue to ZZZ. We were able to utilize IRS (Inertial Reference System)/DME/DME for the remainder of the flight; as our GPS remained jammed until landing. We also lost onboard WiFi connectivity after the jamming event. The FMS waypoint sequencing never was lost; and we landed without further incident in ZZZ. A logbook entry was made upon gate arrival in ZZZ.An unexpected jamming of our onboard GPS equipment. My sole recommendation is for a more appropriate method to conduct electromagnetic/gps testing which respects the integrity of onboard navigation equipment used by the flying public."

column121: We were scheduled to operate from ZZZ-ZZZZ in an aircraft with an inoperative Hot Air Valve per MEL. After engine start the air conditioning system appeared to operate normally. We departed from runway XXR and passing 8000' the inflight crew contacted the flight deck with a report that the air is blowing very loud; all passengers are turning off gaspers; the air is surging and there is a loud whistling sound. They indicated it was not normal and something was wrong. At the same time the cockpit became uncomfortably hot and the air was not blowing from any cockpit vents. I briefed my FO and we decided to level at 10000' enter into holding and troubleshoot the issue; for concerns of pressurization. After transferring control and radios to the FO; the CA reviewed the system pages of the Bleed Air; which did not indicate any faults and reviewed the system pages of the Pressurization which did not indicate any faults. The CA then contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control and discussed the malfunction. Maintenance Control could not find any issues on their end; however we clearly had a malfunction on our end that was not producing any ECAM messages. After consulting with Dispatch and Maintenance Control I advised them that we felt taking an aircraft into mountainous terrain; would not be the safest course of action. They both supported my decision to return to ZZZ. All checklists and procedures were conducted at this time; including diversion and overweight landing checklist. The CA setup a return to ZZZ and throughly briefed the FO on our approach. The crew was briefed and passengers were advised. There were no issues with the return. Once we completed parking checklist the CA made a logbook entry for the malfunction and overweight landing. The Chief Pilot and Assistant Chief Pilot then made their way to the cockpit and asked for a detailed explanation of what occurred. A offline commercial pilot was in the cabin and commented as he deplaned that he knew that something was wrong with the system. We debriefed the inflight crew and they all heard the same loud noise; whistling; surging of air; and abnormal air pressure coming from the gaspers. We then debriefed with the Chief Pilots at the gate in the terminal.

column121: Flight ABCD was scheduled for departure at XA:40Z from ZZZ to ZZZZ. Departure occurred 44 minutes behind schedule due to cargo loading delays in ZZZ.During the takeoff roll; the flight crew observed abnormal aircraft acceleration performance. Additional thrust was applied in an effort to improve aircraft acceleration. The First Officer was the Pilot Flying during departure.At rotation; crew experienced unusual handling and flight characteristics. The aircraft remained controllable and recovery actions were effective. No EICAS messages; cautions; or warnings were generated during the event.After departure; the crew coordinated with Dispatch regarding the abnormal takeoff performance. Dispatch subsequently advised that the aircraft was approximately 56;000 kg overweight. This information was later confirmed with ZZZ Operations.The flight continued to ZZZZ without further incident and landed safely.Dispatch and flight crew coordinated effectively in flight after identifying abnormal aircraft performance. The faulty load sheet and resulting overweight departure condition created a potentially hazardous situation that required immediate operational assessment and risk management.Captain A was DH (Dead Head). He assisted us through out the flight and sure be full paid for working the flight.Cause: Preliminary FindingsAircraft departed significantly above allowable weight limits. Initial indication of the issue was abnormal acceleration during takeoff roll. Abnormal handling characteristics were experienced during rotation and initial climb. No onboard system warnings or EICAS indications alerted the crew to the overweight condition. The issue appears related to an incorrect or faulty load sheet and/or load planning process.This event presented a significant operational and safety risk. An overweight takeoff condition of this magnitude could have resulted in: Reduced takeoff performance; Inability to meet required climb gradients; Runway excursion or rejected takeoff complications; Structural exceedances; Loss of aircraft controllability during critical phases of flightImmediate coordination between the flight crew and Dispatch was essential in identifying and managing the situation safely.Suggestions: Recommended Follow-Up Actions1. Conduct full investigation into load planning and load sheet generation procedures.2. Audit cargo weight verification processes in ZZZ Operations.3. Review dispatch release validation procedures for overweight detection safeguards.4. Evaluate communication and cross-check procedures between load control; dispatch; and flight crew.5. Determine whether additional automated protections or alerts can be implemented to identify extreme weight discrepancies prior to departure.

column121: At 2500 ft; instructor was talking a student through emergency landing profile (ELP). While scanning instruments and then looking at the Ipad for traffic to safely conduct the ELP the instructors eyes then transitioned to the right and at this point observed a high wing aircraft at the same altitude; going the opposite direction; within 500 ft of the instructor's aircraft. Instructor performed evasive maneuvers while the other aircraft maintained their original heading. No calls were made by the other aircraft on CTAF and the aircraft was not on ADS-B. Instructor had been making calls advising of the intended practice emergency landing. The rest of the flight was uneventful with the instructor and student landing safely. Corrective actions would be requiring all aircraft to be on ADS-B. Most mid air collisions happen on clear days below 3000ft within 5 miles of an airport. All participating aircraft using ADS-B-out would vastly aid in collision avoidance. The only other corrective action is using the see and avoid doctrine and diligently scanning in a figure 8 pattern 60 degrees to the left and right and 10 degrees up and down of the aircraft. A lapse of the scan pattern for 10 seconds while talking to a student and glancing at an Ipad can mean the difference between a collision and an NMAC.

At the time of the event; the aircraft was configured for landing at low altitude and low airspeed consistent with normal final approach procedures.Upon the loss of engine power; I; acting as the certificated flight instructor; assumed control of the aircraft. Due to the aircraft's landing configuration and the significant drag associated with flaps 40; glide performance was substantially reduced and the aircraft was unable to reach the runway threshold.The aircraft subsequently touched down approximately 30-40 feet short of the paved runway surface; striking a runway end light prior to contacting the transition area leading onto the asphalt runway. The aircraft remained upright and controllable throughout the event.There was no operating control tower at the airport; and wind conditions were not considered a contributing factor. No injuries were sustained by either occupant. Following the event; the aircraft was shut down and removed from service for maintenance inspection. No immediately apparent structural damage was observed by the flight crew at the time of the incident.Subsequent maintenance inspection reportedly identified a leak in the engine induction system/induction lines; which may have resulted in the introduction of un-metered air and contributed to the total loss of engine power.The purpose of this report is to document the circumstances surrounding the engine power loss event and subsequent forced landing short of the runway.

column121: Arriving at ZZZ flight following was used with ZZZ1 and ZZZ Centers and ZZZ CTAF and ASOS prior to arrival and landing. Turbulence was a factor in all operations for landing; taxing and departure during the XA:45 landing period on RWY. XX (wind 260@26G36) and the departure on Rwy XY at XC:00 (wind 280@21G33). During our time on the ramp at the FBO; the ground crew chocked and tied down the plane due to the extreme turbulence on the surface. While landing; taxing in and out and departing we had the CTAF in the active position on the GTN 650Xi and the Center frequency in the standby position. Conditions seemed to favor a departure on Rwy XX; but at that runway hold line a recheck of the weather strongly indicated that XY had less of a crosswind component. I taxied to the 1 hold line of RWY XY and did pre takeoff checks and setup the GTN 650Xi for the departure route. On the takeoff I noticed over the intersection of Rwys XX and XY that I was passing several hundred feet above a jet that had departed on RWY XX.In analyzing the situation I discovered I had not heard any calls for the jet and that during my setup of the GTN 650Xi at the runway hold line. I must have inadvertently touched the standby frequency block which brought the Center frequency into the active position as the aircraft was rocking in the ground turbulence and thus not allowing me to hear the calls from the jet and the jet not hearing my departure calls either.The learning experience for me is recognizing how close the HOME and Direct buttons are to the active and standby communication frequency selector on the 650; and to recheck the communication setup while at the hold line. This piece of navigation equipment is a relatively new addition to my aircraft. My previous radio equipment had a button which would exchange the standby and active frequencies. Another thought would be to have the CTAF frequency in both the active and standby positions; and the Center frequency on the number 2 COM/NAV unit.I fully understand how this kind of a human failure can cause a devastating accident and I will be more attentive to this detail.

column121: I decided to land at the ZZZ airport while enroute. I had never landed there before so I gathered the airport information from my phone enroute.  The runway is fairly short. There was another aircraft in the pattern as we were approaching and it was on the ground before we entered the pattern.My first mistake was with my radio calls. I was making calls stating the wrong runway end.  I believe I was confused based on the calls the other pilot was making and the direction he said he was coming from. I should have verified with my chart. I didn't. I mention this because I realized that I was making the wrong calls on final and I think that the realization of this mistake just added to the situation.    My pattern was a little tight and I ended up coming in fast. I was in landing configuration with 40 degrees of flaps. I felt I might not be able stop in time due to the short runway and decided a go around would be appropriate.  However with a short runway with trees on the end and 40 degrees of flaps I ended up struggling to climb to clear the trees. I didn't want to start removing flaps as I was fairly slow and fairly low over the trees and didn't want to settle into the trees if I lost any lift. Once clear of the trees I milked off the flaps as I began to accelerate and decided not to make a second attempt.I was too slow and too close to the trees for my comfort level and due to the short runway with obstacles really didn't feel I had many options other than keep the nose down and allow speed to build. Had it been a warmer day with less aircraft performance it could have ended badly which is why I am filling out this report.There are several things that could have helped avoid this situation: 1. I should have done a more detailed review of the airport prior to landing there for the first time as printed resources don't always tell the whole story.  Perhaps I should have looked at some aerial photos or maps. 2. I should have made a better approach; because my pattern was tight I ended up high and ultimately too fast.  A slightly wider pattern would have provided for a more stabilized slower approach.  3. I should have made the go around decision earlier. I ate up too much of the short runway trying to 'save' the landing. 4. I do think that some complacency and perhaps over confidence in flying a familiar  airplane contributed to getting too far down the road before calling the go around. I did some additional go-around practice at a local airport with a much longer runway later in the flight and intend to do more specifically focused on seeing if letting some flaps out particularly in a 172 with 40 degrees would be more helpful or harmful in this scenario as the flaps are almost all drag at 40 degrees and provide very little if any additional lift.I did discuss this situation with some pilot friends to debrief the flight and brainstorm ways to improve and was given some helpful insight.

column121: On returning from a part 61 training flight in the practice area to the west of ZZZ; I instructed my student to pass to the south of the right downwind of runway XXR; in order to set up for a 45 degree entry. While sufficiently far enough south the downwind leg; I noticed an aircraft turn an early right crosswind and cut in front of another aircraft already on the crosswind. The traffic; a Cirrus SR-22; announced via CTAF that they intended to depart to the south. They began tracing straight towards my aircraft; and at this time I took flight controls from my student. I attempted to reach the other pilot to coordinate via CTAF but was unable; or my calls were not acknowledged. At this time I began a descent and a turn towards the airport to allow the traffic to pass off my right side; to my south. The departing traffic; which originally was headed southwest bound; began a turn towards the west; again tracking towards my aircraft. Seeing the other aircraft's ground speed of approximately 180 knots; and knowing my ground speed was approximately 100 knots; I knew it was only seconds until we would collide. At this time; both aircraft had descended to approximately 800 feet MSL. To avoid the collision; and to avoid turning into other traffic established on the downwind to my north; I initiated an aggressive descent to pass beneath the opposite direction cirrus. During this descent; my altitude dropped to approximately 480 feet AGL. After passing the cirrus; I resumed a climb back to pattern altitude of approximately 1022 MSL; and conducted a normal 45 degree entry to the right downwind. The landing was uneventful. To avoid another near miss in the future; I will emphasize to other pilots the importance of departing the pattern in a manner consistent with the AIM's guidance (downwind; then depart) instead of flying on course immediately.

column121: While operating a passenger flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we planned a departure on RW XX with a right forward quartering headwind /crosswind. We taxied to runway XX and announced our intentions on the Unicom frequency. We received our IFR clearance on the ground via ZZZ CTR on the radio as well.We heard no other traffic on the Unicom frequency of XXX.XX We saw no visible traffic during our taxi; in the air or on the ground. The Cessna 182 had taxied much earlier than us so assumed he had departed on his flight to ZZZ2. There were no radio transmissions from the Cessna 182 and that was confirmed via the FBO audio recorded during that time period.Our transmissions were on the recording stating our intentions to taxi to RW XX. We completed our taxi check and were holding short of RW XX. The Co-pilot transmitted our departure intentions for ZZZ RW XX and we began our normal takeoff roll. The aircraft accelerated normally and the Co-Pilot called V1 and Rotate; At that moment the C182 appeared at about 11 o clock in the windshield and approximately 50 to 75 ft. in the air. It was too late for an aborted takeoff as it appeared we would pass barely underneath the the C182. A rotation at that instant would have caused impact with the C182. I felt the safest option was to delay the rotation and remain on the runway for a couple of seconds as the traffic passed over us. It happened very quickly and we rotated and resumed the climb away from the runway. The remainder of the flight was normal and uneventful. The incident occurred due to lack of situational awareness resulting from a lack of radio communication. I was unaware visually of another aircraft positioned at RW XY prior to beginning the takeoff roll. This incident could have been avoided by pilots verifying correct Unicom/ CTAF frequencies in use at uncontrolled airports. Visually verifying other aircraft when possible and the use of all available appropriate aircraft lighting to enhance visibility.
column123: Our aircraft was departing on runway XX. I made CTAF calls taxiing out of the FBO via 1 and made a call once on runway XX ready for takeoff. Another aircraft was seen taxiing on the other side of the airfield via taxiway 2. No radio calls were heard from that aircraft. Visual contact was lost as it blended in to the airport environment at the approach end of runway XY. We started our takeoff roll and as we passed V1 speeds we visually saw the other aircraft departing runway XY. It was approximately 75-100 ft. AGL as it passed directly over us at the intersection of Runway XX and Runway XY. We elected to stay on the ground/runway at takeoff speed until the overflying aircraft was not a factor overhead. We then executed our takeoff with sufficient runway left to safely get airborne.Once airborne at approximately 1000 feet AGL I made another call on CTAF that we were turning northbound and departing the airport environment. No response was heard from any other aircraft in the area; including the aircraft we narrowly missed.Once landed at our destination in ZZZ1 we called airport personnel via cell phone to determine if they could hear our calls on the radio. They returned our call the next morning and stated that they heard ALL of our radio calls but none from the other aircraft. We had briefly talked with the other aircraft's pilot/occupant and knew that they were heading to ZZZ2. We called company at ZZZ2 and determined the aircraft's identification to be Aircraft Y. We did not make any contact with the crew of Aircraft Y as they had left the airfield.We believe that Aircraft Y may have been on the wrong CTAF frequency in ZZZ which is why we did not hear any radio transmissions from them nor did airport personnel. If true this directly caused the problem. To prevent this from happening again; we should have attempted to make direct radio contact with the other aircraft we saw taxiing either on CTAF or Guard frequency. If no contact made; we should have delayed taking our runway until we could absolutely confirm that other aircraft had taken off from their runway and was no longer a hazard.

column121: In regards to the incident of a hard landing at ZZZ.This report is being written by the Pilot in command of Aircraft X at the time of the accident. The trip was intended to be a day trip into ZZZ; we had departed earlier that morning with a VFR request from ATC to give us vectors in route to ZZZ1. This request was canceled shortly after the plane was no longer under control of ZZZ1's Class C Airspace. The intention behind this action was simply to take a more well defined route down the coast which we would follow south to ZZZ.The exact time of the event is not clear to me; I know that when I was roughly 25 miles to the North East of the field I had received the ATIS and information 1 was in effect. It stated that the active runway was Runway XX and the winds were coming from 060 at 11kts; gusting to 18kts.Upon contact with ZZZ Tower; it was communicated the active pressure in inches of mercury and that I was to advise when I was established on a right downwind for Runway XXPrior to my advancement into the downwind the controller in the tower had called asking if I was setting myself up for a straight in approach into Runway XY; as far as I was aware I was not only far east to the runway but also east of the tower that sits on the east of the runway. The tower communicated that from their perspective; I was in position for the unactive Runway XY; however I was still at pattern altitude and at least a mile away from being lined up with the centerline for Runway XY. I continued my approach into the right downwind and advised with midfield; everything seemed in order and even still; turning to base appeared normal; it wasn't until I had turned to final that it was clear to me that I had not adequately accounted for the wind correction due primarily to the gusts at 18kts. I was blown off to the west by roughly 0.5sm - 1sm; and with the gusts now coming in on the headwind; losing attitude on final proved itself to be a challenge; to the degree where this first approach resulted in missed/go around actions being taken. ZZZ Tower at this point advised me to turn back into the right downwind for Runway XX; however it was not advised that this turn was to be made while midfield with the runway; this required a sharper turn of of the runway heading; while working against the gusting 18kt headwind. My initial plan through this missed approach was to clean up the plane's flaps and trim while maintaining the runway heading until 700ft AGL. This request from the tower; while not the primary cause of the hard landing; was in some key details a reason behind the unstable final approach that lead to the events regarded to in this report. I made the needed adjustments to clean up the plane; however I was only up to 800ft AGL throughout the pattern instead of the pattern altitude of 1000ft AGL. upon this second attempt at a right downwind I extended my downwind to allow for more room for adjustments on base and final. The turn to base was standard and by this point I had only applied 10 degrees of flaps and no trim. Upon my second attempt for a final approach I had started off with 10 degrees of flaps but soon realized that I needed to lose more altitude than anticipated. This is because I knew I was below pattern altitude so I held off on the 500ft decent following the plane being abeam the runway numbers. By my approach into final the plane was still roughly 800ft AGL; this prompted me to add in 20 degrees of flaps; however the trim stayed neutral. The plane was well pitched for 65-70kts on the decent because of the heavy use of flaps and everything was steady on the approach until around 150ft - 200ft AGL the turbulence and gusts had rapidly gotten more intense. This pushed the plane back and while I was able to maintain a steady angle of attack until around 100ft AGL; I was just barely crossing over the runway threshold when a final gust pushed the plane on an uneven angle and slowed it into a stall; the final airspeed I rememberseeing was 38kts right before the stall. This happened so close to the runway that I was unable to go around again or glide comfortably to the runway. Aircraft X impacted with the runway and rolled in the grass between the runway and taxiway 1. It stopped in the grass and the mixture was leaned to idle before pulling out the throttle and turned off all electronics to the plane. The plane was swiftly evacuated and rescue crews arrived on the scene. No damage to property or injury to any body involved was found. The only known damage to be found was a chip to the front wheel's rim which was still able to hold air and the windshield had shattered leaving only half of the glass remaining in frame.

column121: On a Part 135 flight operating from ZZZ Airport; the aircraft experienced an in-flight abnormal/critical event while in cruise flight.During cruise; smoke and an electrical burning odor were observed in the cabin area near the galley microwave. Based on observations during the event; I believe the microwave inverter or associated electrical component may have shorted and produced smoke. I began troubleshooting and addressing the smoke source in the cabin.While dealing with the smoke the aircraft experienced a loss of cabin pressurization; resulting in the automatic deployment of passenger oxygen masks. The combination of electrical smoke/fire indications and loss of pressurization significantly increased cockpit workload and created what I believed to be a critical situation requiring immediate priority handling.During the event; I was instructed to advise ATC that the passengers wished to change destinations rather than declare an emergency. The flight subsequently diverted to ZZZ1 Airport. While enroute to ZZZ1; repeated requests were made to ATC for lower altitude and direct routing to the ILS approach. We were not given priority; instead we were given vectors and lower altitudes; but not direct to the approach.I believe we should have declared an emergency because we had: suspected electrical smoke/fire; loss of cabin pressurization; passenger oxygen mask deployment; and an increased cockpit workload and abnormal aircraft condition.Had I been the Pilot in Command; I would have declared an emergency and requested priority handling to ensure expedited routing and appropriate emergency response coordination.The flight landed safely in ZZZ1 without further escalation. Next time I believe the correct action would be to declare an emergency; especially if the source of the malfunction is not immediately confirmed.

column121: On the evening of Day 0; I conducted a Part 107 UAS operation at Location X in support of media coverage activities for a public event. The initial launch location was adjacent to the event area. The later portion of the operation was intended to capture concluding event activities and the final scheduled performer for the evening as part of the event media coverage scope.Prior to the operation; I coordinated with event organizers; informed onsite event and public safety personnel that UAS operations would be occurring in support of the event and conducted standard preflight planning activities. I obtained applicable LAANC authorizations for the operational area; including authorization approved at approximately XA:08 and an extension authorization approved at approximately XB:32.During preflight planning; I reviewed applicable airspace information and mistakenly believed that no event was occurring at the nearby stadium during the planned operation window. Receipt of the LAANC authorizations and my incorrect understanding of the TFR schedule contributed to my mistaken assumption that all required airspace considerations affecting the operation had been adequately addressed.The aircraft was operated with additional safety considerations appropriate for a public event environment; including the use of propeller guards and operational procedures intended to minimize risk to persons on the ground. The operation was not intended to involve sustained flight directly over open-air assemblies of people.Flight operations began at approximately XA:25. During the later portion of the operation; fireworks became visible and audible near approximately XC:28. This immediately prompted concern that a TFR was active. Upon recognizing the possibility of an active TFR; I immediately terminated flight operations and safely recovered the aircraft without incident.Following the operation; I reviewed the applicable NOTAMs and confirmed that a TFR was active. No injuries; property damage; loss of separation; or interference with manned aircraft occurred during the operation.Contributing factors included incorrect assumption regarding incomplete verification of event-triggered TFR status; and confirmation bias after receipt of valid LAANC authorizations for the operational area.As corrective action; I am implementing additional preflight verification procedures for all operations near stadiums or event venues; including direct verification of active schedules; final NOTAM review immediately prior to takeoff; and secondary cross-checking through multiple planning sources to prevent recurrence.This report is submitted voluntarily in the interest of aviation safety and continued operational improvement.

column121: Climbing out of ZZZZ passing through 18;000 feet; a senior Flight Attendant called the Captain in flight deck very distressed. She said the aircraft was vibrating significantly by door 2L. The Captain had the relief pilots go check out the vibrations. They called the Captain and said it was abnormally loud and you could feel the vibrations in their feet.At the same time the left vibration indicator on the engine instruments was steadily increasing from an indication of 1.1 to 1.7 as we continued climbing to FL320. The right vibration indicator stayed constant at 0.9. The crew elected to level off and as power came back the left vibration indication slowly reduced back to 1.1.The crew contacted dispatch on SATCOM and asked to be connected to Maintenance Control.There was no 787 mechanic available for over 10 minutes.
