column121: This was a scheduled flight between ZZZZ1 and ZZZZ2 with operating crews and company jump-seaters.  This event occurred within ZZZZ FIRWhile operating flight to ZZZZ2 as First Officer and PF we were established at initial cruise at 31100. We were continuously in and out of cloud tops during this portion. After a few minutes the wing and nacelle anti-ice systems automatically turned on. Almost immediately we had a bleed #2 EICAS alert with associated inop light in #2 bleed air switch. The PM ran the bleed #2 checklist; after complication we got WAI L;R EICAS  messages .  While working that checklist we received bleeds 1;3;4 EICAS alerts as well.  This was followed shortly by the return of bleed 2 EICAS alert. We noticed cabin altitude climbing and at an altitude of 5700 we elected to put on O2 masks and activated supernumerary o2 switch.  The CPT ran those checklists and managed to get two bleeds back on but we eventually lost all 4 bleeds a second time. Unable to maintain cabin pressure; we advised ZZZZ ATC and coordinated a rapid descent to 3000 meters. During rapid descent the highest cabin altitude noted was 12000 and highest rate of cabin climb was 2000 fpm.  Once below 10000 we removed masks and continued running the EICAS generated non-normal checklists (Cabin Altitude; Bleed 1; Bleed 2; Bleed 3; Bleed 4; Packs 1+2+3; Cabin alt auto; Outflow valve r/l; Suprnmry oxy on; Pack mode 2; Pack mode 1; Pack mode 3). Once below 10000 we struggled to maintain communications with ZZZZ [TRACON] Control even using 121.5; we required multiple relays with other aircraft. It took multiple attempts to verify our final altitude and confirm QNE vs QNH.  Also during this low altitude cruise with center Autopilot engaged and no other crew engagement; power began to increase with a corresponding climb commanded by Autopilot. PF disconnected auto-pilot and auto-throttles and returned aircraft to level flight at 3000 meters. We also noticed lights in Mode Control Panel (MCP) flickering continuously bright to dim. Once stabilized the left Autopilot was selected and auto-throttles were re-engaged.After evaluating options and communicating with dispatch we elected to continue the short flight to ZZZZ2. Once in terminal area we requested short delay vectors to allow for flaps to extend in secondary mode due to lack of bleed air to actuate leading edge in primary mode and landed safely off ILS-Z to runway XX. We maintained our aircraft in distress status until landing due to abnormal aircraft condition.This was a fairly challenging situation.  Time of day; complexity of system failures; communications with foreign controllers; cabin altitude and use of oxygen mask all contributed to high workload.  I was surprised how much the O2 mask decreased our ability to effectively communicate and maintain a high level of situational awareness.

column121: While descending into CYYC on the EBGAL 7 arrival RWY 36R; I was PM; and the first officer was PF.  We had been held up due to traffic below us; and once cleared to descend to 9;000 feet via the arrival; the PF chose to descend in open descent mode.  We had a restriction to cross EBGAL below 14;000' and TIDUK at 9;000.  I felt that descending in managed descent would have been more appropriate; but did not articulate that notion; because the altitude of 9;000 was in the altitude preselect window; and the FMS showed that we would cross EBGAL below 14;000. We requested the RNAV Y 35R with approach control and they cleared us for it via the TIDUK transition.  At that point the PF set 5200' in the altitude preselect window; and I reminded PF to select APPR mode. When PF selected APPR I noted that column 3 on the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) annunciated APPR NAV in green and column 2; line 2 showed ALT FINAL in blue. What I did not notice was that we were still in Open Descent in column 2; line 1.The PF chimed sterile at 13;600; and got the exterior lights at 10;000.I was reviewing my charts when I looked up and realized that we were at about 5;800'. I immediately instructed PF to climb back to 9;000' for the crossing restriction at TIDUK; which we did make.  We were not in dangerous proximity to the ground at that time; and in fact were in VMC; but we actually were between 200-500 feet below MEA on that segment of the approach. After climbing to 9;000'; the remainder of the approach was flown correctly and we landed safely at CYYC.Cause:  I feel that while checking the FMA was appropriate; my missing the Open Descent annunciation in my scan is what allowed this event to occur.  I understand that Open Descent ignores constraints; but I did not realize that selecting APPR would not cancel the Open Descent and capture the vertical path as I anticipated it would. We should have selected managed descent before arming APPR.

column121: Flight ABC from ZZZ to ZZZZ. Flight was late off the gate because of a tire change in the hangar then cleaning and catering once it got to the gate. Pretty chaotic off the gate; so much so that someone mentioned it felt like a training exercise. There was also a delay in our final weights as we were taxiing due to an error with the initial weights we were pushed. Something to do with an electric wheelchair.Captain's leg; I was pilot monitoring. Climb and level-off were normal. Relief pilot calculated breaks and left for his rest period. Received and OK'd ETOPS WX. We had sent a message but were waiting on reply.Almost exactly two hours after takeoff at XA:38; cruising at 35;000 feet; about 110 miles almost due north of Location X; the amber R ENG OIL PRESS caution popped up and I pointed it out to the captain. Looked at oil indications and right pressure was red; showing pressure of 0. I pulled up the FM Non-normals for ENG OIL PRESS L(R). Pressure indication at or below red line limit: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist." What!? A little bit of disbelief and surprise as I process the fact that this is an actual problem. The captain pulls up the non-normal emergency checklist on his side and verifies the issue. He directs me to request priority handling with ZZZ center and request lower altitude.I requested priority handling and get receive descent to 290. Captain then directs me to take over flying duties so he can work the checklist engine shutdown. We transfer controls and I start down in VNAV. I inform ZZZ of 170 SOB and 7+48 fuel on board while CA shuts down right engine. He then calls FA to wake relief pilot and have him report to the flight deck immediately. I am speaking with ZZZ; descending; and receiving vectors to the south while the relief pilot joins us and CA works checklist and coordinates with Dispatch and FAs. I notice the R Engine Temperature indicator in the red. I feel the yaw in the plane but; admittedly; took too long to remember that I needed to step on the left rudder pedal since the right engine had been shut down. Now in trim.A report from the cabin let us know a passenger noted flames coming from the right engine; though we had no indication of fire in the flight deck. The fire handle was decidedly pulled out of sequence from checklist but no extinguishing agent was discharged.I was working the radio and descending. I was trying to VNAV down to 290; then 200; then 6;000 feet; when I realized that was too many steps. I chose V/S out of FL200 because it was right in front of me on the panel. I realize after that I should have done FLCH; but it did what I needed done at the moment. Kind of a frenzied blur of a descent but at some point coordinated for divert to ZZZZ1; put it in the FMC as alternate; CA activated ILS approach RWY XX; coordinated with dispatch; and FAs; and Control for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting). Through 10;000 feet I was fast but recognized it and started slowing to 250 knots while continuing down. I was aware of but not focused on my distance from the airport and knew that I was high and fast. I was coming up on 6;000 feet; but I was still at 250 knots and high. I was cleared to 3;000 feet and direct to ZZZZZ (IF) for straight in to RWY XX; and shortly thereafter cleared for approach to RWY XX. Still high and 250 kts; though. The single biggest mistake of the night was my not arming APP mode here when cleared for the approach. This led to me being below glide slope on final which was trapped at 1000 feet but could have been avoided had I armed when cleared for approach.We completed the checklist and had a quick brief. There was a question if I felt comfortable performing the landing. I was comfortable but offered if the captain wanted to take it. We stuck with SOP; and I was going to make the landing and he was going to continue monitoring the situation. Relief pilot was an invaluable extra set of eyes and mind offering timely advice and mental support. We were coming up on 3;000 feet but hadn't fully restored our PM and PF rolls. I was worried about ALT CAP at 3;000 because I misinterpreted the approach chart thinking the glideslope started at ZZZZZ. This error was not trapped and 700 was put into the altitude window because we were at ZZZZZ and cleared for the approach. Altitude should have remained at 3000 since it was a level segment until GS intercept but definitely not lower than 1900 per the approach plate. This error when unrecognized and I ended up below GS with the runway in sight. Gear went down around 3;000 feet to help slow the plane and flaps were configured as we slowed through the flap speeds. The "Glideslope" EGPWS warning went off and I shallowed my descent to catch the glideslope. At 1000 AGL it was caught that I needed to level off to intercept the glide slope. I disconnected the AP; leveled off; and armed the approach. LOC was captured right away; I stayed level and moments later intercepted the GS and then continued to follow it to the runway. I got right of course initially with A/P disconnect but worked my way back to the left for a stable approach at 500 ft and a 'buttery' landing; if not a little left of center line.Pulled off the runway; got checked out by ARFF; and coordinated a gate. All cleared and taxied in for an otherwise normal shutdown."

column121: Scheduled flight was ZZZ1-ZZZ. The Wi-Fi was discovered to be inoperable on this flight and was not previously written up. Dispatch was notified about this and did an excellent job of keeping us informed with the changing conditions and helping build our situational awareness. Enroute to ZZZ; the flight experienced a rapid onset of moderate clear air turbulence which caused the airspeed to rapidly increase above VMO by 10-15 knots for about five seconds. The captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. The PF maneuvered the aircraft further away from enroute storms and the turbulence became consistent moderate. Once the turbulence died down; the captain told the flight attendants to take their jump seats; followed by a check in. There were no injuries. ZZZ was calling for thunderstorms; hail and tornadoes at the ETA. Flight held over ZZZ [VOR] at FL310 in smooth air to allow the storm to pass. After about an hour of holding; once the extreme precipitation was north and east of the field as reported by ATC and verified by the weather radar; the crew decided to begin the approach to runway XX. On the descent; at approximately 11;000 ft MSL the aircraft was struck by lightning and immediately showed an Eng 1 Reverse unlocked ECAM message. The approach was aborted; the PF leveled off at 10;000 and made a right turn direct to ZZZ2. Priority handling was requested and the ECAM was actioned; resulting in bringing the eng 1 thrust lever to idle; where it remained for the rest of the flight. There was no buffeting so the engine was not shut down but it was treated as a single engine approach. The captain accomplished the brief with the flight attendants. The crew received vectors for the ILS XYL at ZZZ2. On approach; with flaps one selected; a momentary overspeed occurred due to gusty wind conditions. The overspeed lasted less than five seconds and exceeded VFE by approximately five kts. Emergency equipment was standing by. A normal landing was accomplished followed by an uneventful taxi to the gate. Postflight inspection revealed lightning strike damage to the left engine nacelle; right inboard trailing edge flap; and right sharklet and static wick.
column123: We departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ anticipating the need for holding due to lots of severe thunderstorms enroute and near our destination. We had no WiFi on board which limited our ability to monitor everything; but we notified dispatch of our limitation so they could help keep us informed. Our first issue occurred at 37;000 feet enroute to ZZZ. We hit instant moderate-severe clear air turbulence and our airspeed increased by 25-30 knots and we oversped the jet for about 3-5 seconds. The ecam appeared for less than 1 second. After the initial entering of the turbulence; it stabilized to continuous moderate. We coordinated with center to descend and turn away from the storms to try and improve our ride; which worked. When hitting the turbulence the captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. After we exited the turbulence; he had them check in and confirm there were no injuries. We relayed that to ATC and continued on to ZZZ.Getting closer it became apparent that we would be unable to continue our approach into ZZZ due to the severe storms. We coordinated for holding at ZZZ [VOR] for about an hour while we worked with dispatch and center to monitor ZZZ. The WiFi was inop on our aircraft so our situational awareness was limited on what was going on at the airfield and around it. We received reports that the conditions were improving and with dispatch made the decision to shoot the approach. We were informed that the area had light thunderstorms with light to moderate rain and up to moderate turbulence. A RJ had gone in 15-20 minutes prior and had reported lightning and moderate chop before discontinuing the approach. We checked the weather again with approach and conditions still appeared to be improving. The 319 weather radar showed only light-moderate rain around the airfield as well. We were told the airfield still had gusty winds but high ceilings and we were told to expect the visual approach to runway XX. This clearance reaffirmed our belief that conditions were improving; so we elected to continue the approach. Around 11000 feet we were struck by lightning. We instantly got an eng 1 reverser unlocked ecam. We leveled off at 10000 feet and coordinated with approach to turn away from ZZZ and head to ZZZ2. All engine conditions were normal; so we started the turn and then ran the ecam. It directed us to pull the power on 1 to idle and leave it there. We then treated it as a single engine aircraft and declared an emergency. The capt did a brief with the FAs and informed the passengers that we were diverting to ZZZ2. We set up for an extended final for the ILS to XYL and ran all Checklists. ZZZ2 also had gusty winds and light to moderate rain; and on approach we oversped the slats at flaps 1 by 2-3 knots for 2-3 seconds. Aside from that we landed normally and emergency vehicles followed us into the gate where we shut down engines and terminated the flight.

column121: While operating Flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ on Day 0; at approximately XA:22; we were cleared direct to the Final Approach Fix (ZZZZZ) by ZZZ Tower for the visual approach and cleared to land on runway XX. Visibility at the field was reported to be 10 statute miles and weather was VMC. We verified the ILS frequency and course were tuned for Runway XX at ZZZ. With preview selected on the guidance panel; the First Officer selected Approach mode with the autopilot still coupled and while still in magenta lateral and vertical modes. Prior to the aircraft intercepting the localizer; the lateral and vertical modes both turned green and with the autopilot not yet captured on either the localizer or glideslope; autopilot performed an uncommanded descent from the assigned altitude and what appeared to be a smart turn inside the final approach course. The aircraft descended to approximately 800 feet AGL. We heard the 'one thousand' aural altitude alert; which prompted immediate disconnect of the autopilot and the First Officer climbed back to the charted altitude of the ZZZZZ (1;600'). We suspect the aircraft may have inadvertently captured a false glideslope and the combination of PREV mode active with APP armed prior to localizer/glideslope capture may have caused the autopilot to respond to spurious vertical guidance.Upon hearing the 'One Thousand' alert; the pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and initiated an immediate climb back to FAF altitude (1;600'). Shortly thereafter; Air Traffic Control issued a low altitude alert. As PM; I acknowledged and noted that we were correcting.No terrain conflict; obstacle contact or loss of separation occurred. The remainder of the approach was well within company standards and the landing was completed uneventfully.Cause: APP mode selected prior to localizer and glideslope capturePotential false glideslope signal in the vicinity of the FAFPossible smart turn intercept prior to localizer captureEmbraer 170/175 autopilot susceptibility to spurious ILS signals prior to valid course captureAutomation dependency Automation responded to vertical guidance signal before established on the published ILS pathSuggestions: Consider company training emphasis on delaying Approach mode selection until fully established on both localizer and glideslope; even when cleared direct to FAF for situational awarenessConsider training emphasis on direct-to-FAF clearances where autopilot and localizer/glideslope anomalies are most commonplaceConsider encouraging RNAV approaches whenever cleared for visual approaches to avoid mode confusion (both on the part of the aircraft automation as well as on the part of the pilot)
column123: During arrival into ZZZ; the visual XX backed up by ILS approach was briefed and the aircraft was configured in preparation for a stabilized visual approach. The aircraft was about 5 miles out navigating toward the FAF at a 70 degree angle to intercept with the published FAF altitude set and protected in the altitude selector. approach guidance was properly set up and verified prior to selecting APP mode. the autoflight system unexpectedly captured both localizer and glideslope indications despite the aircraft being outside a normal intercept profile. The aircraft then initiated an automated smart turn toward the localizer while simultaneously beginning a descent with a potential false glideslope capture while we were fully deflected from the localizer; Due to the close proximity to the approach and not being required to intercept outside FAF on a visual; the automated behavior was not immediately recognized as a problem. After a few seconds of monitoring what was happening and getting the 1000 foot call while still fully deflected; the autopilot was disengaged and corrective action was taken to return the aircraft to the appropriate FAF altitude and flight path towards FAF. at the same time at which we received the 1000 foot callout; a low altitude alert was given to us by tower. Once reestablished on profile; the remainder of the approach and landing were completed without further issue.Cause: Aircraft capturing localizer and glideslope when not established on final approach pathSuggestions: Wait to engage APP mode until fully established on final

column121: We were assigned Aircraft X to fly from ZZZ. When we arrived at the aircraft l was met by the FO that had flown it in. He advised me they had received an EICAS message about the Cargo Fire Extinguishing system and that line maintenance was onboard working on the write-up they had made for the message they had received on landing. We continued to complete our preflight duties while line maintenance cleared the message and the aircraft was cleared by maintenance. We departed and all was normal operations until approximately 30 minutes into the flight at 34;000 feet when we received a EICAS message CRG AFT FIREX HI ARM" Advisory. The message was displayed for just over a minute and then extinguished. During that time we referenced the QRH for direction and it stated this was a "Crew Awareness" message. Immediately after the "CRG FIREX HI ARM" message extinguished a second advisory message briefly appeared "CRG FIREX LO ARM" and was quickly replaced by a "CRG FIREX HI DISCH" status message. The QRH states that this message means that the "Cargo high-rate discharge fire extinguisher bottle has been discharged." We did not see any other indications of a Cargo Smoke warning (lights or EICAS messages). At this point in the flight I opted to send an ACARS message to dispatch to advise maintenance control that the Cargo high-rate bottle had discharged into the cargo compartment and asked them (dispatch and maintenance) if they wanted us to return to ZZZ. Our thought being that we still had over 90 minutes remaining to fly to our destination; but we were now only approximately 30 minutes from ZZZ. I opted to establish a SELCAL phone patch with dispatch shortly after sending the ACARS message to expedite the communication that we needed to have due to the complexity of the possible decision to divert. While establishing the phone patch through Company radio we received the message "MAINTENANCE SAYS ITS CREW DIFEREABLE".Once the phone patch was established with dispatch we discussed the message we received; what I thought was now the state of the compromised cargo fire suppression system; and some possible options with our dispatcher. The dispatcher again restated that maintenance said that we could continue to our destination and defer the cargo fire suppression system there. I told our dispatcher that this would mean we probably would not be able to carry cargo out of our destination. When a Cargo bottle is used to respond to a "CARGO FWD (AFT) SMOKE" warning message and the contents are discharged the QRH states to LAND AT THE NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. While we DID NOT have a CARGO SMOKE indication (Cargo Smoke push lights; or EICAS messages) our high rate bottle had been discharged and our ability to respond to any future CARGO SMOKE messages during the flight was compromised. Upon further discussion I opted to return to ZZZ to address the issue.My concerns regarding this particular in-flight event are the lack of safety minded real time decision making support from the team (dispatch and maintenance control) on the ground. A statement like "Do what your QRH directs" does not help in this situation. Especially considering the fact that the EICAS messages we were referencing in the QRH did not expressly state what to do given this particular set of circumstances. If we had opted to continue to our destination we would have flown for over 90 minutes with a compromised Cargo compartment fire suppression system to a destination that could probably not service (repair the system or replace the halon) on the aircraft while dealing with contract maintenance in a foreign country. According to the FAA; inflight lithium battery fires and smoke incidents on domestic flights now occur at a rate of roughly two incidents per week. A fact that I was made aware of while attending recurrent ground school less than a month ago. We were carrying cargo and according to the EICAS messages present we did not have a high rate bottle option available to fight a fire in either cargo compartment. Guidance to continue to a foreign country destination and overlook the possible inflight risks; as well as deferring equipment that removes or seriously impacts the ability to carry cargo is at a minimum a bad business decision; or worse; our company is left trying to explain to the families of our passengers or the FAA why we opted to continue if we had an actual cargo fire happen without the possibility to fight the fire in the remaining flight. The decision to RETURN TO ZZZ should have been made as a consensus by all parties involved. After returning and landing safely in ZZZ we were advised by line maintenance that this aircraft has a history of these types of messages occurring. A side note to this incident; after being reassigned another aircraft and completing the flight several passenger thanked us for getting them safely to their destination; despite arriving a couple of hours late."

column121: Upon blocking in at gate XX; I set the Parking Brake In Accordance With (IAW) SOP's and the Triple Indicator showed normal Brake and Accumulator Pressure.  I then took my feet off the toe brakes and the aircraft began to roll forward.  The FO promptly called 'We're Rolling!' just as 'Brake System Fail' and multiple other ECAM messages populated with aural alerts.  I immediately applied maximum braking to stop the aircraft and noticed that the Brake Pressure indications in the Triple Indicator were at Zero; with normal accumulator pressure.  The airplane stopped abruptly as the ground personnel ran away from it.  Thankfully; the airplane stopped prior to impacting ground equipment; the jet bridge; or personnel.  I estimate we were a MAXIMUM of 5' from impacting equipment in front of the airplane.  I held the brakes until communications were established with ground personnel; the aircraft was chocked; and the tug was connected.  At that time; both engines were shut down and the aircraft was pushed back by the tug to the appropriate parking position.  Shortly after the aircraft was pushed into the appropriate parking position and after the last engine spooled down; normal Brake Pressure indications returned to the Triple Indicator and the ECAM faults cleared.  A detailed Discrepancy was entered in the logbook software. Maintenance was called and I personally described the problem to the responding mechanic.  NOTE:  I did discuss the situation with Union Safety and the Committee volunteer who handled my call stated that this same problem had occurred with another Airbus in the previous few days.Cause: I have no idea what the causal factors were - there was clearly some issue with brake system of that particular airplane and based on my discussion with union Safety; there MAY be an issue with the fleet. Regarding mitigation; I sincerely hope Maintenance; Union Safety; Company Safety; Flight Ops; and all other relevant departments investigate this situation THOROUGHLY.  As mentioned in my narrative above; the airplane was a MAXIMUM of 5' from impacting anything from ground equipment to a jet bridge; to a person.  Had the FO not immediately noticed the unexpected forward motion of the airplane; we would be dealing with an accident; a damaged airplane; and almost certainly injured personnel / passengers.
column123: After normal flight at gate arrival; crew taxi'd into gate XX.  After park brake set; each pilot started their flow for shutdown when as pilot monitoring I saw ground crew scattering and noticed aircraft was still rolling forward with the brakes set.  I said we're rolling forward and called for brakes as we jumped over the chocks and were picking up speed.  CA as pilot monitoring hit the brakes bringing us to a stop.  We noted no pressure in the hydraulic gage except for the accumulator and the brake handle was still in the set position.  Then a slew of brake failure cautions presented with no audio ding.  We held the brakes until ground crew connected the tug.  Once the engines were shutdown and the last engine stopped spinning. all cautions corrected themselves and the brake system returned to normal.we were tugged bake into position at the gate.Cause: Complete brake system failure. Recommend review of aircraft data and awareness to flight crews that this can happen during shutdown.

column121: While enroute; we had a system 3 hydraulic malfunction that required us to land at the nearest suitable airport. We found a spot on the ramp after exiting the runway. We contacted operations to send a tow team to tow us to the gate. In anticipation of the tow team's arrival; we shut down both engines. After waiting about 20 minutes for the tow team; suddenly the aircraft started to roll forward and then stopped. Without realizing it; we had been parked in an area that had a slight pitch.In hindsight; we realized that by shutting down the number two engine; we lost hydraulic pressure on the brakes. Due to the non-standard configuration of the hydraulic pumps with the hydraulic three malfunction; the normal brake pressure applied by that system was not on. Keeping hydraulic two system on would have prevented this problem.Cause: The non-standard configuration with the hydraulic system and the high workload related to an unplanned diversion both contributed to this event.Suggestions: During non-standard operations with hydraulic system malfunctions; it would be great to have some kind of checklist or reminder to double-check the systems for any non-standard scenarios that might be anticipated. Due to the nature of an unplanned diversion; and all the details that come with that non-standard scenario; it was difficult to remember the non-standard situations to expect with system malfunctions.

column121: Severe turbulence encounter over OBK aboard Aircraft X; ZZZ - ZZZ1; XA:14 Day 0.Aircrew was aware of a large weather system along the route of flight and; on the previous flight (ZZZ1 - ZZZ); had coordinated a significant deviation from the originally filed flight plan due to this weather system. Prior to departure; we reviewed the flight plan filed by dispatch; and assessed that; as the route of flight took us to the north of the weather pattern (as opposed to going through the south of it; as we had been filed on the previous leg); we would safely avoid the weather.I conduct all of my welcome aboard announcements via face-to-face communication at the galley. During my PA; I stressed that we would be encountering significant weather during the first 1 - 1.5 hours of the flight; and that it was very important for the passengers to remain seated while the seatbelt sign was on; for their safety; and that I anticipated turning the seatbelt sign off during the remaining hour of the flight.In flight; Center (Chicago Center?) recommended that we add OBK to our route to avoid the northernmost boundary of the weather. We entered OBK into our weather application; assessed that this was a prudent route modification based on the developing weather; and accepted OBK. I also communicated the change to dispatch. We observed an area of moderate turbulence over OBK and did not see that as a significant threat; however it was enough for me to ensure that both FAs were seated while we penetrated the turbulence in accordance with the FOM.I initially directed the FAs to remain seated during the initial climb based on other turbulence I observed we would encounter early in the flight; then I released the FAs to perform service at their discretion. When I initially released them; I informed them that they would be able to be up for approximately 30 minutes; then they would need to be seated to penetrate an area of anticipated moderate turbulence (over OBK). After approximately 30 minutes; and about 5 minutes until we reached OBK; I called them to direct them to return to their seats.We had been operating in full IMC for about 20 minutes prior to reaching OBK. (The weather at OBK was visually embedded from our perspective.) ATC advised that there was an area of moderate to heavy precipitation around OBK; I was tracking this area via both the weather application and the onboard aircraft radar. I noted (via onboard radar) that there was an area of heavy precipitation depicted just south of OBK; and that our route appeared to slightly bypass that area to the north. Weather application still showed moderate turbulence.We encountered substantial turbulence as we reached OBK. Altitude and airspeed deviations were so violent that it was nearly impossible to keep up with them; I estimate that we had +- 500 ft. of altitude loss/gain at one point. FO as PF slowed from Mach .77 to .75; and I engaged both Continuous Ignition and the Turbulence Mode on the FCP.Based on the information displayed on our weather application; I believed that we would not be in the worst of the turbulence for very long; so it was in our best interest to continue in our direction of flight instead of turn around. The event lasted approximately two minutes. After exiting the severe turbulence; I assessed that we had just experienced a severe turbulence encounter and called the FAs to assess the conditions in the cabin. The FAs reported no injuries or known damage. I then reported a severe turbulence encounter to ATC; consulted relevant guidance on the FOM; notified dispatch of the encounter and requested maintenance to meet us at ZZZ1.After reaching the Western Michigan area and exiting all turbulence; I turned off the seatbelt sign and the flight continued normally.In my opinion; the weather in the area around OBK simply progressed worse / faster than forecast; and there just was not a viable means available to any of the relevant actors (flight crew; ATC and dispatch) to detect that area of severe turbulence.Dispatch provided what appeared to be a safe route prior to departure (having immediately prior to that fight to initiate a route modification to that same departure point; I closely scrutinized the proposed route to avoid a repeat of that situation). ATC SPECIFICALLY recommended OBK to further isolate us from the weather. Dispatch was informed and did not object to the route modification. Flight crew was actively monitoring the weather during our approach to OBK via weather application and onboard radar; there was simply nothing to indicate an area of severe turbulence via the resources available to the crew; and likely dispatch or ATC.Risks to passengers and crew were successfully mitigated by direct and constant communication and ensuring cabin preparation for turbulence penetration.Suggestions: Information only.
column123: Severe turbulence in flight. During cruise flight at approximately FL340 the aircraft encountered severe turbulence while enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Prior to the encounter we just received reports of moderate chops along our route. We were following ATC reroute that took us to a fix north of the weather system and then on our filed route.We had a change in altitude of +/- 300 - 500 ft. and a change of airspeed of +/- 20 kt. for around 3 - 4 minutes. The autopilot remained engaged and the crew maintained positive aircraft control throughout the event. Cabin crew was contacted as soon as conditions permitted which reported no injuries or damage.The remainder of the flight was conducted without further complications. The captain requested to meet with maintenance upon landing and on the gate for maintenance inspection.

column121: Aircraft was in cruise flight; 34;000 ft.; on a weather deviation approximately 35 miles east of route between the ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 intersections. Flight was proceeding normally; we were anticipating a turn back on course to rejoin before ZZZZZ2 (turning back approximately abeam position ZZZZZ1) as we tracked the weather via radar and satellite data from the Weather App. Aircraft was dispatched with 2 MELs - 21-XX-XXX Packs and A46-YY-YYY Domestic Enroute (USA) CPDLC Restricted. The first MEL meant that we were operating with a single PACK - #2. (Pack #1 was OFF per the procedure of the MEL.)Due to reported SatCom outages - Dispatch just happened to choose our flight to do a SatCom voice check. As the non-normal unfolded this fortuitous SatCom call from the company helped expedite communications to prep ZZZZ Operations for the divert. We were able to communicate our intentions and had both dispatch and Maintenance Control looped in on the issue as it was happening live. We received the following ECAMs: Air Pack 1+2 Fault. CAB PR Lo Diff PR. CAB PR Excess Cab Alt.We followed SOP in accordance with an aeronautical decision-making model and worked the ECAMs as they presented themselves. I called for priority handling on 121.5 (guard) - announced our intentions to divert to ZZZZ and we began an expedited descent to 10;000 ft. ZZZ [ARTCC] Air Traffic Control responded to our distress call - gave us a new frequency; established radar contact; and gave us a vector towards the airport (ZZZZ). We donned our O2 masks and established flight deck communications. Continued to work the non-normal while on the expedited descent. The situation continued to evolve as the associated ECAMs began appearing - i.e.; CAB PR Lo Diff PR & CAB PR Excess Cab Alt. I communicated to inflight via the call button - they answered right away. I told them that we were in a situation. Explained the reason (loss of pressurization system) and told them our time to landing. I also made a PA to the passengers letting them know that we would be making an unscheduled stop; giving them a non-technical explanation of the problem; and that we'd have more information for them on the ground for how they would continue their journey to ZZZ. I was told during the post-flight debrief with the inflight crew that I did a stellar job pushing and pulling the information to both inflight and the passengers. Inflight felt very calm about the whole non-normal as it evolved. (Aside from the ear-popping) inflight told me that the passengers were very calm and nonplussed the whole time. My PA from the flight deck diffused any cabin stress that would have led to an undesirable outcome once on the ground.We continued working aspects of the non-normal and transited into the arrival and approach phase of the flight. Our new destination was inputted; weather obtained; approach was built and briefed; charts and airport company pages reviewed. In this phase of flight - everything was stable. The cabin altitude was at a safe breathable level; we had removed our O2 masks and reestablished flight deck comms. Important to note; the passenger O2 masks DID NOT deploy from the Passenger Service Units (PSUs) during the non-normal. We were proceeding on a vector to our approach - RVAV XX into ZZZZ. I took the time to review the Overweight Landing QRH Checklist. (Our landing weight was 147.8 - a couple of thousand pounds higher than max for that particular weight variant.) Also; the divert checklist in the Manual. I wanted to ensure that we were covering all of our bases and not missing anything. I also reviewed the steps we took during the non-normal up to this point - I talked out loud" while FO and I discussed what got us from 34;000 ft. to this approach into ZZZZ and plainly asked; "Did we forget anything?" The aircraft was expertly landed in ZZZZ by FO. He followed the guidance in accordance with the overweight checklist. "Soft" touchdown and the brakes did not heat up above approximately 200 C. We taxied to the gate where we were met by Station Operations; Local Crash Fire Rescue (CFR); Local Customs and Immigration; and Local Maintenance Control representatives. Times were noted and passed to dispatch. I made the following write-ups in the logbook: AIR Pack 1+2 Fault Inflight - may have been due to OVHT condition. CAB PR Excess CAB ALT ECAM - associated with the above write-up. CAB PR LO Diff PR - associated with write-ups. Overweight landing due to divert - Landing Weight: 147;800 lb.; soft touchdown; temperatures less than 210 C. NAV Tuning LS Disagree Inflight - reset as per QRH - continued normally. The 5th write-up was not associated with the situation; non-normal; or divert. After that I talked with the Maintenance Control representative; Station Operations; and made a PA for the passengers talking about next steps. Passengers were deplaned and the non-normal was debriefed (informally) with all of the crew. Aircraft was taken out of service and a flight was dispatched. Any unintentional (or otherwise) deviations from SOP were done under Captain's Authority under the appropriate FARs. Any errors were trapped using our Threat and Error Management (TEM) model. I would like to commend (and sincerely thank) the crew - FO and FAs - for their professionalism and skill during the event and divert to ZZZZ. Their quick thinking; calm demeanor; and adherence to SOP made this a very easy problem to navigate. I may be the final authority and ultimately responsible for the flight; but we couldn't have done what we did without the support of the whole crew doing their jobs competently and without delay. They are all the best. I'd also like to thank the instructor pilots at Company. Every instructor that I interacted during every training event for the past years contributed to the safe outcome of this non-normal. In conclusion; we had a safe and successful outcome. I can tell you honestly that I will be debriefing this incident internally for the rest of my career - with many lessons learned. Our flight had a serious mechanical problem and we stayed off social media and out of the news. The passengers seemed genuinely not annoyed with the outcome - they still got to their final destination; albeit a little later than they hoped. Our training and the safety systems worked the way that they were designed. It wasn't perfect - no real world non-normal is. As the plane started to turn it quickly turned into a ground loop that the flight instructor tried to correct for. Suddenly we were pointed towards the grass on the edge of the runway. In an effort to stop the aircraft before rolling off my flight instructor tapped on the brakes in hopes of slowing us down but the plane instead stopped in its tracks causing the nose of the aircraft to fall over and onto the ground.After the aircraft stopped moving and the nose was positioned into the pavement I turned off the engine by cutting the mixture and throttle; turning off the fuel selector; turning off the magnetos and the electrical system. My flight instructor got out of the aircraft first and I followed getting away from the aircraft and assessing ourselves for any injuries. After confirming no injuries we proceeded to talk to the authorities.Contributing factors for this event would be the gusting conditions; my little experience in a tailwheel aircraft; and the sensitivity of the aircraft brakes. column121: On Day 0 while operating Aircraft X the flight crew experienced an un commanded movement of the aircraft during the shutdown portion of the flight. After being guided to a complete stop at the gate; the parking brake was set and PARK BRK message verified along with normal pressure indications. The shutdown flow continued in sequence and during the portion of the flow while heads were down; the aircraft began to roll. Once the un commanded movement was realized; the Captain slammed on the brakes immediately. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop. At some point during the roll or just prior to toe brakes being applied the crew received a BRAKES PARK BRK FAULT ECAM message with zero pressure indicated on the accumulator. There were no injuries to ground crew; flight crew or passengers. There was no damage to either the aircraft or jet bridge. The crew followed standard operating procedures and maintained positive control of the aircraft to the best of their ability throughout the event. Once the aircraft was confirmed chocked; the toe brakes were released and the parking brake recycled which then cleared the ECAM and returned hydraulic pressure back to normal. The aircraft was subsequently repositioned via tug vehicle and secured. Maintenance was contacted shortly after.Cause: This event appears to be purely an aircraft systems failure. Per the logbook; the aircraft has a history of this very same problem and clearly needs to be fixed permanently. One recommendation that the crew can add to help mitigate the risk of injury to the passengers would be to relocate the seat belt sign off to one of the last items on the shutdown flow and checklist. The passengers were thrown forward when the brakes were slammed on bc the seatbelt sign had been turned off per the second step of the flow. Engines were still running which allowed the aircraft to move forward quickly. Had the engines been shutdown prior to the seat belt sign being extinguished; we may not have had the high risk of injuring a passenger.

After brakes had been set the ground crew moved the tug in front of the aircraft beneath the line of sight from the cockpit.  After a pause; one of the rampers on the Captain side of the aircraft gave a hand signal quickly.  I interpreted this as the opening hands signal to release brakes and did so.  There was a short pause and the aircraft began moving.  I initially perceived this as tug movement on the aircraft.  The FO said something expressing concern; which I first thought was due to him not having seen the signal directly.  Within another second or so we both applied brakes and I reset the parking brake.  The aircraft had moved a few feet; but I couldn't give an exact distance.  Via interphone we resestablished positive comms with the ramper and the rest of the tow-in was uneventful.  No aircraft damage or personnel injury occurred.  I met with and debriefed with the rampers.  I don't believe any passengers were alarmed by aircraft movement.  I phoned the Chief Pilot and relayed the above information.
column123: During taxi in to gate XX in ZZZ; a miscommunication occurred and the aircraft moved without concurrence or expectation from the ground crew.  Gate XX is noted in the company pages as requiring idle thrust from the taxi lane into the gate entirely; and that the gate is upsloped. This was briefed prior to arrival and we discussed possibly needing a tow into the gate if the turn couldn't be successfully accomplished at idle thrust.  It could not in our case; and we stopped about 50 feet short of the stop bar. The tow  in procedure was initialized by us and the ground crew and we shut down the engines. The incident occurred during the hook up of the tug unit. The tug and ground crew approached the aircraft; and being under the aircraft only briefly; the captain said out loud; ok brakes released" and the captain did so; to which I was alerted as being too soon in the normal sequence. I looked up and around the aircraft and saw the aircraft quickly yawing to the left and said; "whoa; no no no"; and began to depress the brake pedals from my side as I was trying to confirm my belief that this was premature. The captain stated; "I have the brakes released hand signals! They're towing us!" And I responded; "no; no you don't!"; the captain joined me on the brakes and I saw multiple ground crew from my window with the now-visible tug giving us the 'stop' signal; and relayed what I saw to the captain. We realized the aircraft had swung nose-left uncommanded/unintended and put the ground crew at very high risk.  The distance the nosewheel rolled I estimate to be about 10-15 feet.  The ground crew plugged in their headset and they confirmed brakes were set; and the captain asked if everyone was safe and ok; which the ground crew confirmed.  We froze the scene; discussed what happened; and ensured and agreed we could safely continue.  We; the flight crew; realized the ground crew already had the nosewheel bypass pin installed when the aircraft rolled; and the reason the aircraft yawed was the nosewheel free castering under the weight of the unbraked aircraft.  The captain stated he mistook this movement as being towed. With the ground crew; we discussed how to move forward safely; including how to straighten the nosewheel to restart the tug connection. This was accomplished safely and the aircraft was pulled into the gate and proceeded normally after that.  We debriefed the event very thoroughly between ourselves and with the ground crew. We identified the primary cause of the event was the captain and one of the ground crew confused the "brakes set" vs "brakes released" hand signals between each other; either through expectation bias or vague signaling; and the parking brake was released prematurely prior to completing the tug hookup."

column121: While in flight around ELP we experienced GPS jamming. After a while we received GPS and GLS FMC alert messages. I verified RNP value of .24 and referenced the Flight Manual (FM). Both left and right GPS were failed at this time. It was anticipated that once clear of the GPS jamming that all systems would return to normal. For some additional context at this point of the flight we had been navigating through thunderstorms and I had all the flight attendants seated. When approaching the portion of flight that was about to cross the gulf I reached out to Dispatch and Maintenance Control to try to recover our GPS as I was thinking about the GPS issue more and was concerned that being away from land base nav aids for such a long time would cause the ANP to drift to unacceptable levels for a long segment over water. Maintenance Control directed to pull the Multi-Mode Receiver (MMR) ILS-1 Circuit Breaker (CB) per FM. It was during this reset both FMC failed; autothrottle; autopilot; disengaged and the aircraft went into Control Wheel Steering (CWS). The first officer flew the aircraft and was able to recover and engage the CMD with Alt hold/CWS. We received radar vectors from ATC to stay over the Houston shoreline at FL330. At this time Chief Pilot also was on the line and together we walked through a recovery of the right FMC was accomplished with the return of the Control Display Unit (CDU) FMC functionality.  It was at this time the options were discussed about how to proceed and I made the decision to divert due to the amounts of threats with the current aircraft maintenance status and external factors such as thunderstorms; overwater operations; international operations; remaining fuel on board; and weather upon arrival.
column123: The night prior I hadn't slept very well; I laid down at midnight and got out of bed in the morning but spent a lot of that time unable to fall sleep and didn't feel very rested going into the day. I made sure to give myself time before work to rest. I was able to nap for roughly three hours before getting ready for work. There was some traffic so the drive took me longer to get to the airport. I felt relatively rested through most of the flight and ready to continue with no concerns. I think the workload involved with the GPS jamming which eventually let to the Dual FMC failure and divert; along with weather deviations for thunderstorms throughout the issue was very fatiguing; especially for a late all night flying flight. When we lost our FMCs we reverted to ALT HOLD and Control Wheel Steering (CWS) R; Autothrottles disengaged and wouldn't reengage; I was hand flying; and coordinating with ATC to deviate around thunderstorms. The captain was talking with Maintenance Control; dispatch; the Chief Pilot and keeping the flight attendants and passengers informed. With this particular event there wasn't really much guidance in our manuals or procedures on how to proceed. It took a lot of discussion; troubleshooting and decision making to come up with a decision. We ultimately diverted. After arriving at our gate; the captain and I talked about whether or not we should continue. We agreed that it would not be a safe decision to extend our duty day and accept another flight. I think the whole event was just fatiguing on an already late night. While debriefing on the ground and trying to recall the details of the issue; it was apparent we were showing signs of fatigue.

column121: The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 started off uneventful. Everything was going smoothly and as expected. During our climb to FL330; at FL320 I noticed a faint amount of smoke coming from the PTT button panel. There was also a noticeable burning plastic smell. The smoke did not stick around very long and was gone in roughly 20 seconds. The burning smell did remain throughout the flight though. Captain was the pilot flying when we noticed the smoke and smell. Captain transferred controls to me and requested priority handling with ATC. It was a very small amount of smoke; but it was still smoke. So we did our smoke fire and fumes memory action items. We established communication but the Captain was slightly hard to hear with the masks on. Captain tried making another call to ATC but they could not understand anything he was saying due to the mask not being clear. We transferred controls back to him and I took over communications and checklists. I cleared up confusion with ATC that was present from Captain not being understood. We established we were a priority aircraft and would like to divert to ZZZ2. We were told to descend and we could expect vectors for the ILS XX into ZZZ2. While we started a fast descent; Captain sent a message through ACARS to dispatch that we were diverting. I got out our QRH after confirming our memory action items from the QRC. I started the Smoke Fire or Fumes QRH. While going through this checklist I did get interrupted a few times. I needed to relay to ATC our situation. I told them our fuel on board and the souls on board. I needed to make this call a couple times as they did not hear clearly the first time. Once that was clear we called back to the flight attendant that we were diverting and seeing if he had any smoke in the cabin. He could not understand the Captain and after a couple attempts; I told him we were diverting and learned he did not have any smoke in the back. While this conversation was happening ATC was giving us instructions to swap frequencies and to keep descending. I believe we got swapped to approach at roughly 14;000 MSL. Approach gave us a heading to fly as well for the ILS XX. While we were descending; and I was handling communications; the Captain got the approach loaded and frequencies set up. Communications were set up and the approach was loaded. I continued the QRH and got to the point of executing an emergency descent; at this point Captain said to pause that checklist as we needed to focus on preparing for landing. We were also at roughly 10;000 MSL so we did not need any more of an emergency descent as we had acted quickly about getting lower. On our descent I called the FA for a briefing. I told him there was smoke and we are landing in ZZZ2. I told him he had roughly 5 minutes or less until landing. No special instructions as we should be going to the gate as normal. No bracing signal. I had him report that back and he did so perfectly. Continued our descent; we broke out of IMC at roughly 8;000 MSL if I recall correctly; after having being in IMC up until this point through the issue. Captain gave a briefing on the approach. Afterward; I ran the Cruise; Descent; and Approach checklists. Both of us verifying items were complete and accurate. After running the approach checklists; I checked our weight and told the Captain we would be over max landing weight. We got swapped to tower and continued our approach. I ran the overweight landing checklist and we utilized the new landing distance that we were still in compliance with. We were cleared to land by tower on runway XX. With the landing; Captain came in slightly below glide slope to have some time to arrest our descent. He did so very well and we touched down very smoothly. Tower told us we could stop on taxi way 1 after exiting the runway but we elected to get to the ramp. While we taxied I gave a passenger announcement that we were in ZZZ2 due to a precautionary event and we would give them an update when we have one.I apologized about the inconvenience of the diversion and for not addressing them in the air as we were quite busy. Tower gave us instructions to cross runway XY on 2. We got to the ramp and a fire truck was parked in front of the intersection; 3; that we took. The Captain came to a stop as it seemed two firefighters were approaching us and wanted us to stop. The firefighters came up to the plane with both engines running. They did not appear to see anything abnormal as they were very calm. They wanted to communicate and gave us some hand motions to their ears. The Captain and I opened our windows and I tried shouting to them that we could still smell the burning plastic. I had the goggles and mask still on which made this hard. They handed up a note pad to the Captain and we coordinated to taxi to a gate with passing the note pad back and forth. I told the Captain that we can still smell the smoke and mentioned evacuating there. He said no; it will be much better getting passengers off at the gate and I agreed. We did not confirm with the FA that everyone was seated before we started moving again. Later; FA did tell me that everyone was seated when we started moving. We did not contact company ops in ZZZ2; which looking back could have made the ground operations a bit smoother for us. While we taxied to the gate I addressed the passengers and apologized again about the inconvenience and thanked them for their understanding. While addressing the passengers I did not use an alarmed tone or emergency terminology. We parked the plane and continued to run all of our check lists on the ground as normal. The passengers started to deplane and while everyone was exiting; they were very grateful for keeping them safe. Many expressed their thanks to our entire crew. No passengers reported any sort of illness or injuries. Firefighters came aboard and utilized their heat camera and said they did not see anything triggering it. We assumed the source of the smoke was confirmed to be out. We talked with dispatch and maintenance and got everything situated for the day. The crew took a deadhead back to ZZZ.Suggestions: I would suggest that during training there be a little more emphasis of what to do with issues when safely on the ground. Our situation was time critical but did not constitute an emergency evacuation that would have drawn much more attention to the situation. The communications on the ground were lacking as well. I had assumed tower would have gotten a spot set up for us to go to when on the ground but they seemed very laid back with the mentality that we can go wherever we want.

column121: Shortly after retracting the gear on takeoff we received a HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR ECAM.  Initially it was intermittent; with Green pressure showing between 100 - 1100 psi.  It shortly dropped to zero quantity.  I delayed running the ECAM until we had gained a little more altitude and completed the initial part of the ZZZZZX departure.  Climbing through ~ 7;000-8;000 ft; I called for QRC.  With no QRC; I transferred control to the FO with instructions to tell ATC that we'd stop our climb at 11;000 ft; which was our current assigned altitude.  ATC was informed of the issue and that we'd need a few minutes to run some checklists and talk to company…with a likely return to ZZZ.  I ran the ECAM; and once that was complete; I began the QRH.  Once that was completed down to the Emergency Gear Extension; we paused the QRH.  I then contacted company via Satcom (dispatch and Maintenance Control).  The phone patch from dispatch to Maintenance Control took a while; so while we waited to be connected; we started to run the Overweight Landing Checklist to make good use of our time.  I also spoke to the cabin crew to bring them up to speed on what was happening and told them I'd get back to them when I knew what we were going to do.  Once connected with Maintenance Control; they confirmed that we had lost all green pressure.  With thunderstorms forecasted for the ZZZ1 area; with the possibility of a divert; we agreed that the best course of action was to return to ZZZ.  Dispatch reminded me of the overweight checklist; which we had already begun.  Dispatch sent us the re-dispatch back to ZZZ; which we received via the printer as well as on the Operations Management System.  Once done with dispatch and Maintenance Control; we informed ATC with our intent to return to ZZZ; that we'd need about 20 minutes to finish checklists and to prepare for the return.  I also requested priority handling; requested Crash Fire and Rescue (CFR); and we notified ATC that once on the ground we would be unable to exit the runway due to the loss of nose wheel steering.  With the aircraft ready for the return to ZZZ and having spoken to the customers as well as cabin crew; we informed ATC that we were ready for the approach.  I briefed the cabin crew and made them aware it should be a normal landing with the exception of the CFR equipment meeting us and our inability to exit the runway/need for a tow to the gate.  Prior to returning to the airport we completed the Overweight Landing Checklist and reviewed the remaining portion of the QRH from the Emergency Gear Extension to the End; so that we had both seen it before needing to accomplish it.With everything prepared for the return; we notified ATC we were ready for the approach.  I allowed ample time to get configured before the final approach fix.  I instructed my FO to note the touchdown rate of decent and we noted the landing weight as well.  The touchdown rate was less than 50 fpm and I let the aircraft roll most of the length of runway XXL.  Brake temps initially were around 85 degrees; warming to roughly 160 degrees by the time the tug arrived.  Once stopped on the runway; I made a Remain Seated" PA and then spoke to cabin crew as well as made an announcement to the customers.  CFR and airport operations met the aircraft.  In roughly 10-15 minutes our tug arrived and we were escorted back to gate XX.One last component to mention was that we had an Air Carrier X pilot on the Jumpseat.  Once the issue started; he got on the Jumpseat headset and was a good help in monitoring radio calls while we got busy with checklists and briefing the course of action."

column121: On an ETOPS flex power takeoff prior to 80kts ECAM: T/L NOT SET.  Rejected takeoff.  Cleared the runway; ran the QRH Takeoff After Rejected Takeoff Below 80 Knots."  Discussed the possible causes of the ECAM with the FO.  Verified that the Flex temperature had been properly entered and the requirement that the Thrust Levers (T/L) were in the Flex detent.  Taxied out for a second Flex power takeoff attempt.  Prior to taking the runway; verified Flex temperature was on the Perf page.  FO was pilot flying (PF) again.  Flex power was set; and immediately noticed MAN FLEX was not displayed in Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) column 1 followed by ECAM: T/L NOT SET.  Rejected takeoff.  Cleared runway; called Maintenance Control and was instructed to return to the gate.  Aircraft removed from service.  Resulting maintenance action: replaced engine #1 & #2 T12 sensors and engine throttle control units.Cause: The Airbus AOM discusses this ECAM.  The AOM direction to select TOGA would only apply in the event that the FLEX temperature is not entered (or was inadvertently deleted due to runway change) on the Perf page and a FLEX takeoff is attempted or when the T/Ls are not in the FLEX detent.  This being an ETOPS departure; the decision was made to investigate further by rejecting the takeoff. This decision was validated after getting the same ECAM on the next takeoff anttempt and the subsequent maintenance actions that were taken to return this aircraft to service.  Recommend the AOM expound on the ECAM recommended TOGA selection to include the possible reasons this ECAM may be present.  Our experience and system knowledge prevented us from blindly selecting TOGA and flying an aircraft with a throttle control issue to destination."

column121: This report documents a loss of system A hydraulics on short final followed by a landing and QRH accomplishment.  Landing Gear was pinned and aircraft towed to the gate.  During the approach to ZZZ ILS XX at 800 ft AGL; a Master Caution light illuminated with an associated Hydraulic Elec 2 low pressure light (system A). Pilot Flying (PF) was the FO and Pilot Monitoring (PM) was the Captain. Both pilots acknowledged the light. The PM announced the condition and the PF maintained aircraft control.  Based on the facts that we were fully configured; below 1000'; had sufficient brake pressure; and were landing on a long runway well below required landing distance; we confirmed with each other and agreed to continue the approach to landing and delay the QRH until after landing. The PM subsequently extinguished the master caution light. At 500 ft AGL the Master Caution light illuminated again with associated ENG1 and ELEC2 Hydraulic pump low pressure lights. The simultaneous illumination of both System A hydraulic pump low pressure lights indicated a probable loss of System A hydraulic fluid.  At this point; since we were below 500 ft AGL and conditions were still favorable for a safe landing; we once again confirmed with each other that to continue to a landing was the safest option. At this point in the approach; the PF noted that a small amount of increased right aileron input was required to maintain control. While abnormal; it was easily controllable. From this point on; both pilots focused on landing the aircraft safely. During touchdown and rollout the aircraft performed normally. Automatic spoiler deployment occurred upon touchdown and the aircraft decelerated normally on autobrakes 3. Manual braking was applied shortly after touchdown by the PF. The transfer of aircraft control to the Captain occurred at approximately 70 knots. Initially; nose wheel steering was operational and we cleared the runway on taxiway Charlie cautiously and at a slow taxi speed. Upon the completion of the turn on to taxiway Charlie; the nosewheel steering failed. Once clear of the runway the parking brake was set. At this point we determined that we had a complete loss of system A hydraulics. We informed Tower that we needed to hold position to address a hydraulic leak.  We did not declare an Emergency; as the aircraft was on the ground and under control with the parking brake set.  The Captain then directed the Loss of system A" QRH and the FO read the checklist and we accomplished the applicable items. Communication was established with the Flight Attendants by the Captain and they confirmed that the situation was normal in the cabin.  Since the checklist calls for the gear pins to be installed prior to taxi; we determined the safest course of action would be to shut down the aircraft on the taxiway; have a ramp crew come out to the aircraft; install the gear pins; and tow us to the gate.  The Captain made a PA announcement explaining the situation to the passengers and informing them that we would be towed to the gate and all was under control.  When the tow crew showed up; they plugged in to the intercom and we devised a plan to pin the gear and tow the aircraft to the gate; escorted by airport operations.  We were advised us that they did not have gear pins available.  We then briefed a plan to shut down the aircraft engines; and remain on APU power.  Once safe to approach the aircraft; we would drop the gear pins out of the flight deck window; then clear him to pin the gear.  Once the gear was pinned; we were towed to the gate by the ground crew.  Upon post-flight inspection it was noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from the number one ground spoiler actuator on the left wing. Also; Airport Operations said that there was hydraulic fluid on the runway.Recommendations to mitigate the riskAfter debriefing as a crew we discussed some other options.  Option 1:  We could have gone around to run the checklist and to devise a plan. However; with the gear stuck down; we had a higher fuel burn rate and no alternate fuel (there is a warning in the checklist about this).  We would have had to maneuver without the use of half the flight spoilers.  We both believed that this option would have prolonged a dangerous airborne situation.  We had the proper configuration for landing; adequate brake pressure; excess runway available (8700' avail).  This option is worth discussing; but we both believed in this particular situation it was better to land.  The difference between a normal landing and a non-normal with loss of A hydraulics is only 400'.Option 2: Stop straight ahead on the runway; pin the gear; get towed to the gate.  We both agree that this may have been a better option.  However; we would have been on an active runway at night;  closing down the runway to other traffic.  That being said; it would have been the most conservative action. Option 3:  Coordinate with ATC to have ARFF available on site and follow us to the gate; since we had a hydraulic leak.  At the time; we did not consider this.  In retrospect; we believe it would have been a more conservative option. If we had accomplished the Non-Routine Landing Considerations QRH; it would have reminded us to do so."

column121: On approach to Chicago; we were cleared for the ILS 9 center. Slowing the aircraft down commanded by ATC from 170 kn to 160 kn; diligently painted a mental model of the traffic around us. We were paired up with Air Carrier X on nine left; nine right; and behind a regional in front of us which I verbalized im actively looking for traffic. At approximately 2000 feet AGL; I verbalize how there's traffic underneath us depicted on the Navigation Display (ND). As my attention went outside the aeroplane I physically saw Aircraft Y climb turn and descend underneath us for which I stated I had the aeroplane in sight within seconds if not tenth of seconds; my first officer was already manually flying the aeroplane preemptively in the best efforts to see and avoid. As as I proactively scan for traffic the only indication of an issue that I had was a second later when the TCAS system alerted us of a traffic advisory. I had not checked in with Tower as my attention was on guiding and managing the safety situation and near miss. Laterally we flew above Aircraft Y vertically last indication I saw on the ND was a vertical separation of about 500 feet if not less. In the best efforts of avoiding further traffic separation my first officer went slightly above wide path if not shallow or decent. I checked in with Tower; our checklist was complete and was clearanced to land and hold short of 9 center. We had another traffic advisory and on the end it was from the aeroplane that had already landed. We landed with no further incident.We had no advisory from air traffic control in protected airspace. Factors that contributed to our success was a good qualified trained crew; pilot judgement; and crew resource management and coordination. I stated my pilot duties to properly and mentally picture our movement through the airspace and how conflicting traffic can be seen and avoided. my first officer assumed the flying duties as expected. I was 10th of a second from taking controls when I needed to however I relied on the good pilot judgement for my first officer to help manage the situation. I can't stress this enough that I could not have done what was required of us unless we properly coordinated as a crew like we did. The professionalism and experience of both of us in the cockpit is inimitable and irreplaceable to safety and security for an efficient and safe operation. My question still stands as far as where and why ATC had no idea of the situation. Furthermore; where was the protected airspace and why was it intruded? The environment that we operated is dynamic so should the availability of protected airspace laterally and vertical. The dimensions should be and meet the operation to the fullest extent to extend bravo airspace if required and other air spaces for special use not just control airspace but specificly more restrictive requirements like bravo airspace. Even if we had an orb of class bravo airspace around the aeroplane; nothing could have contributed more to a successful outcome then two pilots doing the job that was expected of us at all costs.
