column121: On Flight ABCD from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Day 0; we encountered multiple areas of turbulence along our route of flight associated with convective and ride activity depicted on our weather and information systems. Prior to departure and throughout the flight; the First Officer and I actively monitored ride reports; weather depictions; and turbulence forecasts in order to mitigate exposure to passengers; flight attendants; and the aircraft.After departure from ZZZ on the ZZZZZX Departure; we initially experienced intermittent light to moderate turbulence during climb and cruise. Based on turbulence depictions along our route; particularly over portions of States X and Y near the ZZZ VOR area; I briefed the flight attendants in advance that we would likely require them to remain seated for an extended period in accordance with turbulence mitigation procedures.As we approached the area near ZZZ; we requested ride reports and altitude advisories from ATC in an effort to identify smoother ride conditions; however; ATC advised that aircraft in the area were reporting similar ride conditions at multiple altitudes. During this phase of flight; we encountered periods of light to moderate and occasional moderate turbulence; intermixed with smoother ride segments. Due to the continuing ride conditions and forecasted turbulence ahead; I directed the flight attendants to take their jump seats and repeatedly advised passengers to remain seated with seat belts fastened.While operating east of the river and north of the ZZZ area; both the First Officer and I began observing abnormal lateral/directional aircraft response characteristics during otherwise routine light to moderate turbulence encounters. Specifically; the aircraft began exhibiting a Dutch roll-type oscillation following even minor turbulence inputs. We noted that the oscillations appeared to amplify with time after turbulence encounters rather than dampen normally.The First Officer; who was Pilot Flying; remained prepared to assume manual control if necessary while I continued monitoring aircraft systems; ATC communications; and cabin coordination. During this time; I made additional passenger announcements emphasizing the need for all passengers to remain seated due to ongoing turbulence. Flight attendants also reported continued passenger movement in the cabin despite repeated announcements.Shortly north of ZZZ2; we again encountered light to moderate turbulence during which the aircraft's lateral oscillation increased further. The autopilot disconnected; and the First Officer smoothly assumed manual control of the aircraft while intentionally avoiding abrupt control inputs in order to minimize unnecessary aircraft motion and provide the best ride possible for the cabin. During this event; the aircraft experienced an altitude deviation of approximately 600-700 feet while in turbulence. I immediately requested and received a block altitude clearance from ATC between FL350 and FL360 to safely manage aircraft control and ride conditions. Other aircraft on frequency were simultaneously reporting similar turbulence-related issues and requesting altitude blocks in the same area.The First Officer stabilized the aircraft promptly; and we returned to our assigned altitude shortly thereafter. While monitoring aircraft systems; I observed the Yaw Damper switch in the OFF position with the associated Yaw Damper light illuminated. I checked the annunciator panel and noted no associated FLT CONT annunciation. Based on system knowledge and QRH guidance; I reengaged the Yaw Damper switch; at which time the Yaw Damper light extinguished and the aircraft's flight characteristics returned to normal. The First Officer concurrently referenced and completed the applicable QRH non-normal procedures while I monitored aircraft performance and flight path.After the aircraft returned to normal handling characteristics; I contacted the flight attendants to assess cabin conditions. The flight attendants advised that there were no injuries among passengers or crew; although several passengers in the aft cabin and one flight attendant experienced nausea associated with the lateral oscillation and ride conditions. At no point did the aircraft experience severe vertical acceleration or abrupt up-and-down movement; the primary ride issue involved lateral oscillation and rolling motion that was particularly noticeable in the aft cabin.Following coordination with ATC; stabilization of aircraft systems; and confirmation from the flight attendants that there were no injuries; we elected to continue the flight to ZZZ1. An ELB (Electronic Logbook) message was sent in flight to advise Maintenance Control of the event and to facilitate maintenance evaluation upon arrival. For passenger comfort; we subsequently reduced cruise speed to Mach .75; and ride conditions improved significantly as we progressed north of State Z. Once conditions permitted; the flight attendants resumed cabin duties; and I made a passenger announcement apologizing for the turbulence and advising passengers that multiple aircraft in the area had experienced similar ride conditions.Upon arrival in ZZZ1; we coordinated with maintenance personnel to debrief Maintenance Control regarding the event and aircraft behavior observed during the turbulence encounter.
column123: While cruising at flight level 360; the aircraft began to respond with rhythmic yoke movement after encountering continuous chop and turbulence events. All appropriate actions to sit the FAs and customers were completed prior to encountering this area of turbulence. Both pilots discussed concerns with the airplanes rhythmic movements. We checked for any anomalies on the annunciator panel as well as the overhead panel. As the pilot flying I chose to request a heading to disengage the LNAV function in an effort to see if this was causing the rhythmic response. As we encountered more turbulence; the movements became more abrupt at which point in time the autopilot disengaged as the aircraft entered into a progressively building dutch roll. I immediately confirmed the auto pilot was disengaged and asked the pilot monitoring to request a lower altitude as I began to turn into the tail role slightly and then maintaining a steady profile with the wings while engaging in a slight descent to counter the roll force. I then asked the pilot monitoring to slow my bugged speed to .75 from .77 which correlated initially with N1 speed recommendations for the environmental conditions. After approx 30 to 45 seconds of dampening the aircraft's movement utilizing flight controls; thrust and speed reduction the aircraft settled into a level profile. During this time we were approved off of heading and into a block between 350 and 360 feet. Once reestablished we climbed back to 36;000 feet and engaged initially the heading function followed by the LNAV function; direct to our next checkpoint and on course; then finally the autopilot flight control systems. At that time we noticed that the Yaw dampener light on the overhead was illuminated; and the magnetic switch was in the off position. Checking again the recall there was no associated flight control light or the master caution annunciator. In accordance with the QRH; we performed the action procedures listed to reengage the yaw damper. There are no further actions or anomalies for the remainder of the flight. The captain completed the appropriate write-ups while we debriefed the scenario. Of note the encounter with turbulence as well as the rhythmic rolling motion; which led to the auto pilot disengaging; and what appears to be the disconnection of the yaw damper; resulted in numerous sick passengers as well as flight attendants in the back half of the airplane. These items were also addressed in accordance with the reporting profiles outlined in the FOM by the CA.

column121: For our flight we had an observer in the back right seat. It was our first take off out of ZZZ; we got cleared to takeoff XXL and we were performing a soft field takeoff where we had a crosswind. As the student was initiating takeoff we started to veer to the left of center line so I appropriately added right rudder to get us back on course but when we lifted off; we heard the stall horn and my student added right aileron to get back on centerline. This caused us to drift to the right of centerline. I then appropriately took controls and added forward pressure to avoid a stall or spin and get us back on centerline. During this takeoff the wingtips briefly made contact with the ground. I then safely landed the aircraft on the runway aborting the takeoff and taxied back to the ramp with no further issues. During our walk around we saw there were scratches under both of the wingtips and scratches on the right side of the horizontal stabilizer. There were no injury's and we then wrote up the aircraft.Cause: As the CFI/PIC of the flight I understand that I am ultimately responsible for the correction and outcome of the flight. This was caused due to improper aileron input with the winds and not enough rudder usage.Suggestions: In hindsight after having time to reflect on this event that occurred over the span of about 30 seconds as the CFI; I might have been able to take controls sooner and reacted to the aileron input faster. Other solutions for this fast paced event could have been blocking the controls and better defensive positioning.
column123: During a soft-field takeoff; the aircraft drifted due to the wind after liftoff and struck a pavement near the edge of the runway.Cause: After rotation during a soft-field takeoff; insufficient right rudder input caused the aircraft to drift left. While attempting to correct back to the centerline; the aircraft continued drifting in the crosswind and struck a ground object near the runway edge. The wind at the time was approximately 210° at 12 knots; creating a crosswind component of about 10 knots. column121: Received the aircraft at ZZZ and determined it was airworthy after reviewing the documents and completing the preflight inspection. The flight departed ZZZ with no delays or issues. Approximately 45 minutes into the flight; we received a HYD 2 LO QTY" crew awareness message; but it disappeared quickly. By the time I opened the HYD synoptic page; it reappeared. When we first looked at it; the quantity in System 2 was at 20%; and we decided to monitor it for a couple of minutes. After 3-4 minutes; it dropped to 18%; and we realized it was actually leaking.We decided not to continue to ZZZ1 due to having roughly 450 miles remaining. The captain relayed this information to dispatch; and dispatch relayed it to maintenance. After a couple of minutes; we received a message directing us to divert to ZZZ2. The captain and I discussed the situation and came up with a game plan: I would fly the airplane and handle the radios while he informed the flight attendants and passengers of the situation; handled the new release; calculated fuel; and programmed the box.I quickly got on the radio and advised ATC; "We have a minor HYD issue and would like to divert to ZZZ2. We are not declaring an emergency at this time." ATC then gave me a heading and altitude toward ZZZ2.By the time we were at 9;000 feet; 250 knots; and approximately 50 miles from ZZZ2; the airplane was fully set up. We decided to review the QRH item "LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2" to familiarize ourselves with it in case we lost all the fluid prior to landing. We came up with a plan to lower the landing gear early since we were close enough to the field and still had plenty of fuel remaining. One of the items we would lose according to the QRH was normal landing gear operation due to the HYD 2 loss; requiring use of the alternate gear extension lever. We also agreed that if we lost the system completely at any time prior to landing; we would discontinue the approach; run the QRH procedures; and return to land with the required items and equipment secured.I slowed to 230 knots; and we lowered the gear. Approach vectored us for the ILS XXR approach and asked about the nature of the problem. We advised them that we were not declaring an emergency at that time; but Approach provided priority handling. From there; I joined the final approach course and flew the ILS XXR approach into ZZZ2.Shortly after touchdown; we received several red and yellow EICAS messages; and both the master warning and caution lights/buttons illuminated. I did not pay close attention to them because we were in a very critical phase of flight; but I only deployed the number 1 reverser; knowing the lights and messages were related to HYD System 2. We rolled to the end of the runway to avoid overheating the brakes; exited at taxiway 1; and stopped on taxiway 2 facing east.Tower instructed us to switch frequencies to Fire/Rescue for communication. Shortly after speaking with them; we noticed the right outboard brake temperature rising quickly; and we asked them to monitor it in case it caught fire. We waited there for approximately 25-30 minutes; and the brake temperature eventually cooled off. We then taxied to gate XX; and the remainder of the taxi to the gate was uneventful."

I made my first radio call about 8 miles out; stating our distance in cardinal direction from the field and stated we were on a straight in traffic permitting doing a practice approach. We did not hear any traffic calls nor observe anything visually or on ADSB data. I called a 3 mile final; and about a minute later when we were on short final an airplane says they are taking the opposite runway (16) and will turn out early to the west to avoid us. Since we were basically on short final I cued up and said okay we will break off and turn out east to avoid the conflict. It appeared the aircraft was still barely rolling past the hold short line on the 16 side when I said this; so it seemed very obvious to me that he never made a hold short call and just decided to try to cut out in front of us. I would have happily broken off the approach early to accommodate him had I known he was holding but his first call did not come until he announced he was rolling opposite direction. He then berated me for turning east where the jump zone is. I am very familiar with this airport and know the hazards of the jump zone on the east side of the field but there were a few things going through my mind; #1 my first and immediate concern was avoiding the head on conflict created by the other pilot; #2 turning east was of course not my ideal choice but if my understanding was that he planned to turn west then I of course would not turn west myself and #3 I was very confident the jump zone was not active as I fly at this field regularly and am very vigilant regarding the warning calls the skydive pilots give prior to commencing a jump; so given all of these factors I made the decision to make an immediate turn to the east and continued the turn southbound out of the area. I think there should be some advisory circular or other relevant publication surrounding operations at the YOLO County airport in the event an airplane needs to take evasive action and side step towards the east side of the field.

The arrival proceeded normally until the opposite wing walker detected an immediate hazard and threw up an emergency 'STOP' (X) signal with his wands. Recognizing the urgency; I instantly mirrored the emergency 'X' signal to ensure the flight crew received a unified; immediate directive to halt. The flight crew reacted quickly and brought the aircraft to a stop.Simultaneously; a truck traveling southbound in the alleyway failed to yield the absolute right-of-way to the arriving aircraft. The driver; seemingly unaware of the active arrival; breached the safety zone and braked heavily at the last possible second. The truck came to a sudden stop right next to my position; nearly driving past me and narrowly avoiding a catastrophic collision with both the aircraft and ground personnel. The immediate situational awareness and rapid communication of the wing-walking team successfully averted a major incident caused entirely by the vendor vehicle's failure to follow airport SOPs.Afterwards; we directed the truck to back up and clear the area. Once the hazard was removed; we attempted to resume the arrival; however; the pilot was unable or unwilling to apply enough engine power to get the aircraft moving again after the sudden stop. Because the aircraft could not complete its forward momentum into the gate under its own power; the crew followed procedures to safely secure the flight.

column121: While on takeoff roll; as pilot monitoring; the airspeed readings on the FO's and Captain's PFD (Primary Flight Display) were grossly off. I saw the FO's PFD read an airspeed in the 40s while the Captain's PFD read in the 60s. I also noticed the FO's PFD did not read any airspeed until in the 40s. It seemed to be a delay not usual to any aircraft in the fleet. About the same time; the SPS (Stall Protection System) advanced message dinged on the EICAS. The Captain called 'Reject'; slowed the aircraft down without any harsh braking; I called ZZZ tower and told them we were rejecting the takeoff. Tower instructed us to make a right turnoff of the runway and to then stop on an adjacent taxiway to determine our next steps. The Captain called the Flight Attendant and made a PA to the passengers. The Captain also called maintenance and told them what happened; I overheard in the conversation that the Captain was deciding to return to the gate to have the plane looked at by maintenance. I called operations and informed them we would need to return to the gate. I then called ZZZ Tower and was given taxi instructions to return to the ramp and ultimately the gate. We parked at the same gate that we initially pushed off from. The passengers deplaned and we boarded a new aircraft which was taxing in to park next door to gate. I thought the Captain handled the reject superbly especially with low ceilings and IMC conditions. According to the Captain the previous crew informed him that the airspeeds were reading unreliably. The Captain included in his initial pre-takeoff brief a reference to what his intended action would be should he receive any abnormalities regarding any unreliable airspeed indications. The Captain also stated he would see brief 'check EICAS' indications on his PFD. I don't recall ever seeing this message appear on the FO's PFD.Cause: Unknown mechanical fault causing the airspeed indicators onboard to be grossly off in cross reference to one another; making any reading unreliable.suggestion: Repair the mechanical malfunction to the aircraft before placing it back into service.

column121: I was inbound for landing at ZZZ after flying a 2 hour cross country flight with landings at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2.  I obtained the METAR at approximately 10 miles south of ZZZ around XA:50.  I did not realize the METAR was nearly an hour old.  The wind was reported as light and variable at 4 knots.  I requested vectors to visually fly the RNAV approach for runway XX from the approach controller as well as clearance for touch a touch and go.  I was advised to fly heading 040.  Later I was advised to intercept and hold at ZZZZZ; the initial approach fix for the approach.  During this interval I began experiencing heavy up and downdrafts which required more workload to maintain aircraft altitude.  I was circling in the hold at ZZZZZ from approximately XC:05 until XC:20.  During this time; I failed to obtain updated weather from the METAR due to my increased workload maintaining altitude.  I was cleared for the approach for runway XX.  While on short final; the tower controller notified me the wind was at 060 at 4 knots.  I realized I was going to have a crossing tailwind and briefly considered requesting to change runways.  Since the wind velocity was low I elected to proceed with the landing.  I safely landed the aircraft on center line without issue.  At this point I succumbed to plan continuation bias and applied full power; and raised the flaps to perform the touch and go.  I did not take into account the full effects of the tail wind and slight crosswind component.  As the aircraft accelerated; it began to excessively drift left of the runway center line.  My airspeed slow to build and was not adequate to rotate.  I aborted the takeoff; and simultaneously applied full brakes while setting the throttle to idle.  I attempted to correct for the lateral drift however was nervous to make excessive rudder inputs considering my speed which was approximately 40-45 knots (airspeed) and higher (unknown) ground speed.  Once I realized the aircraft was going to depart the runway I cut the mixture; placed the fuel selector valve to off.  I departed the left side of runway XX shortly after crossing taxiway 1 and entered the grass running parallel to the runway.  The aircraft continued through the grass. The aircraft entered the displaced threshold for run XY where if finally came to a full stop.  There factors associated with the incident started when I failed to get an updated METAR.  I did not realize how much time had elapsed or that my initial METAR report was old.  Had I received updated weather before I was on short final I would have changed runways.  I had committed to a plan and did not realized the changing conditions.  Additionally when the controlled advised me of the wind on final; I could have aborted the landing and requested to land on runway 090.  Finally after having the smooth and relatively easy landing; I had a confirmation bias that the take off would be the same.  I did not consider the additional take off roll that would be required or the effect of the cross wind which pushed me left.

column121: It was my take off out of ZZZ. Right as we were about to hit 100 knots or the high speed regime we got a master caution for and right side IRS (Inertial Reference System) fault. Captain said continue so I did. We rotated as normal. However as I started transitioning from flying visually to inside I looked down and realized I had the VERT HDG AND ATT flags as well as no flight director guidance. I glanced over and saw the captains instruments and flight director were there and working. Being a more critical phase of flight I didn't say anything to the captain yet due to not wanting to startle him more than necessary and I knew I could fly based of his instruments and visually. Once we got through 1000 ft and I knew we were safely away from the ground I stated that I didn't have any of that guidance. The captain said well let me take the plane and radios so you can run checklists to try to fix the issues. Once we transferred the controls I started looking through the non normals. I started by trying to look for any checklist relating to my instrumentation failure. I looked and read through display failure but we both stated this didn't make sense cuz the display was fine. After talking we said the first indication was the IRS FAULT light so let's start there. I started reading through that checklist and performing the actions it stated. It was around that time I realized we had performed a bleeds off TO and we hadn't switched the bleeds to the engines yet. So I performed that action before we got into any type of unsafe situation. Continuing that IRS FAULT checklist it had me turn the IRS selectors switch to both on left. As soon as I did that my side had all instrumentation and guidance once again. At this point we had leveled off at 270 because neither autopilot was working and they wouldn't let us into rvsm airspace without a working autopilot. I had sent a message to Maintenance Control stating our failures so that we could try to get the best guidance possible in trouble shooting. We transferred the controls back to me so he could talk to dispatch and manage the situation. Due to being 10000 ft lower than planned we weren't sure we would make it to ZZZ1. So we made a plan to go to ZZZ2 if needed based on how our fuel burn was going. We also made a plan to change controls back and forth so neither of us get too tired due to having to hand fly. We realized after a while we hadn't updated the cruise winds. Once we did that we realized we were right above bingo fuel. Then after flying a little while long we got below bingo so the decision was immediately made to go to ZZZ2. This entire time we were conferring with dispatch and they agreed. On the descent into ZZZ2 every time we started descending my vertical guidance went out on the flight director. So I again just used other instruments to back up my descent and every time we leveled off the vertical guidance came back on my flight director. Once we got on the approach both my vertical and lateral guidance went out. I was comfortable with flying it raw data and visually so continued flying to landing. Due to the added stress of everything that had gone on the entire flight and having to hand fly for over 4 hours by the time we got to the gate both of us felt somewhat fatigued and weren't sure if we really felt safe to continue. I talked to maintenance to add the failures on decent and approach to our list of failures we had already reported. While I did that captain called the chief pilot about everything and why we needed to do now. The manager asked how we felt and he said we are both on the fence. He went through the fatigue questions and he said based on those answers you guys aren't fit to fly and you are fatigued and will not continue. I don't think we did anything wrong on the flight in any way and I think we worked together well to divide or manage the workload. All of that added stress to flying and having to do so much more work than normal I know drained me which lead to me being fatigued.
column123: During the van ride to the airport; the FO and I reviewed the flight plan. The dispatcher notes included 'WILL NEED RWY XXL FOR TAKEOFF IF CALM WINDS OR WINDS FAVOR RWY XXL' and 'PLANNED BLEEDS OFF FOR T.O.' It was also noted in the release that the First Class Cabin outlets were inoperative. We mentioned the noise abatement as a possible reason for the opposite direction takeoff; or better weight/climb performance. Upon reaching the airport; we walked straight from security to the aircraft. Rather than stopping for coffee on the way to the aircraft; the FO decided to return to the terminal for coffee after stowing his bags on the aircraft. After briefing the flight attendants; to include the potential wait of an opposite direction departure and the First Class outlets; the FO had not yet returned to the aircraft. In the interest of time; I completed the entire initialization of the FMC; with the exception of requesting takeoff data. One of our ACARS messages had revealed a weight restriction; so despite the close proximity between the reserve and REMF (Remaining Fuel); I opted not to add additional fuel; and decided to wait until fueling was finished to request more accurate takeoff data. The FO returned with his coffee and then performed the walk-around. While on the walk-around; the gate agent brought down the reconciliation; and I briefed the passengers about today's flight. Upon returning; the FO began his preflight flow; and I went to the bathroom. When I got back; he then went to the bathroom. The flight attendants had completed their checks and were ready to close the cockpit door; but needed to wait until the FO was finished to do so. Once he returned to the flight deck; the door was closed. At this point; I realized that the autothrottle was not engaged; and so I checked the TAKEOFF page in the FMC and realized that neither of us had sent for the appropriate data yet. When asked; the FO stated that he had requested it; but our current weight was sending back an error for RWY XYR. As a result of his lack of initiative; I suggested that he send for numbers on XXL; as dispatch had requested. He did so; and it also returned an error for being overweight. The suggested value; was roughly 300lbs below our current weight; and due to the line of aircraft that had formed for a XYR departure; I was willing to accept this weight since our wait for an opposite direction departure would likely; burn enough fuel. He believed the weight for XYR was close; and so I permitted him to send it again. The required weight for a XYR departure was roughly 1000 pounds below that for a XXL departure. I told him to send for numbers at the maximum weights specified in the error; and if we got below the number for XYR before our opposite direction departure is permitted; we can do that. I also acknowledged that this weight would be extremely close to our required reserve fuel. Once he sent for a successful solution; I reviewed it and realized that the auto function for the bleed air was recommending a bleeds on solution. I then had him send for takeoff data forcing a bleeds off takeoff; at which point our current weight returned a valid solution for RWYXXR. We were past our scheduled departure time at this point; so we quickly briefed the departure; noting the threats of complacency from day-4; the bleeds off takeoff; and the line of aircraft we would be waiting in. Despite acknowledging these threats; I permitted the first error to be introduced by not requesting a more thorough brief of the clearance and SID; or verifying that the selected altitude was correct. It was not. 3000 feet was still selected from the arrival crew; despite our being cleared to climb via the SID; and the top altitude of the ZZZZZX being 13;000 feet.After completing the before push checklist; we notified the ground crew and pushed off the gate approximately 5 minutes late; and a line of approximately 8-10 aircraft had already formed. The ground crew advised us toturn on our lights; at which point the FO turned on two light switches. I did not verify which switches. During our taxi; the ground controller asked us to re-cycle our transponder. The FO had not turned on the transponder during push; and turned it on now. All checklists and callouts were accomplished satisfactorily through our clearance for takeoff on RWY XYR. During the takeoff roll; approaching 100 KIA; a Master Caution illuminated corresponding to an IRS (Inertial Reference System) annunciator. I extinguished it and verbalized continue; followed by the 100 knots; V1; and VR callouts. Once airborne; the FO directed me to retract the flaps and perform the after takeoff checklist. During final flap retraction; the FO verbalized that he had lost some of his displayed instrumentation. I assumed he meant his Flight Director; and opted to take the aircraft as my displays were operating normally. I continued to fly the departure and climb. Approaching 3000 feet; the Flight Director commanded a level off; as this was the altitude selected in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). I began decreasing power and leveling off as I recognized the VNAV ALT in the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) and cross checked the MCP to deduce that this was not due to the departure. I grabbed the printed PDC and quickly located the clearance to climb via SID. I then resumed the climb noting the next 5000B restriction at ZZZZZ1. Due to the timing of this mistake; it resulted in neither pilot accomplishing the After Takeoff or No Engine Bleed Checklists. This small error that was not repaired during the briefing permitted additional errors to occur; contributing to a lower fuel state.As we continued the climb; the FO continued to troubleshoot his displays and I eventually became aware that in addition to losing the Flight Director (FD); the FO's ADI and HSI were black; with yellow ATT; HDG; and VERT annunciations; but accurate speed and altitude was still displayed. He began searching for a non-normal checklist associated with the malfunctioning display. At this point; I opted to take the radios in addition to flying the aircraft. Passing 10;000 feet I switched the sterile light; 'double dinged' the flight attendants; checked and verbalized that the cabin was pressurizing; and attempted to turn on the autopilot. However; the sterile light was apparently in the wrong position; so instead of turning it off; I inadvertently turned it on. I typically engage the autopilot at this time; but it failed to engage on either the A or B channel. I cycled the FO's FD switch; to make my source the master; and attempted to engage the autopilot again. It did not engage; so I continued to hand fly the aircraft. To prevent myself from overwhelming the FO; who was still searching for an appropriate checklist; I decided not to inform him that the autopilot was not functioning until it became pertinent. The FO reviewed several non-normal checklists and we deduced that they were not the correct checklists. At one point; the Flight Attendants called the flight deck. The FO took the call; as I had my hands full. They were asking why the sterile light had been turned on; and he notified them of our predicament; and I turned the light back off. This was the consequence of yet another error that was not repaired on the ground; adding additional complication to this situation. The flight attendants also informed us that in addition to the outlets being inoperative in the First Class Cabin; they were inoperative in the entire aircraft; all of the screens at the seats were inoperative; and there was no internet connectivity. During this time we passed FL180; and set 29.92 inHg at which point I chimed in that it is possible to use one of the reversionary switches to simply force my display onto his. In reviewing the overhead panel; the FO discovered that the bleed air was not appropriately set. He quickly performed the procedure to set the bleed panel without referencing the No Engine Bleed Checklist. He then set the gear; auto-brakes; and igniters to complete the After Takeoff Checklist. Thankfully the APU was still pressurizing the cabin despite being above 17;000 feet; and maintaining an approximately 5;000 foot cabin altitude. Although we repaired this error before it became an undesired aircraft state; we simultaneously introduced another error as the appropriate checklist was the No Engine Bleed Checklist. Therefore; the APU continued running.Returning his attention to the overhead panel; I attempted to help guide him to the appropriate switch while keeping my eyes on the gauges because I was hand-flying. I then mentioned that there are also reversionary switches on the dash; and perhaps it was one of those. He did move several of these switches but only the upper and lower DU'S (Display Units) changed; so he returned to the overhead. He eventually actuated several of those switches; and again got no positive resolution. As a result; I guided him back to the original indication - the IRS Master Caution. On the overhead panel; the R IRS FAULT and ALIGN lights were illuminated. He located the IRS FAULT checklist. During the climb; ATC eventually cleared us to an RVSM altitude. Knowing that autopilot is a required piece of equipment; I declined that altitude and was cleared to FL270. At this point; I filled in the FO that the autopilot was not functioning. After performing the checklist steps; the FO's instrumentation was restored; but the autopilot still would not engage; and the #2 transponder displayed a fault; so the #1 was selected. We interfaced with Maintenance Control via ACARS for any additional assistance. With the FO's display functioning correctly; I asked if he felt good enough to fly. He confirmed that he was; and I handed aircraft control over to him. We agreed to trading off who would fly every 30-60 minutes to avoid fatigue. At this point; I started my timer and began interfacing with dispatch about our options. This included requesting to transit RVSM airspace as a non-RVSM capable aircraft; which was denied multiple times. While at cruise in ZZZ Center's airspace; we discussed divert options with dispatch and opted to continue as the FMC computed FOB at ZZZ1 was 5.7; which was above the required 5.5. I also sent multiple ELB (Electronic Logbook) reports for the various issues we encountered. We also discussed the possibility that this was a larger electrical malfunction; as opposed to simply an IRS FAULT. I then realized that I had not requested new winds for our lower altitude. After doing so; our calculated FOB decreased. However; dispatch revised the alternate which decreased the required fuel to 5.1; which we were above. As a result of some storms in the area; we needed to use the Engine Anti-Ice; again decreasing our FOB calculation; now below the required 5.1. Shortly thereafter; the center tanks were emptied; the center fuel pumps were turned off; and dispatch notified us that an alternate was no longer required. The required fuel was now 4.4; and the FMC calculated to have 4.7 FOB at ZZZ1; so we continued. As a result of the inadvertent APU usage; the use of ENG ANTI-ICE at cruise; the variations associated with hand flying; and common fuel system anomaly associated with a decreasing FOB after turning off the center fuel pumps; our fuel total slowly decreased below the 4.4 FOB requirement. At this point; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ2. During our descent; the FO's instrumentation began further degrading. During descents in VNAV; LVL CHG; and V/S; the FO would lose his vertical Flight Director; but it would reappear at the level off altitude. I offered to fly as my display was functioning correctly; and he declined. I made sure to keep an eye on our flight path; and the FO was doing a great job without my interference. column121: We were flying into SDL. Winds were mostly calm but favoring runway 3 (I believe it was 320 at 3kt) and visibility was clear and unlimited. We do not have any approved approaches to this runway; so we were planning a visual approach using the Garmin visual". My partner and I both noted that the PAPIs for runway 3 are 4°. We also referenced the RNP Y & Z approach angles. We noted that the approach angles for those are both 3°. We are not approved for these approaches so we were simply referencing them for situational awareness and noting how they avoid the terrain to the southwest of the airport. Sometime during our approach brief we decided that a 3° glide path for the Garmin visual approach would suffice for terrain avoidance. We were proceeding to the airport from the west when we were cleared for the visual about 9 mi west. We cancelled IFR and proceeded to turn onto a left base for runway 3. We did this by proceeding direct to the "STRAIGHT" waypoint on the visual. My partner set a lower altitude; I forget the exact amount but I believe it was the Garmin calculated altitude that coincided with the "FINAL" waypoint. My partner engaged VNAV and APR mode. We began our descent on the VNAV profile. As we began the turn from base to final; the glide path was captured which I believe created a pitch down moment. It was in the turn and simultaneous glide path capture that we received at GPWS "terrain" and "pull up" alert. It took a moment of recognition but my partner disconnected the autopilot and we leveled off our altitude of approximately 3000' MSL. Immediately after level off; we stopped receiving the GPWS warning. Our pre briefed pattern altitude was 3000' MSL so already being there and having the GPWS alert stop; we did not perform a full escape maneuver. We also knew that the terrain was behind us during our level off. At this point we were still in a position to commence a stable approach; so we continued and landed without further event. Looking back there are a few things that I would have done differently. I do believe that we should have programmed the VNAV profile to match the PAPIs approach angle of 4° instead of the standard 3°. That would have given us more altitude over the terrain. I also think that we should have performed an escape maneuver. Even if it meant only climbing another 1000' it would have been the safe and correct thing to do. It also would have given us more time to do a lap in the pattern and re-attempt the approach with a 4° approach angle or a closer in base leg to avoid the terrain. Going forward; I will be much more caution of the terrain to the south west. We train and brief so much for approaches to runway 21 into SDL; but runway 3 should also be treated with equal caution. I do believe that perhaps we need a feasibility note or FOQA alert published for this runway and lack of approved published approach and the terrain. We simply don't have any guidance currently and perhaps a guided visual approach would be helpful in the future as well.Suggestion: I do believe that perhaps we need a feasibility note or FOQA alert published for this runway and lack of approved published approach and the terrain. We simply don't have any guidance currently and perhaps a guided visual approach would be helpful in the future as well."
column123: Going into SDL between XA:00-XB:00 local; the wind was slightly favoring runway 3. In SDL I have never landed runway 3. Looking at the available approaches there were only two RNP approaches that we were not authorized for. So we decided to use the visual approach the Garmin builds. We weren't worried about terrain coming in for runway 3 like we usually are for runway 21. We also did not see anything in the feasibility notes regarding suggestions for runway 3. After getting cleared for the visual approach we joined the visual approach set at a 3 degree glide slope. On a roughly 5-6nm final we got a pull up" message. Surprised; I deactivated the autopilot and pulled up. The message immediately cleared and we continued the approach; flying about a dot high or so the rest of the way. In hindsight there were things we could have done better. The PAPI's were set to a 4 degree glideslope and we should have matched the visual approach glideslope to that as well. The reasoning for keeping it at a 3 degree glideslope was the RNP approaches (although not authorized) used a 3 degree glideslope. So I am assuming the Aircraft's terrain sensitivity is part of the reason they're not authorized for the RNP approach's. Secondly; we should have flown a full go around and rejoined the pattern. This was agreed upon after landing.Suggestion: I would suggest adding a feasibility note recommending a 4 degree glideslope on the visual runway 3. Or I would suggest to join final inside maybe a 4nm final for runway 3."

If we need a longer runway; we can go to ZZZ1 airport.  • Questions/Comments/Concerns? I called out "Abort; abort; abort". My copilot's hand was still on the thrust so we aborted. column121: I was operating from ZZZ as the First Officer and pilot flying. The aircraft was an Airbus A319.  It was the first flight of the day. Upon arriving to the aircraft; the plane had been powered up (assuming by maintenance); however APU was off; Pre-Conditioned Air (PCA) hose unplugged and tangled up by aircraft nose. The three temperature sensors in the plane read; CKPT 90; FWD 94; AFT 98". This became a top priority to try a cool the airplane prior to boarding. With the APU Bleed on; we were able to cool the aircraft and no issues noted. All things considered normal up until after engine start. We noticed Pack 1 was still showing a fault; but both myself and the Captain agreed it was probably a "sticky valve" and once we added a little bit of engine power; that issue would go away. Prior to calling for taxi clearance; the fault went away and everything was normal. However; when taxing out to the runway; the fault came back; but would go away when engine thrust was added and would come back again when thrust was brought to idle. This process repeated itself for about 3 cycles until we decided to tell Ground Control we'd like to pull over and troubleshoot the fault. The CA worked with dispatch and maintenance to eventually MEL Pack 1. Maintenance gave us the MEL 21-XXX "Packs Pressurized Flight (A319) X. Option 2 - (Limited Effectivity) (Speed Brakes Operative)". The main takeaway for this MEL is that the aircraft altitude is limited to Flight Level 370. The day prior; the same CA and I flew another very similar A319 with an inop APU and a MEL'ed Pack 1. The MEL associated with that flight was 21-XXY ""Packs Pressurized Flight (A319) Y. Option 1 - (Limited Effectivity) (Speed Brakes Inoperative)"; with the main takeaway from that; was it had a max altitude of Flight Level 310. Our filed flight plan for our flight was Flight Level 350. We had some discussions on what the differences were and why on one flight we had Y and this one we had X. We discussed the two different altitudes and noted our flight level was right in between them and would monitor the cabin altitude. But according to the MEL that maintenance gave us; FL350 was still legal and we pressed on. On the climb out the aft cabin was "ok" with temperature; but the front was high 70s/low 80s and the cockpit was 90°+; with the aircraft not cooling down on one Pack. While still in the climb to FL350; I started having the discussion on different possibilities to resolve this issue. We were in the process of reaching out to Dispatch via ACARS to send us a fuel plan with a much lower altitude so we could potentially use the APU Bleed to cool the plane off. During that time; we were passing FL330 in which the CA mentioned the cabin altitude passing ~8;000'; which then prompted him to immediately request a level off; then a lower altitude. Our descent started somewhere in the mid FL340s heading back down initially to FL330; never reaching our filed FL350. That's when we received the Master Warning and the "CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT" ECAM. We donned the oxygen masks; established crew communication and continued the ECAM steps. I took the aircraft and the radios and requested a descent down to 10;000' and a westbound heading to get us heading back over land (our flight path was in a Northeast heading out over the water). The CA was busy with checklist; dispatch; flight attendants and passengers; so I initially elected direct ZZZ1 to have something to aim for. I'm not sure the exact altitude the cabin got to; but it was less than 14;000' because there were no issues or indications of a pressurization issue in the back since the passenger oxygen masks did not deploy and the Flight Attendants had no idea any issues were going on up in the flight deck. Once at 10;000'; the cabin altitude was back to normal (300' or so) and we were able to take our masks off; regroup and come to a logical solution for what would be next. Dispatch requested us to head back to ZZZ; which we deemed was safeand appropriate. We landed back in ZZZ with no further issues and taxied to the gate. Our debrief questions that we wanted answers for; 1. Was there any correlation at the start of the morning trying to cool off an extremely hot airplane; and essentially overworking the packs? 2. We still never received an explanation for the 2 different MELs and why they would have 2 different max altitudes?Cause: The temperature of the aircraft was unacceptable; especially with the plane already being powered up; a working APU (that was off) and working PCA which the hose was disconnected. It set the tone of the morning with; "here's something else we have to deal with." -Recommendation: With summer pretty much here; and with locations that are known for hot summers; planes need to be cooled prior to crews getting there.Having a fault while on taxi out is distracting; especially when running checklist and dealing with Ground ATC. To then have a fault that affects the cooling of the aircraft; which again was already an aggravation for the entire crew (flight attendants included). The cockpit temperature was extremely distracting; and it took away some of our situational awareness away with the Pack 1 MEL and the cabin altitude.Having essentially the same aircraft the day prior with the same issue(s); yet a different max altitude per a different MEL has huge expectation basis. Having a better understanding of what and why maintenance is giving us that MEL as well as addressing our concerns about the max altitude would be very beneficial. It's practically impossible for our specific situation where the CA is dealing with all of that while I'm monitoring ATC frequencies. No blame or fault to the CA; again for the reasons listed; but all of my questions came after he was done talking to maintenance and answers were left to interpretation of how we were reading the MELs."

column121: Flight number: ABCD / ZZZ-ZZZZAt XA:07; ZZZ parking position was 1. Taxi clearance was received from Tower to taxi via 1 across Runway XX and continue via 2-3 to Runway XX. No correction or clarification was provided by ATC following either readback at the time.In a dynamic runway environment at ZZZ Runway XX; the crew's actions; including runway entry during the rollout phase; were based on real-time interpretation of the received transmission and a visual scan of the runway environment.After establishing position on the Runway XX centerline; the preceding aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. Tower then instructed the subsequent arriving aircraft to go around and advised that our runway entry was not authorized. We were subsequently instructed to vacate Runway XX via Taxiway 4 at ZZZ. The event was subsequently classified as a runway incursion.Contributing Factors (Human Factors)Contributing factors included ambiguity in the timing structure of the clearance phraseology ('line up and wait after arrival') in the context of operations on Runway XX at ZZZ; requiring real-time interpretation in a dynamic runway environment.VHF communication characteristics and associated audio conditions may have resulted in perceived audio degradation and reduced intelligibility of the transmission. Post-event review of recorded ATC communications was conducted using a high-fidelity audio playback system with slowed playback to enhance intelligibility. This review suggested that portions of the transmission may have been subject to audio degradation during high cockpit workload conditions; resulting in reduced transmission intelligibility.The flight crew independently perceived the transmission in real time as a Line Up and Wait-related clearance.The absence of ATC correction to two separate readbacks may have reinforced the crew's understanding of the transmission.At the ZZZ Runway XX 3 intersection; runway guard lights were available as the primary visual cue; and no runway stop bar system was present. The available lighting configuration provided limited additional visual confirmation or redundancy for runway entry verification between ATC and flight crews. This may have reduced an additional layer of defence that could otherwise assist in resolving ambiguity or reinforcing runway entry status during high-tempo operations.Safety Actions TakenContinuous traffic monitoring was maintained prior to runway entry at ZZZ Runway XX. No evasive maneuver was required during the event; and no collision or loss of separation occurred.Corrective Action / PreventionIn future operations at ZZZ; greater emphasis will be placed on positive confirmation of runway status prior to entering a runway under LUAW clearances; particularly when sequencing is referenced in conjunction with arriving traffic.Enhanced cross-checking of ATC instructions between crew members will be reinforced to mitigate potential interpretation divergence. Additional awareness will be maintained regarding VHF communication degradation and the importance of seeking explicit clarification when any ambiguity exists in runway-related clearances.

column121: My student and I were flying on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ - COS - ZZZ. We were in full IMC conditions and tracking the V389 airway from LUFSE to ADANE. I normally keep very close track of his altitude so I can prompt corrections but got momentarily distracted loading the approach and getting the weather and when I looked back he was over 200 ft below altitude. This is absolutely my fault as I should have kept a closer eye knowing he struggles with holding attitude at times. As soon as I checked it; he noticed it and started correcting but by that time we were probably almost 300 ft low. Right then springs approach contacted us and advised to climb; check our altitude and low altitude alert. We immediately went full power and got back up quickly. This was not safe and I have learned a lot about when to step in as the instructor and how I need to be even more vigilant; especially when on an IFR flight plan as I don't want to cause traffic issues or terrain dangers. This was a r3ally big learning experience for me as an instructor and something I will absolutely learn and change because of.

column121: Flight from ZZZ on a A321T model. After number 1 engine start after our initial pushback from gate XX at ZZZ; we received Elec Gen 1 fault ecam message.  We followed the ecam actions to reset the Generator but was unsuccessful.  We asked ramp if we can hold our current position and the Captain called Maintenance Control to ask if there is another procedure to follow and how to proceed. We were advised to return to the gate for maintenance to board the aircraft.  After further inspection maintenance advised us that they were going to apply MEL (24-XXX)  They asked us to start the #1Engine so that they could disconnect the Integrated Drive Generator (IDG) as to their procedures. APU was checked and as per the MEL; should remain on for the entire flight. Additional fuel was loaded on the aircraft and we pushed back for departure.During our initial climb through approximately FL240 the APU did an auto shutdown. We accomplished our procedures and transfer of aircraft control from the Captain(PF) to the FO(PM). The captain proceeded with checklists and communications between dispatch and the cabin to come up with a solution. With concurrence from dispatch the decision was made to divert to ZZZ1; the closest suitable airport since we were operating on just one generator. We notified ATC  and started towards ZZZ1 airport while the Captain continued with the necessary checklists.  One of the checklists was for an overweight landing. Captain accomplished that checklist and we decided to request priority handling so that ZZZ1 would have the fire trucks ready to meet us upon arrival to inspect the aircraft.Approach and landing was without issues; landing at 180.0 lbs. speed at touchdown 145 kts and rate of decent 200fpm. Brake temps never exceeded 200 degrees after touchdown with brake fans on. We cleared runway XXL and after an inspection we were cleared to the gate.Cause: During the event I feel like our CRM was very good; reverting to our training. We worked together and had a positive outcome in the end. My one suggestion would be; even if some item is deferrable by MEL/Configuration Deviation List (CDL) doesn't always suggest that it is the correct action for that particular mission. In this case; we had a multiple hour flight ahead of us while needing to run the APU continuously. That in turn required us to have a bigger fuel load for APU operations and the fact that we restricted below FL330. It was a nice VFR day in Area X but it could have been the opposite. Operating on one generator could have been a whole different animal had the weather not been as good as it was where she had the failure. Also; the extra fuel caused us to be heavier than we needed to be; and luckily we were in a T-model A321; with less passenger seats. In short; deferrable doesn't always indicate a wise plan of action depending on the situation.

column121: Final approach into ZZZ on the RNAV XX. I received a low altitude alert from ATC after intercepting the final approach course on the RNAV XX into ZZZ.  I was cleared to maintain 2400 until intercepting; with a final approach fix intercept of 2500.  As I was intercepting; the aircraft continued descending; down to approximately 1500 MSL.  After receiving the low altitude alert from ATC; I immediately climbed back up to 2400.  I was handed off to tower; and did not have any further discussions with ATC over the matter. I was not given a phone number or asked to call ATC once on the ground.I believe I inadvertently put the autopilot into pitch mode.  I think it had to do with when I adjusted the altitude alerter.  I was descending to a clearance of 2400 while being vectored to final; but during my final vector I was told to maintain 2500 and cleared RNAV XX; which I asked ATC to confirm (because I was already below 2500) and they responded back with 2400.  I think moving my altitude alerter from 2400 to 2500 put me into pitch mode; which I did not catch.  I was fixated on the CDI as I was watching for my course to come alive and capture while I was turning to my cleared vector heading of 210.  Because of my fixation on the CDI; I missed that I had not leveled out at 2400.I believe the reason I went into Pitch mode is because I moved the altitude alerter from 2400 to 2500; then back to 2400.  However; because the autopilot in Aircraft X levels out (on the descent) 100' low; I believe I was actually slightly below 2400; as the plane was capturing; and then I moved the alerter to 2500; then back to 2400.Human Performance Considerations: I was alert; well rested; and otherwise in excellent condition for being PIC.  I was not distracted; but I did fixate on the Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) for my course capture as the plane descended well below the authorized altitude. I noticed the error a moment before and was just beginning to react when ATC issued the low level alert.To avoid recurrence: I need to not fixate and continue my instrument scan; especially during a critical phase of flight; and confirm Autopilot mode more diligently.

column121: The primary objective of the training flight was to improve and master landing techniques in the Pipistrel Alpha Trainer aircraft. At the time of the flight; I had accumulated approximately seven (7) hours of flight experience in this aircraft make and model.During one of the landing attempts; while on final approach at approximately 200 feet above ground level (AGL); I encountered gusty wind conditions that adversely affected aircraft control and approach stability. As the aircraft transitioned through the landing phase; I failed to apply sufficient aileron correction to compensate for the crosswind and gusting conditions. Additionally; I did not maintain adequate power to preserve the desired approach airspeed and positive control of the aircraft.As the approach became increasingly unstable; I delayed initiating a go-around procedure. Although I ultimately requested that my instructor assume flight controls; that request was made later than it should have been. During the landing rollout and recovery sequence; the aircraft momentarily departed the runway environment before control was regained and the situation was safely resolved. No injuries occurred; and the aircraft was secured without further incident.Upon reflection; several contributing factors were identified:Limited experience in the Pipistrel Alpha Trainer (approximately seven hours total time in type).Inadequate crosswind and gust correction inputs during the landing phase.Failure to maintain proper airspeed through appropriate power management.Delayed recognition of an unstable approach.Delayed decision to execute a go-around.Delayed transfer of flight controls to the instructor.Lessons learned from this event include the importance of maintaining positive aircraft control throughout all phases of flight; recognizing and responding promptly to unstable approach conditions; and executing an immediate go-around whenever approach parameters cannot be maintained. Additionally; effective crew coordination and timely communication with the instructor are critical to safe flight operations.Moving forward; I will place greater emphasis on stabilized approach criteria; crosswind correction techniques; power management; and early decision-making regarding go-arounds. I will also seek additional landing practice in varying wind conditions and will not hesitate to request instructor assistance at the earliest indication that safety margins are decreasing.This event serves as a valuable learning experience and will be used as a tool to strengthen my overall airmanship; aeronautical decision-making; and aircraft handling skills.

column121: I was conducting a long cross-country flight. Flew for a total of 8.2 Hobbs. Preflight was normal; no issues with aircraft; and set out. No issues for the entirety of flight; until nearly 30 minutes out from arrival back at ZZZ around 35 or so miles north. Minutes away from entry into the Mode C veil of ZZZ1 the transponder began turning on and off again; resetting itself. I tried turning it on and off to reset it; but it then refused to turn back on. I began skirting around the veil to troubleshoot; when shortly after the Garmin radio/nav setup failed. Thankfully; the aircraft is a analog six-pack so flight remained nominal. I immediately suspected alternator failure; and checked the ammeter; to still see it curiously showing charge. So at the moment; I simply suspected a Garmin system failure. I still had an alternate radio/nav system through Bendix/King setup; and I began getting the ATIS for ZZZ and planning the entry. Midway through that ATIS; that system died too and reinforced that suspicion of an alternator failure. Now with no comms; transponder; and navigation system; I thankfully had my foreflight pulled up and loaded with the flight plan and navigated off of that. During these events; I realized that with no radios; there was no way to enable the pilot operated lights at ZZZ. I began formulating a worst case scenario of calling ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 to communicate the issue through bluetooth and my Bose A20's; but I saw through Foreflight ADS-B In; thankfully; there was someone doing touch and goes at ZZZ and knew the lighting would be on. So I continued heading towards ZZZ; skirting the Mode C veil and staying low; and saw the lights were indeed on. From there; I decided it best to land at an airport with lights currently on that I was familiar with; rather than risk it at a local airport outside of the Mode C veil with no lighting; or to enter busy airspace with no lighting and transponder and disturb the heavy traffic flow unless absolutely necessary were ZZZ lights to go out and the manager not accessible via bluetooth. Also of note; I had around two hours of fuel remaining and was not in a critical emergency state yet. It was around the approach about 15 miles out I began testing the exterior lighting and noticed I had no strobes; no beacon; navigation lights were still oeprational; and I suspected my landing light was either out or would be out upon arrival. I entered the Mode C veil with no transponder knowing ZZZ lighting was still on and remaining hypervigilant to aircraft. The approach lights for XX remained on; and the prior aircraft had fully landed and taxied clear of all runways; when I turned a longer final. With no landing light and no operational flaps; we put it down successfully.After landing; and shutting down; I checked the alternator and belt and found no obvious abnormalities. I squawked the aircraft and reported it to maintenance for further investigation. Ammeter at the time was still showing a positive +1or2 amps of charge. Prior to shutdown.

column121: After arriving at the gate around XA50 for our turn we were notified of a plane change to aircraft coming from the Hangar. At XB18 maintenance operations notified us that the Aircraft left the Hangar. At XB29 maintenance operations notified us that ZZZ1 went into a ground stop for Thunderstorms with an update at XD00. I called Dispatch; who confirmed the ground stop and EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time) situation. There were slow moving thunderstorms almost directly over the field. The aircraft arrived at the gate around XB43. The crew boarded the aircraft and started the APU to cool the aircraft.The ground stop was extended to XE00 around XC43. Boarding had been delayed so all passengers were outside [gate] XX during the weather delay. Passengers were brought a snack cart. Around XD52 the ground stop was extended again to XF00. The FO shut the APU down and had ground air plugged back into the aircraft. I once again called Dispatch to verify the ground stop and EDCT situation. After XF00 I took a food order from the Flight Attendants and went into the terminal to buy them some food and bring it back to the airplane. I dropped off a sandwich for the gate agent upon my return around XF30 with the crews food.At XF51 maintenance operations notified us that the ground stop had been lifted with a delay now in effect and no EDCT. We called clearance to verify no EDCT. ZZZ Clearance Delivery notified us we had a wheels up time in about 20 minutes. I called Dispatch to confirm and asked the Flight Attendants how soon they could board. I notified the gate agents to start boarding in 5 minutes. We started boarding all passengers with 2 flight deck jumpseaters. We pushed around XG36. After going through the normal pushback procedures; we were cleared to taxi on 1 to holding pad 1 where we would incur an ATC delay to ZZZ1. We decided to shutdown Engine #2 while we waited out our 30 minute delay. While taxiing on 1 and around the time of shutting down Engine #2 we received an ECAM for 'ENG 1 STALL'. While starting Engine #1 we noticed it hang up slightly and accelerate slowly from N1 45% through N1 52%. Once parked in the holding pad I called Dispatch/Maintenance Control for guidance and to see if they received any data from the aircraft. Maintenance Control advised us that they did in fact received an alert on the #1 engine and advised us to return to the gate for maintenance. We subsequently called ZZZ operations to start the gate return process. I put the 'ENG 1 STALL' in the logbook. In addition; I notified the passengers of the unfortunate news that we had to return to the gate now for Maintenance.Once ZZZ operations decided on returning us back to gate we notified ground and started the slow process of taxiing back to gate. I got out of the aircraft to speak with gate agent that we would need to deplane all passengers and that there would most likely be a gate/plane change. The mechanics came on board and debriefed myself and the FO. While passengers were deplaning I called Dispatch to inform them that Maintenance personnel recommended an aircraft swap (#3). The dispatcher informed us of our new aircraft #. I informed the Dispatcher that I would be notifying scheduling of a fatigue call. Prior to notifying scheduling; I notified the crew of my intentions.I subsequently called scheduling and was released from duty. The flight was re-crewed with new pilots and pushed ZZZ.I had flown a ZZZ2 turn the day prior that was delayed 2 hours for aircraft maintenance as well on the inbound flight. It required an engine run with passengers on board to MEL the ENG 1 IDG going to ZZZ2. This delayed my drive home and eventually led me to falling asleep late the next morning.

column121: After a number of operational distractions on our first leg to ZZZ earlier that day we taxied out late on a single engine (#1) headed for ZZZ1. While on Taxiway 1; we attempted to start ENGINE #2 using APU bleed air and received an ECAM message indicating insufficient bleed air pressure. The start attempt was terminated. The ECAM message cleared without secondary indications. We attempted to start ENGINE#2 a second time with the same results. About the time the second start was terminated; an aircraft behind us reported visible sparks coming from the underside of the right (#2) engine.We stopped short of Spot XX on Taxiway 1 and requested a Crash Fire and Rescue (CFR) inspection through Ramp Control. CFR response time appeared longer than expected; approximately five minutes. There were a number of comm challenges with CFR but we eventually received an all clear. With a CFR escort; we taxied back to the same gate on a single engine; completed our inbound checks and deplaned the aircraft.After debriefing two mechanics we completed the Electronic Log Book (ELB) write-up. I instructed the First Officer to contact Dispatch while I contacted the Chief Pilot. Considering the cumulative distractions and threats of the day; I determined that the most prudent course of action was for my First Officer and me not to continue the next leg to ZZZ1.I communicated this assessment to the Chief Pilot; who encouraged me to characterize the situation as either fatigued" or "not fit for duty." I believe this situation is more appropriately categorized as a Human Factors issue and that replacing the crew was in the best interest of safety and operational decision-making. The Chief Pilot was resisting that assessment..Risk factors included:Late-night operationsHunger and cumulative fatigueMultiple maintenance and operational delaysEmergency response involvementReturn-to-gate following engine abnormalitiesLack of immediate replacement aircraft optionsElevated operational stress over an extended period.The Chief Pilot understandably may not have been fully aware of the cumulative operational context. In situations like this; management should rely heavily on the personnel with the greatest situational awareness: the operating flight crew.The Chief Pilot appeared uncertain and repeatedly referenced checking with Crew Scheduling and other management pilots. He later stated that he was relatively new to the position. Pilot pushing is rarely overt. It is not the Chief Pilot "putting a gun to your head." It is more subtle than that. It occurs when pilots experiencing and managing evolving operational risks; request support for a reasonable; fact-based safety decision; only to encounter resistance or hesitation from management instead of support for Captain's authority and the safety values.Pilots are highly susceptible to mission completion bias. For an experienced pilot to objectively assess the totality of circumstances and conclude that continuing the operation is not prudent is not a trivial decision. When that occurs; management should support that judgment."

I noticed my lead was driving; was directly in line with engine 2. Suddenly the aircraft powered up and moved forward. My lead instinctively accelerated the tug in reverse to avoid a collision with engine 2; unaware that my teammate Person B directly behind the tug disconnecting the towbar. As I noticed him moving; I yelled to alert my Lead and my teammate that the push tug and aircraft was moving Immediately. I kept enough distance from the push tractor and from the aircraft that was able to get out of the way. I maintained situational awareness through the whole event. My lead reversed until he was clear of the aircraft as it drove right by us. My team and I returned to the office to address what had just happened. We were informed by our Supervisor Person C and Person A that there will be an updated SOP and procedure will be sent out to the station to ensure everyone is informed of the protocols for return to gate and towing aircraft moving forward to avoid an incident in the future. Following the events; I reached out to the trainer on how to handle the procedure as well.

column121: I was just made aware of the runway excursion on Day 6. In the morning of Day 0; two student pilots and one instructor pilot were practicing a soft field take off on runway XXR at ZZZ. The student pilot lined the aircraft up on the centerline for takeoff and; when cleared by ATC; started the roll down the runway. There was a right crosswind during the takeoff. We started the takeoff with proper wind correction; but as we continued through the takeoff; both Flight Instructor (IP) and Student Pilot's (SP) attention was on the pitch attitude for the soft field takeoff. The student pilot had entered an excessive amount of positive pitch; and the instructor pilot stepped in to help correct the excessive pitch and to maintain flying in ground effect; as our speed was getting pretty low. While making these corrections for the soft field takeoff; the IP did not input the proper crosswind correction; causing the aircraft to be blown off to the left of the runway. After getting the aircraft to a stable airspeed and pitch attitude; the instructor pilot then realized we were left of the centerline and maneuvered back to be lined up with the runway. During this occurrence; neither the instructor pilot nor either of the student pilots saw; felt; or heard any collision between the aircraft and any runway signs or lights. The instructor pilot stated to the students how unsafe the takeoff was; but due to being unaware of any collision; the instructor pilot did not file a safety report. The crew failed to do a detailed enough post-flight inspection and missed the signs of damage from the runway sidebar light on the bottom right side of the horizontal stabilizer. Although neither the instructor nor any of the students was aware of the collision with the runway light; it was made clear that there was impact and damage done to the aircraft's airframe. The Instructor is completing a recurrent training to take action and learn from his mistakes.

column121: Experienced engine roughness and surging at cruise near ZZZZZ intersection; approx. 13 miles ZZZ. Symptoms included a rough running rough; and surged between 1000 and 2300 rpm constantly; the a/c was unable to maintain 6500' altitude consistently. Immediately I executed a turn to head towards ZZZ1 as I had it in sight and there was still some daylight left. To triage; I increased throttle to full; increased my mixture; turned on carburetor heat; cycled through the magnetos to check spark plug issues. I elected not to switch fuel tanks as the fuel selector was already on 'Both'. I also noted lower CHTs on cylinders 1; 3; and 5 per the engine monitor.I drifted down to 5000' and was able to maintain partial power approximately 5-10 knots above glide speed with engine surging. I contacted ZZZ Center and let them know I was having engine trouble and asked for vectors to the closest field (I did not elect for emergency services). Because I was able to maintain altitude; I determined it was feasible to head to the closest field which was ZZZ. I was able to make the field and performed a power off steep spiral into a straight in approach. Throughout the approach and descent I was never able to reestablish full power to the engine. I performed a ground runup with the engine continuing to sputter slightly. I believed it was either severe carb icing; or some form of vapor lock. I also inspected the engine post-flight and did not see any immediate damage to the engine or cylinders.I left the aircraft tied down and the operator's mechanic inspected the engine more closely. They discovered a wasp's nest in the fuel vent and a leak in the fuel line between primer. This likely caused excessive leaning of the mixture and a partial vapor lock. I did not experience any indication or symptoms of the oncoming failure during runup nor during the cruise portion. Oil temperature and pressure continued to be stable through the entire sequence of events. And no indication of fuel contamination or vent blockage during preflight inspection.

column121: On Day 0 and Day 1; I made 5 UAS flights totaling approximately 35 minutes from Location X. During this time; I was not aware of a TFR that was in place. I was attempting to fly directly up and hover my UAS over Location X for recreational pictures and videos. I checked the map in the DJI Fly app used to control the UAS and it appeared to show only a restricted flight zone for ZZZ Airport; which I was just outside of. The status indicator in the top left corner of the DJI control app showed green indicating good satellite connection and showed the message 'Takeoff Permitted'; which I believed confirmed that no flight restrictions were in place. I maintained line of sight; kept the UAS over private property; remained below 400 feet and believed I was following all FAA UAS operational rules. I was not aware of the TFR until the final flight when I was approached by law enforcement personnel.Reviewing my DJI app flight log shows the following:On Day 0; I made one flight for approximately 2 minutes and landed without incident. On Day 0; I made another flight for approximately 7 minutes and landed without incident.On Day 1; I made one flight for approximately 23 minutes and landed without incident.On Day 1; I made another flight for approximately 2 minutes; lost connection and the UAS returned to the take off point.On Day 1; I made another flight for 3 minutes. As the UAS was hovering I was approached by several law enforcement personnel. They informed me I was inside a TFR and directed me to land the UAS. I immediately landed the UAS and complied with all instructions. They informed me I should use an FAA approved mobile app to monitor for current TFRs and that the manufacturer's proprietary drone application was not sufficient. This issue was caused by inexperience; insufficient understanding of how TFRs work and the incorrect assumption that the UAS manufacturer's control application showed both temporary and permanent flight restrictions; which I now do not believe it does. I have no experience operating this UAS or other types of flight experience and should have waited but I was excited and wanted to try it out.In order to prevent this from occurring again I have downloaded the FAA approved AutoPylot app to remain aware of all NOTAMS and TFR's and I have completed the FAA WINGS safety course ALC-42: Airspace; Special Use Airspace and TFRs (Know Before You Go: Navigating Today's Airspace).To prevent this in the future; I believe training certification should be required to purchase and operate all drones. The extremely small size; low cost and ease to purchase my DJI drone gave me entirely the wrong idea about how serious the regulations are for its operation and I had no idea I could get into such trouble for its use.  In conclusion; I regret flying my drone before I fully understood its possible implications. I should have had a better understanding of the FAA rules and restrictions. Thank you for taking the time to read this and I hope it contributes toward something useful for the future.
