column121: My student began to set up for eights on pylons; a commercial single-engine ground reference maneuver. The objective was to have her practice explaining and demonstrating the objective; tolerances; and execution of the maneuver. Her pylon selection was satisfactory. However; she was going to begin the maneuver noticeably low at about 1100' MSL where pivotal altitude today was closer to 1400' MSL. She was reminded of this and she climbed to 1400' MSL using the pivotal altitude table. She began the first turn a few minutes later which was performed well. She recovered to 1400' MSL and began setting up for the second turn in the maneuver. But in doing so; a combination of turbulence and overbanking caused my student to get too low. Overbanking in this maneuver causes pylons to seem to move forward; resulting in an illusion that the aircraft is higher than actual altitude. This prompts the pilot to push forward on the controls when otherwise unnecessary. My student was inadvertently overbanking the airplane (not keeping the bank fixed); resulting in a large descent to which I did not intervene in time. She was reminded to keep the bank angle fixed. In the process of instructing her to do so; we descended to 681 indicated altitude which I believe is below 500' AGL; prompting this report. Besides greater vigilance on behalf of instructors like myself who may find themselves too low; it is important to draw the line higher such that students do not get anywhere near the 500' AGL limit. Fixation on pylons and bank angle may be beneficial to the maneuver itself but can cause a loss of altitude awareness which has resulted in controlled flight into terrain in past general aviation accidents. I plan on drawing the line higher for students performing this maneuver; especially for students who are new to the maneuver from the right seat or students who have not flown the maneuver for some time.

column121: I was the Pilot in Command of Aircraft X operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Approximately 25 minutes into an otherwise uneventful flight; while established in cruise at FL320; we experienced a right engine failure.The event was immediately apparent to the entire crew. We heard two distinct and extremely loud bangs that were consistent with compressor stalls and were accompanied by significant airframe vibration. The severity of the noise and vibration left little doubt that we were experiencing a major engine-related event. Immediately following the bangs; numerous EICAS messages populated the displays. The most prominent message was a Right FADEC FAIL indication; which was followed by High ITT; Low Oil Pressure; and indications consistent with a rollback of the right engine.At the time of the event; I was serving as the non-flying pilot and immediately began running the applicable checklist associated with the Right FADEC FAIL message. As we worked through the checklist; the aircraft indications and system responses were consistent with what we were observing; reinforcing our assessment that we had experienced a significant engine malfunction.Given the loud compressor stall events; severe vibration; and multiple engine-related indications; our initial assessment was that we may have suffered a catastrophic engine failure rather than a simple FADEC malfunction. At that point; our primary focus became aircraft control; system management; and determining the safest and most expeditious airport for diversion.As we transitioned from ZZZ Center to ZZZ1 Center; communication difficulties introduced additional challenges during an already high-workload situation. Although we had been communicating on the ZZZ1 Center frequency for several minutes; when I advised ATC that we were operating as a priority aircraft; the initial response was a question regarding whether we were attempting to pick up an IFR flight plan. This response led us to believe that there was a significant lack of awareness regarding our situation.I immediately restated that we were requesting priority handling and required a diversion to ZZZ2. ZZZ1 Center then requested our position and destination; further indicating that they did not yet have a clear understanding of the nature or urgency of our circumstances.From a crew resource management perspective; this lack of situational awareness created additional workload at a time when both pilots were heavily engaged in checklist execution; aircraft systems monitoring; diversion planning; and threat assessment. Rather than being able to focus exclusively on managing the situation; we found ourselves dedicating valuable attention to ensuring that ATC fully understood the seriousness of our condition.To remove any ambiguity and ensure immediate recognition of our status; I selected transponder code XXXX and transmitted to ATC on the frequency. My intent was to clearly communicate the urgency of the situation; obtain priority handling; and expedite vectors toward ZZZ2. Following these actions; ZZZ1 Center recognized the nature of the situation; coordinated appropriately; and provided the assistance necessary for us to continue the diversion and prepare for landing.As the flight progressed and we began preparing for a single-engine approach into ZZZ2; we became aware of additional system abnormalities involving Hydraulic System 2. We received a FLT SPOILERS FAULT message and observed multiple yellow cautions on the flight controls synoptic page. The indications suggested that the flight spoilers were deployed and were not returning to their normal trail position.To verify the indications; both pilots visually inspected the wings from the cockpit. We observed that spoiler panels 3 and 4; as well as panels 7 and 8; appeared deployed on both wings. These observations matched the indications displayed on the aircraft systems pages and confirmed that we were dealing with an additional flight control anomaly beyond the engine failure.We completed all applicable checklists associated with the hydraulic and spoiler indications. These procedures included actions intended to restore Hydraulic System 2 functionality through electric pump operation. Despite completing the prescribed procedures; the spoiler panels remained deployed and the associated cautions persisted. No corrective action restored the system to a normal configuration; and the aircraft continued to experience the associated aerodynamic drag. It was then as PIC I took control of the flying and the SIC (Second in Command) took control of the radios.As we approached ZZZ2 and entered the downwind for Runway XXR; it became evident that we would be landing with a combination of degraded aircraft performance factors: a failed right engine and substantial additional drag from spoilers that appeared to be stuck in the deployed position. This additional time allowed us to evaluate aircraft handling characteristics; verify performance expectations; review landing considerations; and effectively 'learn how to fly' the aircraft in its current degraded state before committing to the approach.The approach and landing were ultimately completed without further incident. Following a normal touchdown and rollout; we taxied clear and completed the appropriate shutdown procedures. The aircraft was subsequently towed to the FBO ramp where emergency response personnel met the aircraft. Firefighters conducted a visual and thermal assessment and reported no evidence of fire; overheating; or external engine damage following landing.During the post-flight inspection; no visible external damage to the right engine was observed. However; after all hydraulic systems were powered down; the flight spoilers remained physically stuck in the deployed position; confirming that the spoiler anomaly persisted beyond aircraft shutdown. The condition of the spoilers appeared consistent with the indications we had observed in flight and likely contributed significantly to the increased drag experienced during the diversion and landing.While the crew successfully managed the event and landed safely; the combination of an apparent engine failure; subsequent hydraulic and flight spoiler anomalies; and initial communication difficulties with ATC created a complex and rapidly evolving situation.

column121: I was SIC (Second In Command) on Aircraft X which was a ferry flight operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We had been flying for approximately 30 minutes and were in the descent to ZZZ1 when we heard and felt numerous bangs which sounded like compressor stalls and had intense vibrations throughout the aircraft. We both confirmed that the right engine had failed and received many EICAS messages; most prominent being R FADEC (Full Authority Digital Engine Control) FAIL. I was pilot flying throughout the engine failure; and the captain in the left seat was PM and he began running the checklist and communicating with ATC to start our diversion. Trying to get ahold of ATC was more difficult than it should have been. The Captain was trying to communicate with ZZZ Center. When ATC got back to us they asked us repeat our callsign and say again our request. I think they were confused. When we requested that we wanted to divert to ZZZ2; they asked if we had a flight plan on file. It was at this point that ATC understood who we were and that we needed priority handling. We were given direct ZZZ2 and began to descend. Throughout this; I was flying the aircraft and keeping an eye on engine parameters. We had very high ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) ; low oil pressure; and rapidly reducing N1; consistent with an engine shutdown. We also had HYD PUMP 2B FAIL EICAS message. We got the engine shut down; and were slowing and descending to land in ZZZ2 when we got an amber FLT SPLRS FAULT message. When we checked out the window; we had some spoilers that were out; even with the handle stowed. The captain had made a call over the PA to the Flight Attendant earlier to let he know what the situations; but sometime around this time; the Captain called her up and quickly gave her a brief of what the situation was; where we were diverting to; and told her he would communicate with her if we needed to evacuate once we were on the ground. We were aware of numerous other hydraulic issues with system 2; so we were trying to make the best plan of action to get down safely being single engine and having multiple hydraulic issues. I elected to had over controls to the captain for the landing. The captain did an excellent job on the landing and safely taxied the plane off the runway before we had the fire department look at the right engine to assess any damages. The told us there were no heat readings and no visible damages; so we completed all appropriate checklists and we got a tow into the FBO.

column121: Flight Following from ZZZ to ZZZ1 coordinating with ATC following the coast and keeping clear of convective weather; as I also avoided clouds. At XA:45pm aircraft started to experience turbulence and a strong desire to climb above 11k'. Once I brought us back down to 10500 and stabilized us; at about XB:05pm a heavy mist blew in from the S and overtook my visibility. We were sucked up into a climb more much more quickly and violently than before. I turned R to the N toward the coast; and tried descending us to get out of the mist/cloud and back to VFR conditions. It was a very light rain; but total white out. During my descending turn to the N it felt like the aircraft was pushed by a strong gust of wind; the right wing lost lift; and we went into a spiraling dive/spin. As I worked to regain control of the aircraft; I think it was a combination of me recovering from the spin and the atmosphere rapidly changing condition (we were experiencing up and down drafts) that led to the aircraft shooting straight up in the air until stalling. My passenger and I were unsure of what was happening at that point; as all the up; down; and turns had us disoriented. All of our instruments were spinning in circles one way one second; then spinning the other direction the next second. All this in white out conditions. We experienced weightlessness; then increasing gravitational forces. ATC came on asking if we were ok because they had us 'losing altitude rapidly.' Not having any control over the aircraft; all instruments spinning erratically; and total white out visibility... I responded: 'Requesting priority handling; we are not ok. Please stay with us.' My passenger pointed out the VSI got to 9 o'clock by going 'down' and I saw the airspeed indicator increasing in the yellow arc. We were in a power on vertical dive. I saw the airspeed approaching 185mph and I struggled through the g forces to pull the throttle back to idle. I then crushed the right rudder to the floor. I believe this deflection to the side of the fuselage was what slowed our straight vertical dive (maybe we were spinning in the dive too). Either way; the Attitude Indicator then became stable and indicated a diving left bank. Knowing not to pull back on the yoke hard; I gently and intermittently gave the yoke right and back pressure inputs. The g forces lessened; and the instruments all began stabilizing. We became level; but were still falling. Like a parachute. In total white out still. After a few seconds of that; we gently fell below the cloud layer; like coming down an elevator. I put the power back in; and we were on our way. ATC came on asking if we were ok. I said something like 'I love you. Thank you so much for being there for us. Please get me an airport to land at as soon as possible.'I never exceeded the 214mph Vne of my Piper Arrow II; and I do not believe I reached the positive load factor of 3.8 G. Regardless; before my next flight I called my home airport aviation mechanic and performed a visual and tactical inspection of the aircraft with him via video call. I would not have flown my aircraft again if I had any doubt about her airworthiness. Regardless of not hitting the structural limitations of the aircraft... in an abundance of caution; I am having it professionally inspected by my aircraft mechanic.  Although I aimed to remain 20 miles away from the convective weather; I believe it was the outer edges of the cell that caused us to experience the updrafts; downdrafts; and strong wind gusts that caused us to lose control of the aircraft. I kept power in thinking I could keep control of the plane against the winds that way; but in hindsight I think I should have decreased power sooner. Losing altitude and diverting N was difficult because there were other clouds to avoid beneath us; intense air traffic coming and going from all the airports in that area; and lots of different airspace; including military airspace that I was trying to remain clear of for safety. I thought my altitude and heading would keep us safe from the weather; heavy traffic in the area; and the airspaces. In hindsight; maybe I should have asked ATC if it was ok for me divert more N. There was a storm that had just come over the shore from the S to the N that I was trying to stay below as well though. So there was a lot going on. It also looked like small cells; but heavy precipitation over the airports I would have liked to divert to before the event happened. I kept hearing of the 12k' ceiling above me; and ceilings at different airports at 2500' and 4500'. I didn't want to get stuck in IMC trying to descend to land at an airport to avoid the weather; only to end up in it so close to the ground. I wanted altitude for safety; and it was a major factor in why I was able to recover. Not only am I going to make sure my aircraft is just as good as it was before the incident; but I am also intensifying my weather knowledge; and I am going to pursue Spin Training and Aerobatics. These are 'advanced pilot techniques' that I think should be taught to every Private Pilot. Especially since inadvertently getting caught in IMC conditions is such a killer of GA pilots.What could ATC have done differently... I don't think their equipment showed me getting 'too close' to the danger zone that day. A lesson we can learn is how dangerous a tightly formed cell with heavy precipitation consuming its growth can create extreme wind shear around its outer perimeter. The radio was very busy that day with aircraft diverting due to rapidly changing weather conditions. I was very grateful ATC came on to let me know I was losing altitude rapidly. As tossed around as we were; this was helpful in the moment. I was hoping they would call out my altitude repeatedly as it changed; and hoping they would call it out as I was losing or gaining it. Any information they could have given me like that could have helped. I understand they are not pilots; and probably shouldn't give the pilot in an unknown flight condition piloting advice; but the altitude and possibly heading call outs could help in a situation like that. I have no complaints. ATC did a great job handling the weather and workload they had that day. I have a new respect for weather; and this will make me a better pilot; and sharing my experience with others hopefully will help them stay safe. I want to be in compliance with all that is expected of me as a pilot. I want to be an incredible pilot. Please let me know if anything else is expected or needed of me. Thank you for the time you devote to our safety.

column121: Our facility is understaffed. We are allowed 12; 14 with training. We have 9; with 1 controller medically disqualified since the start of the busy season. Day 0 is the final day of the busy season. All our controllers are burned out. Everyone has been doing 6 day work weeks; lots of 10 hour days. Additionally in an attempt to get more staffing; our manager has increased our required time on position and reduced break times and lunch breaks. Moral of the story; we are burnt out. I had been fighting a cold or sickness of some sort and am not 100% at this time. I'm tired; I'm sick. I'm now in my 9th or 10th hour of work. The airport had an event on Day 0. There were several aircraft participating. Before the event; the aircraft altogether did about 100 separate ops in the traffic pattern; wearing out my supervisor and I; the only two there that morning. Luckily a third; fresh controller worked the event itself when he arrived to work at XA:15.During the event; all ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) units staged at Location X; which is across the airfield from the fire station. After the event was over; they called to relocate back to the fire station; needing to cross both parallel runways. My supervisor was working LC; at my request; as I was just so worn out and could barely talk or think anymore; that I felt I would only be safe on ground control; if that. So ARFF calls me and requests to cross both runways back to the fire station. At this time; Aircraft X is lining up to depart rwy XXL. I coordinate a conditional crossing reference the departing aircraft. My SUP approves the conditional.'ARFF and company; CROSS runway XX right at 1. HOLD SHORT runway XX left at 1.'I receive a perfect readback. I watch very carefully as the 3 ARFF units cross XXR. They get to the other side (Taxiway 2) and come to a full stop after clearing the runway. I literally nod my head and say to myself; that's what I want to see. I turn to watch this beautiful aircraft depart XXL and to know when it has passed Taxiway 1 so I can cross the ARFF units. Looks good; roaring down the runway. I make one last check on the ARFF units and turn my head toward them one more time. As my eyes see ARFF; I observe them moving fast (25-40 mph) across TWY 2. I key up the frequency and pretty much yell; 'ARFF; STOP!!!' The lead fire truck slams on it's breaks. I watch as the truck tips forward in its best attempt to stop. The other trucks also stop. ARF is over the hold short line. Seeing that they have all come to a complete stop; I quickly glance over to the aircraft to see if there is any way to cancel take off clearance. It is just airborne between taxiways 3 and 1. At this point; it was safer to let them takeoff. I clutch my chest because I literally can't fathom the thought of what had almost just occurred.The aircraft has now passed and I give the ARFF units clearance to cross runway XXL. I got off position quickly thereafter and left for the day.Recommendation: All of our controllers have had negative experiences with ARFF and how many mistakes on the airfield they have made. I love fire fighters; but these guys (and gals) need more training. The controller's have talked about having them over to the tower and giving them classes during our slow period; but it never seems to happen. Given incidents like this; perhaps the FAA can mandate some driver's tests or something for ARFF on the airfield.Nothing follows.

column121: I was flying patterns at ZZZ.  At approximately XA:30; I was on left downwind for RWY XX. There were several aircraft in the pattern.  I was unable to get the ATC recording but to my recollection I had been cleared to land.  ATC called me as traffic to a 172.ATC informed them they were gaining on me; 20kts faster and to widen their pattern. I was unable to see them at this point.  I do not recall if they acknowledged having me in sight.  LiveATC.com was incomplete and I have not heard any other recordings.  I confirmed later the 172 did veer slightly right.I was flying consistent patterns and having heard the instruction for them to widen; I proceeded normally to reduce power abeam the numbers; reduce speed; deploy 1st flaps; then began my base turn about 1nm to the west of the runway and about 1.5nm southwest of the intersection of XY/XX.As I rolled out of my turn on cross wind and looked left as my wing raised; I saw the 172 coming what appeared to be straight at me.  Simultaneously ATC directed them to 'Climb immediately!'  I received no instruction.  There was really no time for me to do anything but stay my course as they passed directly above me.  Close enough to make out the landing gear.I finished my stop and go and completed one more pattern to finish my flight. I do not recall any further radio communication about the near miss.Cause?  The 172 was flying faster than typical for a 172 and my PA-22 is slower to begin with.  Knowing they were gaining on me and inside I would have expected them to make a sharper turn to the right and slow down.  I suspect they did not have me in sight.ATC could have been less vague with them.  They also could have cancelled my landing clearance; extended my downwind; and let the 172 go first.  OR they could have had the 172 do a right 360.  But I do not know what traffic was behind them.For my part I might have had a closer look at ADSB; however at that critical phase I try to keep my eyes outside and not let the ipad interfere with my night vision.I also could have made a radio call to ask if the 172 was clear before I made my base turn.Things added up for potentially a very bad night for all.  I feel like we all got lucky.

column121: While taxiing out to depart runway XX a Citation landed and made a radio call that they were going to depart the runway then taxi down to runway XY and depart again. Winds favored runway XX so we continued taxiing down and did our run up at the hold short line of runway XX. After finishing our run up I made a radio call to the Citation that we were ready to go but wanted to know how long they would be and that we were fine waiting for them if needed. We didn't hear anything for about 30 seconds. We could see them and they were still holding short of XY so my pilot flying made another radio call asking if they could hear us. My pilot flying made a third radio call about a minute later asking them the same information. We then briefly discussed it and decided to depart; I made a radio call telling the local traffic we were taking runway XX departing to the east. As we were pulling out to the runway the Citation made a radio call that they were departing runway XY and they began to taxi onto the runway. We then made a series of radio calls to them trying to alert them to the fact that we were already on the runway about to start our takeoff roll. We still received no response so proceeded to taxi towards the first taxiway 1 in an attempt to get clear of the runway. My pilot flying made the right call realizing we weren't going to make 1 in time and pulled off to the side of the runway. I continued to make radio calls to them until they were rotating. They passed over us at roughly 200' and didn't make another radio call. The FBO called up after we cleared the runway and confirmed that they could hear us but the FBO was never able to hear the Citation. I suspect (but can't confirm) it was a radio issue on their end. The big takeaway here is recognizing the potential signs of another airplane having a radio issue early on and taking defensive action against it.

column121: During an instructional flight with a student pilot our aircraft briefly skidded into the grass at the edge of a runway-taxiway intersection; while exiting the runway onto a taxiway. This occurred due to the student's decision to exit the runway at a higher speed than is appropriate for turning on the ground. I took control of the aircraft; returned us to the taxiway; and continued back to our ramp.I believe my failure to immediately take controls was a contributing factor. I could have stopped the turn from occurring. I notice a lack of emphasis in training on the rollout phase of landing. AIM 4-3-21 states; 'Exit the runway without delay at the first available taxiway or on a taxiway as instructed by ATC.' It does not make any mention of decelerating to a safe speed before attempting to turn. I believe instructors; especially those instructing in aircraft with differential braking; should receive some reinforcement regarding the possibilities for loss of control while students are turning the aircraft on the ground. The brakes are fundamentally different from other controls in that it is not possible for an instructor to simply override a student's faulty inputs. The instructor must fully take control. Instructors who regularly correct; for example; aileron and elevator inputs may feel a false sense of security vis-a-vis the brakes. Instructors must understand when it is appropriate to correct/override student inputs and when it is necessary to fully take controls. The brakes are unique.
